en: The Great Master Without Peer praises True Stillness;
his broad seal swallows the head of a dead cat and gnaws away the gall of the living. His heels do not tread upon the grass; his nostrils naturally soar through the heavens.
His eyebrows are so coarse that demons and heretics lose their mettle; his gaze is so piercingly radiant that Buddhas and Patriarchs find it hard to contain him.
His spiritual mechanism is as swift as a thunderclap; his eloquence flows like a spring. Only this one move of "concealing the body" remains unrecognized by anyone;
indeed, he has truly inherited the lineage of Shouchang.
Hymn for Master Yongjue by his disciple Zheng Xuan of Zuofei Hermitage:

This old master is the direct bloodline descendant of Shouchang. As clumsy as a hideous stone and as hard as stubborn iron, he greatly propagated the principle of the "Subtle Embrace within the Center" (*zhèngzhōng miàoxiá*), truly inheriting the former glory and directly returning to the original tracks, far continuing the footsteps upon the Path to the Sky.
With a single branch of the fly-whisk, he sweeps away the clouds of delusion for a hundred generations; with a seven-foot rattan staff, he points out the bright moon across a thousand mountains.

Chan, Teaching, Vinaya, and Esoteric practices are unified as one family; Confucianism, Buddhism, and Daoism all return to the same point like snow falling on hot coals. In five hundred years, there has been only this man;
whether he is a saint or an ordinary man, let there be no idle talk.
Preface to the Extensive Record of Master Yongjue.
Three years after the passing of the Great Master of Gushan, Yongjue Xian, his dharma heir,
the current abbot Weilin, compiled the master’s lifetime records of his sermons and various writings, namely:

The *Chan Yu Nei Wai Ji* (Collected Works on Chan Practice, Inner and Outer), the *Wan Lu* (Record of Late Years), the *Zui Hou Yu* (Final Words), the *Dong Shang Gu Che* (Ancient Tracks of Dongshan), the *Yi Yan* (Sleeping Words), and other works, have been compiled and edited into thirty fascicles, titled the *Guang Lu* (Extended Record). I have requested that you, Master Fan, compose a preface for the beginning of these volumes.

Reflecting upon my own dull faculties, I have missed the "arrow-head" (the sharp, instantaneous) pivot of the teaching on several occasions; how then could I dare to write such a preface? Furthermore, I consider that while I resided beneath the Master’s seat, I was personally...
Having received his instructions and having immersed myself in them for refinement over many days from youth until old age, it cannot be said that I have gained nothing from my teacher.
How could I dare not compose this preface? I respectfully state the preface: Formerly, at the assembly on Vulture Peak, the World-Honored One—
Before a multitude of one hundred thousand people, he held up a flower to show the assembly. Only Venerable Kāśyapa alone broke through with a smile;
he was thus entrusted with the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, which is called the "Special Transmission Outside the Teachings.

From that time on, through the four patriarchs and seven successors, the twenty-three patriarchs, and all the ancestors of the five schools, they have been transmitted in an unbroken succession, like lamps reflecting one another. There is none who did not employ this very device to transmit this very Dharma, just as water flows into water.

The transmission of the Dharma-vessel is entirely without leakage. Alas, as the Dharma endures for long, decay arises; true men rarely appear, leading to the transmission of falsehoods by those who are false, which causes much confusion and error.
Our Master has returned by virtue of his vows to serve as a patron (*dānapati*) for the Dharma. Possessing great merit and wisdom, he bestows great eloquence.
Taking ignorance as his teacher and non-duality as his friend, father, son, and brothers have successively inherited this excellence, beating the drum [of the Dharma].
He propagated this Way, reviving the fallen pillars of the Cao-Dong school and healing the terminal illnesses of the Dharma-ending age.

His golden chapters and jade verses, delivered with bitter-tasting yet compassionate intent, are entirely in accord with the heart-blood and marrow of the Buddhas and Patriarchs of antiquity, forming a single, unbroken lineage.
One who possesses the discerning eye of the Goose King (Hamsarāja) recognizes [this work] at a single glance; how could one allow even a single word of disparagement?

In the future, there will surely be a "Son of Heaven with the Buddha-mind" who will include it within the Great Canon (*Dazang*), so that it may circulate alongside the *Zongjing* of Yongming, the works of Mingjiao and Tanjin, and the recorded sayings (*yulu*) of various venerable patriarchs, washing the light of the Buddha-sun and polishing the brilliance of the ancestral lamp.

This is because I take the Great Dharma as my public standard; it is not that I dare to show partiality toward what I personally prefer. Furthermore, the Master has practiced the Way throughout the land for nearly thirty years.
Standing alone and acting independently, he was never swayed by worldly trends. He was like Mount Emei in the snow, rising from the earth and soaring into the sky, towering and far-reaching.
Who among the people of the world would not look up to him in admiration? How much more so now that this record exists to dispel their ignorance!
Yet, by awakening him, did not the Master’s Way thereby become even more vast and brilliantly illuminated?

The Master himself composed further commentaries on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and the *Vajracchedikā Sūtra*, as well as the *Heart Sūtra: Pointing to the Palm*, the *Synopsis of the Meaning of the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya*, and the *Introduction to the Study of Vinaya*.
The *Hongshi lu*, the *Jiding* and *Budeng* two records, the *Jingci yaoyu*, the *Gushan zhi*, the *Kaiyuan si zhi*, and other such works are all circulated separately;
they shall not be further elaborated upon here. This serves as the preface.

Composed by Lin Zhifan, a recipient of the jinshi degree, Grand Master of Instruction (Fengxun Dafu), Director of the Examination Bureau in the Ministry of Personnel, former Censor of the Zhejiang Circuit, and Disciple of the Bodhisattva Precepts;
prostrations. Preface to the *Chan Yu Nei Ji* (Collected Works from Leisure in Chan).
When Master Yongjue returned from Zhejiang to Min, he again retired to live out his final years at Gushan in Fuzhou.

His attendant, the venerable Taichong, recorded the teachings from his three assemblies, categorized and compiled them into the *Chan Yu Nei Ji* (Internal Collection of Leisure from Meditation). Once the collection was completed—
He came to Zhu-li to request a preface from me. Although I have the honor of having read Buddhist scriptures, regarding the Way of the Buddha, I truly have no insight or comprehension whatsoever.
How could I possibly understand the Great Master? To compose a preface for him while ignorant of his teachings would be my own transgression.
The Master respectfully entreated him, and he could not decline. He then said, "If you will not permit me to refuse, may I briefly recount what I know of the Great Master?

The Great Master’s learning permeated both the human and celestial realms, and his insight reached across the present and the past. As for the great matters of the causes of order and chaos, and of rise and fall—"

Whether minute matters such as the subtle junctures of human conduct and advancement, or profound subjects such as the mysteries of the Yellow River charts, Luo River maps, astronomy, and calendrics, or manifest complexities such as ritual, music, law, and governance—he investigated their essential principles with complete precision. Sometimes a single word of his could endure for a thousand autumns;
this is how I came to know the Great Master, for I knew the refinement of his learning. His spiritual radiance surged forth boundlessly, flowing wherever his brush led.
His principles were without lack of refinement; his intentions were without lack of penetration. In the shifting transformations of his discourse, no beginning or end could be discerned.

Yet all was pure, true, elegant, and serene; it was spacious, harmonious, and flowing. It was devoid of the habit of ornate embellishment or superficiality, and free from the spirit of agitation or reckless display.
This is how I know the Great Master; I know the purity of his writings. Having reached nearly sixty years of age, he has only now sounded this bell;
yet after two years of presiding over the hall, he already intends to fold his tongue in silence.

He leaves all affairs to external conditions, as if doing nothing at all, and is utterly devoid of any desire for cleverness or any thought of greedy striving. This is how I know the Great Master; I know the cultivation of his character.
Tranquil. With an iron backbone supporting the void, his solitary style was peerless. His conduct was firm and upright; in all his movements, he took the ancients as his teacher.
Although he presided over four monasteries, his feet never entered the secular world. Though he daily encountered men of high rank and nobility, his speech was never sycophantic or compliant.
This is how I came to know the Great Master; I knew the loftiness of his integrity. Within his quarters, he held aloft the ancestral seal alone, firmly grasping the iron [staff].
The Barrier. Although eminent monks gathered there like scales upon a fish, they all retreated at the sight of the precipice;

it was utterly unheard of for him to grant permission indiscriminately or to hand over the whisk and robe merely to create a bustling scene within his lineage. This is how I know the Great Master and how I know the strictness of his discipline.
As for his ascending the hall to preach the Dharma, he spoke spontaneously as it arose; his skillful eloquence was sovereign, rolling like lightning and dispersing clouds.

Although [the teachings] appear to follow a single path, in reality they do not restrict themselves to one way. Sometimes they are forceful and direct; sometimes they are subtle and dense; sometimes they are lofty and ancient; sometimes they are plain and substantial.
This is like a *maṇi* jewel that reflects all five colors indifferently, or like the great ocean where waves surge and subside without constancy.
This is precisely what the Great Wisdom Sūtra refers to as "the skillful means of the masters of the Great Dharma. Is this not what is meant by Chan encompassing all styles?
This is merely gazing across the river at the reflection of a temple spire, sketched in a state of dimness and vagueness; such is the case here.
How could my own meager abilities possibly know the Great Master? Nevertheless, I have heard it said that the Great Master once remarked:
"In this present age, I am truly like a form and its shadow lamenting one another; indeed, I have not yet seen anyone who can truly know me. And yet, I too...
"I do not seek to be known in this present age. Yet, as long as these words have not perished, my Way remains here.
Should there be, in days to come, one who can perceive my heart through my words, then the single school of Shaolin may perhaps avoid extinction.
May I now request that these words be placed at the beginning of this volume? The Master [Shangren] replied, "So be it. Thereupon, he committed them to writing as a preface. At that time...
Written on the Buddha’s Birthday in the fourth month of the early summer of the Guiwei year of the Chongzhen era (1643), by the disciple Cao Gu, who bows his head in homage,

to his teacher Li Ju— who was born with the title of Jinshi (Presented Scholar) and received an imperial edict to supervise the educational administration of the Nanjing Yingtian Prefecture and other districts,
having previously served as a Censor of the Huguang Circuit in the Ministry of Justice.
Preface to the *Chan Yu Wai Ji* (Supplementary Collection from Beyond Chan).

Throughout antiquity and the present, there have been three types of those who have made their voices heard through writing: those with writings of virtuous nature (*de-xing*), those with writings of inquiry and learning (*wen-xue*), and those with writings of talent and emotion (*cai-qing*).
What are widely circulated in the world are, for the most part, the writings of inquiry, learning, talent, and emotion alone. As for the writings of virtuous nature, however—
Since the Six Classics, those who have composed works have not been few; yet while authors are certainly rare, those who truly understand them are even fewer.

Master Yongjue early on specialized in the Confucian scriptures and was well-versed in the learning of Zhu Xi and Cheng Hao. In his prime, he abandoned these studies and entered the Dharma community of Shouchang.
After a long time, he returned to Min and resided at Gushan in Fuzhou. His disciples recorded his collected writings and circulated them.

The Master himself titled this work *The Supplementary Collection from the Leisure of Chan*. In the spring of the Dingchou year, various scholars and officials from Zhejiang invited him to reside at Zhenji Monastery in Hangzhou.
His disciples increased in number, and there remained eight fascicles and twelve chapters that had not yet been carved for printing.
I have therefore collated them and set them into woodblocks. How could I possibly understand the Great Master? I merely read his writings and observed—
That he does not indulge in the display of his literary talent is something that none but those truly rich in such talent could achieve;
that he does not engage in the systematic arrangement of his learning is something that none but those deeply versed in inquiry could express.

It is as direct as the work of spring’s transformation, universal yet leaving no trace to be found; it is also like a melody of white snow, so sublime that few have ears to hear it. Moreover, whenever I observe him...
When he took up his brush, he wrote with such speed that a thousand words were completed at once; there was nothing lacking in their vigor or their profound perfection.

As for revealing the subtle and elucidating the obscure, he brought forth from his pen all those things that neither ancient nor modern scholars had dared to utter. He expressed himself with simplicity, ease, and elegance, free from the habits of pedantry or ornate affectation.
Is this not what is called "literature born of one's virtuous nature"? Indeed, the Master had received the Dharma-seal of Shouchang and possessed [profound] wisdom.

His brilliance was perfectly rounded, and he was esteemed by the monastic community as the foremost. In truth, his sincere heart and authentic practice were such that there was nothing that did not conform to the standards of former sages;
he established a model for future students. It is truly fitting that he is called a "buttress against the current" in these degenerate times. Such is what is seen in his writings.
How could he possibly be compared to those who merely possess literary talent or scholarly erudition? Not daring to underestimate my own ignorance, I have ventured to compose this preface.
At the beginning of this brief preface, I am well aware that my words are as defiling to these pearls and jade as they are trivial;

yet, I have merely recorded them here to express my lifelong private devotion and admiration. Written on the day of the full moon in the eighth month of autumn in the Gengchen year of the Chongzhen era by Chen Guan, a graduate of the Jinshi examination, holding the rank of Zhongshun Dafu, former Magistrate of Changzhou Prefecture, and disciple of Guian.

Regarding the final sequence of events during the Putong era of the Liang dynasty: Bodhidharma came from South India and established the Chan school, which does not rely on written texts but points directly at the human mind to see one's nature and attain Buddhahood. His verse of entrustment says: "I have originally come to this land."
The transmission of the Dharma rescues deluded beings; one flower opens into five petals, and the fruiting occurs naturally.
Following this, the robe was transmitted through six generations and the five schools emerged in competition. From the Tang through the Song dynasties, its influence grew ever greater.

As for these five schools—the three schools of Guiyang, Yunmen, and Fayan—ended along with the destiny of the Song dynasty. Those whose lineages have continued to the present day are only Linji and Caodong.

Regarding the two schools: the Dongshan school had also been in decline for a long time until the Wanli era, when the venerable patriarch Wuming of Shouchang emerged and began its revival in the world.
Among the several disciples who entered Shouchang’s room, the most renowned were Master Wuyi of Boshan and our late teacher, the Elder Yongjue of Gushan.
The Elder was born at twenty-five and entered the monastic life at forty. He attained enlightenment at forty-six and emerged into the world at fifty-seven.
He passed away at eighty. During his twenty-odd years of public ministry, he sat upon the seat of enlightenment four times and performed great deeds for the Buddha’s work.
His words filled the world and his Way covered the realm; among all the long-resident elders of the monasteries, there were none who did not pack their bags to follow him.
He came to pay his respects, and many virtuous scholars and officials within the realm likewise humbled themselves to inquire after the Way.
His life’s collection of recorded sayings and writings is extensive and has all been published for the world; these ten thousand words or so constitute his final masterpiece.
That he titled it "The Final Words" was a designation chosen by the Elder himself. I humbly reflect that the Way of this Elder is vast...
Greatly refined and subtle. His learning was comprehensive and vast; his insight was perfectly clear and transcendent;
his preaching was bold and fearless; his integrity was strict; his cultivation reached its ultimate fulfillment; and his merit, virtue, and longevity were truly complete and perfect.

On the day of his passing, he spoke a verse to bid farewell to the assembly and sat uprightly until his death, with head and feet perfectly aligned—a feat rarely found even among the ancient patriarchs, let alone among those of the present age.
Alas! The school of Bodhidharma has been transmitted to this day, yet its decline has reached its ultimate limit;
the Elder arose to pull it back, exerting himself through practice and stabilizing it with integrity and rectitude.
He bound them with the fundamental principles and verified them through their words and deeds. He firmly guarded the iron gate, granting no concessions whatsoever.

Thus, even those from various quarters who were reputed to be "饱参" (those who had completed their training) would, upon their first arrival, inevitably display an air of arrogance, holding their heads high like horned beasts;
yet the Old Man, without shifting his voice or expression, would subtly lower a probe for examination, whereupon they would all collapse like crumbling earth and flee in shame. Only...
A true practitioner of the Way, possessing the eye that discerns the Dharma, is able to humble himself before the furnace and bellows, undergoing long refinement without ever retreating.
This is because he knows that in these present times, it is solely upon the Elder that the single thread of the Shaolin lineage depends for its survival, lest it fall to the ground.
Before long, his worldly conditions came to an end, and he suddenly withdrew his transformative power. With the Eye of Humanity and Heaven extinguished, who would not grieve and yearn for him? At—

This is the disciple from Jianzhou, Xie Feiqing, who requests that these final words be engraved upon woodblocks to circulate throughout the realm, so that those who seek the Way in the future may know that the path lies herein and not wander into the groves of heterodoxy.
This is a most noble aspiration. I, the junior monk Pei, have had the honor of attending the Dharma assembly for many years and have now further been unworthily entrusted with this task.
Postscript. I have obtained considerable detail regarding the life and travels of this venerable elder. Therefore, I have respectfully inscribed this outline at the beginning of the volume.
All other particulars may be found in the *Detailed Record of the Venerable Layman Lin Hanzhai’s Conduct*.
Written on the final ten days of the second month of winter in the year of Dingyou, by the dharma-heir disciple Daopai, who burns incense and bows his head in reverence.
Preface to the Drum Mountain Records of Late Life:
In my later years, I have mistakenly entered the net of the world and become such a mere creature. Fortunately, I have not met an early death, but have been extended to this present day.
In total, twenty years have passed. All the words spoken in response to others were like insects boring through wood or wind whistling through hollows;

I could not restrain them myself. Thus, from the time before the year Jiashen until the present year Renchen—eight cycles of changing between winter and summer robes—I have not ceased these "drunken words" (zhīyán).
My attendant has already cast them toward the world for all to criticize and shoot at as they please.
I further compiled these writings into a single volume and intended to have them carved into printing blocks, requesting a title from me.
At that time, I was already seventy-five years old; was this not late, even later than late? I therefore titled it the *Wanlu* (Records of Late Years).

Indeed, when the year is late, the transformative mechanisms of nature are closed off; when the day is late, all creatures retire to rest; and when the tree is late, its branches and leaves fall away.
Regarding the roots of right livelihood, as one grows old, one's daily sustenance and protection are exhausted, and one stands on the very threshold of death.
On this day when I am now to stand on the threshold of death, I possess only this faint, lingering breath, which has not yet suddenly ceased.
My lifelong skills are exhausted at this point; my lifelong deeds come to an end here. What more have I left to say? I still...

What more need be said? As for whether these [teachings] are correct or incorrect, whether they may be preserved or discarded—leave this to those in the world who possess the eye of discernment regarding the Dharma.
Written by the Old Man of Shigum, Yuanxian, as a preface to the General Table of Contents for the Extensive Record of Master Yongjue.

Instructions to the Assembly upon Opening the Ordination Platform. A single heart of compassionate grandmotherly concern from Vulture Peak, Brings forth the void to offer for sale to people. Guanyin...
Catching sight of this from the side, he gave a subtle smile. Upāli emerged from the assembly and was ready to receive it; clearly, it was nothing but waves without wind.
Carrying water and dragging mud, this has been so from antiquity to the present. If there were any *siddha* guests here, they would not walk where the Tathāgata walks.
He held up his staff and said, "Upāli has arrived. He struck the staff once and said, "The recitation of the precepts is finished. Does the great assembly understand?
If you can understand, there is no need for further trivialities; you will then be able to stride across Mount Sumeru and swallow the world whole."
Pointing to the sun and moon as they rise in the west, he causes heaven and earth to revolve to the right. How extraordinary!
Is this not the mark of a true man? If it were otherwise, I, this mountain monk, have transmitted a manual; in a moment, I shall recite it for you all one by one.
Do not say that this mountain monk is deceiving the assembly.

To the assembly on the Lantern Festival: Since the beginning of the New Year, the Dragon King of the Eastern Sea and the Buddha Sun-Moon-Lamp have been locked in a great battle, with neither emerging victorious.
This morning, my nature flared up, and I struck each of the two thirty times with my staff.
"Tōfū! You have already gone beyond Northern Uttarakuru. [The Master] set aside the dispute between the two men for a moment.
"But as for that phrase 'beyond clear skies and rain,' how would you say it? A monk stepped forward and said, "Clear skies and rain. The Master said, "I knew you only understood it in such a way.
As the monk was about to offer further words, the Master gave a shout and said, "Since no one can speak it now, I, the Mountain..."
The monk has gone off on a tangential digression. The great void has no boundaries; the vast ocean has no covering. In clear weather, one watches the silver bamboos hang down;
in the rain, one dries the *kāṣāya* robe in the sun. The wildcat and the white ox, however, know this; the Buddhas of the three periods have been caught and defeated.
Furthermore, there is the wine stand and tray before the altar, which is most adept at manifesting the extraordinary.
Riding backward upon the Buddha hall, he exits through the three gates, startling the Vajrapāṇi outside the door. This night, the Dharma of all Buddhas and patriarchs has been fully expounded.
Yet there remains one further phrase, that which none of the Buddhas or patriarchs have ever reached in their teachings; I originally intended to explain it to you all with complete sincerity.
Broken! Alas, the mountain monk’s duties as abbot are many. Once the Hall of Heavenly Kings is completed, I shall explain it all for you. The night is cold; take care.

A Teaching for the Assembly on the Dragon Boat Festival. In days of yore, the Elder of the Snowy Mountains pointed a deer as a horse; the various patriarchs of the East and West certified a tortoise as a turtle.

This succession has now reached this mountain monk, who likewise cannot avoid taking what is wrong and making it right. Now that this auspicious Dragon Boat Festival has arrived, it must not be passed in vain.
We can do no other than take the vast emptiness of space and mold it into a small *zongzi* (rice dumpling), which we shall offer to all...
When people have filled their bellies and satiated their hunger, he lifts the incense box with his hand and shows it to the assembly, saying: "O Assembly!
If you can chew through this, then when you see the dragon boats racing and hear the chanting of the *chūsō* hymns, you may roam freely amidst the misty waves as you please;
there will be no need for *pú* wine or hanging *ài* flags, and the traces of demons will naturally cease. But if you cannot chew through it, it is merely a single small *zòng*."
"Disciple! You have blocked the mouths of all people. Heh! At the edge of the abyss, there is no limit to places that wound the heart;
how could one obtain gold to cast Qu Yuan?
On the anniversary of his birth, the Master addressed the assembly. Holding up a fan, he said: "Just this thing—when let loose, it differs from case to case. He pointed toward the valley stream.
The mountains are each different. When gathered and held, the ten directions are cut off; the clouds and moon are the same. But as for not gathering and not releasing—how is that?
Today, the Buddhas of the three periods of time are emitting light and shaking the earth upon this old monk’s fan.
If there is any clever patch-robed monk, please come forth and meet me. A monk asked, "How many years of age is this staff? The Master said:
[The Master] said, "The pillar testifies. The student asked, "How old are you, Preceptor? The Master said, "Ask the pillar. The student asked, "What is immeasurable life?
The Master said, "Moment by moment. [The student] asked, "How was it before emerging from the mother's womb?"
The Master said, "People suspect murder. The monk asked, "What about when one has already emerged from the mother's womb?

The Master said, "People suspect murder. The monk asked, "What about when neither of these two situations applies? The Master said, "A mirror. The monk asked, "'Above heaven and below heaven, I alone am honored.
What is it that you honor? The Master said, "A broken wooden ladle atop a pile of refuse. The monk bowed. The Master said, "Clear."
The year has new branches once more; the spring wind’s vexations have not yet ceased. Standing for a long time, take care. Addressing the Assembly on the Mid-Autumn Festival:
If you wish to understand the meaning of Buddha-nature, you should observe the conditions of time and season.

Tonight, the golden wind penetrates the curtains, and the jade dew hangs from the branches. The bright moon flows with radiance, and the azure sky is as if washed clean. Falling leaves dot the forest as they drift, and the cold—
The sound of the cricket enters the ear; the green mountains beyond the curtain are bathed in the light of dawn, and the white waves upon the river shimmer with radiance.
Within these very conditions, does the meaning of Buddha-nature exist or not? If one says it exists, one mistakes the bridge of a donkey’s saddle for a horse.
If one says it does not exist, one faces south and looks at the Big Dipper. Ultimately, how is it? *Ei!* Were it not for the wild geese arriving last night, how could one see the sea gate?
Autumn. On the Winter Solstice, he addressed the assembly: "The first yang returns; the yang lines accumulate to form Qian. The first yin appears in Guo; the yin lines accumulate to form Kun.
Movement and stillness revolve like a ring without end; the transformations of creation and destiny proceed from this opening and closing. It is just as in the Great Changes (Yi Jing)."
The Master said, "Does this not reveal the heart of Heaven and Earth? How do you all understand this? A former Confucian scholar said, "One sees the heart of Heaven and Earth in movement.
Others said, "One sees the heart of Heaven and Earth in stillness. Still others said, "One sees the heart of Heaven and Earth between movement and stillness.
Yet others said, "One sees the heart of Heaven and Earth in that which is neither moving nor still. Everyone, try to say something about these four views.
[The Master] spoke: "Which of those two words is more intimate? Today, Drum Mountain cannot help but provide a commentary for you all. Striking the desk with his whisk to the left, he said:
"In movement, one sees the heart of heaven and earth. Striking the desk to the right, he said: "In stillness, one sees the heart of heaven and earth."
In the *Ji’an* (Recorded Sayings) it says: "Within movement and stillness, one perceives the heart of heaven and earth.
[The Master] gathers his whisk and says: "Neither moving nor still, one perceives the heart of heaven and earth. He suddenly raises the whisk and asks: "Do you see? He lets out a shout and says:
"Do not say, all of you, that Drums Mountain has heavy habitual tendencies; today he is still reciting the *Book of Changes* before people."
A Night Address to the Assembly: Tonight is the tail-end of the old year; tomorrow is the head of the new year. What comes now passes as the ancient; every moment is truly difficult to retain.
Within the three realms, all undergo birth and death—when will this cycle of saṃsāra ever cease? If you do not diligently practice self-examination, how can you differ from horses and oxen?
Only the clever cat can laugh until his face breaks open and remains free of sorrow. Even if one were to preach the Way of True Permanence, it is...
How foul-smelling are those excrement sticks! Everyone, tell me: what excellence does this wildcat possess? Have you not seen the ancient saying:
"Only the wildcat knows there is something; he travels directly upon the crown of Vairocana"?
Address to the Assembly on New Year’s Day: Amidst the sound of exploding firecrackers, the year draws to a close. The spring breeze sweeps vast and wide; the heavens and seas are expansive.
Where now lies the Buddha-dharma of this new year? Peach and plum blossoms bloom, reflecting against the jeweled balustrade. Reflecting against the jeweled balustrade—do not be heedless!
If you do not penetrate this message here, you have come to this mountain in vain for yet another turn. A monk asked: "Please, Master, provide another message."
"News. The Master gave him a slap and said, "What is this? The monk was speechless. The Master said, "Why do you not say:
'The beginning of the year opens the reign; all things are renewed'?"
A Teaching for the Assembly on the Lantern Festival: Today is the auspicious festival of the Lantern Festival.

Taking advantage of this favorable occasion, I, the mountain monk, have set up a small shop at the head of Shigushan to sell lamp-wicks. Is there anyone among you who wishes to transmit the lamp and continue the flame?
If so, please come forward. When no one stepped forward, the Master said: "In the past, Baizhang picked up [a spark] from within the brazier..."
Xing suddenly caused Mount Gui to illuminate heaven and reflect upon the earth; Longtan, amidst the black night, blew out the paper candle, directly causing Deshan to crumble like ice melting away.

Thus, the Buddhas of the three periods have passed the torch from one flame to another, and the seventeen hundred patriarchs have continued the flame from lamp to lamp, each shining through antiquity and soaring into the present. Tonight, this mountain monk also wishes to join them.
All you people have completed this transaction; it ensures that everyone’s torch of wisdom shall illuminate the heavens and its auspicious light pervade the wilds.

Then, making a gesture with his hand like a flame [symbol], he asked, "Does the assembly understand? After a long pause, he laughed and said, "In our shop, every purchase is sold for its full price—no discounts are given."
Addressing the assembly: Empty space is pulverized, the great earth sinks level; the Buddhas cannot show their heads, and the ten directions are entirely cut off.
How solitary and steep it is! How utterly liberated it is! Yet, this is only within the gate of Gushan.
They remain stuck halfway through, all becoming dead men. This is why Luopu went to visit Jia Shan;

Shan said, "It is not that you cannot cut off the tongues of everyone under heaven, but how can you make a tongueless person speak? Some provide a substitute response, saying, "He should give another shout.
This too is like a shrimp leaping out of its bucket—it has never even dreamed of Jia Shan. For the most part, these patch-robed monks...
Householder, by all means do not sit idly waiting for a withered stump, taking that to be the ultimate principle. You must know that at times it is thus;
at times it is not thus. At times it is thus yet not thus; at times it is not thus yet thus. At times one sits high atop the crown of Vairocana;
at times one stays low beneath the feet of an ant. At times, the whole platter is laid out before you.
Sometimes it is treasured away in a nested casket; sometimes it deceives all the world; sometimes it fails only itself.
Sometimes it emerges openly from Mount Qi; sometimes it crosses the Cang River in secret. In such topsy-turvy ways, even Buddhas and Patriarchs must knit their brows.
It is not right, yet it is not wrong; throughout past and present, none have been able to deliberate upon it. Everyone, tell me: why is he so elusive? Hehe!
As long as the shirt that clings to the skin has not been stripped off, it will be difficult to reveal the elegance of one’s naked body.
A Teaching for the Assembly on New Year’s Day: The golden cock crows at the break of the fifth watch; Boundless auspicious light floats across the earth.
The great assembly has added another year to their lives; To meet and offer congratulations is quite superfluous. As for the whisk in this old monk’s hand—
Does it not increase by one year? Let no one say that there is no year; a tongueless child speaks with his own mouth:
"The spring and autumn are discerned upon the ungerminating branch; the crimson sun shines brightly within the shadowless waves. Even the dark-skinned slave and the white ox know this."
When one leaves the gate, there is a path that falls into the wild weeds. Today is the day of the New Year, the moment of inaugurating the reign;

for this reason, I, the old monk, have specially ascended the seat to offer prayers for the longevity of Your Majesty’s life. Now, regarding the single phrase of "Protecting the Country through Gratitude"—how do you speak it?
May the Golden Wheel forever stabilize the three thousand worlds; may the precious mandate extend for billions of years.
Invited by the old friend Hengru, the Master addressed the assembly: "In years past, I and my old friend Hengru entered the community at Boshan together.
At that time, the Elder of Boshan used only the phrase, 'When this single breath does not come again, where will one go?
to leave the people of the world at a loss. Twenty-five years have passed since then. Today, Hengru has specifically come up the mountain."
I have come to visit you. Unable to avoid it, I shall once again take up this old story to repay the kindness of Boshan.

From where does life come? A steel saw dances the *Santai* (Three Platforms) dance. To where does death go? The *Santai* swallows the steel saw. Do not encounter it through light; do not encounter it through darkness.
Cut off both ends at once, and silver blossoms will bloom upon the iron tree. How laughable that Master Boshan of old— [The text ends abruptly.]
The practice of liberation. It was merely held fast; today, this old monk lets it go. Do you all understand? Heh!
At midnight, the stone man finally turns over; to whom can one tell of such a fine dream?
I heard that when an elder entered the seamless stupa to request instruction, he addressed the assembly: "Within the withered tree, a dragon roars;
its thunder shatters the void, yet it reveals no body. Within the skull, there are eyes; they illuminate heaven and earth, yet not a speck of dust is seen.
Today, all is gathered back into the seamless stupa; even the hands and eyes of Great Compassion cannot find it. Do you all recognize this seamless stupa? Long ago, in the Tang..."

Emperor Suzong asked National Teacher Zhong, "After a hundred years have passed, what will you require? Is it within the realm of master and disciple, or within the path of benevolence and righteousness?

The National Teacher replied, "Build for me a seamless stūpa. [The Emperor thought: "His compassionate heart is too earnest; this is also like an old man who does not know when to rest. Suzong said, "I request the Master’s design for the stūpa.

The National Teacher remained silent for a long while and then asked, "Do you understand? The Emperor was a masterful sovereign. The National Teacher remained silent for a long while and then asked, "Do you understand?"

There are no words with which to respond; there is no principle to be set forth. Herein, how many people have fallen into a living trap? Emperor Suzong did not understand; he was ultimately a master of the craft.
The National Teacher said, "I have a disciple who has attained the Dharma, Tan Yuan. You may issue an imperial decree to question him. Thus, he shifted the calamity away from himself.
After the National Teacher passed away, an imperial decree was issued to question Tan Yuan. What was the National Teacher’s intent? Go seek it within a piece of flatbread.
The *Ju* (Soup/Exposition) states: Danyuan’s verse says, “South of Xiang, north of Tan—what place is this, after all?
Within it lies gold sufficient to fill a nation, yet it has been lost. Beneath the shadowless tree, the contract boat awaits; do not mistake it for something else.”
"In the lapis lazuli hall there is no one with knowledge. What need is there for anything else? Today this old monk has brought forth the seamless stupa, layer upon layer.
If you have not yet understood, the old monk shall once again provide a commentary to break it open for you. Be careful. He descended from his seat.
Address to the Assembly on New Year’s Day: For three years at Gushan, I have not opened the hall for formal instruction;
within this, the sweet dew has always flowed abundantly. Why then stir up windless waves? To take up a hare’s horn and discuss its length or shortness!
[The Master] raises his whisk and says: "Do you all understand? This was first brought forth by Old Man Shouchang thirty years ago atop Mount E’feng."
Today, he has fallen into the hands of this mountain monk. I cannot help but bring him forth to celebrate the New Year with you all.

If you can understand this, you will be able to cause earth and heaven to harmonize, the seas and mountains to be level, the smoke of war to cease instantly, and the waves of the whale-sea to no longer rise.
Like a "startled-chicken" jewel-pillow, it shines perfectly and boundlessly; like a divine *maṇi* pearl, it gives birth to the inexhaustible.
A sword hangs from between his brows; killing and giving life occur simultaneously. An amulet is suspended behind his elbow; unfolding and rolling it up is entirely at his own will.
Setting aside the congratulations for a moment—there is yet another person who does not accept such greetings. Can you all approach him intimately?

Even if Linji were to enter directly with a single blade, he would not dare to peer at him with a direct glance; even with Dongshan’s jade thread and golden needle, one cannot avoid being left speechless.

The Patriarchs' Hall: godly heads and devilish faces, donkey lips and horse tongues; receiving echoes in the void and taking a turtle for a soft-shelled turtle.
The Temple of the Guardian Deity: "If one recognizes the mind, there is not an inch of land in the whole world.

The opening of the hall. The Master approaches the seat and holds up the ceremonial document (shu), saying: "The Buddha-dharma of Vulture Peak was entrusted to kings and ministers.

Having finished proclaiming the document, the Master points to the seat and says: "In the past, the Layman Vimalakīrti used this very seat at Vaiśālī..."
In the city of Vaiśālī, he sat upon the vast assembly at Vulture Peak; there, he clarified this inconceivable realm.

What aspect of reality does he clarify? Do you understand? If you do understand, scatter the great assembly with a shout and topple the Dharma-seat! Would you still dare to blame him then?
"If you have not yet understood, this mountain monk shall perform his play upon the stage. He then ascended the seat, held up the incense, and said:

Under the clear and bright heavens, the four seas rejoice in the transformation of universal harmony. This single offering of incense is respectfully offered for the officials of the Great Dao Platform, as well as those of this prefecture, this county, and the entire commandery;
may you forever be compassionate fathers to the four classes of people and eternally act as the warm springtime for all under heaven.
This single offering of incense is respectfully offered for the great patrons of this temple, the Dharma-protecting officials, and the lay devotees.
[And so forth. We humbly pray that you shall long serve as the pillar and foundation of the Imperial House, and forever act as the golden rampart and moat of the Buddha-land.

[The assembly] adjusted their robes and took their seats. After the mallet was struck, the questions and answers were not recorded. The Master remained silent for a long while.
He said: "To understand it in such a way is already the secondary meaning. Before this mountain monk has even stepped out of his quarters, you have already clearly understood and manifested it.
To wait until the mallet is struck once more would be like wind stirring up dust;
how much more so to wait for this mountain monk to open his mouth? Since you have arrived here, one can do nothing but take the non-existent as existent to provide an answer."
Regarding the seasons: does the great assembly still know the primary meaning? Is it not the four dhyānas and eight teachings?
Is it not the five vehicles and ten mysteries? Is it not Linji’s three mysteries? Is it not Dongshan’s five ranks? Is it not Yunmen’s three phrases?
Is this not the Nine Banners of Fushan? For now, let us rejoice that there is no connection. Nevertheless, when held fast, even gold loses its luster;
when let go, even tiles and pebbles emit light. The Nine Banners of Fushan are thus; the Three Statements of Yunmen are thus; the Five Ranks of Dongshan are thus;
the Three Mysteries of Linji are thus—even down to the cawing of crows and the chirping of sparrows, the movement of the wind, and the drifting clouds.
Arising. There is nothing that is not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Do you understand?
If you do not, I shall have no choice but to become a schoolmaster in a village of three households. Long ago, the Great Master Baizhang said: "One must simply penetrate these three phrases.
The first phrase is: one must not grasp at objects. The second phrase is: one must not dwell in non-grasping. The third..."
One must not form a conceptual understanding based on these three phrases that fails to abide or attach. If one can transcend these three phrases, one will naturally penetrate heaven and earth;
it will be as startling to elephants and as awe-inspiring to dragons. Whether governing a state or ruling a nation is fine; discussing the patriarchal lineage or explaining the teachings is fine;

devoting oneself to the fundamentals of farming is fine; engaging in commerce or trade is also fine. This is what is called the perfect interfusion of all phenomena (*dharmadhātu*); what obstruction could there possibly be?
The great assembly, tell me: what is the phrase that penetrates through the three statements? (He strikes the meditation staff. He descends from his seat.

On the occasion of the opening of the retreat, the mountain monk entered the city of Wénlǐng. Greatly startled and alarmed, people called him a "Living Buddha," yet he is merely a worn-out, ordinary man.
Looking at it thoroughly, there is not a single thing; he speaks neither of the five ranks nor the three mysteries. Whenever he encounters...

Green is the pine; lush green is the bamboo. Black is the crow; white is the crane. Nine times nine is originally eighty-one; six times six is simply thirty-six.
If you understand it from this point, you will still be lodging in a thatched hut outside the gate. Do you know yet?
"Is there a phrase within the gate? A wooden staff at the corner of the Purple Cloud Hall was struck once; the stone pillar of the Ritual Practice Pavilion wailed aloud;
the East and West Pagodas clapped their hands and laughed loudly, saying, "A pity! A pity! Do you all understand?
It is well to return to the hall when there is nothing to do. Entering the hall:
In the lineage of the patch-robed monks, everything is of one flavor—straightforward and direct. There is no need for Chinese or barbarian speech;
who cares about "the three before" or "the seven after"? If asked for Shide’s name, he stands with his hands folded across his chest. It is also like Baizhang clearing the fields.
Extending his hand, he entrusted the Great Meaning. It happened that the old monk was washing his feet. Zhaozhou’s words were plain and straightforward;
the Great Way has always been thus. What need is there for any artifice or secrecy? As soon as one begins to deliberate or reflect, a fine steed cannot catch up with the wind;
it is like heading south when traveling to Yan, or searching for the sun in the dead of night. Today, this mountain monk shall once again act [as follows].
"How is it? "I have stood for a long time. Take care.
