It is said: "The year has drawn to a close; where do you return? Day after day of toil and management—all is suffering. I exhort you, O worthy one: you must look within yourself.
The nest knows the wind, the burrow knows the rain. Clouds follow the dragon; winds follow the tiger. The peacock unfurls its beautiful plumage for the guest;
the old crane spreads its sturdy wings to dance with the breeze. Zhaozhou spoke a 'No'; Yunmen, however, said 'Universal. Puhua merely shook [his staff]."
Bell. Heyshan explained the striking of the drum: He raised his whisk and asked, "Do you understand? After a long pause, he said, "Munī is not in Western India;
Zhòngní does not dwell in Eastern Lǔ."

Ascending the Dharma Hall on New Year’s Day: "Today is the first day of the first month; it is the dawn of a new era of prosperity. The old peach-spirits have been replaced, and the new official calendar has been taken up.
All five blessings are brought forth and bestowed without any sense of stinginess. Even the lanterns and the pillar pillars have each offered their congratulations.
Yet, is there yet another person who also receives these greetings? Setting aside for a moment whether they receive them or not—what, ultimately, is this?"
How can one see this person? An ancient said: "Directly beneath, it is still difficult to comprehend; seeking through words, it becomes even more remote.
If we speak of Buddhas and Patriarchs, they are by nature separated by the ends of the earth. Since neither seeking through words nor directness is permitted, how can one attain comprehension?
If you can comprehend it, what need is there to speak of Linji’s Three Mysteries, or what need to speak of Dongshan?

The Five Ranks. What is being said about Returning to the Source and Beheading the Snake, the Arhat’s Writing Characters, Xuefeng Rolling the Ball, and the Great Sui Burning the Slash-and-Burn Fields?
Such ancient and strange things—how could they even reach the strings of one's ears? Why is this so?
Hehe. Once one has crossed the great ocean, there is no need to boast of the water; once one has left Mount Sumeru behind, there is nothing that is not a mountain.
Entering the hall: This first month of the year has already passed five days. The Dharma-bell is struck and the Dharma-drum is beaten. There is no need for "how" or "what";
there is no need to bring up the present or cite the ancients. Rising and extending both hands, he says: "The Buddha-dharma is right here in the hall."
The two hands join; the pillar and the lantern dance together. "All you worthy ones, can you take this up?

After a long silence, he took up his staff and said, "If you do not go while the weather is clear and dry, you must wait for the rain to drench your head. He struck the ground once with the staff and descended from the seat.

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The three yang energies stir their movement; all things are renewed. Peach blossoms can turn red; willow eyes can turn green. Clear and bright is the intent of the Patriarchs;

clear and bright is the mind of the ancient Buddhas. It is only valued that you understand it directly beneath you; do not hesitate or ponder in confusion. Furthermore, there is another extraordinary matter:
a frog leaps across the waters of the Eastern Sea. Does the assembly understand? After a long silence, he said: 'Appropriate.'"
At first, one only speaks of the length of the thatch; it is only after burning it away that one knows the ground was uneven.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The clear faculty is naturally obscured; when thoughts cease, one is lost to the source.
Speech and silence cannot reveal it; affirmation and negation are incomplete. Ultimately, how can one attain resonance? Is it by pointing a finger? Is it by raising a fist? Is it not?"
Is it this letting out of a shout? Is it perhaps drawing a circle? Is it perhaps spinning around once? Is it perhaps performing a somersault?
Is it perhaps knocking over the Dharma seat and sweeping the sleeves before departing? For now, let us say there is no connection at all.
"Good sirs, each of you return to your hall and observe carefully.
[The Master] ascends the hall. In the past, Layman Pang visited Mazu and offered this verse: "The ten directions gather together as one;
Each and every one studies non-action. This is the field for selecting Buddhas; With an empty mind, one returns having passed the examination. Later, Huo’an went to visit Cigan.
At Tiantai Huguo, [Huangbo] recited this verse: "Arriving here is the field for selecting the Buddha. As he reached this line, the Hermit (Guishan) shouted.
The Hermit attained great enlightenment and composed a verse on his realization, saying: "At the limit of deliberation, one sees the title; At the end of the journey, one enters the examination hall.
Grasping the tip of the brush, wind and rain rush forth; This time, I shall not be a 'Plum-Blossom Gentleman'. "Today, this mountain monk does not..."
To avoid following along with the headnotes and footnotes: Huochan (Or-Am) visited this Chan Master at Tiantai Huguo. "Stinking meat attracts flies.
When the verse reached the line, "This is the field for selecting Buddhas; one shoulder is laden with Zen," this Chan Master gave a shout—snatching food from a starving man.
Huochan attained great enlightenment; it was completely shattered and torn asunder. At the limit of deliberation, one sees the title.
"Up there is the Great Man, Qiu Yi Ji. On the long road to the edge of the world, he enters the examination hall.
Hearing thunder, he commits the five rebellious acts. Grasping the tip of his brush, wind and rain come swiftly. Eight *ke* have already passed; this time he will not be the 'Plum-Blossom Graduate.
There is still a trace of that poor, shabby air about him. Friends, tell me: what is it to pass the examination? Is it learning the practice of non-action?"
"Ma! Is it that you have awakened to the emptiness of the mind? For now, rejoice that there is no connection [to be made].
After all, what is the matter that passes the examination? Hehe! At every point of intimacy, one must know for oneself when meeting the occasion."

Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "If one discusses this matter, it has nothing to do with movement or stillness, nor does it involve existence or non-existence. How could it fall within the reach of verbal explanation? There is no room for deliberation.

A single blow of the staff or a single shout is precisely the growth of branches from a long joint; to speak of the 'mysterious' or the 'sublime' is nothing but being buried in dust or hidden by mist.
This is not the Way of the Patriarchs, nor is it the vehicle of the School. What, then, is the matter within the vehicle of the School? The mountain monk—
Today I have a toothache.
[The Master] ascends the hall, takes up his staff, and taps it once, saying: "Do you all recognize this wooden monk?
Since this monk was born, no one can record the year; with his god-like head and ghostly face, he is unfit for transmission. He is accustomed to acting like a madman, unfathomable to others."
He swings a swing on the back of empty space. Holding his staff horizontally, he says: "The Buddhas of the ten directions have no place to emerge. Holding the staff vertically, he says:
"The Buddhas of the three periods of time have no ground to hide their bodies. If it is neither horizontal nor vertical, the Buddhas have eyes but cannot see it;
they have mouths but cannot speak of it; they have hands but cannot touch it. Even unto this day, it responds to conditions.
"A single phrase to show the assembly: how about this? He struck the meditation seat once and asked, "Do you hear it?

If you have heard it, you all have been for many years with this Wooden Seat Abbot, your eyebrows entangled with his. If this is not yet so, the Wooden Seat Abbot is going to the Kingdom of Ryūkyū to open the hall. He descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Mistake! Mistake! Mistake! Those with copper heads and iron jaws vie with one another over strength and weakness.

If even a hair’s breadth of right and wrong remains unexhausted, how can one ever escape being bound by Yama? Do not mistake a broken clay bowl from beneath the hedge for the green stone almsbowl before the Buddha."
"Let you startle the heavens and shake the earth; yet, upon close inspection, it is better not to do so. Ultimately, what is the phrase that lies beyond right and wrong?
There are no traces left behind by the five schools; even the hands and eyes of Great Compassion cannot touch them."
On the day of the Buddha’s *parinirvāṇa*, he ascended the hall and said: "Śākyamuni Buddha was born on the eighth day of the fourth month.
He performed a complete script for a legendary play, exclaiming his own applause. After the opening scene, there were moments of separation and reunion, of sorrow and joy.
On the fifteenth day of the second month, the music reached its conclusion and the act ended; he made a grand finale by manifesting his extinction at the twin śāla trees. Great assembly!"
One must not merely act like a short man watching a play; one must recognize that trace of poisonous intent before it can be resolved.
Today, this mountain monk, without sparing his own eyebrows, shall annotate this for you all.
(Striking the table with the whisk on the left side) Śākyamuni Buddha was born here within the Lumbinī Garden. (Striking the table with the whisk)
To the right, he says: "Śākyamuni Buddha manifested his parinirvāṇa here beneath the twin śāla trees.
As for that which is neither born nor extinguished—how is it? He raises his whisk and says: "What is this? Ei!"
Ascending the hall: Within this very ground, weeds naturally do not grow; beyond this ultimate principle, the mysterious mechanism is such that mulberry trees and lotuses flourish everywhere.
There is no need for Mañjuśrī to manifest multiple bodies to transcribe it repeatedly; what use is it for Arhats to come one by one from within dreams?
The lamp-wielding practitioner only increases his confusion, and the bare-shouldered monk toils in vain through the streets. If you knew...
Dampness is simply water. The sweet nectar flows drop by drop; it does not descend from heaven. If you mistake a servant for a lord, purple clouds will shroud your vision forever.
Is there anyone here now who can burst open the seal of the purple clouds and spit out the taste of that nectar?
This would leave some seventy-odd eminent monks with nowhere to hide their bodies—just like a pair of ancient dragon-eye wells.

Utterly cool and refreshing. *Ei!* A stone pagoda soars into the void ten thousand fathoms high; how many travelers have gazed upon it in vain! (In the Kaiyuan era, there were once the "Ten Wonders" guests.
When they approached the Master as he emerged from the hall, they requested that the Master preach the Dharma by means of these Ten Wonders.)
Ascending the hall, he said: "Each and every one is perfect; everywhere is wondrous. Every dharma is identical to the upward-opening aperture.
If you can dissolve beginningless views and knowledge, there will be no obstruction in movement or stillness as you propagate the essential pivot.
Strike the golden bell atop Mount Sumeru; release the iron hawk beyond New Korea. Drive out the mud ox to walk upon the sea; beat the stone tiger until it lets out a roar. He raised his whisk.
He said, "What do you know? And what have you seen? He struck the sounding block and said, "What is there to obstruct?
He threw down his whisk, let out a shout, and descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said: "In the past, there was Lady Ji of the State of Qin, who questioned Master Kai-shan Xian about the Dharma. Xian replied:
'Our Master of Mount Jing-shan teaches people only to contemplate whether a dog has Buddha-nature or not, as well as the story of the bamboo stick.
One must not offer words; one must not engage in deliberation; one must not seek understanding at the moment the stick is raised; one must not seek it at the moment it is opened...'"
One must take this up personally and simply inquire: "Does a dog have Buddha-nature? No. If a person practices according to this, they will immediately attain enlightenment.
Dàhuì once spoke of it extensively and praised it with his whole heart. Yet she was merely a woman within the inner quarters;
she had no fellow practitioners with whom to deliberate, nor any master to provide her with exhortation. How could she have attained such realization so easily? It is because—
Because his faith was so profound, he was able to apply himself to practice with genuine intensity; thus, his realization was swift.
Setting this matter aside for a moment, there was also a certain old woman who sent someone with money to Zhaozhou’s Guanyin Hermitage to request that the Tripitaka be recited.
Zhaozhou descended from his meditation seat, circumambulated it once, and said, "The turning of the Tripitaka is finished;
I transmit it to you, O Lady. The lady said, "I invited you to turn the entire Tripitaka; why have you turned only half?

At that moment, hearing these words, Zhaozhou had no words with which to respond and no principle by which to justify himself; he simply let the matter rest. Now, if someone were to say, "Zhaozhou saw her act thus..."
When the Way is encountered, one should simply shout right at the person's face, or strike them across the face, or descend from the meditation seat and circumambulate once more.
With such insights, when have you ever even dreamed of the realm of the old woman?
If you all can recognize Zhaozhou’s point of turning, you will recognize that "half-canister. If you recognize that half-canister, you will recognize the Lady of Qin.
Regarding the point of awakening: if you recognize the point where the lady attained awakening, you will then recognize Zhaozhou’s “no. Look at these two;
they were both worldly wives, yet they were able to penetrate the lifeblood of the patriarchs. How could you, who are men, instead let this slip by? The period for Zen practice is drawing to a close;
you must apply yourselves with earnest effort so as not to辜负 (disappoint) Lady Su, the Grand Tutor, today.
The intention behind this person’s offering of a vegetarian feast is most precious.

[To the assembly: Entering the hall: The period of Zen practice is nearing its end. Throughout these eighty-nine days, this mountain monk has opened his two flaps of skin to speak of yellow and white;
it has been nothing other than burying you all. You have been listening with ears pricked up and eyes fixed; listen now as this mountain monk speaks.
Huangdao said, "White! This is nothing but adding shackles and chains; what benefit is there in it?

There was once a Dharma Master named Liangsu who lectured on the sutras and engaged in debate, possessing a vast store of Buddhist teachings. Nevertheless, he could not find inner stability, so he came to visit Magu.
When Magu saw him approaching, he paid him no mind at all and simply took up a hoe and went into the garden. Liangsu followed after him as well.
He entered the garden, but Gu did not look back and returned directly to the abbot’s quarters. Liangsui attained great enlightenment and said, "Master, do not deceive me today;
there is another 'Venerable Guest' who carries a load of Chan about everywhere. He went to Wuzu Yan and asked, "How is it? How is it?
Yan simply replied, "Venerable Guest, you should also distinguish between black and white. When he came again and again, Yan said the same.
Next, it was thus for about a year and a half. One day, he saw Master Yan ascend the hall and say:
"Fellow practitioners entering and leaving together—enemies from past lives. Suddenly, it is like a scale-weight falling into place.
Look at him! What were these two masters saying? What did these two students realize? For such masters as these are truly... heaven.
These are the foremost patriarchs of the first rank. These students are the foremost students in the world.

If you merely seek and investigate within the "Seven Mysteries" and "Eight Subtleties," and simply keep on "meditating" whenever you meet someone, by the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, your meditation will not have gone anywhere.
Now that the period for meditation is drawing to a close, you must by no means regard it as being nearly finished. Each of you should [exert yourselves].
Gripping the rope-head tightly, let us join in wielding the Patriarch’s whip. Take care.
Ascending the hall upon the conclusion of the retreat: For three months we dwelt in seclusion; for ninety days our feet were bound.

If you can break through the Great San Pass, pull open the mouth of the cloth bag, stir the holy arrowhead, and release the falcon soaring into the vast heavens, then look back and see this mountain monk at ninety.

What you have been saying all day is nothing but the sound of a hot bowl clinking. If you merely memorize one bellyful of texts and study a single volume to perform like a ghost in a play, what use is there?
In the past, Dongshan, at the conclusion of the retreat, said: "Brothers, go east or go west."
"You must go directly to the place where there are ten thousand miles and not an inch of grass. But as for that place of ten thousand miles without an inch of grass—how do you go there?
Cuiyan, at the conclusion of the summer retreat, said: "Throughout this entire summer, I have been speaking of east and west for the sake of you brothers.
Look: are Cuiyan’s eyebrows still there? As you all depart, behind each of your heels are two old fellows."
You must examine this with great care; it is not permissible to say that only ninety days constitute a single period. A black-lacquered Kunlun moves his steps slowly;
an iron falcon soars through the void, refusing all tethering. Underfoot, you must ensure there is not even an inch of grass; do not let the eyebrows of Cuoyan be brought to shame.
The Extensive Record of Master Yongjue, Volume One;
The Extensive Record of Master Yongjue, Volume Two.
Re-edited by the Dharma-heir Disciple Dao-pai.
The Record of the Sayings of [Master] Residing at the Zhenji Chan Monastery in Hangzhou:
Three Gates. This gate has been opened wide with its eight characters displayed. How will you proceed, Great Assembly?
Do not add any more mud beneath your own feet.
In Maitreya Hall, he drags his cloth bag across the floor and laughs aloud. At the crossroads, he waits for someone.
But tell me, whom does he wait for? *Pfft!*

In the Buddha Hall: the golden Buddha does not pass through the incense burner; the wooden Buddha does not pass through fire; the clay Buddha does not pass through water—let us set those aside for now.
But as for Zhaozhou saying, “The true Buddha sits within the house,” I do not know how thick his face-skin is. Great assembly, today...
Now tell me: to what Buddha do you prostrate?
In the hall of the monastery, the Dharma is fundamentally without dharma; what dharma are you now protecting? Protect the monastery deity by remaining ever-vigilant.
The Patriarchs’ Hall. A group of incompetent fellows; they all raise waves where there is no wind. If you examine them closely, none can escape the staff.
Within the way of human affairs, let us for now pay three prostrations.
Occupying this chamber, I continue the old protocols of Zhenji and carry out the orthodox commands of Shouchang. The white silk is long within the stream of the Tiao River;
the yellow clouds are pure atop the peaks of Kong Mountain. Tut!
The opening of the hall. The Master proceeds to the front of the seat, holds up the proclamation (shu), and says: "To propagate the Great Dharma, one must rely upon a golden fortress.

I shall now take this hand that supports the heavens and turn it into a fist to strike at the barrier. He then requests the Rector (Weina) to read it aloud, item by item. Once the reading of the proclamation is finished.
The Master pointed to the seat and said, "The Tathāgata Sumerudīparāja has brought everyone to the end of their exhaustion.

If you have not yet heard this, wait while this mountain monk provides you with a commentary. He then ascended the seat and, holding up the incense, said, "This single offering of incense is specifically for the long life and prosperity of [the Emperor]."

May the present Sovereign’s holy life be ten thousand years of peace. We humbly pray that the Golden Wheel may forever stabilize the eight directions and the Tortoise-Pole remain secure for ten thousand generations.

This single offering of incense is respectfully dedicated to the officials of the two courts, the three ministries, and the various prefectures, as well as to the Dharma-protecting magistrates, donors, and lay practitioners of these several districts.
We humbly pray that they shall always be held in the singular favor of the Emperor and remain eternally...
This single incense offering, upon which the myriad people gaze with reverence, is respectfully presented for Great Master Wengu of Zhenji Hall.
May he vow that in every lifetime he shall forever sit within the sandalwood forest, and in every place he shall constantly let out the lion’s roar.

This single incense offering is respectfully presented for our Root Teacher, the Great Monk Wuming of Shouchang Hall, to look up to and repay the kindness of the Dharma-milk. [He] adjusted his robes...
He took his seat. After the mallet was struck, a monk came forward and asked, "Today the field for selecting Buddhas has opened; it is truly a joy that this assembly of eminent talents has gathered.
What is the phrase for transforming the ordinary into the holy? The Master said, "I dare not let you down.

The monk pressed further, "The sentence for transforming the ordinary has been pointed out by the Master; as for the matter within the inner sanctum, how is it? The Master said, "What about right now, you? The monk—[hesitated].
The ritual concluded. [A monk] asked, "It was said that the Eye of the True Dharma was extinguished with this blind donkey;
why then do you seek another half-person or a whole person so that it shall not be severed? The Master raised his whisk and said, "Is it severed, or is it not severed?
The monk stepped forward and said, "The gates of old are reopened today; as all ordinary and holy beings arrive, how will the Master receive them? The Master—
[The Master] said, "In my place, I allow nothing at all. The student asked, "Why do you not allow anything? The Master said, "I cannot blame you. A question was asked:
"I do not ask about the precious sword held aloft in the sky; what is the discourse that transcends Buddhas and patriarchs? The Master said:
"I dare not defile you. The monk stepped forward and said, "If that is so, then everyone will become a Buddha.
The Master said, "That, too, is unnecessary. The monk bowed and withdrew. There was another who wished to come forward and ask a question; the Master said, "Stop, stop!

Even if you had a hundred thousand tongues, each tongue a hundred thousand voices, and each voice a hundred thousand questions, they would all be exhausted by this mountain monk striking [the gong] once."
He lowers his whisk and says: "I have finished answering you all. If there were any point left unanswered, it would be as if one were looking toward the mountain passes from ten thousand miles away.
Raising the whisk, he says: "This is the primary meaning. As for the secondary meaning, do not rashly give rise to conjecture.
No matter how much you may exert your strength with copper heads and iron brows, or how clever you may be with ghost-eyes and dragon-gazes—it is all in vain. He strikes.
Sharp and severe words are nothing more than scolding the rain and mocking the sun; meticulous needlework and thread are entirely the catching of wind and grasping at shadows.
Today, having been invited here by various officials, lay devotees, and venerable elders, how am I, this mountain monk, to expound the Dharma?
My approach is one of total rusticity; I possess no novel phrases nor flowery compositions.
However, the matter brooks no delay; I have no choice but to rend my heart and cut open my gallbladder, exhausting my tongue to explain it for all of you.
Heh! Much empty talk is not as good as a little reality. Take care. The Layman asked: "To 'kill the Buddha' and 'kill the Patriarchs' is entirely to fall within the patterns of the ancients;
to 'strike with the staff' and 'shout with the *han*' does not escape the old traps of the present day. I beg the Master to overturn them completely from the very bottom."
[The Master] said, "I have already pointed directly to the great meaning of the Western Coming. The scholar bowed. The Master then descended from his seat.
The scholar gave a shout. The Master smiled and said, "You have added too much of this."
On the Buddha’s Birthday, the Master ascends the hall. A monk asks: “The World-Honored One had already finished saving sentient beings before he even emerged from his mother’s womb.
Why, then, today, does he point one finger to heaven and one finger to earth? The Master says: “His whole body reeks of stench. The monk asks:
“If Siddhārtha had not been born, ten thousand ages would have remained like a long night. Yunmen said, ‘Kill him! What is the meaning of this? The Master says: “To stop the sound.”

[The monk] raised his voice. He stepped forward and said, "If that is so, then 'the grass withers and the hawk’s eye becomes sharp; the snow melts and the horse’s hooves grow light. The Master said, "Excellent, you who show such respect.
A monk asked, "All dharmas are fundamentally beyond words. How does the Master expound them while remaining beyond words?
The Master held up his whisk. The monk said, "Is it only this, or is there something else? The Master lowered the whisk. The monk bowed and withdrew. The Master then said, "Śākya..."

Karmic debts from the past have not yet been settled; year after year, they are doused once with hot water. It is all for the sake of descendants coming to offer their respects—how many are there who merely echo what they hear?
Only Yunmen knows how to repay this debt of gratitude: he would strike them dead with a single blow, which is no mere clever trick.
Zhenjing wanted to further suppress Yunmen; to turn the noble into the lowly is truly difficult to understand. (He then planted his staff on the ground.)
Today this mountain monk acts according to his mandate. Would the Elder Zhenjing have let him pass?

These three great elders vied for excellence and contended for loftiness, each displaying their own elegance. If you wish to know that they obtained but a single peg, how would this mountain monk speak today?
Upon the mandarin duck pillow, twin streams of tears flow; half are thoughts of you, half are resentments toward you.
At the request of the Magistrate Huang Hai-an, the Master ascended the hall. Layman Hai-an asked, "Venerable Sir, you received the Dharma from Shouchang;
what did you receive? The Master extended both hands. The layman then bowed. A monk asked, "I do not ask about holding fast at the vital ford."
"How is it when you let go of even a single thread? The Master held up his whisk. The monk stepped forward and said, "When a dragon gains water, its spirit increases;
when a tiger encounters mountain terrain, its ferocity intensifies. He then swept his sleeves and returned to the assembly. The Master smiled at him.

[The monk] asked, "When neither existence nor non-existence is established, and one does not rest even in the middle, how is it? The Master said, "What you have offered is true. The monk stepped forward and said, "Is this not the student's [doubt]?"
"Is this where you settle your body and establish your life? The Master then gave a shout. A monk asked, "When kings and ministers personally arrive, their light shines upon the springs and rocks;

the grace of protecting the Dharma is profound—how shall one repay it? The Master said, "What is there to protect? The monk pressed further, "Truly, in every place, even amidst the motes of dust, one may halt the carriage;
there is no need to loosen the belt to guard the mountain gate. The Master said, "For now, just pay your respects. A monk asked, "I do not ask about those who have arrived..."
To resolve the essentials of the Three Mysteries and the Five Ranks of Dongshan, I request the Master to proclaim them. The Master said, "Bring forth your question.
Question: "What is 'the partial within the central'? The Master said: "The ancient mirror naturally contains its radiance. Question: "What is 'the central within the partial'? The Master said:
"Snow covers the summit of Mount Kunlun. The student asked: "What is 'coming from the center'? The Master said: "Not coiling within stagnant waters. The student asked:
"What is 'arriving through the integration'? The Master said: "Moving freely in all directions without inhibition. The student asked: "What is 'reaching through the integration'?
The Master said: "Ancient halls accumulate mist and clouds. The student said: "The five positions of the orthodox and the deviant have been pointed out by the Master; [I do not...]"
"How should one go about establishing meritorious deeds? The Master said, "Look upward. The monk bowed and withdrew. The Master then said, "In the past, Guo Gongfu visited Baiyun Yuan.
Yuan ascended the hall and gave this teaching, citing: 'The Great Man of Shang, Qiu Yiji; he transformed three thousand seventy scholars.
You, the young student, with your eight or nine disciples; your fine work on benevolence shows you know the rites. Yuan said, 'This..."
This verse can cause all people under heaven to cast off their greasy hats and untie their rank-smelling undershirts.
Yet, when I, this mountain monk, look at it, for one in the position of a high official, this verse actually adds yet another greasy hat and rank-smelling undershirt.
Today, Layman Hai-an has graced Zhenji with his presence; how then shall Zhenji act?
The Layman Gu said, "It is no small matter for you, Layman, to have traveled so far. The Layman asked again, "What is 'the Superior Man' (shàng dà rén)?
The Master said, "Look downward. The Layman said, "Is it not 'Qiū Yǐjǐ'? The Master said, "Look for yourself. The Layman said, "..."
"How can a person of immeasurable greatness be inside a kiln? The Master said, "This is not your realm. The scholar said, "Why have you come to be inside a kiln?
The Master said, "The moon over East Mountain rises upon West Mountain. The scholar said, "Where does the road of Jing Shan lead?
The Master said, "It goes straight ahead. The scholar said, "Has Wufeng ever been there? The Master said, "There is no deceiving him at all."
The Master descended from his seat. The scholar escorted the Master up to the upper floor and asked again, "One who wishes to exhaust the view for a thousand li must ascend one more floor.
What is this 'one more floor'? The Master snapped his fingers once. The scholar asked, "Is there perhaps any further ground for progress?"
The Master said, "Do not engage in false conceptualization. The scholar said, "I have seen through you. The Master did not look back. The scholar said, "Shouchang is most fortunate.
The Master still did not look back, but went straight into the abbot’s quarters.
Ascending the hall on his sixtieth birthday, a monk asked: "The fragrant clouds drift and waft; we gaze long upon the springtime of agelessness.
The assembly of dragons and elephants stands in perfect order; we look up to offer prayers for boundless longevity. May I ask, what is this 'boundless longevity'?
The Master said, "Mañjuśrī could not calculate it. The monk pressed further: "When one searches with all one's might and finds nothing, what then? The Master said, "It fills and pervades the void."
“Empty,” he said. The student asked, “What is it like when one places the entire platter out before you? The Master said, “A thousand hands cannot reach it.
The student asked, “I have received your words that the manifestations differ according to the abundance or scarcity of each household; thus there are the distinctions of the five houses.
But how about that single phrase which does not fall into any of the five houses? The Master said, “Space shall speak for you. The student asked, “What is the direct path?”
Regarding the "Gate of Swift Action," the Master said, "One blow, one streak of blood. The student asked, "What is the 'Gate of Subtle Intimacy'?
The Master said, "The golden needle is not permitted to be known. The student asked, "What is the 'Gate of Secret Accord'? The Master said, "Like space merging with space.
The student asked, "What is the 'Gate of Plain Reality'? The Master said, "Drinking tea and eating rice. The student asked, "What is..."
This is the style of the steep and perilous gate. The Master said: "An iron wall ten thousand fathoms high. Furthermore, a monk asked: "Today is his birthday.

Setting aside the question of him condescending to manifest inferiority, he spoke falsely of overturning mountains and emptying valleys. Yunmen said, 'Strike him dead with one blow and give him to a dog to eat.
What is the meaning of this? The Master said: "It only supports half of it. The monk pressed further: "Suppose today it were Yunmen himself..."
"Come forward. [The monk] approaches. "And how do you see me? The Master says, "A-ha. The monk asks, "Is there anything further beyond this?
The Master says, "An eyeless stone man does not plant flowers. The monk bows and returns to the assembly. The Master then says:
"Sixty years ago, I was born on this very day; sixty years from now, I shall speak on this very day. The sixty-year cycle of the Yellow Emperor turns like a ring—how wonderful!"
Like a single flake of snow amidst the kiln’s fire, you masters grasp at the vast void; you have come specifically to celebrate my festival.
Alas, burdened by this stinking skin-bag, it arises moment by moment and perishes moment by moment. To arise is arising; to perish is perishing.
Su Qin exerted his three-inch tongue in vain. Birth is not birth; extinction is not extinction. Sun Bin left the gate only to have his feet cut off.
Even if one reaches the point where arising and ceasing do not interfere with one another, Li Bai grasped the moon at the river’s edge with his hand. [The Master] raises his whisk and says:
"Is this arising? Is this ceasing? Is it not arising? Is it not ceasing? Do they interfere with one another, or do they not? He lets out a shout and says: "For..."

"You all have already commented upon and resolved this. Do you understand? Even if you were to understand it in such a way, if you wish to see true stillness, you still lack one eye. Descend from your seats."
At the request of the filial and incorruptible Tang Qiyuan, [Master] Shouchang ascended the hall and said: "I, the unworthy son of Shouchang, am the most perverse in my conduct.
This morning, having run into Layman Tang, I have unconsciously shattered my entire body. At times I take withered grass and turn it into gold;
at times I point to gold and call it withered grass; at times I roar and reduce the great earth to fine dust."
At times he gestures toward the void and brings forth a hundred jewels; at times he turns toward the space beyond the void to pin on flowers;
at times he goes into a mud cave to bathe. When Yan Hui heard this, he could not remain ignorant; when Confucius heard it, he simply laughed himself down. Guiguzi lost his tortoise within the cavern;
when Sun Bin was questioned about it, there was nowhere to be found. Hehe! Great assembly, have no further concerns and return to the hall.
"Very well. Layman Tang asked, "What is the point where practicing Chan becomes effective? The Master said, "Three children embrace a flower drum;
do not come to block my path to the goal. He then descended from his seat.
The Dharma Master was invited by Chang Yi to ascend the hall. A monk asked, "Throughout day and night one seeks and inquires, seeking only to see one's nature.
What is the phrase for seeing one's nature? The Master said, "Today I do not answer questions. The monk pressed further, "Once one recognizes one's own nature, one is liberated from birth and death.
When the single breath does not come again, how will one be liberated? The Master said, "The mouth is naturally horizontal and the nose is naturally vertical. The monk stepped forward.
[The student] asked: "If one has escaped birth and death and clearly knows there is a place to go, when the light of the eyes falls to the ground, where does one go?
The Master said: "Where are you right now? [The student] asked: "When a solitary person faces a great enemy, what is it like? The Master said: "What enemy is there to face?
[The student] pressed further: "And after facing him, what is it like? The Master said: "Do not let yourself down. [The student] pressed further: "When the halberd is brandished and turned..."
[The Master] said, "Three times outside the borderlands; at midnight, what was the purport of the imperial decree? The teacher replied, "Please show me respect.
[The Master] asked, "An ancient said: 'Do not say that no-mind is itself the Way; no-mind still leaves one gate behind. How does one penetrate this one gate?"
The Master said, "Are you now inside the pass or outside the pass? The monk prepared to speak, but the Master said, "Go. The monk bowed and withdrew.
The Master then said, "If it were the sea, how could there be any difference in its flavor? If it were the void, how could there be any distinct boundaries?

It is only because one is deluded by attachments and stuck in the shell that there arise 'one's own village' and 'another's village. The reproach of being like 'a golden ball struck by a pellet' has had its origins for a long time. Now, I take my leave with a formal bow."

Dharma Master, you have traveled two thousand li from afar to the region of Min to propagate the teachings. Seeking out this mountain monk to request the exposition of the Dharma, you may truly be said to possess the profound discernment that is free from partiality.
Long ago, someone asked whether the meaning of the Patriarchs and the meaning of the Teachings are the same or different.
An ancient worthy replied: "When the rooster is cold, it climbs the tree; when the duck is cold, it enters the water. Another said: "A block of ice; a ball of snow."

Although each possesses the penetrating, orthodox, and correct eye, they have not yet escaped the conceptual traps of identity and difference; neither has discovered the pivotal mechanism that lies beyond.
If someone were to ask this mountain monk whether the meaning of the Patriarchs and the meaning of the Teachings are the same or different:

The mountain monk strikes you right across the face. Why? Because if one is to act for others, one must act with thoroughness; if one is to kill, one must see blood. This is the opening address for the formal retreat period.
Today, the time has come to refine yourselves through practice. Everyone should shake off their lethargy; at every step, hold fast to the end of the guiding rope;
at all times, keep the mouth of the sack securely closed. You must become like a single bar of iron extending ten thousand miles—do not imitate the reed.

The willows along the banks of the mountain stream; the great earth, its mountains and rivers, become a mass of snow. Suddenly they transform into the roar of a lion, instantly causing even the void to split its brain.
Startled, Mount Sumeru runs upside down. The Buddhas of the three periods are but spirits in ancient graves;
the seventeen hundred koans are discarded straw dogs. Even if it were like this, would it suffice for the matter beneath the patched robe? He laughed and said:
This too is like a shrimp that cannot leap out of its basket. As for leaping out with a single phrase—how would you say it? After a long silence, he said, "Ugly. He then descended from his seat.

At the request of the Vice Magistrate Yu Runfu, he ascended the hall. A monk asked, "Having burst through hundreds of thousands of layers of great waves, the golden fish has passed through the net. [The Master replied: "How about now? The monk was silent. The Master struck him and said, "You have been here before! He then descended from his seat.
The spirit and momentum of the scaled one are majestic. Let us not speak of the great waves parting; what is this "golden-scaled fish that has passed through the net"?
The Master said, "If it were so, it would have already passed through the net. The monk turned around and said, "Now, at this meeting of wind and clouds, he soars upward to the Nine Heavens.
The Master said, "For now, return to your original position. A monk asked, "A single thought is perfect and complete, with no before or after; it does not fall into stages."
"What is the matter? The Master shouted, "In what rank does it fall? A monk asked, "The single sail lies peacefully on the sky, bright and clear;
the rain has ceased on the mountains ahead, and the cuckoos no longer cry—what is this like? The Master said, "Your feet tread upon the black pearl; do not ask about the moon in the vast heavens."
Jin said, "What is the ultimate meaning? The Master said, "Sitting with eyes closed at home, one instead complains that the moon has no light.
He asked, "The former Great Master asked Master Yifeng, 'The ten realms arise from the mind; from where does the mind arise?'"
The monk asked, "I beg to ask: from where does the ultimate mind arise? The Master said, "From where does the intent of your question come, Venerable?

The monk bowed and returned to the assembly. The Master then said, "Today is the day when the Gentleman Officer Yu Runfu of Jintan has completed his Great Compassion Repentance and has requested this mountain monk to ascend the hall.
Mr. Runfu is as noble in substance as sandalwood and as refined in character as gold and jade."
His virtuous influence has long been disseminated throughout Minnan, and his reputation stands as high as the North Star. Yet it was said: "Man is not a sage;
who can be without fault? Thereupon, he commanded several lay practitioners (*ālaṅ*) to go to Zhenji Monastery to perform the Mahākāruṇika Repentance Rite.

Generally speaking, the method of repentance is like polishing an ancient mirror. Although the labor of polishing is not without merit, one must realize for oneself that the inherent radiance does not depend upon polishing.

If one recognizes this inherent radiance, then picking up incense and selecting firewood are nothing other than the site of practice (dharma-śālā), and prostrations and recitations all return to the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa). Yet, even this is merely the periphery of the gate of transformation.
Furthermore, one must know that there is what the ancients have said. An ancient asked: "How is it when an ancient mirror has not yet been polished?
He replied: "It is not far from Hanyang. "How is it when an ancient mirror has already been polished? He replied: "The Yellow Crane Tower and the Parrot Isle. There was also another who asked:
"How is it when an ancient mirror has not yet been polished? He replied: "It cannot be obscured. "How is it when an ancient mirror has already been polished? He replied: [The same].
"How is it? he asked. "It is black, as if more has been added. Again, someone asked: "How is it when an ancient mirror has not yet been polished?
He said: "An ancient mirror. "How is it when it has already been polished? He said: "An ancient mirror. Do these three great elders have any distinction between intimacy and estrangement?

If there is no distinction between intimacy and estrangement, where are their eyes? If there is a distinction between intimacy and estrangement, which one is more intimate? Try to discern this. Ancient...

Furthermore, there was a lay practitioner who asked the Second Patriarch, "My disciple is bound by past karma; I beg the Master to perform a rite of repentance for me. He was like a boat stuck in glue, pleading to be ferried across.
The Second Patriarch said, "Bring forth your sin so that I may repent for it for you. This can be called striking a snake at its vital point.
The practitioner said, "I search for the mark of the sin but cannot find it; the thief has already revealed himself. The Second Patriarch said, "I have finished repenting for you. It was fitting.
"Abiding by the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. This is like adding a point to an arrow; it is gone.
A man said, "The characteristics of this offense are not within, not without, and not in between. As it is with the mind, so it is! "Tut! What kind of talk is that?
Even the great and small patriarchs speaking such casual words still fall short of awakening. I, however, am not like this: who cares whether he has repented or not?"

Who cares about the marks of sin or the marks of innocence? Today, this mountain monk shall cause the five mountains to collapse all at once and the four great oceans to dry up instantly. (He strikes the whisk. He descends from his seat.

Ascending the hall on the Winter Solstice, a monk asked: "The myriad yin energies have been stripped away and the first yang has arisen; the auspicious breath has just arrived and the dawn light is fresh.
I do not ask about the stripping away of the myriad yins; what is the principle of the arising of the first yang? The Master said: "Pao-xi could not have completed his [hexagram] lines.
The monk pressed further: "A single phrase clearly encompasses the ten thousand phenomena; let the entire earth return to yang. [The Master said: "Just so."
[The monk] prostrated. The Master said, "Return to your place. [The monk] asked, "When the leaves fall and the tree withers, what then?
The Master said, "Underfoot you tread upon a dragon of mud. [The monk] further asked, "Does a subsequent shadow still remain? The Master said, "In the palm of the hand one holds the sun and moon.
[The monk] asked, "'Contemplating the true mark of the body—contemplating the Buddha is likewise so. What is the true mark? The Master said, "Molded clay and carved wood. The monk covered his ears.
He bowed. The Master said, "You have missed it. He then continued: "The first yang has just arisen; beneath the sea, the earthen ox roars. The six yins are gradually vanishing;
in the void, flowers fall before the cataract-stricken eyes. With hands reaching into the Moon Cave, feet treading upon the Celestial Root."

To be able to turn the heavens with the left hand and revolve the earth with the right—how extraordinary! How truly extraordinary! Yet, these are still matters pertaining to the realm of birth and extinction.
Consider this: the white sun circles Mount Sumeru, yet day and night do not affect it; the vast void encompasses the celestial bodies, yet waxing and waning have no concern for it. This is indeed so.
But compared to the school of Bodhidharma, it is still as far off as the northern continent of Uttarakuru. What about it?
This is a single phrase from the school of Bodhidharma: "The asura holds the sun and moon upon his palms; the yakṣa treads on the mud-dragon beneath his feet.

"I, too, cannot find this monk strange. As for whether the events of two thousand years ago and the events of two thousand years later are the same or different—please let this staff judge it!
[The Master] took up the staff, struck it once, and descended from the seat.

On the day of the New Year, the Master ascended the hall. A monk came forward and asked, "On the thirtieth day of the twelfth lunar month, if someone comes to the Master to collect a debt, how will you settle it with him?
The Master extended both hands. The monk asked, "The fourfold assembly is gathered, the bells and drums are clearly sounding;
before one's eyes, sounds and forms are fully manifest. Among this, who is the person of the moment? The Master said, "Look for yourself. The monk stepped forward and said, "My family is lost."

[The monk] said, "The house has been destroyed. Who is the master? The Master said, "Look for yourself. [The monk] further said, "When the year’s winter solstice ends and spring arrives, the plum blossoms on the cliff edge will send their fragrance through the nose.
The Master said, "That is two extra lines. [The monk] asked, "I have received the verse shown by the Master, which says:"

"When dwelling in the mountains, you must by all means avoid being stained by the floating dust of the world. [The student] asked, "When one studies mountain dwelling in the midst of a heap of floating dust, how should it be?

The Master said, "A sliver of moon travels through the sky; white clouds move with ease. [The student] further asked, "When the body and mind are in a state of quiescent extinction and the Way abounds, how should it be?
The Master said, "A sliver of moon travels through the sky; white clouds move with ease. [The student] further asked, "If one simply manages to exhaust all hatred and love within the breast..."
The monk asked, "What is it like at such a time? The Master said, "A sliver of moon travels through the sky; white clouds move with ease.

The monk further asked, "What is it like when one does not practice Chan, yet this is still a state of cultivation? The Master said, "A sliver of moon travels through the sky; white clouds move with ease. The monk bowed, and the Master said:
These four turning words should be investigated and examined with care. A question was asked: "The myriad phenomena of the forest and the ten thousand images are all manifest;
how can they be hidden? The Master said: "A solitary peak stands out alone, unattached to misty vines. The student pressed further:
"What about when a long sword leaning against the sky cuts off the old man’s tongue? The Master said: "Why do you indulge in such empty pretenses? You have not yet understood the previous talk."

The monks prostrated. The Master said, "A lowly woodcutter merely boasts of his books and sword. He then continued, "This mountain monk has grown so accustomed to indolence that it has become a chronic habit;
I embrace my simplicity to sustain the remainder of my years. Since matters have come to this, I shall engage in a verbal drum-roll with you all.

I am neither able to catch dragons nor strike phoenixes, nor am I able to scoop up eels or hook shrimp. This is entirely because the mountain monk’s knife for dealing with people is not sharp enough."
This is not the fault of all people. Now that the thirtieth day of the twelfth month has arrived, the Old Man Yama is about to come to settle the bill for our meals.
Furthermore, you all wish for this mountain monk to speak a verse of perfect completion (*pūrṇa-gāthā*).

This mountain monk recalls an ancient saying: "To kill a person, one must use the sword that kills; to bring a person to life, one must use the sword that brings to life. There is also another saying: "To kill a person..."

"One must use the sword that brings life; to bring life, one must use the blade that kills. Generally speaking, the ancients possessed great wealth and power, so they could employ such a multitude of swords and blades.
This mountain monk is as destitute as if washed clean; I have but a single inch of iron. When I wish to kill, I simply kill."
To live is to live. Sometimes life is treated as death; sometimes death is treated as life. Do you all understand?
Today, this mountain monk has one more final, ultimate phrase to speak to you all.
Take care. [He then descended from his seat.]

Ascending the Dharma Hall on New Year’s Day: Last night the cycle of the year reached its conclusion; this morning the auspicious scenery opens anew. Rising early at the fifth watch, what busy affairs are there?
Holding up incense, I offer prayers for the Emperor and celebrate the new year. After the meal, the drum beats to urge the assembly to the hall;
look, every single thing is manifest as it truly is. Yet I must open my mouth to speak further—then the lanterns will laugh themselves down and the pillar will be filled with resentment.
Nevertheless, listen further to this old monk’s verse: The willow knows how to lift its brows; the peach knows how to smile. Lingyun has fallen drunk and still does not wake.
The stone ox has sucked dry the mists of the three springs. Only upon reaching this point does one clearly realize the single mind.
Ascending the hall to mark the conclusion of the retreat: Today is the day we conclude the retreat, brothers. It is inevitable that you will all go here and there, east or west.
I, this mountain monk, have three phrases to entrust to you: First, upon leaving the gate, do not walk dragging a corpse behind you.
Second, when arriving at people’s homes to eat, do not let the food touch your lips. Third, do not dwell in a place where there are ten thousand miles of land without a single blade of grass. If...

If you can refrain from violating these three points, then on another day, when you burn a single stick of incense to make an offering to this old monk, it will not be considered an extraordinary act.
However, if among these three points there is any violation, do not say that you spent the winter at Zhenji. Take care.

At the Lantern Festival at Cuīyún Ān, he ascended the hall and said: "Today, the Ancient Buddha Dīpaṃkara, knowing the time and responding to the season, wishes to emit a great radiance for the sake of all sentient beings and preach the dharmas never before heard by the Buddhas.

Yet, the Elder of the Snowy Mountains has anticipated his move and acted first, causing the four flowers to fall in profusion, instantly monopolizing the green mountains so that the four walls are completely filled."

A mound of cold jade; a thousand peaks are all shrouded in crimson clouds. May all sentient beings everywhere together roam within the Great Treasury of Radiance, each abiding at the fundamental limit where Buddhas and sentient beings are equal.
The incense pillar then comes forth and says, "The great earth, mountains, and rivers are a single expanse of snow.
The lantern, however, comes forth and says, "The egret standing in the snow is not of the same color. The incense burner again...
He came out and said: "You two elder brothers, why such a desperate hurry? Tell me, where do these fine flakes of snow fall?

*Duh!* Although these three men were traveling together within the Great Radiant Treasury (*Mahā-ābhāsagarbha*), how could they avoid having their nostrils pierced by the Elder of the Snowy Mountains? Only the old monk Cuiyun remained unaffected by his arrangement.
Ultimately, how is it? Yuan An lies high in bed with his door closed; who cares how deep the snow is before his steps?

On the day after the Lantern Festival, at the request of Chief Administrator Falin, [the Master] ascended the hall and said: "Last night, a thousand homes were ablaze with lamps and ten thousand households filled with the sound of pipes and songs.
The fire-trees shone with silver blossoms, and the star-bridges were linked by iron chains. Dharma Master Miaoguang has finished reciting the Lotus Sūtra."
"Let us simply cause the thick-juiced peaches and the wandering courtesans to dance in intoxication; let the princes all become Buddhas of Universal Radiance.
As for today, where has the Dharma Master Wondrous Light gone? Setting this aside for a moment, tell me: what is the sūtra that was preached?
After a long silence, he said: "The subsequent text is long; it shall be entrusted to a future day. He then descended from his seat.
Record of the Sermon for the Opening of the Summer Retreat at Baoshan Hermitage in Jianzhou.
"Today, at Baoshan, we begin the summer retreat. For these ninety days, you must be thorough and meticulous.
Resolutely straighten your iron backbone and focus single-mindedly upon your own nostrils. Thus, all dark demons and scattered ghosts shall be utterly dispelled. From...
All previous entanglements have been cast aside. There is no need to further inquire about the mind of the ancient Buddhas;
there is no need to further inquire about the meaning of the Westward Journey. Dongshan and his father were not clever; Linji’s descendants have become something extraordinary.
Though hundreds and thousands of samādhis are all wondrous, when brought before this old monk, none are correct. Since they are all wondrous, why are none correct? This old monk’s age—
The old man understands how to conceal his body; he does not permit others to lightly conjecture or deliberate upon him.
Take care. On the occasion of the Buddha’s Birthday, he ascends the hall: "Today is the day when Siddhārtha descended to birth.

You great virtuous ones who have come from the four quarters, chasing after scents and seeking out sounds, seek for this old monk to preach the precepts. An ancient said: 'The single word "precept" (śīla) is that which all Buddhas take as their teacher. Sweet melons..."
"Sweet to the very core. It is also said: "The single character 'precept' (śīla) is what the patriarchs dread. The bitter gourd is bitter from root to tip;
the Buddha and the patriarchs are fundamentally one and the same nostril. Why, then, do they diverge into different paths?
Some say: "Let the Master be as he will; let him dread as he will. This may seem plausible, yet it cannot avoid being relegated to the left side. Others say: "The Master..."

There is no teacher; there is nothing to fear, yet nothing is not feared. It resembles a model, yet it merely resembles one. You have not yet escaped being placed on the right side. This old monk is advanced in years;
my physical strength has declined and my mental vigor is diminished. I no longer possess such elaborate calculations.
Monks, it would be better for you all to return to the hall.

Ascending the hall at the conclusion of the summer retreat, a monk asked: "When all four hooves have already passed through, why is the tail unable to pass? The Master said: "The nostrils obstruct people. Another monk asked:
"When neither the orthodox nor the biased is established, and there is no reliance on stages or positions—at this very moment, I pray that the Master will point directly.
The Master said: "Today I have a headache. The monk bowed and withdrew. The Master then said: "In the past, within the period of confinement..."
[The Master] said: "In the 'untying' (jie) of this morning, there is 'tying' (jie). Passing ninety days in such a manner, it is seen that at every moment there is arising and ceasing.
In the 'tying' of former days, there was no 'untying'; in the 'untying' of this morning, there is no 'tying.
Passing ninety days in such a manner, it is seen that at every moment one is free from arising and ceasing. If you can penetrate these two gates, you are indeed a follower of the Teachings."
"This is the ultimate limit. As for the matter of the Dharma-gate of Bodhidharma, there is not even a single point of connection. [He] holds up a whisk and says:
'Just as it is here, is this binding or is it liberation? Is there arising and ceasing, or is it free from arising and ceasing?'"
It is better to have no affairs than to have affairs. Do not drive another stake into the void. (He let out a shout. He descended from his seat.
On the Buddha’s Birthday, he ascended the hall. A monk asked, "When the World-Honored One was first born, he clearly revealed [the truth].
Why did Yunmen want to strike him dead with a staff? The Master said, "Yunmen was too busy. The monk asked, "How about you, Teacher? The Master—
[Yunmen] said, "To give birth, let it be as it is to give birth; to kill, let it be as it is to kill. A monk asked, "Why, Master, do you lack any independent judgment?
The Master replied, "Does empty space ever increase or decrease? A monk asked, "When Siddhārtha was born, he could not avoid being like a sacred tortoise dragging its tail.
When Yunmen wielded his staff, he merely sought to stop the sound and silence the noise. Setting aside these two paths, I ask the Master to grant us an instruction. The Master held up his whisk.
The disciple bowed. The Master then said: "An ancient said, 'Before the World-Honored One had even emerged from his mother's womb, he had already finished delivering all beings.

Since he had not yet emerged from his mother's womb, for what reason had he finished delivering all beings? I, this old monk, say: 'After the World-Honored One had already emerged from his mother's womb, there was not a single person he did not deliver.
Since he had already emerged from his mother's womb, for what reason was there not a single person he did not deliver? If you can recognize this..."

If you recognize the old monk’s [point], then you will recognize that of the ancients. Today, atop this incense burner, the Buddhas of the three periods and the patriarchs of successive generations turn the Great Dharma Wheel here. Now tell me: is this saving, or is it not saving? After a long silence, he said:
"The text below is long; take care."

The Provincial Governor, Mr. Sun, requested prayers for rain. Upon ascending the hall and finishing the incense offering, he said: "Today, we humbly receive the command from the Provincial Governor, Mr.

Sun, as well as the dignitaries of the entire prefecture, the various scholars who passed the spring examinations, and the literary masters, to entreat this old monk to venture onto this seat to earnestly seek sweet rain.
O virtuous ones, from where does the wind come? From where does the rain arise? The Thunder King flies forth from the head of the black clouds."

"Ask him where he ultimately dwells. When the Dragon King Sāgara sends down rain, he need only move a single thought, and the rain falls everywhere throughout the Sahā world. Look closely: it does not depart from this very place.
What is this place? Do you know? [The Master] picks up his staff and says: 'This old monk’s staff has transformed into a dragon and spews forth mist.'"
Raising clouds that shroud the heavens and obscure the sun, he spreads forth a great torrent of rain that completely pervades all of Jambudvīpa. The assembly, tell me:
by whose power of grace does he receive this? (He plants his staff upright and descends from the seat.)
Ascending the hall, he said: "To argue about right and wrong is like a general merely cursing from the battlefield. To leave no trace or shadow is like a stubborn rock blocking the gate.
To speak of the wondrous and the profound is to labor in vain, chasing the wind and grasping at shadows.

To strike with the staff or shout with the *ke* is to be mired in water and mud, making it difficult to free oneself. At this point, what can this old monk do but open his mouth? (After a long silence) He said:"
Listen to this verse: In Baoshan Hermitage, days seem like years; I recline by the north window, as if before the time of Fuxi and Huangdi.
The crimson leaves upon the branches have no concerns of their own; They let the wind blow them at will to fall by my pillow.
On the day of Zhongyuan, at the request of the lay practitioner Hai’ruo, I ascended the hall.
Today, the lay practitioner Hai’ruo has commissioned this old monk to ascend the seat and expound the Dharma in order to offer merit for his late father, Lord Huaitan.

I recall that on this very day in the past, the Buddha instructed the Venerable Maudgalyāyana to establish the *bowl-offering* (*bōlan pén*) and rely upon the power of the *saṃgha* of the ten directions, whereby his mother was able to escape from suffering.

They will be reborn in the Flower Radiance Heaven (*Puṣpārāma*). Furthermore, they recall the Buddha’s teaching that making offerings to hundreds of thousands of Buddhas is not as good as making an offering to a single person of no-mind (*acittaka*). But what, pray tell, is a person of no-mind?

Some say it is one who cannot distinguish east from west or north from south, who follows conditions with unrestrained ease and lets their nature roam at will. How is this any different from looking toward one's hometown from ten thousand *li* away?
Today this old monk, not begrudging his verbal karma, shall reveal the truth for the sake of all people: the mountains are thus green, the waters are thus blue;
birds naturally know how to fly, and fish naturally know how to swim. If one forms a view that there is Buddha-dharma here, one shall be banished to the Two Iron Ring Mountains;
if one forms a view that there is no Buddha-dharma, one shall likewise be banished to the Two Iron Ring Mountains. Do not form views of existence or non-existence.
Simply follow conditions with carefree expansiveness; let your nature roam at ease. Even if you were banished to the two Iron Ring Mountains, [the Master] strikes his whisk and says:
"The two Iron Ring Mountains have collapsed! The mindless man has arrived! Now tell me, how will you make offerings?
Golden fruits need not be plucked by monkeys; why should jade flowers be carried by phoenixes?
Ascending the hall, [the Master said: "In the past, Han Wen Gong asked Grandfather Dadian, 'How old are you, Preceptor?
Dadian held up his rosary and asked, 'Do you understand? Wen Gong said, 'I do not. Dadian replied, 'One hundred and eight, day and night.
Regarding this kōan, when I was formerly at Zhenji, I once remarked: 'Although Grandfather Dadian was a veteran of great experience, alas, his teeth could not close against the wind.'"
I, this old monk, am not like that. If someone were to ask me how old I am, I would answer: "Sumeru weighs nine *jin*.

This turn of phrase indeed possesses the true breath of a *śramaṇa*. However, now that I am old and my strength has faded, and the Buddha-dharma has further changed, if someone were to ask me how old I am, I would likewise hold up my rosary and say: "Understand?"
"Ma. He said he did not understand. [The Master] also said: "One hundred and eight times, day and night. Everyone, tell me:
is my staff the same as or different from that of Dadian? If anyone recognizes Dadian’s staff, I shall beat the drum on the Western Continent of Aparagoyānī.
If anyone recognizes my staff, Dadian shall perform a dance on the Eastern Continent of Pūrvavideha. East!
Although there are differences in the West, the North and South are largely in accord.
Take care. Ascending the Dharma Hall on the Anniversary of His Birth: This old monk is sixty-six this year; I borrowed a night’s lodging in Baoshan Hermitage.
Today everyone says it is my birthday, So we all go together to the Southern Mountain to offer congratulations. In the past he did not come, and now he does not depart; The two...
If the head does not move, how can the center continue? In this very moment, one should rightly awaken to non-arising. Do not say it is like two wheels turning on an axle.
Even if one’s lifespan were as vast as Mount Sumeru, I would say it is as swift as a snap of the fingers.

Even if one’s lifespan were as immense as empty space, that too is merely painting eyes and brows upon the void. Only the "Black Ox" (Línú) does not record the passing years; he has trampled through empty space until nothing remains.
The two feet—none of the Buddhas of the three periods can know them. The pillar laughs and the lantern weeps.
If you, O worthy one, wish to understand the definitive point, please look at the grove of bamboo at Duofu.

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The Ultimate Way is profound silence; numinous wisdom is beyond dependence. Even if you were to employ shouts or blows at will, you would already have fallen into the second or third [level of conceptualization].
To further ask 'how' or 'what,' it is truly a journey of a thousand miles and ten thousand leagues.

Therefore, the Buddhas of antiquity had no choice but to tie their tongues, and the Patriarchs of successive generations had no door through which to point it out. As the Third Patriarch’s *Inscription on Faith in Mind* says: 'The Ultimate..."
The Way is not difficult; it is only that one dislikes discrimination. Simply do not harbor hatred or attachment, and you will be transparently clear and bright.

Is this not opening up one’s heart and liver to speak to later generations? Yet, since it says "only dislike," there is already discrimination; since it says "simply do not," there is already hatred and attachment.
Moreover, if there is a "clarity" to be pointed toward, how can this be considered the ultimate teaching? You must know that the Supreme Way is without...
There is neither difficulty nor ease; there is neither discernment nor non-discernment; there is neither hatred or love nor non-hatred or non-love;
there is neither clarity nor non-clarity. Just as this old monk speaks thus, does he avoid falling into error?
Although this old monk does not fall into discernment, hatred, or love, he nevertheless borrows discernment, hatred, and love as a prelude to his performance.
"How could one possibly avoid transgression? Ultimately, how can it be avoided? I am a descendant of the Dongxia lineage, and I recall the words of the Dongshan masters.
Entering the hall: Today, the lay practitioner Zhang Huayu has requested that I, an old monk, venture onto this seat to proclaim the Great Dharma."

The Great Dharma of our Buddha takes the realization of the mind and the attainment of the fundamental source as its ultimate principle, and taking the forgetting of emotions and silent resonance as the entrance.
If I were to expound upon the fundamental portion [of the teaching], it would surely be utterly at odds with you all.
For now, I shall borrow from your ordinary daily fare and roll it along the ground, hoping that you will find a point of entry. It is like the *Zhongyong* opening its mouth and—
The Way. That which Heaven mandates is called "nature. The *Great Learning* opens by stating, "To illuminate one's own inherent virtue.
Mencius likewise said, "Exhaust the mind and know nature. Is this not taking the realization of the mind and the attainment of the fundamental source as the ultimate goal?
As Confucius said, "I desire to remain without words," and again, "In silence, I recognize [the truth]. And as Zigong said, "The Master’s literary expressions can be heard."
"Furthermore, the Master’s words concerning human nature and the Way of Heaven are things that cannot be heard [by the common person].

Is this not to take the forgetting of emotions and attaining silent resonance as the entrance? Since then, later scholars have drifted into mere exegesis and transformed it into the pursuit of the examination curriculum."
To be in accord with this Way is indeed a journey of a thousand or ten thousand *li*; how could it be that the learning of the Confucians alone is thus?
Today, you gentlemen who have set your wills upon the Great Way must by all means avoid falling into intellectual understanding or becoming stalled by words and language.
You must cast aside sensory sounds and colors, concentrate your minds, and unify your wills. You must employ the entirety of your spiritual essence and the full measure of your strength in this.
Upon the head-word of a single phrase devoid of meaning, through long and diligent investigation, one day the black lacquer bucket suddenly bursts open.
Naturally, one penetrates heaven and earth and radiates a great light. An ancient master once said:

It cannot be understood through the mind, nor can it be understood through the Way. Ordinary people use it daily without knowing it;

the Buddhas know it, yet find it difficult to name. If one were to give it a forced name: that which is between the eyebrows of the World-Honored One is called the light of the white tuft-mark (*ūrṇā-kośa*);

The old monk strikes his staff and makes a sound; this is the arising of the sound. From where does this arising come?

Having struck it, the sound ceases; this is the cessation of the sound. Where does this cessation go? Since there is neither coming nor going, one knows that arising is illusory arising and cessation is illusory cessation.
Once one knows that arising is illusory arising and cessation is illusory cessation, one knows that from the beginning there has never been any arising. From the beginning...

It has never been extinguished. If one realizes this ground of neither arising nor ceasing, then the daughter of the Chen family need not so much as snap her fingers before entering the pool of seven jewels and sitting upon a sublime lotus flower.
Setting aside the daughter of the Chen family for a moment, what then shall we say of a monk who reaches this point?
Do not raise your voice in a great shout or look down upon the four seas with empty eyes; I, the old monk, entrust this very matter to him alone.
He stayed overnight outside the gate and hauled manure within the garden. Why was this? "The chisel-headed axe on Mount Qingyuan has never been allowed to flow abroad recklessly.

A person raises this topic for discourse. A monk asked an ancient worthy, "What is Chan? He replied, "A monkey climbing a tree, tail trailing behind.

This is not a matter of being weak when encountering strength; it is not a case of withdrawing oneself to yield to others; it is not a lack of intent to deliver sentient beings;

One must indeed understand every detail clearly and be thoroughly conversant with every circumstance before one can truly be said to have reached Shuangji Temple; yet even so, this old monk would tell him, "It is not there; it is not there."
In the past, Qingyuan granted Shitou a hand-axe and told him to go live in the mountains. Shitou then made his request, and Qingyuan simply lowered one foot.

Ascending the hall on the Winter Solstice: beneath the accumulation of yin, the single yang renews its birth; this is the renewal of cosmic transformation (*zaohua*).

When it returns to its original state, from what direction does it come? Once it has returned, by what means is it pointed out? Do you still understand?
If you investigate this to its ultimate limit, you will know that it is without interruption between past and present, and that movement and stillness do not interfere with one another.
