A sword. An amulet suspended from the elbow. If one enters this gate, one cannot avoid having one's brow marked with ink. Why is this?
"Having once crossed the great ocean, one no longer boasts of water; except for Sumeru, there is no mountain."
Upon concluding the retreat, the Master ascended the hall. A monk asked, "The orthodox lineage of Cao-Dong has been transmitted to you, Master;
to whom has your own orthodox lineage been transmitted? The Master said, "I have not received it from Cao-Dong, nor have I received it from the Buddhas.

The monk pressed further, "If that is so, then from where was it transmitted? The Master struck the incense burner with his whisk and said, "From where did it transmit itself? The monk [remained silent].
After the prostrations, the Master said: "Ninety days ago, this old monk spoke of this and that; was there any Dharma to be spoken to you?
If there were Dharma to be spoken to you, you, my disciple, would have been failing me.
If there was no Dharma to be spoken to you, I, the old monk, would have been failing you. Ninety days from now, I shall not speak of this or that; will there still be [anything]?"
There is no such thing as having a Dharma to speak to others. If there were a Dharma to speak to others, this old monk would be failing you, my disciple.
If there is no Dharma to speak to others, you, my disciple, would be failing me, the old monk. This morning marks exactly ninety days;
how then can one avoid failing? Three thousand miles away, do not mistakenly utter [this teaching] when meeting people.
At the request of Layman Erhe of Lushan on the birthday of his Root Teacher, the Master ascended the hall and said: "The true pulse is difficult to penetrate, while false views easily flare up.

To 'surpass the Buddhas and transcend the Patriarchs'—when examined closely, this is nothing more than a rungs on a ladder. The wondrous song and profound guidance—this very thing is called a nest or a trap.
Beneath the White Cloud Crag, many outstanding talents remain submerged; at the head of the Fragrant Grass Ferry, they have long been stranded in a foreign land."
This is why, within the lineage of Cao-Dong, a distinct principle was established: the golden phoenix soars through the void, not merely perching atop Mount Sumeru;
the iron ox rides the waves, penetrating specifically to the heart of the great ocean. Without striking the head-on, one still prizes having a path for turning back.
To act among those of different species, one must ensure there is no private bias beneath one's feet. Even so, this is not a matter of following step by step.

Arrangements are made as circumstances arise; one must know that where there is effort, there can be no penetration, and where there is a fixed position, there can be no encompassing of a single stroke.
If you understand this stroke, then in a single thought-moment it can be suddenly perfected, and in a single moment it can be fully present.
Therefore, the Elder Dongshan said, "It is like the great earth bursting into flames. Today marks the anniversary of Master Hengru’s reaching the age of sixty.
His disciple, the Venerable Ruhé, prepared a vegetarian feast and requested an elder monk to ascend the seat specifically to expound upon this matter.
As for the phrase "Celebrating and Praising through the Meal," how would you say it? "The sun and moon are renewed year after year;
the eternal universe remains the same age after age."
At the request of Master Jinghe, he ascended the hall and said: "In years past, this old monk and my longtime friend Jinghe went together to Cold Cloud Nest atop Double Peak.
There, in a single room, we sat in silence facing each other by a solitary lamp. Later, due to a single moment of error, this old monk fell into the ranks of a common, worldly teacher.
But Master Jinghe’s backbone is like iron; he has sat upright in the empty mountains for nearly thirty years."
"Today I have specifically come up to Mount Guṣan to offer a memorial service and request the Elder Master to ascend the seat.
I do not know what his state of mind will be; today, as it is said, 'the ugly daughter-in-law must inevitably appear before her parents-in-law.

Long ago, when the Elder Master Dongshan saw his reflection while crossing water, he attained great enlightenment and composed a verse, saying: 'One must by all means avoid seeking from others; to seek afar is to distance oneself from me. I—
"Now I go alone; everywhere I encounter him. He is now precisely me; I am now not he. One must understand it in this way to attain accord with suchness.
This one verse contains the five ranks and ten mysteries, as well as the three falls and four prohibitions.
Everything is contained therein. Today, before this great assembly, I shall annotate and dismantle it point by point.
"Do not seek it elsewhere"—after all, from where would you seek it? To wander far away is to distance yourself from me;
who is more intimate than I? "I now go alone"—why roam about in confusion? "Everywhere you encounter him"—you see gods and ghosts. "He is precisely me right now"—still...
Separated by a single mountain range. I am not he now. How many have missed the mark? You must understand it in this way. But how can you understand it?
Only then will you attain accord with suchness (*tathatā*). To whom shall I give these thirty blows?
The old monk has finished his rambling exposition. Do you all understand? For thirty years before this, I studied Linji Chan; I would not accept death.
Having been within the cave of Linji for thirty years, he then studied Caodong Chan; yet he refused to die within the cave of Caodong.
Why is this? A filial child is born from a filial parent, and a rebellious child is born from a rebellious parent.

The Imperial Historian Chen Lianshi, having completed the construction of the Shenguang Dharma Hall, commissioned the Venerable Huichao to enter the mountains to preside over a vegetarian feast and ascend the hall.
The first yang-energy begins to stir; with joy we behold the heart of Heaven. May the Sage’s longevity be boundless, as heaven and earth are about to flourish in prosperity.
When the Imperial Historian Chen Lianshi responded to the summons of the Magistrate Shiyi, he moved the Dharma Hall of Shenguang to Mount Gu;
I, this old monk, followed the road back home. Subsequently, the Dharma Hall of Mount Gu was moved to Shenguang. Within this process, the distinctions between self and other were obliterated.
The traces of coming and going have been severed; there is only the Iron Storehouse Buddha (Tiedizang) radiating light from his very core, and the Stone Tathāgata whose entire body is mouth.
Within this, all sentient beings, each unaware and unknowing, are fully satiated by the flavor of the Dharma.
Why, then, wait for an old monk to beat the drum, ascend the hall, and move his lips and tongue before the Dharma is preached? Nevertheless, even so, now...
The old man’s gate of contemplation stands wide open; the old monk has the right to bear witness.
On the occasion of the Master’s seventieth birthday, he ascended the hall. A monk asked, "On this day of the Master’s birthday, is it the Limited Life or the Unlimited Life?
The Master said, "An octagonal millstone turns in the void. The monk asked, "When a sage appears in the world, the wind does not whistle..."
[The rain] does not break up clods of earth. Today is the anniversary of the Master’s birthday; why then do the wind and rain blow so fiercely?
The Master said: "The Stone Drum resounds through the void. [The monk] asked: "This year you are seventy years old. I venture to ask: what was it like before the seventy years?"
The Master said, "Just look at today. The monk bowed, and the Master continued, "Floating light does not last long;
worldly phenomena are not solid. Surveying the world throughout its course, it is entirely like a dream. I recall when I was forty years old, first shaving my head at Shouchang Temple.
At that time, the objective appearances before my eyes were intensely burning, and there was no way out. When I was fifty..."
He withdrew from the world to Mount He in Jianzhou, where he lived with a dusty head and a dirt-stained face, planting rice to earn his meal.
Although at that time he had already settled his nostrils, he was nonetheless obstructed by those very nostrils.

At the age of sixty, on the banks of the Xiao River in Hangzhou, he cast a vast golden net across the heavens, intending to scoop up dragons and strike down phoenixes; yet in reality, he could not even catch a single gnat.
"I have attained it. This year I am seventy years old. I dwell at the summit of Shigufeng Peak; my hearing is deaf and my vision is dim, and my vigor has utterly faded away.
I remain only upon this seven-foot mat, realizing nothing more than the samādhi of dozing. Looking back over the past thirty years, I have seen how many times things have changed;
it was all merely empty names and illusory shadows, entirely devoid of reality. Even today, there is absolutely nothing [to be found]."
There are many points that could be spoken of. However, since we have arrived here, I shall force myself to offer a single phrase for the sake of you all:
Before the hall, several rounds of wind and thunder have subsided; ten thousand miles away, songs of praise celebrate the peace of the age. Take care.
At the request of Zen practitioner Setsuko, the Master ascended the hall and said: "This old monk is seventy-one this year; after the white dew has fallen, the west wind blows fiercely.
In years past, the pillar suddenly gave birth to a child; everyone said it was a fine day.

For many years I have practiced empty deception and fabricated wonders, deceiving the sages and hoodwinking the common folk without a single person recognizing me. Having played this out until today, my household goods are all gone, leaving only what remains in my hand."
"One single staff. Though one may not understand the Three Mysteries and Five Ranks, it supports heaven and earth through its power.
Sometimes brought forth before the Dharma Hall, it startles and breaks off half the nose of Vajrapāṇi.
You people of virtue, tell me: from where did this staff come? After a long silence, he said: Wait another thirty years, and I shall explain its origins for you."
Chan Master Zepu requested that I ascend the hall. The entire population of Jianzhou had been slaughtered by the great army;
Chan Master Zepu took pity on them and offered them memorial services, further requesting this old monk to ascend the seat and expound the Dharma.

Now, those who have life must inevitably face death—this is something all people know. Yet they do not yet know that while one has life, one has never truly lived, and while one faces death, one has never truly died.
The deceased cannot be plundered by water or fire, nor can they be harmed by weapons or blades.

It is like the reflections in a mirror that come and go while the substance of the mirror remains unmoving; or like the waves of the sea that rise and fall while the substance of the sea is ever tranquil.

To realize this substance of eternal tranquility and immovability is to transcend to the other shore; to cling to its functions of coming and going and rising and falling is to flow [with the mundane].
The waves are inexhaustible. Formerly, on the day of the winter solstice, while eating fruit, Dongshan posed this question:
"There is a thing that reaches up to heaven and down to earth; it is as black as lacquer; it is ever present within activity, yet it cannot be grasped within activity."
"Where does the fault lie? Chief Seat Tai replied, "The fault lies within active engagement. Dongshan called to his attendant to remove the fruit table.
This question from Dongshan was not without significant intent; although the Chief Seat was a veteran of many battles, [he had failed to grasp it].
Alas, it was as if one had been denied entry at the Dragon Gate. Later followers vied with one another to avenge the Head Seat;
it appears they were all seeking to eat Dongshan’s fruit, yet none have succeeded. Only Tong’an Xian spoke differently, saying he did not know.
This is what is called "passing straight through while casting one's body across a raging fire," or "walking alone with arms swinging through a forest of swords and spears. As for...
The old monk says: Not so. Simply answer, "Can you still retrieve it within the state of non-activity? Take it for granted that Dongshan will then have his tongue tucked back in.

On the eighth day of the twelfth lunar month, at the request of the Vinaya Master Weishan, he ascended the hall and said: "In the past, the World-Honored One stayed in the Snowy Mountains for six years. [He held] a reed...

Sprouts pierce the knees; spiderwebs hang from the brows. To clarify this matter, [the Buddha] waited until the eighth day of the twelfth month, when at night he beheld the morning star and attained great enlightenment, finally achieving perfect awakening.
Those who come after, the descendants of later generations, have inherited the empty and taken up the echoes to proclaim it for him.
But tell me, everyone: what is that which was awakened to? If you say it is the mind, the mind does not see the mind. If...
The Way is the Buddha; yet the Buddha does not become a Buddha. If the Way were Chan, then Chan would not be called Chan.
Since it is neither mind, nor Buddha, nor Chan, then what is it? The above is a general offering, all of which is in accordance with reality.
May you all take care not to mistake a donkey’s saddle bridge for your father’s chin. Take heed!

At the request of the lay practitioner Xu Erchang to honor his parents, the Master ascended the hall and said: "In the life of every human being, there is none that does not originate with one's father and mother.
Therefore, the kindness of one's parents is like the sky that universally covers all, and like the earth that universally supports all; there is no one who can fully repay it.
Now, if you wish to fully repay the kindness of those who gave you life, you must understand the principle of non-arising. After a long silence, he said: "The clay ox plows the silken field."
Form: A wooden horse whinnies in the spring breeze; not a single drop remains in the two rivers, flowing vast and deep toward the eastern sea.
Entering the hall: The spring breeze is vast and expansive, its auspicious energy swirling and dense. On the branches, the oriole sings; every note calls the traveler to return home.
Beyond the wall, the peach blossoms bloom; every hue reveals Vairocana’s transcendence of his station. If there were a seeker of the Way here— (He stops mid-sentence.)
"You may take this entire burden upon yourself. Nevertheless, you must not treat it with casualness; you must know that there is the teaching of Master Dongshan.
Master Dongshan said: 'He is now truly I, but I am not now he. Since he is indeed I, for what reason does he further say that I am not he?
If you do not understand this meaning, you will fall into Dongshan’s three leaks."
Falling into the two kinds of light of Qianfeng, one does not penetrate through; falling into the four prohibitions of Caoshan as well, how can one become a true descendant of the Dongshan lineage?

Today, this old monk has unwittingly exposed the family’s shame, desiring only that all of you obtain the true nostrils and do not lose the bloodline of Cao-Dong. Is there anyone? *Ai!* Look out beyond the heavens where the head emerges.
"Who is the one who stands within this circle?
At the request of the lay practitioner (upāsaka) Sun Jue-lin, Vice Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, he ascended the hall and said:

"Today, the lay practitioner Sun Jue-lin has invited this old monk here to clarify the principles of rebirth for the sake of commemorating his late wife, Lady Lin. Now, as for our own mind, it is fundamentally..."
There is a pure land that is neither born nor unborn, nor even non-unborn;
it is only because sentient beings cling to delusions and give rise to radiance that it has been transformed into this mundane realm of the five turbidities.

Thus, the Buddhas of antiquity taught people to cultivate the practice of detachment from defilement and the merit of adornment, whereby it was transformed into the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. Now, as for this mundane realm of the five turbidities...
The Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss is entirely a shimmering light and a fleeting illusion; it possesses no reality.

If one investigates its true substance, then the body, mind, and world are none other than the single suchness (yīrú), fundamentally free from change. It is just as it is today: clouds obscure and mists gather.

During a torrential downpour, the sky has never actually been moved; in an instant, the clouds withdraw and the mist disperses, and the bright sun stands in the midst of the heavens, yet the sky has likewise never been moved.
It is simply that this body of suchness cannot be easily conceptualized or deliberated upon.
If you merely speculate within the realm of emotional consciousness and vaguely perceive a thing existing there, it is nothing more than a lump of clay.
You must all shatter this lump of clay and leap out into the void;
then the entire world of the ten directions will be entirely the body of the Buddha of Infinite Light, and the entire world of the ten directions will be entirely one [Dharma-realm].
In the Pure Land of the Precious Lotus, what further rebirth could one desire? Where else could one go? This very place is precisely where all of you shall be reborn;
it is essential that you know this. The assembly has stood for a long time. Take care.
At the request of Chan Master Buyuan for the memorial service of his deceased parents, the Master ascended the hall and said:

"Long ago, Prince Nalajita, wishing to repay the kindness of his parents, dismembered his own bones to return them to his father and dismembered his own flesh to return it to his mother. Only then did he manifest his original body to preach the Dharma for his parents.
Now, having already dismembered his bones and flesh and returned them to his parents, what would you call his 'original body,' and what would you call that which possesses this original body?"
Regarding this teaching, Yunmen said: "The fan leaps up to the Thirty-three Heavens and pokes the nostrils of Śakra.
A carp from the Eastern Sea is struck with a single blow, and the rain pours down like an overturned basin. Fudaoshi said: "Empty-handed, I hold a hoe;
walking, I ride a water buffalo. People pass over the bridge; the bridge flows, but the water does not flow. If you can understand this—
If that were so, then all sentient and insentient beings would attain Buddhahood simultaneously; how then could one’s own parents not be delivered?

Yet, matters are different today. A Zen practitioner who wishes to repay the kindness of their parents need not go so far as to "divide the bones to return to the father and divide the flesh to return to the mother";
it suffices simply to take this very body born of one's parents and offer it to the Father.
The mother requested the Dharma; the old monk likewise used the mouth born of her parents to expound it for the great assembly. Now tell me:
is this the same as the ancients, or is it different? Alas! Were it not for the guidance of the fisherman, how could one have entered the Peach Blossom Spring?
Be careful.
At the request of the Venerable Mauxi on behalf of his deceased parents, [the Master] ascended the hall and said:

"The single character for 'filial piety' (xiao)—the Confucians call it the celestial principle and terrestrial righteousness, the supreme virtue and essential path. As for our Buddhist school, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* expounds the Bodhisattva precepts;

opening its mouth, it declares that 'filial piety is named the precept,' and also calls it 'the dharma of the ultimate path of filial compliance. Thus, both Confucianism and Buddhism regard it as such."
Filial piety is the foremost of all that is weighty. However, our Buddhist concept of filial piety differs from that of the Confucians.

The filial piety of the Confucians does not go beyond providing for the mouth and body, exhausting one’s sincerity and respect, establishing one’s character and spreading one’s fame, and performing burials and sacrifices according to ritual.
This is the extent of the Way of filial piety for them. Our Buddhist Way, however, is different from this; it concerns the *dharmakāya* (Dharma-body) possessed by a person’s son.
This is none other than the very person of one’s parents. If one can know this Dharma-body, thereafter one should apply the effort of veneration, keeping it in mind at all times.
When it comes to taking full responsibility and bearing the burden, if one suddenly forgets [all else], then one will merge with the Dharma-body without interval.
An ancient said, "Exerting effort, push the father toward the interior," and it is also said, "The whole body returns to the father."

Only upon reaching this point can one truly be called a filial and obedient child. Otherwise, even if one is able to establish oneself, bring fame to one's name, and perform burials and sacrifices according to ritual, these are merely matters of a dream;
they remain utterly at odds with the spiritual essence and life-force of one’s parents.
Furthermore, how can one truly practice filial piety? The great assembly must not fail to understand this. Take care.
At the request of the Daoist Master Zheng Daogong of the Three Mountains, he ascended the hall and said: "Today is the fifth day of the fourth month; beat the drums of Gushan!"
Startled, the stone man was in a hurry; he leaped out from before the courtyard and began to dance. The wooden man asked, "Why are you like this?
He replied, "It is simply because the Prince Siddhārtha has been born in the royal palace; how much joy, and how much sorrow!
The wooden man said, "Why not settle yourself in the state prior to the birth of your parents? [The Master] struck his staff and said, "Today, the Old Monk’s true command is being enacted."
"Go! Give each of these two thirty blows of the staff and drive them out through the three gates. Why? Look:
from the time the World-Honored One was first born until his entry into nirvana between the twin śāla trees—has he ever once emerged prior to the birth of his parents?"
All of this is later generations seeing flowers in the sky and vainly creating complications; within the realm of true purity, such things do not exist at all. Take care.
On the occasion of [the Master’s] birthday, Chen Tairen and others of Wenzhou requested him to ascend the hall. "The one-stump Chan before the withered tree cliff—do not fail to understand it."
Throughout the five ranks and the three mysteries, I have reached seventy-three years of age. Stubborn and unyielding, I have never undergone any change.
I care not for the laughter or abuse of those from all quarters; I lie peacefully and loftily amidst the white clouds. Let the sages and worthies revile me as they will.
"A single peg is about to cover the heavens and the earth. O worthy ones, this old dhūta is like something useless;
he would be better suited for filling pits and blocking caves. Why must you invite him to ascend the hall? Yet, as things have come to this, it cannot be left empty-handed.
I shall take this one peg and form a karmic connection with all of you. He raised his staff and said, "Does the assembly understand? He struck the ground with it.
One seat. Descending from the seat.
At the request of the practitioner Haizang to offer funeral services for his teacher, the Venerable Daochen ascends the hall. The Venerable Daochen personally attended Boshan;
his practice was sincere and his conduct authentic for nearly thirty years. Now, having come to Gushan due to illness, he fixed a date and time and passed away while sitting upright. This—
On this day, the fourth of the seventh month, as my followers have invited me, an old monk, here, I cannot help but raise an old case of "entanglement" to deliberate upon with you all.
Long ago, a monk asked Xuefeng: "When a deceased monk passes away, where does he go?"

Feng said, "It is like ice returning to water. Later, he related this to Xuansha. Xuansha said, "I do not say so. Feng asked, "How would you put it? Xuansha said, "It is like water returning to water. These two great elders serve as a mirror for ten thousand ages; those of later generations receive their legacy from them. How could I, An, dare to merely follow in their footsteps? I must instead offer another way. If one were asked about the passing away of a deceased monk: [The Master] said: "He has returned to his original source. A monk asked: "What is the meaning of 'returning to the source'? The Master said: "When the moon sets in the west, it does not rise in the east. The monk said: "If that is so, where does he go? The Master said: "He goes to the place where there is no going. The monk said: "And what is the place where there is no going? The Master said: "It is the place where the four elements have never been born and the five skandhas have never arisen. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be reborn? The Master said: "He is reborn according to the conditions of the Dharma-realm. The monk said: "What is the Dharma-realm? The Master said: "It is the realm where the three times are eternally still and the ten directions are perfectly bright. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he manifest transformation? The Master said: "He manifests transformation through the non-obstruction of the Dharma-nature. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he enter nirvana? The Master said: "He enters nirvana by means of the non-duality of birth and death. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he benefit sentient beings? The Master said: "He benefits sentient beings through the non-arising of self and other. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he leave behind relics? The Master said: "He leaves behind relics because the Dharma-body is indestructible. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be enshrined in a stupa? The Master said: "He is enshrined in a stupa because the true mind is eternal. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be worshipped? The Master said: "He is worshipped because the Way is beyond form. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be commemorated? The Master said: "He is commemorated because the Dharma-essence is unchanging. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be remembered? The Master said: "He is remembered because the Buddha-nature is ever-present. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be forgotten? The Master said: "He is forgotten because the ultimate reality is beyond thought. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be found? The Master said: "He is found within the silence of the mind-ground. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be lost? The Master said: "He is lost when the deluded mind grasps at appearances. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be restored? The Master said: "He is restored when the true eye is opened. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be extinguished? The Master said: "He is extinguished when the waves of thought subside. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be manifested? The Master said: "He is manifested when the light of wisdom shines forth. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be hidden? The Master said: "He is hidden when the clouds of ignorance gather. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be revealed? The Master said: "He is revealed when the sun of the Dharma rises. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be concealed? The Master said: "He is concealed when the gate of the senses is closed. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be disclosed? The Master said: "He is disclosed when the treasury of the eye of the true Dharma is opened. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be bound? The Master said: "He is bound by the fetters of attachment. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be liberated? The Master said: "He is liberated by the power of non-attachment. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be trapped? The Master said: "He is trapped by the net of views. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be freed? The Master said: "He is freed by cutting through the net of views. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be obstructed? The Master said: "He is obstructed by the barriers of dualistic thought. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be unobstructed? The Master said: "He is unobstructed when the mind is free from discrimination. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be hindered? The Master said: "He is hindered by the hindrances of the five skandhas. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be unhindered? The Master said: "He is unhindered when the five skandhas are seen as empty. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be limited? The Master said: "He is limited by the boundaries of space and time. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be limitless? The Master said: "He is limitless in the expanse of the Dharmadhātu. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be finite? The Master said: "He is finite when the mind clings to forms. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be infinite? The Master said: "He is infinite in the realm of the unborn. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be born? The Master said: "He is born through the power of great compassion. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he die? The Master said: "He dies when the cycle of birth and death is exhausted. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he live? The Master said: "He lives in the eternity of the Dharma-body. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be old? The Master said: "He is old when the body of flesh decays. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be young? The Master said: "He is young when the mind of wisdom is fresh. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be sick? The Master said: "He is sick when the afflictions arise. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be healthy? The Master said: "He is healthy when the Dharma-nature is clear. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be suffering? The Master said: "He suffers when the mind is deluded. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be blissful? The Master said: "He is blissful when the mind is enlightened. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be happy? The Master said: "He is happy when the mind is at peace. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be unhappy? The Master said: "He is unhappy when the mind is disturbed. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be joyful? The Master said: "He is joyful when the mind is free from sorrow. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be sad? The Master said: "He is sad when the mind is attached to loss. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be indifferent? The Master said: "He is indifferent when the mind is equanimous. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be active? The Master said: "He is active when the functions of the six sense organs are engaged. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be passive? The Master said: "He is passive when the mind is in a state of non-action. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be moving? The Master said: "He is moving when the wind of karma blows. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be still? The Master said: "He is still when the mind is unmoving. The monk said: "If that is so, how can he be changing? The Master said: "He is changing when
"Where are you going? he asked. He replied, "Returning to emptiness from emptiness. Everyone, tell me: how much difference is there between this old monk’s [state] and that of the ancients?
I cannot help but offer another verse on their behalf: When ice comes, it returns to water to await its melting;

If water were to return [to its source], traces would still remain. Empty space is fundamentally without joining or parting; In the end, there is nowhere to return, utterly beyond distinction or sameness.

At the request of the Head Monk Shousheng Jing, the Master ascended the hall. A monk asked, "When a person who has received the precepts kills living beings and takes life, yet recites mantras and performs repentance, and happens to encounter one who 'kills the Buddhas and patriarchs'—how does he repent?
The Master said, "Can you kill them yourself? The monk gave a shout and said, "They have been killed! The Master laughed and said, "Wrong. He then continued: "The Buddhas and Patriarchs..."
The wondrous Way is most easy and most near; it lies within the midst of ordinary daily life, with nothing difficult to know or difficult to practice.
Furthermore, why trouble yourself with so much effort to "kill the Buddhas and kill the patriarchs"? Just consider today’s drumming and bell-ringing:
each person puts on their robes, takes up their implements, moves with light feet and swift steps, and hastens up to the Dharma Hall to spread out their mats.
Three prostrations. Having set aside their implements, they listen to the Dharma. Each and every thing is true and spontaneous; each and every thing is luminous and wondrous.
All of it accords with the proper time and occasion. This very thing is precisely that which the World-Honored One spoke without speaking, and that which Kāśyapa heard without hearing.
It is also that which none of the Buddhas or Patriarchs have ever been able to express. Furthermore, what need is there to "kill the Buddha" or "kill the Patriarch"? Therefore, an ancient said:
"Excellent! Strike the board three times. Friends and acquaintances have all come to visit. Since you already well know the proper timing, I shall not speak further.
When the ancients revealed themselves in such a manner, what more was there to say? Nevertheless, one must also know that there is a point of avoidance.
What is this one phrase of avoidance? It permits knowing in this way, but it does not permit understanding in this way."

The two abbots, Bānxue and Shànsēng, requested [the Master] to preside over the assembly; subsequently, they invited him to Yǔzhòng and then to Jīnjiāng. Upon ascending the hall, a monk asked: "An ancient said:
'The moon’s reflection in a clear pool, the bell’s sound in a still night—unimpaired by what it strikes, undispersed by the waves it touches.
Yet this is still a matter of the shore of birth and death. Tell me, where does the fault lie? The Master said: "A fall."
The monk Shansi asked, "What is it like when one has transformed and attained a new body? The Master said, "A thunderclap shatters the silence of the empty mountains.
The monk asked, "Is there yet another phrase of supreme dignity? I pray that the Master will speak it himself. The Master said, "I am weary today, old monk. The monk bowed.

Question: "To pick up the golden needle and jade thread and pass through before the mechanism [of thought], to cut off the hare's horns and tortoise hair, and thereby reveal that which is above—this is still a matter of 'this side.
What is the matter of 'that side'? The Master remained silent for a long while. The questioner pressed on: "As for the ancient saying:
'When the finger points to space, heaven and earth turn; when the path is turned back, the stone horse emerges from the gauze cage'—what does this mean?"
The Master said: "Though one may have traversed every mountain and stream, there are no tracks left beneath one's feet. A monk asked: "All words and speech fall into the present moment.
What is the phrase that points beyond? The Master held up his whisk. The monk pressed further: "That is still a matter of the present moment. The Master then gave a shout.
The monk bowed. The Master then said: "In the past, Gaofeng said: 'Where meaning and phrasing do not reach, and where the essence and its explanation do not penetrate.'"
The blind turtle and the lame tortoise—both their intent and phrasing have arrived; both their school and their teaching are thorough.
The blind turtle and the lame tortoise, seeing Xifeng issue such a proclamation, thought they would find a separate livelihood apart from this, yet they too are blind turtles and lame tortoises.
Gaofeng’s three categories encompass all patch-robed monks; how can one emerge from these three categories? The old monk now—
Every day he employs a skillful means. Holding up his whisk, he makes a dot in the air and says:
"In this very little bit, there is the provisional and the real; there is illumination and function; there is the orthodox and the deviant; there is the guest and the host.
If you all can take this up upon your shoulders as a single burden, you will be like a divine colt from a thousand miles away, chasing the wind and pursuing the lightning."
He has gone! How could he be encompassed by the three categories? Do you all know? Descend from your seats.
It is not in vain that the Elder has entered the stupa. Entering the hall: The Buddha of the East, the Buddha of the West—exhausting the source to its depths, there is not a single thing.
The soil of the East, the soil of the West—though one wears out one’s straw sandals, there is no place to be found. Everyone says there is a going.
Birth. Birth is itself non-birth; why do you not realize this? To cling to "non-birth" is also extreme delusion. When a Zen practitioner reaches this point, they must look within themselves.
Layman Not-Xu of Quanzhou, who had long cultivated the Pure Land practice, has today seen his ashes fly and his smoke vanish;
he has found a place to hide his body. Everyone, tell me: was this rebirth? Was it not rebirth? Or was it both birth and non-birth?
"Is it neither arising nor non-arising? "Tsk! A turtle flies into the sky at midnight; the old king of the eastern village schemes in vain.
Be careful! This was for a single line of Chan practitioners to request [the Master] to ascend the hall on the birthday of their founding teacher. A monk asked: "This is clearly before one's eyes."
[The monk] said, "When hungry, one comes to eat; when tired, one comes to sleep. Aside from this, is there anything else? The Master said, "There has never been a time when there was nothing.

The monk pressed further, "What else is there? The Master said, "The eyebrows cover the eyes. The monk bowed. The Master then said, "People of the present age merely say, 'When hungry, one eats; when tired, one sleeps.
They take it for granted that by bringing a thousand things to rest and ten thousand things to an end, they have attained realization."
Little do they realize that there is a great matter within this. Today, this old monk cannot help but point it out for them:
"The stone ox constantly breathes forth spring mist; the wooden horse neighs loudly in the midnight wind; upon the gourd vine, one swallows the Northern Dipper."
"Laughing at empty space beneath the shoulder pole. Within these four lines, there is the real, there is the provisional, there is illumination, and there is function.
Do you all understand? If you do not yet understand, you must not simply claim that all matters are settled and at ease.
Today marks the sixtieth birthday of Master Zhiguang; his disciples, following their single lineage, have specially prepared this vegetarian feast for him.
"Please, Elder, ascend the seat. The Elder said, "Just now, because of the wind, I spoke in a rambling manner and did not manage to utter a single word of blessing for your longevity.
He then picked up his staff and said, "Now tell me, how old is this monk? He struck the ground once with the staff and descended from the seat.
At the request of his Dharma nephew, Chan Master Jingxin of Juelin, [the Master] ascended the hall and said:
"In the past, Bai Juyi asked Chan Master Niaoke, 'What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? Niaoke replied, 'Commit no evil; practice all that is good. Bai Juyi said..."
"A three-year-old child can also speak in such a way. Niaoke said, "Though a three-year-old child may be able to speak thus, an eighty-year-old man cannot act accordingly.
Niaoke was a eminent monk of the Tang Dynasty; how could he not have been capable of discussing the profound and expounding the subtle?
It blocks the doors and gates. Why is it so? It is because these two phrases—“Do no evil” and “Perform all good”—are easy to speak, yet difficult to know, and even more difficult to practice.
What is meant by "difficult to know"? Who is it that does not commit any evil?
As for the practice of "practicing all that is good," who is it that practices? What constitutes evil? What constitutes good? To know this is to say that these are the seeds of humans and devas;
they are, in fact, the wisdom-life of all Buddhas—is this not difficult? What makes their practice even more difficult?
If one speaks of the ultimate limit, only a Buddha alone can hope to be without shame; from those at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) downward, all possess a sense of shame.

Virtue. Thus it is said: "To practice it is even more difficult. Lately there are certain people who employ the staff and the shout, discoursing on the profound and the subtle, claiming they have transcended the three realms.
Yet when even a minor matter comes before them, they find they cannot bring themselves to utter a single shout.
When you wish to stand upright, you cannot remain so; delusive sentiments drag you away. When you wish to stop, you cannot do so;

illusory circumstances press upon you from all sides. There is no choice but to fall prostrate within the ranks of the three miserable realms, spending one’s days indulging in greed, anger, and ignorance.
Thus we know that these two phrases of Niaokuo are truly a mirror for a thousand years and a medicine for this modern age. Today...
Juelin Jingxin, my elder nephew, has come specifically to Mount Gu at Drum Mountain to provide a vegetarian feast and request that this old monk ascend the seat.
Although Juelin cannot open the hall to preach the Dharma, he is capable of practicing with sincerity and integrity to transform and guide the region.
That Juelin preaches the Dharma is no small matter; that Juelin’s exposition of Chan is profound is something the assembly must not fail to know. Take care.
When Qingliu Chen and his brother Hui invited [the Master] to ascend the hall, he said: "Students who study the Way should regard the practice of Zen as most precious.
In the work of practicing Zen, one must first recognize one's illness. If one does not recognize the illness, Zen becomes false Zen;
when Zen is false, the Way becomes a heterodox path. This is why people today compete for status, vie for self-importance, and pursue fame and profit."
"Zen is it. "What, then, is the illness? "Since I first opened this hall twenty years ago, whenever I have encountered people, I have spoken of mind and nature;

I have spoken of the Way and Zen; I have spoken of the provisional and the real; I have spoken of illumination and function—all of these are deep-seated roots of illness from beginningless kalpas that I have not yet been able to eradicate.
"What, then, is Zen? "On the thirteenth day of the sixth month last year, because of..."
While sunning my books, I slipped and fell. My left foot has been in pain, and I have lain bedridden for over a month; yet it has not healed.
People still come in groups of threes and fives, forcibly bringing this old monk to the Dharma Hall to preach the Dharma.
This is the old monk’s true Zen. If you can recognize the old monk’s true Zen, then you will recognize the old monk’s true self.
"Illness. If you can recognize the true illness of this old monk, you will then recognize the true Chan of all Buddhas and patriarchs.
However, there is yet another phrase: 'the simultaneous forgetting of both Chan and illness. Wait until the day the illness is cured, and I shall reveal it for you all."
At the request of Layman Xie Erbin of Ninghua, the Master ascended the hall. A monk asked, "Dongshan said, 'At that time, I almost misunderstood my former teacher's meaning.
I dare ask: what was it that he did not misunderstand? The Master replied, "The clear pool does not permit the azure dragon to coil.
The monk pressed further, "Caoshan said, 'Going forth, there is no change or alteration. But as for spring growth, summer flourishing, autumn harvest, and winter..."
[Zang] asked, "How do you speak so that there is no change? The Master said, "From antiquity to the present, when has it ever changed?

[The monk] further asked, "Yunju said, 'Everywhere one arrives at understanding, every thing is clear; yet such a person is merely called one who has accomplished their task, and is not ultimately noble.
What is the noble one? The Master held up his whisk. The monk bowed and returned to his place. The Master then said:
Beyond the Stone Gate, the sea breeze is clear; vast and boundless, the Dharma-realm is deep. Though one may soar ninety thousand feet on the whirlwind, people do not recognize it;
they instead seek the traces of wild geese along the edge of a small stream. To the east is wrong, to the west is wrong; the slightest movement gives rise to horns upon the head.
To the front is forbidden, to the rear is forbidden; it is as if one were binding oneself without a rope. It is neither ordinary nor holy.
To seize the void and attempt to flay its skin—this is it! "Ho! This is not it! "Ho! Right Army loved his geese and lost his cranes;
today this old monk makes such an announcement. Although it is for the sake of the assembly’s urgent need, it is like painting legs on a snake.
"Setting aside for a moment the matter of adding legs to a snake, where is the snake right now? A monk stepped forward and made a gesture of fear.

The Master said, "When the waves of the three-tiered cascade are high, the fish transforms into a dragon; yet the deluded person still scoops out the water from the night pond. He struck his staff and descended from the seat.
At the request of Layman Changgong of Qingliu, he ascended the hall and said: "An ancient worthy said, 'It is easy to transform the mountains, rivers, and the great earth back into oneself;
it is difficult to transform oneself back into the mountains, rivers, and the great earth.

When the ancients spoke thus, they were still clinging to their own private selves and had not yet dissolved the images before their eyes. They did not realize that the mountains, rivers, and the great earth..."

What is this? And what, moreover, are one’s own body and mind? Furthermore, to distinguish between what is difficult and what is easy within them is like comparing the density of flowers in the sky or debating the length of a rabbit’s horns—is this not a great error?
Everyone, simply cast open your true eye before your parents were yet born, as it is said in the teachings: "When one person awakens to the truth and returns to the source..."
Originally, the empty space of the ten directions has entirely dissolved away; how, then, could there still be mountains, rivers, the great earth, or one’s own body and mind?
Today, this old monk cannot help but clarify this according to the teachings and use provisional means to dispel delusions, merely engaging in this bit of idle talk.
But Du Man Chan of Gushan is not like this; he takes no account of mountains, rivers, or the great earth, nor does he take account of...
Regarding one’s own body and mind: it does not matter whether before the parents were born, nor does it matter whether after the parents have already given birth.
Holding up his staff, he said: "Simply realize it right here. What else is there? Do you understand? A fishing boat has been carried to the banks of the Xiao and Xiang rivers;
stifled by breath and weary, one asks the white gulls."

At the request of the lay devotee Gao Kaixi for the memorial service of his deceased mother, the Venerable Monk ascends the hall. Today is the seventh-day anniversary of the passing of Lady Lin, the mother of the lay devotee Gao Kaixi;
he has requested this old monk to ascend the hall. During her lifetime, Lady Lin was devoted to the cultivation of Pure Land practices.
At the time of her death, she passed away seated in meditation with full clarity and awareness, and she specifically instructed her son to come to Gushan to invite this old monk to ascend the hall.
The Hall. To clarify the principle of being born in the Pure Land and beholding the Buddha:

at this very moment, jade dew spreads across the river, the golden wind pierces the curtains, fragrant red cassias drift through the front courtyard, and golden cicadas raise their clamor in the evening trees. Everyone, tell me: what do you say?
"Is this the Western Land? Or is it not the Western Land? If you say it is the Western Land, you have mistaken the bridge of a donkey’s saddle for your father’s chin.
If you say it is not the Western Land, you are seeking Chang’an inside the Han-yuan Palace.
Only when the ancients spoke that single phrase, 'The body alone is revealed amidst the myriad phenomena,' was it most intimate. If you all can understand this," [he said].
You will immediately behold Amitābha Tathāgata, who lies across his body for the sake of sentient beings; the ground of golden sand and jewels will appear clearly before your eyes.
Lady Lin An is now within the pool of the seven treasures, sitting upon a precious lotus flower, having attained equal and perfect enlightenment.
If this is not yet so, the Western Land is one hundred and eight thousand [yojanas] from here. Take care!
At the request of the lay practitioner Liu Weiyi of Fucheng, the Master ascends the hall and says: "I, this old monk, am seventy-five years of age;
carrying my illness, I have come to beat the drum of Mount Gu. Stupidly and blindly pursuing things without ceasing, I have caused the cypress tree in front of the courtyard to laugh itself to tears.
I recall that when I was fifty-nine, I first opened the hall at Wenzhou; from then until now, seventeen years have already passed."
I have not preached the Dharma for a short time; I have presided over four monasteries, and my tongue has trailed upon the ground. I have not preached the Dharma for a small amount;
yet now that I am both aged and infirm, it would be fitting to withdraw into the deep mountains to await my natural end.
How could I once again ply my verbal drum before others? Now, because Layman Liu earnestly entreated me to ascend the hall, I have thus addressed the assembly.

The great assembly took their leave. Following this instance, there was no need for further invitations. This is because this Way transcends the characteristics of speech and transcends the characteristics of written words.
Words can clarify the Way, yet they can also obscure it; they can convey the Way, yet they can also cause its abandonment.
In the past, Vimalakīrti remained silent, and Mañjuśrī praised him as having truly entered the Dharma-gate of non-duality. Subhūti...
Dizang sat in meditative seclusion within a cliff cave. Śakra then came and scattered flowers before him. You all should understand this meaning well;
otherwise, even if I, this old monk, were to speak for another seventeen years, what benefit would there be? Do you understand? "To weep until the blood flows is of no use;
it is better to keep one's mouth shut and pass through the remainder of spring. Take care.
On the occasion of the Master’s eightieth birthday, the assembly of this mountain requested him once more to ascend the hall. Grasping the void, he staged a performance;
for over thirty years he has specially expounded the Way. For five years he kept his three-inch tongue deeply hidden, yet now, in his decline, he ascends the hall again as the wind carries him.
This ascent to the hall was specifically requested by the brothers of the family on the occasion of the old monk’s eightieth birthday.
This old monk responds to the occasion. Since we are all people of the same household, it is fitting to speak the language of the household.

From the very inception of the Zen school, the various masters have each established provisional and skillful teachings according to their own inclinations to accommodate those with specific capacities.
Only the Cao-Dong tradition is otherwise: its words and deeds must correspond, and its principle and phenomena must be perfectly integrated. Wisdom...
Practice must necessarily be esteemed as a unified whole. One may sit high upon ten-thousand-fathom peaks, yet one may also dwell deep beneath the nine abysses.
Those at the heights do not fall into the perilous and eccentric; those in the depths do not sink into the mundane and pedestrian.

This is the Great Way in which a thousand sages have traveled together; it has been practiced for ten thousand generations without decay, for it was not established as a mere temporary expedient. Its...
In the beginning, one must necessarily take the realization of existence as the gateway to entry.

Once existence is known, only then can the work of veneration be applied, the station of honor be established, one may soar upon the path of birds, and one may blend one’s traces among the common species.
Yet, as long as physical traces remain, this is not the ultimate realization; one must now reach the point of exhaustion, concealing the body within the coals.
One roams the land of "Nothingness," yet one must not remain stagnant outside the kalpas.
You must know that when the stone ox breathes forth the mist of the three springs, and the numinous magpie does not perch in the shadowless forest, only then can it be called the "effortless effort.
There is no gap between past and present; thus the essential task of the Cao-Dong school is complete. Today, this old monk has leaked his secret for the sake of you brothers.
"Number one! It is like a parent who, out of affection for their child, does not perceive their ugliness; it is like a poor man who treasures his few household jewels.

Brothers, do you understand? After a long silence, he said: 'When you encounter people three thousand miles away, do not misrepresent [this teaching]. He struck his staff down and descended from the seat."
At the request of the Venerable Xianxin, he ascended the hall and said: "An illusory sojourn among humans for eighty years; half my life’s traces have been at the edge of white clouds.
I did not study Bodhidharma’s futile wall-gazing, nor did I follow Confucius in breaking the bamboo slips. When people come to celebrate one's longevity, where is that 'longevity' to be found?
Momentary arising and ceasing—phenomena are not solid. As soon as one speaks of the 'immeasurable,' it becomes a measure again; attempting to delineate the void is like painting space."
Falling into self-defeat. In general, worldly affairs are all empty and false; celebrations and mourning follow one another in rapid rotation.
It is better to sever all idle knowledge and understanding, and walk hand-in-hand through the sky of primordial antiquity. The sky of primordial antiquity is the supreme Chan;
its wondrously luminous essence is pure—what more need be said? As soon as words are attached, it becomes defiled. Do not transmit the Mind-Seal haphazardly among the currents. [He raises his whisk.]
The Master said: "Now tell me: is this the primordial antiquity, or is it the present age? Is it finite, or is it infinite?
He let out a shout and descended from his seat.

The Abbot of Shuangfeng led the assembly to request that he ascend the hall. "In the past," the Master of Dongshan said on the day of the winter solstice while eating sweetmeats, "I pose this question:
There is a thing that reaches up to heaven and down to earth; it is as black as lacquer;
it is ever present within the midst of activity, yet it cannot be grasped within the midst of activity. Tell me, where does its fault lie? At that time, there was one...
The Senior Seat Tai replied, "The fault lies in the act of movement. Dongshan then ordered his attendant to remove the fruit table.
This one public case has been transmitted for nearly a millennium; while there have been many who offered critiques, none have truly grasped its meaning.

According to this old monk’s view, there is a thing that reaches up to support the heavens—yet beyond this thing, there are heavens; it reaches down to support the earth—yet beyond this thing, there is earth.
"Outside of this thing there is earth; it is constantly within the midst of movement and function.

If it cannot be gathered up within movement and function, can it then be gathered up apart from movement and function? This question is nothing more than Dongshan’s skillful provisional establishment, acting as a probe and a decoy.
If one seeks within this whether there is a fault or no fault, it is like seeking broth in a sesame cake—empty space.
Driving in the nails from within. Today, this old monk has demolished the military camp of a thousand years and opened up the heart-mind of ten thousand ages.
My transgressions fill the heavens; I still permit you to descend from your seats to repent. Having stood for a long time, take care.
At the request of the various mountain monasteries and the assembly of Dharma-protecting patrons, the Master ascended the hall.

"Today, the great virtuous ones from within and without Fucheng, together with the lay devotees led by Lin Kongshuo, have come specifically on the occasion of this old monk’s eightieth birthday to offer a vegetarian feast and request that I once again preach the Dharma of non-arising.
Now, where there is a dharma, there is arising; where there is no arising, there is no dharma. If one were to speak..."
There is no time of birth. How could phenomena ever have been phenomena? Today, this old monk shall briefly provide a single thread of lateral insight:
all ordinary beings merely give rise to the notion of "having birth," while all sages and worthies merely begin with "non-birth.

This state of birth and non-birth is truly the great distinction between the holy and the ordinary. If you wish to clarify the principle of this non-birth, the ancients said: [...]* *Note: The source text appears to be truncated.*

There is a precedent. It is said in the ancient treatises: "All phenomena do not arise from themselves, nor do they arise from another; they do not arise from both, nor without a cause. Therefore, it is said that they are unarisen.
Most masters of past and present have relied upon this interpretation. However, according to my own view as an old monk:
It is not so. Since there is fundamentally no self, how could it be that the self is unarisen? Since there is fundamentally no other, how could it be that the other is unarisen?
Since there is fundamentally no combination, how could it be that the combination is unarisen? Since there is fundamentally no causelessness, how could it be that causelessness is unarisen?
This is what is meant by "the essence is fundamentally unarisen. Do you all understand this meaning? If you can understand it, you may immediately transcend.
To transcend the three realms and forever sever the cycle of rebirth—there is no other dharma than this. Take heed!
At the request of the assembly at Kaiyuan Temple in Quanzhou, the Master ascends the hall and says:
"I recall that when I was fifty-nine years old, I first opened the hall at Kaiyuan Temple in Quanzhou. Since then, I have been twisting my own nostrils and wagging my lips."
I have spoken of the Yellow Path and the White Path until this day. My years have already reached eighty, and my clumsy words have been circulated in more than twenty varieties.
Yet, the various brothers from Kaiyuan have come again to request that this old monk preach the Dharma. They seem to think that this old monk has some Dharma not yet exhausted to speak;
is it only today that I shall finally speak? They seem to think that this old monk has some Dharma he is unwilling to speak.
"Only today do you finally speak thus? You fail to realize that not a single word or phrase from this old monk fails to empty out the granary and overturn the storehouse;
there is nothing else remaining. Furthermore, what dharma is there left to speak? Nevertheless, since we have arrived at this point, it would be a pity to let it pass in vain.
Thus, I shall entrust one sentence to the assembly. Long ago, Bodhidharma made a prediction, saying: 'The sentient beings of this land who clarify the Way...'"
Those who practice the Way are few. Later ancient worthies also said, "To speak ten feet is not as good as to practice one foot.
All of them meant that while speaking is certainly easy, practicing is extremely difficult.
However, this old monk says that even if one can both speak and practice, there is still something more to attend to. One must not think, "I alone am able to speak, whereas others cannot," nor...
One can act alone while another cannot; upon meeting someone who praises oneself, one smiles broadly with open mouth, yet upon meeting someone who slanders oneself, one’s face darkens with a frown.
In both cases, the marks of self and other have not been forgotten, and the views of right and wrong have not been extinguished.
Though they may speak of the profound and the subtle, claiming to transcend Buddhas and patriarchs, they do not realize that in truth they remain among the common folk of the villages.
This old monk reflects upon himself and finds much cause for shame. Therefore, I report this with utmost sincerity to you, my brothers:
do not seize the mouth of the flying dragon, nor fall into the disgrace of the lame turtle. This is the old monk’s final instruction.
All of you, exert yourselves! Take care of yourselves.
At the invitation of the assembly of fellow practitioners from Jianzhou, he ascended the hall and said: "The golden wind sweeps the earth, giving rise to sorrow and suffering;
the tides of worldly change flow on, impossible to stem. For twenty-four years I have been at a loss, doing nothing more than beating a cloth drum right before the dais.
How can a cloth drum awaken those who hear it? What benefit is there in my tongue trailing upon the ground? An eighty-year-old old man enters the theater—how pitiful!"
The sleeves dangle as they dance; now that all is settled, what more need be said? Yet I must offer one further word of exhortation.
As for this one word—how would you say it? Today is the fifteenth day of the seventh month.

This one word is that which all Buddhas have never spoken and all Patriarchs have never transmitted; the hundreds of thousands of Buddha-dharmas are all contained within it. If there were anything beyond this...

To seek the extraordinary is like calling Qi a man of Lu. Today, the many fellow practitioners from Jianzhou have come out of old local ties to celebrate the old monk’s birthday and requested that I ascend the hall; thus, I cannot help but let slip a bit of my true nature.
Nevertheless, if one clings to a narrow, one-sided view and lacks a perspective beyond its borders, there are many in the Western Heavens who would not approve.

At the request of Chan Master Zhuan’an of Shouchang, he ascended the hall and said: "Today, Chan Master Zhuan’an of Shouchang has dispatched the venerable Xinyue and others to celebrate the old monk’s birthday and has requested that I ascend the hall. Shouchang is the monastic center established by my late master;
it does not solicit outside contributions nor seek patronage from the powerful elite, but obtains its sustenance solely from beneath the plow and the hoe. He resided there.
Ten years passed, and Shouchang was completed, resplendent as the preeminent center for the Dharma in the region.

When the Ming dynasty fell and bandit armies rose up like swarms of bees, Shouchang was reduced to ashes. Later, Zhuan’an came forward with resolute determination to take sole responsibility for the project.
At that time, circumstances were fraught with contradictions and public sentiment was divided; yet Zhuan’an was able to employ [his resolve].
Using flexibility to employ strength; bearing both favor and resentment to accomplish the task. Thus far, for eight years, the buildings from beginning to end are now largely complete.
The achievement is indeed magnificent. However, the position of abbot is not an easy one. As an ancient worthy said:

"An abbot must possess the five qualities of benevolence, wisdom, trustworthiness, courage, and integrity before he can become a great vessel. During the Wanli era, I, this old monk, traveled extensively...
I have consulted various renowned masters; only the Great Master Yunqi and our late teacher Shouchang could truly be said to possess all five [qualities].
This old monk, having entered the world, has striven to practice three of them, yet still lacks two. Thus, having reached this day, I have merely become a village lion.
Now that Zhuan’an serves as the abbot, does he possess all five, or does he lack the two? For the sake of the nation...
Is it a lion of the wild? Or is it a village lion? Zhu’an, you are in the prime of your strength; you must not fail to exert yourself.
I, this old monk, hold high expectations for you, Zhu’an. Take care.
At the request of the Elder Zaojian of Baoshan, he ascended the hall. Baoshan is the site of the Great Master Wengu’s practice center;
since the Master’s departure, it has been desolate and devoid of people. This old monk lacked the strength to manage it all, so he entrusted it to the Elder Zaojian.
Zaojian was indeed able to carry on the work well: the buildings were renovated, Zen practitioners gathered there in great numbers, and the influence of the Way flourished once more. It is said:
Among the four prefectures of Yan, Jian, Shao, and Ting, Baoshan is renowned as the foremost monastic community (*saṃghārāma*), with none able to equal it.
Now, having come to Drums Mountain (*Gushan*) to celebrate the longevity of this old monk, I am requested to ascend the hall for a discourse. Please bear this in mind:
thirty years ago, while I was at Baoshan studying under Master Wen Gu, the Master asked me, "What is the fundamental Dharma? At that time, I remained silent.
After a long silence, the Master said, "I know full well that you are making your living inside a ghost cave.
The monk asked, "How about you, Master? The Master replied, "I do not refuse to tell you, but I fear you may not hear it well.

The monk said, "Master, you have well explained the fundamental Dharma," and he prostrated himself. Subsequently, another monk asked, "What is the Treasure of Goodness? The Master spread his two hands.

[The Master] held up his hand. The monk was at a loss. The Great Master said, "Are you not a Persian merchant who can discern jewels? After a short while, during tea, [the Master] said: "If you recognize the jewel, you will truly treasure it;
if you treasure it, you will recognize the fundamental Dharma. If you recognize the fundamental Dharma, there is no dharma that you will not recognize."
The Great Master said, "One must not speak in such a manner. I asked, "How would you, Great Master, put it?
The Great Master said, "If one recognizes the fundamental Dharma, then all phenomena are like an enemy born of oneself.

Now, because Bao Shan has come, I have specifically brought forth these two cases of karmic conditions to bestow them widely upon the great assembly, thereby repaying the debt of gratitude for the Dharma-milk of my late master. However, as for this old monk—
Today, the circumstances are once again different. Not only am I unable to expound upon the fundamental Dharma, but I am furthermore unable even to understand it.
It is difficult to boast of one's swordsmanship before others; I can only join with the woodcutter in singing mountain songs. Take care.
The two venerable masters Dingxi and Fenghua shared the same longevity. To celebrate their anniversary, the monastics and laypeople of Ning, Qing, and Yuan read the Tripitaka on their behalf.
On the day of completion, they invited [the Master] to ascend the hall. Since the time of its reconstruction, Drum Mountain had been uniquely lacking a complete set of the Tripitaka;
fortunately, the lay devotee Huang Zhisan of Quanzhou conceived the aspiration to have it printed, and subsequently obtained the support of various lay devotees both inside and outside Rongcheng.

Adorning the brocade with further splendor, it has been bound into volumes. Furthermore, the dharma-friend Shousheng of Shouning, together with his dharma-relatives, exhorted the assembly of both monastics and laypeople to propagate this canon, which has now reached completion. I request that the old monk ascend the hall to chant a verse of perfection.
The old monk recalls that in the past, there was a woman who sent money to Qizhou, requesting the turning of the canon.

The Sutra [Master] Zhaozhou descended from his meditation seat, circumambulated once, and said, "The turning of the Tripitaka is finished. When the old woman heard this, she said, "I originally requested the turning of the entire Tripitaka;
why have you only turned half of it? What kind of hands and eyes does this old woman possess to dare speak in such a manner?
When I, the old monk, look at her, this woman is stuck in the duality of existence and non-existence, and her mind remains caught in likes and dislikes; she has merely become a worldly person.
That worldly woman was buried alive by Zhaozhou over eight hundred years ago; she remains there to this day, still not having risen.
How will I, this old monk, turn the situation today? He brandishes his staff and strikes it once, saying: "Tell me, assembly, is this the *piṭaka* (half-treasury) or the complete *piṭaka*?
Is it perfect or imperfect? He gives a shout and descends from the seat.
At the request of Zen practitioner Jinghui, the Master ascended the hall and said: "This old monk is now eighty years of age;
all worldly affairs have been gathered up and set aside. Only the preaching of the Dharma remains unabandoned, exhausting the power of my three-inch tongue.
Today, the venerable Jinghui has requested that I ascend the hall to celebrate my birthday. I do not know by what means Jinghui considers this a 'birthday'—for me, the old monk."

I have investigated this myself and found no such thing as "life-span" (āyus). To take years, months, days, and hours as one's life-span is merely the shifting of the great transformation, a cycle that is inexhaustible; it has absolutely nothing to do with this old monk.

If one takes spirit and vital energy as one's life-span, then they fade with the passing of years and months, tending toward exhaustion day by day—what "life-span" could there be to speak of? Since both of these...

One cannot speak of "life span. By what, then, could life span be defined? If one were to say that a person possesses an indestructible diamond-like nature that can be called life span, one would not realize that this nature is fully present in all beings, from the Buddhas above down to the most minute insects below.
How could this belong to me alone? Furthermore, this nature is like space; it has neither arising nor ceasing, neither length nor shortness.

Because of the destruction of conventional reality, it receives the name "indestructible"—even these four characters, "Vajra-Indestructible," are merely using the language of worldly truth to adorn empty space, which is entirely baseless. Zen practitioners, how can you possibly be deceived by this?
How deluded you are by empty names and false titles! Zen practitioners, what is the ultimate way? When the void is shattered, perform a somersault;
let the world at large debate its merits and flaws as it pleases.
At the request of his younger brother Zhang Ke-yi and his son Sheng-mu, who submitted a written memorial, [the Master] ascended the hall.

The golden world is fragrant with osmanthus; the wind blows crimson leaves, filling the courtyard. Holding the golden needle in hand, one must sew with care; do not follow illusory shadows and give rise to madness.
Once the great task is done, the hoe is set aside; only upon reaching this point does one know how to enter one’s hometown. To enter one’s hometown.
One must turn one’s steps; the snow-covered house bewilders the traveler, leading to self-deception. The golden rooster does not remain upon the phoenix terrace;
the silver crane soars onto the path of the cloud-tops. Traveling alone to and fro along that path of clouds, one finally departs from the old gateways of one’s native village.
Today, there is not a single record remaining. Together with my younger brother Ke-yi and his son Sheng-mu, [I recall] our forty years in our ancestral home...

Formerly, you came specifically to offer congratulations on this old monk’s birthday and requested that I ascend the hall. This old monk shall not decline your request, even at the risk of being overly talkative.

However, you must further understand that throughout the ten directions there is not a single inch of soil; in what place, then, can one speak of "foreign land" or "hometown"? The entirety of the ten directions is one's hometown;
in what place, then, can one speak of "entering the hometown" or "leaving the hometown"? Do you understand? If you have not yet...
I understand. Listen further to this one verse from this old monk: The Way is vast and boundless; where does it end? Empty space falls over, yet is raised up again.
A tongue without bone—whom does it proclaim for? It is not out of local sentiment that I speak thus. Be careful.
He appointed Fawei as the Head Seat (Chanshou). Ascending the hall, he said: "I have once crossed the Shauchang Bridge;
how could I follow worldly customs and sprout branches in vain? To preserve the lineage of the thousand sages with a single strand of hair—how many can truly know this mind?
In my declining years, now eighty, the Great Matter is finally entrusted to you. For thirty years, the matter of salt and sauce—the ancients had it."
"Speech shall not deceive one another. Only with the strength of a thousand *qun* to steer the rudder against the wind can the foundation of eternal peace be firmly established.
He then bestowed the robe and whisk, descended from the seat.
