Minor Sermon.
Small Assembly for New Arrivals at Kaiyuan Temple. This mountain monk is but a single blade of wild grass; for half my life I have carried a wooden board upon my shoulders.
For thirty years, I have never uttered so much as a single word of Chan before others. Today, meeting you on this narrow path, I cannot help but display my awkwardness and ugliness.
As for the Buddha-dharma, it is fundamentally without dharma. Today, seeing that the monks and the Buddha-dharma are too numerous, I do not see the ancients.
It is said: "In every dharma, how has there ever been a dharma? And it is further said: "For forty-nine years, I have never uttered a single word.
My brothers, do not because this mountain monk speaks of the absence of dharmas, drive a stake into empty space.
If you were to drive a stake into empty space, then the absence of dharmas would become a presence of dharmas. Now, my brothers, for the time being...

You must maintain your fundamental integrity; do not give rise to groundless deliberations. Nowadays, there are certain people who merely dabble in empty pretenses, prying and dissecting the public cases of the ancients.

They practice composing verses, practicing "picking up" (the case), and practicing "answering. They parade these words before others, sometimes shouting, sometimes striking with a staff, raising their fists, or pointing their fingers.
They move from east to west and from west to east, waving their sleeves and walking away, or even pushing over the meditation seat.
He gets down from his seat, turns around, performs a woman’s bow, does a somersault, and goes out the door.
Although these are samādhis already employed by the ancients, today they are variously imitated until they have become mere clichés. What, then, is the Buddha-dharma?
For this reason, I, this mountain monk, pay them no mind at all; it is simply because I lack such idle energy. Great assembly!

"Do you want the Buddha-dharma? Tonight, I, this mountain monk, shall speak my heart out to you brothers about all the Buddhas of the three periods, the patriarchs of successive generations, and all dharmas—is that not well? After a long silence, he said: 'The lantern has leaped out before us.'"
Now it is said: "The Master has worked hard today opening the hall; take care. Small Assembly Instruction:
When Deshan entered the gate, he would strike; when Linji entered the gate, he would shout; Bimozhi only knew how to hold up his fork.
Juzhi was merely pointing his finger. Today, this mountain monk has cast down the drum of Gushan and come to sweep away the clouds of Ziyun.
I have taken those previous entanglements and bound them together into a single bundle; I am throwing them off at Luoyang Bridge. Now tell me, what excellence does this mountain monk possess?
After a long silence, he said: "Enough, enough! It is best to return to the hall when there is nothing to do."
The Small Sermon on New Year’s Eve: An ancient said, “On the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, how will you settle the account?
These words are most critical and perilous. It is because for many years you have merely been at the street corners and alleyways, passing your days by scavenging for leftover spittle;
this is entirely not the reality. On the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, how will you make use of it? To truly grasp this matter, you must—
Only when it breaks through toward one's own local scenery does there begin to be actual utilization.

There are some people who merely pore over public cases (gong'an), dissecting them to determine what is "upward" and what is "downward," or what constitutes a "full presentation" versus a "half presentation."

Having understood each point thoroughly, they must then study the "picking up" (of the whisk) and the composing of verses, study the formal lectures (*shàngtáng*) and the informal discourses (*xiǎocān*).
As the disciples present their compositions for review, the masters mark them with corrections. They pass their days in this manner, which is called "practicing the school" (*cāozōng*).

Furthermore, there are those who focus their attention solely on the cleverness of language and the agility of the *jīfēng* (critical pivot); all day long they practice questioning and answering, like the lips of a donkey or the tongue of a horse.
They wander about recklessly everywhere. Furthermore, there are those who recognize only a state that is nameless, formless, neither existent nor non-existent, and take this to be the ultimate limit;
they wander about recklessly everywhere, cutting and sweeping away at will. Little do they realize that this is merely a vague and indistinct understanding.
Within the True Suchness (Tathatā) school of the Zen Gate, there remains a path not transmitted by the thousand sages; one must not be so superficial and negligent.
Go! Furthermore, there are those who recognize only that which is able to see and able to hear as being fully present everywhere, and they cling to this as the truth.
This is precisely to mistake the servant for the master—a perverted view. Generally speaking, these several types of people—
He is like a destitute beggar leading a tailless monkey. From village to village and from inn to inn, he performs everywhere.
Performing and performing, he thinks to himself that his business is flourishing. But when the thirtieth day of the twelfth month arrives, the drum is broken and the monkey has run away;
he stamps his feet and beats his breast—by then, what can he do to remedy it? Long ago, Beichan...
"Virtuous one! To slaughter a white ox in the open air and distribute it among the people for the year’s provisions is no different from using public property for private gain;
even so, you deserve thirty blows of the staff. Tonight at Kaiyuan, as the monastic community is newly established, the communal assets are meager."
Lifting his chopsticks toward the air, he drew a circle and said: "I, this mountain monk, simply take this single steamed bun and share it with you all for the year-end celebration.
It is entirely up to you to partake of it; if you can partake, you will surely be satisfied and pass the remaining year in joy.
If, however, this is not yet so, then this steamed bun will turn into a thorny acorn burr—you will want to swallow it, but you cannot."
"You cannot spit it out! This is the fault of all people; it is not the fault of this mountain monk.
Small Talk: 'Heedfulness harms one's virtue; silence truly has merit. Let the vast ocean change as it may, I shall never communicate with you.
Although this is so, today I shall lower my clouds and briefly open a single thread. Holding up his prayer beads, he said:
One must not say this is a pearl; one must not say it is not a pearl. One must not give a shout straight at the person.
One must not snatch the pearl and throw it on the ground. One must not say, "Put it down. One must not shake out one's sleeves and return to the hall. Please each provide a response;
if your response corresponds to the truth, this mountain monk shall bestow his whisk upon you in the very hall—not only from me, but from all three [ancestral patriarchs].
"The Buddhas of the world cannot do anything for you; try to say something. The assembly remained silent. The Master said, "Each of you should return to the hall and contemplate this well.
Small Assembly Lecture on the First Day of the New Year: "Tonight is the First Day of the New Year. There is no need for this mountain monk to speak; every household has its flower lanterns."
The bright moon hangs suspended in the sky. At the place where the sun, moon, and lamp-light Buddha have thoroughly revealed it for you, amidst the vast and tumultuous clamor, joyfully take it up;
let it warm you through and through. Do not engage in discrimination. Even so, there is yet another phrase for taking a secret step forward.
How would you say it? "Cold as the sun, warm as iron. At the Amitābha Hall, during the informal lecture (*xiao-chan*):
This matter is not far away; it is like a person in space, like a fish in water. Whether entering or exiting, advancing or retreating, there is nothing that is not space.
Swimming with the current or against it, there is nothing that is not water. It is only because views arise and emotions are produced that [it seems otherwise].
"Ten thousand miles of white clouds. Long ago, Touzi went to visit Cuimwei and asked, "What is the meaning of the West?
Cuimwei simply looked at him with his eyes. As Touzi was about to offer a word in reply, Cuimwei said, "Do you want another ladle of foul water?
At that, Touzi attained great enlightenment. Look at this—could there be even a single speck of conceptual attachment here? Later...
When Xuefeng came to visit Touzi while he was staying in a hermitage, Touzi stepped down from his meditation seat and stood there.

Xuefeng stood there lost in thought, whereupon Touzi shoved him out of the hermitage. Xuefeng could do nothing but weep. Look at this: can he tolerate even a single speck of conceptual attachment here?
Therefore, today I am merely acting like a doctor treating a dead horse, teaching people to practice by departing from mind, intellect, and consciousness.
To penetrate through and manifest this innate radiance is not a matter of dull stagnation, brothers.
This is because it is not a matter of intellectual understanding. A monk asked, "What is this innate radiance? The Master let out a laugh. The monk said:
"How was it before you had even smiled? The Master said, "You have not yet understood. Small Assembly:
A thousand thoughts and ten thousand anxieties are no match for rest; a thousand words and ten thousand phrases are no match for cessation.
There is no need to bring forth the broken sand-pot; why must one pick up the dry dung-stick? Nevertheless, one must not always speak in such a manner.
As for the Amṛta Precept Platform, it has already leaped right into your eyes. Furthermore, how could you fail to notice when the Master walked behind you with his shoulders bared?
What more need be said? You must apply some spirit and discernment before you can succeed.
A Small Sermon: All you monastics of the Chan school need only eliminate four maladies. First, do not seek spittle along the way.
Second, do not stake yourself to a post and rock the oars. Third, do not seek to stay alive by cutting off your own head.
Fourth, do not place a head upon a head. If you can distance yourselves from these four maladies, then naturally all under heaven will be at peace.
Small Assembly. In the past, Mazu said to Damei, "This very mind is Buddha. This is like a nine-transformation elixir;
whoever ingests it is instantly transformed from an ordinary body into the skeletal remains of an immortal. Later, he further said, "This is neither mind nor Buddha. This is like a vajra-jewel sword;
with a single stroke across the head, one must directly sever the life-root of man. Later...
Nanquan also said: "This is not mind, not Buddha, not a thing. This seems like an overly earnest maternal heart;

he thoroughly assists the student by saying there is no need for deliberation. Amidst a thousand abstruse and ten thousand wondrous things, one must simply pass through these three turning phrases, and then one can return home and sit securely. However, under the gate of Drum Mountain, it is otherwise. Not...

Partaking in the banquet of the King and Lord, who cares to ask about the village of apricot blossoms? Do you know? A black tiger prowling at night with snow upon its head—this makes the old holy monk in the hall burst into laughter.
A Small Sermon: Curved like an arrow, straight like a hook. The small is the ocean; the large is a bubble. An earthworm leaps across the Eastern Sea;
a lame turtle flies upon the crest of the clouds. *Chan*.
Small Sermon for the Twenty-Seventh Day Memorial of Mrs. Cai’s Mother, Requested by Mrs. Cai. Frost settles white upon the treetops; the moon casts chill beneath the courtyard.
To understand the meaning of this day, one must recognize the very first barrier. Today marks the twenty-seventh day of the passing of Mrs. Liu, the mother of Mrs. Cai.
This autumn, I passed through Shazhen and stayed at the Changfang Monastery; there, the lady repeatedly [sought] the Dharma...
He came to inquire about my affairs of a hundred years hence. I explained to him in great detail the excellent conditions of the Western Pure Land.
After several months had passed, he fell ill; after being ill for several days, he passed away. According to worldly reckoning, this was fifty-five years before the birth of the Lady (Rujin).
Fifty-five years later, upon the death of Lady Ru, I said: "Since the time of King Vairocana, Lady Ru has been born at every moment;
there is not a single moment she has not been born. She has died at every moment; there is not a single moment she has not died.
Worldly people perceive her coarseness but do not perceive her essence; they perceive her manifestation but do not perceive her subtlety. Thus, they claim that 'today is [the beginning]...'"
In two weeks, one might count the tracks of fish at the bottom of the water and discern the footprints of birds in the sky; how truly lamentable this is!
Yet, once one knows the state of constant birth and constant death, one must further know the state beyond birth and death.
Since it is the state of constant birth and constant death, what is the state beyond birth and death? Is it simply that which is neither born nor dies?
Therefore, can one constantly be born and constantly die? Or is it that precisely because one constantly is born and constantly dies, one can be neither born nor die?
This is the ultimate limit of the teaching schools. In my Dharma-gate, however, we are still separated by a river.
For now, let me ask you: the Lady has passed away; it has already been two weeks. Where, at this very moment, does she dwell and establish her life?
Before the second seven-day period [after birth], while the four elements were still untroubled, where was one’s body and life established?
Fifty-five years ago, before entering the womb, where was one’s body and life established? [The Master] lets out a shout and says:
"If you can understand this one shout within this context, today the meaning of the first barrier shall be overturned at once."
It is understood. Sitting and watching the spirit-casket, one enters samādhi; it makes one laugh that tears fall from both sides of the lamp-stand.

Entering the hall for a small *śamaya* (private instruction): elsewhere, there are those who can explain the Dharma, those who can deliberate upon *kōans*, and those who can employ the devices of staff and shout.
But here, at this old monk’s place, it is simply a single flavor of closing the door and sleeping. Tell me, is there still anyone who...?
There is no such thing as "humanity" here. An ancient said: "To look into a mirror or to frown and groan is to act for the sake of those of middling or inferior capacity;

to close the door and sleep is to engage with the highest faculty. This old monk entering the hall tonight is already "dragging through mud and water," let alone speaking of long and short for the sake of you all.
Nevertheless, since we have come to this, I cannot avoid following the custom and prattling on for a while. Generally speaking, as for study...

As for practitioners of Chan, the foremost rule is that you must not bore through a wall to steal light. There are certain students who focus exclusively on ancient kōans, engaging in analytical dissection and explanation, believing this constitutes realization;
yet they remain unaware that although their explanations may be as flawless as a watertight seal, they have missed the point entirely.

It remains as it was with the ancients; it has nothing whatsoever to do with you. Second, do not try to scoop up water by disturbing the waves, thinking to yourself, "Today I am deluded, so I shall seek enlightenment for another day," and claiming that all the myriad phenomena before one's eyes, as well as the inner mind and consciousness, are entirely illusory and false, while seeking to perceive the true mind right here.
Little do you realize that this very speaking of the false is itself the truth.
Truly, you are already a dull-witted fellow; how much more so when you discard the provisional teachings to claim they are the ultimate truth! Thirdly, one must not drive a stake into empty space.

There are students who cling to the skillful means of the ancients and refuse to let go, regarding them as something extraordinary—such as Linji’s Three Mysteries, Dongshan’s Five Ranks, or Yunmen’s Three Statements.
Some foolishly maintain a state of solitary peril, while others fall one-sidedly into a flat and mundane reality.

Some are greedy for the higher [stages], while others delight in the unconventional; this is precisely the failure to forget attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*), and their distance from the Way is more than ten thousand *li*.
If you can free yourselves from these three maladies, only then will you be true "grass of the house.
Nevertheless, there is yet more to it. In the past, Mazu said: "Since the time of chaos thirty years ago, I have never lacked salt and sauce. First, harmonize.
Shang further remarked: "Since I first fell into disorder thirty years ago, I have never had salt or sauce.
Those two great elders demarcated their territories and established boundaries; they are said to have a place where they can benefit others. But I am not like that.
Since I first fell into disorder thirty years ago, I have simply done my best to drink tea when I meet tea and eat rice when I meet rice; I have paid no mind to them."
There is salt and sauce; there is no salt and sauce. If you can understand this, I, the old monk, have a worn-out alms-bag bowl case which I shall hand over to you with both hands.
If this is not yet so, then for now, you must continue to investigate it thoroughly within the midst of your practice. Examine it again and again.
Small Assembly: To cut directly to the root is to be free from conceptual understanding. To manifest it right before one’s eyes costs not the slightest effort.
If you even raise a single eyebrow, you have already missed it; as soon as you fall into deliberation, you are separated by a thousand mountains.
Therefore, when Muzhou saw a monk approach, he would close his door; when Luzu saw a monk approach, he would turn his back to the wall. This may be called truly acting for others' benefit.
"How could this be like our kind of people, who are all muddled and confused, speaking of the Three Paths and the Four Directions, asking about the wondrous and answering with the profound?
Nevertheless, you must first recognize the point where the ancients were at cross-purposes before you can succeed. Take, for example, Lu Zu facing the wall;
Luoshan said, 'If I had seen him then, I would have given him five strokes of the fire-brush. Why was it that he let him go but did not know how to bring him back? Xuefeng said, "I..."
If one had seen it at that time, one would have well given five strokes with the fire-brush. But tell me: was the intention of [Master] Luoshan the same or different?
These two great elders both borrowed the lamp from the western house to illuminate the wall of the eastern house; each possessed his own hand-eye.
Today, as this old monk examines them, I would well give all three great elders five strokes with the fire-brush. Do you understand? "Lying across the body."
When the universe is thus, who is the one who emerges?
A small session of instruction. Master Mazu said: "Whatever forms you perceive are all perceptions of the mind. The mind is not the mind itself; it exists because of form.
You need only speak according to the occasion, and whether it be phenomena or principle, there will be no obstruction whatsoever. This is the fruit of the Bodhi path."
It is likewise so. That which arises within the mind is what is called form (*rūpa*). Because one knows that form is empty, arising is itself non-arising.
If one understands this meaning, then one may, according to the occasion, put on clothes and eat food, nourishing the noble embryo (*āryagarbha*) and passing through time with effortless spontaneity.
"What else remains? The Master said, "Mazu was like an old woman who has vomited her heart and blood for all of you to hear.
Yet recently, those who have gained some proficiency in literary texts all claim they understand.
When a monk asked Mazu, 'What is the meaning of the Westward Journey? Mazu immediately struck him, saying, 'If I do not strike you, I am not your teacher.'"
Just as he was laughing at me, everyone present said, "This is difficult to understand.
Since it cannot be understood here, why can it be understood at the front? If it cannot be understood here, then those who claim to have understood it at the front are all in error.
Some might say, "I understand! I understand! But the very place where he strikes him is precisely the direct pointing.
What is the underlying intent? Some say that striking [the student] at that point is merely to sever their conceptualizing mind.
Alas, alas! Mazu’s "True Dharma Eye" simply continues to circulate in this manner. If someone were to ask me today, "What is it to know that form is empty, such that arising is non-arising?
I would simply strike them. How will you all deliberate upon this? Do not take it lightly.
Study and understanding bury the mind of the Patriarchs.
In a small-scale discourse (*xiao can*), he raised the case of Layman An’s first visit to Baizhang, where he asked: "A student wishes to recognize the Buddha; what is it?"
Baizhang said, "It is very much like riding a cow while searching for the cow. An said, "After one has recognized it, what then?
Baizhang said, "It is like a person riding a cow home. An said, "I do not yet understand: how does one maintain this from beginning to end?
Baizhang said, "It is like a cowherd holding a staff and watching over it, not letting it trample the crops. From this point on, An understood the meaning. The Master said, "This is one public case."

Consider this: one can see that the ancients were complete and perfect in their realization. Generally speaking, the ancients were profound, steady, meticulous, and subtle—far beyond comparison with people of today.

Baizhang was among the disciples of Mazu; having personally encountered Mazu’s single shout and attained great capacity (*dajī*), how could he have been unable to employ a shout or a blow when answering Master An’s question?
Yet he instead said, "It is like riding a cow while searching for the cow," and when asked about consciousness...
"How is it after attaining [this state]? He replied, "It is like a person riding an ox home. Once one has reached home, everything is secure and settled; what more remains to be done?
Baizhang then asked again, "How does one maintain this from beginning to end?
If a person of today were to answer this question, he would immediately shout, "I thought you were a man of substance! It turns out you have such a view as this!"—Baizhang.
But it was not so. It is further said: "It is like a cowherd who holds his staff and watches over them, ensuring they do not trample upon the crops.
From this, An understood the essential meaning and was thus able to raise a white ox that roams freely in the open air. That he did not fall away from his teacher’s instructions was just like this.
If people look at this today, they might call him a truly incompetent fellow. For now, let us set aside the talk of "providing assurance" that everyone speaks of these days.
Is there anyone here who can recognize the ox? Bring it out and show it to the old monk. The assembly remained silent.
The Master said, "Do not say that the ancients were incompetent."
Small Assembly Sermon: A monk of the fundamental portion is naturally vast and empty; no discrimination arises. This is utterly distinct from all other studies.
One does not inquire about the state prior to birth, nor does one concern oneself with pure awakening. As for *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*, what are they but broken wooden ladles?

To point to a mere hair-tip as Mount Tai, and to regard the vast ocean as a single spoonful—this is to be topsy-turvy and without cause. Even the thousand sages, upon hearing this, would [be struck dumb].
His eyebrows are knitted; why is this so? It is simply because the golden rope has been snapped asunder; it cannot be found here in this land or in the West.
Small Assembly at Chengtian Temple. This present-day Chengtian is the ancient Zhaqing. The First Patriarch was Master Lingmo.
There is a koan that remains unresolved for seven hundred years. Chao-ch’ing once said: “Within the myriad phenomena, the body alone is revealed.
How do you all understand this? Is it by setting aside the myriad phenomena, or is it without setting them aside?”

If you say he negates the myriad phenomena, he also says that [the Buddha-nature] exists within those myriad phenomena. If you say he does not negate the myriad phenomena, he also says that it is "uniquely revealed.
Since he permits neither the claim that he negates nor the claim that he does not negate, how exactly do you explain this?
Do not think it is sufficient merely to let out a shout, give a slap, or wave the sleeves and walk away as if the matter were settled; there must be something more.
This is a place where one truly meets reality. If you are a *siddha* guest, you will know the tail as soon as you raise your head.
If this is not yet the case, then simply learn from Master Ling to sit until seven *pūtana* cushions are worn through. Nowadays, many people say that there is no need to apply effort.
Simply let go. Little do you realize that as soon as you give rise to the thought of letting go, that very thought makes it impossible to let go.
Or some may say that one must simply accept things directly; little do they realize that as soon as you give rise to the thought of accepting, [you have already missed it].

This single thought-moment already separates one by a thousand mountains. There are those who specialize in "donkey lips and horse tongues," answering west when asked about east, claiming they do not accept being arranged by others and do not accept being bound by others, taking this to be their final realization. Little do they know.
The very moment you give rise to this thought, you have already made arrangements for yourself; you have already bound yourself.

This is because as soon as a single thought arises, there is a subject that possesses an object; how could this be anything other than delusion? Heh! A crane may have nine peaks, yet its wings find it difficult to soar.
"A horse that lacks the thousand-li stride cannot chase the wind in vain.
Take care. At Xinghua’s Bodhi Hermitage, a small assembly instruction: "If one discusses this matter, it is fully manifest everywhere.
Just now, the sea winds were like thunder and the great earth shook; I have already finished preaching the Dharma for you all. If you can understand from this point, [you will see it clearly]."
What is the use of such idle chatter? If this is not yet so, you must know that the nature inherently possessed by all people is no different from that of the Buddhas.
For what reason do the Buddhas become the Unsurpassed Honored Ones, while we remain merely ordinary beings of the mundane stage?
It is because we possess deluded consciousness and deluded emotions. What is meant by deluded consciousness? It is that which gives rise to various... upon all objects.
This refers to the views of existence, non-existence, right, and wrong. What is meant by "deluded feelings"?

It is the arising of various sentiments of love, hatred, grasping, and rejection toward all objects. Because there is deluded consciousness, deluded feelings arise; because there are deluded feelings, one creates deluded karma.
By creating the karma of a deva, one is born as a deva; by creating the karma of a human, one is born as a human; by creating the karma of a ghost, one is born as a ghost.
As for ghosts, up to those who create karma for the hells, they are born in the hells; there is no one who is born without being caused by karma.
Birth is caused by karma, and karma is created by emotion. Emotion arises from consciousness. If all people can, regarding all objects...

If one does not give rise to views of existence or non-existence, right or wrong, then one will be able to remain free from feelings of attachment, aversion, grasping, or rejection toward all objects of experience.
Such a person cannot be categorized within the ranks of either the holy or the ordinary; how, then, could there even be talk of birth and death?
If there were a man who, upon hearing such words, came forth and overturned the Dharma seat, one would have no reason to resent him.
It seems you have not yet attained stability; do not indulge in empty pretenses. For now, I shall instruct you in the "medical treatment of a dead horse.
At all times, day and night, arouse a courageous and resolute mind to contemplate this critical phrase (huatou), keeping it ever-present before you.
Like a cat catching a mouse, like a dragon guarding its pearl, there is not a single moment of letting go.

As days pass and months deepen, when emotions are exhausted and principle is reached, one suddenly strikes it—take it for granted that this will penetrate heaven and earth. An ancient worthy said: "When worldly toil is utterly cast off, the matter is extraordinary;
hold fast to the rope's end and make a scene. Were it not for a single instance of freezing to the bone, how could one obtain the plum blossoms falling?"

Nasiang. Small Assembly at Dadao Cliff. This morning, I, the mountain monk, left Guifeng and crossed the Jinji Bridge; traveling gradually through the fields and countryside, I only reached Mituo Cliff at noon.
After the midday meal, I took the path to Chaoyun. The stone walls are high and the sky is vast; I climbed by grasping the creeping vines.
A hundred turns; cold springs pour down from heaven, splashing against people’s clothes. After winding for several *li*, one finally reaches the Great Way Cliff.
Upon arriving after the evening recitation, I met with everyone. "If you come in such a manner, is there any Buddha-dharma here or not?
If you say there is not, where are your eyes? If you say there is, where exactly does the Buddha-dharma reside?"
"Eh! The entire grove of peach and plum trees is filled with spring colors. I ask the Lord of the East: how many know this? The Small Sermon for the Mid-Autumn Festival:
Every year in the eighth month there is Mid-Autumn; on this night of Mid-Autumn, it is even more cause for sorrow.
Upon the ridge, the wooden rooster races toward the moon; by the stream, the stone dog barks without ceasing. Startled, Old Wang the Second from the eastern village lights [the lamp].
Seeking traces beneath the lamp-stand, one catches a toad that has grown two wings; it turns and flies away, its form like a gull.
Friends, do not strive in vain. Guigu burned the tortoise shell and lost five divinations; Jingping cast the stalks and lost his pair of counters.
Small Session (Xiaocan). The staff falls like raindrops; the shout roars like thunder. Three thousand blows in the morning, eight hundred in the evening.
When the ancients acted for others in this way, was it not exhilarating?
However, I, this mountain monk, here refuses to merely follow in their footsteps or accept their various poisons. If a guest comes, I simply say to them: "Five, three, nine, seven. Kill!
"The human blade and the life-giving sword—each shall receive them for themselves.

Hearing that the Great Master was entering his stupa, he gave a small-scale sermon (*xiao can*). Now, on this occasion of the Great Master’s entry into the stupa, the monastics and laypeople from the four quarters have gathered.
Mist enshrouds and clouds gather; is there anyone who knows where the Great Master dwells?

Is it not said that he sits in meditation within his nostrils, or leaps and bounds upon his eyebrows? Is it not said that the clear breeze passes beneath the corridors, and the autumn moon turns before the eaves?
Is it not said that he is vaguely south of Xiang and faintly north of Tan? Is it not said that the crimson clouds do not...?
Leaving the azure void—does the white sun merely circle Mount Sumeru? Is it not the case that "heaven and earth cannot contain it, and the sun and moon can hardly encompass its light"?
To speak in such a manner is indeed plausible, yet it is not yet the ultimate point. [The Master] suddenly raises his fist and says:
"So, it has all along been right here on this old monk’s fist. Wishing to meet everyone face-to-face, he strikes the desk once with a resounding *sheng*.
He said: "A single sound is preached, yet each according to their kind understands it differently. He then clenched his fist and said:
"Suddenly, he transforms into a golden dragon emerging from the sea, soaring straight into the azure heavens. You all must not mistake the bridge of a donkey's saddle for your father’s chin."
Small Assembly for the Day of the Retreat’s Commencement: Brothers, today we once again encounter the commencement of the retreat.

You must know that while there is a beginning and an end to the period, there is no beginning or end to the cultivation of merit. You must simply go forth as a single bar of iron across ten thousand miles; there is only this fundamental koan, your mortal enemy, remaining.
One does not even inquire whether there is awakening or non-awakening, let alone anything else.

As for the words and phrases of the ancients, you must by no means recklessly engage in forced interpretation or attempt to give rise to a conceptual understanding. This Dharma is not something you can achieve through forced interpretation;
it is not something you can attain through conceptual understanding. Furthermore, there is no need to cite all those many strange and eccentric anecdotes from the ancients; simply...
As Deshan said: "You simply have no mind toward things, and no things within the mind; naturally, it is empty yet spiritual, still yet wondrous.
These four lines explain everything with full sincerity, leaving nothing hidden; they are not difficult to understand.
However, as soon as you say "no-mind," you have already become "with-mind"; as soon as you say "no-things," you have already become "with-things. This is because...

Is it empty? Is it tranquil? Since it is neither empty nor tranquil, then even if you possess mouths all over your body and your eloquence flows like a rushing river, it is nothing more than the realm of birth and death;
it is merely the circulation of turbid wisdom. Therefore, the patriarchs of past generations taught you only this:
to take the courage and the spirit of your entire being and apply them entirely to a single phrase of the teaching. Look and look again.
Go! Suddenly, with a single explosive crack, the body, mind, and the world sink away all at once. A thousand differences and ten thousand distinctions are, in an instant, harmonized.
The seven mysteries and eight subtleties are, in an instant, extinguished. At that time, what more can be said?
Whether there is nothing or something, whether there is no-mind or mind—these four characters, "empty," "luminous," "quiescent," and "subtle"—simply have nowhere to be placed. Who cares?
The old man Deshan called him over and broke his donkey’s back. If this is not yet so, do not speak in such confusion.
During these ninety days, you must investigate and contemplate with great care.
A Small Assembly for the One Hundredth-Day Memorial of Lady Wu, Consort of Attendant Cáo. The small boat has drifted to the bank of fragrant grass;
the warbling yellow oriole pierces the green willow branches. Last night, once more, the rain that hastens the blossoms fell, adding to the springtime splendor throughout Mù Creek.
There is no need for Bodhidharma to come and face the wall; why must the Buddhas reveal their full mechanism? If you can [turn the light] behind the head...
Open your eyes! The causal conditions for Buddha-nature lie in this very moment. Has the Lady realized this within?
If you have realized it, you shall immediately go to the Immaculate World in the South to attain Buddhahood. If you have not yet realized it, this old monk cannot help but deceive you.
Sixty years ago, when you were born into the Wu family, it was solely due to your father’s vital essence...
Birth occurs through the provisional conjunction of the mother’s blood; after sixty years, one eventually dies at the Cao residence.
This death likewise occurs solely because the father’s semen and the mother’s blood have dispersed. If the prior birth were real, how could there subsequently be death?
If the prior birth were not truly born, then the subsequent death is also not truly dead. Therefore, birth and death are merely identical to an illusion.

Transformation and [the original] are utterly unrelated; you must observe this for yourself. As for that which is now vividly and clearly manifest, capable of hearing this old monk preach the Dharma—does it have birth and death or not?
Furthermore, you must know that there is the Way of Dao-wu. Formerly, Dao-wu and Jianyuan went together to a house to offer condolences.
Jianyuan tapped the coffin and asked, "Is he alive or is he dead? Dao-wu said: [He is neither alive nor dead.]
Wu said, "When alive, it is not the Way; when dead, it is not the Way. Yuan asked, "Why is it not the Way? Wu said, "Not the Way, not the Way.
Yuan said, "If you will not speak of it to me, I shall strike the Master! Wu said, "Strike as you please; as for the Way, I do not speak of it.
"Everyone, try and look at the Way! Where does my intention lie? He struck his whisk and said:
Suddenly shattering the dream of Jambudvīpa, he laughs himself into oblivion—Namo Avalokiteśvara!

A Small Sermon Given in the Presence of the Spirit for Layman Cao Jiayu: Alas, layman, why have you departed so suddenly? Your serenity, harmony, reverence, and frugality would have brought you long life;

your filial piety, fraternal kindness, benevolence, and generosity would have brought you long life. You turned your heart toward the True Vehicle and served the Buddha with diligence. How could you leave us so soon? *Note: "閻浮" (Yánfóu) is a phonetic transcription of Jambudvīpa. "南無" (Námwú) is a transliteration of *namas*, meaning "homage. "觀世音" (Guānshìyīn) is the Chinese name for Avalokiteśvara.*
"Qian was also worthy of longevity. How could he receive such a premature retribution and depart so suddenly?
Judging by worldly standards, one would surely feel unending grief and resentment, crying out in indignation.

However, if one can comprehend the fundamental cause of receiving one's mandate and grasp the deep-seated currents of karmic retribution, then whether life is extended or shortened, or whether fortune is abundant or meager, these are not bestowed from Heaven."

All this is fundamentally self-invited; what cause for resentment can there be? One must understand that retribution results from karma, karma arises from consciousness, and consciousness originates from illusion.
It is just as a reflection exists within a mirror, manifesting only in dependence upon objects, or as waves arise upon water, moving because of the wind.

The deluded person clings to the idea that the mirror definitely contains the reflection or that the water definitely contains the waves, failing to realize that their essence is actually non-existent.
All arises from illusion. If one realizes the source of this illusion, then that which is non-illusory and indestructible can be known.
Once this non-illusory and indestructible reality is known, illusion need not be eliminated but will be purified of its own accord. Is there, then, birth and death?
Or is there no birth and death? Alas! Layman, if you can clarify this, then the karmic causes of kalpas past can be understood through it, reaching back to the beginningless.
Habitual tendencies can be extinguished from this point on; so what more need be said of long lives or short reckonings?
Now, having received your late father’s solemn command, I shall expound the Dharma for you before his spirit. You must bear this in mind.
Small Precept Assembly at Tianning Monastery. The Patriarch said: "The ultimate Way is not difficult; it only dislikes discrimination.
Simply do not harbor hatred or attachment, and all will be transparently clear. If you can directly grasp this right now, what further matter remains?

If you have not yet been able to do so, I, this mountain monk, shall unravel some complications for you. This is why sentient beings wallow in birth and death, remaining in darkness for kalpas on end.
There is no time of escape because you possess a mind of selective discrimination. Where there is discrimination, there is beauty and ugliness;
where there is beauty and ugliness, there is love and hatred; where there is love and hatred, there is acceptance and rejection;
where there is acceptance and rejection, there is good and evil. Consequently, the good ascend and the evil descend; their retribution lies among gods and humans. If you wish—
To abandon both good and evil and yet take up the retribution of neither-good-nor-evil is the path of the Two Vehicles;

for this reason, they ultimately cannot transcend birth and death, precisely because they possess the consciousness of discrimination and the emotions of love and hatred. Therefore, the Buddhas and the Patriarchs...
To teach people how to emerge directly from saṃsāra, there is no other method than simply requiring you to extinguish this deluded consciousness and deluded emotion.
To extinguish this consciousness and emotion, one must apply the "deadly effort" of a single step. The efforts of the ancients were not fixed;
they all stemmed solely from their singular, urgent, and desperate concern for life and death, acting as if—like a person making... [the text ends].
A great misfortune was at hand; while it was yet half-revealed, he pondered over and over again, seeking a way out.
It was as if, upon a narrow path, one encountered a mortal enemy—one who must be fought to the death.

As days and months passed, worldly attachments were forgotten and consciousness severed; suddenly the flower of the mind blossomed, and as he encountered various conditions and circumstances, [realization] arose.
The spirit of death has been utterly exhausted. Those who come later possess inferior faculties; their thieving minds grow heavier by the day.
Although they speak of investigating the *huatou* and practicing *kung-fu*, their mind of superficial longing increases daily, and their resolve for the Way grows ever more thin.

Furthermore, wild wisdoms compete to arise, leading them to follow worldly currents and fall into ruin. What the Master transmitted and what the disciples received is now merely a matter of words and tongues.
To take gāthās as the correct study for samādhi is truly not to understand.

Your answers may resemble those of Zhaozhou, and your gāthās may surpass those of Xuedou, yet they all merely lead back to the den of birth and death. Thus, the ancients said: "Brother, your phrasing..."
"Even this old monk has not yet passed it; he has merely not yet escaped birth and death. Or again, it is said:
"Let you be able to ascend the hall, able to deliver a small discourse, able to pick up a koan, and able to compose a verse—none of these matters are yet resolved."
Why is this? Do not take idle intellectual understanding and bury the mind of the Patriarch.
Wanghui’s Small Lecture: On White Cloud Slope atop Mount Wanghui, Outside the gate, falling petals are like crimson rain.
Green pines and lush bamboos vie with one another for beauty; Purple swallows and yellow orioles converse together. The void is filled to the brim with the spring breeze.
What need is there to say more? Yunmen universally severed Xuefeng’s turtle-nosed snake; he rode astride Xuansha’s white-browed tiger.
Linji was merely a lowly servant; where could there be a true lion in Xihe? Let him have a hundred wonders and a thousand subtleties—when looked at to the very end, it is simply this.
Why is this so? A sweet melon is sweet all the way through to its stem; a bitter gourd is bitter even to its roots.
The Roots of Suffering: A Small Public Sermon at Zhuangping Hermitage. In the midst of the noisy world, one should withdraw early; in secluded valleys, one should apply the mind with particular care.

King Hui did not tire of the depths, and now I have once again arrived at Zhuangping. Is this for the sake of indulging in solitary pleasure? The age has declined and the Way is difficult to practice; thus, in a quiet place, I fold my hands in stillness.
To act for others, yet not for oneself—just as it is in the midst of deep mountains and secluded valleys, what is the phrase that acts for others?
Gathering acorns and chestnuts with the mist, irrigating the potherbs with the moon. Take care.
A Small Sermon at Zhizhe Monastery. Wuzhou is a place where ancient sages left their traces; Master Zhizhe was one of them.
Now that this old monk has arrived in Wuzhou, he has first had the opportunity to pay his respects. Recalling the Great Master of old, I remember how he once sat cross-legged inside a washbowl.
Was it that he expanded the bowl to accommodate his body, or did he contract his body to fit within the bowl? If one considers this a supernatural feat...
To deliberate is to mistake the bridge of a donkey’s saddle. If one does not deliberate through supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), how else can one deliberate?
An ancient said: "When meeting, do not bring it forth; as soon as the intention arises, one knows it exists.
Today, I, this old monk, have met with you all and have brought it forth. What is the matter of "knowing it exists"? You should look well toward black and white.
Before the differentiation, look! At the Small Assembly at Puming Monastery:
The green grass and clear spring are the mountains of old; The cowherd has departed and never returned.
I have long been accustomed to herding the clay ox; In a casual moment, I have laughed through several layers of barriers. In days of yore, there was Nanquan, who was called...
The Good Herdsman once said: "Since my youth, I have tended a single water buffalo. If I intend to graze it on the west bank of the stream, I cannot avoid infringing upon the King’s grass and water;
if I intend to graze it on the east bank, I likewise cannot avoid infringing upon the King’s grass and water.

It is better to accept things as they are, little by little, for then nothing at all can be perceived. Upon reflection, this seems like drawing a line in the ground to create a pen—one that allows no movement.
He has attained it, yet he is not yet a master. Furthermore, there was Lan’an, who was called a skilled herder. He once said:
"I have raised a water buffalo until it became a white ox in the open air; standing solitary and remote before my eyes, even if I try to chase it, I cannot catch it."
At first glance, it seems as though one’s breath is exhausted and strength spent; if one cannot drive [the ox] away, one is not yet a master of the art.
Only Master Puming has grasped the beginning and traced the end, dividing [the practice] into ten sections so that the meaning of "herding the ox" is left nothing wanting.
However, I, this old monk, am not like that; I have merely herded a single hornless clay ox, and I care not whether it is to the east or west of the stream.
Whether south of the mountain or north of the mountain, sometimes he plows and turns over the great earth, and sometimes he strikes through empty space.
Do you all recognize him yet? After a long silence, he said: "HŪṂ."
A late evening *xiaochan* (small session) on the Winter Solstice. A monk asked, "What is the true person of no station? The Master remained silent for a long while and then said, "Do you understand?
The monk stepped forward and said, "If so, then there is neither entering nor exiting. The Master said, "Even 'non-existence' cannot be apprehended.

The monk asked, "The ancients also said, 'Entering and exiting through the face. Why is that? The Master said, "Pointing to the reflection is merely a means to indicate the reality. The monk asked, "How is it then?"
The Master further said: "What kind of dried piece of excrement is this? The monk replied:

"If it were not for your later words, how could there be Linji? The monk bowed, and the Master said: "The *Great Changes* (*Da Yi*) says: 'At the solstice, the ancient kings closed the gates; merchants and travelers did not travel.
This is a warning against people's reckless movement. Regarding the great matter of one's own fundamental nature, it must not be disturbed. To disturb it in the slightest degree is to go astray."

To speak of "original substance" as the means to become a Buddha or a Patriarch is like placing a head upon one's own head. To speak of "clarifying the mind and seeing the nature" is like putting grit in one's eyes.

To speak of "great capacity and great function" is to lose the essence while pursuing the marvelous. To speak of "returning to the root and going back to the source" is like abandoning one's home to wander abroad.
"Everyone, do not see my speaking in this way and immediately take it to mean a state of 'nothingness' or 'no-mind.
If you take it to mean a state of nothingness or no-mind, that too is merely sitting inside a ghost cave behind the mountain.

Even if you do not act in such a way, you are still like a cicada that has shed its shell but cannot avoid clinging to a cold branch. I, the old monk, have already placed the entire platter before you and handed it over to all of you."
Furthermore, if you continue to fix your gaze, there is no need for us to meet.
A brief instruction: From where does life come? Do not rashly conjecture that it is a fragment of cloud in the void.
To where does death go? Where do the empty flowers filling one's eyes fall? Cease speaking of "yesterday" and "today"; do not calculate between birth-and-death and permanence. The ancients...
Bitter words were once bestowed as instruction: existence and non-existence are just like a vine leaning against a tree. When the tree falls, the vine withers; yet people continue to seek in vain.
With a single laugh, he clearly points it out once more. He points it out again: in the end, where does this one phrase return? *Du!* (A shout)
A small informal sermon for the deceased layman Ye Zixuan. Layman Ye Zixuan of Fudang, possessing a brilliant mind and a refined nature at a young age, has suddenly passed away;
his clan and neighbors all lamented his loss. Yet this old monk says that the layman has, in truth, never died;
it is simply that his numinous true nature remains alert and unclouded here now, listening to this old monk’s discourse.

As for the Dharma, does it have existence or non-existence? Since this [Dharma] is devoid of both existence and non-existence, then all prior births and deaths are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows;
they possess no reality. Indeed, this illusory delusion originally arises from the interaction between mind and objects.
The mind is originally without mind; it exists because of objects. Objects are originally without objects; they manifest because of the mind.
When mind and objects interact in delusion, illusory karma is created. Once illusory karma exists, it draws one into the cycle of birth and death.

Now, if you can simply recognize that this birth and death is illusory, then the nirvana of all Buddhas truly does not go beyond this. He then raised his whisk and said: "Zi Xuan, lay brother, wake up!"
Be alert! If you can realize this, there is no need to speak of delusion, nor need there be any talk of non-delusion.
There is no need to speak of extinction, nor need there be any talk of non-extinction. There is no need to speak of knowing, nor need there be any talk of not knowing.
All the Buddhas of the three periods of time and all the wondrous Dharmas are entirely contained within this; one must penetrate to the very source. This old monk [says]: Ge.
There is no shortage of wisteria. Layman, take care. A small discourse.
[The Master] raised the case where Master Pang asked Mazu: "Who is it that does not consort with the myriad dharmas?"
The Patriarch said, "Wait until you can suck up all the water of the West River in a single gulp; then I will tell you. Thereupon, the Master attained enlightenment.
Later, Cudapanthaka Qing commented, "If one speaks in such a manner, where would the fish, dragons, shrimp, and crabs be placed?
Today, let everyone at Gushan take the place of Mazu and offer a turning word in his stead. One monk said, "As soon as he spoke, I would have given him a shout. One...
A monk said, "The Hermitage Hall deserves a blow from the old monk’s staff. Another monk said, "Wait until you can suck up all the waters of the West River in a single gulp, and then I will tell you.
Another monk said, "What do you call 'fish, dragons, shrimp, and crabs'? Another monk said, "If that is so, then they are born of water.
The Master said, "Each of you is able to speak on behalf of Mazu; this may truly be called..."
There is no difference in the soil within the same pit; it is simply a matter of supporting the strong rather than the weak.
According to my view, Mazu’s words were indeed forthright and easy to understand, yet they were merely appropriate to the occasion and reached only eighty percent of their potential.

Later, Guangyan Ze said to Mazu: "The green-storied pavilion in the city, the high peak pagoda beyond the clouds. Guangyan should have called them: [the green-storied pavilion in the city, the high peak pagoda beyond the clouds].
"Come, help Mazu wash his feet. [The Master asked: "Do any of you have a saying that achieves tenfold perfection? Please each of you speak it.
One monk stood before the Master with his hands crossed behind his back and said, "I pray the Master examine me. The Master said, "A good seven strokes of the rattan for you.
Another monk said, "Within the myriad phenomena, the body alone is revealed. The Master said, "Precisely! How precise! But this is merely..."
He borrowed a lamp from a neighbor. One monk said, "Today my affairs are many; I cannot explain it for you. The Master said, "How intimate! How intimate!
But I fear that if this becomes a habit, it will turn into a prevailing custom. Another monk said, "The heavens cannot cover it; the earth cannot support it."
The Master said, "Wrong, yet not wrong; it is simply that there is no strategy of a great man. One monk merely stood before the Master with his body erect.
The Master said, "Not wrong, yet not right; right, yet not yet right. Another monk said, "Tsk! What do you mean by 'giving' and 'not giving'?
The Master said, "It is like this, it is like this; it is simply a pity. Another monk said, "I would just seize him and question him."
"Who are you? The Master struck him across the face with his palm and asked, "What would you have done then?
One monk said, "The Stone General at the mouth of Lingyuan Cave. The Master said, "You truly could act as a disciple of Guangyan. Another monk said, "I do not know.
The Master said, "If you do not know, what is it that you do not know? Another monk said, "This humble one, today..."
He could not utter a word from his mouth. The Master said, "I grant you thirty blows for now. The Master continued, "Today, everyone here possesses a modicum of knowledge and understanding;
each of your responses has its own source. However, they vary in depth, and most find it difficult to escape the ancient tracks.
As for perfectly realized expressions, wait for another day. He then descended from his seat.
For the sake of the lay practitioner Chen Zhongmou, Grand Historian, and his wife Lady Li, before their spirit tablets:

All sentient beings are submerged in the ocean of birth and death, surfacing and sinking again and again with no time of escape. This state began solely from a single moment of delusion, leading them to this point.
Thus they give rise to greed, anger, and ignorance, manifesting through body, speech, and mind, cycling through the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence.
Because [the cycle of] rebirth does not cease, the World-Honored One, at the assembly of the Vajra, finally offered this earnest instruction in verse:
"All conditioned phenomena are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, and a shadow; they are like dew and like lightning—one should contemplate them thus.
To be able to contemplate in this way is the primary gateway to attaining Buddhahood and the essential path for transcending birth and death. Today, you, O Zhi-jia...

He was like iron bones soaring through the air, untainted like celestial flowers.

For thirty years he dwelt within a single thatched hut, every thought dedicated exclusively to the Pure Land, and every step firmly grounded in the reality of the Way. In the tenth month of winter, he lay ill, until the eleventh month.

On the seventeenth day, he sat in meditation while reciting the Buddha’s name and passed away. The mark of his rebirth in the Western Paradise was clearly evident, as his cranial aperture felt as if it were being scorched.

He may truly be called a preeminent figure among monks and a paragon beyond the mundane world. There are those who, like the winds of Māra, do not apply themselves to practice but merely study the words and phrases of the ancients; they wag their tongues and ply their lips, habitually practicing empty pretenses and feigning outward appearances.

Consequently, he slanders the koans as having degrees of depth or shallowness. What he fails to realize is that the fault lies solely with his own conditions.
He is unable to plant both feet firmly to the bottom within a single koan; therefore, he says, "If I can penetrate here, I can penetrate elsewhere."
It cannot be attained. Little do they realize that if it cannot be attained elsewhere, then that which is attained here is likewise not it.

In truth, Zhaozhou had nothing: "Where does it all return? "The cypress tree in the courtyard," "Three pounds of flax," "A dried-up shit-stick," "The bamboo rake," "Baima’s staff," "The master in sleep"—all these are universally penetrating; how could there be any distinction? If, regarding this—

they simply take the temporary cessation of worldly afflictions or the attainment of some slight light and shadow as their awakening to the Way.

Moreover, when they encounter the words and phrases of the ancients that they cannot penetrate, they proceed to reflect upon and annotate them one by one, failing to realize that this is utterly different from...
To know this—that which is explained through conceptualization—is precisely the tethering rope of the firebrand.

"A single basketful—how deeply regrettable! If you people wish to illuminate this matter, you must let go of everything with your whole being and engage in sincere, earnest investigation until you reach the ground of the ancients.

If these were taken as the precepts, they would entirely belong to the realm of arising and ceasing and ultimately remain within the outflows (*āsrava*); how then could they be called ultimate *śīla* (morality)?

What constitutes compliance? If the reality of filial piety is not yet clear, how can one recognize the precepts? Furthermore, it is said that "restraining the mind is called the precepts.
Do you mean that people take the restraint of the mind itself to be the precepts? Now, what kind of thing is this "mind" that can be restrained?

And what kind of thing is this "restraint" that can restrain the mind? If water cannot wash water and gold cannot be bartered for gold, then where does the meaning of "restraining the mind" ultimately reside?

Furthermore, the Sixth Patriarch said: "The fundamental nature has no 'non'—this is the self-nature precept. Does this mean that people take the absence of "non" within the fundamental nature to be the precept?
These words of the Sixth Patriarch can indeed be called a pressing concern for others, pointing directly and straightforwardly;

yet they still cannot avoid being somewhat entangled in secondary branches. This is because "non" does not arise from "is"; rather, it arises from "non. Since the fundamental nature has no "non," then...
If there is nothing that can be called "is," since its original nature is devoid of such, how could there be anything that can be called "is not"? Yet you speak of it as "not non-is.

The essence is fundamentally quiescent and extinction; it is pervasive and pure, leaving no room for anything else within.

Because the Buddhas of the past relied upon this meaning, they taught that the ten realms—saints and ordinary beings alike—and all phenomena of the environment and its inhabitants, as well as all causes and effects, are entirely empty and still. The Great Way reaches ultimate oneness.
There is no change or alteration; whether in a state of defilement or purity, its essential nature and characteristics remain unmoving.

Because the Buddhas of the past relied upon this principle, they taught that birth-and-death is itself nirvana, afflictions are themselves bodhi, and greed, anger, and delusion are themselves precepts, concentration, and wisdom.

All three of these points refer to the fact that the fundamental substance of reality is originally quiescent. Since beginningless time, sentient beings have given rise to ignorance through delusion, and thus [these phenomena] appear to exist.
The characteristics of the mind. Once the characteristics of the mind take form, delusive objects appear. Once delusive objects appear, one begins to distinguish between the beautiful and the ugly.

Once there is acceptance and rejection, there is then good and evil. Once there is good and evil, there is then cause and effect. From this arise the four modes of birth and the nine realms of existence, as well as the three realms and the six paths.

A Tea Talk at Dàdào Yán: Linji’s shout is gathered back into the rear rack; Deshan’s staff is cast forward into the front pit.

The Twenty-Ninth Case of Niangu (Picking up the Ancient):
It is recorded that after Bodhidharma passed away, he was buried on Mount Xiong’er. Later, the Wei envoy Song Yun returned from the Western Regions.

They encountered him at the Pamir Mountains (Congling), where they saw him holding a single sandal and walking away gracefully and alone. Yun asked, "Where are you going, Master? The Patriarch replied, "I am going to the Western Heaven.
When Yun returned and reported this to the Wei ruler, the tomb was opened for inspection; it contained only an empty coffin, with nothing remaining but the single sandal.
The entire court was struck with wonder and admiration. By imperial decree, the relic sandal was taken to Shaolin Temple to be enshrined and venerated.
The Master said: "This is the final stroke of Bodhidharma. How do you all understand it? When Song Yun encountered him at the Pamir Mountains, he should have struck him dead with a single blow;
that would have shown that there were people in this land of China. Since you have already missed it," [he continued].
He returned to report to the Wei ruler. Upon opening the inspection, the coffin was empty; there remained only a single pair of worn-out sandals.
To leave such a legacy for future generations is truly a state of utter confusion.

When he said, "I have only managed to get the hall-keeper to come," the Master should have replied, "Do not blame the śrāmaṇera;

Case: A monk visited Píngtián. Tián struck him immediately. The monk stepped forward and seized the staff. Tián said, "I was too hasty just now, old monk.

[This] cannot be grasped.
[Case] raised. When Baizhang went for his second audience with Mazu, Mazu saw him coming and held up his whisk.

The Master said: "Regarding this koan, many who have raised and discussed it throughout ancient and modern times claim that Baizhang’s footing was not yet fully secure, and that only upon receiving Mazu’s single shout could he finally attain resolution.

This is the marrow of the matter. Therefore, Xuedou took it up and said: "Refined gold from a great furnace should not change its color.
However, since Baizhang was already refined gold, when Mazu’s shout entered his ears, it could not even strike the strings of his lute.

Deaf! Why do you say there should be no change of facial expression? This one public case (gong'an) is the very beginning of Linji’s teaching.
If this point is not clarified, how can one even ask about anything else? You must know that the path of turning the body [back] is not transmitted by the thousand sages;

Case: When the monks had finished constructing a memorial stupa for Shushan, Baishan asked him, "How much money will you give to the craftsmen?

The monk replied, "No one has been able to say it. Daling said, "When you return, tell Shushan:

"The master craftsman has contributed his own hand. If you were to give even a single coin to this craftsman, it would cause him such distress that his eyebrows and beard would fall out.
The monk returned and reported exactly what had been said. The Mountain Master assumed a dignified demeanor, faced the Great Ridge, and prostrated himself, exclaiming:
"I thought there was no one here; yet upon the Great Ridge dwells an ancient Buddha, whose radiance shoots forth and reaches this place. Even so, it is still..."
Regarding "The Lotus in the Twelfth Month," Daling heard these words and said, "In my saying this, it is already like a tortoise’s hair growing three feet long.
The Master said, "When Shushan delivers such words, there are no few pitfalls; fortunately, Daling has shed his light. One.
"A single flash shatters it all. Nevertheless, to build a stupa for Shushan is still a very long way off. Everyone, tell me:
how will you provide for the craftsmen?"
Case: Dongshan, at the conclusion of the summer retreat, said: "At the end of summer and the beginning of autumn, you brothers will inevitably be traveling here and there.
You must go to a place ten thousand miles away where not a single blade of grass grows. But as for that place ten thousand miles away where not a single blade of grass grows—how does one go there?
After a long silence, he said: "This matter must be like flowers blooming on a withered tree; only then will it accord with it."
The Master said: "Dongshan speaking in such a manner is truly like a magnificent phoenix not perching upon common wood, or a golden dragon not remaining in a cold pool.

While it is not that there is no 'shifting function to occupy the position' or 'shifting position to employ the function,' when one looks closely, it is merely like a monkey climbing a tree—discarding one thing and grasping another; this does not yet make one a master. Now tell me, how is it?"
"This is the place of one's own fundamental nature. After a long silence, he said: "The fishing boat has arrived at the banks of the Xiao and Xiang rivers;
stifled by breath and weary, I ask the white gulls.
He further cited: "Zhao Puna pointed to the half-moon one night and asked Upādhyāya Pǔ, 'Where is that other half?'"
[The Master] went away. Fupuo said, "Do not engage in false conceptualization. Zhaoruo said, "You have lost half of it. The assembly collectively praised them.
The Master said, "Everyone, tell me: where was the fault of Elder Fupuo? Although Zhaoruo and Bunan gained the advantage, they were merely 'degrading the noble to the base.
Though the assembly praised them, they were nothing but 'drunkards eating dregs. But...
Puhua merely lacked the final words. Had he waited for the other to say, "I have lost half," he should have immediately replied, "Indeed, your deluded thoughts are not few.
One can be certain that this would have left Master Zhao with a profound sense of shame.
Case: When Shishuang passed away, the assembly requested the head seat of the hall to succeed him as abbot. Jiufeng said, "Wait until I have questioned him;
if he understands the meaning of our late master, then serve him just as you served our late master. He asked: "Our late master said: 'Rest! Cease!
A single thought for ten thousand years! Like cold ashes or withered wood! Like an incense burner in an ancient temple! Like a single length of white silk!'"
"Go! Tell me, what matter do you understand? Zhaozuo said, "I understand the matter of the 'single color' (the monochromatic).
Feng said, "So, it seems you have not yet grasped the meaning of our former teacher. Zhaozuo said, "Do you not approve of me? Just bring some incense.

Jingfeng then patted the back of the seat and said, "To die while seated or pass away while standing is not impossible; however, I have not yet dreamed of the meaning of my former teacher.
The Master said, "The Head Seat could not help but follow the literal phrasing, and thus he incurred Jingfeng’s censure.

Yi-se (One-Color) falsely accused him. Tian Qi (Heavenly Wonder) annotated the *Guzhu* (Verses on the Ancients), directly claiming that this was the realization of the dharmakāya’s virtue of severance (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).

To regard this as the ultimate consummation is precisely to be lost within "one color. How could the error of following each [erroneous] phrase be anything less than being three thousand li away from the truth?
Since he neither permits it to be recognized as one color nor permits it to be recognized as the dharmakāya, [the true meaning remains hidden].
What was the intention of the former master? Ultimately, how is it? [The Master] raised the case:
A monk asked Qinglin, "When a student goes directly ahead, what then? Qinglin said, "A dead snake lies across the main road;

"How is it when one is right at the head? Lin said, "There is likewise no place to evade. The monk asked, "How is it when it is exactly like this?
Lin said, "It has already been lost. The monk asked, "I do not know where it has gone. Lin said, "The grass is deep; there is no place to find it.
The monk said, "The Master must also be on guard. Lin clapped his hands and said, "All the same," and left.
"This is a lethal poison.

[The Master] raises his whisk. One day, Nanquan, because two halls were disputing over a cat, picked up the cat and said, "If you can speak, I shall not kill it."

The Master said: "When Nanquan issued his command, it was vast and open, leaving no room before him; both halls could do nothing but stand with folded hands and listen.

[Case] presented. Layman Pang took his leave of Mount Yao. Yao ordered ten Zen practitioners to escort him to the gate.
The Layman pointed to the snow in the air and said, "This fine snow falls flake by flake, never landing elsewhere. The practitioner Quan said, "Where does it land? The Layman struck him.
Yunquan struck him once with his palm. Xuedou said, "The layman must not be so casual. Xuefeng said, "If you call me a Zen guest like that, Old Yan [Yama] will not let you off.

**The Eye.** Case:
When Mazu saw a monk approaching, he drew a circle and said, "If you enter, I will strike; if you do not enter, I will strike.
The monk stepped inside, and Mazu struck him. The monk said, "Master, you may not strike me. Mazu leaned his staff against the wall and ceased.

Case: Jianyuan was visited by Bao’ai. Jianyuan then rolled up the curtain, entered the abbot’s quarters, and sat down. Bao’ai lowered the curtain and returned to his guest seat.

Jianyuan instructed an attendant to deliver a message, saying, "It is no easy matter to have traveled so far; you are still separated from the ford. As soon as he finished speaking, Bao’ai gave him a slap across the face.

"It was precisely because there was a monk present that I struck you. When the Master related this to Yuan, Yuan said, "There is still a gap across the ford.
The Master said, "Jianyuan’s concealment of his body was secure and subtle; Baogai’s manifestation throughout his entire being was complete. Jianyuan saw Baogai."
When Bao-gai had not yet seen Jian-yuan, he was merely waiting for the opportunity, as the ford remained unbridged. At that time, he should have replied:
"I thank the Master for his dharma instruction; I shall certainly take Jian-yuan’s saying 'We have met' as our conclusion. Instead, Bao-gai struck the attendant.
How could it be anything less than crossing the ford?
For instance: Qianfeng addressed the assembly, saying, "The Dharma-body has three kinds of illnesses and two kinds of radiance; you must penetrate each one thoroughly.
Furthermore, there is still a 'higher opening' beyond. Yunmen stepped forward and said, "Why does the person inside the hermitage not know?"
"This is a matter outside the hermitage," said Feng. He laughed loudly. Dumen said, "This is still a point of doubt for students.
Feng said, "What kind of mind-set do you have? Dumen said, "I also wish for the Master to grant me full understanding.
Feng said, "You must be like this before you can sit securely. Dumen said, "Yes, yes."
The Master said: "Qianfeng has deployed a great battle formation; it is no ordinary affair. Yunmen, however, stepped down upon his head.
Setting aside matters outside the hermitage for a moment, how is it with matters inside the hermitage?
If you can speak of this, I, Gushan, will recognize him as a fellow student."
Case: Shigong saw a monk; he took up his bow and fixed an arrow to show him. When Sanping arrived, Shigong said, "Watch the arrow!
Sanping thrust out his chest to meet it and said, "This is an arrow that kills people. What about an arrow that gives life?
Shigong drew the string three times, and Sanping immediately prostrated himself. Shigong said, "For thirty years I have drawn a single bow and fixed two arrows, yet I have only shot..."
He attained the state of being half a sage and subsequently snapped his bow and arrows.
The Master said, "To bare your chest and face the arrow truly possesses the strategy of a great man; yet you still regard it merely as a 'killing arrow.'"
Next, let us ask about the arrow for the living. How many have missed the mark? Gong treated it like a dead horse, applying a remedy;
though he managed to save it, it was still only half-cured.
Case: A woman was sitting in meditative absorption before the Buddha. Mañjuśrī then addressed the Buddha, saying, "Why is it that this person is permitted to sit near the Buddha while I am not?
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī, "Simply awaken this woman and cause her to arise from samādhi."
"You must ask him yourself. Mañjuśrī then exercised his supernatural powers and ascended to the Brahma Heaven, yet he was unable to bring [the monk] out of samādhi.
The Buddha then said, "The Great Being Wǎngmíng from the lower regions can emerge from this samādhi. In a short while, Wǎngmíng arrived; the Buddha commanded him to bring [the monk] out of samādhi.
Wangming snapped his fingers once, and the woman immediately emerged from her meditative absorption.
The Master said, "Tiantong remarked, 'Whether in stillness or movement, it is the person who manipulates them. This is indeed so, yet he only spoke half the truth.

While still within meditative absorption, he raised [the matter].
Once, while Xuefeng was traveling with Sansheng through the mountains, they saw a troop of monkeys. Xuefeng said, "Just these monkeys."
Each of them wore an ancient mirror upon their person. The Saint said, "It has been nameless throughout kalpas; why do you characterize it as an 'ancient mirror'?
Feng replied, "A flaw has arisen. The Saint said, "As a teacher of fifteen hundred people, you do not even recognize the critical pivot of the teaching.
Feng replied, "The abbot’s duties are many and pressing."
The Master said: "The divine edge of Sansheng was sharp and keen; looking down upon all quarters, he alone encountered being set aside as dull-witted here.
It was like Xuefeng, who had already passed over the bridge after dropping a heap of stinking excrement, yet Sansheng went back to pick at the side of that excrement;
for this reason, Xuefeng told him, 'A flaw has arisen. Later, he still lacked the means to turn himself around."
As for the method: simply proceed forward. It would have been best to strike him with a staff right at the outset. Fortunately, Xuefeng possessed the magnanimity of a great man;
he was like heaven covering and earth bearing all—a fine standard for a thousand ages.
Case: A monk asked Linji, “What is the ‘hair-blowing sword’? Linji said, “A disaster! A disaster! The monk bowed, and Linji struck him.

The Master raised an example, citing the verse of Wòlún: "Wòlún possesses skill; he can sever a hundred thoughts.

"Please, Preceptor, speak. Yan then laughed heartily.

Establishing the appropriate means, the hidden and the manifest harmonize; father and son sing in resonance, a guiding rule for a thousand ages.
Case: Xuansha asked Jingqing, "The ancients said, 'Not seeing a single dharma is a great calamity. Now tell me, what do you say?"

[Zhaozhou] did not see any dharma. Qing pointed to a pillar and said, "Is this not that very dharma? Zhaozhou said, "The clear water and white rice of Zhejiang you may eat as much as you like, but as for the Buddha-dharma, you have not even seen it in your dreams."
The Master said: "Jingqing’s saying was not incorrect at all. Why, then, did Xuansha penalize him?

It was simply because his words did not transcend the common run and he still suffered from the 'pursuing clods' disease. Had it been Gushan, he would have immediately asked: 'What is this tattered straw sandal?

Xiji raised [the case]. Three Sages said: "Whenever I meet a person, I come forth; once I have come forth, I do not act for the sake of others. Xinghua said: "Whenever I meet a person, I do not come forth;

The aperture is present. [He] picks up his staff and strikes it once. He says:

Baofu said, "Yunyan is much like pushing a cart through mud; every step is laborious.

Under the Gate: It is not that I say it is not so; under the gate of Yaoshan, there is a simultaneous mastery of the wondrous harmony.

The true mark is signless; it is a subtle and wondrous Dharma-gate that does not rely on words and letters, but is transmitted separately outside the teachings. I entrust this to you:

The dragon’s head and horns are already complete; suddenly encountering a thunderclap, he leaps into the sky, overturning the pools and shaking the peaks—a clamor that resounds through the ages. Yet, even this single phrase is not yet fully realized.

Father and son at Deshan vie as heroes; the final word is as alive as a dragon—truly, like a flash of lightning that cannot be caught. One seeks the tracks of a fish from within the water.
Case: A monk asked Tong’an, “What is the Teacher of Gods and Humans? An said, “The horns on his head are incomplete;
the hair on his body does not emerge.
Before the hair and horns have grown, what is it? “How could the five eyes ever have known him?”
Calling for the horse, calling for the ox—neither is it they. The body is hidden within the white clouds;

"The magpie cries upon the tree; its intent lies within the hemp field. The woodcutter recognizes only the sound, mistakenly seeking it at the branch tip."
"Nevertheless, does Jiufeng still understand the meaning of his former teacher? It is like being vaguely in Yue Province and faintly in Yangzhou.
[The Master] raised [the case]: Chan Master Qing of Bājiāo ascended the hall and, holding up his staff, showed it to the assembly, saying:
