The Master spoke these words to Elder Benzhao, pointing out:
"You have been a Buddha from the very beginning. Why, then, do you choose to sink into delusion? You possess the treasures of your own home; for what reason do you cast them aside and wander abroad?"
It is solely because a single thought of delusion arises that a hundred wrongs gather together. Consequently, one willingly endures the *pātaka* (transgressions) and cannot escape on one's own.
It is just like a person in a dream who undergoes great suffering and distress, unable to break free from it; if one says it exists...
It is clearly a dream. If you say it does not exist, you are currently suffering its consequences. Suddenly, a rat overturns the basin and emerges from the dream;
once this occurs, there is no need to further debate whether the events within the dream exist or not. How much less, then, can one speak of abandoning them or grasping at them?
Elder, the events within your dreams are manifold and not just one; your afflictions are likewise manifold. You must grasp what is to be grasped.
One cannot escape. Even if one attempts to renounce it, one cannot renounce it. Day follows day; year follows year.

There is no time of awakening, and thus there is no end to suffering and affliction. One should know that within this state, there is no other way to find liberation than to recognize that it is a dream.
To recognize that it is a dream—how could there then be anyone else? At that point, who is there?
Regarding the matter of dreams, one forms thoughts of acceptance and rejection, stirring emotions of sorrow and joy. Yet, as sleep is already deep, it is likewise not easy to awaken.
I recall that a former Buddha once spoke this verse: "One borrows the four great elements to constitute body and mind;
originally there is no cause for birth, yet objects appear before the mind. If there were no mind, there would be neither sin nor merit—like a phantom."
"Arising is also ceasing. Elder, you should be able to take up this verse and constantly maintain it without interruption, deeply investigating its meaning.
If one day you happen upon it by chance—striking or touching it—the great dream will surely awaken; you can be certain of letting out a hearty laugh.
Having reached such a state, there is no need to ask others. Whether you dwell alone or lead a community, you will be free and at ease in every direction.
Appearing and disappearing without fixed direction—how much more so can one discuss such trivial and minute details?

I have resided at Mount He for eight years, and it was only with the Senior Monk (Dharma Seat Holder) that I shared the closest intimacy through our constant coming and going. Now, as he is departing for Mount Gu, he has requested a discourse on the Dharma from me.

Yet, the Dharma is fundamentally without dharma; what dharma-discourse could there be? All speech and language are entirely devoid of ultimate reality. It exists only within the realm of benevolence, righteousness, and the Way.
It cannot be that there is nothing to be said; thus, I have been so insistent. On another day, after you have awakened from this great dream, it will be my good fortune if you do not scold me.
This is shown to the venerable Master [Name] as he closes his retreat.
I have heard that those of old who studied the Way traveled extensively and sought knowledge afar;

they submerged themselves in humble service and lowly labor, exhausting their sinews and bones and withering their flesh and skin, undergoing every kind of hardship without exception. Yet none of them ever merely sat quietly in a single room, closing the door to maintain silence.
This was intended for those who study the Way. Since the beginning of the Yuan-shi era, there has been the teaching of "closing the gate" (bi-guan).

However, when Gao-feng closed the "gate of death" at Tian-mu, this occurred after the *Zhen-zhen* had already fallen to the ground; it was not a case of delimiting oneself by drawing lines on the ground before the Great Matter had yet been clarified.
It was only upon entering the Ming dynasty that the practice of closing the gate to study the Way became prevalent. As for closing the gate to study the Way, its...
The very first thought is that which seeks stillness while loathing movement; this single thought alone constitutes an obstacle to entering the Way.

How much more so when, in Guanzhong, one neither receives the hammering of a wise teacher nor the encouragement of fellow practitioners, but instead remains in a state of dull stupor, clinging to a single phrase like one embracing a withered stump.
As days turn into months, one’s resolve gradually weakens and one’s strength fades away.
Gradually one grows weary; the "head-word" (hua-tou) becomes tasteless, and doubt does not arise. Suddenly, the second thought has already emerged.
There are even those who, though sitting in a single room, find their hundred thoughts flying about in confusion—so what is the point of the cloistered retreat?
Now that you, Venerable Sir, have resolved to enter the retreat, you must possess a sincere heart and develop a resolute will regarding the two matters of life and death.
Write these characters and paste them on your forehead. Advance with courage and vigor; do not hesitate or deliberate further.
It is like a single person facing ten thousand enemies. If I do not kill him, he will surely kill me.
If one does not risk one’s life to fight one’s way out, how can there be a day of survival? One must simply be more diligent today than yesterday, and more diligent this month [than last].
After a month has passed, if you press forward and retreat back like a mouse entering a cow's horn, then there will naturally be a way out for you.
To the Venerable Weiqian, I have often said that for those who study the Way, first, one must be able to believe thoroughly; second, one must be able to let go completely. First...
Third, one must maintain these firmly. Only when these three essentials are present can one study the Way. What is meant by "believing thoroughly"?

It means believing that I am originally a Buddha, lacking not even a single hair’s breadth [of deficiency]. Furthermore, it means believing in every word and phrase bestowed by the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
It is like a long sword leaning against the sky; it must be able to sever the life-root of a person. Only when one possesses this true faith can one advance.
If there is even the slightest trace of doubt, there is no way to advance. Therefore, one requires someone who can truly believe. What is meant by "being able to let go"?
A person is entangled by many kinds of illusory fame, floating profit, affection, and karmic conditions, as if bound by iron.
The copper locks of the city cannot be opened by themselves; one must exert oneself with courageous vigor, severing everything completely and never looking back again before one can advance.
If there is even the slightest lingering attachment, one will surely be tripped up. Therefore, one requires the ability to let go.
What is meant by "holding fast"? It is because when a person is moved by inspiration and moves forward, it seems as though they believe in letting go.
One has attained letting go; yet there is only the fear that one might be blown away by the two winds of adversity and favor, whereby the believer becomes a non-believer.
One who has truly let go will, as before, still take up the burden and carry it away. Therefore, one must find someone whose resolve is firm.
Only after possessing these three qualities should one contemplate a single phrase of the *huatou*, regardless of life or death, and regardless of leisure or busyness.
Be diligent. If you exert yourself in constant mindfulness over a long period of time, awakening will naturally occur. This is the path traversed by the patriarchs of all generations;
you, O superior man, must strive in this.
To the layman Huang Mengyang, [the Master] showed why sentient beings are unable to transcend birth and death: it is simply because they are deluded. What is meant by "delusion"?

It is because their false consciousness arises perversely, perceiving the existence of external objects. Once they perceive the existence of external objects, there is beauty and ugliness; and once there is beauty...

If there is ugliness, then there is love and hatred. Once there is love and hatred, there is grasping and rejecting. Once there is grasping and rejecting, there is good and evil. Once there is good and evil, there is karmic retribution.
When goodness reaches its extreme, one is born in the heavens; when evil reaches its extreme, one sinks into the earth. All of this belongs to saṃsāra, from which there is no rest.
Now, if one wishes to shatter these external objects, the primary requirement is to sever this deluded consciousness. This deluded consciousness...

Since beginningless kalpas, this has been deeply rooted and firmly established; how could it be easily overcome? Yet, this deluded consciousness possesses no substantial reality at all, and for that reason, it is not difficult to sever.
If one attains a single penetration of the fundamental radiance, it can be immediately shattered.
That there were those in ancient times who, upon a single word, attained realization on the spot, is no empty boast. It is simply that the faculties and capacities of sentient beings are slow.
Those of dull faculties are unable to attain sudden enlightenment; therefore, the patriarchs of successive generations have taught people to contemplate the *huatou* (critical phrase).
Contemplating the *huatou* is not a matter of passing the time indifferently; one must apply oneself with the utmost intensity, pressing forward with courage and vigor.

It is like a lone soldier on horseback with a single spear encountering an encircling army of three divisions—one must risk one’s life and charge through. If one is even slightly delayed or hesitant, there will be [no escape].
One who is truly capable of self-sustenance must attend to various conditions every day; though there is not a moment’s leisure, this *huatou* must never be interrupted.

Should it be lost due to external circumstances, one must immediately whip it back into being. By investigating and investigating in this way, as days turn into months and years pass, [the realization will emerge].
Suddenly, a state of doubt arises all at once. Internally, one no longer perceives the five organs or the hundred bones;
externally, one no longer perceives the mountains, rivers, or the great earth. There is only this single *huatou* (critical phrase), continuous and dense.
Reaching this stage, one must exert even greater brilliance. Suddenly, with a "clunk" (*lìdì*), the *huatou* is shattered. When the *huatou* is shattered, the external realm is shattered.
When the external objects before one are shattered, birth and death are shattered. At this moment, the old green mountains and blue waters remain as they were;
whether it be hell or heaven, one may freely proceed. Thus, it is appropriate to tell others that one is originally a Buddha; it is also appropriate to say there is neither purity nor defilement.

It may be said that there is neither Buddha nor sentient beings. However, if deluded consciousness has not been extinguished, and one continues to engage in a thousandfold discrimination with greed, anger, ignorance, and pride burning incessantly, yet still claims to others that there is neither Buddha nor sentient beings, this is merely the demonic seed and the influence of evil spirits.

When this *huatou* has not yet been broken through, if one’s practice becomes so intense that various extraordinary visions appear, or various heterodox interpretations arise, these are all merely the aberrations of deluded consciousness; one must immediately sever them with a single stroke of the sword.

Once the "great earth-shaking" sound is attained, everything will naturally fall into place, perfectly resolved and secure. When first beginning one's practice, it is inevitable that progress will be difficult, for...

This is dullness and agitation; these two demonic habits are so deeply ingrained that they are difficult to dispel. Even if one fails a thousand times or ten thousand times, one must resolutely succeed.
It is like the "Foolish Old Man Moving the Mountains" mentioned by the ancients.

By persevering through trial after trial, one’s practice will naturally become proficient, and the day of arriving home will surely come. Sentient beings have endured such manifold sufferings since beginningless kalpas.
Chu Gan: "To willingly accept these minor difficulties yet to knit one's brows in fear is what is called folly.
If you say they need not be accepted, then there must be some other method to transcend birth and death; such is the teaching of the non-Buddhist paths.
It is merely a temporary self-deception, for in the end one enters the cycle of saṃsāra. Why? Because their deluded attachments have not been shattered."
"To show that Layman Ding Yuanpei’s numinous light shines alone, utterly transcending the sense organs and their objects"—these two lines have already said it all.
If you can understand this, how would I, this mountain monk, dare to speak further? If not yet, let us first untangle the vines. The numinous spirit of sentient beings...
Light is fundamentally without obstruction; yet, alas, deluded emotions arise falsely. Consequently, there are the six internal faculties and the six external objects.
As faculty and object stand in opposition, false consciousness arises recklessly. One performs good and evil deeds, giving rise to wholesome and unwholesome karma.

Because of this karma, one receives retribution, cycling through the six realms of existence like a waterwheel drawing from a well—wave after wave, kalpa after kalpa, emerging and submerging without end.
At that time, they all felt deep compassion for him. For their sake, he expounded the Great Dharma, summarizing its essential point as nothing other than this:

the solitary radiance of the numinous light. If this numinous light is not obscured, the sense organs and their objects are instantly extinguished; the mind is forgotten and the environment is stilled.

There is perfect illumination without exteriority, and the essence of awakening is suchness (*tathatā*); this is what is called the Buddha. If, however, that light has not yet been revealed, one must possess a skillful means (*upāya*). This "skillful means" is not—
This is to seek out someone to lecture and explain; it is not to engage in the pedantic dissection of scriptures, nor to perform excessive meritorious deeds, nor to sit with eyes closed as if dead.
Rather, amidst the activities of daily life, you must pluck your eyebrows and open your eyes to look: "What is this original face?
You must not calculate whether it is difficult or easy, nor discuss whether it is far or near. Furthermore, you must not lament that your faculties are dull, nor harbor anxieties regarding yourself.

With such heavy karmic obstructions, one must simply press forward and act. After a long time and many years, one will suddenly encounter it and only then realize that rice is indeed grain, and that what makes a lamp is fire.
These words are truly fit to be handed over to the spirits of fire (Bingding). Hehe!

To know that which is fundamentally non-existent is called the "object" (*viṣaya*). When the mind and its object are clearly distinct, where, then, can that which is called "fundamentally non-existent" be found?
This is precisely as you have asked. The "inconceivable object" (*acintya-viṣaya*) is the contemplative method (*dhyāna-dharma*) of the Tiantai school.

That teaching states that a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*) is replete with the three thousand natures and characteristics (*tri-sahasra-svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*), being simultaneously empty (*śūnya*), provisional (*prajñapti*), and the Middle (*madhyama*). This is called the inconceivable object. However, it has already been said:

The "object" (*viṣaya*) is a designation established in contrast to "contemplation. If one does not forget the contemplation of the Truths, one remains entirely outside the gate; how could there be anyone of truly excellent wisdom?
Only when both contemplation and the Truths are forgotten can one be said to have entered the gate. Yet even this is still separated from the affairs of the Patriarch’s school by a river;
how can you lightly cite it as a point of comparison? Benevolent one, from now on, there is no need to drag out this tangled hemp.
Fengxue: "But concentrate your mind and sharpen your will. Direct yourself toward the Original Master; apply the deep probe and the piercing strike until you do not rest.
When the morning comes and you touch your own nostrils, the mountains will still be green and the waters still clear. Is it the mind? Or is it the environment? Winter is cold and summer is hot."
"Not the Way, not the Way. He showed this to Liu Kongxue, the Mochaixue (Mochizuki), who said to the world:
"The Way of Zhou and Confucius is appropriate for governing the world; the Way of Śākyamuni is appropriate for transcending the world. Each should choose [accordingly]."
To take them as one's primary model simply because they are appropriate [to the secular world] is a shallow way of discussing the two teachings.

For if the Duke of Zhou and Confucius had not possessed the actual virtue of transcending the world, then what they call "governing the world" would either be mired in profit and utility or else bound by names and forms.
If Śākyamuni lacked the practical utility to sustain the world, then that which is called "transcending the world" would either fall into erroneous views or be confined to self-interest;
how, then, could it transcend the world? Therefore, one knows that sustaining the world and transcending the world are in truth not two, and the Way is in truth not two minds.
Confucius and the Duke of Zhou likely attained the subtle function of Śākyamuni to propagate [the teachings].
Regarding economics: Śākyamuni surely obtained the secret seal of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius to realize *nirvāṇa*.
Yet, worldly people merely cling to their external traces and treat them as two separate things, as if ice and fire could never coexist; this is because they have not examined the matter deeply.

Since you, sir, now wish to establish yourself within the Great Way, there is no need to debate their differences; rather, discuss their commonalities. Whenever you cite a sage or a worthy, [you will find that their essence is one].
First, one must thoroughly investigate the depths of language; however, one must not fall into the realm of emotional consciousness (*qing-shi*).
As Confucius said, "I wish to remain wordless," to which Zigong replied, "The Master’s discourse on human nature and the Way of Heaven is something we cannot hope to hear."

This can be understood. It is not a matter of emotional consciousness (*qing-shi*). If you attain the state where emotions are forgotten and consciousness is severed, then the original "nose-ring" (*ba-bi*) will naturally manifest;

it cannot be described by words. Once this nose-ring is attained, one may be a Confucian, one may be a Buddhist, or even neither Confucian nor Buddhist—there is nothing that would not be acceptable. Strive toward this!
"To show that all phenomena arise from conditions and likewise cease from conditions"—this is the verse of the Elder of Mount Lingyan.

To know that phenomena arise from conditions is to realize that phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Since phenomena lack intrinsic nature, they neither cease nor arise. Neither ceasing nor arising.
Thus, the essence is inherently as-it-is. Since the essence is inherently as-it-is, to say that there is a nature is delusion;
to say that there is no nature is likewise delusion. Even to say that the essence is inherently as-it-is is not itself non-delusory.
Nevertheless, even if you speak in this way and understand it in this way, have you truly attained awakening? Since there is a path upon which to ascend, one must go higher than others.
Practice! You must cut off the path of words and extinguish the sphere of mental activity;

only when you have personally realized this once will you know what all that was previously said—those "profound beyond the profound" and "sublime beyond the sublime"—actually is. It is merely the sound of a hot bowl clinking. Reflect on this.
It appears that nowadays the ancestral style has been swept from the ground; demons and devils have arisen to manifest their wiles.

Everywhere, those who falsely claim to be "men of knowledge" (jñānin) use the "gourd-seal" to recklessly confer certification upon others, leading one another into the Avīci Hell. Looking at this, it would be better to simply devote oneself exclusively to reverence.
One who practices the precepts still possesses the cause for attaining Buddhahood. As for this mountain monk, having reached this point, there was no other recourse but to speak these various words;

yet even so, it appears to be nothing more than a failure. Nevertheless, my humble intention is to allow all people, amidst the long night of darkness, to catch a glimpse of a single thread of light. However, the host of demons is flourishing; what can one person do alone?
I hope that you, O Illustrious One, will emerge from within the investigation of reality and enter through the place where words fail.
You must not fall into the ghost cave, nor be entangled in the creeping vines. Whether it be the White Horse Pit, pass straight through with hands hanging down;
whether it be the Yellow Dragon Barrier, walk past with arms flung wide—this is still not the business of a true man, let alone merely studying the empty.
"Hu! A wild shout and a flurry of blows! There will be great matters ahead. If one is a man of the waters, their nature is naturally simple and flourishing;
having shut themselves away for three years to read the entire Tripitaka, they may indeed be called a diligent seeker of the Way. Yet, they do not yet know the single aperture that points upward.
It is like a rat entering a rice jar—it ultimately has no way out. You must take all that you have read during those three years..."
Set it free so that not even a trace of a word remains. Then, with a firm resolve and exerting courageous power, direct yourself toward a single koan.

Investigate it with all your might and exhaust its depths; do not permit the formation of intellectual interpretations, do not seek out explanations, do not allow the mind to wait for an awakening, and do not give rise to self-defeat.
Simply practice in this manner, and there will naturally come a moment of breakthrough and liberation.
One day, looking back upon the entire Great Canon, I saw that there is not a single word that is not the direct pointing of the single transmission—the great intent of the West.
Strive on!
This was shown to the venerable Master Wuan.

Regarding the single gate of the Pure Land, there is no other subtle teaching; it simply requires this one phrase of the Buddha’s name to be maintained at all times without interruption and kept constantly in mind.
It does not matter whether this is maintained through principle (*li*) or through phenomena (*shi*).

Once this one phrase becomes thoroughly familiar, it is like clouds parting to reveal the sun: both phenomena and principle are resolved, and even that which transcends both phenomena and principle is likewise resolved.
However, today those who recite the Buddha’s name are many, yet those born in the Western Paradise are few. What is the reason for this?
It is simply because your mouth speaks of the Land of Ultimate Bliss while your mind remains attached to this Sahā world; how then can you go there?

Therefore, practitioners of nianfo must take up a blade of the Vajra-jewel and sever all these worldly attachments one by one; only then will you have the capacity to advance toward that goal. Furthermore, there is...
There is a certain class of people who, as soon as they begin to recite the Buddha’s name, worry that they will not realize the Way and thus insist on practicing Chan meditation.

Their minds are suspended between two ends, and their practice fails to reach fruition because they do not understand at all that the mind used for reciting the Buddha’s name is the same mind used for practicing Chan;
what is attained through Chan can also be attained through recitation. In the past, Su Dongpo initially practiced Chan but found no entry point.
Later, he met Donglin Zong, who said, "Your karmic obstacles differ from those of others; you must apply yourself with 'dead heart' and recite a single Buddha-name before you can succeed.

Once subject and object have emerged, errors give rise to the four views: some see it as existence, some see it as non-existence, or some see it...

There is both existence and non-existence; or one perceives neither existence nor non-existence. Once these four views arise, a hundred negations follow, and one moves further and further away from the Way.
It is just as when an eyelash is right before one's eyes, yet one cannot see it; is it that the eyelash is truly far away?
Thus we know that these four views alone are the very root of birth and death. To be free from these four views is to be without birth.
Death can be escaped. However, one must fundamentally extricate oneself from these four views. This is not attained through scholarly investigation of the scriptures;
it is not attained through deliberation with teachers and friends; it is not attained through the practice of *śamatha* (calm abiding) or *vipaśyanā* (insight meditation);
nor is it attained through performing good deeds or cultivating merit. One must truly turn back upon oneself and investigate: "What is this state before one's parents were yet born?"
What is this original face? This *huatou* (critical phrase) is the proven, efficacious prescription of Xiangyan.
Formerly, while Xiangyan was in Baizhang’s assembly, he could answer ten questions for every one asked, displaying his mastery of intellectual understanding.

Later, when he arrived at Mount Gui (Weishan), Weishan asked him, "What is your original face before your parents were born? He was unable to answer; thus, he set aside all that he had previously studied and...
"Understand this! Cast it away into the great ocean of the Eastern Sea and go south to Nanyang. There, dwell in a thatched hut.
One day, because of striking a bamboo stalk, he attained great enlightenment. He composed a verse and presented it to Guishan, who then patted him on the back and certified his realization.
Layman, simply take these words and investigate them with earnestness of heart; you must be courageous and diligent, as if your head were on fire. Then, your doubts will naturally...

If your sense of inquiry is earnest, the numinous faculty will spontaneously open. This is like the extreme cold of winter reaching its limit, where the first yang returns and the three yang lines initiate the state of Tai;
this is the natural order of principle and the natural course of events. Exert yourself!

The faults of the Chan studies of the nun Jingguang are generally twofold: first, falling into a state of vague indistinctness; second, falling into a state of fragmented disintegration. Thus, our Way is lost.
To fall into vague indistinctness means to cling to a sense of a "blunt" and "indifferent" Buddha-nature as being of a single flavor, [remaining in a state of] emptiness...

When the arrogant encounter others, they shout "Hu! and wield their staffs in disorder, forcibly assuming the role of master. Yet, within the gate of differentiation, they fail to pass through entirely;
they merely become commoners carrying a single board. Those who lose themselves in fragmentation deliberate on every single item, exhausting their mental and physical strength;
their critical analysis becomes increasingly refined, yet their fragmentation becomes ever more severe. Within the fundamental source, they remain as dark as a lacquer bucket. Only...
To become a salt-and-iron magistrate and wish to avoid the fault of being blunt and uncouth, one cannot do so through mere deliberation or intellectual understanding.
To avoid the fault of fragmentation, one cannot do so by blindly clinging to a single point. One must, from the top of a hundred-foot pole, take a step further out;
then, naturally, the sun will be high in the sky, mountains and rivers will have no place to hide, and one will move with total freedom in every direction.
His entire body is his mouth; regarding all dharma-gates, whether establishing or sweeping away, opening or closing, he is everywhere sovereign.
This is what is meant by the two defects being naturally absent without needing to be discarded. The nun Jingguang of Taicang held up paper and requested a discourse on the Dharma.

I have jotted down these few words to encourage you. To the Venerable Shiyun: The sun’s orb is in the heavens; there is nowhere it does not illuminate. Yet beneath an overturned basin, the darkness remains as it was. Is this the fault of the sun? Or is it the fault of the vessel?

It is simply that the light cannot penetrate the obstruction. You, too, are like this. Your virtue is vast and your wisdom is profound, yet you remain hidden within the mountain forests, where no one knows you. This is surely because the vessel is inverted, not because the sun lacks its brilliance. If you can turn the vessel upright, the light will naturally shine forth. Do not let your mind be constrained by narrow-mindedness. Strive to broaden your perspective and expand your capacity for receiving the Way. May you soon emerge from the mountains and bring benefit to the world. I hope you will take these words to heart. Written by [Your Name]. 10th day of the 3rd month, Year X.
If the illumination is not all-pervasive, it is because the basin acts as a deep obstruction. You, Venerable One, have been practicing for years, yet the Great Matter remains unclarified.
This is not due to any other power obstructing you; it is solely because the two demons of dullness and distraction daily cover you over.
From where do these two demons come? To what direction do they go? What kind of nature do they possess?
"Sir, what traces or signs are there that could act as an obstacle for you? These illnesses all arise because your master lacks vigorous energy;
thus, external afflictions are able to take advantage of the opening to enter. If you can apply yourself with fierce effort and examine this critical phrase (huatou), [the obstacles will vanish]."
It should be like extinguishing a fire on one's head, like rescuing a drowning child, like suddenly losing one’s parents, or like suddenly encountering a great enemy.
If there is such earnestness, the two demons of dullness and distraction will have no opening through which to strike.

Furthermore, if you can strive with tireless diligence—advancing like a single iron bar for ten thousand li—after a long time, your anxieties will gradually clear and your resolve will gradually unify. Suddenly, you will encounter it; you will strike upon it. Break through!
By overturning the old molds, you will be able to open your eyes at the crown of your head and radiate light from behind your brain;

thus, the three thousand Buddhas and seventeen hundred patriarchs will all withdraw without the slightest effort of a single gesture—how much more so the two demons of dullness and distraction! Exert yourself, O superior man!
This demonstrates that among all things above heaven and below man, nothing is more concise than the mind; likewise, among all things in the world, nothing is more expansive than the mind.
Why is it said to be concise? Because its substance is most subtle, yet it is that which all existence collectively venerates.
Why is it said that this [mind] is vast? Because its application is so extensive that it cannot be confined by empty space.
If this is so, where should those who seek the mind apply their efforts? They should simply apply their efforts to what is concise.

One who is dedicated to their covenant must not divide their resolve nor confuse their spirit. Throughout the day, they should be ever-urgent, as if they had lost something and must surely recover it;
they must maintain this for a long time and preserve it with purity, like water that inevitably flows toward the east.
Yet that which has passed does not return, just as the sun must necessarily revolve; yet that which illuminates does not cease.
If this is truly so, then one can intuitively grasp the essence of its covenant. Once the essence of its covenant is grasped, its application will be vast.
Being able to encompass the universe and illuminate both ancient and modern times—how could this depend upon cultivation before completion, or learning before attainment?
May the Master exert himself in this endeavor.
I show you, Layman Sun Yetao, that the Way of Chan is subtle indeed. It cannot be transmitted through words, nor can it be reached by the intellect;
how much less can it be imitated through outward appearance and demeanor, or grasped within the sphere of one's spirit and resolve? How would this differ from seeking fortune at a divination stall?
To don the crown of the Yellow Emperor like a mountain pheasant is to falsely assume the plumage of a phoenix; one must necessarily understand what the ancients meant by the Way.
For instance, there was once a monk who asked, "What is Chan? and the reply was, "A common brick. Again, another asked, "What is Chan? and the reply was:
"Fry it in oil over a fierce fire. Again, someone asked, "What is Chan? He replied, "A monkey climbing a tree, its tail trailing behind its head.
These three turning words: one person can kill but cannot bring to life; another can bring to life but cannot kill;
the third can both kill and bring to life. If you can discern these, only then may you come before this old monk to receive a severe beating.
Addressing the assembly in the meditation hall of Yihaosi:
We live in the final age of the Dharma, when the winds of Māra blow fiercely. People are largely indolent and delight in negligence;

they busy themselves with worldly affairs, never wearying even after a hundred hardships, yet when it comes to cultivating the Right Path, they find it troublesome after only three prostrations. How much more so when each harbors a light and frivolous disposition!
With such a mind, they delight in displaying groundless views and take arrogance as their primary concern. They vie for superiority with their lips and tongues;
yet when examined against reality, they possess not a single point of substance. When their faults are discussed, a thousand grievances converge upon them.

Lacking any sense of shame, they presume to act as teachers to others, claiming that they have ascended high into the ancestral realm and look down upon the mundane world. Yet, in a single moment, they may encounter but a tiny mustard seed and be struck down, leaving them utterly defeated.
The flower has eight petals; it is entirely devoid of a sovereign controller. How much more so, then, regarding birth and death?

This is not merely the case within the gate of the Buddhas and Patriarchs—it is not something they can arbitrarily claim as their own. Even the miserable realms of the hells (niraya) cannot possibly escape this.

O virtuous ones, if you have left the household life with a sincere heart, do not draw near to such followers of Māra. First, discipline your person through the virtue of the precepts; do not allow even a hair’s breadth of transgression.
After committing such transgressions, one may either engage in Zen meditation to seek sublime awakening or practice the recitation of the Buddha's name in hope of rebirth in the Pure Land;
by being sincere and diligent, the day will surely come when one naturally arrives home.
To the Layman Wang Ziyeyi, it is shown that this Sahā world is a burning house, a realm where the five turbidities converge and the five desires rush about.
Sentient beings dwell within this place; if there were not the Buddha-dharma to rescue and deliver them, few would avoid falling into ruin. Now, wishing to escape...
This burning house has no other method [for escape] than simply purifying one’s own mind. Regarding the methods for purifying the mind, the Buddha has many approaches.
Yet, if one seeks a simple, direct path that is easy to practice and leads straight out of saṃsāra, none is equal to the single gate of mindfulness of the Buddha (nien-fo).
This gate requires no extensive learning, nor does it require great talent; regardless of whether one is old or young, [it is accessible to all].
Whether noble or base, male or female, monastic or lay—it matters not; you need only be able to recite this single phrase:
"A-mi-tuo-fo. These four characters are like Mount Sumeru, which cannot be shaken at any time.
They are also like a precious vajra sword, which, when encountered amidst any circumstance or condition—
This is immediately refuted. If one possesses such power, then in this very life one will see Amitābha, sit upon a lotus pedestal, and roam within the pure pool of the seven treasures;
there is no need to ask further—rebirth in the Pure Land is already assured. If, however, one's power is deficient, [the result will differ].
One must also urgently spur oneself on. Taking the affairs of this Sahā world as the object, one should daily cultivate revulsion and detachment until reaching a state of profound tranquility.
With such urgency and haste, one should seek birth in the Pure Land, like a fledgling yearning for its mother or a long-traveling guest longing for home.

By employing these two emotions—joy and revulsion—one will have the very boat and oars for rebirth; at the moment of death, one will surely be able to transfer the spirit to the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Ultimately, one reaches Bodhi.

[The Master] showed the King that his own mind is the sovereign of the lay devotees, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth, as well as the boundless void; these are called the "ten thousand dharmas. These ten thousand dharmas are entirely identical to bubbles.

Reflections are illusory and unreal; they all arise as manifestations of the single mind. Yet, while people today all know that the single mind manifests these things, they do not know where this mind actually resides.
Do they think it is within the body? Do they think it is outside the body?
Or do they think it is neither inside nor outside, but somewhere in between? All such views belong to delusion; none of them are correct.
Furthermore, as for that which is taken to be the mind: thoughts arise and perish, flickering and unstable;
now good, now evil, shifting and never constant. By what, then, can one define the mind? Since none of these states are the mind, does this mean there is no mind at all?
How could there be a person who is without a mind? Layman, you should investigate this matter with earnest sincerity.
Investigate thoroughly to find the ultimate point of resolution. Simply investigate in this manner;

do not attempt to provide intellectual explanations, do not engage in speculative reasoning, do not seek someone else to explain it for you, and do not waver between advancing and retreating. With single-minded resolve, investigate until death.

Do not concern yourself with whether it takes twenty or thirty years; if you investigate with relentless effort, there will surely come a day when you penetrate through to the truth. Strive diligently!
I show Layman Huang Erxun that there are not many arts to study; it simply requires recognizing one’s own true mind. Now, observe within this body:
the four elements are but a temporary conglomeration, tending daily toward dissolution. As for what is called the "true mind," why do discursive thoughts arise so profusely? Birth... [arises].
It ceases and is not constant; it is not the true mind. Whether good or evil, it undergoes change and lacks stability; it is not the true mind.
Furthermore, it arises entirely dependent on external objects and manifests as those external objects; if these objects were absent, where would this mind abide? It is not the true mind.
Moreover, within a single membrane, this mind cannot see itself; it is dark within, and thus not the true mind. One membrane.
Apart from this, painful afflictions do not affect it at all; thus, it is separated from the external and is not the true mind.

If one says that by turning the light inward to illuminate, there is an awareness of something profound, secluded, still, and unified, and takes this to be the true mind, one fails to realize that this profundity, seclusion, stillness, and unity arise from the illumination of the deluded mind.
Since there is a mind that illuminates and an object that is illuminated, [it is not the true mind].
This state of profound stillness and solitude belongs entirely to the internal realm;

it is what the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* refers to as "internally maintaining a state of profound stillness," which remains a mere reflection of the discrimination of mental objects (*dharmas*). How could this be the true mind?
Since these states are all not the true mind, what then shall we take to be the true mind? Layman, try during the twelve hours of the day and night to observe what constitutes your own true self.
Mind. Do not use it to engage in speculative conjecture. Do not apply intellectual commentary. Do not seek for others to explain it to you. Do not look for separate expedients.
Do not calculate whether the years and months have been long or short. Do not calculate whether your own strength is great or small.
Simply, in this manner, silently pursue and investigate for yourself: "Ultimately, what is my own true mind? Listen! One day, suddenly—

Only upon breaking through this barrier will you realize that the Three Teachings and Nine Schools are definitively not two different things, and that the myriad sages and thousand worthies are definitively not on divergent paths.
Whether one is a Confucian or a Buddhist, whether engaged in worldly affairs or transcending the world, there is not even a hair’s breadth of separation between them.
Layman, exert yourself!
The Chan of Drumshan, as demonstrated by the excellent attendant, is significantly different from that of other regions. In other regions, people are made to study verse compositions;

here, people are not made to study verse compositions. In other regions, people are made to study the art of responding to questions; here, people are not made to study the art of responding to questions.
In all other quarters, people study formal lectures and informal sermons (*shàngtáng* and *xiǎocān*). Here, we do not require people to study formal lectures and informal sermons.
Therefore, the Chan of other quarters is easy to investigate, while the Chan of this old monk is difficult to investigate.

This old monk desires only that you, in places where explanations fail to penetrate, become filled with indignation—as if your hair were on fire, as if you had lost your parents—and exert yourself urgently to drill into and investigate them. Drill into them! Drill into them!

Come and investigate this! Suddenly, the great earth sinks level; one’s entire being falls away, leaping out beyond the void and mounting the crown of Vairocana—only then may one be called a true student of the Way.

If you remain petty and trivial, following in the footsteps behind others' heels, chewing on the spittle from others' mouths, or lingering outside the gates and walls of others, [you have not yet arrived].
Relying [on others] is like a person born blind relying on a staff. Yet they say, "I am of the Linji school," or "I am of the Caodong school.
One does not know how thick their skin has become. An ancient said: "Do not admire the various sages; do not prize your own spiritual brilliance.
If you are the true offspring of this house, you will naturally not join the theatrical troupes of other houses. Strive toward this!

I show Layman Yujin that the nature inherently possessed by all sentient beings is such that it shines upon heaven and reflects the earth. Yet, alas, ignorance arises abruptly within the state of non-arising;
from this, deluded consciousness suddenly emerges. Once deluded consciousness exists, there is a deluded environment. Once there is a deluded...
Objects have their beauty and ugliness; once there is beauty and ugliness, there is love and hatred; once there is love and hatred, there is acceptance and rejection;
once there is acceptance and rejection, there is good and evil; once there is good and evil, there is ascent and descent.

As good and evil contend with one another, the nature of saṃsāra is like a well-drawing wheel, without interruption. Although it is said that suffering and pleasure differ according to heaven, in reality...
All are false and illusory. Out of compassion for them, the Buddhas have expounded the essential method for escaping suffering, which lies solely in destroying primordial ignorance (*avidyā*).

Yet this ignorance cannot be dispelled through reasoning, nor eliminated through words; it cannot be overcome by meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), nor dissolved by ascetic practices (*duṣkara-caryā*);
it cannot be removed by the power of the Buddhas, nor extinguished by the merit of accumulating goodness.
The essential point is that you must personally develop a sincere resolve and investigate this matter with earnest application to yourself. It is like capturing a bandit—you must capture the leader;
or like clearing away weeds—you must kill the root. Push it forward and push it back; exhaust it and exhaust it further, and the day of arriving home will come of its own accord.
There are many precedents from the ancients. Formerly, Dahui constantly instructed people to contemplate the following: A monk asked Zhaozhou, "Does a dog have the Buddha-nature? or...
"Does the Buddha-nature exist or not? The Master said, "It does not. "All sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature; why do you say it does not?
This word "no" is truly brilliant—it surpasses even Yan Hui and Min Ziqian. There is no place for you to grasp its meaning. Now, simply investigate this word "no";
do not explain it through intellectual understanding, nor calculate it with the mind. Just...
Doubt it in this way. One day, when you have captured him, Zhaozhou will recognize his true face, and you will naturally attain complete mastery in every direction.
What is called "illuminating heaven and reflecting the earth" must not be obscured.
The venerable elder Shōjitsu has emerged from his seclusion and, having passed through four monasteries, has uttered many profound words and perilous phrases;
his sole intent is nothing other than to ensure that people do not fall into intellectual understanding and instead attain right knowledge and vision. Looking at it now, there is no need for this.

Can it be attained? If one speaks from the perspective of the most urgent point of ordinary practice to a superior person, that superior person who wishes to study the Way must first cease the mind of攀緣 (pān-yuán—clinging to external objects) and the mind of知解 (zhī-jie—conceptual understanding). By causing the mind to become like wood or stone, it will naturally and mysteriously accord with the Way.
Deshan said: "You need only be without mind regarding phenomena, and without phenomena regarding the mind; then naturally it will be empty yet spiritual, still yet wondrous. Layman Pang said:
"I only wish that you would empty all that exists, and take care not to reify all that does not exist. Baizhang said:
If the mind-ground is empty, the sun of wisdom appears of itself. All such statements are the sincere and truthful words of former masters.

This is because the mind is inherently numinous and luminous; all wisdom and spiritual powers are fully possessed therein. It is only because it is obscured by external objects that they do not manifest.
Therefore, it is not exposed. If that which obscures it were dispelled, what further matter would remain? It is just like one who polishes a mirror:
by merely rubbing away its grime, the original clarity manifests of itself; why then wait for external light? It is like one who smelts gold:
by merely refining away the ore, the original gold becomes pure of itself; why then wait to borrow its color from another? The method for clarifying the mind is likewise so.
It is likewise so. It does not depend upon anything external. Nowadays, most practitioners look outward, borrowing many idle curiosities;
alas, these only increase their obstructions, placing them thousands of miles away from this Way. You, O Master, should reflect upon this.
I showed this to the Venerable Master Lingsheng.
When I was eighteen years old, I happened to obtain the *Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch* and read it.

Seeing the principles explained therein—perfect, wondrous, transcendent, and vast—I attained great joy and considered myself to have achieved some realization. However, regarding the points where the language of various masters was obscure or contradictory...

I did not understand it at all. I thought to myself that this was merely a cryptic expression fabricated by later generations through forced interpretation. One day, seeing the *Xinxin Ming* (Inscription on Faith in Mind), which states:

"The object arises from the subject; the subject arises from the object," I finally realized that what I had previously attained was merely the mental faculty grasping at dharmas as external objects—nothing more than a reflection—and was not the ultimate reality. It was from this point that I began my formal practice of inquiry (*chan*).
Investigating this to its ultimate conclusion, I see that among those who practice Chan these days, those who claim to have attained enlightenment generally settle for this as their livelihood.
Furthermore, they engage in deliberations on *gong'an*, study verses and dialogues, and take these as their standard of conduct.

Consequently, their intellectual understanding increases daily, their verbal facility becomes more polished, and they pride themselves on having attained great eloquence; yet, they move further and further away from the Way. This is because they... [practice] Chan.

Chan requires nothing more than forgetting all attachments and severing all conceptual understandings, exhausting the thieving mind until it dies out, and attaining the essence of the mind that is free from thought.
Now, however, you turn outward and bring in a great many antiquities; this is precisely what is meant by "only named carrying manure in," rather than "carrying manure out.
How can you ever accomplish the Great Matter? If you, Venerable Sir, are willing to believe me, simply take that which you have [accumulated]...
Whatever you have previously attained or studied, cut it off in a single sitting. Focus exclusively on investigating a single "dead phrase" (huatou).
This dead phrase, which cannot be known through intellectual understanding, is precisely close to the fundamental matter.
You must rub and polish here until suddenly the mind of conceptual understanding is completely exhausted; then, the innate radiance will manifest spontaneously.
It shines upon heaven and reflects upon the earth; yet people today deliberate over that which is beyond comprehension, seeking a path to walk.
Is this not a great error? At such a time, who would be willing to listen when an old monk speaks these words?
However, this mind cannot be deceived of its own accord; thus, I have no choice but to speak the truth as it is. Whether you listen or not is not my fault.

Furthermore, for Chan practitioners in these times, there is nothing more esteemed than the Way of the Buddha of Enlightenment (Bodhidharma). As for the method of practicing Chan, it values sublime awakening (*miaowu*). This so-called "sublime..."
Awakening cannot be assisted by even a hair’s breadth of human effort; it is solely through natural, divine illumination that one enters into a dark resonance with the inconceivable.

Why is it that among the students of today—ten of whom might form five pairs—all of whom desire to practice Zen, ultimately fall into unworthy ends? It is because they do not seek wondrous awakening. Not so.
Why is it that those who attain wondrous enlightenment do so? It is because they know nothing to avoid or shun.
If you now wish to study this Way, you must know there are four things to avoid. First, the establishment of the mind must not be improper;

for the establishment of the mind is the very foundation of realizing the Way, just as a foundation is essential for building a house. If the mind is established improperly, the foundation will first be flawed; even though—
To possess meditative concentration and wisdom while [still harboring these attachments] is entirely the work of Māra; how could such a state possibly enter the Way of the Sages?

Therefore, at the very beginning of entering the Way, all seeking of fame and reputation, scheming for profit and sustenance, the arising of birth-and-death, and the competitive mind of self and others—[these must be abandoned].
It is appropriate to eliminate all such things completely. Second is the application of the mind: it must not lack concentration.

The unsurpassed, wondrous Way cannot be entered by those with coarse minds or superficial temperaments; one must unify the will, concentrate the spirit, and seek it with single-minded devotion. Only then may one hope to reach it.
If the mind is divided among other paths, the inner heart will become cluttered, turbid wisdom will circulate, and evil influences will enter from without.
One rides [the vehicle], yet gallops away from this Way. Third, one must not fail to discard long-held interpretations.
When students previously analyzed scriptures or deliberated with teachers and friends, various views arose;

if they cling to these as being real, the spiritual mechanism will be obstructed and wondrous realization will not manifest. One must sweep them away before one can give rise to new awakening. Fourth—

A new understanding must be eliminated; it cannot be allowed to remain. After long and diligent study, a new understanding may suddenly arise all at once, or upon encountering an object, it immediately manifests as the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

This is the realm of cleverness and is precisely the affliction wrought by the *yāma* demons. If the practitioner does not realize this and mistakes it for a sublime awakening, the calamity will not be slight.
One must necessarily awaken to this oneself. Generally speaking, although such an understanding is extremely ingenious, it is [still a delusion].

In short, [the mind] must arise in dependence upon objects; therefore, it is not the ultimate reality. If one does not urgently strive to eradicate it, by what means can the divine mechanism be cleared and penetrated?
These four aforementioned types are all grave illnesses of birth and death. To commit even one of them is to ensure that one's merit will surely be wasted.
One must deeply examine oneself and cut them off completely; only then can one be said to be within the lineage of the School of the Patriarchs.
This is one who applies their mind with true sincerity. Strive on!
To the Chan practitioner Hunpuk:
Those who study the Way today are many, yet those who clarify the Way are few. Is it that the Way is truly difficult to clarify? The fault lies elsewhere.

This is because there is that which is clarified. For the essence of the Way is profound and mysterious; it cannot be sought with a mind possessed of intention, nor can it be realized through a mind devoid of intention.
It cannot be attained through words, nor can it be communicated through silent stillness. Its essential point lies in forgetting emotions and extinguishing views;
then its essence will manifest of itself. Yet, it is like the vast, limpid void—how could it have coming or going? Suddenly, thunder and lightning...
If one gives rise to horizontal proliferation, one loses that which is inherently present. Only when the thunder ceases and the lightning becomes still will the profoundly serene essence be seen.
A practitioner who has investigated for many years cannot be said to have no insight at all; however, because their vision of the truth is not yet pure, the obstructions are not few.

One must simply sweep away all entanglements and, single-mindedly toward that place where there is no seam or fissure, apply the effort of death with intense resolve. From this, [the realization will arise].
However, there is one path of life that penetrates both heaven and earth. The Patriarch said: "There is no need to seek the Truth;
one need only cease seeing. These are the sincere words of the ancient sages; how could they deceive anyone?

To those practitioners of the Way who cultivate the dhyāna of non-arising: one must first empty and still the mind. For it is only when the mind is empty and still that one can mysteriously realize the wondrous principle.
If the mind is not empty, it is like a bottle filled with donkey’s milk; how then could it contain the lion’s [milk]?
Milk. If the mind is not still, it is like a candle in the wind or water with rising waves; how then could it reflect and illuminate the myriad forms?
Therefore, a student must first quiet their thoughts and reduce external conditions so that the mind becomes empty and still;

only then does one have a foundation for entering the Way. Deshan said: "If you simply have no mind regarding affairs and no affairs regarding the mind, it will naturally be empty yet numinous, and tranquil."
This is precisely what is meant by "wondrous. However, one must not settle into a state of empty stillness, drifting aimlessly and idly dwelling within the armor of non-action.
One must instead possess a single thought of genuine and earnest resolve, diligently investigating and vigorously practicing with the urgency of one whose hair is on fire.
Only then can the barrier of delusion be broken and the Great Matter be expected. However, since beginningless kalpas, human beings have been burdened by deep-seated habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

To now seek to overturn these along with one's faculties is no easy task. One must possess firm resolve and constantly apply diligent effort, disregarding the passage of years and months to press forward in one's practice.
Once this has been cultivated for a long time, the mind will naturally become tranquil and unified. How could it be otherwise?
You should seek other expedient means; strive on!
To Zen practitioner Fazhen:
In the past, during the year of Bingzi, I opened the Dharma at Wēnlíng. There I saw that many of the monks within the city placed great weight upon their karmic conditions for merit. I showed them...
Regarding the practice of pure karma at the gate of Shaolin, there have been few who have truly set their minds upon it.

Yet, this spring of the Gengyin year, when the Chan practitioner Fazhen visited me on the summit of Shigushan, I saw that he has set his mind upon the Way of the Patriarchs, refusing to enter the social circles of other schools;
one may truly say he is a man of outstanding resolve, not confined by worldly conventions. However, the present age is in decline.
The Way has become subtle; the style of Chan practice is greatly corrupted. Among students, most value only intellectual understanding and habitually rely on what they have seen and heard;

few are able to take wondrous enlightenment as their goal. Now, the single word "enlightenment" was that which the ancients esteemed; even after attaining enlightenment, one should still sweep it away—how much more so for those who have not yet enlightened at all?
This is because when the conscious mind confronts objects, it discriminates each one individually, being clearly capable of [such discernment].
I understand. Although it may seem that there is Chan to be realized and a Way to be cultivated, the moment even a hair’s breadth of movement occurs, one immediately falls into contradiction.
Therefore, the World-Honored One used the metaphor of wishing to burn Mount Sumeru with the light of a firefly; such a thing can never be achieved.

To the Chan practitioner Hanhui:

This practice is intended to resolve your beginningless ignorance right now; it is no easy matter. If you wish to seek ease, there are other methods available:

One possesses spiritual awareness; for what reason, then, does delusion arise? It is because one is obscured externally by material objects and internally by emotional attachments.

Therefore, the ancient sages spoke with bitter urgency and repeated instructions, not because they had some other teaching to offer, but simply to have you clarify your own mind and realize your own nature.

Later, many gained entry through this very means; it is truly the most expedient among all expedients.
However, regarding this practice of contemplating the *hwadu*, one must possess a sincere mind, resolve upon a steadfast and enduring will, and remain undisturbed by external influences.
Regarding these matters, there is now a time for their illumination. If one lacks a sincere heart, then this very thought is already deluded from the start;
how can one seek awakening? If one does not establish a firm and enduring resolve, then one will act and then desist, like a hen brooding over her eggs whose warmth does not continue;
by what means could anything be achieved? If one is enticed by external things, then distracting thoughts will fly about in confusion, and the mind will become like a monkey.

The monkey is restless and agitated; by what means could it enter? This is precisely why everyone speaks of "investigating Zen" (chán), yet not one in a hundred attains awakening—it is solely due to these three factors.
If you can now follow my instructions and proceed directly forward, how could there be anyone who has investigated for a long time and yet failed to gain power?

I urge the attendants of the assembly and those who study the Way: first, you must maintain the precepts with purity; thereafter, you may either practice Chan meditation or recite the Buddha’s name, according to whichever is most convenient for you.
If you practice Chan, you must be diligent day and night, regarding only the failure to realize the Great Matter as urgent. Observe—
Take up this *hwadu* (critical phrase) and investigate it with single-minded persistence until you reach the state of great rest; only then will you have attained completion.
If there is even the slightest thing unresolved, you must by no means deceive yourself or others by pretending to be an enlightened master (*jñānin*).

If you practice the recitation of the Buddha’s name, simply take these six characters and constantly bring them to mind. Cut off all worldly affairs with a single stroke, leaving nothing behind to which you might cling.

If one possesses this sincere mind and practices diligently without ceasing, there is no need to worry about not being reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang) or failing to achieve the fruit of sainthood.
Strive toward this!
This was shown to the attendant Feijing.
For those who study the Way, nothing is more essential than seeing one's nature (*xing*). Nature has no form or trace; how, then, can it be seen?
It requires nothing more than for you to bring all seeking to rest and not be deluded by various delusions.
Therefore, the ancients said: "Do not seek the Truth; simply let go of views. This reveals the point at which the ancients truly benefited others. When later students see this...
There is absolutely no place to enter. When instructed to contemplate a *gong'an*, those who examine such cases must by all means avoid giving rise to extraneous thoughts.
To give rise to extraneous thoughts is to harbor a "thieving mind"; even in a lifetime as long as that of a donkey, one will find no point of entry.

Therefore, simply give rise to the doubt regarding the *gong'an* and do not abandon it for a single thought-moment. Like a hen brooding her eggs, let the warmth continue uninterrupted. After years and months have passed, [the breakthrough will come].

One will naturally achieve penetration and liberation. However, at the juncture between awakening and non-awakening, if you are turned by false objects, all prior effort will have been in vain. Be careful!
It is shown that every person possesses the fundamental nature of Constant Radiance (*nityaprabhā*). If one constantly reflects inwardly, it will manifest clearly before one;

yet if one pursues external conditions, one will fall into confusion and remain unawakened. Therefore, when the ancients contemplated a *huatou*, they would simply bring their thoughts back to a single point. Not...
Drawn by external objects, after a long time, the objects are forgotten and conditions subside; thus, the originally inherent light naturally reveals itself.
If you give rise to false conjectures, you will enter a mistaken path; if you seek to ask others, it will only increase your confusion.

Therefore, the method of contemplating the *hwadu* (critical phrase) lies solely in maintaining this focus with unwavering persistence so that the spirit of doubt does not dissipate. Great doubt leads to great [awakening].
Awakening: A small doubt leads to a small awakening; without doubt, there is no awakening. This is a matter of certainty.
Nowadays, people are unwilling to examine the *huatou* (critical phrase); they merely spend their time discussing it in groups of three or five, asking, "What is this *huatou* like?
or "What is that *huatou* like? Once they have explained it clearly, they claim to have attained great awakening. Since the masters themselves lack true realization...
With eyes that see only superficial similarities in others' speech, they immediately apply the "winter melon seal" and claim to have attained realization.

Thus, masters and disciples deceive one another, which is why today the ancestral style has declined and grown cold. Consequently, packs of foxes and dogs go about everywhere claiming supremacy to deceive the world;
their entry into hell will be as swift as a shot arrow. If you, Venerable One, wish to practice Zen, [you must do so with true discernment].
By all means, do not fall into the faction of other schools or the host of demons. Exert yourself!
To the Chan practitioner Hanzhang:
My Dharma is fundamentally without words; my words are not the Dharma. Simply knowing that the Dharma is without Dharma is itself the true Dharma.

Why is this? As soon as one enters the realm of language, it conversely becomes a source of defilement. You must know that when understanding is severed and emotions forgotten, a single phrase naturally reflects the earth and illuminates the heavens.
If you merely dwell upon words and phrases, scrutinizing them one by one, it is just like a firefly wishing to burn Mount Sumeru;
such a thing is impossible. Now that you have resolved to investigate the Way, simply take up a single phrase that has no meaning.

Taste the words. Constantly maintain this mindfulness. After a long time, clouds will naturally part and the sun will appear; what need is there then to worry that the void is not brightly illuminated?

As a leader of the Sangha, one must first be honest and sincere. In dealing with others, one must always prioritize compassion. To settle the mind in a state of detachment is the essential path for nurturing virtue;
to practice diligently and refine one's conduct is truly the excellent rule for becoming a sage. If you wish to proceed to the Lotus Land, do not harbor lingering attachments to the realm of desire.
To understand the intent of the Patriarchs, you must first sever the thieving mind. When speaking, refrain from causing harm to others; when facing affairs...
One should especially contemplate the principles of reality. Only through magnanimity can one win the hearts of the multitude; only through frugality can one cultivate integrity.

In times of chaos, one must skillfully conceal oneself and withdraw to maintain silence. Since our merit is meager, how else can we avoid regret? By remaining tranquil and minimizing worldly pursuits, one should uphold the standard of the Middle Way and Rectitude.
One should associate with beneficial friends to contemplate the elimination of depraved habits, and never become intimate with those who are unwholesome. Be respectful in one’s dealings with others.
Wherever one goes, nothing will be beneficial. To be arrogant and rely on one's own spirit leads to instability at every turn;
grand claims inevitably invite resentment. A cautious mind ultimately results in few transgressions. Those who lightly disparage the precepts are surely unrestrained monastics;

those who delight in speaking of worldly glory can hardly be considered noble and virtuous men. Those who rush toward profit forget righteousness; those who disregard kindness lack benevolence. Their eyes are blind.

How can one be of service to others if, in the end, one only brings about self-destruction? If your strength is small yet you restlessly contemplate heavy responsibilities, it will inevitably lead to the loss of life.
You may follow the tracks of the sages and worthies; do not neglect even the words of the common folk.

Now that you have entered the ranks of the monastic community, you should adhere to the Buddha’s regulations. Do not follow the company of the mediocre and inferior, nor borrow the support of heterodox resources.

Do not emulate the reckless and arrogant who greedily pursue indulgence and laxity. In establishing your resolve, you must surely model yourself after the ancients; in examining your conduct, you must by no means yield to private interests.
When one examines the books of ancient sages, they are nothing other than precious instructions. To strictly follow the rules of the Vinaya is truly to have an enlightened teacher.

What conduct could ever fail to embody the character of *shu* (forgiveness) throughout one’s life? The words of Confucius are not erroneous; all six lines of the hexagram *Qian* (Humility) are auspicious—let us never forget the teachings of the *I Ching*.
Do not envy the long; for by envying the long, you remain forever short. Do not conceal your own shortcomings; for by concealing them, you will never become long.
Light and frivolous speech is certainly not the mark of one destined for greatness. Only those whose gait and conduct are upright and prudent possess the capacity to undertake the Way.
The style of Chan has already declined; you should maintain the integrity of steadfast poverty. The ways of the world have long been lost; cease attempting to engineer a grand transformation.
This is its name. Those who crave greatness and seek glory achieve little but ruin much; those who lack integrity and have no sense of shame—what honor can they find even if they gain it?
It is better to preserve one’s integrity and follow conditions as they arise; how could one forget oneself to pursue external things?

I have received your instruction, which states that since there is fundamentally nothing to be concerned with, how can one allow deluded doubt to arise? To forget it is oneness;
to doubt it is duality. Therefore, teaching people to give rise to doubt is said to be "using a poison as medicine. In my humble opinion, forgetting it is superior to doubting it.
It is exactly as the Tathāgata has instructed. However, regarding the single word "forgetting," there must also be some clarification.

There is forgetting through delusion, forgetting through awakening, forgetting naturally, and forgetting through deliberate effort (*manasikāra*). If one’s attachments have not yet been shattered, can one truly forget by means of deliberate effort?
Even if one claims to be able to do so, it would merely result in a state of dullness and obscurity.
It is so. If the thought of doubt is indeed an obstacle to the essence of awakening, then for those with resolve, they may skillfully utilize its momentum;
conversely, they can even borrow it as a technique for breaking through obstacles. This is because doubt and awakening—
Their mechanisms depend upon one another; their forces are mutually contingent; and their principle is a single, pervasive unity. Therefore, those who seek awakening must value doubt.
Allow me to explain this in detail for you, Layman. As for the mechanism of the human mind, if it does not coalesce into a state of density, it cannot achieve expansive clarity.

It is like the closing of all passages during the height of winter, which truly nurtures the Great Origin (Tàiyuán). If the vital energy were to leak away without being preserved, then its subsequent sprouting and flourishing would be impossible.
It would certainly lack the necessary power. Therefore, the value of doubt lies in its capacity for focused concentration.
Without deeply investigating the source of the Dharma-realm, one will surely be unable to reach far. It is like a solitary army in a snowy night pressing deep into the city of Cai;

capturing Yuanji upon his bed—how could this be considered beyond one's reach? If, however, one leads a scattered and disorganized force to roam the outer districts, looking toward the city of Cai as if it were... [distant].

It is sublime! Therefore, the value placed on doubt lies in the fact that when one values doubt, one investigates it deeply. Thus we know that doubt is the cause of awakening, and awakening is the fruit of doubt;
it is almost as certain as darkness must have its light, or inhalation must have its exhalation. How can one not doubt? How can one not doubt?
When one reaches the point of awakening through doubt, even awakening no longer exists—how then could doubt remain?
This is precisely what you, Reverend Sir, meant by "forgetting them, they become one. How could I further worry that he might resent this and act like a pharmacist?
These are the deluded and ignorant words of a madman; I fear they may offend your profound discernment. I only hope you will deign to consider them with favor. Sincerely yours.
When discussing with the Sangha, they did not permit me to practice Chan.
