To cling to the literal meaning and adhere to the commentary is for Chan to become the Teachings; to transcend the literal meaning and realize the mind is for the Teachings to be called Chan. Formerly, Yong...
Jia was refined in the contemplative methods of Tiantai; upon reading the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, he attained a realization. Later, he visited Caoxi and received formal certification (in-ka).
He then said: "The Buddha’s explicit command points directly to Caoxi; is there truly a distinction between Chan and the Teachings?

Changshui had mastered the three studies and preached the Dharma like clouds. Upon meeting Langya, he asked: "If the fundamental nature is pure and still, how does it suddenly give rise [to phenomena]?"
"Mountains, rivers, and the great earth. Xue replied, "It is originally pure; how could mountains, rivers, and the great earth suddenly arise? Thereupon, the water suddenly cleared.
He returned to lecture on the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra*, whereupon the heavens rained down flowers. Is there, then, truly a distinction between Chan and the Teachings? Now I have heard this.
The Master offered this instruction: "In one's practice, it is appropriate to follow the Buddha’s teachings; it is not appropriate to engage in Chan meditation.
The Chan school was established as a provisional expedient by later generations. To rely upon it for cultivation leads to many errors.

If the Master’s argument is correct, would it then be right to say that Yongjia and Changshui did not follow the Buddha’s teachings, but instead accepted the provisional expedients of later generations? Furthermore, the Buddha said: [text continues]
From the beginning at the Deer Park until the end at Vaidiśa, not a single word was ever spoken in the interim; what, then, is the teaching that you, Master, follow?
When the World-Honored One held up a flower and Kāśyapa smiled, he said: "I possess a special transmission outside the teachings, the wondrous mind of Nirvāṇa, which I entrust to Mahākāśyapa.
These are all explicit texts of the Buddha’s teaching; why do you alone, Master, reject them?
"Should you follow them? For the most part, the teachings employ many indirect demonstrations, whereas Chan points directly. These indirect and direct methods adapt to the capacities of beings;

the Buddha-mind is not divided between them. If you, Master, insist on abolishing Chan and following the teachings alone, then you not only do not understand Chan, but you do not understand the teachings either."
Furthermore, I have heard the Master say: "If one studies the teachings, one gains excellent understanding as a resource for this life and will surely obtain the retribution of wisdom in the future.

If one practices Chan meditation without awakening, one will remain like someone facing a blank wall for the rest of their life, greatly losing the benefits of the Dharma. Judging by this, he concludes that one should not practice Chan meditation.
I, being ignorant, beg to clarify this with an analogy: practicing Chan meditation without awakening is like studying the classics without passing the civil service examinations.
This is the case. To derive benefit from studying the teachings is like obtaining an official post by paying a bribe.

Now that one can obtain an official post simply by paying a bribe, would it be right to encourage those who study the books to instead pay such bribes, on the grounds that reading them makes it difficult to pass the examinations? Is this permissible?
To leave the household life and set one's resolve, one should vow to attain Bodhi; yet, to settle one’s mind upon the study of scholastic exegesis is not the aspiration of a son of the Śākya.
Furthermore, although those who practice Chan have not yet attained thorough realization, their benefit must surely be greater than that of those who merely study the teachings.
This is because a single thought-moment of practicing Chan is the arousal of the unsurpassed mind to seek unsurpassed wisdom. Its...
How could the merit of this have any limit? With every thought-moment, it inwardly perfumes the mind, secretly increasing the seeds of wisdom.

In the present life, it will surely cause delusions to thin and hindrances to dissolve, bringing forth a gathering of auspiciousness. In future lives, it will surely act as the cause for Bodhi and bring about the fruit of Nirvana. As the Patriarch said:
"When you emerge from the head once more, hearing it but once, you will awaken to a thousand things. These words are ultimately not false. Even if one examines the teachings, although now...
They will be reborn in future lives and both shall receive extraordinary benefits. However, the essential point is this: distraction and cleverness ultimately constitute obstacles to the Way.
In antiquity, there were even those who received the retribution of stupidity; this was because their minds lacked right contemplation and instead roamed toward external objects.
How could one avoid becoming bewildered by the passage of generations? Comparing these two approaches together: practicing Chan without attaining awakening truly serves as the cause for awakening;

whereas studying the teachings and gaining benefit merely increases the path of intellectual understanding. Practicing Chan involves directing the mind inward, which truly combines the merit of cultivating the mind;
whereas studying the teachings involves directing the mind outward, entirely lacking the power of "returning the hearing. Thus, the benefit [of the former] is indeed...

What is greater than this? If one says, "I take the recitation of the Buddha's name as my primary practice, and the study of scriptures to support my correct faith," then the Dharma-gate of Pure Land is perfectly sound and appropriate;
who would dare to dispute it? However, to cling exclusively to one method while rejecting others is the fault of the teacher.

If one says that the single method of Chan meditation cannot be received by those of middling or inferior faculties, and that such people must instead enter the path gradually—[this too is a limitation].

Thus, one should teach according to the faculties [of the students]; this has been the single path for the thousand Buddhas. Who would dare to debate it? Yet, to block everyone indiscriminately is the fault of the teacher.
Moreover, since the restoration of the Ming dynasty two hundred years ago, the single thread of the direct transmission has remained as fragile as a thin strand of silk.
We, your followers, are living in this era of decline and decay; we have been unable to expand and propagate [the teachings] widely.

How could we allow the mind’s cycle of arising and ceasing to run wild, thereby allowing the ancestral Way to become even more obscured? I hope that you, Master, will broaden your boundless great perspective and accept this single insight from a fool;
then this Way would be most fortunate. As I write these words, I am overcome with awe and trepidation. I humbly pray that you, like the vast ocean, will grant me your forbearance.
I have repeatedly received your instructions from Mr.

Cao Zhai of Shaxian, all of which rely upon the scriptural texts. Since the Buddha’s intent can be relied upon, it is clearly not erroneous. Nevertheless, I, this mountain monk, ultimately cannot agree with you.
This is certainly not out of self-conceit or a desire to be obstinate; rather, it is because the scriptural passages upon which you rely are—[and so forth].
This is an expedient, provisional teaching. If one were to rely solely on the words to produce understanding, one would fall into the obstacle of intellectual reasoning.
A true man of great capacity would certainly not do so; he must break free from the nest and transcend the conventional to utter a single word of the Way.

Only then does the stage of "studying the Way" begin. Otherwise, even if one can explain the teachings with flawless precision—drawing insights from fragmentary manuscripts through one's own clever intelligence—how could such understanding ever oppose birth and death?

Under the gate of Bodhidharma, the proclamation of this matter primarily requires the severing of right and wrong, the extinguishing of contemplative wisdom, the forgetting of principles, and the departure from mind and consciousness; only then can one transcend birth and death.
Thus, one continues the ancestral lamp. Therefore, every subsequent word must be like the blade of the Tai-ā sword:
to touch it is to be wounded; it is like a drum smeared with poison: to hear it is to perish. How can one rely on scriptural explanations of meaning as an old *śāstrin* (lecturer) might?

Furthermore, it is commonly said that the matter of birth and death is great and must be urgently eradicated. Yet, when its root source is investigated, it is certainly nothing other than this very moment. Now...
To be "alert and lucid" while investigating principles within the sutras and treatises, and distinguishing between right and wrong, is precisely what is meant [by being caught].
If you now merely continue to pore over and analyze these scriptural wheels, you are only further nourishing the roots and deepening the source;
how could there ever be a day of liberation? Therefore, those who wish to transcend birth and death must directly uproot them.

As for the source: if one wishes to eliminate its very root, it cannot be relied upon by depending on people, nor can it be relied upon by depending on the Buddha, nor can it be relied upon by depending on any of the sutras or treatises.

One must take all that has been studied and understood throughout one’s life and, with a single stroke, cut it in two and cast it away beyond the worlds of the ten directions. Only then may one take up a single phrase that is devoid of meaning.
Lift it up once! Whether regarding birth or death, whether distant or near—once right mindfulness becomes singular, the conscious intellect naturally vanishes.
When the conscious intellect vanishes, the True Eye opens wide; the ten realms settle into equanimity, and the task of the Great Man is complete.
This is what is called "entering birth-and-death and transcending birth-and-death"—they are not two separate things.

Is this not superfluous talk? Your Excellency possesses spiritual bones from former lives; you seem to be of no ordinary rank. Therefore, I have ventured to pour out my heart, unconsciously becoming prolix.

The celestial patterns are distant, yet they are hidden within; the terrestrial veins are submerged, yet they are manifest; the transformations of the vital energies are subtle, yet they must be perceived with penetrating clarity, as if pointing at one's own palm.
When you are then gently asked, "What is your original life-spirit? you will immediately become bewildered and lose your bearings.
That which requires urgency is treated with excessive laxity; that which requires patience is treated with excessive haste. That which is most remote is made out clearly; that which is most near...
This is merely partial darkness. What is the reason for this? It is simply because the ears, eyes, mind, and thoughts are deluded by external objects;

they then rush outward in haste, pursuing every single distinction. Consequently, while one may appear to be clear and precise regarding worldly affairs, as for one’s own original life-source (the *benming yuanchen*), it must not be deluded by external objects.
Only when emotions are forgotten, consciousness severed, and all discrimination brought to rest can there be a silent resonance with the truth. Therefore—
Those who truly know this are few indeed. Furthermore, there is a certain class of people who claim to have devoted themselves to this Way, yet they merely make their livelihood out of books.
They take their deluded consciousness and scrutinize it point by point, or attempt to provide intellectual explanations.

Though they say they are investigating the mind, they actually create great obstacles; how then could they ever attain silent resonance? Now, you, venerable sir, are approaching the age of fifty; you are no longer...
Compared to my youth, how much more so now that my rank has increased, my administration has become more complex, my responsibilities have grown heavier, and my concerns have expanded further?

I fear that the malady of being busily pursued by external affairs is actually far worse than being buried beneath the weeds and brambles; if so, when will this great matter ever be brought to completion?
Is it perhaps that you, venerable sir, require excellence in all matters, yet alone do not require excellence in this one? I pray, venerable sir...
In the autumn of your greatest fame and glory, you must by no means forget this thought.

Even if you cannot set aside your busy affairs to decline worldly distractions and devote yourself exclusively to this Way, you should at least, amidst the clamor and confusion, constantly contemplate:
"Which of these is my original life-spirit? Do not speak of principles; do not form intellectual interpretations. Simply maintain this single thought at all times, and then—
In the future, when one transcends birth and death and realizes Bodhi, it is precisely this single thought that serves as the seed.

If there is a latent affinity from past lives, the spiritual root will suddenly sprout; encountering sound or form, one may strike upon it abruptly, attaining sudden and thorough realization even without waiting to emerge from the midst of clamor and confusion.
Once this stage is reached, one is able to manifest the great capacity for awakening.
He manifests the great function: it is permissible for him to follow in the footsteps of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors;

it is permissible for him to revile Confucius, Laozi, and Zhuangzi; it is permissible for him to discourse on military strategy; it is permissible for him to manage the taming of floods. He cuts off everything at once.

Standing atop a ten-thousand-fathom peak, he gazes at the Milky Way—this is also permissible. This is because, without exception, the wondrous essence is reflected therein; thus, without exception, the wondrous function is inconceivable. From the Monastery.
Friends, only you, my elder, possess true faith; yet regarding the ultimate point, you lack the resolve to take it up and bear it. Consequently, you find yourself overwhelmed by trivialities.
The paths of the monastic and the lay are distinct, and my private concern for this is quite keen. I humbly entreat you to grant me your enlightened understanding; it would be most fortunate.

In response: I have received your kind remembrance, O Zen practitioner of the Three Mountains, as evidenced by the gracious arrival of your jade-like letter. I imagined that you must surely possess some new realization capable of assisting me.

However, upon opening and reading it, I find you claim that the true pulse of the Dharma-gate should consist solely in meeting people through the application of spiritual skill (*jikyō*), and that one ought not to transmit the teaching to others.
"Dead word, dead effort. Alas, what words are these! As for the true lineage of the Dharma-gate, it is not something you know;
let us set that aside for now. Yet as for this "dead effort," one step further upon the word-phrase (*huatou*), it is truly not my own speculative theory.
In the past, Huangbo initiated it, and various masters have followed and upheld it, with Dahui especially advocating for it. Indeed...
Dahui revitalized the Way of the Jiabei lineage. Was it that his spiritual capacity and function were not fully equipped?
Rather, in instructing those who came to study, he uniformly employed a single phrase as a *huatou* (critical phrase) to block their throats and exhaust their cleverness.
Only then did he manifest great capacity and great function to stimulate their essential radiance. Consequently, more than forty people relied upon this method and attained realization.
In short, the pedagogical methods of the master and the diligent practice of the student must both be mutually appropriate before success can be achieved.

If one fails to urge forward their own practice and instead relies solely on pedagogical methods to engage others, then how many of those with superior faculties and capacities—who would understand the ultimate destination upon the spot—could there possibly be?
One will see that those of middling and inferior dispositions will forever lose the benefit of the Dharma.
Yet those who plundered the void took advantage of the prevailing wind and followed the echoes; thus, the single school of Bodhidharma was swept away entirely.
Now, when Bodhidharma came from the West and sat facing a wall for nine years, it may be said that he stood like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high.

Yet, when it came to guiding Shen Guang, he did not abandon skillful means, saying: "You must simply cease all external conditions and let the internal mind be free of agitation, so that the mind is like a wall."
This can lead one into the Way; this is precisely what is meant by the teaching of "unceasing effort" (*gongfu*). If effort does not cease, then emotional consciousness will arise recklessly:
one will either be distractedly pursuing fame and profit, or become deeply mired in intellectual understanding. Even if one possesses functional capacity (*jīyòng*), how could it be applied?

As for the true lineage of the Dharma-gate, how could it involve such functional capacity? This is not only the case for those who contemplate the *huatou*. [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly, leaving the final thought incomplete.]

To give rise to branches and nodes—this is to have already produced such complications as soon as one enters the gate. To strike with the staff upon entering the gate, or to shout upon entering the gate, is already to have generated branches and nodes.

Now, to hold this as the orthodox lineage is not merely a matter of being wrong by a thousand or ten thousand degrees. The Way of Zhou was as smooth as a whetstone; I pray you will quickly change your jade.
If you persist in your former errors, it will be no benefit to you. Be cautious! Be cautious!
In response to the instructions sent by you, the Honorable Ying: To single-mindedly uphold the Name while concurrently reading the Mahāyāna sūtras is an excellent method for the Pure Land;

this dharma-gate is perfectly appropriate and entirely fitting—how could there be need for further elaboration? My only concern is that you might not maintain it with firm resolve or practice it for long, so that on another day...
Without awareness or knowledge, one strays onto a divergent path and loses the sheep; how much more so for those who merely recite the Name—who would not say this?

I have often seen brothers who spend their time muddling through drowsiness and distraction with only the single phrase "Amitābha Buddha," claiming, "I recite it several thousand or tens of thousands of times every day. When the thirtieth day of the twelfth month arrives, their hands—
In their frantic confusion, they say that the Buddha-dharma lacks efficacy. How could it truly lack efficacy? It is simply that their recitation is not the correct recitation.
I, the fool, maintain that the single gate of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation) must never be approached with indolence or sluggishness, nor used as an excuse for procrastination.
You must immediately rouse a single thought, like a long sword leaning against the heavens, leaving no place for the two demons of dullness and distraction to flee;
like a fierce fire in a red furnace, causing the emotional consciousnesses of beginningless time to melt away without remainder. Then, one thought of the Buddha, one thought of the Western Land;
ten thoughts of the Buddha, ten thoughts of the Western Land; a thousand thoughts, ten thousand thoughts of the Buddha, a thousand thoughts, ten thousand thoughts of the Western Land.

When one reaches the point of overturning the old molds and re-establishing heaven and earth, then whether laughing, smiling, scolding, or reviling; whether defecating or urinating—there is nothing that is not the Western Land.

How then could one even ask about rebirth there? If today you remain as you were before, you are merely a person of this Sahā world, ranked among the seven, eight, three, or four, half-up or half-down.
If you wish to be born in that land at the moment of death, will it not be difficult? Will it not be difficult?

Ah! At present, your physical body is healthy and your spirit is sharp and clear. Yet, when you suddenly encounter circumstances and conditions, you find yourself unable to push them aside when you wish to do so, and unable to remain seated when you wish to do so.

You must wait for the day when the eight sufferings press upon you all at once, hoping that a single thought will accord with the Dharma so that the Buddha may come to guide you—can this truly be achieved?
Honored as you are in your inquiry, I shall not decline to reveal these matters; your wisdom is truly lofty.
What do you think of this?

Previously, when I received your esteemed letter from Li Qinglang, the Mochai, I learned that you, sir, are able to turn toward this gate and have resolved your will in such a manner; I sighed in admiration more than twice. Every time I...

In the presence of others, he frequently praised Master Li of the Eastern House. When Layman Han-chu came to the mountain, I further heard that he disciplines himself with integrity and regulates the assembly with solemnity;
thus, it became increasingly clear that Feikong was not one who merely indulged in empty talk. Alas! In this degenerate age of decline, how could such a person exist?
In the marketplace of fame and profit, those who see it scatter their spirits; yet when the words of the Great Way are heard, listeners cover their mouths [in awe].
Indeed, it is not only that the customs of the age have been corrupted by the winds of decadence and that people are unable to support themselves;

it is also because their intelligence is inferior and their natures are vulgar, such that they willingly accept the cycle of rebirth as a wheel-turning monarch. Yet now, you, sir, are able to face this world and resolutely extricate yourself, desiring to reach the very depths of the ancient sages' realization.
I had not expected to see the majestic dignity of a Han official once again today. However, as for the entry into this Way, it has not yet—
It can be easily attained. One must not seek it within one's own thoughts, nor should one beg it from the lips of others.

One must directly forget both person and dharma; only then will the true eye suddenly open. Thereafter, all speech and all knowledge and views will be seen as entirely irrelevant to the essential reality.
Only then is one called a true man (*puruṣa*). If one perceives even the slightest thing as being attainable...

If there is a place where one perceives, a place that is delightful, a place that can be deliberated upon, or a place that can be asserted— these are all demonic heterodoxies and not my followers. Or,
if one slightly perceives a place where nothing can be seen, a place that is not delightful, a place that cannot be deliberated upon,
or a place that cannot be asserted— this too is a demonic heterodoxy and not my follower, just as it is today.
There are certain individuals among the scholar-official class who borrow Confucian exegesis to support Buddhist discourse and cite Buddhist teachings to explain Confucianism.
They do not fail to consider themselves novel and transcendent; yet regarding this Way, they are truly like those intoxicated or insane.

Furthermore, by widely inciting heterodox doctrines and deceiving later students, their transgression reaches unto Heaven. For the realm of the single mind is certainly not all things; if one does not follow...
Pressing into the place where there is not a single seam or crevice, one must undergo the total shedding of the entire body before one can take up the burden.

Even if one possesses hundreds or thousands of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and hundreds or thousands of meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), in the end one will become nothing more than a lowly ghost. If you wish to engage in this matter, can you afford not to choose the correct gate through which to enter?
Should you be able to set aside your busy schedule to enter the mountains, I shall still have further matters to offer my humble devotion.

I, [Name], a scholar of the Zhu family, have by misfortune fallen into the ranks of the monastic order. Being base, impure, and without renown, I have been undeservedly favored with your transformative guidance; for this I am moved by gratitude and feel deep shame.

However, regarding the matter of Mount Hu, I ultimately did not dare to set a finger upon it, not out of any desire to maintain a narrow integrity or exalt myself, but simply because I am not a resident [monk].
I am merely a monk of this hermitage. I shaved my head and entered the mountains solely for the sake of the two characters "birth-and-death" (saṃsāra).
As for fields, households, and kin, I have long since spat upon and cast them aside; how could I now reclaim what I have already discarded? This is the first reason I cannot remain in this hermitage.

Furthermore, by nature I am dissipated and unacquainted with worldly affairs; being迂拙 (yūzhuó—obstinate and clumsy), I follow my own whims and find it difficult to conform to the tastes of the times. This is...

Second, one must not dwell in a mountain hermitage. I have received the precepts and vows of my late master, which dictate that I shall not involve myself in worldly affairs nor seek the favor of the powerful and noble.
My alms bowl and water jar follow wherever conditions lead, and I do not store even a single coin. If I were to dwell in a hermitage, from where would I obtain oil, salt, tea, and rice?
This is why I cannot dwell in a hermitage; this is the third reason. Furthermore, I have heard that when the monks of Jiancheng saw officials and gentlemen—
In ritual propriety, one now ranks below the common people; this is a sign that the Way is perishing. How can one not weep with bitter sorrow?

Therefore, from my arrival here, I have never lightly cast a visiting card, nor have I ever returned a formal call when someone came to see me unbidden. Yet, if I am favored with an invitation, I comply.
I have used various pretexts to avoid it; this was certainly not out of arrogance or contempt. Rather, I considered that such is the proper demeanor for a monk.

This is the fourth reason why I cannot remain in the hermitage. Now, Master Yuan and his son have honored me with their correspondence; their profound affection is exceptional and their humble grace is truly admirable, leaving me feeling deeply ashamed.
Yet, what can I do about my inability to stay in the hermitage? It is simply a matter of the conditions for its construction.
For one who is a son of the Śākya, it is right to exhaust all effort in supporting this cause; how could one dare to cherish oneself?
As for the affairs of the hermitage, they shall still be entrusted to the resident monks for management. There is no need to speak further; I await your arrival with all my heart and soul.
Furthermore, Mr. Li Qinglang, a scholar of refined cultivation, borrowed my bed for lodging;
at that time, he received profound teachings and was moved by your noble friendship, which deepened his sense of gratitude. Since we parted and returned to the mountains, [I have remained here].

News had not yet reached me. In the third month, I received a letter from you, the Minister of Agriculture (Siheng), by which I first learned that you have emerged as the foremost among the many scholars.
It was clear that your jade-like brilliance could not remain hidden for long; I also understood that the pursuit of the Way does not obstruct one’s engagement with the world.
Your letter states: "The people of this world are tossed about by the winds of karma like puppets; it is truly laughable and pitiable. This is indeed as you have said. However, please...
If one pushes back and investigates from the very point where they are tossed about by the winds of karma, the meaning of the "puppet" (*kūttaka*) becomes increasingly refined.
As the meaning of the puppet becomes increasingly refined, there is neither the ridiculous to be seen nor the pitiable to be found. Body and mind vanish of their own accord without being discarded;
the world is not observed, yet it is fundamentally quiescent. Thus, that which was called a "puppet" has already been transformed into the broad and long tongue.
The "Phenomena" (xiàng) are precisely what the Three Piṭakas expound and what the Five Schools point toward; how could there be anything that transcends this?
Now, you, who hold the balance, have summoned me with this note, wishing to investigate the ancient legacy of the Nine Worthies. After the Duanwu Festival, we shall surely meet again.
Is not the meaning of the puppet (kùlěi) thereby made clear? Upon my arrival, I intend to prepare a *bācān* (concluding retreat) feast for you; I only—
I trust you are attending to these matters; it would be most fortunate.

This letter is sent to Cai Siheng, a man of talent, at the beginning of the second month of spring. Previously, when I met with Chen Lianglao, he said that your carriage had not yet arrived at the commandery. It was only upon receiving your letter that I learned of your arrival.
I have now come to understand that you returned to your district immediately upon arrival. Your letter states: "On the day of my return, all worldly concerns were utterly stilled;
yet there remains one great matter that I have not clarified, for which I feel true shame and remorse. All day long I am distracted and listless, as if I have lost something.
If you truly possess such an intention, then you are not far from entering the Way. However, you further remarked: "It was like the dispersal of a late-night game, after the wine had been drained."
When the guest has departed, the state of desolation that arises is precisely what is meant by being "dazed as if having lost something"—this is already discerned in the second moment of thought.

For example, when a person suddenly loses a precious treasure, they are so urgent in their search that how could they have the leisure to attend to the late hour, idle diversions, or the like while experiencing such a state of desolation? Generally speaking, for one who studies the Way...
Gentlemen, you should take only the fact that the Great Way is not yet clearly understood as your concern. You must by no means give rise to a second thought.

Furthermore, worldly conditions are like illusions and transformations; birth is not truly born, and extinction is not truly extinguished. If you perceive birth and extinction as real, you have already erred.
To then respond with joy or sorrow is not it the height of error? [End of] "Nine Worthies' Letter," forged.

The errors in this work are numerous; to distance myself from defiling the wisdom of the former sages by deleting and correcting them has been my long-held aspiration. Having now received your gracious summons, how could I dare not hasten to attend?
I intend to leave the mountain after the Dragon Boat Festival; there is no need for you to send anyone to meet me. As for the affairs of Zhongshan, we shall deliberate upon them once I have arrived.

In reply: When I went to pay my respects at the residence of Great Master Wengu, I was suddenly compelled to return due to worldly obligations. I have not yet been able to fully receive his instructions on the Dharma, which leaves me with a profound sense of regret.

Regarding the encomiums for the portraits of the various patriarchs that he commissioned me to compose, I have been hindered by other circumstances and have not yet completed them promptly; this remains the case until this month.
I have just begun to prepare this; I am presenting it to you in its complete form. Before the box had even left my door, Master Xiong arrived from the capital.
To receive your precious calligraphy and to be further honored by your generous gifts—my gratitude and shame are beyond measure.

Regarding the lower scroll of the Patriarch’s portrait, while it was lost at Yanjin by the scholar Shen, it has now been transmitted from over two thousand li away in Hunan by Grand Councilor Cao. Without prior consultation, these events coincide; first one, then the other.
It is not inappropriate; the opportunity is indeed most extraordinary. However, I reflect that the request made by Lord Cao rests primarily upon the Great Master’s magnificent brush.
Who am I to dare take the place of a master craftsman in carving? Moreover, the Great Master Han’s grand literary style is like the light of the sun and moon;
for me to presumptuously add my own feathers to his ermine fur would mean that the torchlight has long since ceased its illumination. May those who observe this not [view it as such].
It would be deemed vulgar; one would surely consider it madness. This would establish an invitation for slander and open a rift for offense.

However, as the Venerable One has issued this command, I dare not remain obstinate in my own ways; therefore, I have thought to exert myself to compose this work and present it to report back on your instructions.

I do so only in the hope that your compassionate grace will provide the chisel and file to refine it. As for disseminating it throughout the four quarters, how could I ever presume to do so? I previously heard that the Elder of Yifeng—
His lofty character and profound realization serve as a true beacon for this degenerate age. My heart is moved by an intense sense of longing;
considering that such a person exists at this very time, how could we allow him to be obscured and his legacy lost? However, the responsibility for this truly rests with you, Great Master.
I beg you to record his life in detail and have it published for transmission—this would be a great event for our day. What do you think?
I reply to Mr. Weng, a man of talent:

Previously, you honored this humble temple with your visit, yet I had not yet had the opportunity to receive your refined presence. Upon receiving your elegant verse, I first realized that it was no work of the mundane world.
Furthermore, having received your letter, I learned that you have already resolved upon the Great Mind and possess right faith; truly, such a state is not easily attained.
In the past, there were those who knew their way home upon seeing the shadow of a single pagoda; there were those who attained awakening when a hand was beckoned across a river.
Does true understanding, then, depend on physical form or outward traces? However, since you have taken the care of your parents as your primary duty, how could you possibly abandon them?

This is because filial piety is the foremost among the great precepts, and filial piety is the very foundation of attaining Buddhahood. To be able to serve one’s two parents well is itself equivalent to...
This is also making offerings to all Buddhas. Furthermore, the teachings state: "In every dharma there is fundamentally no dharma; when observing the mind, how can there be a mind?

It also says: "Receiving form, it remains empty form; hearing sound, it does not obstruct sound. If this is truly so, what division could there be between transcending the world and entering the world?
It is only because people have traditionally sought understanding through the literal meanings of words and principles that one speaks of "no-dharma."

There is no mind, yet in reality there is a dharma that possesses mind; one speaks of the emptiness of form and the emptiness of sound, yet in reality there is form and there is sound—this is something you cannot deceive yourself about.

Now, if you wish to know the fundamental mastery for entering both the mundane and the supramundane, you must decisively cut off all such verbal explanations and intellectual understandings while seated in meditation, and turn solely toward the words of the sages and worthies, [realizing them] in actual fact.
Go and investigate! It is like the Way of the *Zhongyong*, where "the hawk soars and the fish leap"—this is the manifestation and observation of this very Way.

Now, simply look: how is it that the soaring hawk and leaping fish are themselves the Way? You must not attempt to fathom this with the calculating mind; you must not explain it through words and language;
you are not permitted to seek clarification or debate it with teachers or friends. Rather, silently and in earnest, go and investigate it within yourself day after day.

Many months have passed. Now that the clouds have parted and the sun has appeared, I have naturally attained awakening. Thus, I realize that the previous discussions regarding the existence or non-existence of dharmas were all merely frivolous arguments (*prapañca*).
I am honored by the gift of your excellent verse, which sufficiently attests to your refined elegance. I regret that my own work is withered and clumsy, leaving me unable to offer a worthy response.
I have inscribed this small piece and present it to you herewith. With these renewed greetings.
In response to your letter, Mr.
Pan Maocai, you state that the mark of self and other is difficult to exhaust. Is this not true not only for you, but for all the sages and ordinary people of the Three Teachings?
It is truly determined by this: to have a self is called being an ordinary person; to be without a self is called being a sage. However, the root of this mark of self is extremely deep. Indeed...
This illness arises from the very root of one's original destiny. It cannot be removed by those who explain principles;
it cannot be removed by those who strive to restrain their minds; nor can it be removed by those who clarify the mind and cease their thoughts.
One must directly open a single eye before the birth of father and mother. Then, how could there be any "self" or "other" to be found? Nevertheless...

That which is called "prior to the birth of one's parents" is not something obtained through superficial conjecture or careless estimation. It requires that the person themselves engage in deep investigation and thorough inquiry.
If, suddenly, one penetrates this within the inconceivable, then subject and object will be forgotten, right and wrong will vanish, and the holy and the ordinary will become one.
What, then, are Confucius and Laozi? Not only Confucius and Laozi, but all the thousands of worthies and myriad sages as well.
There is truly no other path to realization. May you exert yourself in this.

Furthermore, Master Fayan, I am deeply honored that you graced my humble temple with your presence and I hoped to receive your great teachings; I did not expect such a sudden parting, which leaves my heart with profound regret. May you carry on [the lineage].

I offer my greetings with these words of praise and thank you for your kind inquiries. Regarding the *Five Lamps* (*Wudeng*) which you have presented as proof of the teachings, it is evident that your heart is diligent in the pursuit of the Dharma;
this is truly not an easy matter. However, in my humble opinion, the conflict between Chan and the Exegesis (*jiang*) is like forcibly carving out space within the void.

From antiquity to the present, this malady has persisted for no small number of days. Why, then, must one specifically compile a single book today? Moreover, your natural endowment is lofty and brilliant.

With a mind serene and profound, one should protect the Dharma-gate and strive for what is truly great. Today, if a school does not constitute a true school, it need not wait for the masters of the Teaching (the Exegetical School) to condemn it;
if the Teaching does not constitute true Teaching, it need not wait for the masters of the School (the Sectarian School) to condemn it. It merely serves to delude and confuse sentient beings.
It is as bitter as arsenic or aconite. Whenever I contemplate this in the deep of night, I cannot help but shed tears again and again.
If you, sir, would now take the trouble to investigate its meaning deeply and propagate it widely, would not the merit of protecting the Way be even more far-reaching and great?

I have previously examined several points from your "Discussions on the Refutation of Catholicism. While the reasoning in all instances is flawless, there are certain passages in the phrasing that seem somewhat obstructive.
I beg you to re-examine these so that they may be put into practice. Other matters I shall discuss in person. With many respects.

I reply: It has been ten years since I last saw my teacher, the Golden Immortal (Kāñcanamuni). Having suddenly received your elegant letter with its consoling words, I know that your noble character has not forgotten this one of little wisdom.
However, your manifold praises cause me only increased shame. Furthermore, having received your precious gifts, how could I fail to receive them upon my head?
I have received your instructions. That heterodox winds are spreading more extensively than ever before is indeed a profound cause for concern within the Dharma-gate.

Alas, I am a person of meager wisdom, my aspirations are insignificant, my virtue is cool, and my intelligence is shallow; how could I possibly turn back the surging waves once they have already collapsed?
My humble hope is truly that the worthy ones will rise up together to sweep away the traces of Māra, so that we may once again behold the majestic authority of the Han officials.
This is indeed proper protocol. That you, my friends in Quancheng, are able to investigate the Tiantai school together and uphold the Buddha’s True Dharma is truly no small feat;
this is a profound cause for celebration within the Dharma-gate. However, the Tiantai school is most subtle and precise, and one must not treat it with casualness.
It is also essential to be proficient in other schools before one may exclusively honor its own fundamental tenets. Most particularly, what must be strictly admonished is that one must not...
Having fallen into the fires of scholastic study, you must surely practice inner contemplation in secret to seek authentic awakening.

If your contemplation of the truths has not yet been forgotten and you remain stuck in the conceptual traps of the profound and mysterious, then the essence of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching will be nothing more than tea and rice for travelers on the road;
all the more so when there is no inner contemplation at all, but only the pursuit of intellectual understanding through words, remaining solely within the fray of disputing right and wrong.
To pass one’s days [in this manner]—how could this be the conduct of a true man? I have often remarked that since the time of Siming, the Tiantai school has degenerated into mere scholasticism;
it seems they have never truly understood what kind of realm it was when the Master Zhiyi personally beheld the assembly on Vulture Peak.
Is this not a matter for lamentation? I had long heard that Master Xinggu’s character was firm and his conduct straightforward; I simply wished to meet him in person.

At that time, while one's own matter remains unclarified, one is in haste to judge right from wrong; thus, even before a person of ultimate clarity, one cannot avoid being shrouded in three feet of darkness.
If the notes you have left behind are of this nature, then you must examine them once more with care.
I humbly entreat you to regard me with compassionate insight. With no further words.
