Re-edited by the Dharma-heir Disciple Daopai.
In my reply to Master Lin Deshan,

I received several of your precious letters in which you repeatedly and earnestly urged me to remain and strongly encouraged me to open the hall for teaching; this clearly demonstrates your heart for the Dharma.

My diligence is not comparable to that of those who merely boast of being *dānapati* (donors). However, I have reflected that we are currently in the age of the Dharma’s decline, where demons and devils cause harm.
Everywhere, they falsely occupy the seat of the master and strive with all their might to open the hall for teaching, thereby destroying the ancestral tradition; nothing is more extreme than this.

For these reasons, for three years at Gushan, I kept my mouth tightly shut—not merely observing the "three silences," but because it was not a matter of complacent resignation; rather, I simply did not wish to...
I have entered the ranks of the common crowd. This year’s campaign in Quannan was undertaken because those people there had no knowledge at all of such matters;
moreover, as circumstances converged and the situation left me with no choice, I acted rashly to serve as a mere precursor.
Nevertheless, this was also because my own resolve was not firm enough, and I was consequently turned by the winds of worldly karma—what is called "gathering the six provinces..."

This iron cannot be forged into this error. I humbly entreat you to grant me your vast forbearance and allow me to follow my own convenience. It is like a deer encountering a person; how could it endure such terror?
To be free to roam where the mountains are deep and the forests are dense would be my greatest fortune. We shall meet again at a future time;
until then, I hope to have the opportunity to explain everything in person.

Furthermore, regarding the various sutras spoken by the Buddha during his two previous assemblies of clouds, there are differences among the three vehicles that cannot be explained with a single, uniform standard.

For instance, eliminating marks to preserve the fundamental nature and discarding deviant thoughts to return to the right path—these are precisely the core tenets of the Hīnayāna. These two points alone...

This is a single principle. One grasps at characteristics because of attachment; one grasps at characteristics because of erroneous thought. In the Mahāyāna, however, one realizes that characteristics are themselves the nature (*dharmatā*).
Since all characteristics are fundamentally empty, why wait to eliminate them? Since the original nature is as it is, why wait to preserve it?
If one must eliminate the former in order to preserve the latter, this is called the dharma of arising and ceasing. This point is fully set forth in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*; [the details are] subtle.
Look! You should know this for yourself. Just as the Three Classics were proclaimed by the August Emperor (Gao Huangdi), the *Laṅkāvatāra* is the sudden teaching of the Mahāyāna.
Upon opening the volume, the one hundred and eight questions cannot be subsumed within two words; it is indeed the *Vajracitta Sūtra*.
Although it contains the doctrine of the destruction of marks (*lakṣaṇa*), it says: "The mark of emptiness of all dharmas is neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure."

"It neither increases nor decreases. What kind of realm is this? If it were as described by those two [previous] statements, then it would precisely involve arising and ceasing, defilement and purity, increase and decrease;
how could such a thing be known as the true mark of ultimate emptiness (*śūnyatā-tathatā*)?

I have received your instruction to compose commentaries on the paths of the three sutras, but I fear my strength may not suffice. However, the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* alone is capable of encompassing the essential purports of all three sutras."

If one thoroughly studies a single sutra, the other three will be like splitting bamboo—once the first knot is broken, the rest follow. The words of the Buddha and the words of the Chan school (Zong) are truly not different;

however, the words of the Buddha possess varying depths and universally accommodate the three capacities of practitioners, whereas the words of the Chan school address only those of the highest capacity.

These are what the Buddha called the "Supreme One Vehicle" and the "Separate Transmission Outside the Teachings. Prior to the Sixth Patriarch, there was no emphasis on sharp, witticistic exchanges (*jīfēng*); instead, there was a straightforward and practical instruction.
If people take up the burden based on the literal words from the mouths [of the masters], then the Way of the Patriarchs will be far off.
Therefore, from Mazu onwards, they employed "sparks" (ji-feng); this was merely to strike and reveal from the side, causing people to awaken for themselves.

Regarding the true essence, they did not dare to utter a single word, fearing that people would produce interpretations based on the literal language. For example, when it is said, "We have met," if one is a person of the inner circle, [one understands].
It is like a mirror reflecting a mirror. If one allows even the slightest trace of doubt to enter, then white clouds will stretch ten thousand miles away;
how could one possibly add further annotations? As it is said: "To say 'it is so' is not permitted; to say 'it is not so' is also not permitted.
This cuts off the path of understanding, leaving the person with no place to find life. If one is such a person, they will immediately transcend the cage. The fool—
If you view it thus, I would be grateful for your guidance.

Regarding the doubt previously raised by Great Censor Zeng Eryun concerning the difference between Chan language and Buddhist language, I have already offered a brief response. However, as for this paper...

I have not yet fully grasped what you have set forth; I now request that you explain it in detail. As for the differences between Chan terminology and that of the Buddha, they lie in the words and phrases;
their essential meaning, however, is no different at all. It is precisely the Supreme Vehicle (Ekayāna) beyond the three vehicles taught by the Buddha.
Its origin lies in the World-Honored One holding up a flower and Kāśyapa’s smile; the Buddha himself already considered this a separate transmission outside the teachings.
Since it is called a "separate transmission," how could it be forcibly made identical to the various scriptures?

Other instances include Mañjuśrī’s striking the gavel, Maitreya’s snapping his fingers, Kāśyapa’s overturning the banner-pole, and even the fact that Bodhidharma did not recognize the Second Patriarch.

Having prostrated and risen, they stood in their respective positions. The Sixth Patriarch’s raising of the net to catch the wind—his words were not uniform, yet each was utterly distinct from the various sutras;
furthermore, they were not something he devised only for the sake of later generations.

Generally speaking, Chan language should not be viewed as something strange or perilous, nor as something obscure or profound, nor as a hidden riddle; rather, it is a direct pointing to this very matter.

This causes people to realize it immediately. If you can, beneath this dais, intimately penetrate the moments when the geese fly and the fish leap in Confucianism, the place where [the Master said], "I have nothing hidden from you," and the place where he said, "I wish to remain wordless," then the words of our school can all be shattered with a single laugh.
Furthermore, how could there be any talk of difference or agreement? If one remains confined within mere phrases and sentences...

When comparing their similarities and differences, names and phrases become obstacles and principles and meanings create hindrances; how, then, could one possibly enter the realm of silent realization?
I am writing this now because the Elder Master Wengu of Zhejiang has passed away; he was the very teacher from whom I received the precepts.

I ought to go and offer my condolences; calculating the timing, I will surely return only after the summer solstice. My *Brief Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra* has barely reached six fascicles. Previously, I was honored by Mr.
Ying of the Surveillance Commission, who took my draft to read and even permitted it to be carved into printing blocks. However, now that I am on this journey, [the matter is unsettled].
I fear that I may not be able to complete this work at once. I respectfully submit this for Your Majesty’s perusal.
How could I feel anything but trepidation?

I, [Name], along with Zhang Ershui, the State Councilor, have ventured forth presumptuously; to mistake a deer for a horse is a deed for which we ought not to be spoken of by great men and gentlemen. How could it be otherwise?

I am fortunate that Your Reverence’s affection for me is particularly deep, and you have condescended to grant me your compassionate guidance. Having resided here in peaceful seclusion for half a year, the monastic community has remained free from all concern;

this is truly due to the protection afforded by your great virtue. How could I fail to engrave this deeply in my heart? Regarding the precious gifts you previously bestowed upon me, I am overcome with shame and gratitude.

Your "Hundred Verses on Mountain Dwelling" clearly demonstrates that you have applied yourself with earnest devotion to your fundamental practice. Although I have not yet seen any superior mastery in your own path of transformation, [I remain deeply impressed].
It is pure, elegant, and flowing, with a spirit that rises gracefully above the mundane. One must surely concede that the verses composed by the various elders fall short by one stroke.

Regarding the *Biographies of Bodhisattvas* (Kaisi Zhuan) from the Ziyun era, I have here re-examined them; furthermore, I have supplemented it with a brief record of the venerable masters from the previous dynasty as well as our own Ming dynasty.
I am deeply aware that this does not resemble the original work, yet I have compiled it specifically because the single lineage of Shouchang has been, at times, severed and at others, continued.

Furthermore, as the winds of Māra have fanned extensively and the gates of the Dharma have been thrown into confusion, I have exerted myself to beat these two pieces of skin [my lips], hoping to achieve a single instance of salvation.
I hereby present these two volumes for your perusal; I humbly pray that you will illuminate them with your insight. How could I feel more than boundless honor and joy?
I have presumptuously occupied this Purple Cloud for two periods of retreat, yet it has been nothing more than a vain expenditure of my tongue.
Not only is there not a single person who has slightly grasped its meaning, but even a true seeker who would engage in authentic investigation cannot be found.
This is because within our school, there is no Zen to be understood through conscious intellect, nor are there phrases to be negotiated point by point; it requires—
He must penetrate into the place where there is originally no seam or fissure; only after his entire being has fallen away can he take it up.

Should he be unable to realize this suddenly, only then do methods such as "examining the head-word" (kōan) come into play. This is intended to exhaust the thief-like mind so that, perhaps, the light of heaven may spontaneously emerge.

Lately, however, the style of our school has undergone a great transformation; people generally value mere superficiality, and the transmission between teacher and disciple consists solely of learning how to give answers.

Question: When those who have studied *niansong* (verses on cases) and have a slight proficiency in the texts are granted the "gourd-seal" transmission, they bring about their own ruin and mislead others.
They even go so far as to drink wine, gamble, and engage in wild, derisive laughter, claiming to be followers of our school while refusing to accept any discipline or restraint.
Disregarding minor details, they regard our exhortations as nothing more than the "Zen of old women. Alas! The ancestral wind is about to perish, and demons are rising to manifest their malevolence.
Reflecting quietly upon this, it is truly enough to break one's heart with grief. However, my strength is frail and my understanding inferior;
I am unfit for such a great responsibility. Therefore, I intend to beat the drum of retreat and withdraw to dwell among the green mountains and white clouds.

I have spent my days merely warming a broken-legged cauldron. Now that I am returning to Gushan, I have not yet had the opportunity to pay my respects in person; I therefore humbly offer this brief note to express my gratitude.
I pray that you will graciously look upon me with compassion. I am most fortunate.

For Lü Tianchi, the Minister of Agriculture, the Dharma of the Buddha was not inherently difficult; rather, it was people themselves who made it so. This is why a distance of a thousand li suddenly came to exist between them.
It is just like a person sitting in the middle of the ocean crying out for thirst. However, if one can simply refrain from giving rise to various views and directly realize it, there is [liberation].
How difficult this is! It is like hearing the fragrance of chrysanthemums in a mountain valley:

although this was indeed due to the power of Huìtáng, at what point did Huìtáng ever add a single word of instruction upon the fundamental ground? He merely cut off all the habitual views of his life.
When expedients no longer function and intellectual understanding has dissolved, one suddenly encounters it.

Now, you, Elder Layman, in the leisure of returning to the forest, have already emptied worldly thoughts and severed your attachment to words and letters. From within this state of letting go, you must let go even further;
thereafter, throughout the twelve periods of the day and night, you should single-mindedly take up a single koan that is devoid of meaning or flavor.
Speak! Examine and investigate at length; contemplate in silence. Look into what kind of principle this is. Do not harbor speculative conjectures or form intellectual understandings.

Simply continue to investigate in this manner. Suddenly, on a certain day, when you do not move from the state of intellectual understanding, you will strike it with sudden clarity, and the Great Matter will be completed. By all means, do not say that you are too old to practice this investigation.
Nor should you say that your practice has been shallow; for this matter does not depend on whether one is old or young, nor does it concern the depth or shallowness of one's cultivation.
It is simply a matter within the range of one’s own eyebrows and eyelashes—once understood, it is immediately realized.

Having returned to Gushan, I am deeply moved by your profound kindness; though I have not yet been able to pay my respects in person, I respectfully offer this small note of thanks to express my humble sentiments.
I humbly pray that you will look upon me with compassion; this is a great fortune.

Although Master Jiang Bagong, the Grand Astrologer, and those of the Confucian and Buddhist traditions follow divergent paths, they ultimately possess no dual nature. It is simply that the Confucians employ it to govern the world, while the Buddhists employ it...
Because it transcends the world yet traverses the world, it speaks only of the human realm and only of the present when addressing worldly matters;
because it transcends the world, it extensively discusses the ten realms and fully explains the three periods of time. Thus, while its teachings appear divided, they are in fact unified.

That you, Layman, alone have been able to engage extensively with both Confucianism and Buddhism and to investigate the single nature (xing) with such precision—how rare this is in Wénlǐng! Yet, as for what the Master spoke regarding nature and Heaven...
The Way is truly something that cannot be heard; this is why one values silent realization and desires to remain wordless—therein lies a profound meaning.
Regarding this single point, I pray you will continue to apply your attention. In this way, the heart-mind of Confucius and the life-vein of Śākyamuni will both rest entirely in your hands, Layman.

I have spent two periods of time here in vain, returning with a sense of regret; how can I ever sufficiently express my gratitude for your great virtue? Sincerely yours, [Name] (Seal) *Note: The character "懡[怡-台+羅]" (mòluó) is a transcription of the Sanskrit term *mlāna*, signifying a state of dejection or regret.*

And having personally prostrated myself, I respectfully submit this brief note of thanks, expressing my humble sentiments. I humbly pray that you will look upon me with compassion; it would be a great favor.
Within the single prefecture of Wénlǐng, Mr.

Huáng Jìtāo’s circle possesses the greatest number of worthy and eminent men and the most frequent success in the imperial examinations. Yet, regarding the school of Neo-Confucian learning alone, he has achieved a truly great [distinction].

Regarding this deficiency: although there were former elders such as Master Xuzhai and Master Zifeng who applied themselves with the utmost diligence, they were all bound by the exegetical traditions of scholastic learning (*yixue*); thus, concerning the fundamental ground, they remained truly bewildered.

Now, you, Elder Layman, alone are able to uphold the study of principle (*lixue*) and shoulder the single lineage of the Southern School of the Way; you may truly be called a "sound of footsteps in an empty valley."

However, you must further understand that there is a point which transcends words and emerges from intellectual understanding. Otherwise, even if one daily lectures on "innate knowledge" (liangzhi) and clarifies "supreme goodness" (zhishan), how would this differ from the study of philological glosses?
I am returning to my native mountains; moved by your profound kindness, I have specifically set forth these expressions of gratitude and my humble sincerity.
I humbly entreat you to grant me your enlightened consideration. With no further words. (Note: This is a formal letter of thanks written in classical Chinese style.)
In his literary and Chan studies with Liu Zhonglong, there was nothing other than the perfecting of one's own fundamental mind. This mind is neither defiled nor pure;
it is neither sage nor ordinary person; it is neither moving nor still; it is neither existent nor non-existent. It encompasses empty space without exterior and transforms into myriad forms.
Yet it leaves no trace. It is that which the thousand Buddhas cannot fathom and the Tripitaka masters cannot expound.
How could this be something to be conjectured through words and thought? Because sentient beings give rise to ignorance and delusion, there arise views of differentiation;
because of these views of differentiation, there arise sentiments of acceptance and rejection. From this, some abandon the defiled and hasten toward...
From purity, one may turn toward impurity; thus, the distinction between the six realms arises, and the demarcation between the holy and the mundane is established.
If today you can suddenly sever all views of differentiation and suddenly forget all sentiments of acceptance and rejection, then the attainment of Buddhahood has been with you from the beginning.
Yet there are a certain class of non-Buddhists who claim: "Neither rejecting nor accepting, we follow conditions with carefree expansiveness, roaming according to our own nature."
Yao, you do not realize that this is precisely grasping at grasping and rejecting; yet by grasping at neither-grasping-nor-rejecting, you fall directly into the sickness of grasping and rejecting.
When have you ever escaped the view of differentiation? To forget the sentiment of grasping and rejecting, one must obliterate the view of differentiation.
To obliterate the view of differentiation, one must break through the barrier of ignorance. Layman, if you can break through it directly—

Once you have passed through the barrier of ignorance, you will emerge beyond the three realms and sit at ease upon the crown of Vairocana’s head. How would this mountain monk dare deceive you regarding the practice of Buddha-recitation?
If this is not yet the case, then for now, apply your whole heart to the single phrase "Buddha. If you can achieve single-minded concentration in your recitation, [you shall attain it].
Ignorance may thus be established and destroyed; there is no need to further discuss rebirth.

Even if ignorance has not yet been destroyed, by relying on the power of this mindfulness, one shall attain entry into the Lotus Land and ultimately achieve Buddhahood—there is absolutely no possibility of error. Having returned to Gushan, I am moved by my affection for the Way and have set down these humble thoughts.
I humbly entreat you to grant me your enlightened consideration; it would be most fortunate.
I reply to Master Mimi:
In our school, we value only direct personal realization; there is no Chan that consists of piecemeal deliberation, nor is there any Chan acquired through gradual cultivation.
For this reason, we require you to practice with total simplicity and do not permit idle or confused thinking.
Do not give rise to false intellectual understandings. If you can gain conviction, then investigate in this manner; there is no need to ask about this or that.

For as long as the Great Matter remains unclarified, all one thousand seven hundred cases are open to doubt. It simply requires that you focus on a single case and press forward with your whole life at stake.
If you can pass through one case, you will pass through hundreds and thousands of cases without exception. According to your letter, you say: [The text continues with the student’s inquiry.]

Suddenly, there was a realization; he instantly perceived that things and self are of one suchness. [He thought,] "This is not the ultimate reality; it is merely a matter within the realm of light and shadow.
It remains, in fact, a manifestation of deluded consciousness. That is why it appears and vanishes so abruptly.

If it were a genuine awakening and entry, it would be like seeing one's own biological parents beneath the bright sun and clear blue sky—how could there be a case of recognizing them today and then having to recognize them again tomorrow?

If one cannot attain it, and later says such things as, "Once deluded enlightenment arises, what are the mountains, rivers, and the great earth?"—this is just like a person binding themselves with creeping vines; how could there ever be a time of release?
From this day forward, you must sever these evil cognitions and evil views while sitting in meditation, and single-mindedly investigate a single phrase that is devoid of meaning. From yourself...
There will be a day when you arrive home; if you inquire about odd-numbered [days], I shall send a reply. This is not worth studying.

Furthermore, regarding the "Explanation of the Robe-Donning" (Dabai shuo) shown by the filial and incorruptible Mr. Fang, what is set forth in the *Mohe zhiguan* and its *Fuxing* commentary is indeed already detailed and clear.
However, one must by no means adhere to this statement and claim that when a layperson receives the precepts, they must necessarily be given the robes or must necessarily wear them.

In the past, Guxin bestowed the three monastic robes upon a layperson; the layperson accepted them and used them regularly, performing prostrations to Buddhas and people exactly according to the monastic rules.
This was highly contrary to the regulations, and thus Yunqi severely censured him, citing Ciyun.
This is evidenced by the "Discerning Delusions" (Biànhuò) chapter. Furthermore, in the "Discerning Resonance" (Biàngǎn) chapter of Cíyún’s [work], it is also stated:
"The lay practitioner has a robe for entering the practice hall, which is merely single-layered stitching and differs from the robes of the monastics.

Thus, one cannot say that Yúnqī was unaware of the "Discerning Delusions," nor can one say that Cíyún was unaware of the *Fǔxíng* (Commentary on the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*). Since both of these great masters were already aware of the existence of the single-layered [robe],...
[This is] a robe for sewing. A layperson may wear it, yet why must there be such strict restriction? It is because this robe is specifically designed for entering the *dōjō* (meditation hall);
it is not something a layperson may wear at all times. Indeed, a layperson may only wear this robe when entering the *dōjō*;
once they have left the *dōjō* and are at home, wearing it is in every case forbidden. Thus, when a layperson receives the precepts...
It is not necessary to receive the robe beforehand; rather, one should receive it at the time when entering the *maṇḍala*.

When I heard that Chai Jiliang intended to enter the Hall of Great Compassion Repentance (*Mahākaruṇā-pūjā*), he entered Yunqi to receive the Bodhisattva precepts. Yunqi then conferred upon him a single-seamed seven-piece robe (*sapta-cīvara*).
Thus, both the conferrer and the recipient acted in accordance with the Dharma, which further demonstrates Yunqi’s lack of laxity. This is especially true regarding this robe.
Once one has received [the robes] after they have been offered, it is not permitted to be separated from them; to be separated from them incurs immeasurable transgression.

Now, among householders today, how many are there who can go out and come in without being separated from them? Therefore, it should be known that for a householder to receive the precepts without receiving the robes does not constitute a fault.
Only when one possesses robes yet cannot remain separated from them does one incur a transgression;

thus we know that a layperson (居士) must certainly not indiscriminately accept the three robes, but may only receive them when entering the dharma hall. As for Lingyuan’s interpretation, there are even more points that are incorrect.
For instance, the Sūtra states: "If one is separated by two *zhang*, one incurs immeasurable sin. This refers to leaving the dharma hall.
At that time, it should always be kept with one’s person. It is further stated: "It must not be separated by even an inch; to separate it constitutes an offense that obstructs the Way.
This refers to the time of entering the *dōjō* (meditation hall), when one must not be parted from it for even a moment. Although the scriptural words are very clear, Reigen (Lingyuan) states:

"The previous mention of 'two zhang' refers to the remaining two robes. This is a grave error. I, the fool, say: this wooden board should simply be split away; I hope you will take the trouble to remove it.
I have not beheld your compassionate radiance since meeting with Vice-Governor Zeng Er-yun;
four cycles of winter and summer have already passed. I am unaware of your well-being or how you have been faring lately. From Min...
For a long time, we have been bathed in the transformative rain of your grace; there is none among us who does not engrave this upon our bones and inscribe it in our hearts.
Yet, alas, the "Spring of Yang" has feet; as your carriage arrived in Chu, the people of Min have thus lost their Heaven.

Since the spring of the Dingchou year, I came to Hangzhou to pay my respects to the Great Master Wengu, whereupon various gentlemen of rank invited me to reside at the Zhenji Chan Monastery. From that time on, the borders between Min and Zhejiang were divided, and I have only felt a deep longing [to see you].

I have looked up to you from afar and heard that you have been appointed to Hupeh; news of you has become increasingly scarce. This spring, while reading the reports, I first learned that you had been assigned as a provincial governor on the eastern coast.
It happened that Governor Chen Baian paid me a visit, and I entrusted him with these inquiries.

I imagine that over the years you have investigated the Great Matter so thoroughly that you have "trampled through the lacquer bucket," such that the life-vein of all the sages does not lie outside the single mirror. Previously, I received your command to compose a brief commentary on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.

It has now been carved into printing blocks and circulated within Zhejiang. I respectfully present it for your perusal; I pray you will graciously take note of it. As I write this upon the paper, my thoughts toward you are beyond measure.
In reply to the Venerable Master Zhanke:

I am as worthless as a piece of useless wood, yet I have unworthily joined the ranks at Zhenji. That I have fortunately found some peace and freedom from affairs is entirely due to the guidance of the Great Master.
This is due to the spiritual power of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, as well as the strength of the various donors, protectors, and administrative officers.

What part have I played in this? Having received your instructions, my sense of shame and embarrassment increases all the more. Regarding the several points you have asked about: the former concern was the doubt that the One Mind has five distinct schools;

the latter concern was the doubt that the One Mind possesses distinctions. Your words total several hundred characters, yet they essentially do not go beyond the principle that essence is one while function is manifold.

It is merely that their essence is one while their functions are distinct. What is called "the oneness of essence" does not mean a stagnant, dead uniformity; what is called "the distinction of function" does not mean a scattered state without a governing principle.
It is like a single mirror manifesting ten thousand reflections: how could the ten thousand reflections hinder the single mirror?

It is also like a single piece of gold casting ten thousand images: how could the ten thousand images not be the single piece of gold? Furthermore, it is like what is before our eyes now: the height of heaven.
Beneath the earth, there is the illumination of the sun and moon and the stirring of thunder and lightning;

the myriad trees have diverse forms, and the thousand flowers possess distinct varieties—their classifications are beyond counting. Yet, there must surely be that which has never been classified to preside over them all.
Will you regard this as different? Or will you regard it as the same? Do you suspect that difference obstructs sameness, or that sameness impedes difference? Therefore—
As for what you have doubted below, none of it need be doubted. Moreover, even the names "same" and "different" are established merely as provisional designations;

"sameness" is established in dependence on "difference," and "difference" is established in dependence on "sameness. If one awakens to and enters into the single mind, then such words are all equally illusory and false.
How could one allow for discrimination or deliberation regarding them? I cannot elaborate further at this time; I humbly entreat you to consider this with clear insight.
"Not one. [The Master] replied:

"In the eastern land of Lu, at Wuyuan, the lay practitioner Jing of the Single Transmission Lineage has, since the entry of the Ming dynasty, nearly faced extinction. Although there have been those who raised the teaching in the interim,"

For the most part, these are merely those who rely on intellectual understanding and those skilled in mere verbal debate. It is not only the northern regions that are thus; the same is true in the south.
This is what Changsha described as a situation that merits weeping with tears streaming down and long sighs of lamentation.

Now, having respectfully read your letter, I see that you alone possess the aspiration for spiritual advancement. Could it be that there is no one among the heroic sages who can cause the Way to flourish even without literary talent? However—
Now that you already know this Dharma-gate exists, you should investigate and clarify it with fierce diligence; you must not abandon your efforts on account of advancing age.

Indeed, this Dharma-gate makes no distinction between those who are newly initiated and those who have long participated, nor does it distinguish between the young and those in their later years. Furthermore, this Way is not far away.
It is like a person sitting in the midst of the great ocean crying out for thirst—how could the water be distant from them? It lies only in one’s own mind.

Reflect only upon this yourself. Furthermore, householder, as you approach the twilight of your years, the illusory nature of worldly phenomena has already been clarified, and the affairs of human life have already been settled.
There remains only this one great matter, which must be treated like fire on one's head—admitting not even a moment’s delay.
If but a single thought can be brought into accord with it, would that not be a most extraordinary and supreme benefit? If its application...

The methods for [recording] meritorious deeds have already been fully set forth in the *Xiaolu* (Small Record). I am deeply grateful for your gracious gift. I thank you and have enclosed five copies of my humble publication;
it would be a great honor if you would deign to accept them.

I am deeply honored by the esteemed visit of Vice Minister Ceng Er-yun and am further indebted for the precious gifts you have bestowed upon me; how can I adequately express my gratitude? Regarding your discourse on the practice of stillness (*śamatha*), this is indeed the primary gateway for entering the Way.
For, in our daily lives, the senses, the spirit, and the mind are constantly distracted by external phenomena as they arise and perish. Without [this practice],...

During moments of temporary rest, once one is drawn away by external objects, the external world conversely becomes the master, while the innate spiritual light is reduced to serving the demands of those external objects;
thus, one remains in a state of dullness and agitation, devoid of any freedom. Now that you have practiced stillness, [the situation has changed].
Thus, external objects may seem impossible to disturb; yet the disease-root of habitual tendencies has long occupied the space within the heart-mind.
It is merely like grass pressed down by a stone—it cannot yet be eradicated. Therefore, even while practicing stillness, one must further observe within that stillness: "What is my original nature?
By the power of this observation, one forces open the inherently present spiritual light (*jñāna-prabhā*). Once the spiritual light...
Then what are called the root of illness and habitual tendencies will naturally vanish, just as when a master stands in the hall brandishing a sword—how could any thieves fail to hide and flee?
Furthermore, even in stillness, you must by all means not mistake the state of stillness for the fundamental essence.
For both movement and stillness are merely objects; there exists within this something that permeates both movement and stillness, yet is neither movement nor stillness.

It is certainly not permissible to recognize a slave as a lord. Having been favored with your recent communication, I venture to present this one account. These words are the reckless and ignorant remarks of a fool;
I hope you will deign to select from them what is worthy. This is all.

Furthermore, I, Zhou Rui, have twice received your esteemed instructions from the Ministry of Personnel. I am aware that your natural endowment and scholarly exertion are far beyond the reach of ordinary peers.

However, regarding this great matter, it does not suffice merely to speak of it and leave it at that; one must withdraw the gaze and turn back the hearing, contemplating in stillness that single thought-moment before it arises.

Before this awakening, what was one’s true face? From the moment one suddenly attains entry [into realization], all mountains, rivers, and the great earth, as well as fame, achievement, wealth, and honor, are none other than objects within wondrous luminosity. There is not the slightest thing to be grasped, nor the slightest thing to be discarded;
this may be called absolute sovereignty. It is only that, due to the habitual tendencies accumulated since beginningless kalpas, people have been following after [phenomena].

The mind arises in response to objects. Since the mind arises by pursuing objects, the mind revolves following after them, and the originally inherent spiritual light is consequently obstructed by external things, leaving no room for autonomy.
Among those who claim to have some knowledge of investigating the mind, they merely engage in conceptual discrimination regarding words and pursue logical reasoning;
this is the foremost deep-seated malady of scholars, and it is entirely useless.
To know the principles of words and letters is likewise merely an object. This mind has aspects that cannot be subsumed by words;
as for those principles that can be expressed, how could they ever be grasped through the conceptual deliberations of consciousness?
If one can directly turn back to observe what the face is like before even a single thought has arisen, then one has struck the snake at its vital point. Nevertheless...
Do not mistake the state of empty stillness for the ultimate goal. For even empty stillness is merely an object; it is not the true countenance.

Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "Even if one were to extinguish all seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, and inwardly maintain a state of profound tranquility, this is still but a shadowy phenomenon resulting from the discrimination of mental objects (*dharmas*).
If one can practice internal contemplation and is not deluded by these mental objects, then that is the Precious Abode."

I am close at hand. I have received your instructions regarding my reckless draft of observations; it would be my great fortune if you would simply select what is appropriate from it. In response to Mr.

Jie’an’s request for a commentary on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: there are no fewer than several hundred commentaries upon it, yet most are merely arbitrary speculations that fail to grasp the true teaching.
The general purport of this work is that as soon as one utters a single word [on this subject], it becomes a source of ridicule.
If one wishes to penetrate this scripture, one must first thoroughly investigate the *Śūraṅgama*, *Awakening of Faith*, and *Lotus Sūtra* three times over.

Only after that should one examine the commentaries of the three Bodhisattvas—Asaṅga, Vasubandhu, and Maitreya—and harmonize them into a coherent whole; only then may one annotate the scripture and avoid the fault of arbitrary fabrication.
[This is] a rebuke. If one follows the commentaries of recent scholars such as Gu Yin and others, then [the text] consists of vulgar language.
As for the words within the Chan school, one must strictly avoid touching upon them; if touched upon, they all become heterodox teachings that slander the Great Prajñāpāramitā.

The learning of Zhou, Cheng, Zhang, and Shao, while certainly that of great Confucian scholars within the Confucian tradition, remains outside the gate of Buddhism. Master Shao spoke only of the waxing and waning of qi and destiny.
As for the "Qi" (Mechanism), it is certainly worth listening to. However, regarding the subtleties of nature and destiny (*xing-ming*), I do not yet dare to grant my full assent.

Zhang Zai’s *Zhengmeng* is already a mixture of excellence and flaws; for the most part, it was produced through arduous contemplation and strenuous striving, and thus remains far removed from the Way.

Both Cheng brothers were pure and correct, yet in terms of their fundamental realization (*ji-di*), the Elder Brother was superior, while the Younger Brother followed him. As for the "Treatise on Stabilizing the Nature," it is truly...
It serves as a guide for Confucian scholars. However, both Cheng brothers followed Master Zhou (Zhou Dunyi).

While the *Tongshu* of Master Zhou is entirely pure and correct, I fear that the *Taiji tu shuo* (Explanation of the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate) cannot be without its flaws. In the past, within my "Sleeping Words" (*Eyan*), I have already argued against it with great effort;
nevertheless, as this is a work of the Confucian school, there is no need to reproach it deeply. Generally speaking, in the pursuit of learning, one must [seek it] at the very root.
Fundamentally, one must exhaustively investigate the intimate truth. Next, when reading books, you must apply your attention to the authentic great classics of the Great Sages and Great Worthies;
if you apply your attention to the fabricated works of worldly convention, you will unwittingly have your eyes swapped for black beans.
Having read your recent writings, I recognize your lofty talent and wise nature. It may be done.
You have sat and advanced along this path, yet you have merely failed to encounter a true master and have not read the authentic scriptures;

thus, you have spent your entire life mistaking a common stone for a treasure until the end of your days. If you are willing to believe me, take all that you have previously studied and heard and cast it away entirely—beyond the eastern ocean, and even further than that—and then, from the very beginning, rely upon a single volume of the *Recorded Sayings of Dahui* and engage in direct practice.
I have earnestly investigated this matter once. If I am unable to do so, I shall at least rely on a single section of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* to examine it with an open mind;

in this way, I may still attain the character of a truly authentic person. These words of a madman are an offense beyond measure; I humbly pray that you will grant me your ocean-like forbearance—this would be my great fortune.
I reply to the monk Zhenji from Caoyu Gongxue Academy.

Having received your letter and instructions, my private heart is deeply comforted. I have received the gold for the stupa that you so kindly bestowed; it has already been placed in the permanent endowment of the monastery. How can I sufficiently express my gratitude?
Previously, I was honored by your commissioning of the carving of the Patriarch’s portrait and the composition of its eulogy; the work is nearly complete, with only ten [characters] remaining.
Regarding the remaining shadow [portrait]: please consult the Changming Temple in Wulin; you will surely obtain it there.
If it is not complete, I have heard that your son mentioned the ancestral shadow at Shuixi is very detailed. I do not know where this Shuixi is located now.
If it refers to Shuixi in Jingxian, then it would be easy to have it brought here by imperial decree. In the past, someone once pointed to the shadow of a high monk and asked: [The text ends here.]
"The shadow is here; where is the eminent monk? It is because of his shadow that one pursues the man.

Now, you have abandoned the man while clinging to the shadow—is this not truly enough to make one laugh out loud? This is the fault of this old monk, which has consequently brought trouble upon my disciples.
Having once again received your instructions to reside at Zhenji Temple, I shall do so; let the world not treat me as if I were Feng Fu."
How much more so now that I am personally charged with the three monasteries; the labor of construction is truly vast, and I have no idea when it will ever be finished.
Furthermore, my infirm body is already at its most decrepit limit, and not even a moment can be spared. How then could I dare traverse the passes and rivers to shoulder this great responsibility?
The sin of disobeying your command is certainly unavoidable. I only pray for your compassionate consideration; it would be a great favor.
I reply to you, Vice Director Yan Chonghan:
Having been separated from you for several years, my longing and admiration have indeed been profound. To suddenly receive your precious letter was like beholding a blue lotus upon Mount Yushan.
I have received your account of how the atmosphere of strife within the Dharma-gate has become a subject of great derision by the common world; how could they not feel such [disdain]?
How shameful they are! They care only for their own partisan interests and refuse to observe the truth with an impartial mind.
They are truly the followers of Pāpīyān, borrowing our monastery’s precincts to destroy our Dharma. This is precisely what is called a portent of the extinction of the Dharma.

Previously, while in a state of true stillness, I already saw this wind of factionalism fanning out fiercely; my tears flowed uncontrollably, and I consequently prohibited the formal opening of the hall for lectures.
I decree: I am likewise willing to endure the extinction of my lineage rather than dare to entrust this to the unworthy. For this old monk’s karmic conditions are meager and my strength is frail;
I cannot turn back heaven or pull back the sun. I can only be cautious regarding the Dharma-gate, not daring to walk in step with those who are corrupt and evil.
This is so that the world may know that the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs does not always conform to them. Thus it is...
This old monk has served the Buddhas and the Patriarchs with a single heart of sincerity; do you, my disciples, believe me?
Having received your command, I was again invited by Zhenji to take up residence there.

However, this is a matter from which I can by no means comply, for I have recently served as the abbot of three monasteries, and the expenses for construction and repairs have already reached ten thousand pieces of gold. I do not know what will become of me in the future.

In conclusion, how could I dare so recklessly cross the mountain passes to retrieve what has already been discarded as spittle? I pray most earnestly that you will grant me your enlightened consideration. As I write these lines, my spirit hastens toward you;
how can I express the depth of my profound gratitude?
In reply to Governor Chen Baian:

Previously, while I was in Jinhua, I heard that you had received an imperial decree to enter the capital and subsequently returned to Min with your monk’s staff. Since our correspondence has grown sparse, I have been unable to hear further news.
I shall no longer hear news of your daily activities; yet, facing the moon and encountering the wind, my deep feelings are constantly stirred.
It cannot be said that a man of the Way has truly forgotten his emotions. Now that the monk Zhenji has arrived, I have been able to receive your written instructions.

Only then did I learn that your return to the lakeside was like Gongye’s innocence being vindicated—a covered basin suddenly receiving the light of the sun. Though this is called misfortune, it is also a great blessing. Furthermore, I have heard concerning your honorable illness.
Since you already possess the joy of "not needing medicine," and your physical vigor and strength are firm, you may further cultivate pure karma (*śukla-karman*).

To practice the Way of Renunciation (*śama*), Concealment (*gupti*), and Gathering (*saṃgraha*) is the ancestral tradition of the Confucians and the disciples of the Buddha. Moreover, with the scenery of lakes and mountains, one can enjoy complete leisure;

why must one tread the path of thorns, ascend the lairs of tigers and leopards, and compete with worldly people for the sake of a mere speck of a snail’s horn? Beyond the remnants of meditative practice...
The compilation has already been completed with great effort. Unexpectedly, amidst the croaking of frogs and the chirping of crickets, I have ventured to trouble you, the Great Vehicle;
how fortunate this is! As for the words at the beginning of the preface, they shall naturally rely upon your esteemed brush; what else could they belong to?

Now, having again received your instruction to reside once more at Zhenji, it allows me to continue beholding your sacred abode. This is truly a profound blessing for three lifetimes. However, recently...

I, Rishen, have been entrusted with the affairs of three monasteries; the actual workload is truly extensive. The main hall of Mount Gu mountain is on the verge of collapsing, yet we are now planning its reconstruction.
At Xingfu Monastery, timber has already been felled for a renovation. Although the Śarīra Hall at Baoshan has fortunately been completed, the pagoda has not yet been cast.
To shoulder the labor of these three monasteries alone upon my one aging frame, and then to abandon them all—this is by no means possible.
I humbly entreat you to grant your gracious attention. It would be most fortunate if you would pardon his crime of disobeying your commands.
This is the reply sent to Lü Tiānchí, Minister of Agriculture.

Direct pointing is pointing without a finger; the essential point lies in silent resonance and the forgetting of words. The Heart-essence has no object of veneration, yet it does not hinder one from awakening through following conditions.
Thus, by plucking a flower or raising a whisk, the originally inherent radiance is revealed; by brandishing a ritual tablet or drawing a bow, the illusions of the past are pierced through.
This is simply because there is fundamentally nothing; how could anything ever arise as something external? Alas, the Dharma...
At this time when the conch has long been silent and the life-force of wisdom hangs by a thread, we know that phenomena arise from conditions and the Way is propagated by men.
We respectfully consider you, sir, a pillar of the Confucian tradition and a golden fortress of the Buddha-land; as a rudder and as rain, you bear the heavy expectations of all living beings.
Like a qilin or a phoenix, you manifest auspicious light in this sagely age. Thus, for the sake of the conditions of the Six Harmonies, you have specifically...
The mandate of the Nine Cauldrons is being bestowed. As for me, having unworthily entered the gates of the saffron robe, I am ashamed to even catch a glimpse of its shadow.
I have not yet beheld the sharp edge of the Holy Arrow of the Stone Drum; how could the iron hoe of Shouchang dare to emulate its solitary loftiness?

Holding this precious document, my heart trembles; hearing these profound sounds, my spirit is stirred. I firmly know that a mosquito’s burden is beyond endurance; how would I dare to remain rooted in my own convenience and private interests?
I, [Name], ought to exert myself to the utmost; yet, alas, my circumstances are constrained. I shall wait until early spring to receive your great instructions.
I humbly pray that you will be as vast as the ocean in your forbearance. How could I contain my boundless joy?

In response to Fu Youxin’s admonition that Confucianism and Buddhism share a common source—being like the vast void where no boundaries can be distinguished—I reply: though the white-robed and black-robed follow divergent paths, they are like one arm that naturally possesses both contraction and extension.
To those who realize this, the single Way is uniform and level; to those who remain in ignorance, a thousand differences arise in competition. If it were not for...

The Key of Wisdom: How to Open the Gates of Delusion. I respectfully reflect that Your Excellency’s learning exhausts both the internal and external traditions, and your insight penetrates the profound and the manifest.

You have briefly tested the blade of your "ox-knife" skill in the music and song of the hundred-li district, yet by imperial decree from the Nine Palaces, you have suddenly transcended the ranks of the "chestnut-horse" officials.

Out of compassion for the long decline of the Buddha-Dharma and sorrow for the failure to transform ignorant minds, you have deigned to issue this supreme command, reaching down even to those clad in the field-robe. I know that the purple... [text ends]

Mount Yun is indeed a place for chanting the Way; I, [Name], am startled to find myself a vessel unfit for such a heavy responsibility. Yet, having received your gracious summons, how could I refuse your command?
Alas, my affairs are bound by worldly constraints, which is why my journey has been delayed. I shall wait until the spring breeze flows freely before setting forth.
I humbly receive the solemnity of this great teaching; I pray you will graciously illuminate me. How could I possibly express my boundless fortune!
In reply to the Honorable Minister Hong Qingyuan of Hangzhou and the various local gentry:
We humbly submit that a mountain of a thousand fathoms cannot be overcome by the strength of a mosquito, nor can the sound of a single faint cry compare to the resonance of thunder.

I am truly unworthy to stand shoulder-to-shoulder with you, yet I have the honor of receiving your instructions from this eminent monastery; I feel deep shame at my lack of talent. I respectfully consider that your wisdom-light is perfectly round and your spiritual resonance is profound and far-reaching.
You transmitted the lineage of the Mind from Eastern Lu (China), attaining silent accord with the fragrance of the cassia; you explored the secret teachings of Western Qian (India).
Having galloped forward upon seeing the shadow of the whip, you have both brilliantly illuminated the light of the Imperial Capital and further fortified the defenses of the City of Dharma.

Without deigning to treasure your tablets and scrolls, you have sent down your instructions even to this one clad in the robes of a field-dweller. How can the glow of my firefly illuminate anything? My skills as a flying squirrel are mostly exhausted.

Having erroneously succeeded to the lamp of Shouchang, I am already called a "mixed jade"; now to occupy the seat at Xiaoshan by the Teao River is no different from "appending fox-furs to a weasel’s tail. I am deeply moved by your profound concern and gracious presence.
I am filled with anxiety, still harboring a sense of shame for my own physical impurities. I respectfully lay forth these words of apology; how can I withstand such trepidation!
In reply to the Chancellor Shi Yuwang of Jiaxing and the various local gentry:

I reverently esteem you, whose wisdom penetrates both ancient and modern times, and whose realization of the ultimate and conventional truths is wondrously harmonized. You serve as a pillar and foundation for the Imperial House, having long bestowed [your grace].
A refreshing rain, serving as a golden bulwark for the Buddha-land, suddenly nurtures the seeds of wisdom.

Having long heard the resonance of the Way yet not having beheld its compassionate radiance, I have unexpectedly received this honor of imperial decree, extending even down to the lowly wearer of the field-cloth robe. Entrusted to continue the preceding waves of the Tiāoxī, I am specifically charged with the final task for Shuangjìng.
It is as if the royal throne were being directly bestowed upon a mediocre talent, or as if Mount Tàishān were being lifted [by a gnat].
Suddenly tasked with a burden as heavy as a mosquito carrying a mountain, I feel abashed as I touch my pillow; it is difficult to illuminate even the light of a torch.

With my spirit wavering as I hold this document, the courage of a minor sorcerer has already been exhausted. Having had no leisure to decline the request, I have forced myself to comply. I respectfully express my gratitude, yet how can I overcome my trembling fear?
Reply to Yu Runfu, Cavalier Attendant of Jintan, and the various local gentry:

We humbly submit this. The ancestral seal hangs suspended in the void; how could it be that one who lacks wisdom knows how to serve it? The Dharma assembly has sprung forth from the earth; how could a wild crane ride upon a lofty carriage?
To decline the command would indeed be insolence, yet when it comes to practicing benevolence, how dare we say we do not yield? We shall simply observe its unfolding and rolling up.

Regarding the significance of this moment: the preservation and stabilization [of the Dharma] must surely rely upon the gate of *dāna*. I respectfully consider that Your Reverence’s sagely mind is as clear as the heavens and your ocean of learning is as profound and concentrated as a deep pool.

Having emerged as an auspicious sign for the state, the wind of your virtue spreads the fame of the Imperial Garden; dwelling as a model for the world, the value of your Way surpasses the renown of Longmen.

You have inherited the profound principles of Zibai and revitalized the declining fortunes at Jinsha. I am ashamed that I have yet been unable to cultivate the intimacy of a "thorn-bush" friendship with you.
Fortunately, I have long gazed upon the Northern Dipper with devotion. My will is content to preserve my uncut jade; my perception is as still as frozen ice.

In vain I have admired the rules for selecting buddhas established by Danxia, and I have ventured into the ranks of Shouchang’s community that presses against the void. Suddenly I probed the tiger’s den at the age when Buyi Chen entered official service;
I remained hidden on Mount He for nearly as many years as it took Confucius to reach the stage of "ear-harmony. Upholding the solemn entrustment of my late master, I have—
My humble talents were once confined within the Yunlin Mountains; yet, upon encountering the compassionate radiance of Old Man Wen, I was able to unfurl my sails at Shigou.
Having thus cast aside my arms and walked on, I inadvertently deceived both sages and commoners, creating waves where there was no water. Thus, I have dared to scatter sand and raise dust.

Now, having come to the waters of the Xiao River, I hold a single瓣 (lotus petal) to offer it once more; as soon as I circumambulate the Crane Forest, I hope for the reappearance of the twin feet [of the Buddha]. How...?

When the mandate for a great office was conferred upon me, I was summoned to fill an empty seat. Though I firmly declined, my refusal was not accepted; thus, I was compelled to accept a burden I could not fulfill.

To take the glow of a torch and seek to follow the brilliance of the sun and moon—is this not difficult? For a tree grown among the cypress logs to be thrust forward as a ridgepole—it lacks the necessary substance.
A donkey assuming the responsibility of an elephant, yet vainly claiming that clouds and moon are the same; a chicken entering a phoenix’s nest—how deep [is the absurdity]?
I am ashamed that the mountain streams differ; I needlessly trouble myself with the fear of stepping on ice, yet how could I forget the distress of being in a deep abyss?
Upon opening this letter, I feel boundless shame and profound gratitude.
In reply to Governor Yang Lianjing, I humbly submit this:

When the river of dhyāna is about to overflow, its protection relies entirely upon firm embankments; when the pillar of the Dharma is intended to flourish, its support must be of girth as thick as a man’s arms.

Having already received the personal entrustment at Vulture Peak, the final age of the Dharma values these defensive walls even more highly. I respectfully honor you, Excellency, in your esteemed commandery.

A man of exemplary virtue and integrity, a great vessel of the enlightened age, whose administrative achievements surpassed those of Gong and Huang. He dispensed the deep dew upon the human realm; his lofty reputation was revered like Mount Shan and the Northern Dipper.

He spread the "Yangchun" (Spring Breeze) throughout this sagely era, such that all commoners were graced by its spring-like radiance, and even the monastic community was moistened by the transformative rain.

Grieving that the principles of the Shaoshi lineage were on the verge of collapse, he encountered the completion of the Ziyun Hall project. The precious records shed their light, and the desolate forest [was transformed].

I shall revise my views. My limited understanding, like that of one measuring the deep with a conch-shell, cannot fathom this; yet, amidst the confusion of the *gong* flute, I feel ashamed for my superficial knowledge.

Formerly, I ventured to speak recklessly like the croaking of a frog; now, I dare once more to display the skills of a donkey. Moreover, as the demonic winds rage on, they have nearly produced a landscape of depraved traces;

while the orthodox pulse flows but a trickle, it is difficult to swell it into the great waves that return to the sea. Can we not turn away from the difficult and pursue the easy? Is it not possible to pull back the tide? One must be cautious in one's conduct.

To keep these matters secret within the archives is what is appropriate for the times. This is why I have beaten the drum of retreat with urgency, leaving it to the weeds beneath the steps to grow as deep as they will.

I do not decline to be compared to a cicada in winter; how could I worry that moss might grow upon my tongue? If I were to strike the *gandī* once more on the main road, [the consequences would be grave].
This is something I dare not presume to hear. Should I be permitted to hang my flask and staff in a quiet room, it would fulfill my long-held aspiration. I await your decision with humble reverence;
I hope you will grant me your compassionate consideration. As I write this upon the paper, I am overcome with the utmost longing to behold you.
In reply to Huang Yurú and the various literati:

I, [Name], have unworthily joined the ranks of the black-robed clergy. Having taken my seat in a renowned monastery, I have long neglected the Three Studies and possess not the skills of the Five Virtues;
lacking proficiency in the Ten Subjects, I am but a mere chirping bird. Now that you inquire after my dwelling at Cuíyún, I intend to emulate the reclusion of Lóngshān. I shall return.
Holding this letter from afar, I am deeply ashamed, like Feng Fu, of my empty reputation that has brought me only weariness. Drifting without rest, I know I cannot escape the mundane net;
laboring without peace, the roads stretch far ahead, and I have yet to hear of the art of shrinking the earth.

The clouds and mountains lie vast and distant, yet I constantly harbor the longing to ascend the dragon. Suddenly receiving these cloud-like missives, I feel as if I were facing the steep peaks of Mount Yu in person—how joyful!

Having read your jade-like letter, it was as if I were drenched by a profusion of sweet nectar. I could not have imagined that my own state of sorrow and indolence would still trouble your lofty wisdom.

Furthermore, having received your generous gifts, my profound sense of shame increases all the more. I only pray that your practice of the *dāna-pāramitā* may ever expand and that the Golden City [of the Dharma] may remain eternally secure.
May the Māras and heretics thus vanish into obscurity, and may the monastic community find peace therein; then, how fortunate for the Azure Clouds (the Sangha), and how fortunate for me as well!
How profound! As I hold this writing in my hands, I am overcome with longing and admiration.
*The Expanded Record of Master Yongjue*, Volume Twelve.
*The Expanded Record of Master Yongjue*, Volume Thirteen.
Preface to the Re-edited Upper Section of the Record of the Propagation of Buddhism in Jianzhou,
Compiled by the Dharma Heir Daopai.
The *Hongshi lu* (Records of the Propagation of Buddhism) is a compilation of those who were able to propagate the Way of the Śākya clan.

This Way, since the dream of the Golden Man and the arrival of the White Horse from the West, has had its proponents appearing in successive generations who greatly propagated its teachings. Consequently, a thousand lamps have vied with one another to shine, their brilliance reflecting through both past and present;
how vast it is, beyond all reckoning! As for our own land of Jian [China], prior to the Six Dynasties, it was generally not so.

I have heard that when the Tang dynasty first flourished, Buddhist monasteries were initially established. Following Mazu’s entry into the Guanzhong region, he began his transformative teaching at Fojie Ling in Jianyang, and it was there that Chan studies first began to spread widely.
Although later on the Chan and doctrinal schools diverged as distinct traditions, and the teachings on Nature and Characteristics differed in their tenets, [the lineage remained].
Together they were able to cause the winds of profound transformation to fly and the fountain of the Dharma to gush forth like arrows; all of them were bridges and rafts for our Śākya lineage.

However, since the rise of the Ming dynasty more than two hundred years ago, the lamp of the school has lost its flame and the ocean of the teachings has gradually silted up. Only here and there have been two or three [who sustained it].
They stand as solitary as the morning stars; to whom, then, shall the responsibility for propagating the Way be entrusted?
I, a humble man from Tam-eup, have unworthily entered the ranks of the monastic order and am fortunate enough to have sought refuge within the Dharma cave.

Although a firefly’s light cannot illuminate much and my skills as a bat-like creature are utterly exhausted, my single-minded devotion to antiquity has always been keen within my foolish heart. As I gaze reverently upon the exemplary figures of the past, I frequently find myself shedding tears. Thus, I reflect:
In antiquity, there were these same rivers and mountains; there were these same sun and moon. Now, too, there are these same rivers and mountains; there are these same sun and moon.
How could the people of today be any different from the people of antiquity? Why, then, is the Dharma-gate so desolate and silent? Why is the gap between the present and the past so vast?
Is it not because, once the former traces have vanished, there is no longer a basis for observation and inspiration? People have become habituated to their recent surroundings.
Is it not because there was no one to inspire them? Therefore, disregarding my own ignorance, I have extensively searched through various records.

I have compiled and transmitted everything concerning those masters who were born in Jian [Prefecture], as well as those who established the Dharma and manifested its transformation there, so that students of later generations may see how the ancients were so diligent, so rigorous, and so...

How vast and far-reaching this is! If one could suddenly change course and head toward the goal, advancing toward the mark, then it may well be that the prosperity of the Tang and Song dynasties could once again be witnessed in our own day; this cannot be said to be impossible. Alas!
"All people can become Yao or Shun"—the words of Master Mencius were certainly no idle speech. For those with resolve, nothing remains unaccomplished. If...

If one is complacent in self-comfort and rigid in self-limitation, even if the various patriarchs were to stand solemnly before them and issue their commands, such a person would merely shake their head and disregard them;
what value, then, would there be in this record? Therefore, in the dissemination of this record, I wish for it to be shared with those who possess the aspiration.
Preface to the *Hokke Shiki* (Private Notes on the Lotus Sūtra).

In recent times, those who discourse upon the sūtras have been numerous. Yet, the more refined they become, the more obscure they grow; the more cleverly they argue, the more erroneous they prove. Is it that the sūtra is truly impossible to clarify?
The obscuration lies in their using their own selves to discourse upon the sūtra, rather than using the sūtra itself to discourse upon the sūtra. This, too, is an obscuration.

To discuss the sutras by means of the sutras, rather than discussing the sutras by means of one's own self; to be able to discuss the sutras by means of one's own self without being obscured by that self;
and to be able to discuss the sutras by means of the sutras without being obscured by the sutras—only then may one be considered fit to discuss the sutras.
When I first read the *Yue-shan Yi*, I heard a monk reciting a verse from the *Lotus Sutra* which says: "At that time, I manifested for him a pure light."
Ming-shen was suddenly overcome with such joy that he could not contain himself; he immediately sought out the sutra to read it, yet nothing was revealed to him.
Nevertheless, he realized that outside the teachings of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius, there existed this other great matter.

Thereafter, he extensively sought commentaries and sub-commentaries and searched thoroughly through all manner of texts, hoping to finally hear the truth of this matter, but he became entangled in a thicket of complications from which he could not extricate himself for more than ten years.
Later, while attending upon Master Shouchang, he heard the raising of the story of Nanquan’s beheading of the cat. Suddenly, he attained realization;
he then abandoned his previous studies and followed the Master to train in "withered Chan" for over ten years. One day, he heard a monk recite the *Lotus Sūtra*.
He said: "At one time, we coughed and snapped our fingers together; these two sounds reached all the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions.
Suddenly, the mass of doubt was shattered, and for the first time I realized that there is no self that is not the sutra, and no sutra that is not the self.
What is called 'the assembly on Vulture Peak, solemnly remaining without dispersal,' is merely a dreamer's talk. Alas! How could the discourse of the sutras ever permit [such delusions]?"
How easy it was! To encounter [the truth] more than twenty years ago, and to form a bond with it more than twenty years later;
to seek it during days of keen resolve and profound reflection, and to find it at a moment when one’s essence was exhausted and one’s strength spent.
How can the discourse on the Sūtras be taken lightly? This summer, having no other affairs, I have therefore provided a lateral thread for the sake of others, picking out its essentials.

The essential points have been recorded and compiled into a volume. Now, as for this scripture, since Tiantai raised its banner and Wenzheng captured the prize, other scholars have been mediocre, with no successors appearing thereafter.
Yet, regarding this matter, I venture to offer a different discourse; is it that Tiantai’s interpretation was not profound?
Is this account of Wēnlíng not essential? It is merely a private record of my own affairs;
it is also a private record intended to be shown to my descendants hereafter. This serves as the preface.
Preface to the *Lengyan Yi Jie*:

How extremely difficult it is to expound upon the scriptures! If one seeks them through the commentaries and sub-commentaries (*shu* and *chao*), one falls into the error of being narrow and拘泥 (constrained).

If one seeks them apart from the commentaries and sub-commentaries, one falls into the error of being diffuse and 放蕩 (unrestrained). To fall into the error of being narrow means that the divine mechanism is not broadened, and thus I am constrained by the scripture. To fall into the error of being diffuse...

The "dissolute" (tàng) are those who have no recourse to the correct path and thus tear the sutras asunder for themselves. Only those who are not narrow-minded can then employ commentaries and sub-commentaries;
likewise, only those who are not dissolute can then discard commentaries and sub-commentaries. Such individuals are called "those who skillfully treat the sutras.
Regarding the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, there have been no fewer than ten or more schools of interpretation and practice. Tianru [Zongjing] has synthesized them...
They were collected [into this work]. During our present dynasty, scholars who study the Classics have generally adhered to traditional interpretations, not daring to alter them.

It was not until the Wanli era that the two masters Xuelang and Jiaoguang first discarded the old commentaries, and the Venerable Zibai also vigorously advocated the principle of contemplating the scriptural text alone.
Consequently, later students developed a spirit of vigorous self-exertion, regarding the collective commentaries as nothing more than miasma.
The waters rush by so swiftly that one dares not look back even once. Before long, those who are clever and quick-witted come to hold their predecessors in contempt;

they compete to display the arbitrary growths of their own imaginations, and the essential purport of the entire scripture nearly meets with total destruction. Those who are somewhat dull-witted find nothing new upon advancing, yet lose what they previously possessed upon retreating;
they are left with nothing more than to pick up the remnants of spittle from beneath the seat. Yet they alone fail to consider the commentaries of those who came before.

Commentary: Since it is unfit to serve as a walking staff for future generations or as the oral tradition of people today, can it alone serve as the "Zhucāi" (the definitive commentary) for people of the present?
Furthermore, one fails to consider that what is newly acquired by people today—how could one know it might not be the very sand already sifted out by those of the past?
And how could the ancient exegeses of former scholars fail to assist in the practical applications of the "niúshōu-mǎbó" (cow-urine and horse-dung) remedies used by people today? Therefore...

I maintain that for one who excels at interpreting the scriptures, all commentaries serve as aids; for one who does not excel at interpreting the scriptures, the scriptural text itself becomes fragmented and disjointed—this certainly does not depend on whether the commentaries are preserved or discarded.
Now, while I am in the quiet seclusion of the mountains, there was a visitor who requested instruction on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
I therefore directed him to take the traditional exegesis as his guide. Where there were points that seemed unsatisfactory, I then consulted other sources.

These various accounts may have been produced from private opinions to supplement [the original], and I do not presume they are necessarily treasures for the world; rather, they are intended to serve as a mere supplement to my own meager learning.
Preface to the Dispatch of Chan Practitioner Hong on His Travels.
The Way cannot be attained without study, nor can it be attained without extensive learning. Yet Ānanda, having heard much over many kalpas, said:

Preface to Sending Off a Monk on a Traveling Excursion:

As for the excellence of streams, mountains, springs, and rocks, many renowned sages of both past and present have loved them and traveled there. Many, too, have traveled there and composed unremitting verses.
Yet, I have never heard of anyone who could truly love them. This is likely because those of the gentry, bound by their official caps and ribbons, are confined...
Regarding the net of the world, though one may enjoy it for a brief moment and feel a sense of mental ease, in the end it is not where one finds true peace;
how, then, could one truly love it? As for reclusive scholars who dwell in silent, empty mountains, they too are constrained by their times and limited by their circumstances;

thus they entrust themselves to such seclusion to wander therein—how, then, could they truly love it? As for the grief and resentment of orphaned ministers and illegitimate sons, or of heroes and eminent talents...
When their indignation flares up and they are moved by melancholy upon ascending to high places, they soak their brushes with ink;
thus they borrow these arts to vent their repressed and uneasy spirits—how could such things be considered true "liking"?

The elegance of poets and scholars, the pure detachment of monks and immortals, who mock the mountain clouds and sing while playing with the moon over the stream, claim that their own "liking" is beyond rival; yet this too is merely external.
It is merely a matter of conforming to their forms; how could they truly be said to love them? If so, what must one do before being called able to love [the Way]?

I have heard that there were those in antiquity who were truly able to love it: they would close their gates and sit in tranquil repose, such that both sight and hearing were extinguished, yet their love was not one of mere indifference.

Marvelous sights and extraordinary landscapes meet the eyes on every side, yet his delight is not in their abundance. A single crag or a ladle of water, gazed upon alone with ease, yet his delight is not in its scarcity.
Lofty peaks and vast oceans, traversed to their infinite limits, yet his delight is not in their multiplicity.

This extends even to grasping the great levers of power at the court’s head, driving the fierce Hu tribes beyond the frontier, mending the azure heavens where they were torn, and supporting that which was about to collapse.
Throughout the ages, there has been nothing that has not been transmitted and promoted by those who truly love it;
only then can one be said to possess genuine appreciation. Did not Confucius say, "The wise delight in water; the benevolent delight in mountains"?
This Venerable Master [Name] has long harbored a passion for springs and rocks; whenever he encounters a place of sublime beauty, he invariably lingers there all day, leaping with joy.

He was so carefree that he forgot everything; he simply did not realize his body was amidst the vastness of heaven and earth. Lately, he has further desired to explore famous regions everywhere to fill his satchel.
I do not know whether he truly possesses such a love for them or not. Now that we have reached Qí, all of you gentlemen have offered words of praise;
you did not consider me too humble to allow me to compose a preface for the beginning of this work. I, however, reflect that the joys of benevolence and wisdom are, by their very nature, [inherent].
Let us set aside the matters of the Confucians for a moment. Formerly, when Dongpo entered Donglin, he presented this verse: "The sound of the stream is the broad and long tongue;
The color of the mountains is none other than the pure body. Last night, eighty-four thousand verses were spoken; How shall I bring them up to others on another day?
*Du!* What a fine scholar Su! He is merely circling outside the gate. As for the Master [Donglin],...
This: if you can recognize the point where the scholar fails, then the great trichiliocosm is but a single sitting mat.
If this is not yet the case, I fear that the sounds of the brook and the colors of the mountains will bury the hero forever. Know this.

Since the era of the Wanli period, our late teacher Shouchang entered Min and widely spread the rain of the Dharma.
People have only begun to realize that there is a matter directed toward the ultimate; yet, while they may hear of its existence, they have not yet attained faith in it.

While they may have faith, they have not yet put it into practice. How much less, then, can one speak of those who possess profound faith and diligent practice, persevering until the end of their lives without weariness?
The venerable Benli of Jianyang is one who comes close to such an ideal. When the Venerable first received his training...

Shengquan came to join me in travel and first resolved upon a great aspiration. Upon visiting the Elder Shouchang, he subsequently severed all external ties, vowing to clarify the matter of his own self.
He next entered Boshan, where he refined himself for an even longer period. Thereafter, he traveled to Yue and reached Wu, visiting all the great masters such as those at Yunqi and Xiansheng.
