Regarding his lifelong resolve, I observe that he has traveled back and forth between the East and West, braving the hardships of ten thousand *li* without ceasing for over a decade now.
Is this not what is meant by "firm faith and vigorous practice," one who remains untiring throughout their entire life?
At such a time, the presence of a person such as this—though they may not yet have achieved great illumination—is nonetheless of noble character.

You have already surpassed your contemporaries by no small measure. Nevertheless, it is said in the *Zhuan*: "To dig a well nine fathoms deep yet fail to reach the spring is still to leave behind an abandoned well.
If you can strike the spring with a single probe and draw water from it with ease, then on another day I shall write for you in large and special characters to instruct those who come after.
Preface to the Essential Words of Jingci What is Jingci?
It is the name of a hermitage bestowed by the Great Master Wengu. Why was the hermitage named Jingci? It refers to the practice of reciting the Buddha’s name and releasing living beings.
What is sought through the recitation of the Buddha’s name and the release of living beings? It is said to be the restoration of the mind.
The fundamental purity is fundamental compassion. This is the inherently such mind, vast and eternally pure.

Because sentient beings are deluded regarding this inherent nature, they perceive phenomena as being external to the mind; thus, the eyes are defiled by form, the ears by sound, and the nose by fragrance.
The tongue is defiled by flavors; the body is defiled by tangibles; and the mind is defiled by mental objects. They flow outward in pursuit of sensory objects, unable to turn back on their own.

Consequently, they give rise to karma and commit transgressions, sinking forever into the realm of the five turbidities with no prospect of escape. Out of compassion for them, our Buddha [taught this].
He then expounded for them the Dharma for treating defilement and returning to purity. Since the capacities of sentient beings are not uniform, the teachings likewise differ;

yet, among them all, the single gate of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation) is the most essential. When one recites the Buddha’s name with a single mind, the will is undivided, the six sense faculties are fully gathered, and pure mindfulness continues without interruption.
Thus, the eyes are not defiled by forms, the ears are not defiled by sounds, the nose is not defiled by fragrances, and the tongue...
The body is not defiled by tastes; the body is not defiled by tactile objects; the mind is not defiled by mental phenomena.
Thus, while currently dwelling within the Sahā world, one’s entire being is already seated within the Land of Lotus Flowers. How, then, could one’s future retribution not be pure?

Nevertheless, although one may practice the Samādhi of Buddha-remembrance, if merit and virtue are not complete, the good fruit will be difficult to achieve. Therefore, one must extensively cultivate all [virtuous deeds].
Excellent. These serve as auxiliary causes, and while manifold virtues are numerous, benevolence (*maitrī*) is their foremost.

While practices of benevolence are likewise numerous, abstaining from killing and releasing living beings is their foremost. This is because among all sentient beings, there is nothing they cherish more than life and nothing they suffer more than death.
For all who possess breath and vitality, these sentiments are universal; it is only because they have become habituated to endurance that they remain so.

The benevolence inherent in our shared essence has become paralyzed and inert; thus, we slaughter beings with complacency, regarding it as nothing strange. How could this be the natural state of the mind?
For this reason, our Buddha spoke with bitter earnestness, first forbidding the taking of life and widely encouraging the release of living beings.
By giving them what they most cherish and rescuing them from their greatest suffering, how great must be the merit that reaches all things! Thus it was established.

The monastics and laypeople of this prefectural city, whether ordained or lay, have for many years faithfully upheld the Great Master’s teachings, particularly the practices of *nianfo* (buddha-recitation) and the release of living beings (*fangsheng*).
Yet, fearing that these efforts might not yet be sufficiently widespread or far-reaching, they consulted with me.

I have therefore selected essential passages from various texts concerning the Pure Land and the cessation of killing, compiled them into this work, and entrusted it to the printing blocks for circulation. It is my hope that the transformative influence of the Jingci tradition may thereby flourish even further.

It overflows into the inexhaustible! Alas, the meaning of "Pure Compassion" (Jingci) is vast; how could it be limited merely to the recitation of the Buddha’s name and the liberation of living beings?
While the recitation of the Buddha’s name and the liberation of living beings may be described as Pure Compassion, they cannot fully exhaust its meaning.

To speak at the ultimate level: when purity reaches its extreme, awakening becomes perfect, and one achieves the Unsurpassed Way—all this does not depart from the single principle of "Purity. Broadly speaking...
To deliver sentient beings—compassion reaching through eternal kalpas—is nothing other than the meaning of "Great Compassion" (*mahākaruṇā*).

Indeed, the various Bodhisattvas seek the fruit of Buddhahood above and transform sentient beings below; from the first stage to the final one, this is elucidated in the Mahayana sutras until they fill the rooms and exhaust the oxen’s sweat.
Now, to encapsulate this in two characters leaves no further meaning unexpressed. I venture to say that these were the names given by the Great Master [Nāgārjuna].
My intention lies merely in encouraging mindfulness of the Buddha and the release of living beings. You gentlemen should well grasp this intent and expand upon it.
Nevertheless, there is yet one more phrase that the two characters "Jingci" (Pure Compassion) cannot encompass.
I wish to explain it all for you gentlemen, but alas, my tongue is too short. You gentlemen must inquire of the Great Master.
Preface to the Re-engraved Record of the Sayings of Chan Master Tieguan At the end of the Yuan dynasty, there were three who were renowned as *shanzhishi* (virtuous spiritual teachers) in Jianzhou:
Yangshan You, Doufeng Zhang, and Tianbao Shu. Of these, only Master Shu was able to occupy a strategic stronghold and establish an iron barrier, commanding the whole world.
Those with eyes could not peer into it; those with feet could not traverse it. Guests who were but "cock-crowers" or "dog-thieves" could only retreat in shame.
Is its merit not truly magnificent? For over three hundred years it has been recorded and transmitted, yet it lay buried in dust and hidden by mist, with no one to inquire of it.
Recently, it was further destroyed by water and ants; even the wooden blocks no longer exist. My heart [is deeply grieved].
I felt deep regret. Just as I was reflecting, I saw Lord Meng Teng coming to Mount Meng to offer a memorial service.
I then entrusted this record to him. Alas! Zhuge Liang has passed away; yet the traces upon the fish-belly rock still remain amidst the river mist and reeds under the moon.
The momentum of wind, clouds, dragons, and birds remains vividly before one’s eyes. But who today could be like General Yuan Shao? Who?
As for that man—if he were to arrange his battle formations according to a diagram and pride himself on knowing the art of war, he would be like Zhao Kuo reading his father’s military manuals.
I cannot help but feel profound pain at this.
Preface to the *Shouchang Xizhu Chan Master’s Brief Discourse on the Direct Pointing of the Fourth Coming*.
The direct pointing has overturned all old molds and traps. Although there may be spiritual awakening, one must urgently spit it out—how much more so regarding words and letters?

Since he began extending his hand to receive others, his functional expressions have flourished in abundance. A single word or half a phrase has drifted down into the human world, and thus [this collection] came to be.
Regarding the transmission of recorded sayings (*yulu*): awakening to the mind is the root, while skillful means (*jìngyòng*) are the branches. Students should seek the root;

For this reason, every person roars like a lion, shaking the earth and startling the heavens;

all this is because the root is deep and the branches naturally flourish, and the substance is perfect and the function naturally becomes divine. Toward the end of the Zhìyuán era, his Way declined daily; people abandoned the root and pursued the branches.
They vied with one another in practicing hypocrisy; it was only Xueyan Qin who was praised as a true successor. Qin transmitted [the lineage] to Tierniu Ding;

After the late Master passed away, my elder brother, Chan Master Qiran, obtained the manuscript from the shelves of a lay devotee.
Yet, among what remained after the ravages of decay and insects, there were but few passages that could be read word by word. Having taken it up, I have corrected its errors.

I have combined these records of his deeds and had them carved into woodblocks for printing. In the summer of the year Yihai, I returned to Shouchang to sweep the pagoda and was finally able to set my eyes upon them.
I have only tasted a single drop, yet have not swallowed the entire tide; nevertheless, by relying on that single drop, one gathers the entire tide, for the entire tide is but a single drop.
Now, observing the flow of his discourse, it is for the most part derived from authentic inquiry and practical cultivation. Although...
While their functional utility has not yet been seen to its full extent, there are not a few who have forgotten words to realize the truth through direct experience.
Compared to those in the world who practice "blind fists" and "blind clubs" to deceive the common folk, this is more than a difference between heaven and earth.

Having the fundamental source while being sparing in its application—does this not still qualify them as followers of the Buddha? Long ago, a man of Song dug up the earth and found a jade ruler; he took it to be...
It is the Zhou cubit. When the Grand Music Master (Taichang) established the standard for music, he took it as the Han cubit. Some say:
"Is this not quite close to the Zhou standard? In my records, I have also stated this.
Preface to the Rosary Wings:
Among objects, there is no distinction between large and small; what is valued is their practical utility.

When it comes to practical utility, there are things that can penetrate the divine and transcend transformation, such that they cannot be fathomed by thought—could these not be the most precious of all objects? As I observe rosaries...

It is for the sake of sentient beings that this is so. Since the time the White Horse traveled westward and Donglin initiated the transformation [of the Dharma] in the East, the prayer bead first found its practical application.
Over time, its efficacy became increasingly miraculous; it reached the point where one could enter water without getting wet and enter fire without being scorched.

Even Yama, the Old Lord of the Underworld, did not dare to challenge such a person, and the Pure Land took these beads as a token of tribute. Thus, the utility of the bead is truly preeminent in the world.
First: One seeks its peerless counterpart, yet none can be found. Master Hai of Tianmu possesses vast learning and grand prose;
his writings are exceedingly numerous. It is a pity that this object—so precious and so divine—is not ranked among the great authors.
Thus, he has compiled these six wings, comparing them to the *Tea Classic* and the *Litchi Record*. I replied: "Not so. Tea and litchis merely provide sustenance..."
The necessities of daily life are difficult to transcend beyond the realm of divine transformation.
Thus, while the cataloging and systematizing of these [scriptures] may be favored by those who are erudite and refined, viewed from the perspective of our Way, they are all merely flowery words.

Now, through this "Wing" (Yì) practice, may those who uphold it revere right faith and shed the worldly miasma, until at last they wander carefree to the Land of the Lotus and sit beneath the Bodhi tree.

A tree— does it not rely upon this to grease its chariot and urge on its fine steeds? Therefore, I have joined my palms in reverence and composed this preface for the *Brief Commentary on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
I, being unworthy, have studied Chan at the gate of the Dharma Master; yet I was unable to receive even a single glance from him.
When my period of intensive study concluded and I returned to Min, I found myself with nothing to do in the mountains. I took up the Tripitaka and read it through extensively.

Regarding the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, I claimed to have uniquely grasped its essential pivot, and thus composed two fascicles of a supplementary commentary (*Yijie*) to briefly set forth my humble views, supplementing what had not been reached by other commentaries. At that time...
This was the year of Jiǎzǐ in the Tiānqǐ era. By the time of the Bǐnzǐ year of the Chóngzhēn era, I had begun teaching the Dharma at Kāiyuán Monastery in Quán.

It happened that Master Cényún Zēng was serving as a provincial magistrate in the south of Quán; whenever he had leisure from his official duties, he would frequently order his carriage to visit me so that we might deliberate on matters of great importance.

When questioned regarding the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, [the interlocutor] expressed his distress at the confusion and prolixity of various commentaries and requested that I compose a summary of its essential meaning.

I replied: "Those who practice Chan meditation often delight in grasping the broad outlines; however, because the intricate details remain unclarified, they are ultimately unable to completely dispel lingering doubts.
Instead, they hastily interpret the text according to their own preconceptions, a fault that is not minor. Thereupon, I composed the *Guǎngyì Jiě* (Broad Wings Commentary) and...
I have composed this brief commentary, occasionally drawing extensively from various doctrines to synthesize them into a unified system of thought.

While the general principles are certainly intended to be proclaimed, the subtle nuances must also be clarified. My aim is to ensure that readers, upon encountering the text, will experience a sudden and refreshing realization of its meaning.

It is merely that it has not been obscured by the scriptural texts nor confused by various commentaries. Whether it belongs to the Tiantai or the Xianshou school, I have certainly not yet had the leisure to inquire into its subsequent traces.
The first three fascicles were completed during the humid heat of the Kaiyuan era; in the autumn, I returned to Gushan in Fuzhou and subsequently completed the next three fascicles.
In the spring of the following year, I was traveling to Zhexi, where local gentry requested that I remain at Tiāoshān.

The true tranquility of this valley was finally realized through the completion of the final four volumes. Following the Lantern Festival of the Wuyin year, the Imperial Censor Cao Yugong of Jueli came to visit;
upon briefly casting his eyes over the work, he could not help but express profound admiration. He subsequently commissioned artisans to carve the woodblocks for printing.
Now that the work is finished, I have carefully recorded the date and month herein. Indeed, the merit of the conditions that converged at this particular moment must not be forgotten.
Preface to the Biographies and Eulogies of the Portraits of the Patriarchs.
In the spring of the Guiyou year, Shen Jufu of Jueli traveled to Jianzhou to study, where he visited Master Wengu at Baoshan Temple.
He requested that the Master compose biographies and eulogies for the eighty-eight portraits of the patriarchs. The Master entrusted this task to me, the unwise one.
When I had reached about half [the task], a letter arrived from Senior Censor Cao Anzu of Yangxian, also requesting that I write biographical eulogies for him;
thus, the number increased to over one hundred and thirty statues. From summer until autumn, it was five months before I completed them.

I have prepared this report to inform you of my progress. Coincidentally, while I was at work, Lord Cao was stationed in the Central Plains, and as rebel bands entered the borders, military affairs became extremely urgent.
I was unable to ascend the stone steps. When the raiders withdrew, I managed to inform [the Master] of my departure and returned home.

Upon returning, I fell ill; though ill, I did not expect to recover. Before long, I heard that the Great Master had also passed away. In the spring of the following year, I, Fohui, left the mountain passes to attend his funeral.
The various elders of Zhexi invited me to reside at Zhenji. This spring, due to an invitation from Tianning, I was able to pass through Jueli, where Mr. Cao Jia...
When I, Yu Laijian, saw this, I felt regret that I had not yet put this book into practice. Consequently, together with his younger brother, he made a vow to circulate it.
I, the unwise one, therefore revised and supplemented it and handed it over to them.

Within a few years, both elders have already passed away, and my own frail and decaying body is likewise at its end, gasping for breath. That I am still able to witness the circulation of this book—is this not indeed [a cause for joy]?
How joyous this is! Nevertheless, that which can now be transmitted is but a reflection; that which cannot be transmitted is not the reflection itself.
If the observer can seek the reality through the reflection, and attain the untransmittable through what is transmittable, then the circulation of this book will not have been in vain.
If one merely gazes upon the outward semblance, [the purpose is lost].
In doing so, you are merely searching for dregs and lees; the reproach of "buying a chest and returning the pearls" will surely be unavoidable.
Furthermore, what use is this?
Preface to the *Shimen Zhenxiao Lu* (Record of True Filial Piety of the Śākya School):

How profound is the meaning of filial piety! It is vast indeed. Without filial piety, the person cannot cultivate themselves; without filial piety, the human realm cannot be governed; without filial piety, Heaven and Earth cannot be harmonized;
without filial piety, the spirits and deities cannot be reached. Even the Unsurpassed, Most Perfect, Equal, and Right Enlightenment [of Buddhahood] is not attained without filial piety.

There is likewise no other means by which this can be achieved. Thus we know that among the fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) of both the mundane and supramundane realms, none truly surpasses filial piety (*xiào*).
Regarding the secular interpretation of filial piety, its significance comprises five aspects.

Furthermore, the *Shìfǎ* (Canon of Posthumous Titles) describes filial piety with five meanings, which may be condensed into three: compliance, ultimate fulfillment, and deliverance. In sum, it refers to serving one’s parents well.
To serve [the Way] yet fail to be compliant is not goodness; to be compliant yet fail to accord with principle is not compliance.
What is called "ultimate" means being compliant from beginning to end without interruption. What is called "measure" (du) means being compliant such that rites and ceremonies do not falter.
To fully exhaust this meaning—were it not for the Unsurpassed, Most True, Perfectly Enlightened One—how could one possibly be worthy of it?

How remarkable! Thus we know that the filial piety of the secular world is but a minor form of filial piety, whereas the filial piety of the Śākya [Buddhist] tradition is the great form of filial piety.
How can it be that those who have become monks in this world generally borrow the gateway and courtyard of our Buddha to cultivate private gain for their own persons?
Is it any wonder, then, that the secular world censures our Buddha as being one who has neither father nor sovereign? — *Qiantang Meng* (The Dream of Qiantang)
The layman Zhai, harboring a sense of lamentation in his heart, has compiled the various passages on filial piety found in the sūtras and śāstras into this single volume.

He intends for those who have left the household life to understand the Buddha’s profound intent regarding the supreme path of filial obedience, thereby avoiding the worldly slander that Buddhists lack fathers and sovereigns.
His dedication is truly earnest and laborious. Having now arrived at Taizhou, he has requested me to compose a preface for its opening.
This is a path I have long delighted in; therefore, I dare not decline with the excuse of my lack of literary skill.
Preface to the *Chuanxin lu*:
Examining antiquity, we find that whenever a Great Sage arises, they invariably bring about a profound transformation for the world; it is never a matter of chance. During the Liang dynasty...

During the era of Emperor Wu, the study of doctrine surged like surging waves, and people devoted themselves exclusively to lecturing and exposition. Its corruption inevitably led to a fixation on empty words and a casting aside of actual practice.

How could the transformation of Śākyamuni Buddha have been nearly extinguished without this? Therefore, when [the Sixth Patriarch] emerged at Shaolin, he did not establish written texts but transmitted only the seal of the mind;
when [the Buddha] emerged at the Twin Trees, he did not spare his own life but widely propagated the ten thousand practices.

The methods employed by these two masters appear as if they were as different as heaven and earth; yet, insofar as they both aim to rectify deficiencies and remedy defects, and to establish all sentient beings in a state of peace and happiness, their ultimate intent is one and the same.

As for the various verses on the Dharmakāya at the Twin Trees, they have become the ancestral progenitors of the Chan school, appearing almost as if they were unfolding the potentialities not yet manifested during the time of Shaolin. Were it not for his being the reincarnation of Maitreya, how could he have been capable of such a thing?
Ah! I have been in Wǔ for one month and immediately encountered this record of the Great Being (Mahāsattva), as if having obtained a supreme treasure.

The *Dharmakāya Verses* and other sections still survive; like sifting sand to find gold, their refined brilliance dazzles the eyes. Thus, the transformation of the Great Being remains undying.

Now, in recounting the purport of these four sutras, I shall simultaneously address the old-day "entanglements" here. This is not done out of audacity toward the Buddha.

Regarding the preface to the newly carved edition of the Letters and Dharma Discourses of Chan Master Dahui:

When the Patriarch came from the West, he transmitted the Buddha’s mind-seal alone. This seal does not fall within the realms of the aggregates, sense-bases, or elements; therefore, it is beyond thought and deliberation.
That which can be penetrated transcends names and forms; therefore, it cannot be understood through words and speech.
It lies solely in abandoning all expedient means and merging with it through spiritual wisdom.

Thus, those in the world who seek the Way often suffer from having no gate through which to peer and no path upon which to advance, like a horse halted with its reins slackened beneath a precipice or a sheer cliff, seeking its way out.
Is it not difficult indeed for one to gallop forth as a spirited steed?

For this reason, the Buddhas and Patriarchs extensively established skillful means, including the method of investigation and inquiry, so that one may enter the state of no-thought through thought, and enter the state of wordlessness through words.
From the Tang dynasty through the Song and Yuan, all the patriarchs relied upon this very method to enter the Great Radiant Treasury of the Buddha.
However, those who do not apply their minds skillfully become stalled in discursive thought and submerged in words, and thus the maladies of Chan arise.
As for these maladies of Chan, their symptoms are manifold; some fall into a state of solitary peril, which they then take as... solitude and peril itself.
Regarding "taking [this] as meditation": some fall into the trap of the "plain and real," taking the plain and real to be meditation;

some fall into the trap of the "dangerous and strange," taking the dangerous and strange to be meditation; and some fall into the trap of the "frivolous and trivial," taking the frivolous and trivial to be meditation.

All of these arise because their views are biased and one-sided, such that their emotions lean toward some things and turn away from others. There are even those of a certain class who... [entirely...]
There is no place for views; yet some merely dissect the words and phrases to engage in investigation, or sit with eyes closed in stillness, waiting to become Buddhas.
This is the most inferior of all ailments. Formerly, after the Southern Song dynasty had retreated southward, the Elder Miaoxi appeared in the world.
From the perspective of "having a phrase" and "not having a phrase," he clarified the Great Matter with extraordinary brilliance, surpassing his contemporaries.

Rarely has anyone been able to equal him. Observing the maladies of the world, which could never be cured by ordinary means, he employed his unimpeded eloquence to strike directly at their roots and penetrate deeply into their nests.
It was as if one were holding up a torch of rhinoceros horn to illuminate the spirits; no demon could hide. It was like a sudden clap of thunder shattering the silence; even the deaf could hear.
His expositions were so incisive and exhilarating that he was truly a peerless figure in a thousand years. During the Wanli era...
The layman Taiyu Yang of Pumen in our province of Min selected the "Questions on the Dharma" from among those records and carved them into woodblocks for circulation;
he may truly be called one who skillfully dispenses remedies. It is a pity that these blocks were destroyed by the fires of war.

When Wenzhong separately carved the "Questions on the Dharma," they ultimately omitted the six letters addressed to Ceng Tianyou, leaving no small sigh of regret over this deficiency. Now, Yang Jiaosi...
"Householder, you have further inherited the former intention and thus completed the work by carving it anew. Once the carving was finished, you brought it to me to show and requested a preface.
I said: 'Excellent! You are truly able to assist me; you are truly able to inspire me.
I reflect that the maladies of the Chan school today are more than ten times worse than they were in the time of Miaoxi. In short, they are all of the lowest sort."
This is a malady. It mostly consists of deliberations between teachers and friends, transmitted from mouth to ear.

For instance, Tianqi’s commentaries on the *Gusong* (Verses on Ancient Cases) and the lectures, critiques, and chants at Shaolin are not merely incapable of being free from thought—they are all perverse thoughts; they are not merely incapable of being free from speech.
These are all false claims. Not only are they unable to transmit the Buddha’s seal, but they instead wear the seal of the Demon King.
This is what is called a chronic and incurable ailment; how could it be cured by an ordinary physician? Formerly, the heir of the Guo state suffered from a "corpse-stiffening" seizure (shi-jue).
Ordinary physicians folded their hands in helplessness, considering him dead. Only Hou Qi knew he could be saved, and he applied needles to the Triple Yang channels.
He revived him by performing five massages. Nowadays, those who suffer from "corpse-fainting" (shi-jue) are numerous.

The words of Miaoxi are precisely the golden needle of the physician Qin Huan. Should one not contemplate them deeply and take them to heart? Nevertheless, this book was written for the sake of those who are ill.
As for those of superior intelligence, such as Qingyuan and Yongjia when they saw Cao [Dongshan]— [End of provided text]
Xī: When Nánquán and Dàmé met Mázū, they were like fine horses that gallop upon seeing the shadow of a whip;
had it been so, this book would have become superfluous, and our Way would have been fortunate indeed. How can I find such a person to meet?
Morning and evening, I shall wait with bated breath.
