Preface to the Abridged Commentary on the Diamond Sūtra (Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra):
Sentient beings are submerged in the ocean of birth and death, surfacing and sinking again and again, with no prospect of escape. What is the reason for this?
Ah! It is truly because the mirror of the mind is fundamentally pure and the forms reflected therein are originally void, yet sentient beings perceive them as real.
Consequently, they give rise to attachment and aversion, produce grasping and rejecting, and create deluded karma; thus they willingly invite the cycle of illusions and endure suffering.
It is like seeing a tiger in a dream—the person and the tiger are both non-existent; or like flowers blooming before the eyes—the eye and the flowers are both equally afflicted.
They cling to them and will not let go; how could there ever be an end to this? Out of compassion for them, our Buddha taught the Dharma for destroying existence, titled the Mahāprajñāpāramitā.
There are eight sections of the Prajñāpāramitā in total, and the Vajracchedikā is one of them. There are six translations of the Vajracchedikā in total.

Now, the translation by Master Qin constitutes one such version. Its phrasing is concise yet its meaning is abundant; its expressions are clear yet its principles are profound. It truly represents the essential core of the eight sections [of the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*].

Its ultimate aim is to shatter the false attachments to both persons and phenomena, to realize the true mark of the single mind, and to cause all sentient beings not to grasp at appearances, remaining as they are in unwavering suchness. When I was in my early twenties, I already knew how to read it.
Seeking the meaning of this sutra in various commentaries, my heart grew weary of them. For while the principle is fundamentally direct, they explain it with circuitous detours;
while the phrasing is fundamentally clear, they seek it in obscurity. This is largely because they are entangled in the "ivory vines" of the two treatises and cannot liberate themselves from them.
Yet, when there are those who do not follow these two treatises, they in turn recklessly indulge in their own [speculations].
In their hearts, they have transcended the essential tenets and contravened the Buddha’s intent; thus, those who discern them censure them.

Consequently, there are no fewer than several dozen commentaries on the *Vajracchedikā*, yet among them, one has rarely heard of any that may be called a "good commentary. In the autumn of the year of Xin-si, I returned from Wuzhou to Jianzhou.

While residing at Baoshan, Master Xinshi composed the *Jingangdu Meng*. Although the traditions of this school trace back to Guifeng and Changshui, he abridged the redundant and retained only the essentials to facilitate the practice of beginners. He commissioned me to edit it;

though I participated in the process, I merely provided interpretations based on others and accomplished the task through their influence. In my own mind, I could never find true peace with it, and therefore—

The single commentary on the *Vajra* has, conversely, resulted in the karma of incompleteness. Upon concluding the retreat in the spring of the Yiyou year, I grew weary of expounding Chan and spent my days lying flat on my back.
Having no means to dispel my leisure, I took up this sutra and commented upon it daily.
I have utterly eradicated the tangles of former days and alone revealed a brand-new sun and moon; I have sought correctness in principle and fluency in expression. There is nothing [else].
It is merely the fault of being circuitous, obscure, and obscurely ambiguous. After three revisions of the draft, the commentary was completed. A visitor challenged me, saying:
"In ancient commentaries, the patriarchs above and the *Compassionate Honored One* (Maitreya) below followed the two treatises; there was not a single word or character that did not have its source.
Now you discard them and do not follow them—is it because your wisdom can surpass that of all the great sages? I replied: "This is..."
"Not so. Do you say that Vasubandhu could have turned his back on Asaṅga? I say no. Do you say that Asaṅga could have turned his back on the Inner Court (the Maitreya tradition)?

I say no. Since you maintain that these three sages transmitted the teaching to one another like water being poured from one vessel to another, it would be appropriate for them to strictly uphold their master’s teachings, not daring to alter even a single word.
Yet, when we examine it now, we see that Vasubandhu established twenty-seven doubts."
This is already not the intention of Asaṅga. Asaṅga’s division into eighteen stages (*vihāra*) is likewise not the teaching of the Inner Court.

Why, then, do you diverge from the path in such a manner? If you knew that Asaṅga and Vasubandhu would certainly not contradict the Inner Court, then you would know that I today certainly do not contradict Asaṅga and Vasubandhu. The guest apologized and withdrew.
I have therefore recorded this together and placed it at the beginning of the fascicle to serve as a preface.
Regarding the *Sifen jieben* (The Four-Part Code of Precepts),
in the year of Gengchen, while I was at Zhenji Monastery in Hangzhou, I wished to emulate Guifeng by extracting the essentials of the *Vinaya*.

He intended to show [this work] to those of later learning, but in the end, he was prevented by illness. This spring, he came from Gushan to Baoshan and declined all requests for audiences, devoting himself solely to the propagation of the Vinaya.
When others requested him to annotate the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* as a means of facilitating instruction for new ordinands, he complied.

I said, "This is my long-cherished aspiration," and thus I gave my consent. I began writing during the first decade of the middle autumn month and finished during the final decade of the early winter month;

it took three full months, and only after three drafts were completed did it finally take shape. As for the events and principles contained therein, they were all extracted from the *Caturvargika-vinaya-piṭaka*.
All matters concerning what is permitted and what is prohibited are likewise based entirely upon the Buddha’s regulations; I did not dare to rely on my own arbitrary interpretations.
It was ordained. Alas, that this book should be completed on this very day!

Now, at this juncture when heaven and earth are overturned and remade, in this autumn of chaotic beginnings where peace has not yet settled, where white blades pierce the air and corpses lie strewn across the fields, where the inhabitants flee in terror through mountains and valleys, their lives hanging by a thread from dawn to dusk—why have I, despite my failing strength, exerted myself to compose this? It is because...
People know that when the fortunes of the world change, their suffering is extreme; yet they do not realize that when the fortunes of the Dharma change, their suffering is even more extreme.
The suffering of a change in worldly fortune lasts for a single lifetime, whereas the suffering of a change in the fortune of the Dharma lasts for ten thousand kalpas.

The calamity of a single lifetime’s suffering ends with the destruction of one's body, while the calamity of ten thousand kalpas’ suffering reaches its limit in the three miserable realms. When these two are compared, how could [the latter] be anything less than a hundredfold?
How could even ten thousand million people equal one such person? Yet, people see only what has already occurred; they cannot perceive what is yet to come.
Consequently, they are struck with panic and lose their composure regarding this, while remaining complacent and seeking mere security regarding that.

I lament that since the Tianqi era, the venerable elders have perished and those of later generations have declined day by day, like a raging torrent that cannot be turned back. Furthermore, they are deluded...
They flaunt their views of emptiness and treat the precepts as discarded hair-bands, failing to provide any restraint; what end will there be for them hereafter?
This is why I have applied myself with such diligence and urgency to complete this book, not daring to let worldly difficulties obstruct my purpose.

I merely reflect that to circulate this book in the present age is like playing the zither at the gate of King Qi—should it be met with no contempt or derision, that would already be fortunate. How much more so...
May I venture to hope that you will rely upon it and practice it? Nevertheless, this too is like the sheep for the month-opening sacrifice;
whether it is preserved or discarded is up to the benevolent one.

Preface to the *Lüxue fayen xu* (Preface to the Introduction to the Study of Vinaya), Winter of the Bingxu Year. While I was composing the *Jieben yueyi* (Abridged Meaning of the Prātimokṣa-sūtra), a guest came to seek instruction on the *Lüxue jeyao* (Essentials of the Study of Vinaya).
Upon my perusal of his work, I found that for the most part he had not even seen the Vinaya texts himself, but had instead plagiarized other books—much like a crane wading in the floodwaters.

This is what I have compiled. I have therefore composed this "Introduction to the Study of Vinaya" (*Lüxue fayen*) to show it to others. As for the term "introduction" (*fayen*), it indicates the importance of being careful at the beginning.
Now, a journey of ten thousand *li* begins with a single step; if that first step is taken wrongly, those ten thousand *li* will be in vain.
Therefore, students who are beginners must not fail to be cautious. If one mistakenly places faith in the wrong person or erroneously practices false teachings, there will be [consequences].
To remain ignorant of their error throughout one’s entire life, and for successive generations to transmit them as correct—how can the resulting harm be fully described?
What has been compiled here merely indicates the general outlines of the various precepts, so that one may know where to direct oneself.
Although this does not yet reach the ultimate state of vastness and subtle refinement, if one seeks it through these very principles, then what is called "vastness and refinement" will be found.

Those of lesser capacity certainly do not go beyond this. It is just as when one leaves home to travel by carriage: if one first applies grease to the ruts, there will be no destination too distant that cannot be reached.
Although this book is slight, what it addresses is of great importance; this is why I did not shun the reproach of being pedantic, but completed it.
As for those of lofty intelligence, they should naturally consult the complete Vinaya themselves; what need is there for this book?
...is sufficient to say.
Regarding the Preface to the Commentary on the Benevolent Kings Sutra for the Protection of the State:
Formerly, the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai extensively expounded various commentaries, all of which have already been widely circulated throughout China; yet, [of these], only the *Renwang*...
One commentary fell into the hands of those abroad for several hundred years. It was only during the Song dynasty, through the efforts of merchants, that it finally returned to its native land;
yet it failed to circulate widely in the world and remained hidden within the Dragon Canon (the Buddhist Tripitaka).

Recently, as the national destiny has declined and calamities have occurred in succession, the Venerable Benzhao, deeply harboring the anxieties of Goujian, carved this *Benevolent Kings Sutra* [into woodblocks].

It was printed on wooden blocks and widely encouraged for recitation. Subsequently, the Venerable Reirin remarked that the meaning of the sutra is profound and remote, and cannot be understood without a commentary (*sho*).
He therefore took the ancient *sho* of Tiantai and combined it with this text. Indeed, this commentary has been transmitted since the Chen and Sui dynasties for over a thousand years;
yet, existing as if present and then as if lost, it had not been widely manifested to the world, such that even among veteran teachers and long-established scholars, few...

There are those who have encountered it but once; yet now, these two sons are able to put it into practice at this time when the four seas are boiling over and the common people are submerged in the mire of suffering.
From this we know that this commentary shares a great karmic affinity with the sentient beings of the final age;

is it not for this reason that the dragons and devas lent their power to circulate it? I only wish that every person might, by means of this commentary, penetrate the sutras, and by means of the sutras...
When one attains the ultimate principle, the spiritual power of Prajñā is such that there is nothing it cannot shatter, and likewise nothing it cannot protect.
Even the state of Buddhahood and the rank of Bodhisattva depend upon it for their realization; how much more so, then, the governance of a nation and the welfare of its living beings?

Some may argue that order and chaos alternate in a cycle ordained by Heaven, and that reciting sutras while shut inside one’s door is a remnant of the former age’s declining virtue—why, they ask, should one still value this today? To this, I reply: [The remainder of the text follows as provided in the source.]
That is to say: the governance or disorder of a state truly depends on the mandate of Heaven (tianming), yet the mandate of Heaven is fundamentally rooted in the human mind.
Therefore, the human mind is the source of both order and chaos. It is not only the Buddhists who speak grandly of this principle;

even when examining the Confucian classics from antiquity, such as the *Great Changes* (*Da Yi*) and the *Great Plan* (*Hong Fan*), it is fully recorded therein. How can one simply consign everything to the mandate of Heaven while lacking the art of creating that mandate? Truly...
If one can deeply savor the purport of this sutra, then there will be no technique left unexhausted for shaping one's destiny.
I ask that gentlemen who understand destiny pay close attention to this three times.
Preface to the Collected Poems of Yang Weixun.
In the middle of this spring, I proceeded to the imperial residence for the purpose of offering prayers for the Emperor’s well-being. There I met Mr.
Yang Weixun, whose brilliance and refinement were truly those of an extraordinary and eminent man; I had already suspected that he must be skilled in poetry.

After some time, he presented me with his recent drafts, which I found to be profound, elegant, and deeply resonant, placing him on equal footing with the masters of the past. Furthermore, his spirit of loyalty and righteousness—
At that time, Bo Bo saw [the truth] at the tip of the brush; thus he knew that Wei Xun was indeed skilled in poetry. However, I say this:
his natural endowment could have advanced him toward the Way, and his talent could have responded to the needs of the world. Why then did he devote such singular effort to this alone?
It may be that his family was originally poor and they had long been accustomed to hunger; perhaps the stifled and despondent vapors of his distress were all channeled into indignation.
These [feelings] were expressed in his poetry; thus, his verse was uniquely refined. Therefore, I lament that only Xun was capable of such poetry.

Now, having fled the chaos into Min and encountered a sage ruler who promoted him to the position of Director of the Department of the Household, how could he continue as before with his former craft of "carving insects" (trifling literary pursuits)?
He ought instead to exert his strength in diligent public service, laboring for the affairs of the King to pacify the realm within and restore our Qing dynasty.
"Only after [the world] is like felt-cloth can one compose long songs and short rhapsodies to gloss over the Great Peace—is this not a source of joy?
Therefore, I do not wish for Wei Xun to be the sole possessor of such poetry. I am originally a withered monk from the mountains and fields, whose vocation is Chan.
Why is it that toward Wei Xun, I cannot advance him through the study of Chan, but instead urge him toward fame and achievement? It is surely because at this time..."
During the days of lying upon firewood and tasting gall, one receives the rank of others and consumes the emoluments of others;
yet to exalt oneself through the practice of *cān* (abdicating) would not accord with the human heart. Is it truly fitting for you to act thus?

Once your merits have been fully realized and your achievements complete, you may don a coarse robe and yellow cap and seek me out at the summit of Shigufeng; at that time, we shall certainly have a different discussion.

Preface to the *Dànxián jí* (Collection from the Tranquil Studio). Formerly, Zhuangzi discussed poetry, saying: "Poetry is used to express one's nature and emotions; gentleness, warmth, gravity, and thickness constitute the teaching of poetry.
Judging from this, poetry exists solely in attaining the correctness of one's nature and emotions. As for those who discuss poetry in later generations...
On the contrary, they focus exclusively on craftsmanship through artifice and prize novelty and elegance;
consequently, the spirit of gentleness and profound sincerity has vanished without a trace. How could this be the teaching of poetry? The Venerable Lishang of Tanyang has never studied poetry.
Nevertheless, he also possesses a body of poetry. Having encountered various conditions and circumstances, he spontaneously engaged in poetic exchanges;
whether in verse or gāthā, there are several dozen pieces in total. This summer, when he came to Baoshan in Jianzhou, he presented his complete collection to me.
Upon reading his poems, I find that they embody the Way of antiquity: their sentiments are vivid and profound, their spirit is solemn yet harmonious, and their diction is elegant and warm.
Its tendency is pure and elegant; there is nothing therein that does not follow the rectitude of human nature and emotion to express what one has to say.

As for the decadent and seductive forms, the painful artifice of carving and painting, the clamorous atmosphere, and the frivolous rhetoric of the final age—none of these have any place within it. Is this not indeed close to what Zhuangzi discussed? Indeed it is.
The Way of poetry has been in decline for a long time. I did not expect that you would be capable of such [attainment].
However, it is not what the world prizes; there are few in the world who truly understand it. Yet, you do not seek to be known by the world.

As the Master Lao said, "That which is rarely known is precious. Your poetry is indeed worthy of being prized. Therefore, I have specially composed this preface for its beginning to bequeath it to posterity.
The postscript to the *Zhigui ji* (Anthology of Planting Cinnamon) states:

"In the past, the Four Sages expounded the *Great Changes* (*Da Yi*), and Jizi set forth the *Great Plan* (*Hong Fan*); they had already investigated the ultimate limits between Heaven and man and deeply clarified [these matters]."
This is the mechanism of resonance and response (*ganying*). However, people observe instances of worldly resonance that do not always conform to this principle;

consequently, they are unable to have deep faith. Some claim that one may obtain results or escape calamities by mere chance. Others claim that it is like the growth, flourishing, and withering of plants and trees within the Great Creator (*daizao*):
these occur spontaneously through their own nature and transformation, and Heaven truly has no intentionality. This extends even to those who practice benevolence...

Filial sons feel stifled and unable to express themselves; they ultimately have no means of self-exoneration, nor can they help but feel indignation at the fact that the Way of Heaven is devoid of knowledge—how much more so for those of lower station?
Since Buddhism came from the West, it was its foremost teaching to proclaim the doctrine of cause and effect.

It penetrates the three periods of time, leaving no subtlety uncomprehended; thus, the essential principles of the *Great Changes* (*Dàyì*) and the *Great Plan* (*Hóngfàn*) began to become widely manifest and clear in the world.

Yet, there were still those who treated it with neglect and refused to believe it, because their defilements of emotion were difficult to cast off and their attachment to the self (*ātmagrāha*) remained firm;
consequently, they were unable to engage in deep reflection upon the words of the sages. This is what is called "contravening Heaven"; this is what is called "insolence."
"Sages! What offense have I committed? The layman Jiuqi Jiang is devoted to the study of Confucius, yet he fears only violating Heaven and insulting the Sages;
thus, he has carved this inscription on the 'Planting of the Cinnamon Tree' (Zhigui) and requested that I provide a preface for it at the command of his friend Ruo-shan. I said:
'Though your words are excellent, how could they possibly surpass those of the Great Sages? Therefore, one must simply revere Heaven and honor the Sages.'"
This is the preface. *The Preface to the Xifaji*:
The *Xifaji* was composed by Xie Gaoyu, a refugee from the Song dynasty. Gaoyu possessed great talent and bore a heavy burden... [text continues]
Zhi encountered the hardships of his times and wandered as a solitary traveler in foreign lands; yet he maintained his integrity with steadfastness, never wavering in his resolve.
He spent the remainder of his life singing songs of resolute sorrow, and there was no one who heard him who did not admire his righteousness.

Having read the *Records of the Remnant Subjects of Song* and the *Gazetteer of Wuzhou*, I already knew that Gao Yu’s character and integrity were preeminent, making him a remarkable figure among the worthies of the Song dynasty's final years. Now that I have obtained this collection...
Upon examining them, one first realizes that his poetry—if we consider the prose as well—strives mightily to follow in the footsteps of the Tang masters.

His various "Ancient Style" (*gufeng*) poems can be said to ride side-by-side with those of Li He and Zhang Ji, while his five-character regulated verse (*wuyan jinti*) stands shoulder-to-shoulder with that of Meng Jiao and Jia Dao.
As for the various "Records" (*ji*) he composed, they move freely between the styles of Han Yu and Liu Zongyuan. In sum, there is not a single word or character [that does not reflect this].
He captured the very tone of the Song dynasty. Yang Shen (Yang Sheng’an) claimed him to be the preeminent among the literati of the late Song;
is this not so? Yet I, a fool, maintain that the integrity, righteousness, and literary works established by scholars are both held in high esteem for a thousand years.

As for one such as Gao Yu, his singular indignation and his buckets of blood and tears can truly be ranked above those who "gathered ferns" (Bo Yi and Shu Qi) and placed on equal footing with the *Chuci* (Songs of Chu); he is no mere Du Fu.

Even those such as Mei Li and Qinglian were left in a state of rapturous wonder. Furthermore, I have seen in Huang Qian’s collected works that his integrity and conduct were honored by the world as a model;
those of later generations vied to be in his presence, for wherever his staff and sandals reached, every word and smile was nothing other than instruction.
If this is so, then Gaoyu was not merely one of impetuous chivalry, nor was he a man of singular, narrow-minded rectitude alone.
He was truly a man of integrity. How could he merely be regarded as the preeminent literary figure of the late Song dynasty?

As I happen to be living amidst the height of the world’s turmoil, secluded in the mountain forests with my breath held, I recall that man and reflect upon his era; I cannot help but read this collection three times over.
Therefore, I have composed this preface and circulated it.

Regarding the *Jìdēnglù* (Continuation of the Lamp Record), the Chan school has transmitted it through successive generations, likening it to a lamp. This is because it takes its name from the lamp’s ability to dispel darkness and reveal objects; it also takes [its meaning] from...
That it may continue its illumination without end: from the Jingde era of the Song dynasty, Master Daoyuan first compiled the *Chuan Deng Lu* (Transmission of the Lamp).
Following this, there appeared the *Guang Deng*, *Xu Deng*, *Lian Deng*, and *Pu Deng*.

As their accounts vary in detail and brevity, scholars find it difficult to examine them all exhaustively. Consequently, the Venerable Dachuai Ji merged them into the *Huiyuan*, covering the beginning to the end.

This work is systematic and provides great convenience for later students; its merit is truly profound. As for the various masters from the Shao-ding era onwards who were not included in the *Huiyuan*, we still rely on the *Xudeng* to preserve their records.
However, as that collection was also incomplete—ending merely at the end of the Song and the beginning of the Yuan—it has been nearly four hundred years since the Yuan dynasty until the present day.
During this time, the radiance and brilliance of many masters have been obscured and erased, and they have yet to be recorded.

This lack of clarity in the world—who is to blame for it? Without weighing my own limitations, I began in the spring of the Wuzi year to gather materials extensively from various sources, hoping thereby to compile and supplement the deficiencies of previous works.

By the summer of the Gengyin year, I further obtained the *Wudeng xulu* (Continued Brief History of the Five Lamps) compiled by Master Yuanmen Zhugong, with which I supplemented what remained incomplete. Before long, however, my illness became exceedingly severe, lasting for three months.
He began to recover. Upon recovery, however, his eyesight grew dim and his hearing grew dull; his hands could no longer hold pen and ink.

Consequently, his records still lack the period from the Chenghua era onward, for he simply stopped where he had to stop. The collection consists of six fascicles and is titled *Jìdēng* (The Continued Lamp).

Some have remarked that in the Chan school, the priority lies in awakening through the mind, and that language and writing— *Note: The provided text ends abruptly; this translation reflects the fragmentary nature of the source.*
These are but dregs and sediment. Why must one string together pages and accumulate volumes, drawing out branches and extending tendrils like the *Five Lamps*?
Moreover, why add further to it by creating a "Succession of Lamps"? This is because one does not understand that words can both obstruct the Way and carry the Way.
If one clings to them, even the most refined essence becomes dregs; if one understands them, even dregs become refined essence. How could words ever be exhausted?
Is it not so? As for what has been recorded therein, whether detailed or concise, this was necessarily so due to the differences in the times and the capacities [of the recipients].
For instance, the "wall-gazing" of Shaolin and the "settling of the mind" by the Second Patriarch were like the administration of knotted cords in ancient times.
Subsequently, there appeared the *Xinxin Ming* and the *Dafangguang Fo Huayan Jing Tanjing*; these were like the records of Emperor Xuan Yuan.
It is a covenant. In the Tang era, the two lineages of Mazu and Shitou expounded upon Chan in vast abundance; was this not the ritual and music of the Three Dynasties?

In the Song era, five schools vied with one another and the Five Lamps emerged in succession; were these not the Six Classics of Zhurong and Siwei? When the times required brevity, even the binding of knots on cords was not too simple;
when the times required detail, even the Six Classics were not too many. The essential point lies in adapting to the capacities of the multitude.
The mechanism for generating [new works] serves merely to clarify the nature that has existed from the beginning.

If one were to reproach the people of the Spring and Autumn period, saying, "Why did you not create records using knotted cords? would that not be perverse? That such works continue to be produced to this day is not a matter of choice;
it is precisely like how, after the Six Classics, there appeared the Seven Chapters of Master Meng, which speak of the goodness of human nature and extol Yao and Shun.

To advocate benevolence and righteousness and to cease depraved doctrines is likewise to clarify the Way of the former kings; how could it be said that adding to this constitutes a superfluous appendage?
As for the fact that what has been recorded may be confused and excessive, failing to accord with the intent of the Western Transmission, it would be like Wang Tong’s *Five Classics*:
though he claimed they could succeed those of Confucius, he was unaware that they were actually a farce like "dust for rice and mud for soup."
Is this not a grave transgression? This is what I deeply fear and am unable to escape;
I shall still submit it to those of great wisdom, awaiting their correction and refinement.

Preface to the *Supplement to the Lamp Record* (Fozu Tongji): When Bodhidharma came from the West, he first revealed the essential core of the mind, overturning all previous conceptual molds. From this, the lamps were divided and the flames continued, until his transformation filled China.
It was not only those who sat upon the curved-legged throne who could wield their tongues to propagate [the Dharma]; even farmers carrying provisions to the fields...

Wives, fishing elders, and woodcutters were all able to converse with clapping hands on the joy of Chan. How could this be fully exhausted by the ears and eyes of a single person, or fully recorded by the pens of a single hand?

Since the rise of the Tang dynasty, those who chronicled the karmic conditions and encounters within the Gate of the Treasury [the Chan School] first produced the *Baolin Zhuan* (Transmission of the Baolin Temple).
During the Five Dynasties period, there appeared the *Xu Baolin Zhuan* (Continuation of the Baolin Transmission) and...

The *Shengzhou chuan* (Lineage of the Holy Lineage) was transmitted until the Jingde era of the Song dynasty, when Master Daoyuan first synthesized the three previous records and augmented them with more recent events, titling it the *Chuanteng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp).
At that same time, there was Li Zunxu, who claimed that what had been collected was not yet exhaustive; he thus composed the *Guangdeng lu* (Extended Record of the Lamp).
Subsequently, Master Foguo Bai produced the *Xudeng lu* (Continued Record of the Lamp) at the beginning of the Jianzhong Jinggu era. This continued until—
During the Chunxi era, the Master Ming, known as Huiweng, compiled the *Lian deng hui yao* (Essentials of the Linked Lamps).

At that same time, there was also the Master Shou of Leian, who likewise remarked that what had been collected was not yet comprehensive; he therefore composed the *Pu deng lu* (Universal Lamp Record) to broaden it.
These five lamp records were so voluminous that students found them difficult to master entirely. Consequently, the Master Ji of Dachuan began by merging these five lamps into one.

The *Huìyuán* (Compendium of the Source) was convenient for later students; however, under its process of pruning and editing, many were left with "marred foreheads," leading inevitably to sighs over lost pearls.
Furthermore, the collection itself remains incomplete. For instance, regarding the area north of the Yellow River, the Jin dynasty possessed the single lamp of the *Dàdìng* era.

Even Daichuan had not yet been able to see [this work]; thus, were his omissions not already numerous? Subsequently, there appeared a *Xùdēng* (Continued Lamp), of which it is unknown who was the author.
Its collection is the most extensive, yet its inclusion of spurious works is also the most abundant.
Nevertheless, by means of this, one is able to see what was omitted from the preceding five *Dēng* (Lamps); thus, its merit is indeed great. As for the present—
Among scholars, they know only of the single work *Huìyuán*; as for the *Xùdēng*, it is kept secret within the Great Canon (*Dàzàng*).
Thus, even those of renowned virtue and eminent monastic status may go their entire lives without seeing it once. Alas!

The bitter words and subtle teachings of the various masters, delivered with open hearts and bared souls, have ended up merely as dust upon the rafters, satiated by wood-eating insects. Is this not truly a matter of profound lament? Therefore, I have [compiled] it in its entirety.
I searched through the *Continued Lamp Record* (*Xu Denglu*) and, by extension, various other biographies, selecting those deemed worthy of transmission and recording them.

In total, one hundred and eighty-five individuals were obtained. Collectively titled the *Supplementary Lamp Record* (*Bu Denglu*), it is said: "The Great Way is perfectly luminous and vast, transcending the mundane order of things;
what is lost by its omission? What is gained by its supplementation? It is done only for the sake of circulating the conventional truth and inspiring [the faithful]."
To open the eye of wisdom for later scholars by means of the secret radiance of former sages—rather than leaving this [text] deficient, how could it be better than to supplement it?
Do not say that because these are sands already sifted from the great river, they may be discarded and ignored.

Preface to the Guide to the Three Scriptures of the Buddhas and Patriarchs In the Chan school, there are what are known as the "Three Scriptures of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. These have been transmitted and practiced within the monastic communities for a long time.

For the most part, they contain no discourses of lofty or vast scope; rather, they consist entirely of instructions that are immediate and practical for daily life, serving nothing more than to guard against floating emotions and to warn against deviance.
Karma: To guide it toward the Right Path is the primary gateway to studying the Buddha and the precious instruction for enlightening the ignorant.
No one who has become a monk can afford not to know this; it is just as when building a mountain nine fathoms high—the achievement must necessarily begin with a single basketful of earth.
If one discards a single basketful of earth while boasting of a nine-ten-foot wall, even a young child knows that it will surely not be completed.

Contemporary followers of Chan Buddhism vainly admire what is lofty and remote, feeling ashamed to discuss what is humble and near. Upon seeing such books, they invariably shake their heads and disregard them, falsely assuming that those of superior faculties and supreme wisdom would find no need to concern themselves with this.
They do not realize that for those of superior faculties and supreme wisdom, it is precisely not an obstacle.
One may cultivate both the middle and lower [vehicles] simultaneously, as did the Venerable Kāśyapa.

He transmitted the robe with a single laugh and is hailed as the first patriarch of the Chan school, yet he practiced *dhūta* austerities throughout his life without ever abandoning them. How could it be that his faculties and wisdom were inferior?

As for those of the present day, how do their faculties and wisdom compare to Kāśyapa’s? It is simply that their deluded passions are difficult to restrain and they delight in negligence; thus, they resort to such pretexts.
How lofty and far-reaching! Yet they merely indulge their own private whims; I know they will surely end up self-indulgent and self-abandoning.

Now, Zipei has first annotated this sutra to serve as a guide for those of us at the beginning of our studies. He has interpreted its meaning and brought it forth with clarity and lucidity, expressing even a single basketful of his own thoughts.

Preface to the *Shuyu* (Explanatory Discourses) of the Chan Forest. That the Chan Forest possesses *shuyu* is neither a regulation established by the Buddha nor a regulation established by the Patriarchs.

However, since the arrival of the Sangha in this land, in order to lead all sentient beings back to the ocean of the Buddha, whenever matters were represented or circumstances were set forth, there was necessarily a reliance upon [such discourses].

Commentary: Thus, the utility of the *shu* (commentary) has long been established. During the Tang and Song dynasties, this office was held in particularly high esteem within the monastic communities (*conglin*);

none but those who excelled both in talent and learning were selected for it. Since the advent of the Ming dynasty, however, those among the clergy truly capable of fulfilling this role have been rare;
instead, people merely rely on inherited archaic texts and withered phrases to offer perfunctory responses. In my past...
For many years, whenever I held this office, I suffered from the lack of prior records upon which to rely; thus, I was frequently compelled to compose my own responses extemporaneously.

As these accumulated over time, they inadvertently formed a volume. Those with a penchant for such things mistakenly came to prize them, transcribing and circulating them—a process that has continued for over thirty years.
Recently, I saw that Mr. Yu Shidu had carved them into printing blocks at Wulin. And...
The various virtuous friends from Southern Quanzhou have likewise followed the tradition of Wulin in completing this work.

They did so because they believed that although the matter is minor, its utility is indeed difficult to dispense with; and although the phrasing is humble, the meaning can still be conveyed. This was the intention of these gentlemen for its circulation.
Within the great monastic centers, there must surely be extraordinary and eminent individuals whose every utterance is like pearls and gems, and who wield [the pen] with mastery.
When the brush forms wind and clouds, what further use is there for this? I have jotted down a few words to serve as a preface.
The Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra:
The Prajñā is without cognition; all dharmas are fundamentally quiescent. They arise from the wondrous essence of the single truth, appearing as reflections within the two truths.
Floating fame appears real yet seems unreal; it cannot be categorized as either real or unreal. It is both separate and united, yet cannot be clarified through separation or union.
Thus, it is empty yet not empty, existent yet not existent. These qualities mutually establish one another without hindrance, and mutually negate one another while coexisting.
They may also both vanish, such that their dissolution and establishment are unimpeded, and their concealment and manifestation are sovereign. This is called the mystery of Prajñā.
This is the essential point. Yet, alas, the ordinary mind is easily deluded and the fire of wisdom is difficult to kindle.
It is like attempting to catch the wind with a net or grasping the moon from its reflection in the waves; one undergoes toil in vain, which instead becomes an obstacle.

Thus, a hundred sufferings entwine and a thousand calamities converge, all arising from this single moment of attachment. Now, as for this *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya-sūtra*, its text is concise while its meaning is...

This work is truly abundant; its phrasing is manifest, yet its principles are profoundly abstruse. It first opens the two gates of emptiness and form, specifically to refute the two attachments to existence and non-existence.
When existence and non-existence are exhausted, the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) can be revealed; when form and emptiness are unified, the wondrous meaning becomes complete.

If one clarifies this path of Prajñā in daily life, one has already accomplished more than half the task. I have observed the commentaries of various schools, but few have reached its profundity; only [Master] Xian...
From the outset, I have followed the two "Retirements" of Mount Gushan; indeed, they were veteran generals on the field of Dharma.

However, their works extensively excerpted from the sūtras and śāstras, making them overly elaborate and reliant on verbal devices (*śruti*), such that they are not easily accessible to beginners. Therefore, I have specially provided these "Finger-Pointing" instructions so that the meaning may be readily perceived, thereby facilitating the study of beginners.
Nevertheless, a journey of ten thousand *li* begins with a single step; may those who observe this not treat it with negligence.
Preface to the *Benchou* (The Pivot of the Pen):
During the early Ming dynasty, there was a reclusive gentleman named Wang Da who lived in obscurity in the northern frontier. He composed a single volume of writings titled *Benchou*.
Because his words were all simple and devoid of artifice, yet substantially pertinent to the everyday routines of human life, they were like this:
Indeed, one can anticipate that such a person must have observed the transformations of the world and experienced long periods of hardship and anxiety;

therefore, what he has written strikes directly at the evils of the times. It is truly an essential art for avoiding harm and preserving oneself in a degenerate age, and a set of maxims for establishing conduct and perfecting virtue.
Furthermore, as his words are simple and accessible, they need not concern whether one is a beginner or a scholar of long standing; all may profit from them.
It is clear and easy to understand; its exhortations and transformations are especially extensive, and its power to move people is especially swift.
If one were able to follow and practice it, how could the governance of the ages of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties be surpassed? As the saying goes: "Vessels need not all be *hu* or *lian* cups;
practical utility comes first. Medicines need not all be *san* or *ling*; curing disease is the priority. This book is precisely what that refers to.
Indeed. This work was first re-engraved in Jinling by Lin Gushu, the Minister of the Ministry of Revenue;
subsequently, it was re-engraved in Xixia by Han Gongwen, the Vice Censor-in-Chief. Both of these editions consist of thirty-two chapters.
Later, the Vice Commissioner of Shandong, Mr. Pan Yuying, published it in Jinan; subsequently, Mr.
Dai Zhongliang of Xin’an re-published it in Jianzhou. Both of these editions consist of seventy-seven chapters.
Upon careful examination, I find that the editions of Pan and Dai represent the complete original text, whereas those of Lin and Han are abridged versions. Now, I have once again...
I revised and edited [the text], resulting in thirty-nine chapters. Furthermore, for each chapter, I provided a heading, much like Xunzi did.
When Xie Chunyi of Jianzhou saw this and approved of it, he requested that it be carved into printing blocks to share with his fellow enthusiasts; this was a most noble intention.
Thus, I have recounted its origins and conclusion as follows.
Preface for the Seventieth Birthday of Layman Xie Xianke, Composed in the Autumn of the Year Dingyou. On the nineteenth day of the seventh month, coinciding with my own eightieth birthday, Mr.
Xie Feiqing of Jianzhou came from afar with his father, the elder layman Xianke, specifically to offer incense and provisions as a gift, to offer their congratulations, and to request [this preface].
Ascending the seat, he proclaimed the primary truth (paramārtha-satya) to provide an occasion for the joy of the Dharma for the monastics and laypeople gathered from the four quarters.
Thereupon, they addressed him, saying: "We, father and son, have had the honor of residing under the Elder Master’s guidance for over twenty years.
We have been fully nourished by the nectar of the Dharma (amṛta) and have respectfully adhered to his teachings without any lapse. On this day, the twenty-eighth of the eighth month..."

On the occasion of my father’s seventieth birthday, when all his friends and relatives had assembled, I ventured to request a word from the Venerable Elder on behalf of his long life, so that it might be recorded in our family genealogy and ensure that our descendants would succeed one another in an unbroken line, never falling away from the practice of goodness.
Being unable to decline, I have respectfully compiled this record: My grandfather’s name was Yimao (以懋), his courtesy name was Xianke (獻可), and he was a native of Jianzhou (建州).
The wife’s surname was Xie; Nian-dun in Gui-ling was her ancestral home. Her lineage descended from the Song Dynasty Prince Consort, Lord Meixi, as well as the Master of Li-xue, Deyang.
Their family line has been continuous like a string of cicada wings, with no lack of eminent figures throughout the generations. Her father, Mr.
Yiyang, loved goodness and delighted in charity, possessing the character of a great elder. He also once took refuge in the late Master Shouchang at Dong-shan.
Yan observed the fasts and recited the Buddha’s name for over forty years, as consistently as a single day. He fathered three sons; my grandfather was the youngest.

In his youth, my grandfather studied for the civil service examinations, yet he did not achieve his ambition. Nevertheless, he was by nature upright and firm, and possessed a character that was simple and robust.

He was harmonious toward his clan and devoted to his kin; he showed compassion to the orphaned and assisted those in urgent need. Trusting in Heaven and following the Way, he was entirely free from artifice. Consequently, he was frequently [honored] by the authorities...
He was highly esteemed by various local elders, each of whom presented him with commemorative tablets (*biao-xie*) to extol his character and virtue.

He married into the Chen family, fathering six sons and one daughter; all their marriages were completed. The eldest son was named Feiqing (styled Jing), who studied at the local prefectural school and received the stipend of a disciple.
His literary talent and conduct were refined and elegant, and he achieved renown within the artistic circles. The others each remained settled in their respective vocations. [His] grandson...
There were over ten Cao family members. His great-grandson Longjin succeeded him in attending the academy (*pan*).

As for his other grandsons, they are all outstanding and vying for excellence—those who are just beginning their advancement and show no sign of ceasing. I have often ventured to offer my humble reflections on this:

since the upheaval that overturned heaven and earth, the hearts of men and the ways of the world have undergone mutual transformations, declining day by day to a point where they seem almost beyond remedy. What we can rely upon is only the presence of virtuous people.
The gentleman should support it with the Dharma as a protective wing, so that perhaps one-tenth may be preserved from every thousand.
Otherwise, where would there be any place to rest? Formerly, Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty said to his minister He Shangzhi:

"I have just seen the treatises composed by Yan Yanzhi and Zong Bing, which elucidate the Buddha-dharma; they are extremely clear in their principles and both serve to inspire and encourage the human spirit. If one were to..."

From the officials down to the commoners along the borders, all were moved by this transformation. I, the Emperor, shall then simply let my robes hang loosely and sit in peace, bringing about a state of Great Tranquility. What further affairs could there be?
Thereupon, Shangzhi stepped forward and said: "In a village of a hundred households, if ten people observe the five precepts, then those ten will become pure and prudent."
In a village of a thousand households, if a hundred people practice the ten wholesome deeds, those hundred will live in harmony.

If this moral influence is spread throughout the entire world, then among a population of billions, there will be a million virtuous people. For every single good deed one can perform, one evil is eliminated.
To eliminate one evil is to bring rest to one form of punishment. When one form of punishment is stilled within the family, ten thousand forms of punishment are stilled within the state;

thus, Your Majesty’s words that "peace will be brought about by sitting still" are indeed correct. However, in the present age, the pure customs have long since been diluted, and those who follow no rules believe that doing good leaves no trace, thereby vying with one another to rush toward evil.
For this reason, weapons and spears are entangled in chaos, and the net of punishments is cast wide.
It is dense and pervasive, and its calamities extend even to the common people; its cruelty is beyond words.

If throughout the empire everyone were like the Xie family—where ancestors, fathers, sons, and grandsons have transmitted their legacy through generations, honoring the Buddha and receiving the precepts, accumulating goodness and cultivating virtue—then as for the instructions they give to their descendants, they would be only to read and till the land, to be diligent and frugal. In such a case, even if there were armies...
What further use would there be for punishments? That which Emperor Wen of Song called "sitting with arms folded to bring about Great Peace" is indeed not false.
Moreover, you, sir, have reached the age of seventy according to ancient reckoning; yet your beard and hair are white, while your face bears the complexion of a youth.
Your longevity is truly immeasurable. Your talented sons and virtuous grandsons fill your presence in great numbers, and the reputation of your family is mightily sustained.
Thus, he is the locus where auspicious blessings converge; in days to come, he will surely establish a brilliant and magnificent legacy that far surpasses those who came before.
I am old and have long distanced myself from brush and inkstone; for all who seek my writings, I resolutely decline their requests.
Yet, regarding the petition of Mr. Feiqing, I could not bring myself to disregard it. Therefore, I have specifically raised the point of how Buddhism is beneficial to... [the world].
The World is regarded as the longevity of an elder; this constitutes the preface.
Colophon to the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Gumei. Colophon.
The school of Direct Pointing flourished during the Tang dynasty and declined during the Song. By the Yuan dynasty, three of the five lamp lineages had lost their succession;

only the Linji and Caodong lamps remained. Yet, Linji excelled in its vigor but failed in its lack of refinement, while Caodong excelled in its subtlety but failed in its excessive detail. As for this lack of refinement...
Fragile and attenuated, its lingering influence and refined resonance were nearly extinguished.
At that time, within the single lineage of Linji, only Xueyan Qin rose up from amidst the decay and desolation, so that the family tradition might perhaps not be lost.
His successors were only Gaofeng Miao and Tieniu Ding. After Ding came Banyue Cheng; after Cheng came Gumai.
Master You succeeded him. Initially, Master You studied under Moshan Ben; later, he underwent the forging of Prajñā’s hammer.
He finally severed the life-root at the moment the alms bowl moved and settled, casting off all worldly confines.

He subsequently occupied the seat of Gao’ang, grasping the Vajra-ring, reviling Buddhas and scolding Patriarchs, and commanding ghosts to drive the winds. Those who followed him with their monastic packs filled half the sky.
Thus, it was none other than this Master who ensured that the Way of Linji did not fall into ruin. Since the rise of the Ming dynasty, this Way has become increasingly obscured.
Those who ascend the Flower-King throne in various places and claim to be "good spiritual friends" (kalyāṇamitra) often mistake the howling of jackals for the roar of the lion;
such a state of utter confusion has never been as extreme as it is today. How, then, can we ever hope to rouse the likes of Gumai and his peers?
"Old age. Shall I not rectify this once and for all? In the past, the Way of Linji declined upon reaching Fengxue.
When Fengxue ascended the hall to expound the Dharma, he would often weep until his tears fell. Had he known that things would reach the present day, one cannot imagine the depth of his grief.
On this journey to Shulin, I climbed Mount Yangshan and paid my respects at the stupa of the Elder Gumai, where I was able to behold this record. It is exactly as if—"
In the long night of gloom and darkness, I suddenly beheld the luminous pearl; thus, with joy and exultation, I have appended this postscript to the *Xuefeng Yulu*.
Since the flourishing of the teaching began with Nenggui, none has surpassed Mazu in the excellence of those he brought to realization, followed by...

Thus, we turn to Xuefeng. This old man of Xuefeng, having shed the bottom of his bucket beneath Deshan’s staff and emptied all his household treasures at the Inn of Mount Ao, was able to move with total freedom—spanning heaven and earth.
Returning to Min, he expounded the Dharma beneath Elephant Bone Peak; he did not speak of the nature of reality nor engage in negation, but simply emerged abruptly. Every single word...
A single phrase transcends all and stands out from the crowd; it cuts off past and present, a realm unreachable by mind, intellect, or consciousness.

It is truly the life-force of the Buddhas and the marrow of the patriarchs. Thereafter, those who transmitted the lamp and spread the teachings numbered forty-six, flourishing into the two lineages of Yunmen and Fayen.
Were it not for this, how could one say that the source is distant and the stream is long?

Ah! Since my own tonsure, I have thirstily yearned for the words of Xuefeng, regretting that I had not seen them more often. Upon examining the Tripitaka, I found they had ultimately been omitted and not included.
Later, when I obtained the printing blocks from the Xuefeng Temple collection, it was like finding a precious jade gem.
However, I saw only the miscellaneous verses recorded at the end of the scrolls, as well as the "Testament of Lady Lan" and the "Final Instructions of the Great Master," most of which were...
This was a fabrication that, on the contrary, obscured the merits of his predecessor; in my heart, I found this particularly grievous.

One day, while in an old bookstore, I obtained a woodblock edition from the Yuan Zhitai era (1298–1307) produced by Qiaoyin Yisuo. Only then did I realize that the additions at the end of the volume were entirely not authentic.
Now, this has been collated and finalized based solely on the Qiaoyin edition. Those from all quarters who wish to know the matters concerning the "Wooden Ball" (Mogu) should seek them herein.
Colophon to the *Xuanyaoji* (Collection of Profound Essentials) by National Teacher Xingsheng of Gushan.
In the spring of the Jiashu year, when I first arrived at Gushan, I inquired immediately about the *Xuingsheng Yulu* (Recorded Sayings of Xingsheng), but no one was able to provide it.

Later, searching through the Tripitaka, I finally obtained this record; however, it was merely a small volume, likely gathered by later generations from among the remains of decayed wood, insects, and ashes, rather than the original collection compiled by Liaozong. It was incomplete and missing portions.

There is much here, yet the "water cranes" (superfluous passages) are not few. Those who observe it do not long before they yawn and feel drowsy; how then could they possibly comprehend its ultimate intent?

Therefore, on a day of leisure, I have rectified errors such as those of "Hei" for "Hai" and "Shi" for "Gou," and deleted redundancies, hoping that the true face of Xingsheng Temple may once again be revealed.
Generally speaking, the language of Xingsheng does not prize the strange or the perilous, nor does it employ elaborate ornamentation; it simply...
In ordinary speech, he manifests the function of sparks from flint and flashes of lightning; in the blink of an eye, he spans a thousand li, making it difficult for anyone to catch up with him.
Whenever he utters even a single word or phrase, thousands and tens of thousands of people cannot shake him, nor can they fathom his intent.
Could this be possible for anyone who does not wear the talisman beneath their elbow or possess the eye atop their head? One should know that [this is the power of] Xianggu...
This family tradition has been so from the beginning. Because the Master was able to deeply grasp its essential meaning, he was given the title "The Holy Archer" on that very day.
I have now collated and edited this for your high discernment. In the past, Zhuan-an Gui remarked that this record’s singing is lofty while its harmonizing is rare;
perhaps future generations of Chan scholars will not be able to understand it. If, however, there are those today who can understand this record, they shall [sound the drum].
The Way of the Mountain Path does not lead to desolation.
This was inscribed after Zhuowu’s Burning of the Books.
Initially, Zhuowu and Tiantai were inseparable friends; however, because their discussions on learning did not harmonize, they eventually fell into estrangement. Later...
The followers of these two schools also reviled one another until Zhuo’wu met his end; all this was caused by their discussions on learning acting as a medium for such conflict.
The malady lay in seeking the Way through emotion (*qing*). Because they sought the Way through emotion, there was no one who did not become submerged in emotion.

Consequently, even if their learning became increasingly vast and their intellectual understanding more extensive, their self-grasping emotion grew ever more intense. From this, [their attachments] became firm.
Their armor becomes ever more formidable, and their spears and halberds become ever sharper; their momentum will not cease until they have come to mutual destruction.
Regarding the doctrines they uphold: Tiantai takes human ethics as the ultimate, while Zhuowu takes the state where joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure have not yet been aroused as the ultimate.
When I formerly resided in Chu, the monastics and laypeople I encountered all for the most part took the side of Zhuowu. I, however, said that Tiantai’s position need not be discussed.
Indeed, even Zhuowu himself was not without his faults. It is like the hand: when extended, it becomes a palm; when clenched, it becomes a fist.
Although the fist and the palm differ, the substance of the hand remains unchanged; how could there be any room for acceptance or rejection?
What is now called the "ultimate of human relations" is the fist extending into a palm. What is called the "central state of non-emotion" (the unmanifested) is the palm clenching into a fist.
It is the fist. In one case, grasping the palm is considered ultimate; in another, grasping the fist is considered ultimate. How much distance can there possibly be between them?
If one were to know the substance of the hand, then the fists and palms so grasped would be nothing more than the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a hare.

It is heard that the Way does not involve movement or stillness, yet it is the constant embodiment of movement and stillness; the Way does not fall into existence or non-existence, yet it is the eternal sovereign of existence and non-existence.
Those who study the Way today insist on abandoning movement to grasp stillness, and abandoning existence to grasp non-existence;
how can this possibly be the intent of the *Zhongyong*? Formerly, Han Daibai commented on Xuedou’s verse, saying: "One..."
A rabbit lies across the ancient road; as soon as the gray falcon sees it, it seizes it. Later, the hunting dog lacks spiritual acuity;

it vainly searches for it at the site of the old withered stump. Zhuo’wu clings to the state of "the mean before arousal"—this is precisely what is meant by searching at the site of the old withered stump.
How could he know that at the very moment of joy, anger, sorrow, or delight, the state of the mean before arousal is already like the blazing midday sun?
Suspended in mid-air, there is nowhere to escape. Such is what he perceives; thus, he is unable to govern his joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure, but is instead governed by them.
Amidst the meeting of contrary waves and headwinds, in the perilous uncertainty between life and death, he possesses no mastery over himself and ultimately takes his own life. How tragic!
Postscript to the *Prajñā-nirjñāna-śāstra* by the Elder Zibo:
He used it to transcend the world, surpassing all vehicles (*yānas*) and securely realizing one’s own mind;
he used it to navigate the world, wherein phenomena and principle are one, and whether held horizontally or inverted, everything accords with the sagely emperors and enlightened kings.
The Path of the King. There was a guest who harbored doubts regarding the Way of Prajñā, contending that it is unsuitable for governing the world.
I replied: "That which is elucidated by Prajñā is the two-fold emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*). That which is revealed by the two-fold emptiness is the one mind (*ekacitta*).

Since this mind is not obstructed by the barriers of person (*pudgala*) or phenomena (*dharma*), it is empty yet numinous, quiescent yet wondrous. Whether in the mundane or supramundane realms, what use could there be that it does not fulfill?"
It is well. If one were to claim that Prajñā is unsuitable for governing the world, then it would follow that the One Mind is unsuitable for governing the world.
If the One Mind were unsuitable for governing the world, then from what source could the administrative achievements of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu have been established?
Furthermore, when I observe those of antiquity who served as emperors, kings, worthies, and sages, there was none—
It is not by forgetting both person and dharma that one can subsequently attain its subtlety. If one allows the dharma not to be forgotten, the dharma becomes an obstruction;
if one allows the person not to be forgotten, the person becomes an obstruction. When person and dharma obstruct each other, a hundred faults sprout simultaneously.

Thus, even if one wishes to tread the path of benevolence and righteousness or cultivate ritual and music, it will not go beyond mere forced contrivance—merely externally mimicking their traces. Should one encounter honor or disgrace, or praise or blame...
When praise is heaped upon you, can you receive it as if it were empty space? At the juncture of profit and loss, gain and failure, can you regard them as if they were the hair of a tortoise?
In the face of the perilous and evil encounters of birth and death, can you stand firm like a vajra? Not only this.
Even in the minutiae of a single technique or art, if one does not forget the person and the method, yet no one can attain its ultimate subtlety. It is like a swordsman:
he must forget his hand and the sword, and the sword and his hand; only then can he brandish and cast them about in all directions without failing to conform to the proper measure.
Should there be even the slightest failure to forget, he is restricted by that measure. It is like a wheelwright: he must forget his hand and the wheel, and the wheel...
Only when one’s hands have forgotten [the technique] can speed and slowness respond to the mind without violating its proper measure;
should there be even a slight failure to forget, one loses their skill. Viewed from this perspective, who would say that Prajñā cannot be used to govern the world?
In the early spring of the Ren-shen year, having read this postscript, I inscribed these words upon it at the request of a guest.

Inscription for the Scroll on Releasing Living Creatures at Zhaoqing The dharma of releasing living creatures expands the benevolent waves of the Buddha-ocean and delivers beings from the painful traps of the mundane world.
The Elder Yunqi’s tongue has already dragged through the earth for a long time; now, Master Huikong of Zhaoqing continues to propagate its waves by opening a pond and establishing a society.

The moon is the occasion for a single assembly, and people delight in following it. Moreover, because this place commands the excellence of lake and mountain, the ripples of the water reflect the moon, and verdant hues float upon the mist;

Even when the fortunes of the age decline and calamities arise together, the roots and sprouts from which they originate are accumulated misfortunes."

Its merit and benefit are extraordinary and cannot be measured by calculation. During the Song and Yuan dynasties, the monastic communities invariably recited it together on the first and fifteenth days of every month.

In this way, we may hope not to fail the instructions of our Buddha’s entrustment, nor to fail the grace of the Sage Emperor who nurtures and protects us.
If one were to say that this sutra is not suitable for ritual services and thus regard it as a mere leisurely text, [one would be mistaken].

Thus, [the transmission of the Dharma] has merely remained unextinguished during the Spring season. As for Zhendan (China), the Tripitaka is that which entrusts the life-force of wisdom through written characters.

How clear is this intent! Who would dare to question it? Within a mere thousand years, the disparity between prosperity and decline has been as vast as this.

Those who wish to prolong the life of wisdom to await the future—can they not exercise foresight for hundreds or even thousands of years?

How vast is the disparity between us in terms of human character! In the spring of the Wuchen year of the Chongzhen era, the layman Xiushi came to Mount He and spoke of the Tripitaka in book form;

he joyfully expressed his wish to request a copy. Consequently, on the eighth day of the sixth month, I braved the summer heat to cross the mountain ridges, arriving at Lengyan Temple in Zhulin on the first day of the seventh month, where I fell ill due to the miasma of the season.
It was extremely severe. After half a month, the illness subsided. I requested the scriptures to return home. Upon reaching Qiantang, I encountered a tidal surge;
among the residents on both land and water, those submerged numbered in the tens of thousands, yet my vessel alone escaped the peril—this was due to the power of the stored scriptures.
Nevertheless, the sail fell into the water and my boat nearly capsized three more times. When the boat reached Qinghu, the mountain stream...
The waters also surged and overflowed, turning the level plains into rivers for seven days. When the water receded, roads collapsed and bridges broke;
those who attempted to cross were frequently drowned. On the seventeenth day of the eighth month, he finally returned to Puṣpa. Upon seeing him, the lay devotee was filled with great joy.

Yet he was unable to speak. It was likely because several days before my return, word had been spread that I was gravely ill, and I had also heard of the catastrophe of the great flood in Zhejiang, which had submerged vast numbers of people. Thus, when the Elder saw me, it was as if meeting again after lifetimes apart;
his joy was beyond description. Alas! How can this collection be treated lightly? Zibo [Zhixu] wailed like Shen Baoxu.
At the court of Qin, with blood and tears of bitter toil, after an accumulation spanning several decades, this work was finally completed.
The lay practitioner [the patron] generously dispensed his wealth, while I risked ten thousand deaths for a single life to obtain this collection. How could this collection be taken lightly?
Those who view this collection hereafter, if they can refine their understanding through recitation and enter into its profound meaning—
The Spirit. By entering the spirit, one brings forth its utility; thus, may I not fail the diligent efforts of those who carved and those who requested this work.
Furthermore, may the wisdom-life of all Buddhas be sustained by this and shine forth without end. This is the record.

Record of the Restoration of Seongchwanyam (Holy Spring Rock) In the southern part of T'an County, there are few great monasteries. Among those renowned, Seongchwam is the preeminent; it is the place where the Great Master Liu of the Tang dynasty planted his monk’s staff.
Once, while the Great Master was traveling through this mountain, he planted his staff in a rock, and water gushed forth following the staff. The local people marveled at this.
He subsequently established a hermitage for him. From that time on, there were successive periods of prosperity and decline, so remote as to be beyond verification.

Toward the end of the previous dynasty, the monk Pude expanded and enlarged it, making it somewhat conform to the regulations of a monastic forest (*saṃghārāma*). He established over one hundred *mu* of arable land.

Upon reaching the Zhengde era of our present dynasty, the monk Daochao of Dufeng came to preside over the affairs of the monastery. It happened that the county office received an imperial mandate to requisition the land.
After it entered official status, those who remained were few in number. Subsequently, his disciple Desheng succeeded him and was able to greatly revitalize the monastery’s enterprise.
He rebuilt the main hall, the meditation hall, the abbot’s quarters, and the three gates, making them twice the size of the original structures.
This occurred during the seventh year of the Jiajing era. By the thirtieth year, he constructed a nine-bay bridge at the foot of the mountain and further paved the stone path from there.
A bridge was built leading directly to the hermitage. From the surplus of his robes and alms-bowl, he established fields to provide for the fragrant meals.

After Master Sheng passed away, the abbacy was held by successive successors. Internally and externally, the community always numbered several hundred. By the beginning of the Tianqi era, the buildings had again grown dilapidated;
the monks joyfully each exhausted their strength, and whether it was the main hall, the meditation hall, or the abbot’s quarters, they all renovated them. The work—
Having finished his address, it was the first year of the Chongzhen era. This summer, due to the calamity of the river spirit, the bridge collapsed.

The community rebuilt it according to the former design of Master Sheng. At that time, the number of monks increased and the consumption of food became more abundant; the income from the fields was insufficient to meet the needs.

Thereupon, they collectively expanded the landholdings until they reached several *mu*. Alas! How constant are prosperity and decline? It depends entirely on obtaining the right person. [Master] Sheng...
That there are successors to the Duke may indeed be called "having people. To renew what is decayed and to supplement what is deficient—what blame can I find in such later generations?
Nevertheless, the establishment of a Buddhist monastery (brahmacārya-śālā) can it truly be equated with the mere act of new construction as a Buddhist service?

I have traveled to that land since my youth, and I am well-acquainted with the Sacred Spring (Śrī-tīrtha). Those who dwell there—with their frost-white hair and conch-like cranial protuberances—possess a refined and dignified demeanor.
Compared to all other lands, this monastery is uniquely sublime. Now, as I wander here once more, I see its vermilion pillars and painted beams nestled amidst the rocky crags and hills;
its green lattices and azure windows swallow and spit forth clouds and moonlight. To what extent does it transcend the standards of former times?

Yet, do you gentlemen perhaps recall the deeds of those who came before us? I have heard that in the past, during the Jiajing era, the meditation hall was no larger than a bushel-measure, yet it gathered...

There were ten or so monks who practiced the contemplation of *Complete Enlightenment* (*Yuánjué*). At that time, Zen Master Jīnfēng served as the head of the assembly (*zuòyuán*), and Zen Master Tiānzhēn served as the West Hall master (*xītáng*).
After three years of fixed-term practice, many attained direct realization (*xiànzhèng*). Is this not a familiar story from your mountain retreats?
At the beginning of the Wanli era, Zen Master Yúnyáng came to listen to the *Śūraṃgama Sūtra* while dressed as a layman; he subsequently shaved his head and became a monk. Ultimately, he...

Is this not the very teaching of the Great Good Spiritual Friend (Mahākalyāṇamitra) from the old stories of the mountain caves? The model for emulation is not far off; the guidance of the true teacher is methodical.

It depends entirely upon how you apply yourself through practice. Now that you, sirs, are at this juncture of the midday destiny and have encountered this rare opportunity, I pray you do not limit yourselves.
Each of you must spur yourselves on with the whip of the patriarchs; then the gate of Prajñā may be entered, and the Hall of Radiance reached.
It is fit for wandering. It is my hope that the various elders of Jinfeng will not monopolize the beauty of this place as they did in the past.
What need is there to speak of my own meager efforts in restoration? This serves as the record.
Record of He Shan Hermitage He Shan is an ancient monastery that was destroyed by fire during the Hongzhi era of the Ming dynasty.

Subsequently, its sacred grounds were overgrown with lush weeds, and its assets fell into the hands of local magnates for many years. It was not until the beginning of the Tianqi era that the local villager Jianquan [took up the cause].
The layman Xu and his descendants, including Xi, all turned their hearts toward the Buddha-vehicle and vowed to dedicate themselves to the Pure Land.

As they wandered through the old site, they could not help but be moved by a sense of sorrow; they subsequently ransomed the land and rebuilt it from the ground up. Thus, the precious halls towered toward the sky, and the lofty pavilions obstructed the sun.
Meditation chambers reflected the moonlight, and the abbot’s quarters were showered with celestial blossoms. The golden body shone brilliantly amidst the heavens, and fragrant mists...

It pervades the Dharma-realm in a dense, misty haze. Furthermore, mountains were purchased to expand the lands for firewood and timber, and fields were established to provide for the needs of fragrant meals.
Ritual objects and offering vessels were all fully prepared. Construction began in the *Renxu* year of the Tianqi era and was completed in the *Wuchen* year of the Chongzhen era.
Hardly had the work been finished when Master Jianquan passed away. His sons feared the rapid passage of time...
[The stele] was erected. The human heart is unfathomable; to ensure that this undertaking endures for all time, [the donor] has requested a record from me.

Now, this public official, with resolute strength, has transformed a forest of thorns into a precious monastery and manifested the Holy One.
It is like a secluded valley; its generosity may be called vast, and its merit may be called grand. Alas! It is truly difficult for the donor, and not easy for the recipient.
Those who dwell here and partake of these provisions in the future should also consider how they might repay this virtue.

If they can embody the public’s intention and feel no shame before the Buddha’s teaching, and follow the Buddha’s teaching without betraying the public’s intention—then their purpose will be fulfilled.
Thus, for the public, the Sangha is a golden wall; for the Sangha, the public is a Dharma raft. How could this not be a source of merit?

Yet, if there are those among the monastic ranks who play the flute out of tune, failing to follow pure discipline, who wastefully consume offerings and profits while disregarding past merits, then even a drop of water or a grain of rice [is lost].
How could this be anything other than iron pellets or molten copper? The Dharma and the precepts are majestic and stern; the words of the Sage are not false.
It is fitting that we, his later followers, should certainly exercise self-restraint. This is the record.

Upon the mountain, the soil is rich and fertile, and the forests are verdant and dense. Amidst them stands a structure with vermilion pillars and painted beams, soaring loftily in the clear sky.
Nestled amidst the evening mists and twilight glow lies Longtou Hermitage. As for the founding of this hermitage, its origins are unknown;
by the time of our dynasty, it had already vanished into the weeds and withered smoke, leaving nothing to be recognized.

Furthermore, he obtained the support of his disciple Zhēnyù, and thus succeeded in greatly reviving the institution’s legacy. In the [Wànlì]...
In the year of Renyin, he renovated the abbot’s quarters, the refectory, the kitchen, the storehouse, and other facilities;

furthermore, he increased the mountain forests, fields, and estates by several units. Consequently, the magnificence of its buildings and the abundance of its provisions for the Sangha were deemed the foremost among all monastic gardens in the region.
Subsequently, Master Yù passed away prematurely in his middle years; fortunately, there was his grandson Xìngchéng, who was able to...
The affairs of the world are like the rising sun; it is only just beginning its ascent and has not yet ceased.
Now, Master Song is already eighty-four years of age, yet his physical vigor remains as robust as that of youth and maturity. His backbone is like iron, and his two pupils are as black as lacquer.
He governed the assembly with dignity and restrained himself with frugality; moreover, his love for the virtuous and his delight in giving were particularly innate traits of his character.

Thus, he was truly an outstanding figure among the clergy. Now, fearing that the light at the end of the wood might not endure long, and considering that the origins of prosperity and decline, as well as the hardships of founding and maintaining [the monastery], must not remain unrecorded, he requested that I compose this account for him.
This is a brief account, intended to be perpetuated as a mirror for future generations.
A Record of the Reconstruction of Lingyuan Hermitage on Huangmei Mountain:
Traveling east from the outskirts of Jianzhou, upstream for nearly fifty li, one reaches Nanyuan. At the head of this source is...
The mountain that rises loftily above the clouds is Mount Huangmei. In its center stands a hermitage called Lingyuan.
It was here that the Hangzhou śramaṇa Jinghai first established his dwelling in the second year of the Qiánfú era of the Táng Emperor Xiāozōng, the year Yǐwèi (879 CE).
Since Jinghai was actually a successor to the Fifth Patriarch of Huangmei, he named the mountain after Huangmei, intending to commemorate its origins. Subsequently...

Passing through the Song and Yuan dynasties, the structure had long since fallen into ruin. Reaching the fifth year of the Hongwu era of our present dynasty (the *renzi* year), the bhikṣu Jue-ming again raised funds from the public to rebuild a hermitage for residence.
