In the *jihai* year of the Jiajing era, the Marquis of the Princely House, Mr. Qian, summoned the monk Yuan-jing to serve as abbot; [he was granted] five *li* of land from the local district.
This site, where the waters of the four directions converge, was entirely granted for the purpose of ritual cultivation at the original hermitage.
In the [blank] year of the Wanli era, following the passing of the former monk, the local elders unanimously requested that the monk Zhineng take charge of it.

Neng was the fifth-generation descendant of Chan Master Tianzhen of Doufeng; frugal, simple, and diligent, he succeeded in greatly reviving the monastery's legacy over nearly twenty autumns. Upon his...
Observing that the roof structure was about to collapse and its condition could not be maintained for long, he gathered craftsmen and materials to renovate it into something new.

A great hall was established in the center, with three gates in front; to the left was the Gandhakuṭī, and to the right were guest quarters. Some areas were made spacious as pavilions, while others were made intimate as chambers;
only the three-bay "Venerable’s Chamber" remained as it was in the original layout of Huihai. Construction began during the Tianqi era.
On such and such a day of such and such a month in such and such a year; it was completed on such and such a day of such and such a month in such and such a year.
As for this undertaking, it was not undertaken by consulting the counsel of the multitude nor by relying on the strength of the masses, but was accomplished solely by one individual.
Yet its scale and grandeur far exceed those of the past—this may indeed be called difficult. In the winter of the *dingmao* year, I accepted the invitation of Dayun and traveled...
Passing through Huangmei, the resident monks earnestly requested that I record these events. I reflect: the location of Huangmei is lofty and vast;
the produce of Huangmei is abundant and fertile. Is it merely this that the Master left behind for his disciple to receive?
In the past, the Fifth Patriarch of Huangmei encompassed the world with the Diamond Circle (Vajra-maṇḍala); at the end, he only...
A single Lu Xingzhe was able to seize his ring and make use of it; we have relied upon this to this very day.
If future generations can penetrate the depths of Lu Xingzhe’s point of application, then the single lineage of Huangmei will likely not fall into decline.
Thus, the merit of this reconstruction today may well be considered not in vain. This is the record of Jingming Hermitage, written by the layman Chushi.
He dwells upon the banks of the Jinjiang River, where he studies the books of Confucius and cultivates the legacy of Confucius.

He was one who would soon tread upon patterned stone with his sandals and read the secret scriptures within the celestial halls of the wood. Yet his character was profound and far-reaching, possessing a transcendent air that rose well above the mundane world.
In his youth, he built a hermitage on the southern slope of Baling Mountain; there, paths turned and peaks receded, while valleys deepened and clouds thickened.

There the layman occasionally sought refuge from the clamor of the world to rest his shadow; amidst those surroundings, he shared the company of two or three monastics, sometimes practicing meditation and sometimes chanting the sutras.
He engaged in supramundane conduct. When he heard that Grand Master Wen Gu had arrived at Tan, he bestowed upon him the name Jingming (Vimalakīrti) and composed a record for him.

Later, the layman came to Gushan and presented this record to me. As I read the Grand Master’s record, its most essential point was his desire for the master to study the conduct of a layman, to possess the mind of a bodhisattva, and to enter deeply into the Dharma-gate of non-duality, thereby reaching the ultimate goal.
This is the foundation of the inconceivable. Let us now consider this: from where does one learn the conduct of a lay practitioner (*upāsaka*)?

From where is the bodhisattva-mind perfected? And from where does one enter the gate of non-duality? In short, if one wishes to learn the conduct of a lay practitioner, one must first perfect the bodhisattva-mind;
if one wishes to perfect the bodhisattva-mind, one must first enter the gate of non-duality. Once one is able to enter the gate of non-duality, then...
Whatever is manifested from a resolute mind is none other than the Bodhisattva’s mind; whatever is performed by a resolute body is none other than the Bodhisattva’s practice.
This is the ultimate. Even such inconceivable deeds as borrowing a seat from King Lamps and taking rice from Fragrant Accumulation—who could surpass these non-dual acts?
Yet, from where does this gate of non-duality ultimately enter? *Du!* (A sharp exclamation).
Record of the Reconstruction of the Zunseng Pavilion at Kaiyuan Temple:
The existence of the Zunseng [Pavilion] at Kaiyuan likely originated with the "mulberry lotus" of the Huang family.

According to the local gazetteer, in the second year of the Chuigong era of the Tang dynasty, Huang Shoucong, the elder of the prefecture, dreamed one day of a monk begging for his land to establish a temple. Huang Shoucong said, "It must..."

"It must be a tree that produces white lotuses. The monk thanked him with joy, but suddenly the figure vanished; he saw the Thousand-Armed and Thousand-Eyed Bodhisattva ascending into the sky and departing.
Two days later, white lotuses grew upon the mulberry trees in the garden. Shougong then went to the place where the lotuses had appeared.

The Zunseng (Honored Victorious) Cloister was established, and the Great Master Kuanghu was invited to reside there. The authorities reported this as an auspicious omen, and by imperial decree, Lianhua Temple was founded.
Subsequently, the temple’s name was changed several times until the twenty-sixth year of the Kaiyuan era, when it was first renamed its present name.
The temple grounds were extensive, comprising one hundred and twenty courtyards, of which the Zunseng Cloister was the original foundation. During the Xining era, the monk Benquan...
A Hall of Great Compassion (Dabei Ge) was constructed within it. It was destroyed by fire during the Shaoxing era. Subsequently, there were six successive administrators;

their initial construction was humble and inferior, failing to meet expectations. In the fourth year of the Qingyuan era, the monk Faxuan rebuilt the new hall, with the local gentry Liang Kejun and Li Shen providing substantial support.
In the Dingyou year of the Zhi Zheng era, it was again destroyed by fire. In the Wuxu year, the monk Fachih reconstructed it. During the Jiajing era...
For a time, it fell into ruin and was entirely possessed by those who had been granted [the land] as a reward.

In the fifth year of the Chongzhen era, the year of Renshen (1632), the monk Jiehui of the temple, reflecting that the site of its original source must be restored, donated his robes and alms bowl to redeem the ancestral grounds.

With District Magistrate Shuan-an Chen acting as the primary patron, various conditions converged like spokes in a wheel, leading to the reconstruction of a magnificent pavilion to enshrine the Western [Buddha].

The three great sacred images were installed, and small dwellings were constructed around them for the convenience of their guardians. In the winter of the year Yi-hai, the work was finally completed;
its layout was vast and spacious, and its vermilion and white decorations shone with brilliance. The former glory of the Venerable and Victorious One once again rose loftily above the clouds.

That same winter, I began my dharma-teaching at Ziyun Temple; I ascended the pavilion to inquire about its origins, and amidst my lingering reflections, I could not help but feel a sense of profound longing.

I reflect upon this. In the past, whenever the Great Master Kuanghu lectured on the *Sūtra of the Rebirth in the Upper Realm* during the summer retreat, he would invariably attract a thousand followers;
was he not the ancestral founder of Zunseng? Master Shen, a dharma successor of Ciming, appeared in a dream to Luoshan as a teacher for practitioners of Chan;
was he not the tenth-generation descendant of Zunseng? As for the three schools of Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya, those who emerged as auspicious omens for the world were like the qilin and the phoenix.
There are no fewer than twenty or thirty people here. Is it not because the illustrious and exalted have nurtured their excellence and given rise to this source?
This "Illustrious and Exalted" (Zunsheng) was the *chú* at the time of the Zhou and the *pèi* at the time of the Han; Master Mengguan truly knew how to speak!
Yet today’s Illustrious and Exalted—its site remains as it was, its pavilion remains as it was, and even those with shaven heads and square robes remain as they were. Behold them!
I still harbor the regret that the present cannot equal the past. What is the reason for this?

Moreover, I have heard from the elders of old that when the *Zunsheng* (Victorious) [monk] flourished, the temple flourished because of him; when the *Zunsheng* declined, the temple declined because of him.
Thus, the *Zunsheng* was the very inception of this monastery. Now that the *Zunsheng* has been restored, eminent monks have risen like magpies, and the Dharma...
The thunderous resonance of this sound may be anticipated by counting the days; may you all exert yourselves to respond to this occasion.
Thus, I have taken up my brush and composed this record.
Record of the Cuìyún Hermitage:
I have resided at Zhēnjì for two years and have frequently observed those of corrupt and wicked character who have usurped the teacher’s seat.

They discourse on Chan with great clamor, and their disciples follow this trend like madmen or drunkards. These are truly what are called "those who hawk the teachings of the Tathāgata. Thereupon, I reflected:
This was intended as a plan for my own leisure: first, to rectify the abuses of the Chan school; second, to avoid being associated with such people as a "man of knowledge" (jñānin).
Consequently, I came to the western residence of Yuhang, where I obtained a small plot of land suitable for dwelling, namely the mountain of the Huang family.
Upon inquiring of the Huang family, it was found that they were all refined scholars with the air of venerable elders.

They joyfully donated five mu of their land, whereupon the date for breaking ground was determined and the foundation laid. Clay was molded into tiles, laborers were assembled, and materials gathered.
Work commenced in the eighth month of the Wuyin year and was completed in the ninth month of the following autumn. By the time the year of Xinsi arrived, a great famine had struck.
With several dozen people within the hermitage, it was truly difficult to sustain oneself through almsround.
Just then, a letter arrived from Jianzhou requesting my presence, so I moved my staff back to Min. I entrusted this chamber to Zhici to maintain the incense and lamps.
A practitioner of divination told me, "This site is not fit for habitation. I asked, "Why? The practitioner replied, "Those who dwell here ought to face south; now it faces north."
Thus, there would be no sense of radiant transcendence. Generally, one who dwells in a place should have a counterpart;

now, having no counterpart, there would be no one to recognize, encounter, or guide them. For these two reasons, it is unsuitable to dwell there. I said: "It is truly as you say, but it depends on who the dweller is.
If the person is one devoted to fame and achievement, their will being fixed on fame and achievement, they will surely value recognition and long for it."
To transcend and soar. If those in black robes who practice Chan abandon the secular world to enter the mountains, joyfully maintaining austerity and silence, what more would they need here?
Those who dwell here now should simply be able to let their hair and faces be covered in dust, sustaining themselves through alms-rounds;

they should rather seek the seclusion of darkness than the brightness of light, and rather seek self-reliance than worldly favor. In this way, they may perhaps come close to the Way. Thus, I have written this for them.
This record is intended to serve as a warning for those who come after.
Regarding the affairs of the world, things are sometimes flourishing and sometimes falling into ruin; they appear to have no constancy, yet there is also a sense of constancy that cannot be denied.
As for the strong, it is simply a matter of timing. When the time has not yet arrived, even one with immense strength may undertake a task but fail to achieve it;
when the time has arrived, even one with meager strength may lift it up and succeed. I have observed this in the matter of Yongquan.
Since the abandonment of Yongquan in the *Ren-yin* year of the Jiajing era, there have been many monks who have sought to exert their strength to restore what had fallen into ruin.
It took ninety years for people to seek [this goal], yet they were not consistent in their timing, and in the end, no results were achieved.
It was only when Yanyuan invited Boshan and his disciples to preside over the seat that the temple’s restoration became as certain as planting grass in the ground;

for he was highly esteemed at the time, the monastic community delighted in returning to him, and the various donors were happy to protect him. Yet, because Boshan declined the heavy responsibility and departed, was this not indeed...?
When the time has not yet arrived, even one endowed with great strength may undertake a task, yet it will not be accomplished.
My arrival at this mountain occurred during the Jiashu year of the Chongzhen era. At that time, the temple was still half-overgrown with weeds and brush;

there stood a great hall rising majestically in the center, which had been constructed by Cao Gong Xuequan, the Palace Protector (Gongbao), after clearing away the overgrowth. Adjacent to the hall was the refectory.

Behind the hall were established the guest quarters, the incense storehouse (xiangji), and the administrative office (kusī); these were all constructed by the assembly of monks to provide accommodations for Bo-shan.
Behind the main hall was established the Dharma Hall, and to the right of the hall was the abbot’s quarters (fangzhang), which was the achievement of the monk Hongxiao.
In front of the abbot’s quarters was the meditation hall (chandang), which had been converted from the West Hermitage; it was narrow and inadequate.
Because I was dwelling among such a vast assembly, I would often wander about and look in all directions, feeling a chilling sense of being overwhelmed by the magnitude of the task.
That winter, Public Security Commissioner Lin Gong Hongyan constructed the two towers for the bell and drum. The following year, Lord Cao further constructed the Hall of the Heavenly Kings.
In the autumn of the Bingzi year, he built the Tripitaka Hall to the east of the Dharma Hall. In the spring of the Dingchou year, I heard this news.
After the Great Master Toku passed away, he traveled five hundred *ri* to pay his respects at the funeral. He subsequently remained at Shinjaku-ji for five years before returning home.
Upon his return, he found that the main hall had been ravaged by the sea winds; both corners had collapsed, and water dripped everywhere across the floor.

Although the Buddha images appeared as if alive, their gold and vermilion paint were peeling away. He then devised a plan for its reconstruction, immediately commissioning stonemasons to rebuild the hall.
The front terrace and the stone of the great courtyard were established. In the following year, the year of *guiwei* (1423), timber was sought from Jianzhou;

in the winter, laborers were assembled to construct the hall, and the main Heavenly King Hall (*Tianwangdian*) was moved and expanded to its side to serve as the Hall of the Ten Directions (*Shifangdian*).

In the summer of the year of *jia-shen* (1424), corridors were added to the left and right of the Great Hall, leading up to the Dharma Hall (*Fatang*). To the west of these corridors was the Chan [Hall].

The Hall was constructed by the Grand Governor, the Duke Shao Jiechun. In front of the Hall is the Brahma-Practice Hall (Fanxing Tang), which was renovated from the former Chan Hall and expanded to accommodate itinerant monks.
To the west of the Brahma-Practice Hall are twelve bays for the latrines and bathing facilities.
During the winter, he further established shrines for the Gaolantai and the King of Min on the left corridor of the main hall, and erected a shrine for the Patriarchs.
The two shrines for [Master] Shouchang were located on the right corridor of the hall. In the summer of the year Yiyou, the斋堂 (zhāitáng, “Hall of Repose”) was reoriented to face south.

To the east of the Hall of Repose is the Bailing Hall (Báiyún Táng), used for receiving guests. To the east of the Bailing Hall is the Small Guest Quarters; this is where the former guest quarters had been moved.
To the east of the Hall of Repose are six bays of the Xiangji (Xiāngjī, “Fragrant Accumulation”) kitchen. In the year Dinghai, the three [images] were sculpted.

The various great images of the Treasure Heavenly Kings [were restored]. In the year Gengyin, he constructed the Jingye Hall (Pure Practice Hall) in front of the Baiyun Hall, built the Huayan Hall in front of the Fanxing Hall, and established a mill and workshop on the eastern wing of the temple.
By this time, there was no ruinous part of the monastery that had not been restored. This undertaking took a total of fifteen years from beginning to end before the work was finally completed.
All of this is due to the silent protection of the nāgas and devas, the joyful offerings of the *dānapati*, and the diligent efforts of the monastic community.
As for me, I have truly been sitting like a corpse in my small room, merely discoursing on the "vague Buddha-nature" and realizing the "slumbering samādhi.
I had no idea how things could come to this. Is this not because the time has arrived, such that even with feeble strength, one can lift [the burden] and achieve success?
Thus we know that among the affairs of the world, success cannot be achieved by mere chance, and momentum cannot be seized through forceful contention.
The *Great Changes* (*Da Yi*) is the source of the Five Classics, yet fortune, misfortune, regret, and shame follow solely the dictates of time.
Confucius is the most honored among all sages, yet his retiring, serving, enduring, or hastening was governed solely by the laws of time. Time, oh time! How could one ever oppose it?
Thus it was established. Once the temple was completed, it was customary to have a record; therefore, I have chronicled its date and month, inscribing it upon stone for posterity.
This is the Record of the Reconstruction of Baoshan Chan Monastery.
During the Wanli era, the Great Master Wengu received the Dharma seal of Yunqi and propagated the Way along the Xiaoxi River.

He rebuilt the Zhenji Chan Monastery, and monks and laypeople turned toward him in numbers like clouds. In the year of Wumu, having just finished his work at the monastery, the Master traveled alone with his staff over the mountains to the desolate Chongsheng Temple in Jianzhou.
There he hung up his monk’s staff and lived on alms; after some time, people gradually took notice of him.
Those who came to pay their respects gradually increased in number. After three years had passed, Zhenshi came several times to request his departure; only then did he speak of returning home.

His disciples were like children who had lost their mothers, longing for him without ceasing. Master Xinshi, his successor, then consulted with the assembly, desiring to invite the Great Master to return once more so that they might establish a monastery to satisfy the hopes of the multitude.
They divined and obtained the site of Baoshan in Jianzhou. Although Baoshan was in Jianzhou— (Note: The provided text ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)
It belongs to Jianzhou (建州), which is close by, being only forty *li* away. Thus, the people of Jian were delighted to bring it to completion.
This was indeed the year of the *xiyou* cycle in the first year of the Tianqi era. This hermitage was old and cramped, with only a few people residing there.
Master Xinshi (心石) feared there would be no room to accommodate a large assembly, so he subsequently constructed a five-bay pavilion behind the main hall. The following year, within the prefecture...
The local gentry and virtuous friends deliberated together and dispatched messengers to invite the Great Master, but he did not grant his consent.

After seven such round trips, it was only in the autumn of the *dingmao* year of the Tianqi era that he returned once more. In the tenth month of winter, construction commenced and materials were gathered;
the hermitage was renovated anew. A Buddha Hall was established in the center, a refectory on the left, and a meditation hall on the right, with small auxiliary buildings surrounding them.
The administrative office (*kusi*), guest quarters, storehouse, kitchen, and bathhouse were all fully provided. The following year, once these were completed, the Great Master returned his staff.
In the *gengwu* year of the Chongzhen era, the Great Master was traveling to Huang’an; Master Xinshi again went to Hubei to welcome him there.

Upon his arrival, monastics from all quarters came to meet him, their packs slung over their shoulders. Master Xinshi said to the monastics: [...]* *Note: The source text appears to be a fragment of a hagiographical or historical record concerning a Chan master’s activities and the construction of monastic facilities.*
Since the collection was assembled, it was necessary to ensure that the scriptural records were fully provided.
Consequently, he obtained the Tripitaka from Jinling and constructed a five-bay pavilion behind the *zhaitang* (fasting hall) to house them.

Furthermore, as the abbot’s quarters were cramped and situated too close to the guest lodgings, he additionally built a three-bay pavilion behind the *chantang* (meditation hall). At this point, the scale of Baoshan was truly complete. (Section B)
In the spring of the year of Hai (the twelfth lunar month), the Great Master returned to Zhejiang. In the winter of the following year, in the twelfth month, he passed away.
In the spring of Dingchou, I went to pay my respects at Zhenji. Thereupon, the various gentry officials requested that I succeed him on the seat. I resided at Zhenji for five years;
in the autumn of Xinsi, I resigned from monastic affairs and returned to Min to dwell at Baoshan. Master Xinshi said to me, "At Baoshan..."
The work having been completed, there remained one thing yet to be done: the erection of a stone memorial tablet. Master Jian labored diligently on this task for more than twenty years.
Since our late teacher passed away to the West, many of his colleagues have likewise become "strangers" (died).
If I do not record these matters now, how will they be known hereafter? Regarding the origins and conclusion of the hermitage’s affairs, the Master alone is most thoroughly informed.
Among my late teacher’s associates, none was more intimate than you. It is unlikely that you would begrudge me even a single word.
Having received your command, I assented with humility and did not dare decline on account of my lack of literary skill; I have therefore taken up my brush and recorded this.

Record of the Reconstruction of Dingguangyan Cliff Forty *li* south of Jianzhou is Nanya Mouth. Entering the mountains another five *li*, one reaches Dingguangyan Cliff. Within the cliff, the Great Master Dingguang is enshrined;
hence it is named after him. As for the Great Master Dingguang, he is the one recorded in the *Chuan deng lu* (The Record of the Transmission of the Lamp).

The Abbot of Nanshan Rock was a Dharma descendant of Yunmen. Because he was originally a manifestation of an ancient sage, his spiritual efficacy was particularly renowned, and the local people frequently made offerings to him and prayed to him whenever they encountered calamities.
This is not recorded in the gazetteer of this rock; it is unknown from which era his cult began.
Many years have passed since then, during which the temple lands have been lost, the monks have fled, the buildings have fallen into ruin, and the incense...
It was like fire and darkness; the tracks of wandering monks could not reach it. At the beginning of the Chongzhen era, the Great Master Wengu arrived at Jian with his traveling staff.
There, the layman Guifeng, together with several virtuous friends, ransomed the Baoshan Hermitage to serve as the Master’s place of residence.
The layman further took the lead in managing the affairs of the monastery. Subsequently...

Zen monks gathered there in such numbers that the buildings could no longer accommodate them. Consequently, the lay devotee (jushi) ransomed this cliff and rebuilt it to serve as a lodging for Zen practitioners.
This was in the year Xunwei of the Chongzhen era. After three years, the work was completed.
Furthermore, he established several mu of land for the support of their ascetic practices. Upon reaching this point, he commissioned me to record these events. I, for my part, reflect thus:
In the autumn of the former Xin-you year, I stayed at this rock for two months. At that time, the lay practitioner had recently redeemed this rock and had already made a vow to rebuild it.
In the spring of the Bing-xu year, when I came to Jianzhou, the lay practitioner again invited me to stay at the rock.
Thus, the jade palace and flowered halls have been resplendently renewed; this is the fulfillment of every one of the layman’s long-cherished vows.
I have therefore detailed their beginning and end, recording them upon stone. However, I recall that when I parted from the layman in the past, he requested a verse from me, and I spoke this verse:
"The Persian closes his eyes and chews raw iron; the sages and ordinary beings of the ten realms are all..."
It was extinguished. Suddenly he bit through it, and blood flowed profusely. A mute swallowing his words—whom could he tell?
It has now been twenty-seven years since then. I do not know, Layman, whether you have ever bitten through this iron or not. I am recording this matter now for that reason.

I have included this here for the sake of all; not only to spur the layman forward, but also so that future generations will not dare to claim that Dingguang and Hanyue were entirely devoid of the Buddha-dharma. This serves as the record.
Record of the Śarīra Stūpa at Baoshan Ān:
The segmented bodies of this world are like foam, bubbles, or wind-lamps; they cannot endure for long. Once the vital breath is exhausted, they fall into decay before one can turn back.
Only the body of the Supreme Person is not thus; it is able to manifest form through the spirit and transform the vital breath.
Regarding the Path: although the vessel-world (bhājanaloka) is coarse, it can still be instantaneously transformed into a ground of adamantine jewels; how much more so the root-body (indriya-kāya)?

Formerly, when the World-Honored One manifested his parinirvāṇa beneath the twin śāla trees, after his cremation, those things known as the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics were all transformed into śarīra relics—perfect, lustrous, and pure, rarely encountered in the world. At that time, the celestial palaces and the oceans...
In Tibet and throughout the five regions of India, there were none who did not venerate them with competitive offerings;

indeed, these were bequeathed by the compassionate vows of the World-Honored One to serve eternally as fields of merit for the world. Since the Han dynasty, they have circulated and reached this land.
This is like Mount Mao in Zhedong or Gold Wheel Peak on Mount Lu.
In the first year of the Huangyou era of the Song dynasty, Empress Cao commissioned an imperial eunuch to construct a stupa at Hongfu Temple in Tongxu County, Bianjing.

She took all the śarīra relics enshrined within the palace and deposited them in the fourth tier of the stupa. Later, after many years, the stupa fell into ruin. By the Jia [year] of the Chongzhen era...
In the year Wuxu, when marauding rebels invaded the borders, the local magistrate took bricks from this site to repair the city walls. Among the debris, he discovered a stone casket.
Upon opening it, he found seven crystal vases, all containing *śarīra*. One silver vase contained a single fragment of bone from the Buddha;
within it were numerous *śarīra* the size of millet seeds. Another silver casket contained two golden Buddha images. [The magistrate] examined them...
From these ancient inscriptions, I first learned its origins. At that time, military affairs were extremely urgent, and there was no opportunity to deliberate upon how to enshrine it;
consequently, the fragments were each taken away. Cao Anzu, a Military Commissioner (bingxian) from Yixing, obtained one piece.

He intended to build a stupa for it at Nan Yue Temple, but due to illness, he did not succeed. As he approached his death, he entrusted it to Cao Shicang, a Censor-in-Chief from Jiaxing. In the year Wu...
In the autumn of the Year of the Tiger (1590), the Attendant Official (Shiyu Gong) invited me to Tianning Temple. Before long, I returned home, entrusting me with the śarīra relics.
In the year of Xinsi (1591), I brought them back to Min Province; upon reaching Jianzhou, I enshrined them at Baoshan Hermitage. That winter, the monk Dajian...
He first cleared the site for the stupa foundation in the western valley of the hermitage. In the year Guiwei, he constructed the stupa hall.
In Bingxu, the monk Xingqiu raised funds to cast the stupa in bronze and carved stone for its base; however, due to conflicting circumstances, the work was not completed before Xingqiu passed away.
It was only when the Elder Zaojian arrived to preside over the abbot’s quarters that the project was finally finished, in the year Renchen.

On the seventeenth day of the eighth month, the śarīra was respectfully enshrined within the stūpa. Indeed, since receiving the entrustment in the year of Wuyin (1638), there has not been a single day that I have not contemplated the welfare of the śarīra;
yet it has remained unaccomplished until now for a full fifteen years. Was its completion not truly difficult?

Nevertheless, at this juncture when heaven and earth undergo a transformation as vast as a cauldron being overturned, and during this autumn when military dispatches fly in from all directions, amidst the common villages—
Of ten households, nine are empty; half the people have ascended the registers of the dead. Even for the brief duration of a single meal, it is difficult to find even temporary security.
Who, then, could attend to urgent matters? Is it not therefore fitting that its completion should be so difficult?

It is my singular fortune that this one monastery, Bao Shan, remains as secure as ever, and the monastic community is still able to exert themselves here. Regarding this stupa, they have especially brought it to great completion.
Amidst such turmoil, it was like plum blossoms breaking through the snow to bloom, or lotus buds appearing from within fire; how could this possibly have been achieved by human effort?
It was truly due to the sustaining power of the World-Honored One’s compassionate vows and the merit of the protection afforded by the dragons and devas.

Moreover, I have been especially fortunate in this regard. I recall that in the autumn of the year *bingxu*, while I was in the Bao-shan Sutra Repository, I saw a single pillar appear within a śarīra flask; its length was equal to the height of the flask.
Subsequently, the pillar vanished, and an image of a Dharma-protecting deity appeared, approximately one inch and two fen in height. At first, I did not understand its significance. Immediately—
Observing it today, the Dharma-gate of Jianzhou has fallen into extreme decay; yet the completion of this stupa coincides precisely with that time.
Thus we know that this stupa must serve as a central pillar within the Dharma-gate, and will surely be able to protect and sustain it.
It shall not perish; it is a portent of its future revival. Could one not divine this from the present?
Therefore, I have recorded it all together as a voucher for future reference.
A Record of Layman Shen Huaiting’s Return to the Western Paradise.
To the east of Tanzhou lived the layman Shen Gong, known as Huaiting. He was gentle and kind but lacked physical strength;

moreover, having never studied Confucianism in his youth, he was unable to exhaustively investigate the Buddhist scriptures or discourse upon the profound principles of the Truth. Consequently, many people disregarded him because of his frailty and perceived lack of intelligence.

One day he followed me to study Buddhism and asked about the method for spiritual advancement. I said, "Observing your natural disposition, you should focus solely on the cultivation of the *nien-fo* samādhi;
this will surely yield real results. He asked, "Is there any other method superior to this? I replied, "There are ten thousand varieties of medicine, yet treating the illness is paramount.
If the medicine does not correspond to the illness, then even if one takes ginseng and milfoil every day, what [benefit will there be]?"
"Is this beneficial? The Master replied, "Yes, yes. He then resolved his mind upon the Pure Land and maintained his recitation of the Buddha's name without slackening.

At that time, there were some "yellow-mouthed" Chan practitioners who stirred up gossip and tongues; many were misled and confused by them. Only the Master remained firm in his resolve and would not be swayed, saying, "How can one be satiated by merely talking about food?
Twenty years later, in the spring of the Dingchou year, while I was residing at Zhenji in Hangzhou, I heard of the Master.
In the twelfth month of the old winter, he fell ill. He selected a date himself, saying, "The twenty-sixth day is auspicious; it is time for me to depart. At the hour of the Dragon (7–9 a.m.
on that day, the Venerable Honryū came to inquire after his illness. Upon seeing him, the Master smiled and said, "I have long awaited you, O Teacher."
"How can you assist me in my practice? Benli replied, "The effort I have applied over these twenty years is all concentrated on this very day.
Will you, sir, be able to receive its benefit? He held up his prayer beads and said, "Now is precisely the time to exert yourself.

He then called his sons, had them support him out of the main chamber, set out an incense altar and an image of the Buddha, and sat upright and resolutely. At that time, all his relatives and friends arrived.
Hui Da-yu, the lay practitioner, called out to him, saying, "At the critical juncture between life and death at Huaiting, you must by no means allow yourself to be bound by affection.
The Master replied, "I have repeatedly received your ultimate instructions and now am able to put them into practice; however, I lack the means to repay my parents' love.
He then raised his hand in thanks. Guang Yu, the lay practitioner, suddenly let out a sigh. The Master looked back and said, "Ha! At this, all the disciples shed tears.
The Duke rebuked him. He then dismissed his wife and children and merely held his prayer beads while reciting the Buddha’s name from the morning until noon.
His relatives and friends all gathered around him to recite the Buddha’s name together. One of them heard the sound of celestial music and suddenly said, "The time has come; I am departing."

He then raised his hand to his chest and departed from the assembly for good. For some time, the crown of his head felt as if it were being scorched. His remains stayed in the shrine for three days, his countenance appearing as if alive.
Among the gentry and commoners of the entire district, there was none who did not sigh in admiration at this rare occurrence. District Magistrate Shen specially honored him with a memorial tablet.
I reflect that among the heroes and eminent figures of the world, those possessed of great strength and abundant wisdom may advance toward this [enlightenment].
The Way does not consist in exhausting one's energy on peripheral paths, nor in dividing one's resolve among divergent branches.
To be able to cultivate with tireless diligence and to apply one’s will without distraction, proceeding directly toward the Lotus Land—how many such as you, sir, could there be?
Yet you, sir, attained it despite being physically frail and lacking great intellectual acumen. Thus, can you truly be called weak and of little wisdom? This is what the world calls "great strength."

Among those of vast capacity and great wisdom, there has been none equal to him. Fearing that these matters might be lost to oblivion over time, I have recorded them in detail so that they may be transmitted to future generations. Thus it is said.
The Record of the Venerable Master Wuming’s Conduct (With Preface).
In the ninth month of autumn in the Ding-si year of the Wanli era, I carried incense and entered the abbot’s quarters to request a record of my late teacher’s life and deeds.
The late teacher personally composed a piece for me totaling over six hundred words. In the spring of the following year, the late teacher passed away. Thereupon, I...
I composed two records concerning my practice at He-lin, but at that time, detractors were so numerous that I did not dare to publish them;

the venerable Benli obtained them and kept them hidden. Later, when the administrators requested a stele inscription from Master Hanshan, the account they provided regarding the circumstances of my Master’s entry into the Way was largely factually distorted.
This left me with a profound sense of resentment in my heart. This summer, I have come to Jianzhou.

He eventually passed into nirvana. If you, O lay practitioners, raise this matter here and strike at your own true realization—reaching the realm where no flowers grow even at the bottom of the sea—you will correspond with that "other side. In this way, you may not fail the ultimate extent of his compassionate care.
On the thirteenth day, he composed his final testament for Shouchang and wrote a verse to be sent to Boshan, which said: "My Way has flourished for fifty years..."
Chan: It was not right from the start that you confused the lineage; I have handed this down to all quarters as a cause for severe reproach. Meeting you again, I shall once more apply the awl.
On the fifteenth day, his body no longer felt feverish and his phlegm ceased to arise. He still rose to address the assembly, saying: "In human life, there is receiving without retribution;
do not be panicked by old age, sickness, and death. He laughed until he shattered the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and his karmic consciousness naturally dissolved.
They vanish. At that moment, the clouds clear and the constant light shines forth. Buddhas and patriarchs all abide in this *dharma-cakra*.
Therefore it is said: "I now abide in the light of eternal quiescence; this is named Great Nirvana.

Even if Buddhas and patriarchs skillfully reveal profound mysteries through various gateways and expedient means, they do not, in total, transcend the light of great quiescent extinction. Descend from the seat. Again, perform the ritual of taking leave.
The letter from the donor states: On the sixteenth day, the funeral rites for cremation were assigned. The assembly requested that his entire body be preserved, but this was not permitted.
At that time, a monk requested a verse. He wrote: "Not forming a sentence—how could it be the Dharma? Heaven and earth are not like it; Buddhas and Patriarchs find it difficult to harmonize with."
On the seventeenth day, he felt pain in his back. A monk came forward to massage the Master’s back for him. Weeping, [the monk] said, "My affinity is shallow;
I shall not be able to serve the Master for long. The Master rebuked him, saying, "Foolish child! You need only diligently maintain right mindfulness;
that itself constitutes serving this old monk, and it also constitutes serving all Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Why do you act like a child? He then went to fetch water.
He himself instructed his disciples to wash their faces and wipe their bodies, saying, "After I am gone, there is no need for further bathing; it would merely waste the monastery's resources.
Before the hour had struck, he sat in the lotus posture and requested a brush, writing: "Today, I have clearly shown you the way. Having finished, he threw down the brush and passed away.
During the cremation, the flames were five-colored; his cranial bone and teeth remained entirely intact. When the Master first manifested his illness, the sun was still...
He forced himself to rise. He did not eat for more than ten days. All his final instructions and various writings were composed by his own hand.
Those who came to inquire after his health filled the area outside his door repeatedly; although many attendants tried to stop them, the Master would not permit it.
He summoned them all to see him and exhorted them earnestly, setting only true inquiry and actual realization as the goal. Some sought dharma words, while others sought verses or hymns. Or...
When questioned on koans, his responses were like echoes; he showed no sign of weariness. At the time of his passing, he wrote several characters with his hand;
the strength of his brushwork was vigorous and powerful, as if the strokes were about to take flight—a truly extraordinary feat.

Alas! It has been ten years since I first visited the Master at Dongyan Cave in the year Wushen. Deeply entangled in the net of worldly dust, I have not yet been able to escape it completely. Only last year...

At your feet, before the single announcement had even been completed, you passed away at the Crane Forest (Heilin), leaving us with profound sorrow. Your karmic obstructions were deep while your conditions for rebirth were shallow—alas, how painful!

Yet, having personally witnessed these supreme auspicious signs during this one assembly of the *Nirvāṇa*, we have finally come to know that a great spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) is so free and self-possessed at the threshold of birth and death.
Thus, it cannot be said that this was an ill fortune. Burning incense and preparing this blank paper, I respectfully record this.
To transmit this to posterity.

The precept against taking life is that which the Buddhist tradition holds most paramount. This is not merely a private teaching of Buddhism;
rather, it accords with the fundamental sentiments of all beings. For among all things, there is nothing more cherished than life and nothing more dreaded than death.
Therefore, among all evils, none is greater, and among all transgressions, none is weightier than killing. Furthermore, I have heard it said: "The greatest virtue of Heaven and Earth is called Life."
From this, one knows that among the great evils of humanity, killing living beings is foremost. Since the Supreme Lord (Shangdi) loves life, one knows that what the Supreme Lord detests is killing.
Since benevolence is the greatest of virtues, one knows that killing is the greatest of evils.

Since benevolence is the very essence of the human heart, one knows that killing is not the human heart. Should the precept against killing not be treated with gravity? Furthermore, since humans have already [taken this view]...
When benevolence (*ren*) is taken as the mind, its measure encompasses empty space; how could there be any place of paralysis or numbness? Its mechanism penetrates from beginning to end;
how could there be any time of cessation or extinction? That which is called "heaven, earth, and the myriad things as one body" is this mind; it is this benevolence.

Therefore, when the sages of the Confucian school achieve the state of "harmony and centrality" (zhonghe), they must culminate in the establishment of heaven and earth and the nurturing of all things;
when they reach the utmost sincerity and exhaust their own nature, they must culminate in being able to exhaust the nature of all things. This is neither far-fetched nor extravagant;

it is simply how the benevolence of the single body fundamentally is. Since the benevolence of the single body is fundamentally thus, yet when the sage governs the world, he cannot avoid [certain difficulties].
As for the consumption of fresh food, it was because the sages had no other recourse.

I have examined the Buddhist scriptures and found that at the beginning of the kalpa, the people were simple and sincere; therefore, Heaven produced earthy fat and non-glutinous rice to provide for their daily needs.
Later, as their artful minds gradually grew, the earthy fat and non-glutinous rice ceased to grow, and the people...
Food became scarce. Driven by the fires of hunger, the impulse for killing arose falsely; the strong oppressed the weak, and the wise oppressed the foolish.
They took the flesh of birds and beasts to eat them, no different from birds and beasts devouring one another.

Yet their original intent was merely to stave off starvation, whereas in the end they greedily craved the raw and bloody scent. Day by day this grew worse, and slaughter was carried out wantonly. Thus did the Sage arise.
Feeling compassion for them, he established the rites to provide protection for them, saying: "In the second month of spring, one must not permit the breaking of nests or the destruction of eggs.
Fish less than a foot long shall not be sold. Sacrifices must be conducted according to the rites, with fixed provisions. Banquets must be conducted according to the rites, with fixed numbers.
A Great Officer shall not slaughter oxen or sheep except under extraordinary circumstances. An ordinary officer shall not slaughter dogs or pigs except under extraordinary circumstances."
How could this possibly be the fundamental intention of the Sage? Unable to stop their pursuit, he merely provided a means to prevent their excesses;
thus it is said that this was what the Sage could not help but do. Now, as for beings and myself, although our physical forms are separated, our consciousness and perception are truly the same.
In our craving for life and fear of death, how are we any different from humans? Yet now, one inflicts upon them infinite and ultimate suffering.
To provide me with a moment’s slight sweetness—is this peaceful for the heart? Is it right according to principle?

To take their most vital life-force to enjoy my own leisurely and superficial human sentiments—is this peaceful for the heart? Is it right according to principle? To kill their lives in the hope of prolonging my own life;
to kill their bodies in the hope of nourishing my own body; to kill their parents and wives... [is this peaceful for the heart? Is it right according to principle?]
My son, if you hope to preserve your own parents, wife, and children, is this consistent with human feeling? Is it right according to principle?

Even without waiting for self-reflection and inference, try to consider this: can you endure the state of terror and wailing as they are placed upon the butcher’s block and thrown alive into the boiling cauldron?
Can you bear their agony and resentment? Can you eat [your food] while knowing this? If you think it can be endured...
Once one has eaten, their mind is no longer that of a human being. Mencius said: "When a gentleman sees them alive, he cannot bear to see them die;
when he hears their cries, he cannot bear to eat their flesh. How could this be a matter of mere private sentiment or indulgence?

As for the world of recent times, there is even more that is不忍言 (unbearable to speak of). Social customs have become shallow and corrupt, with people vying to pursue frivolity and luxury to the extreme of verbal indulgence.
Regarding the desire for the belly: they exhaust every delicacy found in water and on land. For a single meal, they slaughter hundreds of living beings.
What is most lamentable is that during the mourning period for parents, they drink wine and eat meat as if at a celebratory banquet; the number of lives killed is especially beyond count.
In this one practice alone, they violate the rites of the ancient sages from afar and offend Heaven in their immediate vicinity.
The laws of the present dynasty externally bind one in the enmity of resentment, while internally extinguishing the lineage of benevolence and filial piety. Is this the way of a Confucian?
Or is it not? Is this the way of goodness? Or is it not? Whenever there is someone who attempts to admonish them, they invariably use worldly censure and suspicion as their excuse.

Not fearing the sage’s regulations, not fearing the king’s laws, and not fearing the actual evils of immorality and filial impiety, yet fearing only the superficial criticisms of the world—what kind of vision is this? What kind of vision is this? Alas, the common and ignorant folk!

It is certainly appropriate to follow worldly customs; yet how could men of talent and distinction merely practice them without examining their meaning? Long ago, Huang Shan Valley composed a verse which says: "My flesh and the flesh of sentient beings— Though their forms differ, their substance is not different. Originally they share the same nature, Only separated by physical bodies. Let others endure the suffering, While I take the rich and sweet for myself. Do not let Old Yan pass judgment upon you," [The verse continues: "For what you have done yourself. This is a most excellent teaching. It is truly a matter that should be investigated deeply. If one does not examine this, it is like a person who, while eating meat, does not realize that it is their own flesh. This is a grave error. Furthermore, the *Sūtra on the Ten Evil Deeds* states: "If one eats the flesh of sentient beings, one will be reborn as a beast. If one eats the flesh of humans, one will be reborn as a human. If one eats the flesh of those in the hells, one will be reborn in the hells. If one eats the flesh of hungry ghosts, one will be reborn among hungry ghosts. If one eats the flesh of animals, one will be reborn as an animal. If one eats the flesh of asuras, one will be reborn as an asura. If one eats the flesh of devas, one will be reborn as a deva. Thus, the karmic retribution for eating meat is extremely severe. How can those who wish to cultivate the Way fail to understand this? One must simply cease eating meat. Consider for yourself: the intent behind the precept against killing is fully expressed in this verse. As for the doctrine of cause and effect and karmic response, it is logically inevitable and impossible to evade.
This is not only detailed in Buddhist scriptures but recorded in secular histories; moreover, it is evident and undeniable to what one sees and hears with one's own eyes and ears.
However, when a gentleman restrains evil, it is not out of fear of punishment; he does so for the sake of benevolence. How could it be otherwise?
This is done for the sake of a reward; it does nothing more than ensure one's own personal safety. May those of lofty intelligence take note of this.
Regarding the drowning of women, I have often heard that within the ocean of karma, the karma of killing is the most grave; and among all acts of killing, the killing of humans is the gravest of all.
Among all acts of killing, those between father and son are the most grave. Among the killing of sons, to kill one who is innocent is the most grave.
Now, the common practice of drowning female infants is precisely what is called killing an innocent child; it is an offense of the greatest magnitude.
Yet the world remains complacent and takes no notice of its strangeness, regarding it as a matter of course—is this not truly extraordinary?
Formerly, Mencius said: "When people of today suddenly see a child about to fall into a well, they all experience a sense of alarm and compassion.
This is not for the sake of establishing a connection with the child's parents; it is not for the sake of seeking praise from their village or friends."
It is not that one dislikes the sound [of the child's cry] and acts accordingly; it is simply said: "One who lacks a heart of compassion is no human being.
Now, to lift up your daughter and drown her is to love your own child less than the child of a neighbor. This is not all.
Even when a prisoner in jail has a crime for which execution is mandated, the judicial officers still delay until the autumn or winter to prolong their momentary life.
Now, to lift up a woman and drown her is a love for one's child that does not even equal the concern shown toward a prisoner condemned to death. Not only this:
the compassionate sympathy of a benevolent person pervades all things; even toward wriggling insects and crawling creatures, they cannot bear to cause them harm.
Now, to lift up a woman and drown her is a love for one's child that does not even equal the concern shown toward the most minute of wriggling insects. Not only this: [it is] calamitous.
Nothing is more extreme than stubbornness, yet among beasts and birds, there is none greater. We hear that a monkey, out of grief for its child, broke its own intestines;
a tiger, looking back repeatedly, gazed upon its offspring. How could their affection for their children have any distinction between male and female?

Now, to take a daughter and drown her is to show a love for one's child that falls short even of the benevolence found in these beasts. To act in such a manner as this while being a parent—how can it be called humanity?
Setting aside for a moment the fact that in this world there are laws for retribution for killing, and in the afterlife there is the karmic retribution of a severed lineage, consider this:
as soon as one leaves the mother's womb, one is cast away from the place of death. Too late for cries of distress, with no one to whom one’s agony can be told, one writhes amidst streams and ravines;
even passersby dare not look directly upon such a sight. Is it truly possible for those who act as one’s parents to do this? It is not.
How can this be? Alas! That which distinguishes humans from beasts is their possession of a heart that cannot bear [to harm others].
Now, your heart has become so callous that you are not even equal to a beast; how then can you claim your place among Heaven and Earth?
I have long sought the cause of this, but could find no way to explain it myself. I had thought that you might have entered the service of another school.
Is it that you drown them because they have nothing to do with acting as regents or inheriting the ancestral line?
Yet you do not say, "If a son is born who wanders aimlessly in all directions, what can be done? Is it that you drown them to save on the expenses of dowry?

Yet you do not say, "If a son is born who squanders the family fortune on gambling and prostitution, what can be done? Is it that you drown them because you anticipate they will be unworthy? Yet... [you do not say so].
Is it not said that the birth of a son brings ruin and disgrace to the family’s reputation? How can you bear this? Is it because you think the family is too poor to sustain him that you drown him?
But do you not also say that the birth of a son necessitates clothing and food? How can you bear this?

Is it because you think there are already too many daughters in the house that you drown him? But do you not also say that by receiving this karmic retribution, you shall have no sons for the rest of your life? How can you bear this?
Why is this so? If one examines the origins of this matter, it does not go beyond the habitual practice of killing as a constant custom, whereby the heart of benevolence has been extinguished.

Living in conformity with the prevailing worldly customs, they deceive themselves that the royal law takes no notice of them; they merely facilitate the private interests of their households and utterly fail to fear the retribution of ghosts and spirits.
From this, one knows that for those who have become women, their feelings of grievance and resentment must surely pierce the very sun.
Flying frost! As a parent, one’s own perverse and inauspicious qi will surely obstruct the heavens and shroud the universe;
is this not the commission of a most grievous offense and the bequeathing of endless calamity?

It is heartbreaking to witness such things, which prompts me to speak at length, hoping that you will exert yourself to reform and be persuaded to turn the wind [of fate]. Should you see others abandoning their daughters, please provide them with compassionate care and arrangements.
To preserve life may well be one occasion for transforming calamity into auspiciousness.

Regarding the exhortation to release living beings, I have heard that the minds of all Buddhas and sentient beings are one. All Buddhas, through the love of sentient beings, bring their own [enlightenment] to fulfillment.
Because their compassion is so great, their compassion is supreme. Because sentient beings take the compassion of the Buddhas and seal it as love, their love is profound.
There is no love more profound than that which loves all; yet nothing is loved more than one’s own life.

There is no compassion greater than that which is compassionate toward all; yet nothing is more compassionate than saving the lives of the multitude. Therefore, the gentlemen of antiquity delighted in...
Regarding the practice of releasing living beings (*fangsheng*): it is truly because one embodies the great compassion of all Buddhas above and fulfills the profound love of sentient beings below.
As for the greatest of good deeds, what could surpass this? Alas, once the mechanism of slaughter is set in motion, cruel and poisonous practices are widely carried out;
they are hunted with a hundred stratagems and captured by a thousand means—either confined within cages and enclosures or hung alive upon knives and carving blocks. Their courage... [is crushed].

Their spirits fall and their souls fly; mother and child are separated and scattered. Their mouths are filled with indignation, yet to whom can they cry out? Their eyes gaze longingly, seeking rescue.
They are like prisoners awaiting execution, standing on the brink of the gate of death; or like a peaceful community suddenly beset by a violent raid.
What must the state of their sickness and suffering be like? What must their grief and resentment feel like? For this reason, the Buddhas have established these precepts against such suffering.
Regarding the taking of life: I have extensively exhorted others to release living beings, relinquishing my own impermanent wealth to redeem their most precious lives.

Whether sparing one or two, or as many as ten thousand, I have enabled them to change from peril to safety and to live when facing death. With the heavens high and the seas vast, they may roam at will;
with the sun warm and the breeze gentle, they shall together return to a state of peace and prosperity. Though this is called the smallest of acts of charity, [it yields immeasurable merit].

This is indeed a most profound virtue. Whether one considers them as future Buddhas or as parents from many lifetimes, once the shared nature of their awakening is recognized, it is logically impossible not to feel deep compassion.

Furthermore, whether they receive retribution in this life or undergo compensation after death, once the vital spark of life is touched, the sentiment naturally cannot be forgotten—how much more so when one is amidst the weeds...
When the trees turn yellow and shed their leaves, one still feels sorrow; seeing the gloom and severity of clouds and mist, one likewise loses joy.
From this we may verify that the true mind must pervade the ten voids, and supreme benevolence flows directly through all myriad beings.
How could those endowed with blood and breath lack the sincerity of compassion? I only pray that you will constantly practice ransoming [life], so that the pulse of benevolence may flow eternally;
that you will widely exhort your peers, so that the wind of mercy may be universally spread; that you may perfect the originally existing true mind and preserve the Buddha-nature within yourselves;
and that you may look up in praise of the Imperial Benevolence’s transformation while silently turning the mechanism of the destiny of slaughter.
This is what is called the supreme joy of goodness; it is nothing other than a magnificent event of great peace. I pray that you will extend a single hand and not knit your brows.

In the chapter on "Good Friends," the bond of friendship is held in high esteem. Virtue does not stand alone; benevolence must have its support. Achievement cannot be achieved by one person alone, for a vessel is not formed by itself.
It is accomplished. Though one may occupy a position of high honor, without a friend, one cannot find peace.
Though one may possess rare and extraordinary talents, without a friend, one often falls into self-abandonment.

There are even instances where a father cannot obtain it from his son, a ruler cannot obtain it from his minister, an elder brother cannot obtain it from his younger brother, and a husband cannot obtain it from his wife—yet such qualities always emerge through friendship.
With these few words, he has ultimately perfected his excellence. Is the contribution of a friend not indeed weighty? Yet, while the name "friend" is one, the realities of friendship differ.

There are those who befriend out of emotion, those who befriend for profit, and those who befriend through the Way. What value is there in befriending out of emotion or for profit? It must be through the Way that one befriends. To befriend through the Way— *Note:
This passage appears to be a commentary on the opening lines of the "Jieyou" (Understanding Friendship) chapter of the *Mencius*. The text provided is a fragmentary excerpt.*
Thus, they forget one another beyond the bounds of physical form and trace, and reach mutual accord prior to sound and color. They refine and sharpen one another, returning solely to the Way.
It can eliminate my biases, it can open my obstructions, it can supplement my deficiencies, and it can perfect my strengths.

The *I Ching* says: "The image of the hexagram Dui is that of lakes joined together; the noble person, accordingly, cultivates themselves through discussion and study with friends. This is friendship.
It is clear that righteousness must be held in high regard. Since the decline of worldly customs, the way of friendship has daily decayed;

those in the world who speak of friendship do so only for the sake of profit or personal sentiment. When profit is occasionally not obtained, or when sentiment occasionally happens to falter, resentment arises.
Or, when one’s own demands are excessive while one’s expectations of others are complete, yet one conceals one’s own...
To disparage what others lack while envying their strengths gives rise to resentment and grievance; from this, one becomes filled with indignation and declares to others:
"There are no good friends in the world. Is it truly because there are no good friends in the world?
It is rather because the way one seeks friends has not been correct. Those of antiquity who were skilled in seeking friends did not exhaust others' feelings nor harbor expectations of them.
Do not conceal others' virtues with your own strengths; do not disparage others' shortcomings with your own weaknesses. Be diligent and earnest, seeking only that which is good.

Thus, even one who possesses the brilliance of a sage and occupies the position of the "Nine at Five" (the sovereign) will examine the words of commoners and gleaners and consult craftsmen and the blind;
what then would not be considered a friend? As for emulating the exemplary conduct of former sages, one need not inquire whether they are contemporaries to be friends.
It is ancient wisdom. When one stone grinds another, the friend does not inquire whether it is good or evil. Extending this principle, Heaven takes its model from his loftiness;
Earth takes its model from his thickness; the sun and moon take their model from his brightness; cold and heat take their model from his transformations;

and among feathers, fur, scales, shells, plants, trees, metals, and stones, there is nothing that does not have its standard and nothing that cannot be taken as a model. How, then, can it be said that there are no virtuous friends in the world?
Since my youth, I have often suffered from bouts of madness, which prevented me from gaining entry into the circles of great men and gentlemen.

'A single phrase clearly encompasses the myriad phenomena'—this is the Mystery within the Essence (Ti-zhong-xuan). 'Double Yang, the ninth day of the month: the chrysanthemums are fresh'—this is the Mystery within the Phrase (Ju-zhong-xuan)."
