yet, if one grasps the meaning while forgetting the words, then within a single phrase, there is nothing that is not encompassed. For example, the line "On the Double Ninth, the chrysanthemums are fresh" contains the Three Profundities (san xuan).

The Three Essentials can all be understood through silent resonance. Now, since the Abbot explains the Three Mysteries by analyzing them phrase by phrase, how then could he possibly analyze the Three Essentials?
A monk asked, "What is the mystery within the essence? The Abbot of the Pagoda replied, "As Master Zhao said:
'Only the sage is able to take the myriad things as himself. He also said: 'The three realms are mind-only; the myriad dharmas are consciousness-only. And he further said:
'All dharmas that arise are manifested by the mind alone; all worldly causes and effects, even down to the finest dust motes of the world, are formed by the mind.'"

The essence is such as this; only then is it right view. To lack even a hair’s breadth of this is to fall into wrong view, for there would then be a superfluous dharma, and one would fail to realize that all is but mind-only.
The monk asked again, "What kind of words are 'the mystery within the essence'?

The Abbot of the Pagoda replied, "It is like when the Buddha pointed to the ground with his finger and said, 'A Brahma temple should be built here,' and Śakra, Lord of the Devas, took a single blade of grass and planted it in that spot."
He said: "When the construction of the Brahma-pavilion was completed, the Buddha smiled. When Daluo was kicked down by Mazu with a single step, he rose and said:
'The myriad phenomena and the hundreds of thousands of wondrous meanings are all found right upon the tip of a single hair; there one immediately recognizes the source.'"
A monk asked Zhaozhou, "What is the student's own self? Zhaozhou replied, "Mountains, rivers, and the great earth.
Such responses are what are called "conventional words" (he-tou-yu). To directly clarify the mystery within the essence is precisely like pouring foul water over someone; one has no way to escape.
The monk Jin asked, "What words or phrases clearly reveal the path of self-expression? The Abbot of the Pagoda replied, "It is like when Xingshan asked Shishi, 'Have you ever been to Mount Wutai?
He replied, 'I have. [Xingshan] asked, 'Did you see Mañjuśrī? He replied, 'I did. [Xingshan] asked, 'What did Mañjuśrī say to you?
He replied, 'He said, "The Master's parents have been cast into the wild grasses. The monk then questioned him further.
Ganshui. When Vimalakīrti used his hand to hurl the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system into another direction, what was his intention?
[Ganshui] said, "To fill up the ravines and gullies. A monk asked, "When one speaks it all at once in a single phrase, how is it? He said, "Shattered into a hundred pieces.
Yunmen asked a monk, "Where have you come from? [The monk] said, "From Mount Nanyue. Yunmen asked again, "Why did Master Rang enter Lake Dongting?"
The monk had no reply. Yunmen spoke on his behalf, saying, "Thank you, Master, for condescending from your high station to this lowly one.

Although such words respond to the immediate occasion, they still represent a path of personal emergence; yet, fundamentally, they have not attained liberation or pure clarity. One must further understand that there is the "mystery within the phrase."
Regarding the "Mystery within the Body" (ti zhong xuan) cited by Gu Ming: for the time being, let us set aside the question of whether it is correct or not.
However, its meaning merely recognizes ordinary rationality and has not transcended conventional measurement; how could this possibly be Linji’s “Mystery within the Body”?

The monk asked again, "Since you have realized the mystery within the essence (*tǐzhōng xuán*), every word and phrase you utter already encompasses both principle and phenomenon; why then do you require the mystery within the phrase (*jùzhōng xuán*)?
The Abbot replied, "Regarding the mystery within the essence: when confronting the immediate situation, one must observe the timing and distinguish between guest and host.

Furthermore, if one merely identifies with the Dharma-body or the Dharma-nature, claiming it can roll up or spread out the myriad phenomena and grant or withhold from the holy and the ordinary, one remains entangled by such dualistic views and cannot achieve liberation."

*Sā*. Therefore, it is necessary to clarify the "mystery within the phrase" (*jùzhōng xuán*). If one can clarify this, it is called the single path of transcendence, the pivotal mechanism for ascending.

It is also called responding to matters of one's own fundamental share (*běnfēnshì*), wherein one no longer engages in conventional dialogue. A monk asked: "What kind of speech is the 'mystery within the phrase'? The Abbot of the Stūpa replied:
"It is like when a bhikṣu asked the Buddha, 'What Dharma do you teach? and the Buddha said, 'I teach the Dharma of concentration. [The monk] asked again."
"What Dharma will you preach tomorrow? The Buddha said, "The indeterminate Dharma. [The monk] asked, "What is so certain today, and what is so indeterminate tomorrow?
The Buddha said, "Today is certain; tomorrow is indeterminate. A monk asked Master Si, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?
Si said, "What is the price of rice in Luling? Another monk asked Zhaozhou, "I have heard that the Master..."
He personally visited Nanquan. "Is it so? [The Master] asked. Nanquan said, "In Zhenzhou they grow large radishes.
Furthermore, a monk asked Yunmen, "What is the discourse that transcends Buddhas and patriarchs? Yunmen said, "A sesame cake. [The monk] asked again, "What is the pivotal bolt of the higher realm?"
The Gatekeeper said: "The eastern mountain and the western ridge are green. Furthermore, a monk asked Dongshan, "What is the Buddha? Dongshan said, "Three pounds of flax.

If one can awaken to and enter into even a single phrase among such utterances, everything will be thoroughly understood. Consequently, all intellectual views regarding the mystery within the essence will be instantly purified.
From that point onward, one will be entirely free from the conceptual knowledge and views of "Buddha-dharma," and will thus be able to [accord with]—
The person has removed the wedge and taken off the head-stall; they no longer rely upon a single thing.

However, while they have merely managed to shed their intellectual knowledge and views (*jñāna-dṛṣṭi*), their underlying understanding (*dṛṣṭi*) still remains, and thus they do not attain mastery over birth and death. Why is this? Because they have not yet awakened to the Way.
Regarding the words and phrases used by others, they claim these are "non-responsive talk" (*wuda hua*). In this age, people take this to be the ultimate standard throughout the world.

Great Practice! The ancestral wind has faded and died out, yet there remain words and phrases. If you wish not to involve yourself in words and phrases, you must clarify that which is the "mystery within mysteries.
The Ancients said: "To penetrate the pivot of the higher realm—this is to have no Buddha-dharma or intellectual views. They also said: "One who can bestow [it] upon others..."
It means to remove the wedge and take off the head-stall; it is to not rely upon a single thing.
It is merely said that one has "shed knowledge and views," yet if one's conceptual understanding still remains, one can only say that one has not yet awakened to the Way.

Since one has not yet awakened to the Way, how could what is called "conceptual understanding" possibly penetrate the pivotal mechanism of the higher realm? If the wedge of one’s own self has not been pulled out and the head-stall has not been removed, how [can one be free]?
Can one truly remove the wedges from others and strip away their head-cages?
Thus we know that what the ancients called the "mystery within the phrase" was merely the proliferation of many cryptic words and wondrous phrases by those of scholarly understanding;
how could it be the "mystery within the phrase" of Linji?

A monk asked, "What words are the mystery within mysteries? The Abbot of the Pagoda replied, "It is like when an outsider asked the Buddha: 'I ask neither about having words nor about having no words.
The World-Honored One remained silent for a long while. The outsider then said, 'The World-Honored One’s great compassion has cleared away the clouds of my delusion.'"

"Allow me to enter. Again, a monk asked Mazu, "Leaving behind the four propositions and transcending the hundred negations, I pray that you, Master, will directly point out the meaning of the Westward Transmission.
Mazu said, "I have no mental preoccupation today; simply ask Zhizang. The monk asked Zhizang, and Zhizang said:
"I have a headache today; ask my elder brother Hai. When the monk asked Hai, Hai said, "When I reach this point, I do not understand.
Furthermore, when Linji asked Huangbo, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? he was struck three times for his three questions.
Such precedents are regarded as the ultimate mystery within the gate of skillful means; only those who have realized it know them. If one looks toward...
To claim that the primary teaching of our supreme ancestors was not yet [fully realized] is simply unacceptable.

The causes and conditions cited by the ancients were all those that did not involve words or phrases; they are called the "mystery within mysteries. Only those who have attained awakening can truly know them.
If this is indeed the case, then the examples previously cited—the rice from Luling, the three catties of hemp, and Yunmen’s cake—[are likewise beyond verbal expression].

These are merely the "mystery within the phrase" (jùzhōng xuán); they do not yet encompass the "mystery within the mystery" (xuánzhōng xuán). These are all that can be known by those who have not yet attained awakening.

Furthermore, such cases as those of Fenyang—namely, "Beating the Great Image at Jiazhou," "Bathing the Iron Ox at Shanfu," and "Playing with the Lion at Xihe"—are likewise merely the "mystery within the phrase.
They do not yet encompass the "mystery within the mystery. These are all [the domain of] those who have not yet attained awakening.
To claim that one can know it is a grave error. Thus we know that what the ancients called "the mystery within mysteries" belongs entirely to deluded thought;
how could it be the "mystery within mysteries" of Linji?
The monk said, "The Three Mysteries must be perfectly complete all at once. If they are seen to be not yet complete, what fault is there?

The stupa master replied, "If one only attains the Mystery within the Essence but has not yet realized the Mystery within the Phrase, this person will long retain a conceptual understanding of the Buddha-dharma.

Every word and phrase they utter must be understood as a response corresponding to the Three Vehicles; within those phrases, one must rely upon the proper timing and fully integrate both Principle and Phenomena."
Only when the roles of guest and host are distinguished can one speak of "perfection" (*yuan*); otherwise, it is called "partiality and barrenness.

Because this person does not forget their intellectual views and knowledge, their eye of the Way remains unclarified—like a speck of gold dust in the eye. They must further awaken to the mystery within the phrase before they may proceed.
If one merely awakens to the mystery within the phrase, one penetrates the Dharmakāya; yet, conversely, one may become a slave to this very knowledge and vision, possessing no actual practice.
There was a monk who clung to the self and others, believing that objects exist outside the mind; he had not clarified the mystery within the essence.
Many descendants of Yunmen and Linji are like this. Generally, even if a student of the Way can awaken to these two kinds of mysteries, [they remain unenlightened].

Furthermore, one must clearly grasp the "mystery within mysteries" (*xuánzhōng xuán*); only then can one avoid remaining stuck on the path of mere liberation. Only then can one attain stability and set foot firmly upon the ground of reality.

Having awakened to the mystery within the essence (*tǐzhōng xuán*), yet claiming not to forget cognitive views (*zhījiàn*)—if the eye of the Way (*dàoyǎn*) is not yet clear, then this essence remains entirely [unrealized].

This is delusion. To say that what has not yet been attained is the "mystery within the mystery" (*xuánzhōng xuán*) implies that once one has realized the "mystery within the phrase" (*jùzhōng xuán*), one has already penetrated the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Yet, why do you still say that the "mystery within the essence" (*tǐzhōng xuán*) remains unclarified? Now, the "mystery within the essence" is precisely the matter of the Dharma-body itself.
How could there be a person who has penetrated the Dharma-body and yet still does not understand the Dharma-body? From this, we know what the ancients recognized as the essence.

The mystery within the middle is not the illumination of the Dharma-body; the mystery within the phrase is not the penetration of the Dharma-body. In short, these are merely instances of generating false deliberations.
Generally speaking, regarding the three mysteries, each single phrase must possess all three; they must be perfectly complete at once, and cannot be distinguished by sequence, shallowness, or depth.
If even one is lacking, then both will be compromised and leak away, and they can no longer be called "mysteries."
As for Juefan, he delighted in discussing the errors of the ancients, yet he was unable to deeply clarify those errors;
he merely criticized them for not conforming to his own use of Xuansha’s three phrases to judge the Three Mysteries (sanxuan). Now, the words of Xuansha’s three phrases are fully extant.
Regarding his first phrase, it says: "If you know the measure that transcends the category, then you will not be afflicted by the demons of the mind."
It is brought under one's control; once it has entered into one’s hands, it is immediately transformed and made to fall into place.

To say that one "penetrates the Great Way" while not sitting within ordinary views—such as the common expressions of the ancients and moderns regarding the "ever-present Buddha-dharma and its insights"—is precisely to remain within the confines of ordinary views and have not yet transcended the realm of conceptual measurement. When compared to Xuansha’s "First Phrase," is there not a vast difference?
Regarding Xuan Sha’s second phrase, it is said: "Entering birth and exiting death, extensively benefiting all beings, and utterly transcending the realms of form, desire, attachment, and views.
It is further said that those who are slaves to knowledge and views lack genuine practice; they harbor likes and dislikes, as well as the notions of self and other.
To compare this with Xuan Sha’s second phrase—is there not a vast difference? As for Xuan Sha’s third phrase:
Some say: "When the Great Function manifests, its transformations are without fixed direction; it is entirely used and entirely not used, entirely arising and entirely not arising.

They claim that from ancient times until now, it has been said that this does not involve language, taking as evidence the World-Honored One’s long silence, Mazu’s response beyond the four propositions, and Linji’s three times receiving blows. They propose to characterize this as the Mysterious (xuán).
How far removed from the third phrase of Xuefeng is this! Thus we know that the Ancients certainly did not recognize Xuansha;

yet Juefan not only failed to recognize Xuansha, he likewise failed to recognize the Ancients. To treat them with such contemptuous derision and to cite them erroneously—Juefan’s transgression is indeed grave.

Juefan said: "The teaching-body (dharma-kāya) of this land responds to capacities through sound and hearing. Therefore, those who clarify the Way rely on language to bring forth the function of wisdom.
By using words to dispel words and using principle to discern principle, the wondrous, subtle, perfect, and luminous state is never interrupted;
this is called the 'flowing True Suchness' (pravāha-tathatā). This is what Fenyang meant when he said: 'A single phrase, clearly manifest, encompasses all phenomena.'"

Those who attain it divine it and clarify it; they do not die beneath the words. Therefore, when responding to circumstances and putting them into practice, they all cast aside conventional molds so as not to be hindered by traces and shadows.
This is what is called "having no words within words," which is what Fenyang referred to when he said, "On the Double Ninth, the chrysanthemums are fresh.
The discourse on the Three Mysteries (Sanxuan) originally arose from the need to eliminate afflictions; thus, one who attains [this]...
As for the Dharma, its value lies in knowing its intent. To know the intent is to be vast and empty, following conditions with spontaneous ease; this is called not missing the opportune moment.
This is what Fenyang meant when he said: "When one attains the meaning and forgets the words, the Way becomes easy to approach."

These are what Juégǎn calls the Three Mysteries (Sānxuán). From the passage beginning with "The essence of the Dharma-body" up to "A single phrase, luminously encompassing the myriad phenomena," is the Mystery within the Luminous Essence (Míngtǐzhōng xuán).
From "Those who have attained it for themselves" up to "On the ninth day of the Double Ninth, the chrysanthemums are fresh," is the Mystery within the Luminous Phrase (Míngjùzhōng xuán).
From the discourse on the Three Mysteries up to "When one grasps the meaning and forgets the words, the Way is easy to approach," is the Mystery of the Ultimate Meaning (Yìyì zhōng xuán).
The "Mysterious within the Mind" (*xuan zhong xuan*) is the profound meaning within the intent [of the teachings].

In the past, the Ancient Pagoda Master (*Guta Chu*) allocated the verses of Fenyang to the three mysteries (*san xuan*), which greatly deviated from Fenyang’s original intent. Why has Juefan now followed suit and divided them as well?

Furthermore, Juefan frequently rebuked the Ancient Pagoda Master for improperly establishing arbitrary designations such as "the Mysterious within the Mind," yet here he again tacitly accepts and employs them.
Why is this so? Furthermore, regarding their interpretations of the "mysteries": the first two mysteries are likewise merely the teachings of the ancient Patriarch Xusha;
it is only the final mystery that differs. Thus we know that what Juefan discussed was largely driven by the momentary impulses of the time.
Since such contradictions exist, people often admire his talent and consequently place their trust in his doctrines; the resulting harm [to the Dharma] can be imagined.
"How excellent is the Way!
Juefan said, "It is not only Linji who delights in discussing the Three Mysteries (Sanxuan). The *Cantong qi* composed by Shitou is fully endowed with this principle.

I have often contemplated it deeply; it is simply that the terms 'mystery' (*xuan*) and 'essence' (*yao*) have been replaced by 'light' (*ming*) and 'darkness' (*an*). The text consists of only forty characters."
Regarding the remaining phrases, they are divided by way of the luminous and the dark. At the very beginning of the chapter, it is stated: "The spiritual source is luminously pure and bright;
its branches and tributaries flow darkly. Furthermore, it is explained and elaborated upon: "Darkness accords with the superior and middle [phrases]; 'bright' refers to the clear and turbid phrases.
This means that when in the dark, one must necessarily accord with the superior and middle; when in the luminous, one must clarify the clear and turbid. This is the mystery within the essence.

Furthermore, when pointing to its fundamental principle and revealing its intent, it says: "The beginning and the end must both return to the source; honor and subordination employ their respective expressions.
Thus, the subsequent passage extensively enumerates the phrases concerning clarity and obscurity, unfolding in a continuous and unending succession. This is the "Middle Mystery" (Zhongxuan).
When his words have come to an end, he further says: "I respectfully inform those who study the Mystery: do not let your time and light be spent in vain.
If a practitioner can, in their daily life, avoid wasting time or missing the proper occasion, this is truly repaying the Buddha's kindness; this is the profound meaning within the mind."

To take the light and darkness of the *Cantong qi* as the profound essentials (*xuan-yao*), and then further use the Three Mysteries (*san-xuan*) to categorize the *Cantong qi*, is to greatly lose the intent of both traditions.
Within "Literary Chan" (*Wenzi chan*), there is also one chapter that is largely identical to this, differing only slightly;
it further claims that the *Cantong qi* is precisely the "Mystery within the Phrase" (*zhong-xuan*) of Linji. Now, the *Cantong qi* is the same, and awakening (*jue*) is likewise the same.
Such are the differences in their judgments. How can they hope to command the trust of others?
In my view, Juefan’s errors and delusions seem to surpass those of the ancient Tazhu;
having suffered repeated calamities throughout his life and stumbled until his final days, it was surely because he deserved them. How could one say these were "calamities without cause"?
An Examination of Longtan:
The *Song Jingde Chuandeng Lu* records only that Tianhuang Huizhao succeeded Shitou;

it does not know that there were two Dao-wus at the same time—one who succeeded Mazu and resided at Tiangwang Temple west of the city of Jingzhou, and one who succeeded Shitou and resided in Jing[zhou].
The Imperial Temple (Tianhuang Si) to the east of the provincial capital contains materials that can be relied upon: the *Epitaph for Nanyue Huairang* compiled by Tang Guideng;
the *Memorandum on the Essential Tenets in Response to Minister Pei* by Guifeng; and the *Epitaph for Mazu* composed by Quan Deyu.
Furthermore, the two epitaphs cited by later Da’anguan Ying—those by Qiu Xuansu and Fu Zai—are even more detailed. There is nothing here to be doubted.
However, in Qiu’s inscription, he states that Longtan Xin succeeded Tianwang Wu; this cannot help but raise doubts.
I have previously examined the *Recorded Sayings* (Yulu) of Xuefeng, in which Xuefeng, addressing the King of Min, declared that he had attained the Way of the former masters Deshan and Shitou.
Furthermore, the preface to the *Recorded Sayings* of National Teacher Yan of Mount Gu also states that Yan was a fifth-generation descendant of Shitou.
These two texts were produced during the Five Dynasties period, not long after Longtan; how could they have so hastily forgotten their own origins?
Based on this, we know that Longtan Xian was a successor of Tianhuang Wu, not Tianwang Wu; this is the first proof.
Furthermore, Longtan Xian’s family lived in Tianhuang Lane to the east of the city of Jingzhou, where they made their living selling cakes.
Every day, he would send ten cakes to Venerable Tianhuang. After each meal, the Master would always leave one cake behind, saying, "I give this to you."
He used it to provide shade for his descendants. One day, Xin thought to himself: "I took this cake away; why has it returned as a gift to me? Is there some other meaning behind this?
He went to see [the Emperor] and asked about it. The Emperor said: "This was brought by you; returning it to you—what fault is there in that?"

Xin heard of this and gained some understanding of its profound principles; he consequently entered the monastic life. The Emperor said, "In the past you honored merit and goodness, and now you have believed my words;
you may be named Chongxin (Venerable Faith). Thereupon, Xin served diligently at the Emperor’s side.
From this, we know that the one whom Longtan Xin succeeded was Tianhuang Wu, not Tianwang Wu. This is the second proof. Furthermore, one day Xin asked Tianhuang:
Xinxing said, "Since I arrived, I have not received instruction on the essential point of the mind.

Huangbo said, "From the moment you arrived, I have never failed to instruct you on the essential point of the mind. Xinxing asked, "Where did you instruct me? Huangbo replied, "When you brought tea, I accepted it for you;
when you brought food, I received it for you; when you bowed in greeting, I lowered my head for you. Where else?"

Dazu did not point out the essential core of the mind to him. The Master lowered his head and remained silent for a long while. Huang said, "If you see, see directly; if you attempt to deliberate, you are already mistaken.
At that moment, the Master attained realization. He asked again, "How does one maintain this? Huang replied, "Roam freely according to your nature;

be expansive and relaxed in accordance with conditions. Simply exhaust the ordinary mind; there is no separate 'sage's understanding' apart from it. On another day, he asked, "Regarding the succession of the patriarchs..."
The transmission of this matter—how is it? Huang said, "It is not that you cannot recognize where he has come from.
Xian said, "How many people possess such an eye? Huang said, "In shallow grass, reeds grow easily.
Based on this, we know that the one whom Longtan Xian succeeded was Tianhuang Wu, not Tianwang Wu; this is the third proof. These three segments now serve as proof.
It is as clearly manifest as this. Yet, in Qiu Xuansu’s *Epitaph for the Stupa*, it is recorded that Longtan succeeded Tianwang.

How can this alone be considered exceptional? Upon examination, it is evident that a later person, out of baseless devotion, arbitrarily altered the *Epitaph for the Stupa of Tianwang* to create a point of contention.
Otherwise, they would surely have struck through the passages in the preceding three sections that serve as proof and simply omitted them. Afterward—

This can serve to establish his argument. Furthermore, Zhang Wujin once remarked that Yunmen’s *jīfēng* (pithy, sharp discourse) resembled that of Linji, and thus he should be considered a successor to Mazu.
This, however, is merely the talk of a rustic from Qi-dong. Since ancient times, those who received the same master have been regarded as peers.
Yet, those whose spiritual "edges" (jīfēng) differ are many; how could they necessarily be identical? For example, Yúnmén and Fǎyǎn both emerged from Xuěfēng.
If Yúnmén were to be traced back to Mázǔ, would Fǎyǎn then have to be traced back to Shítóu?
Furthermore, the spiritual edges of Dánxiá and Tóuzǐ were no inferior to those of Línjì. If Āngxuān and Sānshèng both missed their opportunity at Shìshì, then...
Should Danxia, Touzi, and Shishi then be reclassified under Mazu? Furthermore, consider Nanquan and his disciples;
all were successors of Mazu, yet they did not employ staffs or shouts. Huishan and his disciples were all successors of Baizhang, yet they did not pursue austere severity.
Should they then be reclassified under Shitou? Moreover, I have previously examined Xuefeng.

A complete record [of his teachings] has been preserved. His Chan encompasses all styles; its waves are vast and expansive. Thus, at times his speech resembles Linji, and at other times it resembles Caodong.
This was true for his disciples as well, such as Xuansha, Changqing, Baofu, Gushan, Anguo, Jingqing, and others.
Even though Yunmen’s functional deployment of *ji* (critical pivot) was uniquely austere, in reality his speech was not entirely definitive, and his *ji* did not always strike directly at the core.
Furthermore, he successively studied under Caoshan, Shushan, Jiufeng, and Qianfeng;

his recorded sayings remain extant, such as those concerning the "three kinds of illness" and the "two kinds of light," which are entirely identical to those of Qianfeng. This is particularly evident.

How could it be claimed that he was the same as Linji and should have been a successor in the lineage of Mazu? Those who are ignorant are indeed difficult to reason with, but for those of superior intelligence...
This can be verified and known. Therefore, I have written this to inform the wise of the world; may they examine it in detail.

A Memorial for Personally Visiting the Master’s Quiescent Chamber.
To begin with: that which is neither moving nor still is the essence of the wondrous Way; that which possesses both movement and stillness is the function of the wondrous Way.
To abandon stillness and pursue movement is the delusion of ordinary beings; to loathe movement and indulge in stillness is the attachment of those of the Two Vehicles. If this is so, [then...]

Thus, they sit in quietude within deep forests and dwell in seclusion amidst cold valleys; avoiding the dust and vapors of the world, they refuse to enter it, content with the lack of vitality in withered trees.
Would this not be treading upon the deviant tracks of the Two Vehicles and contradicting the great purport of the True Teaching?

This is surely because there is a subtle skillful means (upāya). The Way is not stillness itself, yet it must be realized through stillness before it becomes manifest. The Way is not movement itself, yet it must be realized through movement...
This obstructs and obscures. As the saying goes: "To seek pearls, the waves should be calm; if you stir the water, it will be difficult to obtain them.

Therefore, when our Buddha established the teachings, those of the highest capacity forget both movement and stillness, transcending them to realize the truth alone. Those of the next level first practice the waters of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and subsequently give rise to the light of wisdom (*prajñā*).
It is not that they indulge in stillness as a place of rest; rather, they truly rely on stillness as the essential means for entering the Way. Truly...

One is able to attain clarity through stillness; when the light of wisdom shines forth, one may say that the mountains, rivers, and the great earth—all objective conditions—are transparently void of any substance.
One may say they are certainly not other things. Yet one may also say they are the mountains and rivers, the great earth, and all objective conditions.
When it is thus, the bustling of markets and cities does not constitute clamor, nor do the mountains...
A forest is not "solitude. The great trichiliocosm is not "wealthy. A single valley is not "poverty. A great assembly is not "many. A single person is not "alone.
Even if one faces the peaks ten thousand fathoms high for a lifetime, gazing at the Milky Way, can it be said that they have grown weary of movement and become addicted to stillness?
If the root of birth and death has not been severed, the water buffalo will not yet cease its trespassing upon the crops.

Wandering aimlessly through the mundane world, you do not know how to withdraw and collect yourself. It appears that your mind follows external objects as it rushes away, and your wisdom becomes obscured by things like mist.
Though you have adopted the name of the Mahayana, your self-deception is indeed profound. Shouchang alone has approached his teacher, casting his solitary shadow upon the Seven Stones Mountain peak;
he has already spent three years in the refined cultivation of dhyāna and stillness. Now, furthermore, at Longjin—
Yuan intended to erect a few rafters to serve as a place for seated meditation (*yànzuò*). This was likely to borrow stillness in order to seek that which is neither moving nor still.
In ancient times, Min was known as a "Dharma Cave" (*fákū*); among its officials and lay practitioners, there were none who did not long savor the joy of Chan.
Deeply immersed in the joy of the Dharma, he gave with profound sincerity, and it was completed in no time. How could this possibly require my many superfluous words?
However, as for the single phrase "movement and stillness do not interfere with one another," I ask that you, Master, take it up and carry it yourself.
Preface for the Construction of the Fo-ding Hermitage by Daoxian.
At the mouth of East Kun Mountain there is a peak named Guli; atop Guli there is a hermitage named Fo-ding.
