A Memorial for the Transformation Field at the Tranquil Chamber of Longtan, beside the Shitang Cliff.

Beside the Shitang Cliff, pearl-like trees reflect the light of the white tuft [between the Buddha’s brows]; within the hollow of the Dragon Well, golden cords shine with the colors of the auspicious clouds.
A few rafters of thatched cottage suffice as a place to rest from the shadows; a heart as pure as ice has long since become that of one who has transcended to old age.
This plan: with the meditation cushion and staff, I have already forged a friendship in the Green Mound; with the rain-hat and cloud-cloak, I am about to attend to the green fields.
Yet Mount Yang has no place for planting a spade, and the level plains offer little space for driving a calf.
With no permanent means of livelihood remaining, I must rely on external support. Steaming sand cannot produce rice, and cooking clouds can hardly satisfy hunger. If I wish to seek a hundred...

For a field of ten *zhang*, one must necessarily provide the silver of Master Ganqi; beneath the hoe, one should thoroughly investigate the Great Meaning, and upon the tip of the brush, I pray you will radiate light.
This is the fund-raising appeal for purchasing land to support the Jiaolin Jinxian Hermitage for ten thousand people.
The lush greenery of the banana groves has long shrouded the traces of his former seclusion; the golden spire floats with light, distantly continuing the garden of the ancient immortals.
Amidst the shadows of ten-thousand pines, there is no hindrance to raising one’s thatched hut; at the crossroads of the street, one may well open the cloth bag.

To cause the wheel of food to turn, one must first ensure that the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) is joyfully accomplished. Before driving the ox across the level fields, one hopes to encounter Sudatta as he emerges with his bullion.
Desiring to seek even half a portion from beneath a single stroke of the hoe, how could one dare to look for it within a mere fragment of paper?
Seeking out ten thousand people, he did not decline to raise up the pivot of the teaching; I pray that each of you will open your smiling mouths.
At Baishuiyan, while reciting the *Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, it was said:
"The entire earth is the single eye of the śramaṇa. Where else could there be a sūtra? The entire Dharma-realm is the *Avataṃsaka*.
Having already mastered this single scroll of the scripture, where else could one possibly fix one's gaze? If you can grasp the meaning right here, you will have already shed all entanglements.

What need is there to speak of the ten mysterious gates? You would have entered them without even needing to snap your fingers. Even if it were called the One True Dharma-realm, it would be no different.
To break into laughter, why must one turn back? It is simply because the habitual obstructions have grown ever deeper; alas, they are sealed by the dust of the world and difficult to pry open.
If one does not cause the ocean of sound to shake the earth and roar through the heavens, how could the clouds of radiance illuminate the present and reflect the past?
To enter the sea of Vairocana, one must launch an iron ship across it; meanwhile, at the gateway of Avalokiteśvara, one must directly brandish the "shadow-grass. One sound—
It has entered my ears. Why need one travel through a hundred cities? To contemplate the half-verse with a darkened mind is precisely what is required to transcend directly the nine realms.
As soon as the Brahma-sound is raised, the heart-light of the great earth is suddenly opened; as the precious volume is first turned, the Buddha-fruition of a lifetime is instantly perfected.

How magnificent is the power of the Dharma! How wondrous are sentient beings! Each and every one is inherently possessed of a sūtra; it only requires that they awaken to it and realize it for themselves.
May everyone ascend together to this assembly, and it is certain that they shall share the same title and the same name.
At the head of the Wanshi Rapids, the Zhongyuan Water and Land Feast is established;
smoke-shrouded marshes and clouds darken as the rain falls in a misty drizzle, while the ever-rising waves overturn the void. Upon the sandy islets, the moon is bright, yet the wind is bitterly cold.
At this time, we hear the souls weeping through the night. On the banks of the green willows, it is fitting that a hand reach down to pull the drowning from the water;

upon the marshes of white artemisia, who can provide a boat to cross over the perils? Now, on this day when Maudgalyāyana rescues those in distress, we initiate the ritual of the *zhāi* fast established by Emperor Liang Wudi.
We pray that the Iron Ring Mountains may suddenly vanish beneath the sun, and that the Land of Golden Sands may manifest before our very eyes.

Before the riverbank, the great stream swirls and eddies; yet one may cross it with ease by riding the wind. The traveler’s sail flutters and tosses, yet there is no peril as it breaks through the waves.
I pray that you will contribute from the wealth of the five families to collectively cultivate the Dharma of the three firmnesses. This is indeed evidenced and can be trusted.
I hope you will not take a circuitous route and fail to comply.

Regarding the preface for the Tripitaka at Baoshan Monastery, the Elder of Mount Lingshan has appeared in this world once more; from non-existence he speaks existence, his tongue trailing across the ground. Though it is called a "sutra" and called a "commentary,"...

The Vinaya is called "Treatise" (lun). It is established according to the capacities of beings and arises by relying on conditions. It is like a thousand waves rising in competition or ten thousand peaks vying for their steepness;
yet, in essence, it merely clarifies this very local scenery of the original ground.

Thus we know that within the Great Canon, every word and every phrase is the heart-essence of all Buddhas and the medicinal medicine for sentient beings. How, then, could one possibly discuss whether these are provisional or ultimate?
Is this truly within the teachings or outside of them? Lately, some fledgling Zen practitioners, with their immature mouths, treat the Tripitaka with contempt;
instead, they memorize the words and shouts of the Patriarchal School as their livelihood. Unaware that they are merely clinging to the trap and the snare, they attempt to fathom the Buddha’s wisdom.
Whether in the context of the School or the Teachings, they violate the former and oppose the latter—their delusion is exactly the same. Now I have heard from Master Gu...
The Master traveled south with his flying staff and stayed at Baoshan Monastery in Jianzhou. Zen practitioners flocked there from all directions;

while their capacities were indeed diverse, the Great Master’s teaching hall was vast and encompassed those of all three levels of aptitude. Consequently, the Chief Administrator, Master Xin, conceived the thought of requesting the Tripitaka to universally moisten the various faculties of sentient beings.
At that time, a scholar named Mr. Xu first gave rise to this great resolve, donating gold to initiate the project and setting a noble example. However...
A city cannot be constructed by a single tree; a mountain cannot be completed by a single basketful of earth.

If we can join hands in a common endeavor and together contribute to this sublime plan, then every grain of rice and every thread of silk will become a precious sail upon the turbid sea—a true seed of the Buddha-fruit.
When, in years to come, you have realized the natural splendor of your own ground, you may then say to others: "The sacred scriptures of the Tripiṭaka."
Originally, these were merely old scraps of paper; what fault could there be in that?
The draft for the inscription on the *Lotus Sūtra* bronze bell at Gushan states:
"Sentient beings are hindered by form and constrained by spatial direction; they are separated by mere inches and cannot communicate. That which can truly communicate—"
It is simply sound and hearing. Thus we know that the reach of sound is most extensive, while the penetration of hearing is most wondrous.
Regarding all methods for unifying the masses within the world and means for awakening them, there is nothing that can surpass sound and hearing.

Now, from the imperial court above down to the monastic quarters below, whenever morning and evening are signaled or when the assembly’s movements are regulated, one must invariably rely upon the bell. How could this be?
It is not that the bell has "hearing sound" as its function; rather, it is something those dwelling among the assembly must necessarily rely upon.

As for what is recorded in the Buddhist scriptures—that upon hearing the sound of a bell in the dark paths of the underworld, the instruments of suffering are instantly stilled, and upon hearing the sound of a bell within the passes, skulls are instantly shattered—its utility is thus all the more miraculous.
At Yongquan Temple on Mount Gu, the weeds were cleared and the site was rebuilt from the ground up.

It was Master Cao who first initiated the project by constructing the main hall and the ordination hall. Upon obtaining Master Shanlin, he then erected the two towers for the bell and drum in front of the main hall.
When Lord Shen, the Regional Inspector, came to visit this mountain, he donated his stipend to commission the casting of a copper *Lotus Sūtra* bell.
Thereupon, the monastery sent monks out to beg for alms to assist in completing this magnificent undertaking. Indeed, regarding this *Lotus Sūtra*...

They enter through the sound of the bell, and by means of that sound, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is proclaimed. Thus, let every person, upon the single application of their faculty of hearing, immediately comprehend the entire sutra.
Without the need for wearying delay in a thatched hut, they suddenly obtain what was hidden in their own home;

without the necessity of fleeing from the burning house, they securely mount the white ox. How great, then, must be the benefit of such a field of merit! Furthermore, I have heard that as for the bell—
It is like a vessel. Only when three things combine does sound arise; only when five things combine does hearing occur.
Now, since sound must depend on the combination of three, it is sound that is not sound. Since hearing must depend on the combination of five, it is hearing that is not hearing.
If sound is not sound, then it is the sound of non-sound that fills and obstructs empty space. If hearing is not hearing, then...
This is not a matter of hearing with the ears; it pervades the entire Dharma-realm. From this, one awakens and enters. At Mount Gu, the bell has already been cast long ago.
If this is not yet the case, wait until after the work of the furnace is completed, and there will naturally be a master of great mouth who shall explain it thoroughly for all people.
The Preface to the Request for the Tripitaka in Volumes by Zhongshang Ren says:
"Sutras, Vinaya, and Shastras—like two or three notes of a yellow bird; whether Buddha, Dharma, or Sangha—like three or four fragments of white clouds.
The World-Honored One spoke of existence where there was none, placing hair upon the back of a tortoise; yet sentient beings possess it themselves."
Seeking it in vain, one searches for snow within a furnace; one cannot avoid drilling empty pages of old books. It is just like a fool guarding a withered stump.
If it were a transcendent faculty, it would certainly not enter through the gate. Alas, being mired in delusion and trapped in the shell, one is constantly startled by the "rope-snake" in the dark.
Therefore, it is said that one takes the short for the long and builds a tower in the air. Every dharma proceeds from this.
Go here; the grit is always pure gold. Every word does not come from elsewhere; the jade palace appears within a blade of grass.
Among the three hundred and more assemblies, who has not been spurred by the whip of shifting shadows? Of the five thousand sacred texts, all are medicines to quell madness.
If you can see the moon by following the pointing finger, there is no need to seek Chang’an further; you may return home along the very path you are on.
Hanyang is not far from here. There dwells a superior person of middle rank whose moon of precepts has long been pure and whose flower of compassion has suddenly blossomed.

Desiring to peer into the realm of Great Wisdom, he must rely upon the method of extensive learning. Before turning the Wheel of the Half-Piṭaka at Zhaozhou, he first requests the complete scriptures from Xiushui.
Whether these be the words of the Buddha or the words of Māra, one must simply overturn the banner-pole; this is not a matter of expedient means.
Riding upon that which is not a true vehicle, one need only tread through the lacquered bucket. In the waves of the sea, there is no duality of flavor; how could one calculate their source?
Outside the gate, there are a thousand paths, yet all lead to the imperial capital. The three types of grass and two types of wood alike flourish, nourished by the rain of Dharma;
the seven treasures and eight jewels are left for the poor child to gather as he pleases. With pen exhausted and tongue shortened, I am truly unable to propagate and praise [this further].

This may be fully investigated. Whether it be a mosquito carrying a burden or an ant climbing a tree, how could I dare to lag behind in circulating this? I have inscribed these words as a libation-offering (zhīyǔ) and announce them everywhere to the gates of donors, so that we may together turn the Wheel of Dharma.
Belonging truly to the seeds and sprouts of Bodhi, let us join in extending our precious hands, hoping thereby to plant the roots and shoots of Prajñā.
Respectfully recorded.
Regarding the chanting of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* at Mount Gu:
Mount Gu was formerly a Chan monastery. Since its foundation by Xingsheng, the lineage of the lamp has continued without interruption for over seventy generations. As for Chan...
The Great Practice (Mahācaryā) flourished until the Jiajing era, when it was abandoned by the fire-god Zhurong and reduced to overgrown weeds.

During the Tianqi period, it was restored and the Venerable Boshan was invited to open the hall and extensively propagate the school’s tradition, nearly rivaling its former glory. However, the monks in the meditation hall were required to recite the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* daily as a fixed practice.
Some practitioners found this objectionable; I, however, maintain that the *Avataṃsaka*— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the extant portion.)
The fundamental Dharma-realm and the transmission of the One Mind at Shaolin diverge into two paths, yet they ultimately return to the same principle.
Furthermore, those who truly engage in Chan meditation have traditionally been required to attend to secular affairs;

for instance, Xuefeng and Baizhang both served as stewards (*dianzuo*), while Yangqi and Xingsheng both served as administrators (*jianyuan*). How could a single scroll of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* possibly hinder one who practices Chan?

Furthermore, masters such as Longji (Dragon Mechanism) and Maming (Horse Neigh) both integrated the teachings of the Sutras and the vehicles of practice; Guifeng and Wenling likewise provided commentaries on the sutras and śāstras.
How could one single scroll of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* possibly be an obstacle for those who practice Chan? In the past, Master Dushun composed a verse:
"The ox of Huaizhou eats the grain; The horse of Yizhou has a bloated belly. Seeking a physician throughout the world, One applies moxibustion to the left shoulder of a pig."
[The interlocutor] says: "If this verse is considered to belong to the Teachings (Jiao), from which fascicle of the eighty-one-fascicle *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* does it emerge?

If it is considered to belong to Chan, one can see that its author was also the first patriarch of the *Avataṃsaka*. However, what I wish to clarify is this: it belongs to Chan, yet it also belongs to the Teachings."
There is no need to carve up empty space or compete over "this" and "that," for such things are laughed at by those who possess true understanding.

On this occasion, following the annual custom, I have raised funds to sponsor the recitation of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*; therefore, I have written this to dispel such delusions. As for the discourse on cause and effect and the merits thereof, I dare not elaborate further here.
A Memorial for Soliciting Rice for Drum Mountain:
Stone Drum Peak is the bulwark of the provincial capital; Yongquan Temple is a deep pool for Zen monks. Since the founding by Prince Zhongyi, more than seven hundred years have passed;

since the patriarch Xingsheng began the transmission of the Way, more than seventy lamps have been perpetually linked. Alas!... [unable to provide further translation without the remainder of the text].
The Chan tradition gradually declined and failed to flourish; thus, the power of the Buddha grew ever more exhausted and could not be revived.

Furthermore, as the fire-god Zhurong fanned the flames, the monasteries were reduced to ruins. Broken steles lay prostrate in the grassy courtyards, and cunning hares sprawled across the Buddha’s throne.
Now, wishing to fan the embers of long-extinguished ash, I would pitch a thatched hut amidst the withered grass;

intending to continue the strings already snapped, I would raise my whisk beneath the wild mists. My pack is just gathered and the fields have already been abandoned, yet I have not yet reached the point of single-mindedly inquiring into the teachings or Chan;
instead, I am about to look up and call out for "Geng" and "Gui. With an empty belly, how can one accomplish the Way?
Only when all conditions are prepared may one enter the summer retreat (*varṣā*). The Buddha left behind these regulations: one relies on a single alms bowl for sustenance;
the Sangha possesses no permanent property, but merely seeks its livelihood from the four quarters. If you wish to first set the wheel of food in motion, you must dispatch mendicants far and wide.
While Yunmen’s cakes and Zhaozhou’s tea are indeed things one may partake of, I request that you instead bestow Luolang’s rice and Nanguan’s meal.
In the future, regarding the reconstruction of the Dharma Hall at Ch’ang-ch’ing Hsi-ch’an Temple on Mount Yi:
approximately five li to the west of the city of Min lies Mount Yi; atop it stands what is known as Ch’ang-ch’ing Hsi-ch’an Temple.
The temple first originated in the Tang dynasty. When Chan Master Lanyan came from Daguang to reside here, the white ox ran amok, overturning the great earth;

"having a phrase" and "not having a phrase" threw the world into turmoil at that time. Subsequently, the practitioner Lingdao spread the venomous breath of Xuefeng’s turtle-nosed staff throughout Jambudvīpa.
Through the generations, the transmission of the lamp has continued in an unbroken lineage, and together with Xuefeng and Gushan, they are renowned.
Regarding the three great monasteries of Min: since the entry of the Ming dynasty, the lamp of the Dharma has gradually dimmed until the present day.

Consequently, let alone their inability to revitalize the school or propagate the teachings as they did in former times, even their architectural structures have reached a state of decay that is nearly beyond repair.
Minister-General Cao, feeling this deeply in his heart, exerted all his efforts to advocate for them and commanded the resident monks to solicit donations for their restoration.
The Great Hall has now reached completion after three years of labor; yet the Dharma Hall remains as dilapidated as before.

Those who dwell there feel a sense of shame, and those who visit it heave sighs of lamentation. Thus, Master Cao’s intention remains unfulfilled. Consequently, the resident monks again gave rise to a great resolve and once more set out to solicit donations.
Layman Xue [Name] was the first to contribute gold, setting an example for the community. I, for my part, reflect upon this:
In the establishment of a monastic community, a hall must necessarily be built to expound the Dharma.

This is because, although the Three Jewels are held equally in high esteem, in terms of receiving sentient beings and benefiting their lives, nothing surpasses the Dharma. The Buddha is the one who presides over this Dharma; the Sangha is the one who expounds this Dharma.
If the Buddha were without the Dharma, what would be precious about the Buddha? If the Sangha were without the Dharma, what would be precious about the Sangha?
Furthermore, this is that which all Buddhas have taken as their common teacher and which the entire Sangha collectively honors;

it is the precious raft for emerging from peril and the bright lamp for destroying darkness. Since the Dharma truly cannot be neglected for even a single day, how could its hall possibly be abandoned for a single day?
Thus, it is fitting that the monastic community should find no peace day or night, but rather strive with urgency to construct this edifice.
Yet, those patrons who lament the present and mourn the past surely share in this same sorrow. Now, when one calls out with the wind at one’s back, how could there be anyone who does not respond?
I know that the arrival of gold and silk, and the soaring of the halls and chambers, may be awaited with confidence within days. However, the Dharma must necessarily rely upon...
Only after the ground is established can one expand; the ground must rely upon the Dharma to become significant.
Were there a hall but no Dharma, what value would there be in possessing such a hall? To manifest the body alone amidst the myriad phenomena has been an unresolved koan for seven hundred years.
The profound voice of the kalaviṅka bird must not cease for long, and I, too, cannot help but harbor high expectations. May you all...
Exert yourself!
Petition for the Construction of a Śarīra Stūpa at Baoshan Hermitage:

In the past, when the World-Honored One’s transformative expedients were completed, he withdrew his radiance at the Twin Trees. He further manifested as śarīras, so that his luminous influence might continue to appear.
This auspicious sign ensures that [the Master] shall forever serve as a field of merit for humans and devas. Indeed, his compassionate heart and great vows are inexhaustible;
thus he has manifested his traces in this final age. At Hongfu Temple in Tongxu County of Bianjing, there was formerly a stupa, which had long since fallen into ruin.
In recent years, due to the arrival of bandit rebels, the county magistrate took these bricks to repair the city walls. There he discovered a stone casket, two feet square.
Upon opening it, he found inside a silver casket containing two golden images and a silver flask holding a single bone of the Buddha.
Within the bones were śarīras like millet seeds; there were seven crystal vases, each containing several grains of śarīra.

Examining the ancient inscription, it was found that at the beginning of the Huangyou era of the Song dynasty, Empress Cao ordered an eunuch to inter the Buddha-bones and śarīras in the fifth tier of the stupa.
This was because all the items offered by the palace throughout successive reigns had been collected and enshrined within the stupa. At that time, it was appropriate.
The Grand Councilor Cao Anzu (Cao Xing) served as the Superintendent of Military Posts. He requested one *śarīra* relic and returned it to Yixing, intending to build a stupa for it on Mount Nanyue;
however, due to the onset of illness, he did not succeed. As he approached his death, he entrusted the *śarīra* to the Imperial Censor Cao Yugong of Jiaxing.
The following year, when [the author] arrived at Zhenji Monastery by the Shaoxi River, the Censor sent the *śarīra* there.
I was entrusted with the responsibility for this matter. Unfortunately, as several years had passed without a bountiful harvest, it could not be completed swiftly.

Thereupon, I reflected that while the *śarīra* relics at Jinling, Mount Kuanglu, and Mount Mao all radiate their brilliance throughout the realms of humans and devas, none had yet been heard of in Min.
Consequently, I desired to return to Min to erect a stupa. At that time, Master Huixin and various donors came to invite me; thus, I accepted the honor and entered Min.

Now it is proposed to construct a stupa at Baoshan in Jianzhou. This is because Jianzhou serves as a vital thoroughfare for the Eight Min Regions, yet Baoshan is further secluded deep within the mountains;
it is a place that those who drink wine or consume meat cannot pass by or even inquire about.
Now, these śarīras have traveled more than one hundred thousand *li* away and passed through over three thousand years before coming to rest upon this mound.
For the sentient beings of our Min region, something they had neither seen nor heard of since the beginning of time, they now encounter and pay homage to in person.
How could this be anything but a most rare and auspicious connection? Furthermore, now that this stupa has been completed, it is hoped that—purple [light will shine forth].
Polishing the golden body, he constantly preaches the Dharma; those who gaze upon him even once or pay him homage all receive extraordinary benefits, which shall forever serve as the seeds of Bodhi.
I pray that my fellow practitioners will join me with a single hand.
The Preface to the Ritual for the Repentance of the Pure Land at Fahai Monastery on Mount Luo:
The teaching of the Pure Land is fundamentally based upon such scriptures as the *Great Amitābha Sūtra* and the *Sūtra on the Sixteen Contemplations*.

It proclaims that in the west there exists the World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*), whose meritorious adornments are foremost among all. Furthermore, the World-Honored One Amitābha gathers in and sustains all sentient beings.
They shall return to the Land of Ultimate Bliss. His vows are vast and supreme;
those beings who are born there shall forever sever all suffering until they attain Buddhahood, never regressing. Furthermore, his merit and benefits are likewise supreme.

Those who seek birth in this land take a pure mind as their foundation. Regarding the method for purifying the mind, one may either recite the Name, practice meditation, or extensively cultivate various forms of goodness;
yet the simplest and easiest way to practice is by far the foremost. For this reason, it is widely praised in the various sutras and propagated by the successive Patriarchs.
Since the Buddha’s teachings entered China, the flourishing of its reception and recitation, and the swiftness with which its efficacy has been realized, have been unparalleled.

There is nothing that surpasses this. However, I fear that because the roots of transgression have been deep and heavy since beginningless kalpas, obstructive conditions are truly numerous, making it difficult to accomplish pure virtue.
For this reason, the Chan Master Ciyun of the Song dynasty, relying on the teachings of Tiantai and examining various sutras throughout his life, composed this method of repentance.
It takes the purification of the mind as its essence, the three contemplations as its core principle, and the eradication of transgressions as its function.

This is for practical application, with rebirth in the Pure Land as the goal. When the facts are complete and the principles are perfected, anyone who cultivates this practice should first give rise to three kinds of mind:
first, the straightforward mind; second, the profound mind; and third, the vast mind. Once these three minds are possessed, one may then cultivate according to them.
Thus, not only will the mountain of transgressions be leveled and dark karma extinguished, but one shall surely emerge from the site of enlightenment before long.
Thus, one may personally behold the Buddha’s light and receive his prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). This is to sit upon a precious golden lotus throne within this Sahā world.
Here at Haeinsa on Mount Jirong, the Venerable Eul-hwa has gathered various pure companions to practice this Dharma together.
For the sake of the four debts of gratitude and all beings in the three realms of existence, he spreads the causes for the Pure Land and creates the conditions for rebirth there. Do not...
It is said that the merit of conditioned phenomena will inevitably perish over time; yet one shall behold the seed of the Vajra, which never decays.

If each person can give rise to the three minds and together cultivate the two kinds of giving, then the lotuses in the Golden Pond will flourish day by day, and the wondrous fruit of Bodhi will not be far off. This is respectfully inscribed.
A Memorial for the Reconstruction of Yung-ch’uan Chan Monastery at Kuo-shan:
In the past, during the era of the Five Dynasties, upon the peak of Elephant Bone Mountain, the dark waves surged like the sea; therein, a single branch first emerged.

He who was titled "The Holy Arrow" (Seongjeonja) was none other than National Preceptor (Guk-sa) Heungseong. At the request of the King of Min, the National Preceptor resided at Yongchun Temple on Mount Gu.
There he propagated the "Three Balls" teaching, gathering fifteen hundred disciples clad in coarse wool. The style of Chan meditation spread widely throughout the realm.
Subsequently, those who maintained the lineage through the "linked lamps" numbered more than seventy generations; it can truly be said that few have ever equaled him.
It was abandoned. Although the Zen tradition did not flourish during the Ming dynasty, the light of the Buddha and the sound of the scriptures continued without ceasing.
By the Jiajing era, however, due to a failure to maintain virtue, the temple was destroyed by fire. It remained overgrown with lush grass for nearly seventy years.
During the Wanli era, the local scholar-officials Chen Gong Yiyuan and Cao Gong Xuequan first initiated the movement to restore it.
Before his work was half-finished, his strength was already exhausted, for those entrusted with the task were not the right people.
In the Xinsi year of the Chongzhen era, the hall was again destroyed by a storm from the sea; it stood precariously, on the verge of collapse. Just then, I returned from Zhedong.

The local dignitaries of the various districts commissioned me to oversee this task. Seeing that the current circumstances were untenable, I instead planned a reconstruction. This was in the tenth month of winter in the year Guiwei.
Before long, the world fell into the calamity of the "nine" (a period of great misfortune). The difficulty of the situation was indeed hundreds of thousands of times greater than before;
yet, fortunately protected by the silent guardianship of the dragons and heavens, we were able to gradually carry out the construction amidst great chaos. Seven winters passed.
It is the height of summer, yet the work is not yet finished. This year, the hostilities have only just been settled, yet you still dispatch monks to beg for alms.
This is because the Buddha resides within the human heart; he certainly does not exist or cease to exist based on whether the times are peaceful or chaotic.

Furthermore, since the Buddha’s vows are boundless, how could they ever be interrupted by the ease or difficulty of circumstances? I only hope that all patrons will each relinquish what is insubstantial.

With this wealth, we shall together remedy long-standing deficiencies. Although the undertaking may appear to fall within the realm of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it will ultimately become the cause for supreme fruition.
Although the Way reaches its ultimate in Bodhi, it does not abandon the merit of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). This is respectfully recorded.
A Memorial for the Great Memorial Assembly of the Mid-Autumn Festival at Mount Gu:

Alas, human affairs are manifold and the mandate of Heaven is not constant. Heaven and Earth stand at the juncture of decline and prosperity; the people and all things face a time of upheaval and transformation.
As the calamity of war has arisen, let it be that blood dyes the green mountains; as the disaster of the whale-waves breaks forth, how can we bear to witness...?

Bodies sink into the Black Sea; how much more so when pestilence follows in succession? Every day one hears the sounds of wailing and weeping; as famine arrives repeatedly, it is difficult to avoid the corpses in ditches and ravines.
The common people have no means of sustaining themselves, and the registers of the underworld abound with the grievances of those who died unjustly.
One can rely only upon the excellent wisdom of our Buddha to alleviate the bitter suffering of these people. Maudgalyāyana’s offering to his mother took place on the Zhongyuan Festival.
The period of almsgiving coincides with the *pravāraṇā* ceremony of the Saṃgha; it is truly a day on which all Buddhas rejoice.

The debt of gratitude toward one’s parents can surely be repaid, and the lingering spirits may likewise be transcended together. The Sūtras expound the Ten Mysteries, through which the wondrous gate of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching may be entered.

The ten-volume *Sūtra of Repentance* remains as the bequeathed teaching of Emperor Wu of Liang. By establishing the *Ullambana* offering at midday, the holy and the mundane are universally provided for. May [this merit] be bestowed...

As the day draws to a close, both spirits and ghosts alike return to their source; this is the compassionate vessel of the Great Sage, which likewise increases the profound blessings of those at the lowest level of existence.
Who among us does not aspire to Buddhahood? Let us all harbor the thought of universal salvation. Who among us has no kin? Let us all maintain the remembrance of honoring our ancestors.
I only pray that you will set aside worldly wealth and properly perfect this Bodhicitta; do not decline to take up the task.
When the critical phrase (*huatou*) arises, you may each break into a smile.
Regarding the Memorial for the Repair of Longle Longquan Temple:
Longle is a preeminent district of literary excellence, possessing the Shajing Monastery; and within Shajing, there is furthermore the Longquan Temple.
This is a preeminent site for the patriarchs of Chan. The monastery was founded during the mid-Tang dynasty; it was only during the Xiantong era that it was first granted its current name.

The Great Wisdom Chan Master Baizhang truly shaved his head and received his monastic training here. From the Tang through the Song dynasties, its halls and pavilions were towering and its monks—those "dragons and elephants"—trode upon its grounds;
it was renowned as a magnificent and flourishing monastery. Upon entering the Yuan dynasty, however, the study of Chan declined.
Day by day it fell into ruin, until during the Tiānshùn era of the Míng dynasty, it was completely transformed into a śītavana (cemetery).
This took one hundred and thirty years. During the Wànlì period, the former Prefect Cáo Yù and the Vice Commissioner Yè Shímǐn first proposed its restoration.
They appointed the monk Dàzhèng to oversee the project, and his disciple Chángxīng assisted him. Thus, it was restored.
The thorny forests have been transformed into a land of jewels, and the Northern Máng Hills have been converted into a pure realm.

Thus, those from the four quarters who come to examine past traces and pay tribute to former sages no longer harbor the lamentations of "the millet growing tall. Yet, as the sun and moon hasten on, more than fifty years have already passed;
it has frequently endured the ravages of wind and rain, and there is a chilling fear that the structure may suffer the ruin of its main beams. Indeed...
The fortunes of the world change in succession, and material resources gradually diminish; it is inherently impossible for anything to remain constant without eventually decaying.
However, to rectify deficiencies and remedy decay so as to bequeath these works to posterity, the merit lies with man.
If we neglect repairs now, where will the former achievements be placed, and what will future generations have to rely upon? How, then, can this project be delayed? This—
This is the time to rectify all acts of giving; it is the moment when one must urgently extend a helping hand. Past karmic conditions persist, yet the opportune moment will not recur.
Within the light of the white tuft of hair between the brows, it is precisely right to open the armory; from within the purple silk curtain, I invite you to scatter pearls.
Although families differ in their wealth or poverty and things vary in their value or weight, the single thought of wishing to do good is truly without distinction.
All these, without exception, flow forth from the mind of Bodhi. All myriad virtues converge therein, and all lead to the attainment of Buddhahood.
It is just as the great rivers, streams, brooks, and even the tiniest springs all flow toward the vast ocean and are entirely transformed into salt water;

how then could there be any distinction to be made between small and large, or difference and sameness? Some might say that at the time when Heaven first brought forth the world from its chaotic obscurity, the people were born...
Saving lives from death is the most urgent matter; what leisure is there to attend to such non-urgent affairs? I say:

the cycles of the world have their periods of decline and prosperity, but the Buddha-nature neither exists nor perishes. The Buddhas abide within the thoughts and minds of sentient beings, daily turning the unsurpassed Dharma discourse without interruption;
how could this ever be obstructed by order or chaos? It depends solely on whether the wise can remain free from delusion.
The events of today are spoken for those who possess wisdom; they are not spoken for those who lack wisdom. They are spoken for those who possess Buddha-nature;
they are not spoken for those who lack Buddha-nature. Why then should I weary myself with further words? I respectfully submit this brief exposition.
The Dharma-abiding Bhikṣu [Name],

incumbent of Yongquan Chan Monastery at Mount Gu, respectfully selects the first day of the third month this year to personally lead the assembly of monks in chanting twenty-four recitations of the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra for the Protection of the State*, praying for the pacification of the mists of war.

Regarding the preservation of the state’s destiny: I humbly submit that our situation now dwells in the abyss; who can provide the aid to emerge from this peril? Calamity has reached the stage of solid ice;
how can the power of returning spring be obtained? Looking up to the Great Awakened One and bowing down to receive His vast compassion, I reflect deeply:

I, [Name], was born into the dusty world and have taken refuge in the Gate of Emptiness. Eating wood and wearing grass, even a drop of water is entirely moistened by the Sage’s grace. Dwelling among crags and caves...

Every inch of land is sheltered by the imperial grace; yet though one might sacrifice head and limb, it would be difficult to repay this debt, and though one might offer a mere drop of water or a speck of dust, there is no way to express gratitude.

What a tragedy! That in the midst of the sun’s course, we have suddenly encountered the calamity of an eclipse. Famine has struck repeatedly, leaving the old and the young to perish in the ditches and ravines.
War has broken out many times, driving half the scholars and farmers into the rebellious waters. The waves of the great fish have not yet subsided upon the seas.
To the south, iron horses prance with arrogance beyond the northern frontier; the Central Plains are in turmoil. Battle clouds dye the blood of combat yellow.
The entire state of Chu has sunk beneath the waters; the plains grass turns white like bleached bones. Now that the Passes of Qin have fallen, soldiers cast down their blades and flee like rats.

The peril facing the Jin state has surpassed all bounds; officials receive the imperial mandates and the rebels submit like grass before the wind. Yet the harm threatens the ancestral altars and the very foundations of the state, and the situation is bound to press upon the Divine Capital.
Recently, as communications between the north and south have been severed, the anxiety of those high and low has become particularly acute.

As the clergy are weak, we can only harbor the sincerity of one offering his back to the sun for warmth; yet, as the virtue of the Buddha may be relied upon, we respectfully proclaim the rites for protecting the nation. We humbly pray: [The remainder of the prayer follows.]

The Golden Wheel shall eternally stabilize the realm; the Tortoise-Pillar shall forever remain secure. Blades and arrows shall suddenly vanish, and the groans from the four borders shall quickly cease.

Enemy troops shall retreat far away, and the exhaustion of the myriad people shall be entirely relieved. The sun and moon shall alternate in their brilliance, perpetually casting their light beyond all boundaries.
Heaven and Earth interact in perfect harmony, together brewing the auspiciousness of Great Peace. Throughout the land, the records of the year abound with prosperity;
across all under heaven, the signs of Great Tranquility hang manifest. I, [Name], am overcome by the utmost intensity of my fervent prayers and entreaties.
Liturgical Petition for the Memorial Services for the Ascension of Emperor Chongzhen:

It is with this that we submit: The sky of Yao has long been in motion, and the eight corners of the world have enjoyed the grace of his protection and nourishment. Yet the sun of Shun has suddenly set, and the four seas have lost their sovereign of reliance and trust.
We contemplate the rites for repaying the state, and thus briefly present our sincerity through these sacrificial offerings. We humbly consider that [the deceased], the Fourth...
Relying on this livelihood, these six matters accompany me. Amidst the dense mountains and deep forests, I am content to be a son of the Śākya;
under the vast heavens and broad earth, I am permitted to be a subject of this sagely age. Even the stubborn metal that leaps from the furnace is but the forging of Heaven and Earth;
even the ordinary tree of no utility—who has not been brought to completion by the dew and rain? Unable yet to sing of the Emperor’s power, I bathe in the Imperial benevolence and reflect upon it.
I reply: Though I lack the strength of arms and legs to serve my sovereign with loyalty, I still maintain the diligence to offer prayers for you morning and evening.

How could it be that calamity arose from the green forests, daring to brandish halberds and assault the palace gates; or that a rebellion sprang up within the inner chambers, where one would bear to sell out the nation and open the imperial passes?
Alarmed by the ascent of Xuanyuan, I look up at his dragon chariot in vain, unable to reach it; grieving for the passing of Fuxun, I wish to climb after him—[but am unable].

The celestial guards stand motionless; ghosts wail and spirits cry out. Solitary indignation ascends to disturb the white sun; heaven collapses and earth cracks as deep anguish penetrates directly to the crimson heart.
In vain one harbors the sorrowful sincerity of a blade of grass, unable to respond to the great transformation of the three springs.
Thus, following the legacy of the ancient sovereigns, I specifically proffer the reverence of the tiger-kowtow, and repeatedly invoke the sublime names of the Sugata.
Exhausting my sincerity in cries of "Long live the Emperor," I uphold the secret seals of Yoga. May the rain of Dharma-treasures fall from the void, manifesting the wondrous radiance of *Hrīḥ*;
may the iron city beneath the earth be shattered. By cultivating these minute merits, even as small as a pinch of grain, I look up to repay the vast grace of the Great Chaos.
I humbly pray that the Mandate of Heaven may flourish ever more, that Imperial benevolence may continue to spread, and that Divine majesty may operate far and wide, bringing about a second creation.

Though the mountains and rivers have been ravaged, Your Majesty’s sagely virtue flourishes ever more; You once again raise high the sun and moon of great brilliance, turning back the tide of calamity and elevating all living beings to the realm of benevolence and longevity.
Having utterly extinguished the demonic miasma, You have turned the great cycle of creation toward a domain of purity and tranquility.
I, [Your Servant], am overcome with the utmost intensity of fervent supplication.

**Petition for the Ritual Confession on the Occasion of Emperor Chongzhen’s Ascension to the Afterlife** *Humbly considering:* The course of Heaven has been fraught with many hardships, coinciding precisely with this time of profound shock; yet the Emperor’s virtue is impossible to forget, deepening our filial longing all the more.

Though separated by the realms of the unseen and the seen, our single heart remains unchanged; though spanning from antiquity to the present, the Great Principle shall never be worn away. We contemplate how to repay [His Majesty].

As for the Way of Virtue, there is no fixed origin; we merely set forth our sincerity to offer this prayer. We, your subjects [Name] and others, with utmost humility and trepidation, prostrate ourselves and address Your Majesty:

We humbly reflect that as the destiny of the *zhengyuan* (the True Origin) undergoes transformation, the configurations of antiquity and the present are never constant. Yet, as Heaven’s bounty and its distinctions manifest, the designations of superior and subordinate have long been established.
Within the realm, the Three Great Ones are foremost in veneration; how could we dare forget the heart of reverent cultivation? This is especially true regarding the Buddhist scriptures...
I revere the four debts of gratitude and harbor a profound sense of duty to repay their virtue. Even the most minute insects and crawling creatures cannot turn their backs on transformation;

the grass by the mountain stream and the flowers upon the crags are all moistened by the gentle breeze and sweet rain. Throughout the heavens all are granted amnesty; wherever one goes, one returns to benevolence.
This is because we humbly encounter Your Majesty, the Emperor: divinely gifted with sagacity and naturally endowed with heroic prowess, you regard the people as if they were wounded.
He emulated the supreme virtue of King Wen of Zhou by regulating his own conduct with frugality; he shared the grand plan of Yu of Xia.

Yet, alas, as the fortunes of the state were declining, celestial calamities followed one after another. Amidst hundreds of thousands of changes and difficulties, the burden of toil rested upon him alone.

For seventeen years he labored with weary effort—how could such hardship be eased for even half a day? He suffered the misfortune of the "Ninth Yang" year and endured the agony of the dragon’s excessive heat.
This brings about calamity. Disaster arises from the ponds and ditches; rebel traitors spread their mats beneath the golden net. The mechanism is as deep as that of the rats in the shrine;

the rebellious eunuchs open the gate for the sale of the nation, causing the Dragon Chariot to ascend abruptly, abandoning the myriad affairs of state without a glance, while the countenance of Heaven grows ever more remote.
We grieve for the nine lands that have no refuge. We, [your servants], are lowly ones clad in the robes of the fields, shaven-headed remnants of the common folk.

Stupid and ignorant, what do we know? Having left the secular world, we are content to be like wild deer; living our lives in poverty and hardship, we are truly like drifting tumbleweeds with no home.

Borrowing the moisture of your gracious waves, we feel ashamed that our meager virtues offer no contribution. Seeking to prolong our lives in the grassy wilds, how can we find a way to atone for our hundredfold faults? We possess only...

The rites of the Brahmans and the Zhushis have long exhausted the veneration of the monastic community. Above, we rely upon the vast vows of the Buddha and the Devas; below, we gather the refined sincerity of the Sangha’s conduct.
For seven days, with diligent effort, we have performed the Repentance Rite of Emperor Liang; at midnight, in secret, we have practiced the Yoga of the Ancient Buddhas.

By means of these roots of goodness, we respectfully pray that the Imperial Majesty may be further adorned. We humbly beseech that Your Majesty’s sagely virtue may flourish daily, and that celestial blessings may abound.

Prosperity shall increase further. May your spirit roam the Golden Gate, and may you once again cause the Buddha-Sun to shine upon the various heavens. May you nurture virtue upon the Lotus Terrace, widely proclaiming imperial benevolence throughout the nine realms.
We pray once more that you will not withhold the light of your compassionate illumination, and that you will continue to bestow the auspiciousness of averting misfortune and calamity.

May you sweep away all malevolent spirits and demons, restoring the clarity and tranquility of the universe. May you silently consolidate the imperial destiny, so that we may all rejoice in the eternal covenant of the rivers and mountains.
Your servants are overcome with the utmost urgency and trepidation as they gaze upon Heaven and look up to the Sage. We respectfully submit this memorial to inform Your Majesty.
A Memorial Submitted by Sun Daotai of Jianzhou Requesting Prayer for Rain.
This memorial is submitted to pray for the descent of copious rain to alleviate the distress of the people. Since the onset of summer this year, there has been a prolonged drought.

Although the local Governor-General, Mr. Sun, led his various subordinate officials to offer prayers at all the various shrines without success, he subsequently dispatched an official bearing incense into the mountains to command me to act as his representative in making the plea.
I have assembled the entire assembly of the mountain monastery to recite the Great Compassion Mantra.

Incantation. Following the opening of the altar, I respectfully submit this "Chapter of Exposing the Heart" for Your Majesty’s perusal. I humbly observe that a state takes its people as its foundation; thus, the policy of nurturing and sustaining them must be diligent.
The people take food as their heaven; thus, the labor of sowing and reaping must not be neglected.

This labor necessarily relies upon the irrigation of rain and dew; how could it tolerate the withering heat of the drought-demon? Yet, at this time when the Fire God Zhurong governs the season, there is absolutely no sign of the god of rain, Zuan.
On the day Xu manifested his spiritual efficacy, the clouds were dense and thick, yet the wind caused them to disperse; the sun was bright and radiant, yet the rain could not arrive.

Already lamenting its dryness, it was as if one had encountered the heat of sitting within a steaming cauldron. Lacking the rain to moisten it, who can console the longing thoughts of gazing at the clouds?
The grain stalks, once lush and flourishing, now gradually wither into the yellow fields of Bin; those millet plants, once standing tall, are about to wither away in Zhou.
Originally white, the planted rice has turned into painted cakes; how can parched sand satisfy hunger? Thus, we call upon the Buddha, the King of Awakening, to proclaim the secret scriptures.
Through the wondrous response of Great Compassion, he will surely be able to transform those celestial calamities;

through his inconceivable divine power, he may deliver the people from their distress. We humbly pray that he will suddenly rouse the hibernating dragons and send forth the distant thunder and lightning.
Majestic! Massing clouds arise, shrouding the fierce heat of the sun; copious rain falls, moistening the fertile fields cracked by drought.

Having bestowed such abundant benevolence, auspicious signs of prosperity abound; ultimately, the benefits of bountiful harvests shall be reaped, and the year shall be recorded as one of great abundance.
I, [Name], overcome with the utmost fervent and earnest prayers, respectfully submit this memorial.

On the occasion of my birthday, I respectfully prepare this memorial service for my parents by reciting Buddhist scriptures to repay the kindness of my kin. This year, having reached the age of seventy, the nineteenth day of the first month of autumn marks the anniversary of my mother’s birth.
Accordingly, on the first day of the month, I commenced the recitation of the *Vaipulya Buddha-vaipulya Sūtra*.
The twenty-four sections of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra and the twenty-four sections of the Compassionate Repentance Method of Emperor Liang were recited in succession.
When the five-day period was completed, on that very night, a single altar of Yoga-style ritual food was prepared, and an offering was made to the Buddha for the dedication of merit.
I respectfully recommend that my late father, Cai Yunting, and my late mothers, Lady Zhang and Lady Fan, each transcend the sea of suffering and together realize the state of non-arising.
I humbly submit that all things are formed from the essence of vital energy (*jingqi*), which necessarily relies upon the process of procreation and birth to achieve completion.

As for receiving a body through the fullness of its form, who is not a product of the illusory union of Yin and Yang? The kindness of one’s parents is truly equal to the Three Greats; it is vast and immeasurable. Indeed, the way of filial piety stands foremost.

The Five Relationships are indeed the ultimate virtue; the supreme fruits of the Buddhist gate are all accumulated and perfected through them. Confucius’s practice of benevolence takes these as its primary task to establish its foundation.
Thus, they are what both those in monastic robes and those in white lay dress must equally follow, and what those who aspire to the state of a Sage or a Worthier One must collectively strive for.
As for this ignorant and lowly person, merely possessing an ordinary body, I am ashamed to be a discarded piece of timber in a desolate valley, yet I am honored...

Entrusted with the grave responsibility of this Dharma-gate, I followed the Confucian teachings in my youth, yet failed to reach the method for becoming a sage. It was only in my later years that I returned to the Buddha-vehicle, yet I have long remained ignorant of the essential meaning of illuminating the mind.
As the sense-faculties and their objects arise in mutual interaction, I am stuck in delusion and find it difficult to accord with the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*).

Ensnared by the entanglement of afflictions and karma, I cling to appearances, thereby ever-increasing my outflows (*āsrava*). Thus, I have wasted the endowment of this physical form and betrayed the grace of its molding.
My constant reflections on these words grow ever more poignant as time passes; my filial impiety deepens in direct proportion to the years that have gone by.

Now, upon this day when the bow was first suspended [at my birth], I shall undertake this autumnal journey of departure from the mundane. With reverent devotion, I shall uphold the sacred scriptures and diligently circulate their perfect exegesis.
Through the six aspects and ten mysteries, I shall reveal the heart-seal of Vairocana; through the seven locations and nine assemblies, I shall expound the Dharma-realm.

In the True Sect, it is held that sin arises from the mind; thus, one should labor with single-minded diligence in the five repentances. Since food is provided through the distribution of the Dharma, one should proceed with reverent care in the equal practice of the three types of giving (*dāna*).
By cultivating these minute causes of even a fraction of goodness, one may adorn the Land of Bliss for one’s three ancestors. I humbly pray:

The light of the *ūrṇā* shines uniquely; the golden arm extends compassion. Standing firm, it crushes the mountain of transgressions. Within the *puṇḍarīka* flower, a wondrous essence is nurtured; instantly, the obstacles of delusion are dissolved.
Within the *kinnara* kalaviṅka’s voice, one realizes non-arising. Only then can the heart of even a blade of grass be exhausted, and the debt of unfathomable virtue be repaid.
We further pray that all sentient beings may be liberated from the wheel of suffering, and that our kinsmen may become pure companions—whether as monastics or laypeople.

Together we shall ascend the wondrous gate of Prajñā, following one another step by step; together we shall journey to the other shore of Nirvāṇa, so that the initial vow of studying the Buddha may be fulfilled and the fundamental aspiration to benefit living beings may be fully realized. Respectfully drafted.

The Extensive Record of Master Yongjue, Volume Eighteen.

Epitaph for the Great Master Mingzhiji Wengu (with Preface) When the great sages and worthies of antiquity and the present age arise in the world,
although their paths of concealment and manifestation differ, and their methods of withdrawal and engagement vary, they remain one in essence.

There is nothing that does not serve as a model for the correct standard to prevent the flow of excess; it is merely to cause sentient beings to return to the fundamental ground of original enlightenment.

Since entering the Ming dynasty, the patriarchal seat has been desolate, as rare as stars at dawn. Furthermore, wild wisdom has vied with one another in its display until its source has become utterly corrupted.
In this situation, were there not someone to prevent the waves of transgression and to turn back the surging tide?
What of these sentient beings? I heard of Great Master Wengu in Wulin; I have now met this man. According to his biography:
the Great Master’s name was Guangyin, his courtesy name was Wengu, and Zhangshi was his pen-name. He was the son of the virtuous man Li Jiashan. His surname was Zhou;
his father, Shan, possessed the character of a recluse. His mother was Lady Zhao. She dreamed of the deity Xuwushen, who, bearing a sword, led forth various armored [soldiers].
The scholar protected his gate. Upon awakening, he became a teacher. During his childhood, he constantly saw a stupa suspended in mid-air at the corner of his left eye.
As he grew older, he accompanied his father into the town; passing by Dàshèng Temple, his father called out for him to look at the stupa.
The Master said, "I have constantly seen this before my eyes, but I did not know its name and therefore did not tell anyone. Since then, I have not seen it again.
At seven years of age, he followed a tutor to study elementary texts and was immediately able to master their meaning. His father ordered him to practice Confucian studies, but he was unwilling;
he would often sit upright with his eyes closed, reciting secret gāthās. When he reached the age of thirteen, his father recognized his resolve.
He was then sent to Kaiyuan Temple in Hangzhou to serve as a crow-chaser. The temple was the site of Chan Master Konggu Long’s practice hall.
Once having received the tonsure, the master felt a profound admiration for Master Long and resolved to emulate him.

One day, seeing a diagram of the Dharma-realm on the wall, he asked his teacher, "The ten realms arise from the mind; from where does the mind arise? His teacher was unable to answer. At that time, the West...
The Venerable Yifeng of Shu was dwelling in a thatched hut on the western slope of Qingping. [Zhaozhou] went there to visit him.

Yifeng said, "If you wish to understand, you must attain wondrous enlightenment. The Master asked, "How can one attain enlightenment? Yifeng then instructed him to contemplate the character "Lù" (Dew) from Yunmen’s teaching.
Upon hearing this once, the Master immediately believed it and directly applied himself to its essential meaning, to the point of forgetting both sleep and food. Huifeng deeply esteemed him for this.

Later, while casually reading the story of the Seven Virtuous Women visiting the Śītavana cemetery, he suddenly attained realization. Huifeng then brought up the koan of the "Cinder-Boy coming to seek fire."
The Master asked, "Qingfeng spoke thus, and Fayen also spoke thus; how can there be awakening and non-awakening?
The Master said, "At first, one attempts to settle with the conscious mind, and for that reason does not awaken. Later, by directly taking responsibility, one is able to attain great awakening.
Qingfeng raised his fist, struck the desk once, and said in a stern voice, "If so, then you have attained great awakening!"

He scolded him harshly and drove him out the door. At this, the Master was so overcome that white sweat drenched his back. Thereupon, he redoubled his resolve and applied himself with all his might to his studies.
At the age of twenty-four, when Master Yifeng returned to Sichuan, the Master left his place of training to enter Yunqi Monastery and receive full ordination.
At twenty-six, he followed Dharma Master Jieshan to study the Tiantai school; within one year, he reached its profound depths, to the great admiration of Jieshan.

Whenever a lecture was held, he was invariably invited to serve as the *zhuazuo* (head of the assembly). At age twenty-seven, the local authorities of the provincial capital requested the Great Master Yunqi to open a Dharma center at Jingci Temple;
at that time, a vast multitude surrounded him like dragons and elephants treading upon one another, and they specifically appointed the Master as the *weina* (rector).
By then, his outstanding character had already begun to emerge. For several years, he listened to lectures by day and practiced seated meditation by night.

He practiced both [study and meditation] simultaneously, yet was unable to achieve single-minded purity. Upon meeting Chan Master Wuhuan, he was exhorted to apply himself to "continuous and subtle" practice.
The Master then left his lecture hall and retired to seclusion at Mount Fahu in Xixi. For four years, he lived alone;

sometimes he would go without food for several days, and at other times he would sit in meditation from morning until night. As those seeking instruction gradually increased, fearing that his own practice would be neglected, he took up his staff and departed.

He departed and went among the people to beg for alms. Soon after, he ascended Mount Shuangjing and built a thatched hut at the foot of Baiyun Peak, remaining with his shadow never leaving the mountain for six years.
While contemplating the karmic connection between Master Liang and Mazu, his doubts remained unresolved.

One day, upon seeing yellow *huangruixiang* flowers, he suddenly attained great enlightenment. He composed a verse, saying: "It is indeed empty space that preaches the sutras; the common bricks and tiles..."
Lìzhèng was just about ready to listen. Previously, he had been twisting his natural nose and mistaking a gourd for a ritual vase.

From this point on, that which had been a thorn in his side was completely released. Thereupon, he left the mountains and went to Yúnqī, where he received the Bodhisattva precepts and sought instruction morning and evening;
thus, he fully mastered the Way of Yúnqī. Upon reaching Yíyáng, he visited Master Huàn-yǒu of Lóngchí.
Daci was by the pond warming himself in the sun beneath the steps when the Master asked, "Where is the Abbot? Daci replied, "He is just not here.
The Master then performed a prostration. Daci took him by the hand and went up to the Dharma Hall. After the formal greetings were concluded, Daci said, "Yesterday, he ascended the hall."
He brought up the story of the "Tawny Slave and the White Ox. Although there were further words offered, they did not satisfy the old monk’s mind.
"How would you say it, my son? The Master replied at once: "The Buddhas of the three periods do not know its existence; the tawny slave and the white ox, however, do know it exists.

Since from the beginning delusion and awakening have never interfered with one another, how can you teach them to withdraw their hands? Chi then presented his own work, *Deshan’s Reclining on the Earth*.
Bai said, "Show this verse to the Master. He added, "For now, you compose another verse yourself. The Master then composed a verse, saying: "Is there or is there not that final word?
The father and son of Deshan are too much at odds. Born of the same lineage, yet they die on different paths; Having lived for three years, my regrets grow ever more numerous.
Dachi was greatly pleased and said to the Master, "Why do you not take up this matter and join us in chanting and composing together? The Master did not.
He said, "I am naturally convinced. Chì asked, "What more do you wish for? He replied, "When I look at Yuanwu and Dahui, I feel deeply ashamed.
Chì sighed with a sense of pity and said, "Among scholars today, none have mastered the teaching before they claim to have mastered it; how could anyone else attain such self-conviction as you?"
"I, an old monk, shall yield you a place of refuge. He lingered for several days, and as he was about to depart, Daci escorted him to the gate.
Patting the Master’s back, he said, "Old nephew, I still have my doubts about you. The Master replied, "Where do you doubt me?
Daci asked, "What is the meaning of the secret transmission? The Master said, "Today I will not turn back toward Yixing. Daci laughed heartily.
The Master donned his bamboo hat and set out on his travels. He journeyed north to Mount Wutai and eventually returned to Mount Jing. At that time, the Zen seats throughout the realm were desolate;

even in the regions of Wu and Yue, the Master’s name was unheard of. Feeling deep pity for this state of affairs, he consulted with the masters of Mount Ji to initiate a period of intensive Zen practice (chanqi) in the Avalokiteśvara Hall.
Subsequently, he established further retreats at Lianju and Yongqing, where eminent monks arrived in great numbers.
As he underwent intensive training for a set period, many experienced sudden breakthroughs that seemed to erupt from the ground. At that time, Elder Yifeng returned from Sichuan;

the Master took this opportunity to further his realization, investigate the profound mysteries, and once again discern the subtle distinctions, thereby sealing his understanding of the teachings of Linji.

Not long after, Yifeng departed, and the Master went into seclusion at Jing Mountain by Lake Dongting. The conditions there were exceptionally harsh and cold, which caused him to contract a chronic abdominal ailment. His disciples urged him to leave.
At Mount [Shan], on the day of Renzi, he was about to return to Shuangjing. Taking the route via Pingtao, he stayed overnight at the home of the host Ding Daozhe.
Ding Daozhe considered the path to Pingtao to be a vital thoroughfare for the two eyes of Shuangjing;

however, as itinerant monks had no place to lodge, he wished to erect a simple shelter of straw to serve as a reception hall and requested the Master to preside over the project. Although the Master’s own aspiration was set upon the seclusion of mountain caves, he...
His compassionate vow was profound. Hearing this, he was moved by deep sympathy and subsequently gathered forty-eight like-minded companions.
Each contributed their robes and alms bowls to construct a few thatched huts, providing a mere temporary lodging for those traveling among the clouds and waters.

It happened that the State Councilor Zhu Pinghan entered the mountains to pay respects at the sacred shrine of Master Zibo; hearing of these matters, he marveled at them deeply and proceeded to purchase land to serve as the site. Thereafter—

when words are many, the Way becomes increasingly obscured. When the Way is obscured, practice becomes increasingly deviant. Once practice has become so deviant, what more is there left to say?
Today, those who open the hall to preach the Dharma throughout the land number more than one hundred, and those who have been entrusted with the whisk and transmitted the robe exceed one thousand.

If one seeks those whose words and deeds are sincere and whose practice and principle are perfectly harmonious, such as are called "excellent knowers," [they are exceedingly rare].
As for the one known as Shí (識者), his fingers could not bend more than once; thus, I cannot help but incline my heart entirely toward the Chan Master Gúháng.
According to his biography, the Master’s name was Dàozhōu and his style name was Gúháng. He was the son of Zhèng Wǒhàn of the Zhèng clan in Jìnjīng; his mother was of the Sū clan.

Having lost his father at the age of one, the mother Sū harmonized with a bear-bristle brush and drew on reed stalks to enable him to attend an external school. By nature, the Master was exceptionally gifted.
He was fond of learning and capable in composition; among the great elders of the commandery, there were none who did not regard him as one of great capacity.
In his youth, he had married a wife, but because she was not compliant with Su [Shan], Su ordered him to divorce her. The Master did not dare disobey.

Upon Su’s passing, the Master then abandoned his household and took up residence at Chengtian Temple, where he recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* daily without ceasing. Lin Jichong, the Minister of Rites, held him in high esteem.
One day, while reading the *Recorded Sayings of Shouchang*, he reached the passage where a monk asks, "When one dies and is cremated, what is your original nature?
He became deeply perplexed by this. At that time, hearing that Boshan was flourishing in his teachings, he wished to go there to seek instruction.
The Minister Lin Jizhong then fulfilled his aspiration, escorting him to Boshan to shave his head; at that time, the Master was already thirty-eight years of age.
After shaving his head, he served as the head of the Hall of Practice (lingxing tang). He sat in the Hall of Silent Sitting (buyu tang) through the night for three months without closing his eyes.
At that time, the Imperial Censor Yu Jisheng of Jinling came to visit Master Boshan and invited the Master to Jinling.
There, the Master shut himself in retreat at Mount Wulongtan and presented him with a robe made of plain blue cloth along with a verse. The verse said: "Do you not see? Tianmu..."
A stone upon the mountain peak serves as a boat; the Great Being Gao Feng dwells at its summit. For over thirty years he has lived on necklaces and gruel;
to this day, people pass down his pure reputation. What do we disciples have in our quiet chambers? Our mouths do not open, nor do our feet move.
Naked, with nothing left but two eyebrows; empty-handed and fistless, boasting of vigor. Yet one does not see Master Lang’s Zen: using a hoe as a pillow and grass as a mat.
What likeness is there between the Buddha-dharma and worldly conditions? Upon a flat rock, he sleeps at ease throughout the day.
My disciples have heard nothing of hoes and grass; where could you seek out the flat rocks and creeping vines? Opening the window, one can only see—
The blue sky: a single path of numinous clarity, bright and vast. Do not treat this moment as ordinary. The light does not illuminate the object; the object is not the light.
Suddenly all is expansive, transparent, and unimpeded—this is the "Graduate of Mind-Emptiness. The Master took the verse and investigated it with even greater diligence.
After two years, he attained realization and said to the lay practitioner Liu Xincheng: "I have now, regarding..."

In a situation where there was nothing that could be done, he managed to catch a glimpse of its very core. He met with various scholars and officials in Jinling, who invited Boshan to open the hall at Tianjie Monastery.
While Boshan was away, the Master left the mountain pass to serve as the guest prefect; when Boshan returned, the Master re-entered the pass.
The following year, news of Boshan’s passing arrived, so the Master returned his staff to Boshan. Once the funeral rites were completed, he returned to Min. At that time, Huilong...
The assembly of monks, admiring the Master’s character, invited him to occupy the abbot’s quarters. After three years, he passed away and returned to the spring [of the underworld].
He then lived in seclusion at Dàyún (Cloud-Wearing) on Déhuà Mountain. Dàyún rises precipitously for ten thousand *zhèn*; human tracks rarely reach it. The Master sat in meditation in a single room;
moss coins covered the steps. For four years he remained thus. In the year Bǐngzǐ, when Minister Lín Zōng retired from office and returned home, he invited the Master.
The Master left the mountains and hung his staff at Chengtian Monastery in the prefecture. That winter, Zhongcheng Yu Jisheng came from Xuefeng to welcome him.
In the spring of the Dingchou year, the Master arrived there and constructed the Hall of Heavenly Kings; he also renovated various other buildings.

Because the monastic community was prone to negligence and many were obstructing the transformation through the Dharma, he took his leave. He was then invited by Wang Jingtai, the Grand Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, to the West [Capital].

He spent the winter in meditation. The following year, Grand Councilor Yu Jisheng and Magistrate Huang Yuanqing requested him to return to Huilong, where he opened the放生池 (Fangsheng Pool) and its subsidiary cloister.

Yu and Huang inscribed the account upon stone. In the winter of the Ji-mao year, Liu Chuzi Chunyuan of Xinzhou, noting that the abbotship of Boshan had long remained vacant, led the assembly to invite the Master to succeed him. In the autumn of the Xin-si year, he went there to take up his post.

Yangyi began his hermitage at the foot of Fenghuang Mountain in the year Renwu. He first gathered laborers to construct the dwelling, with the support of lay practitioners Zhang, Shen, Huang, and others who together assisted in its completion.
Previously, when the Master left the household life, he had always carried two wooden spirit tablets with him;
now that this project was undertaken, it was intended as a means to honor his ancestors. Therefore, he named it Baqin An (Hermitage for Repaying Kindness). Upon its completion, he further...
He returned to Boshan. In the winter of the Jiashen year, the Prince of Hui visited Xinzhou specifically to take refuge [in the Dharma] and was granted a set of purple robes.
In the autumn of the Yiyu year, he took leave of Boshan and entered Min; it was a time of dynastic upheaval, as warhorses galloped in all directions.
The Master then withdrew into the deep mountains, dwelling without a fixed abode. In the year Wuzi, he returned once more to Baqin, where he remained for eight years, winter and summer;
his reputation for the Way grew ever more prominent. Whether noble or humble, none failed to admire his fragrant traces.

When monastics from the four quarters came to seek instruction, the Master was like a thousand-fathom iron wall, never granting them assent or refusal; most retreated, looking back at the precipice. In the year Yiwu—
In the third month of spring, he first manifested illness; yet he still attended to his affairs as usual. On the full moon day of the eighth month, his illness became critical.

He then summoned his various patrons and entrusted them with his final instructions. Zhang Jiusheng, a scholar-official, asked: "When the single breath no longer comes, where will you establish your dwelling and find your life?
The Master said: "Precisely this is the very place to establish one's dwelling and find one's life. Zhang said: "Could it not be that you..."
"Is there still any ground for attaining power? The Master replied, "How can you mistake a servant for a lord? He then sat in the full lotus posture and passed away at the hour of You (5–7 p.m.
on the twenty-fifth day of the eighth month. Looking back, he had been born on the twelfth day of the third month in the year of Wanyili Badyou (1605) at the hour of Xu (7–9 p.m.).
He reached a worldly age of seventy-one and a monastic seniority of thirty-four. His disciples...
I collected his posthumous writings, totaling several volumes, and had them carved for circulation in the world.

On the second day of the tenth month in the year of Bingshen, his entire body was enshrined in a stupa on the southern slope of Fenghuang Mountain. His son, Jiyiran, composed a biographical account of his conduct and requested that I write the inscription for the stupa.
Because of my ties to the Dharma gate, I have been able to form a friendship with the Master; however, in truth, I am not yet qualified to do so.
Having tasted the flavor of his Dharma, how could I dare to lightly defile it?

Yet, observing the Master’s vast talent and profound learning as such, one might think he would sit upon a curved couch, discoursing on trivialities to dazzle the local people—a task for which he would surely be well-suited and find sweet.
Instead, he keeps his mouth firmly sealed and hides his depths like emptiness. How could this be the way of a petty man?
How noble! Moreover, I have heard that his natural disposition was austere and upright, and his conduct from youth had been principled and square.
His solitary character and lofty integrity were manifest throughout the world, as people have long been able to say. From this, one can understand the Master’s intention:

he perceived that in these final days of the Dharma, those who preside over the Law mostly engage in empty verbalization. Therefore, the Master sought to pull them back through personal practice rather than words. This is the Master.

Regarding this Dharma gate, he truly wishes to turn back the surging, turbulent waves that have already collapsed; his concerns are profoundly deep, and the conduct he maintains is likewise most arduous.
Therefore, I do not decline my own meager abilities and respectfully compose this inscription for him. The inscription says: To clarify the Way through words.

Do not perform what is not right conduct; it is like returning to one's native land, where one arrives only by setting foot upon the path. Alas for this decadent custom—who can serve as a clear guide?
Only Baoqin was able to truly follow [the Way], his integrity soaring to the clouds and his secluded purity naturally admirable, like a plum blooming on the snowy peaks.
The frosty sky is illuminated by the moon; how sublime is this excellent model! Let those who have preceded us take it as our pattern, and let those who study behind us revere it as their standard.

Thus, instruction by personal example serves as thunder to shatter dreams and as an oar to rescue those drowning. Now that the wise man has departed into the distance, his lofty spirit is difficult to perpetuate. This stūpa—
White clouds shall forever encircle it; here this true jade is enshrined. May it shine eternally like the sun.
Epitaph for the Stupa of Longevity (with Preface).
In the spring of the Jiashen year, the Governor of Wucheng, Chen Baian, seeing that I was aged and ill, prepared a burial site for my longevity.
At the western field of Yongchun Temple, the project was subsequently interrupted by worldly calamities and could not be completed.
It was not until the winter of the *xinmao* year that the work finally reached completion; however, my old age and illness had grown even more severe.
