I then reflected that regarding a single stone tablet within a tomb, later generations inevitably seek to secure honor through high official rank and rely upon grand compositions for ornate embellishment—this is merely to increase my own transgressions. Nevertheless, when examining ancient precedents...

Master: There are those who have described their own conduct and those who have inscribed their own epitaphs upon their stupas; these are widely transmitted in the world and are not considered improper.
Thus, I have imitated them and composed this. My name is Yuánxián, my style name Yǒngjué. I am the son of the Cài family of Jiānyáng in Jiànzhōu.

By nature, I am austere and detached, finding no pleasure in worldly clamor. Furthermore, my talents are truly dull and slow, and I am not skilled at following the currents of the times. Therefore, although—
He studied the Confucian classics and served as a local scholar (*zhusheng*). Yet, he constantly harbored the aspiration for world-transcendence.

At the age of forty, he finally abandoned his wife and children and went to Shouchang Temple in Jianchang, where he paid homage to Master Wuming and received the tonsure. Not long after, he mistakenly received the seal of mind (*xin-yin*).
Upon the master’s passing, he went to rely upon Master Boshan for three years, and subsequently returned to Mount Yin in Min, where he remained in seclusion for twelve years.

Cai had his head covered in ash and his face smeared with dirt, intending to decay together with the grasses and trees. One day, he visited Master Wengu, who earnestly exhorted him to emerge from the secular world.
Consequently, Cai was appointed as the abbot of Mount Fushan, where the master of Great Precepts (Mahāśīla) was entrusted to him;
at that time, Cai was already fifty-seven years old. Thereafter, he successively presided over Kaiyuan in Quanzhou, Zhenji in Hangzhou, and Baoshan in Jianyang.
Later, he returned once more to Mount Gu. He then reconstructed the monastic dwellings. His various writings and recorded sayings total twenty works, comprising over one hundred fascicles.
He did not conceal his shortcomings or crudities, leaving them open to the world’s critique. Alas! My life’s journey is entirely like a dream from yesterday;
with such a record of failure and deficiency, it is difficult to avoid the scrutiny of the high-sighted. As for my entry into the Way, I was the most dull-witted of all. Its...
He appeared in the world at the latest possible time; his engagement with the world was most clumsy. Furthermore, he was unable to widely gather eminent monks to expand the prestige of his school.
Compared to those of other quarters, he is like a lame turtle looking toward a soaring dragon—how could he be worth mentioning?
This year he has already reached seventy-five; before long he will transform into another thing. Therefore, he has prepared this grave in advance to await that moment.
I have also composed an inscription for him in advance. The inscription says: Whose skull is this, that has erected this stūpa? It is the son of Shouchang, the master of the Stone Drum.
Unconcerned with worldly affairs, he was of a singular and coarse nature. His aspirations were great and his words were grand; his eyes looked upon Buddhas and patriarchs with utter disdain.
Occupying the seat of Xingsheng, he reviled the present and cursed the past. Summoning spirits and driving the winds, he rebuilt this edifice. Now, casting aside his skin-sack, he is laid to rest.
Hidden in a desolate ravine, do not say he has no voice; his roar is like a tiger’s. Is he alive? Is he dead? I pray you, unravel these words.
Proclaim this to all who come: who shall succeed to my legacy?
Inscription on the Square Mirror:
Its substance is square, yet its illumination is circular. When an object arrives, it responds; I myself am void and profound.
One must strictly avoid seeking after the reflection; one must directly penetrate before the mirror.
Inscription on a Duan Inkstone Having received its form from the Duan Cave, it serves its function within the Garden of the Gods. Its color is dark purple; its virtue is moist yet firm.

It uses stillness to govern movement, and its square shape to accommodate the round. Its body holds rain and dew; its face bears clouds and mist. A single point of solid heart remains entirely unchanged, regardless of what is done.
The multitude of its channels whirls through many turns.
The inscription on the Drum Mountain bell reads:

"Perfectly round and perfectly dense; thus tranquil and thus void. It sounds only when the time is right; it responds without exceeding [the moment]. It chants with the wind and strikes against the moon."
From this region of white clouds, he did not withhold his "whale-sound" [sermon], thereby awakening those on the path of darkness.
As for that which may be relied upon today as a model, is it not surely this?
Inscription for the Bell of Kaiyuan Temple:
The foremost monastery in Min, how magnificent is Kaiyuan! This great vessel is employed to assist the workings of Heaven and Earth; it resounds with the wind and strikes against the moon.

Reaching far across the boundaries of dawn and dusk, it is empty yet inexhaustible; tranquil yet capable of resonance. Its perfect penetration embodies all virtues; the realms of the unseen and the seen receive its grace.
All people together receive its bounty; it shall endure forever through the ages.
Inscription for the Auspicious Stone (with Preface):
The elder Mr. Songgang lived on the banks of the Yexi River. He had five sons, all of whom were brilliant, talented, and outstanding.

Carrying substantial wealth, they traveled through the regions of Qi, Lu, Yan, and Zhao; consequently, the family’s prosperity increased daily. Furthermore, they were fond of righteousness and delighted in charity, doing so repeatedly.
He was honored with a commendatory plaque by the Magistrate of the District.

Having planned to expand his residence, construction first began in the *wamok* year of the Wanli era (1583) and was completed in the *wamok* year of the Tianqi era (1623). On the day of its completion, he happened to find a stone beside Byan-gi Stream;
it was over ten feet high, as rugged and imposing as a chivalrous knight, yet elegant and lustrous like a literary scholar, standing firm and upright.
It is as dignified and majestic as a nobleman standing at court; it is truly no ordinary stone.

For such an extraordinary stone to reside within the reach of common sight for ten million years, until none could obtain it, and then to be found on the very day the Great Hall was completed—this cannot but be seen as a sign emerging from the occasion of a new beginning to portend eternal prosperity.
What a source of celebration this is! Thereupon, it was moved and placed within the main gate, and a pavilion was specially constructed to face it, named "Auspicious Rock" (Ruishi).
He requested a commemorative inscription from me. The inscription reads: [The text of the inscription follows here.]

The purity of jade contained within its casing; the essence of the congealed river. Substantial yet refined, elegant yet still chaste. Possessing a nature from the Great Antiquity, appearing as an auspicious omen unto the present.
Matching it in virtue and matching it in achievement, let this serve forever as a testimony.
The Extensive Record of Master Yongjue, Volume XVIII.
The Extensive Record of Master Yongjue, Volume XIX.
Re-edited by the Dharma-heir Disciple Daopai.
Discourse in Praise of the Record of the Propagation of Buddhism in Jianzhou (Ten Chapters):
Discourse on Reaching the Root.

The Treatise says: The single dharma of *dhyāna* (meditation) pervades all vehicles; it is entirely attained through cultivation and realization, and thus falls within the realm of conceptual measurement (*kalpanā*).

Only the Dharma [of this school] directly points to the one mind, which is merely designated by the provisional name "Zen" (*dhyāna*). It is beyond what can be said of cultivation, realization, or conceptual measurement.

It is just like the crest-jewel of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), which is noble and unsurpassed, and cannot be equaled by other treasures; it is also like a consecrated prince, who, although still...
The *bāngbǎo* (infant swaddling cloth) cannot be compared to the attire of court officials. Like the Vajra King’s sword, it wields the power of both killing and giving life with total mastery;
it cannot be constrained by formal rules. Therefore, those who are monks must prioritize this above all else. Should one abandon this for other affairs, [the essence of the monastic path is lost].
Though one may practice asceticism for accumulated kalpas, to ultimately fall halfway through the path is not a skillful method.
I establish that since Mazu of the Tang dynasty first opened the gate of the sweet dew, the transmission of the lamp has continued from then on, shining brightly everywhere.
Those who entered the *Chuan Deng Lu* number more than forty; as for officials, laypeople, farmers, and village women, they too were able to partake of the flavor of the Dharma together with us.
Entering the Mirror of the School (Zongjing): How magnificent! Toward the end of the previous dynasty, the study of Chan declined and fell into dormancy.

Yet, with the late emergence of Tieguan, there still remained the spirit of the ancient venerable masters. As for our present dynasty, however, the Huilin Monastery has long been withered away and the authentic lineage has already been lost;
those who study Chan are not even a handful. Even among those who are called "good spiritual friends," they are all...
To mistake a slave for a lord, or to take a mere mouse for a precious jade—this is surely not as well as the attainment gained by those who exclusively cultivate pure karma.
Alas! The azure waters and crimson mountains remain as they were a thousand years ago; looking up and down, leaning upon the railing to offer my lament, how can I bear such desolation?
It is here that I feel a profound sense of grief.
The *Xianhua lun* states:
"In the study of the Śākya clan, the Way (*dao*) is its root and penetration (*tong*) is its branch. According to the Dharma, one ought to devote oneself to the Way;
once the Way is perfected, penetration will manifest. If one’s intention lies in seeking penetration, one will inevitably lose the Way. To lose the Way while gaining penetration—this is [the error]."

If even the practice of meditative concentration can be lost due to demonic interference, how much more so must supernatural powers (ṛddhi) be lost? Therefore, one who possesses right view would rather attain the Way without such powers;
it is not that they loathe the powers, but rather that these phenomena are not worth striving for. Furthermore, there are generally five types of methods for attaining supernatural powers:

those attained by practicing the Mahāyāna, those attained by practicing the Hīnayāna, those attained by practicing the vehicle of ordinary worldlings, and those attained by practicing non-Buddhist [teachings].
Those who attain [the Way] through the Dharma do so either by means of causes from past habituation or through the elicitation of karmic retribution;

as their scales differ—whether great or small—and their orientations vary—whether heterodox or orthodox—they cannot be treated as a uniform whole. This treatise is like striking ice at Ruiyan: it serves as a trace left behind by the ancient sages.

There is nothing that can be considered different [in their ultimate nature]. As for the rest, some have partially attained small fruits; some still remain stuck at the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*);

some fall among the ranks of ghosts; some belong to external sects; and some are even great-power bodhisattvas who employ skillful means (*upāya*) to gather and transform others. Since there are thus several kinds of distinctions, [the text continues:]
It cannot be suppressed in its entirety, nor can it be extolled in its totality. Those who remain within the mundane world are certainly unable to discern this;

yet those who have transcended the mundane should know what their primary concern ought to be. If one merely observes extraordinary traces and gives rise to delight, one will inevitably follow a deviant path from which there is no returning.
Should one not be cautious?

In the late autumn of the Patriarchal Hall, where virtue is honored, wild wisdom flourishes in competition. Those who understand the Way are many; those who practice the Way are few. Now, as for this impending illumination...
It is because one must practice them. To understand them clearly yet fail to practice is no different from not understanding them at all.

Furthermore, if one uses this as a hook to seek fame and cultivate great wealth, then even if one possesses spontaneous eloquence and preaches the Dharma like clouds, I consider such a person nothing more than a mere peddler.
Those recorded in this collection are all men of accumulated refinement and pure sincerity; although their realization may not reach that of Mañjuśrī, [they are nonetheless true practitioners].

The Patriarchs were difficult to equalize through divine transformations; yet by striking the ice [to seek the Way] and practicing according to the teachings, their every movement did not exceed the prescribed measure.
Having reached the ultimate refinement, they finally returned to the fruit of sainthood. How, then, could one take the boastful claims of wild wisdom as authoritative?

As for those practitioners who cultivate in obscurity—whether because their Way is so great that it is rarely understood, or because their virtue is perfected yet they encounter adversity—their forms remain hidden and their voices silenced, such that no one can trace them through outward appearances. Thus...
This record cannot exhaustively cover them all. The *Fujiao lun* (Treatise on Assisting the Teachings) states:

"The teachings of Confucianism and Buddhism are divided, their gateways being vastly distinct. When great Confucian scholars harmonize these through the principle of the spirit (*shenli*), then the thousand differences..."
Suddenly forgotten. When the petty scholar confines himself to the limitations of conceptual measurement, even a single speck of dust becomes an obstruction.
This is why the great scholar distinguishes [the truth] such that it vanishes of its own accord without effort, while the petty scholar desires to cease his slander yet is unable to do so.

Since the Six Dynasties, there have been many who slandered the Buddha; all did so by conjecturing through their own private biases, thereby creating for themselves the opposition of water and fire. As for me—

The Buddha’s domain still lies ten thousand *li* away. Even taking Māng-rì (Mencius) alone as an example, though he resolutely took charge of the transmission of the Way (*dào-tǒng*), his various essays such as "On the Origin of the Way" are merely the rambling words of one who is dazed and intoxicated in a dream.

As for the various Confucian scholars of the Sòng dynasty, they were indeed not Mencius’s equal; yet regarding the Buddhist scriptures, they all approached them with superficiality and haste, unable to fathom their profound meaning. Therefore...
They are constrained by intellectual understanding and do not believe that there exists a realm beyond comprehension;

they are bound by the relations of human society and do not know that there are matters transcending such relations. This is why various divergent doctrines proliferate. Now, if we record the views of the various Confucian scholars, it is not so.
They all studied extensively under various masters and were deeply immersed in the joy of Chan meditation; they never remained confined to their original positions.

Now, these gentlemen were all men of extraordinary talent born of Heaven, with spirits and intellects as expansive as the earth, yet in the end they could not bring themselves to slander the Buddha. This makes it clear that the Buddha is truly not to be slandered.
As for those of shallow learning and immature speech, who have no insight whatsoever yet falsely cite former sages as a pretext to give rise to reckless and perverse views...
How can this deliberation be so utterly lacking in reflection? Alas!

As a junior in the study of Chan, I have harbored presumptuous thoughts regarding the lofty heights [of our tradition], rashly claiming that the precepts are insufficient to uphold and that the Tripitaka is unnecessary to peruse.
Arrogant and self-indulgent, they believe themselves to be outside the three realms, unaware that they have already fallen into the midst of the niraya hells.
Now, observing Master Shi, his discipline of the precepts was refined and strict; his movements never exceeded the proper bounds. In his later years, he read the Tripitaka three times;
considering reading while seated to be disrespectful, he instead recited it standing and perused it while walking. Alas! He is truly a beacon for ten thousand generations.
Xuedou left because he could not bear his habitual tendencies; from this point on, Xuedou was truly unable to overcome his ingrained habits.
As for Huanglong Nan, he relied [on him] for the longest time, which can be called "excelling at relying on others."
Biographical Eulogy for Chan Master Nichuan Zhishun of Tianbao:

When Nichuan first resided at Tianbao, he departed after only a short time. He subsequently stayed at Guiyuan, Dongchan, and Xuefeng, yet in each case he acted in the same manner, dispersing his wealth and retiring from his position while his influence was still at its peak. Were it not for a great man, could such a thing have been done?
Ah! Among those of antiquity who were called "Great Men of Knowledge," there was one who, within a single courtyard, felt such lingering attachment that he could not sever his ties.
Judging from this, Nichiren is truly a teacher for all eternity. It is a pity, however, that his recorded sayings (*goroku*) have not been transmitted to the present day. How regrettable!
The "Biographical Praise for the Method of Self-Immolation by the Daoist Jin" states that the method of self-immolation is permitted in the Mahāyāna but prohibited in the Hīnayāna.

The underlying intention is that in the Mahāyāna, because the weight of compassionate vows is profound and the power of endurance is already sufficient, such acts may be permitted. Those who practice it do so either to make offerings to the Great Dharma or...
If one burns [the body] to protect the Great Dharma, or burns it for the sake of expounding the Great Dharma, the benefit is immense.

In the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), however, the mind is weighted toward self-interest and the aversion to suffering is profound; thus, there is a pressing desire to burn [the body]. Since the benefit is already meager, how much more so when the power of patience (*kṣānti-bala*) is not yet sufficient?
To lose right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) in the face of such peril—how could its harm be overestimated? Furthermore, in this world, there are those who act as Māras...
As for those who have authored [this work], some are motivated by a craving for posthumous fame, while others act out of provocation.
Since these are neither states of right mindfulness, they will inevitably bring about evil retributions; how could one not prohibit them?

In this volume, it is recorded that after Duke Ai’s transformation, several *he* of *śarīra* were obtained, and a monk’s sandal was cast down from the sky by the Daoist Jin. That these items are indeed combustible is beyond doubt.
However, I fear that those who lack understanding might recklessly imitate him; as for this, I do not see it as being appropriate.
Yang Wengong Yi’s biographical eulogy states that Dadian’s insight was transcendent and vast, no less than that of Ciming; moreover, at the moment of his passing, he was carefree and self-possessed.
His course was clear and resolute; he was truly a man of immeasurable stature. The Shi family chronicler noted that his nature was upright and he esteemed integrity and righteousness.
When Emperor Zhenzong wished to establish Lady De as Empress and commanded Gong to draft the imperial edict, he sent Ding Wei to convey the decree, but Gong did not comply.
Ding Wei said, "Strive to do so; you need not worry about not attaining wealth or honor. Gong replied, "If such were wealth and honor, it would not be what I desire.
Gong’s adherence to his principles was such as this; how could one say that he studied Chan and yet found no efficacy?

Those who claim that upon hearing these words he became terrified and lost his composure, using this to mock Gong’s practice of Chan, have likewise failed to examine the matter closely. How could there be...
At the critical juncture of birth and death, his mastery was such as this; yet, amidst ordinary matters of profit and loss, how could he have been moved by such concerns?

This must surely be the fabrication of slanderous accusations by those who were weak and petty at the time, through which the reports became distorted and gave rise to the reproach of "barking at mere sounds."
The Eulogy on the Biography of Hu Wending (An Guo):
Wending studied vigorously and practiced with diligence; his resolve was fixed upon the *Chunqiu*, and his concern for the state and love for the sovereign grew ever more profound as time passed.
Regarding Chan Buddhism, he investigated it deeply and attained its innermost realization. If this is so, how could Chan be detrimental to loyalty and filial piety? As for those in the world who—
Those who reach [this conclusion] often claim that the study of Chan is detrimental to loyalty and filial piety; yet they have clearly failed to investigate the matter. Formerly, Mr.
You Dingfu of the Song dynasty wrote in a letter to Lü Benzhong: "Regarding what is taught in the Buddhist scriptures, even the Confucian scholars of the world have not investigated them deeply."
Senior scholars have often never read Buddhist scriptures; therefore, they disparage them so vehemently.
Little do they realize that those points they seek to refute are precisely what the Buddha himself considered incorrect. Dingfu may truly be said to be one who understands the essence of words.
In the Eulogy for Master Zhu Xi’s Biography, it is said that regarding the study of Buddhism, Master Zhu sometimes praised it and sometimes censured it, employing both exaltation and suppression.

His exaltation was intended to cleanse the vulgarities of the secular world, while his suppression was intended to establish the principles of human relations. Indeed, he did so through his own person.

As he was the preeminent leader of the school of the Way, his words of instruction to others could not help but be thus. In his later years, the Master composed a poem titled "Reciting Sutras While Dwelling in Seclusion," which says:
Sitting upright and alone with nothing to do, I casually open the books of the Śākya Sage. For a moment I rest from the tethers of worldly burdens, Transcending them, I am one with the Way.
The gate is closed, the bamboo grove dense; Birds sing after the mountain rain has ceased. To understand this is— [Note: The original text fragment ends abruptly.]
For the sake of the Dharma, body and mind are equally tranquil and serene. To contemplate this, one realizes that those who have gained an understanding of the sutras do so not superficially;
it is not merely a matter of personal aspiration alone.
Discourse on the Gazetteer of Gushan Temple (Six Chapters):
Discourse on the Record of Outstanding Sites.

The discourse states: Formerly, Wang Jingmei remarked that this mountain is renowned for its steepness and excels as a place for ascending and gazing afar; beyond the Lingyuan [Spring], it is unsurpassed.
It is marvelous beyond compare; yet, critics still lament that its "Phoenix Pond" (Fengchi) has not been reached, for its "White Cloud Cave" (Baiyundong) remains unopened.
Indeed, among the various wonders of this mountain, the most exquisite beauty is called Lingyuan; the most transcendent marvel is called Fengchi;

and the most wondrous and perilous site is called the Three Gates of White Cloud. As for ascending to high vantage points to gaze into the distance, one may simultaneously capture the extraordinary splendors of both land and sea.

As for that which stands as the singular excellence of the Eight Min regions, none surpasses Lishu Peak. Thus, from antiquity to the present, renowned sages have traveled there with staff and sandals;
their sighs and praises were never enough, leading them to express themselves through song and verse until their footprints overlapped one another.
Nevertheless, I believe those who truly excel at such travel are indeed rare. For in an instant it is vast and open, in an instant it is dark and secluded, and in an instant...
While one might cast aside both body and world, it is difficult to escape the dust of mundane existence in an instant; how can this truly be called "wandering"?
How can this truly be called "wandering"? Confucius said, "Ascending the Eastern Mountain, one makes Lu seem small; ascending Mount Tai, one makes the whole world seem small.
This, indeed, must be understood through a distinct argument.

The Discourse on the Record of Construction and Destruction states: "The rise and fall of Yongquan Temple is something even a passerby can speak of; yet, does one truly understand the Way of the *I Ching*? The *I Ching* says:
'Above the ridgepole, below the eaves, to await wind and rain,' which takes its model from the hexagram *Dazhuang*. It takes [the significance] of its four yang lines..."
This refers to being at the height of prosperity, yet it also implies that this prosperity has not reached its ultimate limit. Furthermore, it says:
"The ridgepole is high and prominent—auspicious," because the strength is balanced by the central position. "The ridgepole sags—inauspicious," because the strength has lost its central balance.

Is this not because one does not desire the palace or residence to be excessively grand, and moreover, requires the virtue of a strong center to sustain it? Otherwise, there will be the misfortune of the ridgepole sagging.
And that was all. In the past, when Yongquan Temple was at its height, its soaring eaves and lofty halls already represented the ultimate grandeur of the human world;
yet it still relied on those of virtue residing therein, so that it might maintain its fullness and not fall into ruin.

Later, however, one of meager virtue occupied such a position of extreme prosperity—how could it have avoided being submerged and lost? Therefore, even with the virtues of his ancestors, the King of Min...
Its majesty was such that it could not even rival the fires of common woodcutters—this too is a matter of principle.

Yet now, after being rebuilt for over twenty autumns, it still does not reach half the scale of its former state. Those who dwell here often feel shame over its deficiencies, while those who visit find fault with its lack of grandeur.
Do you alone fail to consider that those who studied the Buddha in antiquity planted [these foundations]...?
One may sleep beneath them; one may dwell among tombs. The spring gushing forth today is certainly not comparable to dwelling beneath trees or among tombs.

Moreover, while the virtue of "stiffness in the center" has not yet been heard of, you recklessly hope for the auspiciousness of a "ridge rising high. Let alone that you will fail to obtain it through such seeking.
If a building project is not completed, even if it can match the beauty of previous models, how could one ensure that it will not suffer the misfortune of structural collapse?
This, too, is a failure to understand the Way of the *I Ching*.
The *Seng Baozhi lun* states:
"Among the monasteries of Min, Xuefeng is invariably ranked first, while Gushan is truly second only to it.

This is surely not because of the beauty of its crags and peaks or the grandeur of its vistas; rather, it is because those who have presided over this seat were, for the most part, successive patriarchs."
All possess the perfectly rounded brilliance of wisdom, sufficient to illuminate both humans and devas, and to glorify the teachings of our Great Awakened Sovereign.

Thus, renowned sages of antiquity—such as Zhang De-yuan, Li Bo-ji, Zhao Zi-zhi, and Zhu Hei-an—were all able to humble their minds and lower their status to seek them out amidst deep forests and remote valleys; was this not because those individuals possessed [such qualities]?

How heavy the burden on one’s feet! Since the fall of the preceding dynasty, the tradition has gradually declined; by the time of our present dynasty, this Way had become a mere echo of the past. What is the reason for this?

It is likely because prior to the Song dynasty, those appointed as *zhuchi* (abbot) were required first to receive imperial edicts and incense offerings, and second to be nominated and requested by the provincial governors (*jiānsī*).
Consequently, the abbots of this mountain were all the most distinguished selections of their respective times. Under the preceding dynasty...
It was solely by examining the extensive teachings that certificates were issued for the administration of the monastic office; this was how those who embrace the Way could be brought forth.

During the Hongwu and Yongle eras, these were recommended by the Sanggang (Monastic Directorate) and issued by the Senglü (Registrar of Monks). After the Xuande era, however, the matter was ultimately left unattended.
Consequently, those who trade upon the name of the Tathāgata have generally used their own power to seize [the office], usurping what belongs to the public domain of the ten directions.
They merely moistened the private coffers of their own families; with sons and grandsons succeeding one another, they remained intoxicated by its richness and satiated by its excellence.

How could they have questioned whether the Buddha-dharma was effective or not? Since its re-establishment, there has been a slight effort to proclaim this Way, hoping perhaps to once again witness the majestic dignity of the Han officials.
Yet, on this day when Māras arise in competition, our precarious state is like a single hair pulling against a thousand-jin weight; and yet we still aspire to—
To follow the precedents of the Song and Tang dynasties—is this not difficult? Is it not difficult?
The Discourse on the Record of Land Taxation states: "To provide for monks, one must use land; to settle upon land, one must possess virtue. Wherever virtue resides, land will necessarily follow."

Wherever a field is located, harm will surely lie in wait for it. In the past, when Mount Gu was at its height, the monastic community numbered in the tens of thousands, and donors vied with one another to be first in their offerings;
thus, even though there were ten thousand *mu* of wasteland, no one dared to covet it.
But when it declined, who could bear to allow the fertile lands of the *dānapati* to be left to the unrestrained desires of the reckless? Consequently, the powerful and the strong seized them...
They seize it; the waves of the sea toss it about and swallow it. Furthermore, the government offices expend six parts of it, or eight parts of it, yet show them no compassion.

When I previously came to Mount Gu, I saw that the monks of the monastic compound exhausted all they could collect throughout the year, yet it was still not enough to satisfy the demands of the authorities.
Once the lashes and beatings became urgent, they sought nothing but the silver of wealthy families day and night. That they did not [fall into ruin]...
Even when their assets were exhausted and the monastic community had perished, they still did not stop. Where, then, lies the fault for this?
Nowadays, secular monks generally amass great wealth to bequeath to their descendants; let them inquire about this at Mount Gu.
The Discourse on the "Catalogue of Arts and Literature" states: The name of Mount Gu was not well-known prior to the Tang dynasty; consequently, poems and prose concerning it are rarely encountered.
During the era of the Zhu Liang, there were the "Record of Lingyuan Cave" and the "Twelve Odes" by Xu Yin, both of which have been lost and no longer transmitted. From the Song dynasty onwards...
When his writings first appeared, those who transmitted them were indeed few. It was not until the Yongle era of our Ming dynasty that the monk Shanyuan first compiled them into the *Lingyuan ji*.
Subsequently, the monk Gujian compiled them once more, continuing until the Wanli era.
Xie Wulin and Xu Xinggong first compiled the gazetteer, gathering materials so thoroughly that it may be called complete.

Now, nearly thirty years have passed, and Xinggong has again collected them to produce a supplementary gazetteer. I, therefore, have been able to build upon these two records and further augment them.
Indeed, this literature has not fallen into ruin; those who hold it are like those clutching a "pearl of Sui," and its source will flow on endlessly. I alone am moved by sorrow.

The mountains and rivers remain as they were; the Buddha-land endures forever. Yet those who grasp the pen and ascend the dais are ultimately like drifting clouds and illusory reflections, appearing and vanishing in an instant.
Though it is said their names endure, where indeed do they truly abide? Moreover, after a long time, even their names no longer exist;

thus, for one to claim that their established words shall be imperishable—is this not difficult? There must, therefore, be something that penetrates both past and present, participates in Heaven and Earth, and stands preeminent—
However, that which must not be obliterated does not reside in the trivial details of names and titles.
Some might still hope to emulate Han Yu and Liu Zongyuan, or stand shoulder-to-shoulder with Li Bai and Du Fu, asserting that their reputations must certainly not fall into ruin.

In my humble opinion, Han, Liu, Li, and Du were merely masters of the "carving of insects" and "engraving on paper. For a man of true character to establish himself, should he not strive for what is truly great?
The *Zazhilun* states:
"What is recorded in this miscellany does not concern matters of great principle and might thus seem dispensable.

Nevertheless, having read extensively through the various Confucian classics and the official histories of successive dynasties, are these not the great canons for transmitting [the teachings] to posterity? Within them, birds..."
The profusion of beasts, plants, and trees, and the abundance of utensils, implements, and cultural artifacts—few who have not extensively consulted various books can fully comprehend these.

Thus we know that Great Shun’s consultation with even the grass-cutters and wood-gatherers was indeed a supreme instruction; that when rites are lost, one must seek them among the common people, is by no means idle talk.
Formerly, there was a man from Min named Wu Hai, who claimed that the various schools of thought and the hundred masters are thieves of the Six Classics. Regarding external...

The *Kin'yōroku* (Records of Kinya) is a thief of the orthodox histories; one might wish to eliminate it entirely, yet one does not know that it contains the "floating fruit" of Chu, the "clapper-birds" of Lu, or the "ashes of the pillage" from the Han.
Who, then, could distinguish these from one another? I say: in the study of a gentleman, one should prioritize the great and subsequently attend to the small;
focus on the root while roaming through the branches. Then, even a single phrase or a solitary character from an eccentric book [will find its place].

The various classics are all items within the medicinal basket. Yet, I still observe those in this world who bear great reputations and are called "erudite and refined," who spend their days investigating trivial and obscure matters to bolster their own standing;

as for the subtleties of body, mind, and the nature of life, the grand matters of ritual, music, law, and governance, and the causes of ancient and modern order and chaos, they are for the most part muddled and superficial in their approach. Should they occasionally offer a discourse, it is like someone suffering from a nightmare.

To speak thus in one's dreams is how narrow and vulgar it is! It is like a minnow in a well, finding joy in a few pints of water to moisten itself, while the vast, boundless expanse of the ocean is not what it desires.
Would it not be better to broaden and enlarge one’s perspective?
Discourse on the Annals of the Construction of Wēnlíng Kāiyuán Monastery (Four Parts) Discourse on the Annals of Construction:

The discourse states that this was an ancient site where purple clouds once settled; its domain was exceedingly vast, and those who resided there numbered in the tens of thousands. Since the Yongle era...

Subsequently, the abbot’s seat was again vacant and the Chan tradition gradually faded away. Eminent monks dispersed in all directions like clouds, while those who clung to the "chicken rib" (a worthless remnant) regarded it as a mere relic of the past.
As virtue declined, lay patrons ceased to arrive; the land became vast yet sparsely populated, and those with covetous eyes began to rise up.
Consequently, there were seven or eight cases out of ten where a temple could no longer preserve its original domain. Nevertheless, it still relied upon...
This was a site prepared with temporary straw mats; thus, the sound of the sutras and the light of the Buddha’s flame did not reach total extinction.

In recent years, the Precept Platform and Dharma Hall have been restored, and the Great Hall has fortunately been renovated anew; this seems to coincide with the auspicious occasion of the "Return of the Seven Days" (the winter solstice).
If one improves one's conduct and responds to circumstances with excellence, then it will lead to the hexagrams Lin (Approaching) and Tai (Great Peace); this remains to be seen.

If, however, you merely harbor resentment over things that have not yet returned to you, while failing to cultivate your virtue, then even if your entire domain were restored, how would you be able to dwell within it?
If you can diligently cultivate your virtue, then even a dilapidated office or an old house is quite sufficient.
The full lotus posture is certainly not confined merely to a snail-shell hut or a grass shack that accommodates only seven feet;
moreover, since the Buddha resides within the human heart and each is capable of emitting light, who knows that the Elder Huang may not appear once again today?
This rests solely upon each of you to exert yourselves.
The *Kaishi-zhi-lun* (Treatise on the Aspiration of the Bodhisattva) states: "I have composed this *Kaishi-zhi* and marveled at the abundance of sages within the Purple Cloud.

Could such a thing exist anywhere other than this auspicious and extraordinary land? Yet, since the manifestation of the auspicious signs of the mulberry tree and the lotus flower, nearly a millennium has passed. As for the ancients..."
It is so now as it was then. Why is it that in antiquity sages and worthies appeared one after another, whereas today they are few and their voices have ceased?
A saying goes: "The Jia-yu gave birth to the Ying-long; the Ying-long gave birth to the Feng-huang; the Feng-huang gave birth to the hundred birds.

Is it necessarily the case that their power gradually declines? Or is it rather that the Dharma-vehicle has declined, and sages and worthies remain hidden? That the present does not equal the past is not due to a single cause alone.
Kṣaya! Alas, how could this be restricted by the ambitions of those who seek the Way?
For all who depend on external conditions, time and circumstance can restrict them; but for those who depend on nothing external, neither time nor circumstance can restrict them.
Thus, although the Spring and Autumn period was fraught with peril, it could not confine Confucius; and although his humble alley was in poverty, it could not confine Yanyuan.
Although they were in distress at Mount Shouyang, it could not confine Boyi and Shuqi; this was simply because those with resolve establish themselves by their own will.

As for those who plan for great accumulation of wealth and pursue illustrious fame, striving diligently from dawn to dusk yet unable to find peace within themselves amidst the currents of time and circumstance—they are the most deeply deluded. How tragic!
The Discourse on the "Treatise on Arts and Literature" states: Alas! As I contemplate this "Treatise on Arts and Literature," I sigh at the difficulty of achieving immortality.

Among the three things the world’s books call "immortal," the establishment of words (establishment of discourse) is but one. Now, while words may indeed be transmitted, if the words lack literary refinement, they will not endure.

Regarding the transmission [of texts]: there are words that are refined and elegant, yet they still do not survive as transmissions. Some say this is because the person [who produced them] was not worthy of transmission.

Now, the rites of the Xia and Yin dynasties lack any corroborating evidence; even the Six Classics of Confucius have lost two of them. How can it be that people are simply incapable of being transmitted?
Alas! Illusions and transformations are not solid; though distant, they must perish. Even Heaven and Earth...
If even this cannot be avoided, how much less so for humans, and how much less so for written texts? Within our Buddhist tradition, there are things that simply cannot be extinguished;
it rests with those of resolve to exert themselves on their own behalf.
The Discourse on the Record of Land Taxation states: The assets of Ziyun Temple were bestowed by various donors since the Tang and Song dynasties.

The monks rely upon them for their livelihood, yet they pay official taxes and provide corvée labor for the local district exactly as private households do; thus, there is no depletion of the state’s resources. As for...

In recent times, it was claimed that monks were neither commoners nor productive subjects and were draining the state’s resources; thus, proposals arose to sell their lands or to confiscate their stipends.
Not only was there no means to provide for them, but they were instead strangled and dispossessed, losing five-tenths of their property.

By the Jiajing era, when the defense against Japanese pirates broke out, the authorities requisitioned six-tenths of their land to provide rations for the troops. Furthermore, Governor-General Jin [Jin Shunzhi] levied taxes upon them as well.
8. Up to the present day, the military forces have been withdrawn yet the provisions have not been reduced; indeed, they have even increased.
How could it be that the monks do not become impoverished and flee? Formerly, there was a high monk named Hongze of Ziyun; the prince bestowed upon him fertile lands.

He declined and would not accept. There was one named Xiexia; when the provincial governor Wang Jixun provided him with a larger residence and increased his provisions for sustenance, he firmly declined, saying, "Do not burden my descendants. There was another named Yuchang;

when people offered him fertile lands, he said, "If I possess such things, my descendants will surely not escape the jaws of wolves and tigers. Looking at them today, these three masters were truly great men!
The Extensive Record of Master Yongjue, Volume Nineteen.
The Extensive Record of Master Yongjue, Volume Twenty.
Re-edited by the Dharma-heir Daopai.

Eulogy on the Spiritual Portraits of the Patriarchs (with Preface) The True cannot be sought through distance; that which is distant is not the True. The shadow does not exist apart from the form, yet the form is truly not the shadow.

If one attempts to grasp it by speculating upon the traces of the shadow, it is no more than reaching for the moon in water. If one attempts to grasp it by speculating upon the absence of shadows and traces, it is still...
A flower blooming in the void: when both existence and non-existence have departed, how can it ultimately be? Puhua exerts his full strength to perform a somersault;
Master Zhi grasps his brush and carves open the gateway of the face. One knows that this has cost a great deal of salt and sauce.
Nevertheless, though this is so, affairs do not follow a single direction; only then do many gates appear. Now, here we are sketching the features of empty space and pointing them out.
The traces of dreams and illusions have already withered away like creeping vines, yet he raises them up once more. The accumulated spoils of years are overturned to their very bottom.
As for the various patriarchs of the past, are they truly one? Are they two? They are simply of a single capacity.
The Dharma’s conditions lie herein. Do not say that the whole body has not yet been revealed; it has already been presented face-to-face. Hehe!
Were it not for the wild geese arriving at night, how could one perceive the autumn at the sea gate?

The beginning of the Sangha-treasure was when the Venerable Kauṇḍinya’s ear was pierced by Kāli’s sword—a fact already revealed long ago. When the first song was sung at the Deer Park, you alone were the first to harmonize with it; thus, there was one who was deaf.
A single word falls; it deceives the great earth. As the presiding elder among monks, he is the First Patriarch, Venerable Kāśyapa, of the various patriarchs of the Chan school.
The moment a single flower was held up, the hearts of a thousand sages fell. When it encountered an ignorant fellow, he smiled and acted;
like fire on dead wood, it shines brilliantly through ancient and modern times. Is this the First Patriarch of the Chan school? Wrong.

The Second Patriarch, Venerable Ānanda, could swallow and regurgitate hundreds of thousands of Buddha-dharmas; with his faculty of tongue, he possessed great learning and dhāraṇī-retention—why then was he designated a Patriarch of Chan? He overturned the flagpole.
The wife’s heart is bitter. Nevertheless, do not say that Qi was transformed into Lu after a single change.
The Venerable Śāṇakavāsin, the Third Patriarch, made a prophecy from the green forest;
the auspicious grass signaled its time. When the Venerable Kāśyapa was born, he appeared at that very moment, using poison to destroy poison.
How could a dragon possibly peer into this? To lay out the ground and erect a temple, one is instead branded on the face by the seal of the "channel.
Whether the Fourth Patriarch Upagupta was seventeen or not seventeen—these words split into two pieces; why such haste? The shaking of the demon palaces is but a dream.

As for these matters, his room was always filled to the brim with tally-sticks; there was never even one missing. Ultimately, what great qualities did he possess? His brows were arched and his nose was straight.
The Venerable Tīrthika, the Fifth Patriarch, said:
"The wisdom of my teacher, who has emerged from the bonds of existence, is like the sun rising above the house; to this day, I still look up to its lingering radiance. It is not otherwise.
People see it as if it were lacquer. Hehe. This is merely talk from a dream; originally, it is not real. Whether existence or non-existence, it cannot be discerned.
Thus spoke the Venerable Master Mijia, the Sixth Patriarch.

In the past, I was born in the Brahma Heaven; having encountered my kinsmen and friends, I have been fragmented through countless kalpas. Whose fault is this? When creditors and debtors meet, one falls into this trap.
Yet it turns out not a single step has ever been moved; only now do I recognize that three times three is originally nine.

The Seventh Patriarch, Venerable Vasumitra, with his golden cloud-like floating canopy, was nurtured in the Land of Sages. Holding the vessel in his hand upon the road back home, his preaching of the Dharma was as vast as space, clearly establishing the distinctions of all things.
How could it be tolerated that Brahma Kings and Śakras would come before his face to defile him? This is precisely the right moment.
Strike him across the spine! This is so that we may not fail the Buddha’s prophetic prediction.
As for the Venerable Eighth Patriarch Buddhānanda, his meaning need not be discussed;
it is as difficult as nailing space. If one attempts to discuss it, it lacks meaning; it is like placing a handle on a bowl. When meeting on a narrow path, there is no room for evasion.
They partake of the flavor of ambrosia; though it is but a single word, they know where to return. Yet, they would have failed their own birth with the *uṣṇīṣa*.

Although the Ninth Patriarch, Vajramitra, did not speak, he had already revealed the meaning; although he did not act, he had already reached the ultimate. It was like a needle meeting its eye—perfectly attuned.
Truly without a trace. He immediately took seven steps, yet he has already fallen into the second [category].

When the Venerable Daobian, the Tenth Patriarch, sat with auspicious light illuminating his seat, the stench was already manifest. His ribs did not touch the mat; his backbone was cast of iron. He sat upon the golden ground.
Spreading out and tearing up one's sitting mat—does it still possess any true meaning? Seven errors and eight mistakes.
O, the eleventh patriarch, Honored One Punyananda:
"You are not the Buddhas, nor are the Buddhas you. With these words alone, he was worthy of being entrusted with the robe and overturned the golden [seat].
The Ground. Having thoroughly pierced the pivot of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, what need is there to speak of the "Awakening Flower" coming into being? It is much like a branch growing from a branch.
The twelfth patriarch, the Venerable Aśvaghoṣa, did not recognize this as Buddha;
yet Buddha cannot be recognized. To encounter it here is like a silver mountain and an iron wall; one day, they shall be sawn apart.
The wood is severed; for the first time, one recognizes that the scale-weight contains sap. Its claws and fangs are exposed in mid-air, crushing and subduing the great illusory enemy.
Alas! An entire field of right and wrong arises from emptiness; in the end, neither demon nor Buddha can be analyzed apart.
The thirteenth patriarch, Venerable Kāpimāra, possessed supernatural powers capable of transforming the vast ocean.
Yet what was that truly? It was merely a strange and illusory phenomenon. Suddenly realizing the ocean of one's own nature, he saw it as nothing more than child’s play.
Whether demon or Buddha, all were but empty distractions; he cast aside hundreds of thousands of supernatural powers and captured [the thief].
The venomous dragon came to be his son; indeed, he did not fail as the successor of Aśvaghoṣa.

When the Fourteenth Patriarch, Venerable Nāgārjuna, manifested the lunar disc on the spot, this was truly unavoidable. Yet, this mere painted cake—though one looks at it, it remains ten thousand miles away.
Neither form nor sound—who would dare to presume upon it? Only one of true bone and marrow can truly not fail this intent.
The Fifteenth Patriarch, Venerable Kanadeva, cast a needle into a bowl;
he was a thief. Beholding the full moon, he saw only its half. He pointed to a wooden mushroom—

The preceding cause demonstrates the later calamities facing bhikṣus; it is like beating the grass solely to startle the snake. Having settled the old case of my own house, the Sixteenth Patriarch, Venerable Rāhulata, relied upon the tips of the branches to hear the worldly melodies beyond the mundane.
The Buddha’s prophecy was not in vain, and the lamp of the Patriarchs has thus been transmitted. One who exhausts the source of the golden river [attains this].
Casting a hook down a thousand fathoms, he held forth a single bowl of Brahma-heaven rice; it was difficult even for a master to avoid a side-long laugh.

The seventeenth patriarch, the Venerable Saṃghanandin, cast aside worldly glory like worn-out sandals and sat in meditative repose within a stone cave. Yet karmic debts pursued him, just as a magnet attracts iron. He took the nectar of immortality and shared it universally.
I drink with the great assembly, merely responding to the occasion. If one asks what its flavor is like, let it leave the entire earth tongue-tied.
The Eighteenth Patriarch, Venerable Gayāsata, came bearing a mirror;
I shall gladly smash it to pieces. The capacity of the Buddhas—what a mere dregs of spittle! It is neither wind nor a bell.
Pointing directly to this is like a monkey climbing a tree; one cannot help but accept the full charge.

The Nineteenth Patriarch, Venerable Kumāralata, was long skilled in preaching the Dharma through the power of Prajñā. When he encountered a poisonous hand, he pointed it out on the spot, and suddenly he grasped it.
The nostrils. Do not say there is no one; space is completely filled. Although it may be settled with a single blow, it is nonetheless eight *kē* (two hours) too late.
The twentieth patriarch, Venerable Śānavāsa.
As a form gives rise to its shadow, one traces the current back to its source; innate wisdom suddenly awakens, and one silently realizes the ultimate origin.
Since the essence is fundamentally unborn, what words can there be for phenomena? Whether conditioned or unconditioned, they are but empty clamor within a dream.
The Twenty-first Patriarch, Vasiṣṭha: Autumn waters and the bright moon; a precipitous cliff and cold snow.
An old fisherman awakens from sleep and moves toward the marshland; only then does he realize that last night his boat briefly rested there.
Black as jade, white as iron—who would dare speak against its very core? My Master, having caught him on the spot, [let him go].
I know where this leads. Indeed, the assembly of worthies was not given to idle chatter.
The twenty-second patriarch, Venerable Mañjarī, was born into a royal palace;

he attained mastery of these profound mysteries and realized that the Dharma is fundamentally unimpeded, appearing exactly like an illusion or a bubble. Thus, he fulfilled the Buddha’s prophetic prediction.
He divided the lamp to guide others through transformation. When the incense was lowered at the Crane Grove (Heli), the fire inevitably sought the dry wood.
The twenty-third patriarch, Venerable Hulan, arrived carrying a ring;
it was not for any other purpose. Having long been a "crane master," how could he act as a beast? When karmic debts meet, they are inevitably reconciled.
The incense formed into tassels; one day, upon hearing a verse, he knew his place of return. The flock of cranes felt relieved and departed.
The twenty-fourth patriarch, Śrīsena, taught that the Way cannot be sought;
when employed, it is not a feat of achievement. Reaching the source, there is no action; the ancestral pulse flows secretly. In the past, there was an extraordinary aura.

It should rest upon your own person; otherwise, your head will fall and your arms will be severed, and both your aggregates (skandhas) will become empty. By all means, do not say that this is a meeting of karmic debts and grievances.

The Venerable Paśyetsūtra, the twenty-fifth patriarch, possessed a divine sword naturally sharp and a pearl in his fist inherently luminous; his coming was due to a specific cause. With the seal suspended behind his elbow, the time for the arising of difficulties has arrived.
The transmission of the robe symbolizes faith; the longer it is refined, the more clearly it shines.
Only when the true succession is first established can the twenty-sixth patriarch, Bodhidharma, be recognized.

As for the Venerable Upagupta, he was once a mountain-dwelling heretic; through the power of his "stupid meditation," he encountered the state of no-mind and brought about his own misfortune, whereby he was led to return to the True Vehicle.
To turn the curved into the straight, people suddenly encounter it. Two times five is ten;
the twenty-seventh patriarch, Venerable Prajñātāra, was not Śrī-vidyut-dhara (Poti), yet he was called Śrī-vidyut-dhara.
Coming from causes and conditions, he served as a vessel for the Dharma and constantly turned the wondrous sutras.
How could it fall within the realm of words? Both hands emit light, yet there is no further handle to grasp.

The twenty-eighth patriarch, Venerable Bodhidharma, came across the sea for no other reason than to overturn the old molds; even heroes were left without a foothold. He sat facing the wall for nine years.
What kind of door is this? It is both laughable and loathsome. Fortunately, there was a master who dealt a lethal blow, so that [the Patriarch] could only depart westward with his single sandal.
To this day, the lingering calamity has not been extinguished; they have all fallen into the number of one thousand seven hundred.
The twenty-ninth patriarch, Great Master Huike, severed his arm to find peace of mind;
after three prostrations, he attained the marrow. It was like space merging with space—what principle is this? He instructed him to seek out his transgression, yet it could not be found;
ultimately, there was no other essential meaning. Although it is said that the Dharma was transmitted from one to another, it was, in effect, like waves without wind.
The Third Patriarch, Master Sengcan, sought his offenses but could not find them.
His home was destroyed and his path cut off; he took refuge in a desolate mountain, solitary and alone like a shadow without a body. He was not such a person.
How could I dare indulge in further words? In his later years, he obtained a youth whose skin was still warm with blood.

The Great Master Daoxin, the thirty-first patriarch, had long since mastered the gate of liberation through past cultivation and early on wore the seal of the ancestral masters. By the walls of Jishui City, the hearts of the rebels were struck with terror; at Mount Poutou, [the Dharma] flourished.

The thunder of the supreme Dharma rolled; though the Imperial Edict summoned him from all four quarters, he did not emerge from the mountains. Only then did one know that the Master of the Way does not serve his commands.
When the Great Master Hongren, the thirty-second patriarch, arrived, there was a prior agreement:
"The place of birth is difficult to verify; do not speak of having no surname, for let him know it himself. Now the fruit of Huangmei has ripened.
Let the wind blow it away. This single scroll of the *Vajracchedikā* has become a public proclamation. It provoked the barbarian to immediately receive the robe.

This wood-seller, the Great Master Huineng, the thirty-third patriarch—who could not recognize a single character—ran straight into the *Vajracchedikā*, which turned to powder. At the third watch, he entered Huangmei directly.
The Plum Room: Truly, this is like casting a net to catch the wind; what need is there to discuss further rules and regulations? From now on, the sweet nectar shall pervade the world;
birds approaching the Golden Mountain will find no difference in its hue.

Chan Master Rong of Niutou Mountain dwelt in the silent, empty mountains, taking birds and beasts as his companions. Fortunately, he encountered a master who sat and cut off the lineage of Buddhas and Patriarchs; there, the tracks of wolves and tigers could not be found.
Suddenly bursting forth was the sun at its zenith at noon. What difference does it make whether it is today or tomorrow? Go ask the hermitage.
The Central Patriarch:

National Teacher Huian of Mount Song occupied the seat of Shaoshi and held the seal of Huangmei. He set aside Nanyue and was entrusted with the Emperor of Ten Thousand Chariots. Only when entering the water did he finally see [the truth].
The Great Man: even at the end, he still upheld the true command. His wild and raving discourse was understood by no one;
yet the wildfire could hear his final instructions. Master Nanyue Huairang.
A single poison obstructs the chest; for eight years, what can be done? Suddenly it collapses—what is this?
A mere brick before the hermitage is the lure of calamity; it draws forth the colt, creating waves upon dry land.

When Master Qingyuan Si was about to take up his duties, he requested passage across a frozen river; fortunately, he encountered a master craftsman, whereupon his thieving intent was fully exposed. Fundamentally, there are no stages or ranks.
There was no need to move a single step. In years to come, he brought forth the "Stone," truly overturning all proclamations.
Chan Master Jingjue of Yongjia perceived the pivot before it was struck;
his spirit swallowed the Buddhas and patriarchs. Carrying his staff, he arrived and met his master just in time; his functional mastery transcended all bounds.
Like a fierce tiger bound, he returned after one night; he opened a separate gate and emerged from Mount Gonggong as the Chan Master Mazu, fulfilling the prophecy.
Awakened by a single brick, he strode and trampled with unrestrained freedom; his functional power was most divine, and those who encountered its venom were transformed.
One hundred and thirty people remain under his feet to this day, like thunder and lightning.

Chan Master Shitou Xiqian received the mandate from Caoxi and entered the chamber of Qingyuan; though his boldness was as vast as heaven, he was merely self-conceited and did not realize that there was [a master] south of the Ling Mountains.

News: The ocean of nature directly roams with the Patriarchs; a single scroll of the *Cantong qi* remains as a model for posterity. Turning heaven and covering earth, its wisdom and function are extraordinary.
The path of Shitou is slippery—who can reach it?

Chan Master Baizhang Hai stands towering atop the Great Hero Peak; he is forged entirely of pure gold. A single shout leaves one deaf for three days; from this moment forth, his fangs and claws are revealed.
He overturns the "wild fox" Chan and transmits the phrase that transcends the hall, drawing forth the red-bearded barbarian until even sages and worthies are left at a loss.

Zen Master Nanquan Yuan was one who transcended the world of things; his every playful stride left behind fragrant traces. For thirty years, Nanquan tended the ox, providing it with ample water and grass.
One day he departed from the mountains, and the great earth suffered a violent jolt. He could shatter dreams by pointing at a flower; who can redeem the cat he beheaded?
Master Zhizhu of Dazhu:

his treasure-store had long been buried; he abandoned his home and wandered abroad. Only upon meeting someone who pointed it out to him did he realize it was originally present within himself. Its illumination and function are boundless.
The dragon roars and the lion bellows; there is no gate for entering the Way.
The Master opens its window for you.
Since the Zen Master Wutian did not dwell on that side, why need one further discuss this side? Once the stone wall is smashed through, it is naturally so.
Neither side remains; standing alone on the summit of a ten-thousand-fathom peak, he causes the entire universe to be swallowed in a single gulp.

Master Huangbo Yun was so exceedingly compassionate toward his father that he allowed his son to become so exceptionally proud; yet upon hearing a single shout, he was so startled that his tongue lolled out, and he immediately attained realization.
The tiger’s roar! On a narrow path, he personally encountered a single fang; the lives of the assembly nearly escaped not.
From this point on, the lineage became exceedingly perilous, leaving the heroes of the four seas at a loss.

When Chan Master Shishuang Qiyuan touched upon a single spark, he finally came to know its existence. He kicked over the pure water jar, refusing to fall into conventional molds; instead, he became a water buffalo.
Unprovoked, he fell into the hands of Yangshan, from whom father and son established their family tradition. Their hidden mechanism was perfected.
Combining these signs to entice and guide:
Chan Master Shenyi of Zhaozhou picked up a radish from Zhenzhou and hung it as a gourd on the eastern wall; he brought forth the cypress tree in front of the courtyard, teaching directly.
The great earth is in a daze; has Zhaozhou passed through the barrier or not? Pointing east to speak of the west is devoid of principle;
whoever encounters this must have their very marrow withered away. The Venerable Master Chen of Muzhou.
His spiritual capacity was like a flash of lightning; his function was like a divine dragon. Seven ancient and eight strange—seek them and they are empty.
In an ordinary gesture of extending his hand, he founded two schools. Hanging up a single straw sandal, he caused Huang Chao’s heart to fail with fear;
the people of Muzhou to this day chant praises for his merit in repelling the rebel. Alas! How could I possibly know this old man?
Chan Master Linji’s thirty bitter blows were intended to see blood; here, one must awaken with sudden intensity—there is no room for branches or joints. Three fists and a single palm.
Snow upon frost; claws and fangs suddenly revealed. The gate is perilous and the path cut off.
Master Dongshan Jia says that even the insentient can preach the Dharma—this itself is the true portrait of the Master. Yet, when it comes to bringing it forth on the spot, how is it?
Still lingering in contemplation, he crossed the water and beheld his own reflection; only then did he realize the grandmotherly heart of the ancients.
From this point on, he freely opened up the five ranks and cut through the dense forest of all views.
National Teacher Guoyi of Mount Jing was the true treasure of the Dharma.

Performing the deeds of a great man, he established the Patriarch’s legacy at Shuangjing; there, the Dragon King offered up the land, while Master Mazu could not unsettle him, and even the Heavenly King met with his blunt dismissal.
He was certainly not merely the sole peer in the nation of Tang, but truly a figure for a hundred generations.
Auspicious omen.

Master Guifeng Zongmi’s Chan and Teachings branched out in different directions, and few were able to unify them. Only this master, upon a single encounter, comprehended both paths and became the patriarch of the Teaching school.
It serves as the outward manifestation of Chan; it extinguishes disputes and awakens the deluded, like the sun at first dawn.

Master Xuefeng Cun received the master’s staff in his youth and later relied upon the admonitions of his friends; his realization was as vast as heaven and earth, and his great function flourished profusely, as the wooden ball rolled forth.
Wisdom cannot reach it. With a turtle’s nose blocking the road, its venom is difficult to approach. Yantou spreads his net as vast as the heavens;
all the descendants filling the earth are phoenixes and qilin. Master Caoshan Ji.

The waters of the cavern flow upstream; the Master inherited his wisdom. From that direction he came, opening these five ranks. The precious mirror stands upon its pedestal, illuminating all myriad things.
Void and profound, without attachment—how could it be grasped through mere intellectual understanding?

When Master Yantou Huo’s rocks split and cliffs collapsed, it was by the command of Deqiao; the Master then succeeded him, his thunderous voice becoming even more rapid. At the lakeside, his oars were like living dragons;
Yantou’s path was as steep as heaven. Whenever he encountered someone, he would let out but a single sigh, and countless ordinary people lost their lives.

Chan Master Wén of Lóng-hú, a scion of the imperial house who served as a minister to the Dharma King, attained the seal of “not speaking” from Shí-shuāng and realized the mind of the “forehead-marked by the mountain.
The dragon hid its scales in its sleeves to avoid punishment; the water rewarded his virtue by becoming clear and still. As he drew near his end, he said: “Everyone, listen!”
Thirty years of secrets have been fully revealed.

As for Chan Master Niaoke Daolin on the peak of Mount Qinwang—what manner of place is it? A bright moon hangs from the pine branches; the red dust of the mortal world cannot fly upon it. How supremely perilous!
Reality is ultimately level; how could the Prefect truly comprehend it? To station oneself as a governor over mountains and rivers is yet too precarious;
standing downwind, one can do nothing but look on with regret. —Master Yunmen Yan.
In the Qin era, [the chariot] crushed and pierced through; he retreated and entered the gate of Muzhou. It was not merely that one foot was damaged, but his very life-root was extinguished.
As soon as he offered a single word at Xuefeng, its fame resounded throughout the great earth. The gateway stands like a sheer cliff of a thousand fathoms;
how many can swallow the steamed cake he brings forth?
Chan Master Fengxue Zhao was not deluded by Nan-yuan; beneath the staff, he penetrated to the very source and revealed the "Iron Ox" kōan.

When Lu-p’o lost what came before and forgot what followed, the life-force of the lineage under Linji was reduced to a single thread. Relying solely on our Master, it was barely sustained. Shedding tears, I now bring this forth.
Stored within the family [lineage], the waves of the Dharma surged from here to the heavens.

When the Way of Linji was about to cease upon encountering the winds of Master Shoushan Nian, it relied on this master to continue it; thus it rose up once more in full force. This is the teaching of the unspoken.
The listener is not the ear. To shake one’s sleeves and depart—what principle is there in that? Within the breast, there is not even a trace of a single character;
the seven scrolls of the Lotus Sūtra have become mere scrap paper.
Chan Master Fayen Yi had a fragment of rock obstructing his chest;
his path was exhausted and his way cut off. Upon encountering a person, he tumbled down; the shadows of the triple world vanished, and all things were manifest as they are.
Why need one twist and contort? This is the Great Dharma Eye; its illumination and function are without deficiency.
Chan Master Fenyang Wude Zhao passed through the seat of Baizhang; he fished out the moon from the empty pool. A lion sits crouched upon the ground; those who approach have their courage shattered.

The three secret seals give rise to the clash of arms; the ten wisdoms produce branches and nodes. A monk of extraordinary character has come for the sake of the Dharma; I specifically request that you diligently proclaim it.

Master Xuedou Xian, who had mastered the sutras through exhaustive study, possessed a power of discernment as swift as a galloping wind. Once he entered the gate of wisdom, all that he had brought with him was utterly lost beneath the monk’s whisk. Under the monk’s whisk—
It is like facing the rising morning sun; its swift current passes over a blade—its mechanism is difficult to describe with metaphors.

When Chan Master Ciming Yuan scolded Fashi, his application was indeed extraordinary; only the Master could withstand it. His wild mind was instantly stilled, and he immediately attained liberation at Dangyang.

A roar! Truly, it makes heaven tremble and the earth split asunder. With a single word, he topples the divine cauldron and its house. Since ancient times until now, where has there ever been a true hero?
—Master Chan Master Yuan of Foyin.

Early and midday, the fierce venom of the *Śūraṅgama* strikes; death lies in wait before the opening of the pickled-vessel jar. With a set of sharp fangs and savage tusks, he makes everyone who hears of him suffer a headache.
He does nothing but insult the sages and deceive the worthy, solely intent on seizing dragons and striking phoenixes. Having painted the true likeness of the Master, he laughs with great joy;
who would have known that this laughter would shatter the dreams of Jambudvīpa?

Chan Master Tianyi Huai dreamed of descending from the stars; this was due to his past conditioning. He traveled extensively among monastic communities and early on excelled beyond his peers. He then encountered a "fierce-handed" master.

Facing an iron wall, one suddenly breaks through with a crash; the nostrils are lost. A ten-thousand-fathom silver mountain collapses instantly, and a single wheel of the sun bursts forth from the void.

Chan Master Yongming Shou suspended the mirror of the single mind, in which the reflections of the myriad practices were perfectly complete; its profound meanings were thoroughly investigated, and a thousand lights shone together, opening the gate of Buddha-recollection.
He demonstrated that it is solely the mind and its objects, extensively encompassing the three faculties and universally extending his guidance.

When Master Nanyuan of Huanglong met Chan Master Ciming, whose backbone was as hard and unyielding as iron, the Master’s heart and gall were instantly shattered upon seeing him. Zhaozhou had already scrutinized and penetrated him.
No cause or condition. How can one speak of a single sheet of snow upon a red furnace? As perilous and steep as heaven, it cannot be climbed;
the three barriers have cut off the tongues of heroes.
Master Chan Master Yangqi Hui.

The supportive ministers assist the Compassionate and Enlightened One, acting as the guiding framework for the assembly. With a single word, one knows when to rest; it dissolves like ice melting away.
"A three-legged donkey tramples people to death"—what need is there to ask whether there is a white-marked tiger on the South Mountain? In days to come, his descendants will surely fill the earth;
facing the wind, each shall possess wings to soar toward the clouds.
Chan Master Baiyun ended with "Carrying a pearl, he comes;
with a single laugh, it is snatched away. Who knows that this laugh can both kill and bring to life? Yet, when one finally recognizes it for what it is—
It is like the bottom falling out of a bucket; only then does one realize that this pearl was originally open and unobstructed.

Regarding the two gates of Chan and Pure Land by Chan Master Ze of Changlu: which is provisional and which is real? He established his teachings according to the capacities of beings; the Way of the thousand sages is one. The Great Being [Avalokiteśvara] provides profound assistance.
At this preeminent assembly, let it not be said that the direct pointing of the Dharma is not the legacy of Master Huiyuan.
When Zen Master Wuzu Fayan first stepped out his door, he carried a single board and bumped into people at every turn; he nearly had his eyes gouged out, yet it was because of Baiyun...
To provide for his livelihood, he purchased the ancestral estate of his grandfather; though it was his own family’s old property, it cost him many layers of calloused feet.
Zen Master Hongzhi of Tiantong encountered a single stroke from Danxia, cast aside the "clay-ball head," transcended beyond the empty kalpa, and touched his own nose.
At the third watch, no borrowed light is needed; his original radiance is inconceivable. He sits firmly atop Mount Taibai, and the milk of the Dharma flows across the great earth.
Chan Master Dahui of Jing Mountain inherited the nostrils from Baofeng and broke out of the shell-seal at Tianning. The Buddha-sun shines upon heaven and mirrors the earth.

With a bamboo switch he chased elephants and whipped dragons; his pungent and stinking fame spread throughout the land of China. Chan Master Hongzhou Linji Huqiu Long did not fail the entrustment of the orthodox lineage of Linji.

Upon entering the gate of Changlu, he recognized Yuanwu’s words; it was as if the scent of fermented vinegar had been produced in his mind. In the end, he joined their ranks. Do not say that what is soft and yielding is easy;
the tiger of drowsiness sat crouched at Tiger Hill, brooking neither Buddhas nor patriarchs.
Master Ying’an of Tiantong explored the lair of the Tiger Hill; it was as if he could not settle there. He sat upon the summit of the Golden Wheel; it was as if he could not be obscured.
He let loose the donkey of Yangqi, and all jackals were silenced. The gate of ambrosia opens, deep as the sea; the mountain is high, the path is perilous, and the clouds—
In the pitch-black darkness, Chan Master Puan Su sought a reflection at the gate of Dayue;
he turned his body within the ocean of Avataṃsaka. His fundamental nature is unfathomable and his traces difficult to find; he reveals himself in a manner distinct from the ordinary.
The ancestral intent of the Patriarchs is profound; alas, during the day people fall victim to calamity. Infinite clouds of demons rely upon you for purification.

Chan Master Wuzhun Fanzhu entered the "Broken Hut" (P'o-an) by mistake and obtained nothing at all. His assembly was as vast as the sea, and his transformative influence was unfathomable. He forged them with literature and tempered them with martial discipline.
His forging and molding were thorough and subtle. On two occasions he entered the inner court, where he cleared away the clouds to reveal the sun and moon.

Although Chan Master Xueyan Qin’s knowledge and views remained, and the pivot of the gate was still obstructed, he shattered the glass-like barrier before the ancient cypress in the hall and borrowed the seat of Mount Yangshan.
He penetrated the lineage of Yangqi and fully upheld the orthodox command; all manner of demons lost their spirits.
Master Gaofeng Miao struck down the "corpse-dragging" phrase and captured the master within the dream. The Dead Gate was as perilous as heaven; he bore it upon his back like a fierce tiger.
Three times he called, yet there was no turning back; his claws and fangs were not lightly deployed. With this single black bamboo staff, he lashes and strikes all Buddhas and patriarchs.
Iron Mountain and Master Qiong’s skulls have been shattered; strike once more, and there will be nothing lacking. One must pass through this experience—dragon eyes and ghostly gaze.
It is still difficult to recognize; from ten thousand miles away, you have come for no reason to pursue the foul odor. It permeates heaven and scorches earth, leaving no place to hide.
The net of Dharma spreads across the heavens, opening even beyond the seas. —Master Zhongfeng Ben.

Upon encountering a flowing spring, he beheld gods and ghosts; having obtained a bamboo staff, he demolished nests and shattered fortresses. Transcending the illusory world, he dwelt wherever clouds gathered;
his preaching of the Dharma was unhindered, like the waters of a whirlpool in the ocean.
Chan Master Duanya Yi trod upon a thousand-fathom cliff and shattered a sheet of snow. His discerning wit was like rolling thunder; his solitary austerity was like tempered steel.
He lived in seclusion for fifty autumns, such that even fire could not heat him. In his final years, he became even more wild and eccentric, extinguishing the tracks left by a thousand sages.
Chan Master Songyin Moshan has, throughout immeasurable kalpas, carried this leather bag. With a single blow, it is like snow cast into boiling water; his entire body is now a mouth.
Light radiates from his pores, cutting off what precedes and follows. Heavenly flowers fly and flutter.
Chan Master Chang of Qianyan has reached the ultimate destination of the Buddhas: a withered tree meets the snow, a vicious dog guards the gate, the path is severed, and a rat overturns the basin.
A lacquer bucket falls and cracks open atop Mount Fulong; one mistakes a tortoise for a turtle.
Chan Master Tianru Weize lacks the capacity to break through;
