withered and compliant, he hides like a six-legged tortoise by the water’s edge or beneath the forest trees—sometimes even appearing before his teacher.
He let out a single roar amidst the grove of trees; thus he did not fail his master, Huanzhu.
Chan Master Led Jitan’s "Five Ranks of the Dragon's Flight" renewed the Dharma destiny, following him like clouds; he became a supreme treasure of the nation, yet ultimately refused to accept office.
The celestial discourse became increasingly intimate; at its conclusion, it was poured forth entirely.
Who could continue its melody?
Chan Master Jinbifeng’s white light blazes brilliantly—a rare omen within the Dharma. Having heard the sound of the felling trees, what further matters remain? He entered the imperial court twice.
The Seals of the Patriarchs: The opening of heaven first celebrates the gathering of wind and clouds; imperial grace is most abundant as they sing of returning home.
The śarīra relics shine brilliantly like strung pearls, initiating the teachings of the various patriarchs.

The Bodhisattva Vasubandhu raised two challenges in succession, unveiling the secrets of the Compassionate Honored One (Maitreya). His magnificent treatises rose like clouds, explaining the meaning without omission. Once the Consciousness-Only doctrine was clarified, both the nature and characteristics [of phenomena] were fully established.
It shall forever serve as a lamp for the Dharma, illuminating ten million generations.

Venerable Kāśyapa Mātanga appeared in a dream to the Golden Man (Emperor Ming of Han), who then carried the Dharma eastward. Opening the heavens and leading forth the sun, his power resided in his person; it was as if those who were blind had finally regained their sight.
Like one who was suddenly cured of deafness, he subdued the external assemblies and forever propagated our school.
Venerable Dharmaratna did not transform the world alone;

he must have had his assistants. Once Kāśyapa Mātanga had gone to the East, the Master followed in his footsteps. When the various sutras were first translated, [Dharmarakṣa] was the one who initiated them.
He began to pour down the rain of the Dharma. As an envoy of the Tathāgata and the patriarch of Zhendan, he came from Kangju when the conditions for the Venerable [Kāśyapa] had ripened in Jiangnan;
there, a light illuminated the heavens, and following that light, he arrived. The Master, appreciating his skillful means, first requested śarīra relics.
He was the precursor of the Great Dharma. When the stupas and monasteries were first established, the torch of wisdom was kindled for the first time.

Dharma Master Kumārajīva manifested his spiritual power even in the womb; his wondrous wisdom was like that of a deity. Holding his alms bowl, he realized the ultimate meaning, and at a tender age, he preached the sutras. Thus, the Buddha-dharma was transmitted to the East.
The erroneous transmission has been inherited through the ages; it truly relies upon the arrival of the Master, who emits great radiance—
the various patriarchs of the Tiantai school,
beginning with the Venerable Huiwen of the Northern Qi.
The Dharma of Chan came from the West; for the most part, it was confined to gradual causes. Only you, Master, rose up in prominence, awakening to that which is innate and natural.
Having inherited the Dharma of Nāgārjuna, you took the principle of the One Mind as your core insight. This wondrous gate of the Perfect and Sudden is like the sun first rising.
Venerable Master Huisi of Nanyue embraced his scriptures in an empty tomb;
his sorrowful weeping was so poignant that Samantabhadra touched his head and silently spoke for him. He received the teachings from Guanding of the Northern Qi.

The *Lotus Sūtra* provides immediate and thorough penetration, expanding the gates of meaning for the perpetual guidance of future sages. Thus we know that those who uphold this through their past vows must belong to the ranks of those who emerged from the earth.
— Tiantai Master Zhizhe.

Having come here by virtue of being entrusted with this mandate, I now encounter you once again. You personally received the transmission from Mount Nanyue and suddenly attained profound awakening. You alone have taken the King of Sutras as your primary school;

the rain of Dharma falls in torrents, and the wondrous sound of the Perfect and Sudden teaching is the single path of a thousand sages. Alas! A master such as you, who upholds and propagates [the teaching] so extensively, may truly not fail the entrustment made at Vulture Peak.
Master Zhāng'ān Guǎndì followed the teachings and contemplations of Nāgārjuna;
Tiantái Shìchāng had masters who compiled [the teachings], causing the Dharma waves to spread ever further. Through successive hardships, he annotated the scriptures.
The snow was covered by ice beds; even a fierce fire could not heat them. His guiding cord remained forever taut.

Venerable Zhizhi (Zhiwei) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* emerged from the residence of a lay official and entered the palace of the Dharma King. As concentration and wisdom were simultaneously manifested, he attained the perfect realization of the *Lotus Sūtra*. He raised his flying staff and settled there in stillness.
The Dharma drum is struck long and deep. Why is it that what you sought was small, yet what you have obtained is so magnificent?
Could it not be that you are one who has emerged from the earth, appearing specifically through skillful means?

The chamber of the Venerable Tian-gong Huiwei of Great Majesty was vast yet secluded; only the Master entered it, where he fashioned a great Dharma-boat and courageously retired to the deep mountains.
Deer and wild boars roamed together; his movements followed the seasons, and his transformative influence spread naturally throughout the region.

Later in life, Venerable Zhang’an Lang of Zuo Xi entered Tiantai, where he mastered all its teachings without exception. He disciplined himself through the dhūta practices, drinking from mountain streams and dwelling among the crags. Beings of different species were moved by his transformation.

The Śāriputra relics hang suspended; his conduct was pure and his Way perfected. Standing out as a preeminent emblem of the faith, he inherited the family teachings and oral transmissions of the Venerable Zhanran of Jingxi.
While his Way had not yet been widely proclaimed, our Master succeeded him, bringing forth a brilliant light before him. He alone wielded the two wheels [of wisdom and compassion].
His vast influence was boundless, and his profound eloquence exhausted the mysteries of the ultimate. He raised the banner of supreme victory.
How magnificent was National Teacher Qing Sui!
How sublime was Master Jingxi! It was difficult for anyone to succeed them. Only my teacher Linghui attained a singular accord with them. Thus, the flow of the Dharma reached beyond the seas.
His brilliance illuminated the horizons, like the rising sun piercing through the darkness.

National Teacher Qingxiu was adept at entering the teachings and contemplation; his profound insights leaped forth like a bounding spring. He was earnest in his practical conduct, yet his practice was rooted in non-action. Thus he sat beneath the fly-whisk.
Divine wisdom naturally expanded; the treasury of the Golden Land shone with radiant light. When the National Temple was cleared of worldly distractions, the Venerable One presided over its destiny.
As the teachings grew dim and submerged, like clouds dispersing and birds taking flight, he stood as a solitary figure in the deep forest, wondrously entering into right concentration.
Shadows fade and dust gathers as a single thread of pulse awaits the light of dawn. National Master Qingxiu is a skilled expounder of the Dharma;
he must surely preach according to the Dharma. Whether the assembly is large or small, it leaves no trace, for the void has tongues. A monk from afar came to listen.
He prostrated himself and took his leave. As [the Master] soared into the air and smiled in farewell, he first realized that this was a bandit.

When the Tang dynasty collapsed and the various heroes vied for supremacy, who could have known that the interior lands were truly dependent upon the King? One must cultivate diligently and exert oneself even more.

In response to the transformation of the nation, lofty discourses arose like gathering clouds. Holding aloft the torch in the deep night, Venerable Jingguang of Luoxi realized his identity with Avalokiteśvara;
his illumination and function were inexhaustible. The thread that had nearly been severed relied upon this Master to flourish once more as he searched through the ancient treasuries.
From amidst the ashes, he retrieved a stray scroll from the east of the great ocean. Splendid was our Master, who was truly able to uphold his lineage:
the Venerable Yitong of Baoyun.

The eminent Fanbiao of Wei was a preeminent figure from the Eastern Sea who came to study in the Middle Kingdom. Having completed the path of the Perfect and Sudden teachings, he spread the Dharma like pervasive clouds;
his religious destiny was transcendent. Stūpas of śarīra were built in rows, as he realized the extinction of nectar-like ambrosia.
Not long after the teachings of the Fourth Patriarch,
Master Fazhi of Tiantai, had fallen into decay, there appeared a true son of the Buddha, a leader among those who cultivate wisdom, who swept away heterodox views.
He let out a lion’s roar; with but a single complete word, he subdued the mouths of the multitude.
This was the Huayan patriarch, Venerable Dushun.
The great ocean of the Avataṃsaka is so vast and boundless that it defies comparison; were it not for one of great wisdom, who could fathom its depths?
It opens the gate of the Dharma-realm and reveals the path for returning to the source. Thus we know that our Master must surely be the Lord Mañjuśrī.
The arrival of the Dharma Master Xianshou Fazang must surely have a cause.
He has burned off his fingers to establish a vow, traveling across the ocean of Vairocana to exhaustively reach the limits of the Dharma-realm, emitting light from the portals of his mouth.
The Divine Capital shook with the earth. How magnificent was our Master! His legacy shall serve as a model for ten thousand generations.

As for the excellence of Dharma Master Qingliang Chengguan’s karmic conditions, I have no leisure to fully extol them; as for the purity of his cultivated virtue, I am unable to point it out or name it.
With the ocean-like wisdom of the Dharma-realm, he has exhausted the ocean of the scriptures; how could I possibly fathom its depth?
As for my teacher, he is not merely the teacher of seven emperors, but is truly a model of conduct for ten thousand generations.
The various patriarchs of Cien, beginning with Master Xuanzang, had already experienced the lecture halls at a young age.

Renowned for their spiritual insight, they underwent arduous trials in their quest for the Dharma, entrusting their very lives to their sincere resolve; thus, they brought back more than five hundred treatises.
Reaching the highest heights and fathoming the deepest depths, the Great Teaching is here fully complete.

As the School of Characteristics (Lakṣaṇa) first flourished, Master Kuiji’s tradition of Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātra) emerged; its principles are most subtle. Xuanzang obtained its secret key—were it not for his teacher, who could have penetrated them? He composed commentaries and compiled sub-commentaries.
Directly raising its banner, it is like finding a torch in the darkness. A teacher for a hundred generations:
Master Huiyuan of Donglin, the patriarch of the Pure Land school.
Deeply entering the gateway of Prajñā, he separately opened an antique shop. Though the turbid waves overflow to the heavens, a single boat lies across the ancient ferry.
Do not say that taking a mistake for right is wrong; when has it ever not been the road to Chang’an?
Master Fazhao’s past must have had its causes; thus, the vision appeared first. Upon reaching that place, Mañjuśrī appeared face-to-face and pointed the way back to the Pure Land.
In these final ages, if one abandons this single path as a skillful means, one will only find further confusion and dizziness.

The various patriarchs of the Vinaya school, beginning with Master Xuanshi of Nanshan, were disciples for whom the Buddha ordained that they abide by the precepts. Once "mad wisdom" arose, they transgressed the boundaries and departed from this path; the Master [Daoxuan] then propagated the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
The radiance of his precepts shines afar; he is the reliance for a hundred generations and a pillar of the Dharma-gate.

Master Lingzhi Zhao mastered the three studies, taking the precepts as his foundation. Like ice and frost, he maintained his integrity with diligent practice, his virtue as steadfast as the Southern Mountains.
Master Lai Xijian succeeded him; when the conditions for the Lotus Realm ripened, celestial music was heard from afar.
Among the various patriarchs of Yoga, there was the Master Amoghavajra.
Occupying the station of consecration and wearing the seal of Vairocana, his spiritual essence responded in silent resonance, like an echo answering a call.

Mañjuśrī specifically manifested his form before him, and the Heavenly Kings also came to receive his commands. This was not merely the efficacy of secret mantras; it was truly the work of an inconceivable sage.

Master Xingxiu possessed the fivefold teachings of the Dharma. Having obtained their seals, he was popularly hailed as a sage for his mastery of the Yin-Yang system and the *chenglun* (astrological and prophetic texts).

Since his mind had already attained harmony within the gate of Mount Song, why did he linger upon the paths of other studies? From this, one knows that the wisdom and application of a great man are such that—
The mani jewel— how could it be square rather than round and reflective?
[It is like] the Sage-Saint who manifested through transformation, the National Preceptor Fotucheng.
The cruelty of the Shi clan was like that of a raging tiger; why did you, Master, come to become their guest? These hundreds and thousands of strange lights—how could they be so divine?
It was truly because you practiced benevolence toward the army, as is said of one who is familiar with seagulls. Yet, they had not yet grasped the Master’s true heart.
Master Huiyue was this great bodhisattva manifesting in the body of a bhikṣu; his precepts arose from his innate nature—how could his supernormal powers have been achieved through cultivation?
Serving as the teacher to emperors and presiding over the great dharma covenant, he was the peer of Master Zhi; his fragrance remains for a thousand years.

The Great Being Baozhi came from an eagle's nest; his extraordinary traces were unfathomable. Emperor Wu of Liang understood him quite well through their close association, yet how could he help but recognize him by his physical form?

Thus, he could not avoid having his face torn open; why should it have hindered him from revealing his entire being? It was only because Gu Kaizhi was no true master that [the painting] failed to capture him.
Causing the clouds for a thousand *li* to darken;

when the Great Master Hanshan sees the people of this world, they appear like the wind or like madmen; when you see these people of the world, they are laughable and pitiable. Sing aloud beneath the pines.

Striking palms by the roadside, a solitary figure against a cold cliff; the grass grows long and the mist is cool. Fortunately, there are Fenggan and Shide, so that everyone may ascend together to the theater.
Thus spoke the Great Being Shide.
Without lineage and without abiding—this is precisely it. When encountered and pressed by others, one’s flaws are exposed in no small measure. Hanshan joins the beat;
laughter and weeping cannot cease. Since he returned to the cold crags, to this day the cool moon shines upon the autumn grasses.
Buddha Bagu’s only possession is this cloth bag. It confuses and deludes many people; whenever he encounters someone, he begs from them. For what reason?
Even if he meets a master who challenges him, the master can do nothing with him. Alas! Let the ancient eccentricities be as they are; one must simply not mistake him for [the Buddha].
The Buddha of the Future.

In the stone grotto of the Elder Long-ear, with its pine-clad doors, the mind delights in practicing asceticism; a hundred birds find their refuge here, and celestial flowers may rain down. For this reason, it is not transmitted [to others].
This is the marvel of its spiritual powers being universally pervasive. Let all you monks with eyes look upon it together!
Master Jidian did not abide by his proper lot;
he was sevenfold fallen and eightfold deranged, churning up the world and deceiving both earth and heaven—let him turn it over until it is exhausted.
The old nest: when has one ever escaped these entanglements? Fleeing back to Tiantai, he could not hide his clumsiness; yet his empty fame continues to be passed down to this day.
From the *Extensive Record of Master Yongjue*, Volume Twenty.
The Expanded Record of Master Yongjue, Scroll Twenty-One.
Compiled by the Dharma-heir Dao-pai.
Various Eulogies.
The praise of Amitābha Buddha is simply this very thing. If you call it "Amitābha," then if it were that [Ultimate Reality], what would you call it?

He provides a precious raft made of floating flowers to receive those dwelling in the illusory Sahā world. To manifest the pure and the defiled is all a scene of self-deception; to abandon the defiled and hasten toward the pure—
In a dream, he crosses a great river. If he encounters a man with an iron forehead and copper eyes, he will certainly follow his own way and not comply with him.
Now tell me: is this rebirth or not rebirth? Alas! Wang the Great of East Village has no clever schemes; he rides a stone horse backward across Silla.

Śākyamuni Buddha praised all the Bhagavans of the three periods of time, saying: "Only our Śākyamuni Tathāgata is most rare and extraordinary. He descended to take birth specifically in a realm difficult to endure;
he took the five turbidities as the path for returning to the source. Though born into the imperial palace in a position of supreme honor, he cast it aside with effortless ease."

He treats worn-out sandals as if they were [the most precious things], demonstrating that he knows his original nature is inherently noble; how could the petty honors of the mundane world ever be equal to it?

He marries and fathers children according to the ways of men, yet at once he cuts them away as if severing silk threads, demonstrating that he knows emotional attachment is a great affliction; thus, at the primary gateway of restoring one's original nature, he severs it first.
He wanders extensively among external paths and personally penetrates through them all; knowing they are not the way, he abandons them with clarity and resolve. This demonstrates his knowledge.

Those dharmas are not ultimate; practicing through kalpas until one's efforts are exhausted is all in vain. For six years on Mount Himavat, Śākyamuni endured the snow covering the thousand peaks without even noticing.
This demonstrates that refining the Way requires diligent effort; once the thorns of the emotional faculties and views are severed, one attains liberation.
Upon seeing the morning star, he attained great enlightenment; greatly amazed and slightly startled, he proclaimed himself a Buddha.

He demonstrated that there is a direct cause for attaining Buddhahood, which is not achieved through forced cultivation or realization external to the mind. Within the Bodhimanda, his original intent was fully realized, like the rising sun shining upon a high mountain.

To accommodate the various capacities of sentient beings, he opened up skillful means; concealing his precious robes as a temporary expedient, he donned tattered garments. Thus, at Deer Park, he first turned the wheel of Dharma.
The Wheel of the Four Truths: as soon as Ājñātakauṇḍinya struck the rhythm, the command was fulfilled. From this point on, the Triple Gem has dwelt in the world;

its radiance blazes forth, illuminating all things. Whether teaching gradually, suddenly, or through the Perfect [Dharma], it rains down transformation according to capacities, saving beings boundlessly.
Without distinction between the three types of grass or two kinds of wood, every single thing touched by it flourishes and thrives. The dharma-waves of the Golden River flow without end. Until...
Now the remaining moisture still drips steadily; a single drop, barely touched, penetrates the very source. Its light swallows the ten voids—whom could dare to rival it?
The ocean of the Buddha’s merit is like the sands of all realms; yet my praise of a single mote of dust has already been thus.

The merit in every mote of dust is vast and immeasurable; even with my tongue-organ, I cannot reach its limit. Even if all the Great Awakened Ones throughout the Dharma-realm were to each diligently produce—
With a long tongue, one might speak in verse for a full hundred thousand years; yet even praising my Śākyamuni Buddha, it would be difficult to exhaust [the description].
Reflecting deeply, I and Śākyamuni have been no different throughout immeasurable kalpas. He wanders through the defiled lands like a lotus flower, while I am mired in the mud, unable to emerge.
There has never been the slightest decrease or increase; it is merely from delusion and awakening that the distinction between ordinary and sage is made. If one is deluded...

When the mind turns back, it becomes external objects; turbid waves strike the heavens, impossible to cross. To awaken is to realize that external objects are entirely but the mind—a perfect sphere, radiantly shining, a mass of brilliance.
Ultimately, delusion and awakening do not interfere with one another; both the paths of purity and defilement are decisively cut off.
The Dharmakāya’s laughter shatters all withered stumps; how can one speak of the phrase that transcends? I now bow my head and question Śākyamuni:
Śākyamuni lowers his eyes and closes his tongue. I only pray that body and mind may serve every dust-mote world, universally causing all sentient beings to attain Buddhahood.

Eulogy for the Image of the Buddha Emerging from the Mountains: The empty mountains are steep and precipitous; frozen clouds have not yet parted. His form resembles withered wood; his tongue is long, covered in deep moss.

Sitting there, solid and unmoving, he lets the world’s doubts and suspicions fall upon him. When he beheld the bright stars at night, he could not contain his own laughter. Unable to restrain his amusement, he sighed once more: "How marvelous!"
Reflecting three times upon this great matter, I have come out from the mountains once more. *Duh!* For forty-nine years I have been muddling along;
to this day, my face is covered in dust.
Praise for Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva (Two Verses)
When one observes with the eye, the nature of hearing is inherently empty; when sound encounters the eye, the nature of sound is inherently extinguished.

Both sound and hearing are quiescent, and there is only this single mind. The solitary light is transcendent and detached, yet it does not abandon sound and hearing; both are universally pervasive, such that nothing is not perfectly penetrating.
As it is with one faculty, so it is with all faculties; they illuminate one another and function interchangeably, their spiritual subtlety being inconceivable.

With eighty-four thousand hands and eyes manifested simultaneously, he is thus called the Great Compassionate One. His virtues are immeasurable, and appearing in response to the capacities of beings in this region, he is foremost among them.
The power of sublime contemplation is the teacher of this bodhisattva; as a disciple making offerings, you ought to examine that teacher.
If you find that teacher, it is true offering.
She is not a woman on the sands of Jinshe; nor is she a traveler by the cliffs of Putuo.
When this old monk sees her half-nosed visage, he perceives her as nothing but an old thief who has no home within the ten realms.

The Praise of the Three Great Beings: The three elders meet; what do they speak of? To prove south as north—what can one do about them? Let them join together and fabricate with their lips and tongues;
it is all but a single *kaṇṭhāra* (nonsense). Even until now, the poison has not ceased; look at this—it is not even a single character.
It forms many. I beg you to grasp the phrase "not yet arisen" and do not concern yourself with waves on windless water.

The Great Being Mañjuśrī praised him, bowing his head to the Great Being who is the eldest son of the Buddha; whose light of wisdom shines everywhere, he is truly the mother of all Buddhas, manifesting her shadow throughout the Sahā world.
The Buddha Śākyamuni, the Good Minister, sits upon the lion throne and beats the drum of poisoned lacquer.
Eulogy on the Bag-Holder Monk (Two Verses) I do not value you for your grinning face; I do not value you for your sagging belly; I do not value you...
Your physical stature is stout and robust; I do not value your chest being so vast and open. I only value how you carry this cloth bag, unaware of the passing years.
Everywhere you meet people, you beg for a single coin; in your foolish persistence, you never find the time to stop.
You linger even in brothels and wine shops. How vast indeed is your compassionate heart! You gather it all back into the cloth bag, leaving no center or periphery. Even so—

It is so. If the conduit lets down the cloth bag, how else can one offer praise? One can only bow one's head and take refuge in the Venerable Maitreya, who has truly large stomachs and broad intestines;
it seems there is no realm he does not contain within. I do not yet know when this vow will be fulfilled.
It can only end in a fit of "he-he" laughter.
Regarding the encomium for Hanshan and Shide:
wearing tattered clothes and with soiled faces, their hair disheveled and unkempt, they hold brooms and look back—what is this for? It is for the sake of those worldly people.
The deluded and the ignorant are many; they stubbornly cling to empty shadows as the bait for calamity. One must simply sweep them away to avoid such wasted efforts.
Words alone are insufficient, so I follow them with a mournful song. If this mournful song finds no resonance, there is nothing that can be done. Grief turns to laughter.
Clapping hands with "ha ha" laughter, I mock those who pursue the trivial. It is like a moth burning itself. Alas! Beyond the gates of Guoqing, the streams and mountains are ancient;
to this day, the bright moon hangs amidst the pines and vines.

In the *Praise of the Venerable Śūnyatā-ja*, since he is named "Born of Emptiness" (*Śūnyatā-ja*), how can there be characteristics? Are they characteristics or emptiness? Are they one or two? Thus, all conceptual attachments are shattered.
To shatter the Tathāgatagarbha, one need not concern oneself with the rain of flowers before the crags; simply take up the staff in hand.
Though it is called the Azure Dragon of the East, it is nonetheless just this very appearance.
Eulogy on the Eighteen Arhats. For the Golden Immortal Hermitage:
If you point with your finger, what does it point to? Is it the Buddha? What is the Buddha? If you point to the mind, what is not the mind? A single finger is perfectly clear.
How utterly laughable! For a thousand years he has been nothing more than a wild fox spirit. Is there anyone who can speak on behalf of this Venerable One?
During the Tang dynasty, however, there was indeed the old Juzhi.
Holding this scroll in his hand— obtained directly from the Buddha himself, its patterns and colors already manifest, like ink revealed within charcoal.
*Du!* Better to take it before the hall and burn it with fire, so as not to let people see the stolen goods and catch the thief.
A single staff to lean upon; its illumination and function cannot be divided. It carries one across the waters of the broken bridge and accompanies one back to the moonless village.
Yet, it is better not to rely on it. Why? Because viewed with the correct eye, it is not worth half a penny.
Brushing aside the eyebrows—parting the long brows—to see clearly face-to-face. Alas, how can one avoid delusion? Still, nothing is seen.
Whether you see or do not see, do not seek lightning in the sky.
Entering meditative absorption in stillness, he heard no sound; celestial flowers fell in profusion, and he was the very first to see the Buddha. For a time, he was deluded by heat.
Such evil forms and demeanors as these can only be relegated to the realms of humans and devas, destined forever to serve as fields of merit for others.

Palms joined, palms joined at the chest—whom do you take refuge in? If you say you see the Buddha, you have clearly fallen into a trap of words; even if you say you do not see him, you cannot avoid being at fault.
Alas! Look at these hands joined at the chest; it is truly not as good as casting them loose and lying long in sleep.
The sounding of the *qing*, the sounding of the *qing*—with a single stroke, the great earth sinks level, the marrow of emptiness is revealed, and the dragon roars from the withered tree.
Yet, were you to come before this mountain monk’s gate, there is much more to it than that; for he perceives only its shadow, not its true form.
Washing the ears, washing the ears to remove dust—this merely results in self-defilement. Though it may be "perfect penetration," it is sevenfold wrong and eightfold mistaken;
it is precisely here that one ought to deliver a punch straight to the chest, regardless of whether you have received the personal instructions of Vulture Peak.
The Dragon-subduing [Śakra] emerges from the ocean; his spiritual transformations are unfathomable. To be like a *hudigū* is not considered extraordinary.
Since it is like a *hudigū*, why is it not considered extraordinary? I ask this of the "White-robbery Thieves" of the Tang era.
The fierce tiger, cowed, loses its majesty and submits in docility. When one wishes to ride it, one mounts it as easily as if crossing a young calf.
Yet, for a monk who has attained his true measure, what use is there for such a beast? Have you not heard it said: "The songs of Ba are not the melodies of Yangchun"?
Leaning on the armrest, I ask the Venerable One: "Is there anything upon which you rely? If there is something upon which you rely, why do you need this?
If there is nothing upon which you rely, what use is this? Therefore, when a monk takes up the command, he cannot help but break it with a single punch. Nevertheless...
Within the gateway of Buddha-work:
formerly one would kneel and request instruction; now one sits with knees drawn up. For many years we have deliberated on this matter in vain, as if—
Having become habituated to indolence, one must now cease this indolence. Since the time these were entrusted at Vulture Peak, I have not been able to clear away these stagnant burdens.
I shall mend my robes.
Gautama’s old patched robe—each fragment cut from clouds and mended together. Weighing seven catties when held, it wraps around a slender waist-drum.
Is there anyone here who wishes to recognize Old Gautama? It is simply this.

Regarding this single scroll of scripture you are reading: from the beginning, it has not been permitted to be turned over. Day and night you have peered through the paper window; being too close, it has instead become distant.
After all, do you truly intend to turn this one scroll? When the eye behind the head opens, the autumn clouds across the great earth will roll away.
Performing the lion dance—perform the lion dance! How many acts have you performed? Six is precisely one; one is precisely six. A skilled hand returns to that veteran master;
amidst the deep white clouds, he is hidden away in a cave of *dhyāna*.

If one were to transcribe this single scroll of scripture using Mount Sumeru as a brush and the great ocean as ink, would it be possible to finish writing it even though all of space were completely filled?
Nevertheless, today, from the tip of the brush, light is emitted that shakes the earth; those who behold it are the *siddhas*.
The guest,
with his bag slung over his broad belly, opened the cloth sack and begged a single coin from every person he met to repay the debts of his past lives at the wine shop.
He mingles with the brothels; everywhere he goes, there is no obstruction. Ha ha! At the crossroads, a scene of total ruin.
The Pagoda-Bearer’s precious stupa comes from the west, startling heaven and shaking the earth. Its strange radiance lasts for a hundred autumns; those who see it find it impossible to fathom.
Do not attempt to deliberate upon this; I fear these are not the relics of King Aśoka.
*Dharmabhadra* (Three Verses):

The old barbarian who came from the West was utterly confused. When Emperor Wu of Liang questioned him about the primary principle (*paramārtha*), he spoke out with great audacity, leaving everything wide open.
Yet there is none. Again he says, "I do not know; it resembles a silver mountain. The entire nation has missed the mark and stands there hesitating;
they can only go in secret across the Long River. For nine years he faced the wall, his mouth silent like that of a donkey.

This heap of stagnant goods—whom will it sell to? On a snowy night, even the marrow of his mind was exhausted. Looking back, even before he had set foot in the Western Heaven, he deserves thirty blows. Why?
Therefore, he established models and patterns for posterity:

crossing the river on a single reed, facing the wall for nine years—when one attempts to deliberate upon it, it cannot be grasped; even the thousand sages cannot recognize it. Its lingering poison has spread throughout China.
To this day it has not ceased. What excellence is there?
A single pair of worn-out sandals, heaped up as he faces the wall—what could he possibly say? To have "attained the marrow" after three prostrations is nothing but a scene of utter failure.
Transmitting the empty and receiving the echoes down to this day is like adding further ripples to the water.
Eulogy on the Diagram of the Three Teachings:
The Three Elders emerge like flakes of ice and sleet, cleaving through the void; with their three-inch tongues, what have they accomplished?
To mistake a tortoise for a turtle—once they have gathered together in one place, what more remains to be said?
Master Daguan praised him, saying:
"His bones are like steel; his spirit is like a rainbow. He shoulders the Great Dharma and exerts the strength to revitalize declining customs, as if protecting a sovereign or a parent."

How could he have looked to his own person? Though he encountered such hardship, his loyalty to the Dharma gate was such that, when the end of the age had become frivolous and thin and the纲 (regulations) of the Dharma had long since collapsed, it relied upon the Master to revitalize them; thus the surging waves were suddenly turned back, as he focused his mind with single-minded devotion.

He returned to the Pure Land, propagating the myriad practices to spread profound compassion. Thus we know that the Master was truly a pillar of his era and a guiding standard for ten thousand generations.
Eulogies for the Three Great Masters Yunqi, Shouchang, and Zhenji:

These three masters emerged together, like the sun illuminating the dark alleys of the world. Whether through Chan or through the Teachings, their paths differed while their destination was the same; they inherited the legacy of the past and opened the way for the future.
He has established an excellent model for all. Although I am not quick-witted, I wish to emulate him, yet have not yet succeeded.
Eulogy on Master Shouchang (Two Verses):
In a single stroke, he leveled the Great Good Mountain; Casually, he leaped through the Patriarch’s Barrier. Fifty years of plowing the rain and tilling the clouds—
Carrying [the staff], he never had the intention to enter the dusty world. His iron bones soar into the void, beyond compare; on the bird-path where no one else travels, he goes and returns alone.
A single staff is as lively as a dragon; to this day, it flows of its own accord at the mouth of the cave.
This old monk has no basis at all; he points east while speaking of the west, truly lacking any principle.
He disturbs sentient beings, raising waves where there is no wind. Having established more than twenty monasteries, he drove ghosts and commanded the winds.

For over fifty years, he filled pits and dug into the earth, yet at the final moment, his entire edifice collapses. Then he says, "Today I have clearly pointed it out. Is this not merely following after the Great [Vehicle]?
"Have you passed over the fine mountains? "Tsk! Do not attempt to deliberate within this.
Master Boshan praised him:
"He cut off the roadhead at Mount Yushan and settled his nostrils upon Mount Emei; from within a brocade pouch, he wafts forth something extraordinary."
Fragrance. Drilling a hole upon the face of empty space; firmly grasping the iron gate, it does not open for a moment.
At the end, who will be able to follow in his footsteps? By the Layman Teng Xiushi (two verses).
Exquisite and radiant; exquisite and substantial. Though this was but a fine dream, what need is there to seek it further upon awakening?
Having studied the Way for eight years, he suddenly passed into stillness. What is to be rejoiced in is that his resolve to inquire into the Way was but recently diligent;

what is to be lamented is that his practice of the Way was not yet complete. Nevertheless, the final song is left to you as the long-lasting legacy: sitting cross-legged, he departed toward the west with clarity and lucidity.
An old crane tramples over the nest atop the pine; Carrying the moon, it flies back home, yet no one recognizes it.
In this single dream of Jambudvīpa, who awakens first? The five desires, layer upon layer, naturally form their own bonds.

The Master had a hundred thousand strings of cash wrapped around his waist, And once more he rode upon a crane from Yangzhou. At the moment of death, he clapped his hands and sang "Returning Home," As the lion suddenly snapped the yellow...
A golden cord—resembling that of Feng Jichuan in years past—cannot avoid taking error for error. He sits steadily upon a lotus as vast as a wheel;
five-colored jewel-radiance reflects and dazzles one another. Celestial robes flutter and soar, brilliant as clouds and rainbows;
upon the ground of lapis lazuli, the music of heaven is heard. How many in this world vie to be heroes? Yet, when viewed, you have lost to him on the final move. Still remains...
This one is here in Saha; a ladleful of foul water is splashed right upon his head.
Eulogy by the Layman Lin Deshan, Military Commissioner:

Your nature is preeminently bold and spirited; Magnanimous and lofty, you are called a peerless hero. Your mind and chest are transparently free of worldly things; Your liver and gall are laid bare before others.

In times of sorrow, you alone submitted a memorial to rebuke the scales of authority; your heroic ambition was set on settling the dust of the Hu. You ensured the military provisions for the three frontiers were sufficient, and the defense of the perilous city struck terror into ten thousand barbarians.

The North Gate’s lock and key could have been entrusted to you, yet, having suffered slander, you shook out your sleeves at the edge of the Eastern Sea. Repeatedly you vowed to don the black robes and strike the stone drum;

why then do you linger here, bringing shame upon the mountain spirits? The achievements of Han and Fan— (Note: The final line "Han Van Gong Ye" (The Achievements of Han and Fan) appears to be a fragmentary title or reference to the great deeds of the Song statesmen Han Qi and Fan Zhongyan.)

Where are they now? Calculatedly, one wins nothing but a hollow reputation. Had you waited until your achievements were complete before withdrawing from the world, the clouds among the rocky crags would have laughed at you.
The entire world is intoxicated by fame and profit; alas, there is no one who can be called "the only one wide awake.
I shall now clear the stones upon the mountain peak in advance, awaiting you to play together upon the stringless zither.
Eulogy for Layman Chen Zhongmou, Attendant Lecturer:
How few are there like you, steadfast and upright? A single branch of cold plum blossoms amidst the snow is spring itself. Clad in black robes, you gaze alone at the moon before the crag;
Yet you are truly a loyal minister of bone and marrow from a former dynasty.

Eulogy for the Woodcutter of Deshan (With Preface) The woodcutter’s surname was Yang, his given name Fengjing, and his courtesy name Taiyu. Deshan was the place where he lived in seclusion. Born of noble lineage, he mingled his traces among the ranks of Chan practitioners.
As for his cultivation of the mind and regulation of conduct, many virtuous men of the month-evaluation (the community) praised him. Yet, despite being virtuous, he remained poor.
Furthermore, it is precisely because of his poverty that his worth is made even more manifest; thus, was his poverty not indeed a blessing?
His descendant, Yi-fan, possesses the character of his father and has requested a eulogy for his portrait. I say: a man such as this layman may well serve as a model for others.
I have scribbled these few words to satisfy his request.
Deep is his inner heart; serene is his outward countenance. He abides in virtue with richness; he nurtures virtue with humility. In the prime of his years, he took delight in the Way.

He further obscured his own person, taking pleasure in giving without weariness; yet in his later years, he became even more impoverished. He resolved his will upon the Western Land, as certain as water flowing eastward.

At the end of life, he passed away with serene detachment, like a wild goose crossing the vast sky. Alas, the Layman! Was it not that while his acquisition of material things was frugal, his acquisition of the Way was profound?
Self-Appraisal (Thirty-nine Verses):
My present condition is most loathsome. I do not raise the whisk, nor do I wield the staff; I sit upon a seat of withered wood.

Speaking Chinese with barbarian tongues, reviling Buddhas and cursing patriarchs, deceiving the earth and defrauding heaven, they drummed up empty rhetoric to delude later students. Eightfold inversions and sevenfold perversions;
the mountain does not reveal its peak, the moon hides half its face. Although there is absolutely no principle here, it nonetheless does not betray the transmission of Cao-Dong.
In the fleeting passage of half a lifetime, having reached the age of fifty, whenever I encounter people, my malice erupts without any sense of restraint or taboo.

I revile all the hundred sages and thousand worthies, claiming that I am merely venting the indignation of the Buddhas on their behalf. My speech never touches upon the classical scriptures, and my every movement is as frivolous as a child’s play;
I am truly a disturber of heaven and earth, leaving it to gods and men to loathe and cast me aside. Is this not the "separate transmission outside the teachings"?
"Ha! Elder brother Kāśyapa, you have not yet reached it either (at the request of Baishuiyan).
Chiyin has spent eight years at Heshan, yet he dares not drive a stake into empty space. While everywhere people talk grandly of Chan, here one hides one's head like a turtle.
Every year one plants rice to buy food, willingly taking gold for iron. This is clearly half [of the truth]."

The writing is not straightforward. How can one claim it is the direct bloodline of Shouchang? It is because "much falsehood is not as good as little truth," and "a thousand clevernesses are not as good as one simplicity" (as requested by Heshan).
I am not you; yet you are me. A breeze in spring; a cloud in autumn. The *huangyang* tree’s Zen: a lock with no seams.
This year I have entered the city of Wénlíng, like a turtle limping through the mud.
*Ei!* The tangerine peels of Wēnzhōu are not fire. (At Kāiyuán Monastery, he was invited.)

This old fellow has spent his life as a "Du-tian" (a scholar of the fields of knowledge), never having understood how to study the Buddhas or the Patriarchs; he only knows how to stretch out his legs and strike while sleeping.
When someone questions him, he has nothing to say in response, yet he claims that this is the "separate transmission outside the teachings. Ha ha!
He once walked across Shouchang Bridge, yet from the beginning, half of his nostrils have been missing.
This old beggar! How base and incapable he is! He resembles neither those of antiquity nor those of today; both ordinary people and sages alike loathe him.
He overturns the teachings of the Tripitaka and extinguishes the lamps of the five houses. What excellence does he possess? A shaven-headed monk, that’s all.
This fellow is ignorant; he cannot even distinguish between the characters for "pig" and "boar. He turns his head and refuses to speak of the lineage of Shouchang;
he lifts his feet and tramples through the precepts of the Xiaoxi River. It is all nothing but employing ghosts to drive the wind, allowing him to buy high and sell low at will.
He has gained a hollow reputation in the world solely because he has failed to repay his debts in Jambudvīpa. (At the Request of Zhenji Monastery)
A single cloud over Mount Gu; a drop of foam on the Teao River. He is but a ruined ordinary man; how could he discuss Chan or the Way?
Do not offer him worship; it is best to bury him deep in a snowy pit (at the invitation of Zhenji Monastery).
He shattered the gate of Nanquan and galloped out from the stable of Shouchang; with not a single speck remaining in his breast, he went everywhere speaking in all manner of ways.
Now he drifts along the curves of the Xiaoxi River, taking a sand basin for a precious vessel of jade.
Although he has presided over three monasteries, he lets himself roam like an empty boat. Do not say that he is merely a spiritual friend to five hundred people.
Yet it is all merely floating and temporary.
To stride across the crowns of all Buddhas, one borrows strength from the blow of Shouchang’s staff; yet it remains on the lips, drumming up right and wrong.
Having a mouth but no mind, there is nothing to avoid or shy away from. Hehe! Who can see even half of its nose?
This fellow is ignorant; there is no Chan within his belly. He recklessly grasps the whisk to deceive gods and men.
Having appeared in the world for only four years and presided over the hall for merely two, he has already begun to shrink his head and pass his days, always fond of stretching out his legs to sleep.
He falsely claims to be the legitimate son of Shouchang; upon closer inspection, he is not worth half a cent.
He casts his line in the Shaoxi River and beats the drum on Mount Gu; he possesses not a single iota of Buddha-dharma, yet he insists on reviling the Buddhas and cursing the Patriarchs.
While the treasures of all quarters are like gold, he flatly disparages them as mere dung and soil. Why does he act so contrary to human sentiment?
It is simply because the bitter gourd is bitter from root to tip.
At the peak of Shigufeng, a scene of total ruin; by the banks of the Tiexi, the family tradition is utterly lost. Whenever meeting people, he specializes in feigned ignorance;
he does nothing but point west when it is east. Now that he has been sketched upon paper, it turns out he is merely an old bald monk.
He met with poison beneath Huanglong Peak; he lost his entire body on the banks of the Yanjin Ferry.
Now his shadow remains in Shayang—take care not to mistake the false for the true.
At the peak of Shigushan, they cast their nets to catch the wind; by the banks of the Tiaoxi, they lower their rods to fish for the moon.

Looking at this, it is all a scene of futility and confusion. It would be better to keep one’s mouth shut and hide one’s tongue, willingly remaining uninitiated for five years, truly being "stupidly and steadfastly simple.
When meeting such a person, do not ask about his lineage; he is not a drop of blood from Caoxi.
This old beggar—what manner of being is he? The three realms cannot contain him; empty space cannot measure him. Without cause, his shadow falls upon the world;
let him be as he is, receiving the offerings of devas and humans.

Having mistakenly entered this great and wondrous mountain, I have ventured to act with the boldness of one who "does not yield when it comes to benevolence. Yet, there is not a single speck of the Buddha-dharma here;
one knows only the ten-foot and the ten-cubit.
A blank sheet of paper may bear some resemblance [to reality], but alas, how can it withstand the defilement of brush and ink? The moon’s reflection in a still pool is not the truth.
Truly! Let all of you indulge yourselves in vain conjecture.
Who can paint my likeness? My features are no different [from others]: in my right hand I grasp a staff, and in my left I hold a rosary.
This results in far too much complication. Why bother with such trivialities? It is better to let go of both hands; only then can one recognize him.
To recognize him is simply to see that he is but a single-headed donkey.
A single sheet of white clouds atop the towering peaks; a single line of fishing line along the banks of the Tiāoxī River.

Neither do you enter the six realms of ordinary beings, nor are you seen by the four classes of sages. Leave it to others to try to paint it out; even so, it is merely a broken fan on a scorching day.
Mistakenly entering the gate of Shouchang, I presumptuously succeeded to the seat of Xingsheng. On the road through the night, who can say where it leads?
Holding alone a single *zhilin* staff amidst the clouds—how many know how to grasp it crosswise or hold it upright? Thoroughly and completely, there is no news at all.
"Alas, you old beggar! You do not recognize the Chan of Bodhidharma. In vain you receive the offerings of devas and humans, lying high on your back amidst the white clouds.
At times you brandish a fly-whisk, deceiving both earth and heaven. When others have sketched you out in all your confusion, looking at you, you are truly pitiable."
Old and ignorant, what am I capable of? Neither ordinary nor holy, I am loathed by men. Do not say I am the legitimate heir of Shouchang;
I am merely a bald-headed old monk.
This old fellow has nothing to say; sitting upright atop Shigufeng Peak, he clearly possesses but a single peg.

He blinds the eyes of all sentient beings, painting a cake and pointing to it as the moon. Do not say that he has attained Dongshan Chan; deep within the white clouds, he simply guards his simplicity forever.
A single spoonful of water creates waves; raising the whisk, he dares to deceive the thousand sages. Shattering empty space, there is nothing to compare it to;
even the ten realms find it difficult to contain.
Beneath the bridge over Li River, he parts the waves seeking water; atop the precipitous peaks, he raises his net to catch the wind.
Utterly devoid of human form, he points west and calls it east. Merely ignorant and driven by his lips and tongue, he deceives people, claiming this is the Dongshan school.
Entering the Shouchang Gate, he followed in the martial footsteps of Dongshan; he spread the waves of the Tiexi and beat the drums of Mount Gu.

In a casual laugh, he shattered the five houses of the lineage; herein, not even a single Buddha or Patriarch can find entry. It is merely an empty fist used to deceive small children, taking pure gold and calling it earth.
A mediocre monk from Shouchang, presumptuously occupying the head of Gushan; failing to grasp the meaning beyond the teachings, he sees a horse and calls it an ox.

He topples the banners and spears of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, forging enmity with the seven assemblies of disciples. To his eyes, the vast ocean is but a trifle, and both ordinary beings and sages alike are filled with sorrow.
The stone drum has been lightly struck for fourteen autumns; it causes both the mundane and the sagely to fall into sorrow.
How much better to lie peacefully within the deep clouds, leaving the mountains high and the waters flowing as they may.
At seventy years of age, he was utterly deluded; when questioned on Chan, he could not understand, and when questioned on the Teachings, he knew nothing.

He possessed nothing more than a single fly-whisk, which he held crosswise or upright, causing people to harbor doubts. Such a hollow old fellow—were the thousand Buddhas to hear of him, they would knit their brows.
Yet he himself took pride in it, claiming that this was the final branch held aloft at Vulture Peak.
The traveler atop the precipitous peaks has no ordinary rules or patterns. His opening of the mouth is not mere speech; neither ordinary beings nor sages can fathom it.
Thief! Thief! Neither this eastern land nor the western realm can contain him.

This old bhikṣu is a thief within the Dharma-gate. Occupying the seat of Xingsheng, he speaks of yellow paths and white ways, destroying the ancestral legacy of the Buddha and severing the life-veins of the multitude.
Now that he is old, he becomes even more reckless; toppling and tumbling, he has no standard of conduct.
Having swindled all the offerings of the world, he will find it difficult to escape the reprimand of Old Yan. Heh!
The ordinary monk of this vast world does not recognize the Buddhas and Patriarchs; he carries a single wooden board across his shoulders, being neither of this age nor of antiquity.

Clinging to a single, narrow perspective without flexibility, he is truly both foolish and dull-witted. Let others laugh and revile him as they will; he remains silent, granting only himself permission.

The solitary wind of Shouchang rose majestically like ten-thousand-fathom cliffs. Gushan attained it and continued to propagate its command. It stirred the waves of Dongshan’s waters and emerged from the pit of Caoshan.
Unaware of the orthodox and the deviant, it gave rise to the illnesses of sentient beings. How many know the golden needle and jade thread?
This is called the life-force of the wisdom of all Buddhas.
At the peak of the towering Lishu peaks is a decrepit bhikṣu who values not his own spiritual nature and seeks not the company of the sages.
Opening his mouth, he singles out Buddhas and patriarchs for abuse as if they were bitter enemies. He cooks rice with no grain and rows a boat with no bottom;
he is truly a monk who has lost his way. Yet he claims that the waters of Dongting Lake flow upstream.
Within the great round mirror, this sudden thing—were you to say it is "him" or "me," you would immediately miss the mark;
were you to say it is neither holy nor ordinary, that too is a lapse into idle talk. When the Boatman hid his body, who could have discerned him? When Dongshan beheld his reflection...
Only then can one truly bear this responsibility. Dao-shun, how could you possibly maintain this? It would be better to spit right in his face (as requested by Attendant Shun).
Shou-chang rose up like a mountain; Dong-shui stirred up waves. Bo-shan followed them, like rivers and streams. What kind of person am I?
He also sang "Li Luo. Three pieces of firewood were arranged in the shape of the character "Pin" (品). Jade and stone were nearly indistinguishable; even now, his shadow remains in this world.
Let those who laugh laugh, and let those who scold scold. (To the right: the three portraits of Shouchang, Boshan, and the Master on a single axis.)
An old bald monk atop the towering peaks, for many years has reclined amidst the white clouds.
When someone asks him about the meaning of the Westward Journey, he smiles and points toward the sun rising in the east.
This old fellow Du Man Chan claims he lived before the time of Vipaśyin Buddha. Shaking his head, he disbelieves the Buddhas and Patriarchs;
in his view, the Five Houses of Chan are not worth half a penny. His mouth is fond of stirring up waves where there is no wind, teaching people to dig into the earth to seek the heavens.
One who acts with such inverted karma of speech would do better to learn from a simpleton: when hungry, eat.

Sleeping when weary; in my youth, I studied the teachings of the East (Confucianism). I vowed to emulate the former sages. In my middle years, I yearned for the West (Buddhism), my ambition no longer resting in the realms of humans or devas.
Having gathered the dust of Shouchang, I have imitated his style in preaching Chan. From beginning to end, four kalpas have passed; for twenty years, I have handled and played with these matters.

Warning the world, I have often spoken with bitter words; protecting the Way is the intent of these various chapters. A lifetime is but a dream within a dream; illusory forms are merely solemn appearances.

Dwelling as a guest in Jambudvīpa for eighty years, half my life’s traces have been by the white clouds. To utter a thousand words from the mouth that deceive the Buddhas and Patriarchs—when looked upon, they are not worth even half a coin.

This old fellow is too biased by nature; he carries a single, stubborn plank across his shoulders. He does not believe in the Chan of Bodhidharma, yet whenever he meets someone, he likes to stir up windless waves.
He tells others to dig into the earth to seek the heavens. Having reached the age of eighty, what has he accomplished?
His laughter has split half the mouth of empty space.
This old man has now reached eighty years of age; all worldly affairs have been gathered up and put away.
Only this shadow remains, spreading throughout all directions—its exposure is so profound that even layers of concealment cannot suffice. Do you know it? Within the body of form is the formless body;

only by bowing one’s head can it be seen clearly and distinctly. (The Master sat in his quarters on the day before his passing to receive the prostrations of the assembly. A monk who held a portrait of the Master and sought a eulogy had him write these words.)
The Extensive Record of Master Yongjue, Volume Twenty-one;
The Extensive Record of Master Yongjue, Volume Twenty-two.
Re-edited by the Dharma-heir Disciple Dao-pai.

The verse above shows Layman Zhang closing his Persian eyes and chewing raw iron; the ten realms of sages and ordinary beings are all extinguished at once. Suddenly, he chews it through, and blood flows.
Dripping away. A mute swallowing his voice—whom would he tell? Shining through heaven and piercing the earth, it is universal radiance;
on every terrace and tower hangs the autumn moon. It illuminates and shatters the gates of east, west, south, and north; Maitreya is originally nothing but a dry dung-club.
There are certain masters who measure and speculate about this, like seeking a flake of snow upon a red-hot furnace. Having once crossed the Shauchang Bridge, one finally recognizes the void.
Emptiness is not color. Master Zhang has pursued the Way for many years; now, let all that was before be set aside. Do not concern yourself with whether demons or Buddhas arrive;
look inward with full intent and tie it within your breast. Upon Dingguang Rock, waves overturn the void;
this is precisely the time to seek the drop of blood at Caoxi. Do not let your physical vessel be busy at both ends; an iron man must always decide for himself.
All day long he manages a single game of chess; when the game ends, his great skill turns into clumsiness.
On his departure, he unconsciously becomes far too talkative—how laughable, like driving another wedge into the void.
Sitting at Night on Jade Furnace Peak. Seeing the Moon Rise over the Paper Window, I Compose Two Verses (on the night of the eighteenth day of the second month in the year of Xin-you).
I have searched for signs of life within withered wood; For several years I have pushed my cart against a precipitous cliff. The Great Image has been struck across the face once.
A fist; an iron ox splashes forth liquid gold.

From the crown of the head, the eye of Maheśvara protrudes. Throughout the ten realms, there is not a single speck of saint or ordinary being. In vain one speaks of the peach blossoms red on both banks;
empty space, to its very depths, admits no staining.

From Shachi, I took a boat to Ganting. On the boat, I heard a monk reciting the Lotus Sūtra, which inspired me to compose these two verses (the twenty-first day of the ninth month in the Guihai year):
The golden cock pecks through the azure lapis lazuli; Ten thousand cessations and a thousand restings are known only to oneself. Reclining peacefully on a single sail, the heavens are clear.
Lǎng! On the mountain ahead, the rain has ceased and the cuckoos cry.
Today, for no reason at all, there is a verse. Neither "four-seven" nor "two-three" is recognized; I set it forth clearly to inform all quarters.
When the eyebrows are raised, the eyes fall to the ground.
A guest asked what he did while dwelling in the mountains. He answered with a verse:
"I do not practice Chan, nor do I study the Buddha. What is this old fellow Śākyamuni? It is simply because, in the end, I have no calculations;
with my tattered robe covering my head, I warm myself by the firewood."
Seeing off a monk who visits Wutai, I am told that Manjusri is not easily encountered. Outside the Vajra Cave, the azure sky is lush and deep. When you meet him, seize his crystal cup directly;
do not concern yourself with the three before or the three after.
Sleeping by day, leaning against a seven-foot mountain vine at the edge of the clouds; at midday, he stretches out his two legs and sleeps.
When a guest occasionally comes to inquire after him, he shakes his head and says nothing of the Patriarchs' Chan.
This old monk’s discourse on Chan follows a different path. In picking up and pointing out [the truth], he does not expend any effort; let it be that both staff and shout are set aside.
Lying straight or lying crosswise—do you understand? Or do you not?
A Verse on the Staff:
Although it possesses no form or likeness whatsoever, it provides support as one enters and exits. Without cause, it is held crosswise or set upright;
even Buddhas and Patriarchs find it difficult to know.
When I occasionally raise the whisk to show it to people, it is like a flash of lightning across the void—still too slow. Who would take a rabbit’s horn as a staff?
I shall hand it to him right here in the hall.
The Verse on the Ruler of Precepts:
Used daily by Xunchang, it deliberately deceives both sages and worthies. With a single stroke, killing and giving life proceed together, instantly causing the skull to dry up.
Baizhang brought forth the verse on the pure pitcher in the midst of the assembly; Hualin, unaware of his own position, was struck with a kick by Guishan,
thereby revealing the mark of the broad and long tongue.
The Verse on the Rosary:

Ultimately, it is the beads that turn the Buddha; ultimately, it is the Buddha that turns the beads. Circulating day and night through the hundred and eight [beads], only when one grasps them and breaks through [the delusion] does one know it is he himself.
A Verse on the Meditation Cushion:
Linji received him and struck him immediately; Changqing simply taught him to wear it out. Let the teachers and monks be as they will in their confusion;
he truly has no dependence and no self.

The verse on the alms bowl has but a single upward-facing mouth; thus one understands the Patriarch’s direct command. Having been transmitted from Vulture Peak, there is no need to specially attach a handle.

The *kāṣāya* robe and the verses [of the Dharma] have spread poison before the Many-Son Stūpa; for generations, they have inherited emptiness and received echoes. Should you wish to give rise to the mind of transmission and reception, I would simply give you a slap across the face.

When the sitting mat is gathered up in verse, it becomes a single character; when let go, it is like a square field. As for neither gathering nor letting go—Sumeru is pulled out right before one's eyes.

Departing from Boshan to Return to Min (Two Poems) I urge myself to carry my jar and staff out of the Min Mountains, To seek the final barrier of my former teacher. Having exhausted every hardship, nothing could be found;
Now I shake my sleeves and return empty-handed.
For three autumns I sat steadily upon the moonlit meditation cushion; today, I instead carry my staff through the clouds. This is simply the indeterminate path of the patch-robed monk;
it is difficult to discuss one’s conduct and movements with you.
Seeing Master Yinnan Off to Dwell in the Mountains (Two Poems) Though young, you have surely experienced bitter hardships;
Your establishment of this hermitage seems like a pretext for leisure. As a monk, you ought to know shame and remorse;
Try to imagine Gautama when he was on the Snowy Mountains.
Severing worldly ties, I depart for the mountains; though empty flowers fill my eyes, let me not grasp at them. In a single thought, one must seek the Unsurpassed Treasure;
how could even a fraction of it be hung within the human world?
Seeing Off the Venerable Monk Yanxin as He Enters the Pass (Two Poems) The Great Intent of the Westward Journey—do not treat it with superficiality.
From time immemorial, the Buddhas and Patriarchs have used iron to forge their passes. Should you one day force your way through them, no one will recognize you;
A stone woman gives birth to a son, and blood fills the mountains.
The Yellow Dragon’s path is utterly beyond scaling; through iron walls and silver mountains, few can pass. Yet Shide, before the kalpa of awe-inspiring sound, gathered a cluster of followers;
with a casual movement, he shattered the three barriers.
Summer of the Gengwu year. My illness was extremely grave. Layman Shen Daochu came to the mountain and composed four verses for me:
"Yesterday I walked with forced vigor; today I lie down in sickness. This physical form is truly not my master; herein one should realize this truth."
Suddenly it is as cold as ice; suddenly it is as oppressive as fire. Water and fire change in an instant; all objective conditions can be recognized.
The form withers like a withered tree; the voice becomes faint like a mute’s. This consciousness, too, is clouded and scattered—who among them is not subject to death?
"You have now come to inquire after my illness, but where does this illness ultimately reside? Try asking Vimalakīrti. Yet even Vimalakīrti remained silent.
To demonstrate the cultivation of pure karma (four stanzas):

Continuous and dense, one diligently maintains mindfulness; How could arising and ceasing ever become a single mass? When mindfulness reaches the point where arising and ceasing do not [interfere],...
Dry. At the soles of one's feet, lotus flowers constantly appear.

Other Buddhas are clearly none other than one’s own Buddha; to think of another is the same as thinking of oneself. When there comes a morning where one contemplates stillness and forgets both self and other, the Land of Ultimate Bliss is gathered back into the western courtyard of the eastern hall.
Do not say that the Western Paradise is not the Infinite Bliss; it is simply because here there is this Sahā world.
Once you have shattered this Sahā world into dust, the West will not be separated by so much as a single speck of dust.

The Sahā world of the five turbidities is originally empty; it is only because of deluded attachment that one is imprisoned within it. Empty flowers appear as real, yet they have no arising or ceasing;
their brilliant display is entirely due to the cataracts in the eye.
To the Zen practitioner: "That which is mind is Buddha;
that which is mind is Buddha—*tāradā*. That which is not-mind is not-Buddha: what is it? Direct pointing and single transmission become circuitous.
What can a thousand words and ten thousand phrases do for the deluded? It clearly illuminates heaven and reflects the earth; yet before one's eyes, there is only darkness. How can you endure this?
Hurrying about; what was near can, through effort, become far. Wandering north, south, east, and west in vain deliberation—cease your conjectures if you wish to seek the light.
Valuing neither self nor other, exert all one’s strength upon the single phrase of the *huatou*. It is like entering a room and further raising a spear;
poison within poison, violence within violence. Slaying one's way through the heavy gates, one strikes straight at the nest. The mountain ends...
When the water is exhausted, the path naturally comes to life; emerging above the heavens, he laughs heartily. Dragging the Buddha Hall backward, he exits through the triple gate;
mounting the Sangha Hall, he passes beneath the hearth. Ten thousand sages and a thousand worthies all fold their hands in submission; neither becoming a Buddha nor becoming a demon.
Xintan Chan Master Requests Instruction (Four Verses) A single phrase of the *huatou* is like an iron stake;

A thousand thoughts and ten thousand reflections are snow in a furnace. When one exerts oneself to the utmost and shatters through it, The great earth, mountains, and rivers become a single orb of moonlight.
A single phrase of the *huatou* is like an iron stake. How could ice flakes ever not be snow?
If one is not casually deceived by the snow and ice, at high noon the bright moon is revealed in the sky.
A single phrase of the head-word is like an iron stake. Snow upon snow, frost upon frost; the spirit of spring always arises from the extreme of cold.
An iron ox roars, shattering the moon over the eastern mountains.
A single phrase of the head-word is like an iron stake; white as lacquer, yet black as snow. Within this, the pivotal mechanism utterly deceives people;
do not seek the moon by following the pointing finger.

To the Zen practitioner who studies "the dry dung pellet," the Unsurpassed, Perfectly Complete Honored One of Right Enlightenment—how can he be called a "dry dung pellet"? Let him employ a hundred subtleties and a thousand mysteries;
yet when he reaches this point, the arrows are spent and the bow is broken. Raising the eyebrows, look closely: it is much like a fierce tooth gnawing.

Raw iron—only when it has been bitten through will one find satisfaction. Without regard for past or present, or for the passage of years, bite until emotion is withered and consciousness extinguished.
When the forms of the ten realms vanish, their shadows perish of themselves; then the dung-stick emits a great radiance, and empty space fully extends its broad and long tongue.
The wildcat and the white ox are one’s own kin; the wine table and wooden ladle become the standard of character. Yunmen.
Too many living beings have been struck down; it provokes the stone man to laugh without end.
To the Zen practitioners: Zhaozhou has no Zhaozhou—why did he say "no"?
Having a mouth but no heart cannot be schemed out. If you seek to penetrate from beneath the words, you will be pierced through.
Chiseling away: Fools chase after clods like Han Lu; skin must be broken, bones shattered, and the marrow must be reached. Do not laboriously analyze along the paths of conventional gates.
Step by step, uphold sincerity as a single bar of iron; it is like drawing up the sea in search of its pearl. One need not concern oneself with its vast expanse of thousands of miles;
one simply vows to exhaust the great ocean until dry. When the dog of awakening fills the entire earth, the world itself becomes the body.
The mind is entirely it. (The first character is read as qiè; the second is read as chèn with the upper radical zhòng and the suffix jiā). Suddenly smashed to pieces, nothing remains.
Zhaozhou’s true face has no place to hide; it is simply that very broken alms bowl from those years past.

In life, one battles for rivers and mountains amidst the leaking gardens of transgression; after death, one is buried empty beneath a mere seven-foot mound. How much glory can be won by struggling for the space of a snail’s horn?
Yet the flavor of long-chewed vegetable roots is far more abundant. A thousand feet of stature are all but covered by yellow dust; how can a hundred clever schemes avail against the white [void]?
What of the bones? Even if the springtime could be made to linger, Chao and You would surely not have lain upon the mountain slopes. On this Dragon Boat Festival, I offer this gift to the patron:

when the boat sinks in the deep, one must lose oneself to dwell among the waters. Only by cutting through the rushing current does one become a true man; even a sword, if buried for long, its light will surely shine forth.
Dew: Gold requires repeated smelting before the ore is removed; within the mirror, one falsely recognizes it and doubts there is no head, yet searching inside the robe, one finds the pearl exists.
Having heard the "Song of Chu," the mist and waters darken at twilight; I stand gazing longingly as the bright moon shines upon my cold hut.
Spontaneous Verses (Ten Poems) Do not mistake a single bubble for the entire ocean; Suddenly seeing through it all, myriad conditions cease. Heaven and earth are vast and boundless;
The nine-thousand-li Peng soars with complete freedom.
Vast and boundless, the misty waves flow day and night. How many autumns have passed for these white hairs in the mirror? Within them lies the path of non-arising:
a wooden horse conceives and gives birth to an iron ox.
The faculties and their objects are non-dual, originally empty; it is only because the arising of the mind is so vastly different. To allow even one of these to falter can cause both to perish;
the clay ox enters the sea, leaving no trace to be found.
Once encountered, they are treated like enemies; the sages and saints all bring them under control with a single blow of the staff. One would willingly take gold and treat it as if it were brass;
until even empty space laughs and nods its head in approval.
In a dream, one knows that mountains and rivers are false; upon waking, one takes honor and disgrace to be real. When dream and awakening are viewed together, both are clearly not obscured;
they shatter heaven and earth and transcend past and present.

Spring has arrived upon the flowers, yet it cannot yet be sought; Forgetting discrimination for a moment, one becomes intimate with them. When gazing with fixed eyes, they especially obstruct the vision;
Fluttering butterflies pass by the western neighbor’s house.
A single sphere of perfect luminosity is fundamentally undivided; yet the ears speak, the nose sees, and the eyes hear.
Since the realm of delusion arose, the family treasures have been exhausted through kalpas, and their vital energy seems as if incinerated.
The Fan suddenly struck the Earth Deity; Vemacitrin suffered the pain and gave rise to anger. Śakra looked on from the side and remained unwilling to accept it;
Vajrapāṇi was struck with the staff until his tears flowed like rain.
The entire world is but a single emotion; returning emotion to its original nature is no small matter. Seek the path back directly from within emotion;
a segment of constant radiance is inherently perfected.
The pine branch suddenly snaps and the crane’s nest overturns; it startles the fisherman’s soul from within his dream. On the reed bank, the moon is bright and its cold penetrates to the marrow;
Mount Kunlun is overturned and swallowed by a stone tortoise.

In discussing "Harmony" (*zhong*) and "Centrality" (*he*) with Confucian scholars, the wondrous essence of these two is fundamentally non-dual. To arbitrarily divide empty space into two parts is like seeking nostrils before they have been born;
it is as if eyelashes two zhang long were to blindfold both eyes.
The celestial image of the cannon hangs suspended just as the cold reaches its peak; the trigger is always pulled as the year is about to begin anew.
If one can penetrate the point where it is devoid of emotion, the entire body will be blown apart, transcending past and present.
When the Master Shiliang asked,
"Why did Zhaozhou say 'No'?"— if you hesitate for even a moment, you will only find it more remote. Once the den has been thoroughly trampled from top to bottom,
you will finally know that the gourd hangs on the eastern wall.
To point out that there is nothing lacking for a superior person—if the Way were already as perfect as the great void, it would already be a case of creating trouble where none exists.
To further say there is "nothing lacking and nothing remaining" is merely a public proclamation on the street. For now, please take off those mother-born trousers.
Regarding the "Sublime Meaning of the Vajra" shown to the lay practitioner Yan Yongzheng of Songxi:
what is it? Even Asanga and Vasubandhu could do nothing about it. One must advance further into the simultaneous emptiness of person and phenomena;
even the state of "suchness unmoving" should be rebuked. To give rise to illumination is already a deviation of thousands of miles; to be without thought is to fall into the realm of ghosts.
The Divine Nest: Only after the flower of the mind has suddenly blossomed does one come to know that the Buddha-dharma is fundamentally not many.
For the Hundred-Clumsy Abbot, the iron gate at the foot of Mount Zizhi was closed; within the light of ultimate purity, coming and going were severed. For three years he cultivated unimpeded mastery.
Power! Transverse and vertical across the great earth, nothing can obstruct it.
To the candidate Chen Yunqi of Songxi:
Do not inquire about myriad conditions—whether they are stirred or not. Though the mind may be deluded, its stillness becomes entangled. All things are identical to bubbles and shadows.
Contemplation is the true pivot for attaining Buddhahood. Objects appear only because the mind has not yet been emptied; once the mind is empty, why worry that objects will not open up?
Old Lu understood that from the beginning there was nothing at all, and so at midnight at Huangmei, he transmitted the robe and bowl.
Shi Songxi Ye Taijiao, the scholar: "Amitābha" (the first character is pronounced with the *qie* of *qiè*).
A thousand miles, ten thousand miles—a single iron rod. Myriad practices revolve back into the gate of non-duality.
The vast earth is a boundless expanse of falling snow. Amidst this falling snow, do not cease your own effort; further, take up the whip for the stone ox and drive it forth.
Blood. A single red wheel protrudes from the void. Amitābha is nothing but a dry piece of excrement.

Inscribing the dragon’s head on the well—this is a single drop of dragon-head water. Those who drink it must value careful investigation; do not harbor thoughts of coming and going. Cease tasting for cold or warmth.
Tracing the current back, one knows there is a source; letting it flow forth, it moistens all things without limit. To discern the pulse of Caoxi, the flavor within this is long-lasting.
To the attendant Shun, I show that the Buddha-dharma has never resided in abundance; you need only investigate your own Amitābha. Be resolute and strive directly to meet the Original Face.
See! Moment by moment, pursue it without letting it go; it is like encountering a fierce enemy while holding a spear, or like steering a rudder through whale-infested waves.
If there is an object to be observed, it belongs entirely to delusion; if one guards silent stillness with a mindless heart, that too should be rebuked.
