When the doubt regarding a single phrase remains entirely undispersed, how can even a million demonic armies prevail? One day, when you crush the clay ball, you will leap out of the void.
"Kongchang lila. To the lay practitioner Xia Diaosheng of Wulin, he showed this one phrase as a *huatou*, cutting it sharply from above.
Ten thousand distinctions and a thousand differences are all extinguished; he teaches only that one must press straight ahead.
To practice is to directly cause even the skull of empty space to split open. The five thousand-plus scrolls are merely paper for wiping sores;
the "dry dung-stick" of the Buddhas of the three periods—Zhaozhou’s true face has no place to hide. The broken cauldron was originally just old iron.

It is said that Master Chen of the Three Mountains, Zhongni, once wished to remain silent; how could you, disciples of You and Xia, ever have dared to transmit it recklessly? It requires nothing more than to sever all idle intellectual interpretations;
eat your rice and wear your clothes, and you will partake in the fundamental source.
Showing the Initial Ordination of a Śrāmaṇera (Eight Verses) When shaving your head, do not sell it;
If you sell your head, your life will perish. In daily life, pass the time as circumstances allow;
Though your robes are patched a hundred times over, the fragrance of the Way is renowned.

Since you have already passed yourself off as a son of the Tathāgata, your offense in peddling the name of the Tathāgata is even more grave. It would be better to return home and grow your hair once again;
do not encroach upon even a drop of the Tathāgata’s legacy.
The food in the monasteries cures the ulcer of hunger; how could one discuss its merits or defects therein? Those who eat should possess a sense of shame and modesty;
those who do not eat may rely on you to advocate for them otherwise.
While Shouchang was alive, he was as hard as iron; he never stooped his back before others to beg. Three meals of thin gruel, he went forth with his hoe;
even in years of famine, there was still wild barley soup in his fields.
The monks of Shouchang have all cleared the fields; this old fellow takes up the plow and goes forward himself.
Although he does not understand the meaning of clearing fields, he at least avoids paying the toll for his rice to King Yama.
Now that you have eaten your fill, there is no need for worry; with nothing to manage in all affairs, it is best to rest. Yet how can one find leisure within leisure?
One gives rise to a hundred wrongs, accumulating faults and grievances.
Do not say that reviling others is not evil; it is the very womb of calamity at the gate of hell.
If you desire only for your own person to be free from restraint, you will surely create boundless karma.
Traveling north and south in search of a good place, who would have known that the good place is within one's own heart? If the mind does not find rest, there is nowhere that is good;
having wandered to the ends of the earth, it meets with nothing but enmity.
To Master Qizong (Two Poems) For a monk, the essential requirement is a backbone like steel;

One must know that through ascetic practice, one’s provisions will last long. Recalling those who cultivated the Way on the Snowy Mountains in the past, They endured many years of countless winds and frosts.
Solely maintaining right mindfulness, one investigates the True School; sitting and severing idle circumstances, the self becomes empty.
Standing alone with feet planted on the crest of a ten-thousand-fathom peak—New Silla lies only to the east of the sea gate.
To Master Yuanchang (Four Poems) The towering peaks of Mount Xizhi block the tracks of birds; At the Stone Gate, such celestial peril—whom can it pass?
Were it not for a man with iron brows and copper eyes, It would remain forever shrouded in blue smoke and emerald mist.
All along the Way through the night, the white clouds are deep. Walking straight ahead, how could it cost any effort?
If you prefer to take a detour, you will remain stuck in the desolate forest for years on end.
The ancients did not venture beyond Feiyuan Ridge; with a kick from their fingertips, they shattered the levelness of sea and mountains.
Whenever I see so many clever fellows traveling thus through clouds and waters across a thousand peaks, I cannot help but reflect.
A patch-robed monk must rely on a single lean staff; when climbing mountains or crossing waters, let not your grip slacken.
Suddenly encountering the place where water ends and mountains reach their limit, clap your hands and sing aloud atop the peak beyond the clouds.
Shown to Master Kang (Two Poems) Where illusory conditions gather, body and mind appear;

One must know that within these phantom reflections there is indeed reality. Directly exhaust the very marrow of empty space, And the myriad worlds of the great chiliocosm will all be perfectly luminous.

Only when both cessation and contemplation are forgotten does one enter the Way; only when neither existence nor non-existence is traversed does one return to the Truth. Leaving the household life is not for the sake of craving idleness;
it is to turn one's body within the thicket of thorns.
Seeing off a Monk Returning to Boshan:
His straw sandals are like tigers as he seeks his way home; He catches the eastern breeze and departs over the ridge. One must remember the moment at Xuan Sha’s Ridge:
With a toe, he kicks through the dawn of heaven and sea.
Seeing off a Monk Returning to Boshan:
Lightly he carries his gourd and staff as he passes through the Min Pass. A thousand-li journey, traversed freely back and forth. Upon his return, he will gaze his fill at the moon over Dongwu;
He must know that it is not at all different from the mountains and streams here.
Admonishing the Multitude (Four Poems) Life is like a lamp in the wind;
the floating senses are like illusory shadows. Why do you stubbornly cling to a self? To the very end, you remain unable to realize it.
Forms and sounds do not arise from without; beauty and ugliness are reckoned by the mind. Chasing after them one knows no rest, like a fish greedy for a baited hook.

When deluded passions are sent away, they return again; when right mindfulness arises, they are extinguished once more. Until the principle of true permanence is attained, the dust of affliction will find it difficult to cease even for a moment.

Ascending, it is like climbing a peak; descending, it is like returning to a valley. Even with diligent effort, accomplishment remains difficult; how could following one's own whims not lead to error?
To the lay practitioner Yu Weikun of Huizhou, I show this:
contemplate this *huatou* as if chewing iron. The world and the body-mind are snow within a furnace; suddenly, a thousand [rays] are released from behind the head.
Light! When both worldly dharmas and Buddha-dharmas have vanished like shadows, one must know that there is still a further barrier beyond.
Even the Old Man Śākyamuni was left tongue-tied; when Mazu’s single shout deafened Mount Daxiong for three days, what could possibly be said?
Show me how it was when the white layman and his mother met.

Not even a speck of dust separates them in the Western Land; it simply requires that the red thread at one's heels be severed, so that by lowering one's head, one sees the Ancient Amitābha for oneself.
To Master Huo of Furuang:
This mountain monk does not open a shop of antiques. When meeting you, O Master, there is nothing comparable; everything is torn to shreds and most disheveled.
All that remains is a broken boat moored at an ancient ferry, vainly guarding the cold night moon over Lujiang. How dare I speak idly before others?
Proclamation: The celestial precipice of Shimen is as calm as water; no one asks anymore about the road leading through the clouds.

Winter of the Jiashu year. While repairing the stupa of Master Xiushantang, it was discovered that the ancient stupa, having been buried for a long time, had suddenly reappeared at the edge of the clouds. What existed in former years has become manifest today. Today...

The Great is not as it was in years past; from antiquity to the present, everything depends on human calculation. Success and failure are merely matters of worldly conditions. Indeed, all that possesses form must perish;
one must know that where there is no fire, there is no transmission. A single phrase that transcends past and present: year after year, the waves flow away into the river ahead.
Zen Meditation Verses (Twelve Poems) Those who practice Zen must not be overly subtle or analytical.
To deliberate upon public cases is truly pitiable; it is only by meeting face-to-face upon the tip of a single hair that one truly sees.
It will surely cause the earth to reflect and the heavens to shine.
Practitioners of Zen must not be reckless; a shout or a blow is merely coarse and wild, leading one to fall into a perilous state of stagnant, lifeless water.
Turning back, one’s path is as vast as the void;
practitioners of Zen, do not seek falsely. Let all myriad wonders and thousandfold mysteries rest; iron walls and silver mountains shall be reduced to powder.
Even Deshan and Linji are difficult to match;
practitioners of Zen must not be complacent. Do not dwell long in the thatched huts outside the gate; until you have returned to the Treasure House, you will never reach completion.
I ask you to sing a song of returning home;
practitioners of Zen, do not demean yourselves. In whose house is there no true Buddha? It requires nothing more than a single thought-moment to accord with the unborn.
A staff made of rabbit horns with a whisk of tortoise hair—meditators, do not seek excessive knowledge;
reading through the Five Lamps only increases one’s delusion. An earthen ox tramples the moon upon the clear pool.
The five-leaf flower blooms upon a distinct branch;
practitioners of Zen, do not act recklessly. Many are the diverging paths where sheep are lost. Having traversed ten thousand mountains and the caves of clouds and water, [one finally arrives].
One must know that there is yet the White Cloud Village beyond;
practitioners of Zen, do not be indolent! A million demonic armies wait for you day after day; at every moment, brandish the sharp blade of your hair-piercing wisdom.
For the first time, I have recognized "Namo Avalokiteśvara.

You who practice Zen, do not busy yourselves with other matters; such busyness can only serve to increase the cycle of birth and death. If you do not fail to recognize the pearl hidden within your own garment, [you shall find liberation].
A single robe covers the body, yet there is more than enough glory;

you who practice Zen, do not disdain poverty. When poverty is not extreme, one’s true nature is not revealed. You must know that this is the matter of wind-and-flow elegance that penetrates to the very bone.
When the cold has ended, there is naturally a spring elsewhere.
Those who practice Zen must not cling to a single thing; the transmission of dead methods has become nothing but a malady. A true hero must be like a dragon emerging from the sea.
In the five schools of the Gate, there are no traces left.
Verses on Mindfulness of the Buddha (Four Stanzas):

One who practices mindfulness of the Buddha must be single-minded. As the breath goes out, one must attend to the incoming breath. When pure mind continues without interruption, the clouds of obstruction will disperse.
Rubbing the nose of one's own face before death, those who practice nianfo must be diligent in heart.
Laziness has long nurtured deluded emotions; let there be a single moment of resolute resolve always like this.
The precious lotus radiates light day after day;

those who recite the Buddha’s name must be firm in resolve. Know that even a single drop of water can pierce through stone; when the thought of mindfulness bursts forth like a fire-drill striking sparks, what need is there to worry about the five-colored lotuses of the Western Paradise?
Those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha must maintain an upright posture; only through such uprightness can right faith be perfected.
Thus cultivating the seeds of Bodhi within oneself, one becomes a true spiritual heir of Amitābha.

To Layman Linpaowan (Two Poems) The sound of the Buddha’s name flows on without interruption, Just like a fierce fire smelting true gold. When the ore is exhausted, the gold is complete, forming a great function;
Reflecting the earth and illuminating the heavens, it shines with a unique brilliance.
The Buddha’s name is as upright as a sword leaning against the heavens; it cuts through thousands and tens of thousands of branches. Before one's very eyes lies the Land of Lotus Flowers;
who has need to concern themselves with the compassionate power of Amitābha’s vows?
To the Good Friends of the Pure Land Society (Seven Poems) A single thought of Amitābha is as solid as iron;

In idleness or busyness, movement or stillness, it is free from birth and extinction. When this land and the Western Paradise have both been reduced to dust, what need is there to speak of "non-arising," like snow in a boiling cauldron?
A single phrase, towering like a vajra, has refused to be forgotten despite being forged a hundred times and hammered a thousand times. It penetrates directly beyond the limit of Vairocana;
it is not apart from this very mind, for it is the Western Paradise itself.

Where the sword-wheel is brandished, the night-light grows cold; the mountain colors and the sound of the stream cannot deceive. One must wait until the golden cock personally crows at dawn, when the five-colored lotus flowers reflect upon the jeweled balustrade.
Holding the name requires no further seeking of the profound; a single phrase instantly transcends sound and form.
Myriad objects melt into a single moon—how can one distinguish between the East and the West?
When will the outward pursuit of a deluded mind ever come to an end? Even if one piles up mountains of gold, it only piles up sorrow.
If you are willing to let go of everything with total sincerity, the autumn moon shines upon a cloudless sky.
Gather all six sense-faculties into mindfulness of the Buddha alone; when fleeting delusions are fully refined away, realization is spontaneously perfected.
Upon the towering pedestal, the golden form is manifest without needing to give rise to a single thought.
Do not give rise to likes or dislikes toward external conditions; when concentrated into a single thought, ultimately there is no division.
Suddenly shattering the lapis lazuli mirror, the sound of the Dharma is heard by you alone.
When practicing the Way with General Shi Qiu, it is like being on the front lines: do not let the golden halberds and iron horses falter. Strike down the chief enemy directly within the ranks;
returning in triumph, the spring fills every path.
Together with Feng Zhongjun and his million demon armies, you shall know the location of the lair; by striking the den and burning the nest, they can be eliminated at once.
Victory in battle will naturally bring peace to the state and the nation, as you seize the bright pearl from atop the Wheel-Turning King’s topknot.
When a guest arrives, the tea master shows him only a single cup of tea; yet it stirs up the monastic groves in a chaos like tangled hemp. This matter is perfectly clear, without front or back;
yet for no reason, it suddenly separates one from the ends of the earth.
The spiritual radiance of the venerable Chaojue transcends the realm of sense organs and objects; how could one know it by clinging to those organs and objects?
Only when you can utterly extinguish the thieving mind will you finally recognize Zhaozhou’s "East Hall" and "West Hall."
Showing the Monks of Guiyang Mountain (Two Poems; the mountain contains the flesh bodies of two patriarchs).
Three purple peaks soar aloft among the clouds. Within them dwells a recluse who guards the Patriarchs’ barrier. One must believe that the skull-bone still possesses eyes;
from the crown of his head they burst forth, illuminating the human world.
The True Body is said to reside at Guiyang; sun and moon hang as a pair, illuminating the heights above. I am ashamed that my incense offerings have nothing worthy of being burned;
after the rain, the mountain colors are truly deep and verdant.
Pointing to the Great Way, the monk of Yanshan says:
"The mountain colors of Qingyuan float with emerald luster. It is heard that a True Person dwells upon its peak. The Great Way is brilliantly clear, as straight as an arrow;
yet coming and going, it is infinitely curved like a hook."
From the beginning, the Great Way has led straight to Chang’an; once Chang’an is reached, the Dharma-realm is vast and wide. Yet alas, people of this age all prefer shortcuts;
though they exhaust every hardship, it remains difficult to arrive.
The Master Shimiyin strikes the Stone Drum before the window; with one roar, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth are startled.
Even you men of iron brows and copper heads must be cast once more into the fierce furnace.

Answer: Niqiao Lin, all phenomena are originally empty; it is only because of the delusions of the mind that they appear to exist. When the deluded mind engages in conceptual discrimination, one speaks of emptiness, yet in reality it is not empty.
When one presses into the nature of emptiness, both existence and non-existence are absent; this is called "original emptiness" and is also called the "ultimate meaning."
At the seaside, Ta-su, my virtuous friend, showed me that birth and death are like the great ocean:
vast and boundless, its azure expanse reaching to the heavens. If one is willing to possess a firm and resolute will, one will naturally find contentment.
Hoist the sail for ten thousand li; how could one linger over a single courtyard? A single leaf rides upon the celestial wind; even a thousand-fathom surge cannot block its way.
Ultimately reaching the other shore, the Jewel Mountain can be plucked by hand. Training in the Way is also like this: the realm of the sages lies but a few inches away.
Exert yourself; do not abandon yourself to fate. You are truly a guest who has transcended the mundane world.
For the Layman Fanmu returning to his village to visit his parents (two poems):
Having endured hardships for many years, he returns with a tattered robe weathered by wind and smoke. One day, he directly beholds his own parents.
Face to face, one knows not what has been offered before the hall;
treading through the high and low terrain, all is but casual. Carrying his staff slung across his shoulder, he returns to the Min Pass. By the side of Danxia Station, the lychees are ripe;
surely their subtle fragrance must waft through the ten thousand mountains.

Those who observe the precepts yet busily manage monastic affairs wander aimlessly; when will they ever find rest? With yellowing teeth and white hair, they still greedily pursue their desires. Their management of a hundred generations is but a dream of three watches;
their establishment of a thousand autumns is like a tiny bubble. All say that accumulating merit ultimately accumulates evil; who knows that increasing joy is likewise so?
This only increases your sorrow. Even if you could calculate everything to your heart's content, when the iron staff falls upon your head, you will have no freedom.
To the Upāsaka Zhixi:
The Ultimate Way has always been free from discrimination; why must you deliberately set yourself to distinguish between east and west? Turn the light back and look at the very base of your feet.
Below: Ordinarily sitting, one cuts off the azure lapis lazuli.
Anping Youmo Daoqiao died and entered the underworld. The Lord of the Underworld ordered him to return and request a verse:
"Clearly there is a road to the Western Land; it lies solely within a single thought-moment of the person. Seeing through body and mind as being like a horse."
The horns, the sword-trees, and the mountain of knives are empty in this very moment.
In response to the scholar Liu Zhonglong’s request for a verse in the rhyme of "Lai," the layman says:

A gentleman can plant lotuses amidst the flames; Manifesting his body to mingle with the mundane, he simply follows conditions. If you wish to clarify the Great Way, do not harbor [artificial] thoughts.
I see it: as soon as one utters profound words, they have not yet escaped conceptualization. When purity and defilement are both forgotten, one is still separated by the riverbank;
when existence and non-existence are both cast aside, it is still not yet Chan. Where deluded sentiments cease, True Suchness manifests; step by step, one ascends to the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
To Layman Zhuang Taizhen:
Grasping the rope’s end with firm resolve, he travels alone; what need to fear the sword-trees and mountain of blades?
Having endured every hardship without retreating, he turns the wheel of Saṃsāra as if it were but a trifle.

I show you, my good friend Wu, that the single gate of nianfo (Buddha-recitation) is the most direct and straightforward. It requires no extensive knowledge or understanding, nor does it employ clever speech.
It demands only this one phrase: "Buddha. Stand firm like a piece of steel; what matters it whether there is kindness or affection, or whether there is resentment or enmity? All other thoughts—
Neither arises; the shadow of the Sahā world vanishes of itself.

Master Shiqi shows us how to seize empty space and make it real for once; ten thousand anxieties and a thousand thoughts are instantly reduced to ashes. Opening one's mouth before the Iron Pillar Gate—how extraordinary!
A laugh. He casually swallows the stone tortoise.

To the Layman Wang Wupian, he shows that one phrase has from the beginning been utterly free of correctness and partiality. Any casual deliberation results only in entanglement. An iron ox roars forth before the mountain.
The Road. Treading through the mists of ten thousand *li* over three springs.
To Layman Xia Jundu:
On both sides are poisonous fires; behind is the turtle-nosed snake. Only this one path ahead, yet there lies an enemy born of life itself.
One must resolutely move forward; there is not a moment’s delay to allow him [the obstacle] to remain. When the morning comes and [the veil] is torn asunder, a lotus flower appears within the fire.
To the Venerable Cimo:
when fighting alone amidst a hundred thousand troops, do not hesitate to whirl the wheel-sword and dance with the blade; let the long serpent coil itself up and lie low.
The Moon: Directly seize the ringleader to repay the lord’s kindness.
To show the elder Ansheng one phrase:
A jeweled sword hangs across the void; though the thousand sages seek it, they find no trace. The white ox lies peacefully before the slope.
Grass. Sometimes it leaps out from the east of a small stream.
To the layman Xin Yu, I show this one phrase:
a precious sword transverse in the void; mountains, rivers, and the great earth all leave no trace. One day, it will shatter the empty sky.
Also: The sun’s orb surges forth from the eastern sea-gate.
To Master Ningyuan (Four Poems):
His beard is red, truly a red-bearded fellow. What man among us would not be a hero? Do not cling to the tea and rice of this temporary lodging.
Matured. A single inhalation must cause the great ocean to dry up.

From of old, the patch-robed monks have never followed others; meeting Buddhas and patriarchs on the road is like encountering an enemy. In vain do they speak of the clay oxen fighting as they enter the sea;
one must know that the iron wall does not grow flowers.
Holding a single sword aloft alone, he cuts through the void; both Siddhārtha and Pāpīyān have their traces utterly extinguished. Transcending empty space, he stands upon one’s head;
Mount Sumeru is tucked within a lotus fiber.
The road before the gate is ultimately unstable; light arising behind the head may well be a demonic omen. An archer from the depths shoots down the sun at the edge of heaven;
the mute man, in a panic, cries out for his father.
Two Poems on Master Zhihui’s Dwelling in the Mountains When dwelling in the mountains, one must never be stained by floating dust.

In studying the Way, one has always had to learn poverty. If you can reach the point where your bag is empty and lacks even a single grain, then naturally the cold will end and spring will arise anew.
Dwelling in the mountains, do not steal empty fame; hold fast to body and mind, forged as if from iron.
Penetrating through hundreds of layers and thousands of folds, the stone ox walks step by step through fire.
To the Venerable Zhuoran:
The waters and mists of a hundred cities stretch out in vast obscurity; with staff in hand, you have come from the south on a long journey.
Though the clay pot of Tiaoshang is of an old design, it has recently been entrusted to emit a thousand rays of light.

Showing the way for Master Yun’an to dwell in the mountains and establish his hermitage far off at the edge of the white clouds: boiling stones and eating pine, there is a world apart. One day, atop the desk-mountain, he points to himself:
Mount Sumeru hangs upside down behind the curtain of the night sky.
Showing Emptiness to the Superior Men (Two Poems) This is neither empty nor not empty;
it is only because of deluded attachment that the various existents arise. When deluded sentiments are completely dispersed, the sun-disk stands solitary;
it shines through the three primes, which are originally nine.
What need is there to speak further of this emptiness? Old Pang chews his food to feed children. A stone man claps his hands and a wooden man sings;
it startles old Wang Liu of the eastern village.

Showing that when the mind seeks a superior person, the seeking mind transforms things; when there is no seeking, things do not obstruct the mind. The incense lion atop the hall—when consciousness breaks through this, it is realized to be gold.
From the *Extensive Record of Master Yongjue*, Volume Twenty-Two.
The Extensive Record of Master Yongjue, Volume Twenty-Three.
Compiled by the Dharma-heir Disciple Daopai. Section on Verses and Hymns, Part Two.
Ten Verses on the Diagram of Tending Cattle:
Before being tended, the horns grow fierce and untamed; Once they leave the gate, who can control their trampling of the fine sprouts? The clouds deepen and the mud slips before the mountain.
On the road, turning one's back on home, the days grow ever more distant.
At the start of the journey, suddenly meeting on a narrow path, he is led by the nose without being let go; how many times his stubborn nature has greedily sought entry!
Grass. Dragged along, it is fortunate that there is a child holding the whip.
Though subjected to numerous lashings and proddings, its nature still persists; merely because it is tethered by a rope, it cannot bolt away. It constantly gazes toward the grass in the level fields.
Form: A mountain child holding a staff observes the dawn and dusk.

Turning his head, he tames his nature which has long been unruly; it gradually becomes supple. Without thinking of pursuing external things, he turns his head back of his own accord. The herdsman’s hand on the halter is not easily let go.
Let go. Only upon reaching the mountain of one's own home does one finally consent to rest.

Tamed and submissive, he follows at evening’s fall along the ancient stream; returning home, there is no need for the tethering rope. Let him roam as he pleases among the spring grasses that reach the very heavens.
Green. When has it ever had the intention to enter another’s field?

Unimpeded, its coat of dappled white reveals itself as it sleeps on the open ground. The green willows and fragrant grasses are naturally serene; the whip and reins have been cast aside among the pine trees.
Below, the short flute is blown crosswise as the sky approaches midday.
Flowing freely, crossing waters and piercing clouds, he comes and goes at will. Eating and drinking according to conditions—who could possibly fathom him? The cowherd boy is simply without thought.
Calculating, he rests his head upon a stone, sleeping soundly by the bend of the winding stream.

For long he has lived in peace and security, forgetting all within the forest; having forgotten both self and others, there is no need for intimacy. Amidst the light of the bright moon, the shadows of clouds drift by.
Transcending, one reaches the point where clouds and moon are both indifferent.

Shining alone upon the traces of the realm, the golden mirror of wisdom hangs suspended; its solitary radiance shines forth with nothing before it. In the silent, empty mountains, people still remain.
While you are here, I shall still strike you once behind the head.
When both mind and object are extinguished and both are gone, there is a single expanse of emptiness. The mud ox enters the sea—what trace remains? Within this, no one knows the message.
Meeting. At midnight, the sun in the east is bright red.
This indicates the first stage of practice (two verses):
Cutting off all thieving minds, right mindfulness will naturally remain constant. It is like a drop of water piercing stone; why worry?
There is no gate for entering the Way.

Excessive knowledge only leads to increasingly many errors; excessive seeking inevitably results in much forgetfulness. You must diligently guard right mindfulness, lest the sheep wander off into other regions.

I show Layman Wang Ziyeyi that worldly conditions are unreal and this illusory form is not solid. Ignorance internally perfumes the mind; like a venomous dragon lurking in a deep pool, grasping thoughts arise.
There are thus humans and devas, like the buckets on a well-drawing wheel; how can there be an end to the ocean of suffering?

Like a rope mistaken for a snake, or a ghost perceived in a tree stump, amidst raging, blazing fires, only the wise person realizes this beforehand. The flowers in the sky suddenly vanish; their essence is fundamentally thus—neither heaven nor earth.
Neither sage nor worthy—what can one call him? A block of wood, a common brick. This visiting superior man has long enjoyed the mastery of refined elegance;
in his later years, he also loves to seek refuge in Chan. Having passed by my banks along the Shaoxi River, he requested that I compose this short poem for him.

Ashamed that I am now old and sick, I embrace my simplicity and lie amidst the forests and springs. When I lift my brush, it feels as heavy as a pestle; when I unroll a scroll, it often takes a year to finish.
How much more so for those fleeting words and phrases—like spring dew or autumn mist—which are no more than fallen leaves on the steps that can never be mistaken for gold coins.
Consider the world of the Great Antiquity, before even a single stroke had been made. Yet there already existed a scroll of poetry that neither Confucius nor Laozi could fully sing.
To the novice monk Chudu:
all those who have left the household life must not allow themselves to fall into mediocrity. Every person possesses the original truth; they are no different from the Buddha.
It is only because deluded sentiments are heavy that the false notions of subject and object arise; consequently, discrimination is born, leading to rejecting and grasping.
Good and evil thus divide their paths, and the cycle of rebirth forms the seven realms. Turning incessantly without end, how could one know there is a way out?
Our Buddha, the Teacher of the Three Realms, has earnestly and repeatedly exhorted us with bitter words. To suddenly realize the original truth is for empty space to fall;
the solitary white ox-cart brings one safely out beyond both the mundane and the sacred. Both the Sahā world and the Land of Ultimate Bliss are overturned in a single stride.
If you fail to realize this, you will merely be painting a cat after the model. A single phrase of "Amitābha Buddha," when brought forth like a vajra, shatters all worldly attachments.
Thus one roams freely toward the Western Land. Simply purify your own mind; why worry that the earth is not pure?
These are words of truth. Exert yourselves; do not abandon yourselves.
Handing over the entirety of empty space as a single burden—how could one ever rest, even with all one’s energy and strength exhausted? It is better to bring forth that which is soundless.
The flute: Turning it upside down and blowing crosswise across the evening mountains;
showing the venerable Shōhōrin as he rows his small boat onto the reed-strewn shore. At midnight, the moon over the stream is at its brightest; suddenly, the golden cock crows and awakens him.
Later, the daughter was born; there is no need to seek her nostrils.

To instruct and enlighten the superior person, one must reach the furthest and exhaust the highest; the will must be firm. One must strictly avoid being tainted by shallow and depraved saliva. Only when Shitou opens his mouth can it be attained.
[The Master] laughed. [He said: "Naturally, the 'Heaven within the Earth' has been dug up.
In response to Layman Lindao Jing (four poems):
On the worldly path there is neither level nor steep; Levelness and steepness arise from the mind. If the heels are naturally firm, Mountains, seas, and all things are broad and even.
In vain one speaks of the gravity of verbal karma; the essence of karma is fundamentally empty. Once the crimson sun has risen, what trace remains of frost and dew?
The thief is one's own kin; he is ultimately no other than oneself. If the master is not deluded, there is no need to capture the various thieves.
The fundamental form is originally not distant; it is obscured by many branches. When conceptual discrimination is suddenly extinguished, one will naturally know it with clarity.
To the Assembly (Twelve Verses): My Way is like empty space;
when sought, what is there at all? If deluded sentiments have not been eliminated, even non-existence is but dust and grime.
My Way is like the azure sky; even joining bamboo poles one cannot reach it. If you are a traveler soaring through the void, you may stand amidst the clouds waving a fan.
My Way is like dark sacrificial wine; do not seek its flavor. The wine from the village tavern intoxicates the traveler, yet it is said to be sweet enough to dispel a thousand sorrows.
My Way is like a broad highway; anyone with feet can travel it. But the human mind is of its own thorns; lost in wandering, one falls into desolate mounds.
What was direct becomes circuitous; what is ordinary turns perverse. As for the affairs of the Patriarchs’ school, it is best to let the dust and ashes fly.
Originally not being a Buddha, the wooden puppet perceives True Suchness (*tathatā*). This mountain monk’s tongue has no bone; it is like seeking fish on dry land.
Holding fast the secure barrier as if it were an iron stake—this single piece of bitter heart, to whom shall I speak? Fortunately, there are moss-covered stones before the gate;
meeting here, we may untie our heart-knots together.
Securing the firm barrier like an iron stake, one gladly allows the white clouds to conceal a thousand clumsinesses.
Upon meeting, one simply laughs "he-he" from within; do not use vermilion to paint the moon.
All that is transmitted by word of mouth is false; only when one sits and cuts it off with no-mind is it called true.
If both truth and falsehood can be utterly swept away, there is no need to seek the nostrils one was born with.
Beyond the Sound of Awesome Power (Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja), do not harbor views; at the crossroads of the street, do not manifest yourself.
Hiding one’s traces is not permitted for idle seekers of knowledge; only the tabby cat attains intimacy alone.
His Chan is easy to learn, my Chan is difficult. Do not fear the cold of green waters and blue mountains. Only when the great ocean is emptied will the pearls reveal themselves;
only when empty space is trodden through will the mind find peace.
In my Dharma, there has never been so much as a single word; were there any words, you should know the Dharma would become increasingly remote. In days of yore, Qingyuan raised the true command:
like snow falling upon a red furnace, the lunar disc stands solitary.
I sing of the Buddha’s tooth at Mount Zhi, which has wandered among men for tens of thousands of springs; protected by devas and dragons, its color remains as fresh as new.
Deep within Mount Zhi, amidst mist and clouds, I have personally beheld the Tathāgata’s purple-golden body.
At Shuangji Temple, one traverses a myriad peaks until the path turns secluded and deep. White clouds and crimson leaves fill the mountains in autumn.
The celestial wind roars against the rocks by the stream, startling the azure dragon to release a round of rain.
I express my gratitude to Layman Xie Ji’ān:
The three teachings are one family; the "one" and "three" do not stand, for they are but empty flowers. It is just as a rope is seen because of the hemp;
how could one speak further of a snake upon that rope? Having opened the two eyes beyond the limit of Vipaśyin, what need is there to discuss Confucius or Laozi?
Śākyamuni, as you depart now, I have no gift to present; simply take care and sail upon the white clouds in your raft.
Exhort Dongseng and Vinaya-master Kebin to not enter this monastic community. The spirit of the ancients was truly fierce and resolute; having been struck, they paid the fine and departed once more.
The Abbot’s entire body is nothing but cast iron. The *vinaya* master must resolve to learn from the ancients; with a sharp blade, he cuts through the fetters of a thousand autumns.
In investigating this matter, do not let up for a moment; with a single blow, he makes it all one stream of blood.
If one can attain a sudden chill that penetrates the very marrow, like a withered plum in mid-winter meeting the snow, a branch will naturally burst forth, its subtle fragrance wafting of itself.
Different from the ordinary, the iron wall and silver mountains are pierced through in an instant. A single moon fills the heavens and covers the earth.

For many years, I have diligently followed my attendant as he has investigated this "yellow-waxwood Chan. How can the message within this be transmitted? One must truly exert oneself with desperate resolve.
He departs, yet he stands before me like an enemy. With the vajra-jewel sword leaning against the void, one must strike him down directly to achieve self-completeness.
Even at this point, there remains the final word; even Yantou was ultimately left in bewilderment.
Exhort the nine visiting attendants and the Zen practitioners: your resolve must be fierce. How can you idly pass the seasons? Keep this very matter suspended upon your hearts;
whether moving or still, remain always like a single block of iron. Do not diverge into idle sentiments or illusory realms; empty the great ocean until it is dry.
Reaching the *kṣaya*, exhausting the *kṣaya*. Coral branches branch out, supporting the moon.
This shows that the matter beneath the feet of the venerable practitioner Hengchu is difficult to explain. How could one ever find heaven by digging the earth? Today, I shall communicate this to you.
A thread. Sumeru hangs upside down as a night-bright curtain.
To show and awaken those with the mind of the Patriarchs:
the heart-mind is fundamentally without things; from what could one awaken? Only upon awakening does one know there is not a single thing. At midnight, the wooden man knocks on the moon.
The door opens; Vairocana awakens and emerges from the ancient capital.
To the Chan master Shouchang he reveals:
the current beneath the Shouchang Bridge has not yet dried, and the snow atop Huanglong Peak is still cold. After Boya finished playing, the frosty sky—
The Moon. Once Zi-qi departed, those who knew him were few. You, O Superior Man, embrace your coarse wool and enter this community; do not follow worldly customs and deceive yourself.
It is better to exhaust yourself in the great wonders of the mountains, lifting up a single sphere of the West River moon.
The Chan practitioner Shi Cuiran has come from the south carrying his mendicant’s staff for several years. This morning he asks the way amidst the white clouds.

Without crossing the definitive phrase of the Stone Gate, Bodhidharma would not have recognized the Patriarch’s Chan. Suddenly, with one shout, both ears go deaf; only then does one know that the Yellow-Faced One [the Buddha] has...
Family Tradition: The universe is overturned—how skillful! Empty space is shattered—how can it be proclaimed?
To the Venerable Guyuan:
A single drop from Guyuan has little flavor; If one can taste it, one is able to emerge from the river of craving. This is no ordinary water.
In comparison, even the Sage Confucius clearly did not recognize him.
To Layman Yang Yifan:

Within this world, all that is in turmoil is but mundane dust; only by leaving the dust behind does one become a person of this school. There is no need for you to don the patchwork robe and call yourself a Chan practitioner.
One who recognizes the dust-sensory bases and immediately manifests the body must study the Way with a resolve as hard as iron.
Entrust worldly attachments to the snow in a cauldron; directly investigate the "Persian biting the arrowhead" phrase.
Leap out of empty space and do not indulge in idle chatter.
I tell Zhang Ke-yi, young scholar:

in your youth you must exhaustively investigate principle. Only when the mind is empty will principle become intimate. As long as subject and object are not yet exhausted, you remain separated by the ford of delusion.
Suddenly, both subject and object are shattered; only then does one see the original mind. I ask Confucius and Laozi: why must you preach the Six Classics?
To Shen Tong and Qing Mao, I say:

though you are young scholars, you must exhaustively investigate principle. Yet seeing principle is not yet being intimate with it. When suddenly there is nothing to be seen, only then have you crossed the ford of delusion.
Neither the Way nor meditation; neither Buddha nor mind. I laugh at the old Confucius, who toiled in vain expounding the Six Classics.
To Huang Zhongxin, Wénxué:
Attaining sagehood is certainly not difficult, yet upon closer inspection, it is also not easy. It is only because deluded views arise that the bright sun becomes obscured by itself.
When nature is obscured, emotions inevitably arise; once emotions arise, external objects become a burden. Chasing after them without knowing when to rest, ignorance and delusion fill the earth.
Everyone claims to possess innate wisdom, yet who regards benevolence and righteousness? Everyone claims to be a true man, yet they willingly sink to the level of dogs and swine.
The illness lies within me, not in emptiness; this is why I have cast myself aside. In the school of Confucius, self-mastery is paramount; Yan Hui was able to request instruction on how to serve.

When the self is mastered, external objects are naturally forgotten; when objects are forgotten, one’s true nature is spontaneously realized. Vast and open, it is beyond naming; even becoming a sage is already not it.

The lay practitioner Jiaorì says that Confucianism speaks of existence while Buddhism speaks of emptiness; one must recognize that true emptiness is inherently different. If one speaks of clinging to existence, it merely becomes a burden;
in the end, it returns to nothing more than the wind at the treetop.
On Ming Confucians (Eight Poems) The Way of the *Zhongyong* lies even with the ignorant and the wives; The leaping fish and soaring kites are even more manifest.
How strange that Kaoting made so many errors, Only to entangle himself further in his own heterodox habits.

It penetrates heaven, it penetrates earth, and it also penetrates humanity; yet the matter at the heels of one's feet is increasingly difficult to clarify. As soon as a single thought arises, the whole body is shrouded in obscurity;
though one exhaustively examines the Six Classics, they only explain names.
The aim of the Confucian school lies in sincerity and illumination. The teaching of "cautioning oneself when alone" seizes the essential passageway.
If one understands from where thought arises, even the two words "sincerity and illumination" are not ultimately real.
Mengzi’s "branching out" speaks of the accumulation of righteousness; Yanzhi’s "four do-nots" likewise is not yet benevolence itself.
Once the root of one's own illness is illuminated and shattered, the vast universe is one's entire body.
One day Zhongni wished to remain silent; he clearly pointed out the source of the Mengjin River. Only when Yan Hui appeared as if ignorant did he truly grasp the essential meaning.
The clouds dispersed across the autumn sky, and the moon filled the courtyard.

The Confucian school claims they exhaust the Way and can govern the world; yet to govern the world, one must first realize the emptiness of worldly phenomena. If even a single point has not been extinguished, it becomes a seed of calamity;
how many who travel westward end up turning east?

A single point of numinous light is inherently perfect and round; it is only because of obstruction by external objects that it cannot manifest in its entirety. Therefore, Master Zeng gave rise to the method of "investigation of things" (*gewu*);
once one exhausts this inquiry to its source, there is sudden enlightenment.
The wondrous essence is empty and void, transcending both views and thoughts; when one minutely contemplates the four negations, how could there be any knowing?
To intend to know much and hope to emulate the sages is clearly to betray one’s own eyebrows.
Seeing off the Chan practitioner Nanxun as he dwells in the Baiyun Cave:
The ancient cave is secluded and deep; when sitting alone, The sound of the spring drips and birds sing in the branches. The shadows of clouds across the thousand mountains seem to have vanished;
A single laugh fills the void—who can truly know it?

Shishi Bi shows that the lineage of Master Chuanzi, the Caodong school, is distinct from the rest; from the beginning, it has not permitted much verbal explanation, but directs one straight toward deep realization within wordlessness.
Even so, this is like gazing at the bright moon from amidst the clouds.

I show you, Layman Chen, that this matter has from the beginning been beyond the reach of views and thoughts. Where language manifests, it immediately becomes discordant; cut off right and wrong, and forget emotional deliberation.
When the ancient Buddhas appeared with such majestic dignity, they were thus.
To Layman Zhengnan on his fiftieth birthday, seeking a verse:
Your countenance is still in its prime vigor, yet you have reached the age of fifty. This is precisely the day when the ancient Master Boyu realized his errors.
Zhongni praised his worthiness, and his fame remains radiant to this day. You, sir, are now able to admire the Way and seek me out in my mountain retreat;
you should sever the roots of worldly dust and bring these illusory dreams to rest early. Direct your thoughts toward the realm of purity, where the lotus flower nurtures its wondrous essence.
Vast and majestic is the Golden Teacher; how could his lifespan have any limit?
The Zen practitioner Nikkō, seeking a verse for his deceased kin, requested:
"The wondrous body is fundamentally without purity or defilement; how can one distinguish between the Eastern Land and the Western Paradise? The golden cock has crowed, shattering the third watch."
Afterwards, the boundless Dharma-realm radiates light everywhere, showing Layman Zhu that all matters from the past have been but illusions.
One who can know illusion is inherently ever-as-it-is; the iron ox leaps across east and west.
The bank. One need not count the three-legged donkey of Yangqi.

To the layman Zhuang, he showed that there is a Buddha in the West who has long been beckoning him. If you are willing to believe, you must know that the path is not far. Look back again: from where does this thought arise?
Arise! Having passed through kalpas in this Sahā world, you shall transcend it in this very moment.

To Layman Zhang Lu: Among the disciples of the Sage of Confucius, Zeng was the most "Lu" (dull). It was precisely because his state of dullness accorded with the Way that he could attain a mind-field as pure as white silk. But let your mind-field be like white [silk].
Only through such training can one seek deeply for a person of superior attainment.
The Master Shidao said:

"A person of superior attainment, though young, must establish firm resolve. Do not follow the vulgar currents that lead one astray. Within the garment there is a pearl; you should retrieve it with haste."
Record. Zhaozhou’s Eighteen Meetings with Nanquan.
Showing a Zen practitioner a hoe:
"Lately, the atmosphere in the monasteries has become thin and corrupt; day and night, the shell of ignorance grows thicker. How many truly practice and earnestly investigate?"

People merely take the remnants of spittle and indulge in arbitrary conjecture. Having learned enough through such conjecture to fill their bellies with Zen, they use donkey lips and horse tongues to insult one another.
They vainly pass down the "winter melon seal," until their very foundation is lost and they fall into ruin. You now do not enter this protective community;
instead, you head toward Gushan to embrace its solitude. At Gushan, there is no Zen and no deliberation; it empties all that exists.
There is this true medicine: one must simply not be divided by external dust. Gather all myriad thoughts back into this single point; morning and evening, let your resolve not waver.
Suddenly, as clouds part and the sky becomes vast and empty, the numinous light emerges far beyond the reach of sight or knowledge.
This is the true learning of Shaolin; it transcends the entanglements of the three realms in a single stroke. How can it be compared to the cranes in the human world that wade through the floods?
The Transmission of the Precepts (Six Poems):

The Chan practitioner Qi Cun and Miaoxie of Gushan [received] the precepts from the Xiaoxi [lineage]. In the Dharma-ending age, this is the foremost defense. To build a lofty tower, one must first have a foundation.
Root Text: Do not say that the sacred peaks transmit only the single dharma.

Chan practitioner Dongsheng [Dongshan Liangjie] drummed the mountain; Miaoxie of Shaoshan followed the precepts of the Teao River. In donning robes and eating meals, emulate the Jetavana Garden; you must remember the final words of Nirvana.
Entrustment: Do not allow Pāpīyān to enter this gate.

The Chan practitioner Zaojian, with the subtle grasp of Mount Gu at the banks of the Tiexi, blows the flute as a stone maiden; those who recognize this are rare. To uphold and explain it, one must first know this.
My friend, do not let celestial flowers stain your patched robe.
Do not violate the Chan practitioner’s drum;
Mount Shan’s wondrous grasp and the Teao River’s precepts are held fast by the void, which may provoke resentment, yet you must believe that the *vinaya* is entirely sublime.
In practice, the Dharma was first transmitted by Dhūta Kāśyapa;

the Chan practitioner Jingxin [inherited it] at Mount Gu, while Miaojie [received it] from the Shaoxi River. The five articles and seven groups of precepts are all profoundly mysterious—how could they be compared to the frantic confusion of recent times?
In the Han dynasty, the feet were bound by the snares of Māra while the mouth discoursed on Chan;

the patriarchs and holy Chan practitioners, these sons of the Śākya, falsely divided Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya. Upon examination, they are all but the radiance of the single mind. First, he propagated the Dharma of the Precepts as his primary task.
The Guide leads all sentient beings extensively to the field of enlightenment.

I urge you, Righteous Lord and Layman, that this Great Matter has from the outset never been within the scope of verbal explanation; let the Six Classics take their course—how could they possibly proclaim it? Please look at the bamboo before Maocu’s window.
*Caosūtra*. Before the Great Ultimate was yet delineated, it was manifest.
To the lay practitioner Zheng Yongbi:
"The mind is pure, and the land is naturally pure. This principle is difficult to alter in ten thousand ways. There is no separate method for purifying the mind; a single Buddha dispels all doubts."
As long as the lotus fiber is not severed, it can pull a great elephant in its flight; only when even a single thought ceases is it called the time of seeing the Buddha.
To the painter Zhulangzhong:

with a single stroke of the brush, a hundred billion forms appear; look closely and they are ultimately none other than yourself—this numinous light manifests throughout all dust motes of the universe.
The realm: only upon looking back do you know the true face.
Strive on for the sake of Chan practitioner Lin;
with each entry, one becomes more intimate. What prevents you from turning around further at this point of intimacy? To the very end, where is the source to be exhausted?
There is. Below the eyebrows, the eyes have always been there.

This shows Zen student Yilun that his wondrous nature is fundamentally perfect and harmonious. He has no attachment to either good or evil. While it is certainly unfitting to be defiled by evil, to stagnate in goodness is likewise an error.
How can those like Pāpīyas act with such unrestrained malice? Under the pretext of speaking of transcendence and vastness, their greed and anger are worse than that of a dog.

Even if they study hundreds of thousands of verses, will it not only increase their poisonous medicine? They may falsely claim to be spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), yet even the Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*) are no place of joy for them.

You who seek the Way for the first time must deliberate carefully when you step out the door. If the deluded mind is allowed to wander even once, it will become increasingly difficult to restrain and bind.
When the ancient masters taught the tending of oxen, how could they ever have allowed the rope to run loose? When both man and ox are forgotten, heaven and earth are truly vast and empty.
To show that it is truly difficult for a practitioner of subtle Chan to leave home and study the Way: advancing in it is like climbing a ten-thousand-fathom mountain.
If one can remain ever non-retrogressive at every step, one will not even realize they are dwelling amidst the white clouds.
To the Chan practitioner Xishi Xuan:
There are no many secrets to the work of practicing Chan. Push aside all affairs and maintain the simplicity of the One. Hang only the Great Matter upon the heart;
take the iron ox directly and whip it until blood flows.
Shi Ke Zhiyan, the Layman:
The Great Way is clear and distinct; it does not belong to verbal expression. As soon as names and words are involved, entanglements arise.
In a single thought, when the subjective and objective are utterly exhausted, the stone ox lets out a roar by the ancient stream.

The Venerable Master Qingyu was shown that arising in a single kṣaṇa is itself ceasing in a single kṣaṇa; this was clearly explained by the mark of the broad and long tongue. Even this "kṣaṇa" is but a provisional name;
from the very beginning, all phenomena are fundamentally quiescent.
To Shì Ruì (Four Verses) To study the Way, one must first recognize oneself.
Most honored and most noble, who can compare to you? Exert your will and seek diligently without slackening;
It is like bailing out the ocean—one must reach its very bottom.
In studying the Way, first contemplate that worldly phenomena are empty; the sense organs, the body, and the physical world leave no trace.
Yet within this very emptiness there is an original bone—this is precisely the true master.

In studying the Way, one must first prize single-mindedness; do not divide your path and pursue it in confusion. Though the colors red and purple follow worldly fashion, who knows that they turn their backs on the person of original nature?

In studying the Way, diligence in self-mastery comes first; when the work of self-mastery is accomplished, the myriad realms merge in harmony. The great chiliocosm is not something other than oneself;
only then does one realize that every phenomenon is originally empty.
To Layman Peng Erren:

The essence of this mind is fundamentally beyond separation and subtlety; the chirping of magpies and the singing of orioles reveal its wondrous mechanism. Do not give rise to conceptual elaborations through idle interpretations;
throughout the vastness of the ages, people have vainly engaged in right and wrong.
I show you, Layman Peng Erda:

your numinous light is vast and penetrating, pervading all of space; how could it reside within the confines of a few mere scrolls? You would do better to exhaustively explore that realm where Fuxi had not yet drawn his lines;
to break off the bamboo slips of the *Book of Changes* three times is but a waste of effort.
To Layman Huang Zhongdan:
The lifeblood of the thousand sages cannot be expressed in words; eating and dressing accord with the original source. Confucius of old spoke of "nothing hidden";
when the osmanthus blooms in the courtyard, one enters the wondrous gate.

Verses on the Pure Land (Four Poems) The ground of lapis lazuli shines with the luster of gold; It is not in the west, nor is it in the east. When deluded thoughts are utterly extinguished, one returns to the One Buddha;
Spontaneously, one sits within a lotus flower as one’s natural body.
The moment a single thought arises, one is bound by entanglements; no method for gathering the mind compares to the practice of Buddha-recollection. Directly cast the entire Sahā world aside;
the nurturing of the spirit rests securely upon the purple-gold lotus.
Every person possesses their own ancient Amitābha; do not let it slip away during the twelve periods of the day.
If you simply ensure that the radiance of the mind remains ever unclouded, there is no need to snap your fingers to leave this Sahā world.
With the single phrase of Amitābha, there is no other thought; when myriad thoughts are all empty, one perceives the primordial suchness. This is liberation in every dust mote;
there is no need to further inquire after the Zen of the Patriarchs.
It is shown that one should simply introspect;
do not pursue superficial appearances, but look inwardly. Peel away layer after layer and do not crave the profound mysteries.
Once the duality of subject and object is forgotten through discernment, the true source will naturally be seen directly.
To the Chan practitioner Shouyu:
The numinous light shines forth alone beyond the sense bases and objects. Where here could there ever be wisdom or folly? At midnight, the wooden man opens the stone door;
indeed, it is only by being without intention that one may encounter him.
To Zen practitioner Zhifazhen:
This Way is manifest and face-to-face; why must you seek it out with such deliberate effort? A nun is fundamentally a woman; the mountain gate naturally faces the Buddha hall.
Thus, when the World-Honored One held up the flower, it was like a flash of lightning in the sky before hundreds of thousands of devas and humans.
Without opposition, the fruit is true knowledge and vision.
To the Layman Tao Tai Liang (Two Poems):
The Buddha-way is profound and vast; it cannot be fathomed by worldly wisdom. One must rely upon the sacred words to use them as a finger pointing at the moon.
If you grasp the finger and mistake it for the moon, you will instead bring about your own error.

To err yourself and further mislead others—though white clouds may stretch for thousands of miles, if one ascends the peak of the Way, the most essential thing is that the path be straight. If the path deviates by even a hair’s breadth, the level road becomes a deep pit.
On the path, do not fear toil; with fierce vigor, press forward. If you reach its summit, only then can you turn back and escape illness.
Strive, O Chan practitioner Jisheng!
Do not be overly attached to phantoms and fleeting light. Space has bones—this you must further investigate. Only when names and words are exhausted will you be upright.
What need is there to seek south for fifty-three years?
I urge you, Dharma brother Bai:

the Heart-Seal of the Patriarchs is fundamentally difficult to clarify; to deliberate over it by even a hair’s breadth is to fall into worldly sentiment. At midnight, the golden rooster suddenly breaks through...
In a dream, a pair of eyes suddenly emerged from the void.

They were shown to the Chan practitioner Juehai to demonstrate that the essence of Chan is quiescent extinction, free from names and forms; even the term "quiescent extinction" is not Chan itself. One need not seek the truth; one must simply bring all seeking to rest.
Behold! The Patriarch, with bitter words, reveals the profound explanation:

he shows the Chan practitioner Cànran that this single phrase of the "head-word" is like an iron stake. Whether moving or still, let it continue incessantly; do not seek to rest. Furthermore, you must raise your eyebrows.
Look! Do not merely wait indifferently for the right moment.
This Way has never been separated from you by so much as a hair’s breadth. There is no need to seek it elsewhere; you simply must bring to rest the thieving mind.
The Three Thousand Buddhadharmas are fundamentally not many.
Showing the solitary man Yueshang:

A single orb of bright moon reaches the heart of the heavens; the azure sky has never been tainted by even a half-point of defilement. When a student arrives here, they must cease their lingering steps;
the nostrils have always been of a different depth.

To demonstrate the essential points for those of superior birth and superior character: set your mind on emulating the ancients; in your practice, do not draw near to reckless Chan. Only by constantly examining yourself and recognizing your own faults can you distance yourself from the mundane and aspire to the sages.
To Layman Zheng:

Sentient beings are deluded and obscured, naturally entangled in their own bonds; discrimination is difficult to forget, and the taint of attachment remains firm. When will the surging waves of the sea of suffering ever cease?
You must believe that in the West there is a wondrous lotus. If pure mindfulness can simply transcend the four propositions, then the great earth, its rivers, and mountains are all [the Pure Land].
Vast and open! The Land of Ultimate Bliss, with its jeweled nets and golden ponds, resides right before one’s very eyes in the ordinary state.

To the student Yang, Layman of Jinjiang, who has traditionally valued intellectual insight, the Master of the Apricot Terrace (Confucius) nevertheless said, "I wish to remain silent. One must know that this "single thread" is none other than this.
Objects—only through silent realization does one come to know how they accord with the source of the Way.
Confucius was right there under his own feet; Yan Hui clearly sought it outwardly. He mistakenly saw what was before his eyes as standing out prominently;
only at the end did he realize that, in truth, there was no way to reach it.

To Shanzi Pan, the filial and incorruptible scholar, I show that this single point of luminous spirit knows neither old nor young; whether becoming a sage from among the common folk, it always depends on this very source.
When one looks back, not being obscured by the dust of emotions, it penetrates earth and sky, fundamentally as it naturally is.
To Mr. Pan Zhongzi, the scholar:

In the school of Confucius, the most urgent matter lies in seeking benevolence (*ren*). When one can take responsibility for oneself, the hundred ailments are cured. Once it is realized that the sense-faculties and their objects are fundamentally illusory, the entire universe appears as one's own complete body in vast openness.
Showing the One Who Transcends Myriad Dharmas (Two Poems) The myriad dharmas originally return to the One;
where does this One itself return? Treading upon the waves, they are but water; the night moon shines with perfect brilliance.
My own body is fundamentally without substance; where could the Chan school be attached? Therefore, those who study the Way need only attain the emptiness of mind.
To Master Shida Li (two verses): The path to the West is not difficult to traverse.
Send your thoughts back to the West and do not linger in the East. Constantly recite the Buddha’s name as a child remembers its mother.
Mother, why grieve that mother and child shall not meet?
It is said that rebirth in the West is very easy; one need only fear that the ordinary mind refuses to cease. When the ordinary mind is fully stilled, one returns to true awakening;
this very mind is the boat for crossing over beings.
Seeing off the Chan practitioner Shiqi as he returns home to visit his kin is fundamentally the business of descendants; yet from time immemorial, the ancestors have never stepped outside the door.
This time, if you should see your own grandfather, you would do well to swallow the entire universe in a single gulp.
To the Zen practitioner Hanhui:
On the ancient path of traveling to study under various masters, one must possess the eye. Upon entering a gate, one must discern the host; it is valued that one knows the true sound.
Nowadays, everyone has a mouth for drumming on the air, but only by walking the correct path does one know who is a true person.
I shall clarify this for you, Master Jun. You have already studied the Way for many years; I will grant you a partial understanding of it.

However, if you wish to attain unimpeded mastery in all directions, you must still pull out one more wedge. Only upon reaching this state will you know that every matter is as it should be; how could you allow vulgar learning to intrude upon this?
Discrimination. In eating and dressing, he is merely ordinary; yet he is a single moon that penetrates heaven and earth.
Addressing the assembly while ill:
"This old man was born with a temperament too biased; he refused to follow the worldly stream into entanglements. His stubborn nature remains as it was even now."

Transformation! I shall use my stubborn bones to rescue Confucianism and Chan. In Confucianism, the pursuit of fame and achievement has truly led to its loss; in Chan, the veneration of cleverness and debate makes right conduct difficult to perfect.
Now that I am on the verge of death, what more is there to do? I shall simply offer this single thought as a requital to the dragons and gods.
The final verse of the臨終偈 (Verses on the Hour of Death) was personally entrusted [to him]. Within and without the three realms, there is no place to be sought.
From the *Yongjue Heshang Guanglu*, Volume Twenty-Three.
The Expanded Record of Master Yongjue, Volume Twenty-Four.
Compiled by the Dharma-heir Disciple Daopai.
Poetry, Part One.

A Five-Syllable Ancient Poem on Traveling to Baisui Mountain Temple Rising at dawn, I depart from the southern suburbs. My traveling robes are cold as iron. Far stretches the path of green pines; Slowly, frigid clouds coalesce.
Layered ridges rise ever more precipitously; as the mountains end, the path seems to cease. A small bridge spans a perilous ravine; I contemplate the Way and take up my staff amidst the clouds.
Winding through the emerald mists, there lies the palace of the Dharma King. Its heavy gates are deep and secluded; an aged monk sits there, his eyebrows white as snow.
Welcoming guests, he hurriedly untied his shoes; with laughter and ease, we greeted one another. From a crevice in the rocks, I drew fresh spring water;

in a bronze pitcher, I brewed *quèshé* tea. From my small pavilion, I gazed upon the precipice; opening the window, I awaited the bright moon. The wind through the pines blew against my frozen ears; the sound of the waves never ceased.
When asked about the meaning of the "Holding Up of the Flower," I cannot utter a single word. Beg me to write a new poem, and it will be like a dyke bursting.
Do not speak of "literary Chan"; I fear it would be the extinction of the nectar of immortality.

In Lu-yang, Mao Jiqi cleared the land to construct a thatched cottage. He built the foundation with great care for its levelness and solidity. Three bays were laid out across the front, with two wings extending to the east and west.
The thatching was woven as neatly as if cut with scissors; the pillars stood as straight as chopsticks. The outer fence was left quite sparse, while the inner walls had to be complete and dense.
Since there are no marks of axe or chisel, it is spared the adornment of vermilion and lacquer. Windows are opened to allow for the free flow of air, and doors are set to regulate entry and exit.
It can avoid the bitter frost; it can avoid the scorching sun. Those of high station are unwilling to come; how could worldly scholars ever gather here?
Only the monk of non-action, who all day long cradles his knees; sometimes he goes out the gate, leaning on a single *khakkhara*;
sometimes he enters the door, wearing a cloud-like cloak and a rain hat. When inspiration strikes, he sings aloud; when weariness arises, he lies down to rest.
Hehe! There is another heaven. Its vastness is truly beyond compare. I send these words to those who have not yet returned home: when will the affairs of this world ever end?
Only after they are finished can one return to the mountains; by then, it may be too late to bite one’s own heels.
At Jinxian Hermitage, I received a letter from the scholar Li Qinglang. Missing him, I sat up after waking from sleep and scratched my head;
outside the window, the rain fell like falling fur upon the void. A guest came to knock at my door, the sound of his tapping resonating repeatedly.
What a handsome man of noble family! Able to convey these twin carp. Unfolding the seal and reading them again and again, they are as vast as a bell that shatters silence.
They drink my rose-dew for me; they brush away the willow breeze for me. I envy you who willingly embrace poverty, pure and slender like a lean walking staff.

The numinous tortoise never abandons its shell; the pine in the snow stands tall and firm. Composing poems that favor the extraordinary and the perilous, Li He and Lu Tong occasionally appear amidst the white clouds, coming and going to explore the Chan school.
Alas for that young man of the eastern house; though he wears the black silk ribbon of office, he also holds the vermilion bow.
A mere glance brings forth wind and rain; he tugs his beard, ever feeling himself a hero. Morning and evening he ascends the heights and ridges, bustling among the common folk of the marketplace.
How base! Truly he degrades himself. Who could compare your jade-like bones to such as these? As we sit long, the incense seals turn white with ash; at the close of day, the lanterns glow a deep red.
Spontaneous Verses on Remembering a Person: The Plantain Tree in the Night Rain While staying at Lengyan Temple in Xiushui, I heard of the circumstances of its recent restoration.

I composed these verses to express my sentiments regarding this site where former sages once annotated the sutras—a great monastery that once dominated the marketplace, yet which, after years of neglect, has gradually fallen into ruin and been transformed into a "Jin Gu" garden.

Famous flowers vie with one another in their splendor; precious beauties likewise compete for grace. Drawing white counters to track the waxing and waning of the day, the sounds of *lú* dice mingle with pipes and strings.

The eminent scholar, a true "Subsidiary Sage," has come to visit the old Lêng-yen Monastery. His eyes meet every sight and he lets out a long sigh; moved by sorrow and alarm, he cannot sleep through the night.

There will come a guest from the azure clouds, whose ornate staff brushes through mist and smoke. Will you not deign to turn those hands that once unfurled the imperial edicts into fists to knock at the gates?

Together we shall contemplate reclaiming the encroached lands and forge a structure to continue our former karmic bonds. We shall dispatch the adamantine flames and sprinkle them with the cool, clear spring.
In an instant, a precious monastery was formed, appearing as if it were the realm of Śakra or Brahmā. Painted rafters and shimmering green tiles adorn golden halls draped with pearl curtains.
Chanting resounds through the spring day; dark clouds gather over the evening assembly. The Great General Linji’s shout reveals the Zen of the common brick.

It was still engraved upon palm leaves, and its transmission spread widely across the seas; how magnificent it was! Yet, as the court torches burn but for a short time, the Great Being has already departed to the West.
His remaining image stands solemnly alone; his vacant hall holds only two green eyes. Who among the worthy shall succeed him?
I have come to be beset by illness and distress, lying prostrate for a long duration. Following behind the elder, I have repeatedly recounted my meager experiences.

Reflecting thus upon adversity and prosperity, I see they are as easily turned over as the palm of a hand; how pitiable! The worldly order is always like this; how could even iron or stone remain firm?
Sitting for a long time, my mind forgets sleep; the autumn moon moves before the eaves.

On the southern road of the city, the fragrant grasses grow thick; on the southern road of the city, it stretches far as one approaches the capital. Ancient locust trees line the path in green, and fine birds still call to one another.
I pray you, traveler, lend me your ear: as you journey forth, do not hesitate. Tread this path of chariots and horses; avoid that road of thorns and brambles.
Pausing by the side of the forked way, I ask you where you intend to go. Alas! A thousand li of error lie within the very first step you take.
Therefore, when the gentleman studies, he must be cautious in selecting his path; this is what I have carefully contemplated.
In response to the gifts bestowed by Liu Yuzhong and Dai Pingzi of Qingzhang upon my visit to the mountain:

The era has fallen after the kalpa of the conflagration, and the ancestral temple has long been overgrown with weeds. Fortunately, there are patrons who offer gold for the land, once again constructing the dwellings of the Śākya clan.
The spring gushes forth in a constant flow; the white clouds still unfurl and fold. The sacred source has not yet run dry; the sound of the water as it drinks remains.
Those of old found this quite miraculous, as ten thousand fingers circled the round mat. Yet, regarding the verse of the Stone Gate, how could there be any difference between past and present?
I have come to succeed him at his seat; like a lame tortoise emerging onto a thoroughfare, how dare I pursue the lightning-fast steed? The gathered onlookers all burst into laughter.

Why do you deign to visit this humble man, Your Excellency, with your lofty carriage arriving from amidst the pines? I would gladly avoid the polished stone steps of the court to invite you into my cottage of mist and clouds.

The mountain children leap for joy together; the fine birds vie with one another in their cries of delight. Even the white dragon cannot restrain itself, sprinkling rain to wash away the dust and mire.

As he wields his brush, dragons and snakes race across the page; every brilliant stroke is like a shimmering jade bead. Resonant echoes fall upon a thousand crags; flowing light illuminates the nine thoroughfares.
We sit side by side to discuss this fundamental matter: what is Chan, and what is Confucianism? Only when one realizes the intent of Bodhidharma does one come to know the books of the Sage Confucius.

Joyfully forgetting both clamor and stillness, the pines and moonlight shine upon the empty window; the mountains are vacant and the clouds' shadows are faint, as a subtle fragrance enters the courtyard.
I sit here in withered desolation, standing dazed like one who forever guards a tree stump. In vain do I await the gaze of Master Shi; I am but an old *chú* tree upon the mountain peak.

Once, on the day I went to sweep the ancestral stupa at Xuansha, I emerged from the pine gate at noon. Winding my way down the azure ridges, the mountain wind blew against my robes as they fluttered at the edge of the crags and peaks.
The river’s light recedes yet approaches; mountain clouds depart only to return. How vast and boundless the green fields appear! How many times I lingered upon the grassy paths.
Winding along east of Yecheng, I gazed longingly toward Feilai Shan. At sunset, I reached its base, reflecting deeply on the hardships of the journey.
The golden spire has long since crumbled; the stone stupa too is half-ruined. There was a monk who could mourn the antiquity of the site, rebuilding it amidst the desolate mounds.
I came to visit these ancient traces, and host and guest shared in full delight. Before the ancient stupa I offered incense; leaves fell as the autumn mist grew cold.
The distinct sounds of the Dharma being preached have not yet ceased even until now.

Ascending the mountain, one feels a profound resonance with the towering peaks that seem to transcend the heavens; gazing upon them, they are both green and azure. Stone steps pierce through the clouds, and at the pine gate, the grass has not yet been cleared.

The immortal cannot be summoned; the vermilion well is choked with accumulated sand. The meditation master has departed and does not return; the stupa lies overturned, sealed by creeping vines and ivy.

The transformation of things is fundamentally like this: what can one preserve from morning until evening? There was a monk who made a plan for his own life; even unto death, his resolve did not waver.
For my own sake, I have prepared this square grave; how could I dare to move the stones of the ancestral stupa? I know not what will become of me after death—who will cherish this grave?
As the sun sets and the evening breeze blows, the cold crickets chirp incessantly.

To ascend the summit of Mount Gushan, one must reach the ultimate peak. This saying I have heard from antiquity. Many times I wished to climb upon the clouds, yet my resolve was repeatedly obstructed by myself.
This morning I resolved to go; though my strength was failing and I relied on a staff for support, I reached that craggy crest. From there, I looked down upon ten thousand peaks.
The five tigers dare not cross; they lie prostrate upon the riverbank. Faintly visible are the various cities, where pale smoke locks the level plains.
The mountains stretch to the sea’s end; drifting on, where do they go? Gazing to the horizon within the vast, azure expanse, the islands appear as if they could be counted.
An evening breeze rises from the horizon; the stone drums roll with a deep, resonant sound. With a sudden, piercing cry, they return, their echoes falling through a thousand crags and ravines.
May the Great Master hear this on his seventieth birthday!

The Great Way has long been submerged in obscurity, yet you rose up like a towering cloud to restore it. Your lofty traces are far beyond easy emulation; may you alone be able to carry on the lineage.

The Dharma-clouds hang thick and heavy; their moisture flows everywhere across the great earth. I, in this Min region, am most fortunate, having been granted three successive transfers through my diligent humility.

Shaking out my robes upon the peak of Lim-zeh, a single laugh makes the surrounding mountains seem low. In the empty valley, startled by the sound of my footsteps; on the shaded cliff, looking up toward the morning sun.
