I only pray that you will dwell long in this world, sustaining us forever with your precious hand. With snowy brows and crane-like hair, may the nations around the seas look up to you for refuge.

This act of supporting one’s mother is called the Way of Filial Piety; it is the very beginning of Buddhahood and is also termed the Dharma of the Ultimate Path. The Buddha’s exhortations on this matter are not limited to a single expression.

Though one who has left the household life departs from the secular world, they must surely repay the kindness of their parents. How could one fall into the net of attachment? A fundamental nature such as this must not be neglected.
He built a hall named "Nurturing Mother"; Huangmei is a teacher for a hundred generations. Carrying his mother on his back while traveling on foot—such filial conduct is truly worthy of emulation.

Alas for those peddlers of profit who flee the teachings of Śākyamuni to enrich their private interests; how painful that this is not the Buddha’s intent! How can one wonder that the world collectively censures them?
Having completed his travels and studies, the Superior could not forget what he longed for; leaning on his staff, he returned to his native village to build a mountain hermitage for his mother.
The majestic and virtuous Minister of State, with a single sweep of his hand, caused spring to bloom upon the willow-lined streets and the moon to hang from the branches of coral.
Upon hearing of this, I could not help but open my mouth in joy. I only pray that your mother may live long, forever filled with the boundless bliss of the Dharma.
In response to Mr. Huang Lifu’s poem in the rhyme of "Yonglai":
Tóngchéng is an ancient and renowned region where extraordinary talent is nurtured. Since the rise of Ouyang Xiu, men of distinction have emerged one after another in rapid succession.
Your family has long held the rank of high officials; you have been known for your brilliance since early youth. A majestic master of great prose, you alone continue his legacy.
Like the sun eclipsing all other lights, you alone hang in the azure sky. When one inquires at Mount Yejing, your reputation for the Way stands higher than the Dipper’s northern stars.
Seeking wonders amidst Wu and Yue, I occasionally mingle with wild monks and their staffs. Everywhere I go, the celestial pipes resound; I rejoice in the reopening of these secluded depths.

Pearls and jade shimmer across a thousand crags; the mountain deities guard these precious paintings. Looking down upon those who toil over their tablets and brushes, their petty pursuits seem as trivial as a mere game.
Wearied by my travels, I have returned home; the springtime has now come to its end. I rest in idleness within the Purple Cloud Chamber and take up my brush in the Lotus Palace.
At times, five-colored rays of light shoot straight into the cold void. Facing south, I embrace ten thousand scrolls, sufficient to establish a legacy for a thousand autumns.
I, this mountain monk, have come to Ziyun, yet I have failed to fulfill my purpose with my single staff. How might I follow you on your travels and paint upon walls a thousand feet high?
Inscription for a Painting of a Daoist’s Pine-Rock Grotto:
Its steadfast form is naturally solitary and prominent, all the more so as it grows within a rocky enclosure. This rocky enclosure embraces stone-milk; its steadfast form harbors *fuling* fungi.
Therefore, beneath the pines, this man alone recites the *Huangting Jing*. Amidst the clear shade, he stands haughtily by the white rocks; the wild expanse is moist, embracing the profound stillness.
Alas for the guests of the world, who bitterly desire to gird their waists with crimson belts.

Inscription for "Zhuozhai" (The Studio of the Unrefined): The green mountains possess a divine spirit; the white jade feet are fit for pure play. The man of high station has ceased his worldly entanglements; his noble heart is shared with the rustic farmer.

Though born amidst toil, he has not yet submitted a memorial to the throne; his lofty spirit cannot be constrained. Once the willows have been swept away, he then seeks to entrust his sorrows to verse.

The eavespider spreads its web in the clear sky; wild cocoons become spring jars. How truly is the transformation of things! Do not speak of the dreams of the deluded. Within the mountains, there is a resonance:
the mountain stretches across emerald mists; the spring waters ripple with fresh green. Fallen flowers refuse to stay; they flow out into the bends of the stream before us.
From where does the Way-man come? He wishes to borrow the white clouds for lodging. The white clouds cannot be relied upon; he merely uses them to avoid the dust and vulgarity of the world.
In spring he tills half a mu of field; in autumn he harvests a load of millet. Whenever he gathers the roots of wild vegetables, he mixes them to make "necklace-gruel."
Once full, what more is there to seek? I lie high upon my cottage beneath the forest trees. Having woken from sleep, I step out the door and plant two rows of bamboo anew.

I have heard it said that the young man of the eastern house chases after gold as if chasing deer; when his gold is exhausted, his pouch is empty once more, and his wife despises him while his children revile him.

One instance of simple preservation is more than enough; a hundred instances of clever cultivation are never sufficient. I send these words to the young man of the eastern house: why not plant many grains?
Carrying the wisdom of the Sage, I, Huaiyue, have come to the land of Zhizhe.
I cleared away the brambles to examine the ancient traces, yet I did not see the monument to his former life; Mount Wulu remains empty and azure.
Green grasses obscure the wild mists; I linger, sighing with long regret. A solitary dragon has extinguished its profound radiance, and human affairs are separated by a thousand years.
Yet the name of the wise one still remains, echoing like a thunderclap to this day. How can I rouse this man from his rest, so that we may once more explore the profound mysteries?
How large is this ritual pitcher? How could it possibly contain seven feet? Send word to those scholars: do not waste your efforts in vain speculation.
It is like the North Star, high above; who could reach out their hand and pluck it down?

The Great Being Huai Bo gazes longingly at Mount Huang, where yellow clouds drift amidst the vast white mists. This solitary peak towers for a thousand autumns; it is but a foot or two from the heavens.

I recall the Elder Shanhui of old, whose Way surpassed that of the sages yet who wore the shoes of a Confucian scholar. He went to court to enter the Hall of Imperial Reception, where he sat upon his mat alone, maintaining his dignified ritual protocol.
Wielding his brush, he expounded the entire scripture; how could the void possibly contain it? Each night, nectar-like dew drips down, and celestial immortals frequently come to rest here.

The temple has fallen into ruin, filled with cold smoke; its beams are warped and the steps have crumbled. Who can preserve this like the Ling-guang Pavilion of Lu? Only these twin trees stand towering and majestic at its base.
Seventy autumns have passed since my youth; now I am seventy years old.
My eyes grow dim and my teeth have fallen out. My limbs are stiff and my steps falter; wind and snow fill my hair.
I have observed the world for a very long time; my dreams and experiences have passed through many eons. A thousand ages are but a single thought; do not sigh over the vicissitudes of the world.
The ten realms are but a shared reflection; the substance of the mirror is fundamentally non-existent. Even Bodhi is not real, much less the remnants of the mundane.
A hundred anxieties have all vanished; at leisure, I open the scriptures of the ancient Buddhas. Deep into the night, I sit alone leaning upon my armrest;
the bright moon fills the courtyard. Presented to Layman Pan Shige on his fortieth birthday:

Mr. Pan was fond of learning from his youth; by the age of twenty, he had already achieved renown. As he grasped his pen, the winds and clouds arose; his conduct and progress approached that of the ancients.

In his middle years, he was able to take delight in the Way, withdrawing from the world to the banks of Qinxi. He found serene joy in benevolence and wisdom, forever renouncing the fame of a snail’s horn.
In his poetry and prose, he found his own amusement; every word revealed his profound integrity. He was like the elusive recluse of Jin, whose willows by the river spread a pure and refined breeze.

This year marks my retirement from official service; the festival of the suspended bow (my sixtieth birthday) has arrived once more. I offer these humble verses as a gift, treating this mere rubble as if it were gold.
Seeing off Layman Shen Junyao returning to his home in Tan County:
Shen Jun is the son of an old friend. From a thousand miles away, he came to Shimen. Out of pity for me, old and infirm, he stayed close by to inquire after my health with warm greetings.
Because of this, I have inquired after my old friends; counting them on my fingers, how many remain? Alas, I alone am left behind; what is there to discuss regarding my own decay and neglect?
This morning he parted from me; white clouds swirl before the village. He did not need to urge me three times; he simply said that he wished for silence.
Due to a fall, I lay ill (ten stanzas):
One foot stumbled and I fell; my four limbs were all afflicted. Lying stiff and unable to rise, both movement and stillness have lost their regularity.
How much more so on the days of the three heats, when one dwells as if beside a mass of fire; sweat drenches the back at every turn, and the fanning of the fan is never forgotten for a moment.
All this arises from the illusory body; what arises through illusion brings injury to itself. One must know that that which is non-illusory dwells peacefully in the realm of non-action.
Mistaken by a single step, one falls into endless sorrow; tossing and turning upon the pillow and mat, the pain never ceases.
Reflecting on the perilous path of the world, every inch is filled with spears and halberds; if for a single thought one falters in vigilance, calamity arises—whom can one blame?

Therefore, when the gentleman studies, he ought to practice with vigilance at every moment. If one wishes to tread the path of integrity without fault, this rectitude does not lie in seeking it elsewhere.
It has been nearly a month since my illness began; bitter medicine has not left my side. When the will no longer governs the vital energy, how can one move even a single step?
The scorching heat now relinquishes its office; the golden wind stirs the cassia branches. Gradually entering this realm of cool serenity, it is as if one were once again free from illness.
Moreover, I rejoice that no guests have arrived; in silence, I find my own delight. This is unlike Vimalakīrti, whose powerful eloquence galloped across the four seats.
After illness, illness is added; skin and bone remain barely joined. Only the bridge of the nose stands high, still just as it was before.
The western wind pierces through the quilt; crickets chirp chaotically against the four walls. Seasons pass by as they may; when will there ever be a "good day"?

Furthermore, there are those who request the Dharma, pointing to what is crooked and calling it straight; this is not out of a desire to deceive you, but because I am speaking the truth for your sake.
Reclining on my side for three months, the morning dew has drenched the banana leaves; the sun and moon leap like balls, and my flesh has already wasted away by half.
At the bedside, I first learned to walk; supported by others, I took my first steps some days ago. This single room, barely more than ten feet square, still feels as distant as a hundred li.
Now that the Ninth Day Festival approaches, the pleasure-seekers’ enthusiasm is particularly grand; yet this sick monk lacks the strength in his legs—how could he dare hope to ascend the heights?
Four months have passed upon this pillow; looking back, it was but a brief moment. Though my suffering has slightly subsided, my gait and stride are still unfit for travel.
The scriptures have long been neglected, yet I have not laid down my brush and ink. When guests arrive seeking verses, I let my hand flow across the paper without hesitation.
A wind deceives my ailing body, which can no longer support itself. Clutching my coarse wool, I guard my skeletal frame, waiting merely for the day of my return.
For over a hundred days, I have been gasping for breath, sighing constantly at the passage of time. The solid ice has now arrived, yet the bitter pain is not yet entirely gone.
My intake of thick gruel has diminished, and my vital energies wither away day by day. My medical skills have already reached their limit, and the efficacy of treatment is truly sparse.
I lack the strength even to hold my staff, still requiring the support of an attendant monk. How profound is my decline! I now bear this mere remnant of a body in vain.
In solitude, I guard my single chamber; the overcast rain brings a twofold chill. The plum shadows before the steps grow thin; beneath the fence, the chrysanthemum blossoms wither.
My ailment has never been cured; tossing and turning, I still suffer in pain. Years have declined and strength is weak; as days count down, how can there be peace?
Simply contemplating the origin of the myriad phenomena, I find myself at peace in the profound stillness. Both the sick and the healthy are altogether without cause.
Now that the tenth month has reached its full moon, the shadows of bamboo lie still across the window. Deep in the night, the lotus-drip clock runs long; a chill arises upon the mat like frost.
Clutching my quilt, I could not fall asleep; reflecting upon myself, I was moved to sorrow. Having been born within the three realms of existence, the bonds of karma have yet to be severed.

My illness has persisted long; how can I avoid taking medicine? I fear it will result in the calamity of lameness. Therefore, I think of the old master Yunmen—what harm would there be in him preaching the Dharma?

I am now seventy-four years old; for several years I have been beset by the suffering of illness. Moreover, having undergone this recent transformation, I have not stepped outside my door for five months.

Now, as the movement of the *lǜguǎn* pipe brings forth the ashes and the clouds clear so that the sun stands at its zenith, I lean on a staff to emerge before the hall and force myself to walk some dozen or so paces.
Gazing out, I see the mountains before the house; their forms are a blend of emerald and purple. An old crane returns to its pine treetop, its posture as it faces the wind appearing ready to dance.
*In Commemoration of Zheng Suonan (with Preface)*:
Master Suonan was but a commoner during the final years of the Song dynasty. After the fall of the Song, his solitary indignation never ceased, and he passed away with his ambitions unfulfilled.
I once composed a work titled *Xinshi* (The History of the Mind). I used iron to fashion a casket and submerged it in a well at Chengtian Temple in Suzhou.
It was not until the Wuyin year of the Chongzhen era that the book finally emerged. Upon reading it, I was filled with a sense of poignant regret.
The world’s situation is like the beam of a scale; every moment it changes anew. Reversals are utterly unstable; why distinguish between ruler and minister?

How is it that Master Zheng remained a loyal subject of the Song dynasty to the end? Having received not even a measure of grain or a pint of rice in salary, he maintained his will with steadfast loyalty and integrity.
The history of his heart, encased in an iron casket, makes every word move gods and spirits to tears. He painted orchids but not bamboo; this intention was truly profound.
He would rather slight the wealth of Lü Wang than endure the poverty of Bo Yi. Even if a Yao or a Shun were to appear, his haughty bones could not be flattened.
Though my noble ambitions remain unfulfilled, until death I shall maintain this single-minded resolve; it is firm and cannot be turned back.

It is not that I crave fame in future lives, but as I light my lamp to read your writings and close the scroll to chant them long, I wonder: how might I borrow a pure breeze to sweep across the people of this world?
Huidream Guan Chanshi (With Preface). Huidream was a native of Quan.
He was the dharma heir of Kaiyuan Foguo. His learning was vast and profound, and his prose was elegant and refined.

By nature, he was strict and aloof, finding few with whom he could harmonize. When the authorities appointed him to preside over Chengtian Monastery, he declined and did not accept. Among his extant works is the *Kai*... [text fragment].
I obtained the two works, *Shi chuan meng guan ji* (The Dream Observations of Master Shi) and [the other], while residing at Kaiyuan Temple;
they were the first I took to heart, for their author was truly a man of the Way. From the Yuan dynasty down to the present day, few have been able to equal his excellence.
The Dharma-gate is in decline, which is truly a cause for profound lamentation. Thus, in my private dreams and visions, I alone feel an intense longing for him.
Southern Fujian is called the Land of Buddhas, where renowned monks have risen like flocks of sparrows; yet Mengguan was the very last to appear—how few in this world can truly know him?

His accumulated learning has a profound source; his writings follow in the footsteps of those who came before. His integrity is most firm and steadfast; he would rather decline official summons than compromise his principles.
His single room is no larger than a peck-measure, yet he sleeps deeply amidst purple clouds. Though the four walls are utterly desolate, his books and scrolls fill every desk.
The sages of old cannot be seen; they are found only upon ancient scrolls. For three hundred years in Min and Yue, who has been able to succeed to their excellence?
Gazing now at those surviving volumes, how profound they are—difficult to fathom their depths. With a serene sense of distant longing, my yearning thoughts cannot cease.
Song of My Ruined House: I have several rooms, long inherited from my grandfather. Ascending the tower, one may compose rhapsodies; facing the moon, one can call for wine.
My attire follows the Han and Tang traditions; at my desk by the window, I sit alone burning incense. I often gather with friends to discuss the classics.
It is only because many years have passed; what can be done against such decay and rot? Though my father spoke of repairs, I was preoccupied with idle pleasures.
One night, dark clouds gathered, and wind and rain poured down in torrents. Walls and roofs were utterly demolished, and all that was beautiful was suddenly consumed.
Men and women flee into empty valleys; orphaned and exposed, they have no place to lodge. The Six Classics have sunk into the mire—what need is there to speak of hemp or beans?
Wild foxes stride across the hearth; mountain ghosts weep beside the walls. Yet, with its unchanging countenance, there remains only the chrysanthemum by the eastern fence.
My life has been plagued by many misfortunes from the start; I spoke only of learning how to avoid the world. Now there is nowhere to hide; I stand alone as a solitary, impoverished man.
Reflecting back on the affairs of my ancestors, at this twilight hour my feelings are unbearable. Alas! A long lament arises; the wind is cold and heaven and earth are shrouded in darkness.
A Heptasyllabic Old Poem: Reading the Collected Works of the Elder Zibo, Moved by Reflection The ancient path is desolate, long since devoid of travelers;
At the ancestral temple, the accumulated snow nearly reaches the waist. On the shaded cliffs, even in broad daylight, mountain ghosts appear.
A Whistle. In the wild weeds and cold smoke, foxes and hares revel in their pride; countless innocent people fall prey to demonic enchantment, dragged into the thorny brambles beyond hope of rescue.
Old Master Zibai’s heart-blood burns with fervor; he raises his voice in a great cry until his very soul seems to dissolve. Behold! Bao Xu wept blood as he stood before the court of Qin;
the ministers and subjects of Duke Mu of Qin likewise shed tears. Once the "Wu Yi" (No Clothes) ode was finished, the sounding of the *diao-dou* drums rang out.
Wielding his brush, he brings glory to the land of Chu; once again we see him: Zhuge Liang, leading his armies without regard for his own person.
Ghosts and spirits wail, dragons and serpents cry out; how could one ever dare to foresee success or failure? At Qishan, he raised righteousness and struck terror into the enemy’s heart.

Whether restoring Chu or extending Han, though their paths differ, their great purpose is as uniform as a rainbow piercing the sun. Now, amidst these late autumn days in the groves of the forest, the old...
How intense were these two gentlemen! Worldly men, knowing only how to preserve their own bodies and value their status, frivolously mock them as "dragons in overbearing positions.
Yet there was indeed reason for their advancing without retreating; they were the loyal subjects of Han who bowed their bodies and exhausted their lives.

Reading old books by lamplight at night, they resolved to propagate the Great Dharma and early on cast away their very persons. A single heart of bitter resolve like the blazing sun, its golden light shining brilliantly across the heavens.
On the eastern road, I sigh: I, who merely guard the stump, weary myself in vain. The life of wisdom is like a single strand of silk; its prospects grow ever more solitary.
How can the miasma of calamity be suddenly cleared away, so that we may sit and behold the era of Tang and Yu this very day?
Section Chief Yuan Shui invited me to reside at Mount Hu while traveling. The former abbot, Master Yinshan, requested that I undertake the restoration of the monastery.
I composed this to encourage his journey, recalling the days when the transformation of Mount Hu flourished:
its soaring eaves and running beams reached toward the celestial thoroughfare; as the drum was beaten and one ascended the hall, ten thousand [monks] stood before.

Pointing [at the past], the flashing lightning and thunderous peals were ever as they were; now, entering this desolate clarity, only a few withered monks remain. Planting grain to procure rice, they maintain their dwellings;
who would have known that Zhurong (the Fire God) still harbors such jealousy? The magnificent pagoda has vanished, leaving only a snail’s shell of a hut.

Weeds grow in chaos over the walls where *luóyī* (climbing vines) once hung; before the steps, *mùxù* (alfalfa) fills the courtyard. The ancient hall is already in ruins, with only the old paving stones remaining; the drums are struck and the bells are tested.
The affairs of the bell have long been neglected. Master Yuan, who loves the Way, has manifested his celestial nature. He treasures the Great Dharma like a precious pearl;

every time he worries about Mount Hu, he cannot sleep. Rising at dawn, he sent me a letter of eight lines. Alas, alas! A lame tortoise has poked its head out; it would make Nanquan and Lord Lu laugh to death.
Although there is no grand hall to house dragons and elephants, there still remains a space to accommodate the round meditation mat.

Do not resent the narrowness of this hut that cannot even accommodate my knees; rather, I recall the ancients who dwelt beneath trees. The Buddha-dharma does not reside in the auspiciousness of a soaring ridgepole;
do you know how one establishes a temple by merely planting a blade of grass? Why do you now labor so hard over construction? It is only because you grieve for the past day and night.
Lower your head like a cloud and emulate the mendicant; for what purpose other than to find peace for this seven-foot frame? Ahead lies the warmth of the sun.
The landscape is beautiful; everywhere the spring is deep, with willows and elms growing long. Taking my single staff along with me, I shall go to ask Jeta for alms among the people.
*In gratitude for the visit and gift bestowed by the Minister Cao Nengshi at the mountain.*
The jagged Stone Drums obstruct the eastern sea; tiered peaks face one another like golden lotuses. The cliff-carvings were first made by Zhu and Zhao;
divine light nightly illuminates the cold void. How few have been the travelers since antiquity? Most are eroded amidst blue mists and green moss.
Only then do I know that integrity and principle are precious for their own sake; how could they rely on stone to demonstrate inexhaustibility? Master Cao arose next.
With the bearing of a courtier in the temple halls, he has returned with two sleeves brushing the pure breeze. His talent, as lofty as eight pecks of grain, has yet to be tested;

for now, he entrusts his labor to the classics to perform the merit of mending the heavens. Having long surrendered his official ambitions to the distant blue river, he rejoices in exploring the Zen school alongside a rustic monk.

Once again spreading golden light, he opens the stone drums; these have been moved from the Brahma and Śakra palaces above. I, riding upon the winds of karma, have arrived here to penetrate [the truth].

Along the path through the mists, encounters are rare. Once again, I see the Patriarch’s mechanism transform the demonic edicts; on the dark precipices, the white sun reveals the横行 (wandering) tracks of ghosts.
The wild waves cannot be turned back as they rush toward the east; my warm blood nearly sprays against the azure heavens. The Great Dharma, hanging at the end of autumn, is but a single thread;

its majestic golden walls and moats rely solely upon you, sir. Seizing this moment of leisure, you have driven your sedan chair here; leaning on your staff, you have trampled through the white clouds.
Clouds seal the sky; with elegant thoughts and ornate verses, he rivals the Seven-Step Sage. The radiance of his brush and the strangeness of his ink shake a thousand peaks.
He pledges his heart to plant the seeds of Bodhi directly below. With might he supports the precious torch to dispel the gloom. I am ashamed that I cannot grasp the wheel of the turning sun;
instead, I envy Zishao’s divine bow.
Together with He Pingzi, a man of talent from Qingzhang, my heart is most fervent in seeking out worthy sages.
To prop up heaven and support the earth requires heroes. Lately, the scholars who peddle the classics have exhausted their flow;
for every ten works examined, nine are found to be riddled with flaws. You, Master, have risen from the city of Danxia; your talent exceeds eight pecks, and your spirit is lofty.
Transcending all bounds, your writings on governance and strategy resemble those of Jia Yi; every word is like tears shed upon the blood of heroes.

You have specially annotated the *Yugong* to assist former sages, providing detailed expositions on the mountains and rivers as their longitudinal and latitudinal coordinates. Your work is magnificent, clear, and a rare treasure of this age; Dong Zhongshu and Jia Yi would not be considered "double-tongued" today.
Yet the Heavenly Qiao of the northern frontier has not yet been subdued, and those who brandish weapons in the Central Plains have still not been extinguished. I pray that you—
Cease resting in the mountain hut of the Southern Hills; swiftly apply the whip of your ancestors to meet the demands of the times.
When the bridge at Yingzhou was completed in Tanyang, Mr. Ding came to solicit a poem. I praise the virtue of Lord Shen:
the mountains upon the lake are crimson and towering; the waters within the lake are deep and surging. A spiritual radiance, refined and refreshing, gathers at Yingzhou.

Island. Many heroes and sages of antiquity and the present have emerged here. In the past, there was the Recluse of Qiaodong River; his understanding of the Way made his household resplendent with autumnal colors.
When Master Lu Jiuyang (Huiweng) offered a cup of wine to bid farewell to Ji Tong, they walked and chanted upon the bridge, forming a magnificent gathering.

How many years have passed since the raging waves swept it away? Its former traces are difficult to pursue, and my heart is moved with sorrow. A traveler stands at the river crossing as the dark spirit fades; the waves are swift and the rapids turbulent.
The lofty winds and rains brought forth tears of joy; together we rejoice that the "Spring of Yang" now has feet. Benevolent breezes sweep and nourish all things, bringing life and growth.

For a hundred *li*, all is peaceful and bright beneath the rain of transformation. As the people’s praises fill the roads, they extol the Lord’s virtue. There is Master Ding, who wears benevolence and upholds righteousness;

like a long rainbow resting upon the waves, he requires no external aid. To donate five thousand pieces of gold was not difficult, yet he drove stones and transported timber to complete the work in a single day.
Have you not seen? When Duannming built the stone bridge across the sea, gold was spent tenfold and materials were brought from many places.

From Minnan to Yanbei, all vied to proclaim it, saying that such divine achievement could not have been accomplished by human means alone. How does this compare to Lord Shen, who issued no command yet sat watching as the work was completed and the myriad people enjoyed ease?
A Birthday祝 for Master Chiyun of Zhiti at Eighty Years of Age:
The Zhiti Peak stands firm at the edge of the Eastern Sea; Layered peaks and overlapping ridges embrace the Chan hermitage. The celestial crown and sacred traces are remote and unfathomable;
The alchemical hearth of the immortal remains amidst the ruins. Within it dwells a high monk with hair like snow, Who sits beneath the Pratyekabuddha Rock, embracing...
Jinyu, you are like a crystal pitcher bathing the moon, or like a cluster of flames revealing a lotus. At eighty years of age, you remain vigorous and alert;

drinking from mountain streams and sleeping amidst the clouds, you always act with spontaneous ease. May you, Master, remain in this world as long as the Treasure-Handed One (Baozhang), acting forever as a bright torch to illuminate the dark alleys.
A Letter Presented to the Venerable Jiu-feng Within the Bodhimaṇḍa, the Dharma-thunder resounds;
In seven locations, wondrous adornments manifest through illusion. At last, beneath the twin śāla trees, he delivers his final testament;
The vast ocean of the four virtues is boundlessly deep. By whose power does the Venerable One wield his brush? From a single hair-tip, he brings forth the inexhaustible.

Past and present, though one were to fill the oceans with ink and write them all, not even a single dot or stroke could exhaust their fullness; within this very midst, all is perfectly round. I have come to burn incense and read them aloud;
the brilliance of the brush and the strangeness of the ink shake the azure heavens. It is like a lion exerting its full strength:
the ancient mirrors manifest all at once, layer upon layer. I feel my body enter the realm of Vairocana; the dharma-realm interlaces and remains eternally serene. Thus I also perceive...
The body floats upon the ocean of nirvāṇa; every drop of ghee contains the fullness of all flavors. Closing this volume, I ask you briefly:

how does it compare to that which has not yet been painted? Master Ying lies in high repose beneath his window of schistophyllum; the lantern in the corner of the wall laughs until it nearly falls over.

Inscription for the Prajñā Hermitage, also Commemorating the Master Qiujiang How vast and boundless is the sea of the Three Zhe! The surging waves rise like mountains, about to strike the heavens. Upon the riverbank stands a hermitage, small as a peck-measure;
Its wooden gate remains perpetually closed, sealed by clouds and mist. Along the winding paths, tall bamboos shed pure dew; The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra* is engraved upon the four walls.

Amidst the jade and agate, there sit serenely two mendicants; elder brother and younger brother, it is difficult to distinguish who comes first. The elder brother’s tone is ancient and untainted by the mundane;
sitting alone upon an empty bed, he contemplates a worn brick. The younger brother has now completed his sixty-year cycle;
with a naturally simple mind, why should he not enter the marketplace? I wish to pluck Mount Sumeru from its base to offer you further blessings for immeasurable years. I laugh at myself.
Though the void cannot be invoked for aid, I shall briefly grasp my hair-pen to compose this short piece.

Last year famine stalked the land as the River Lord wrought great havoc; the green rice seedlings were swept away, and the fields became like the sea. Locusts followed in succession, their swarms obscuring the sky.
O Heaven! The fields have been ravaged and the sprouts destroyed for thousands of miles. Weeping and wailing never cease;
sacrifices are offered to Heaven and prayers made to spirits, yet there is no end. Furthermore, spring snow falls as large as fists, drifting for half a month without stopping.

The displaced have no place to shelter their bodies, and the corpses in the ditches and gullies are beyond counting. Some sell their wives and trade their children to barely survive; others pawn their own [bodies].

The body serves as a servant for the lowliest; parched grain, husks, mud, and dirt are our daily fare. Even grass roots and tree bark are considered delicious. The weak lose their lives and enter the realm of ghosts;
the strong seize by force, rising up like swarms of bees. The mats in the north and south are all covered in gathered dust.
When donors do not arrive, upon whom can one rely? Though the iron board still hangs before the old hall, the alms-bowl returns empty, and only plain water is boiled.
The monastic community has scattered like birds with no place to settle; for a morning they are seen, yet by evening they have moved on again.

Robbers in the green forests roam with great license, making it difficult for both mountain-dwellers and wandering monks to find sustenance. Have you not seen the laywoman (upāsikā) who dwells in Haizhu City? Though her vessel is small, she rains down jewels to relieve the poor and hungry.
And have you not seen the Great Being at the Twin Trees who vowed to burn his own body, willing to sacrifice himself to save the world from calamity?
I am self-reproachful; I am ashamed that I am incapable of both. I do not yet know how I might come to rescue them.
I only pray for a great harvest in autumn, so that auspicious qi may suddenly dispel the stagnation of heaven and earth.
Lamenting the City of Fortune, which has been besieged for a long time; famine and disease press together with urgency, I offer this lament. Alas!
The suffering of the City of Fortune is most pitiable; boundless and profound calamities have converged at this time. Ten months have passed since the military siege...
I do not understand. A household of a hundred thousand cannot support itself; when the three calamities arise together, even Heaven does not grow weary of them.
Corpses fill the city, their number beyond reckoning. It is said that a sage of old once uttered a prophecy: "The three mountains shall flow with blood until they form a lake.

Indeed, one searches everywhere on the banks of this lake for grass to fill the belly; even by cutting flesh from the ditches, one may stave off hunger. When humans devour one another like birds and beasts, the marketplace...
The tiger’s words were no deception; how many have been seen begging along the paths of noble mansions? One day, wives and children are left abandoned and scattered.

It is only because one’s remaining life is difficult to preserve that the family’s reputation has been swept away—yet who would mock them for this? Wuzhu established a kingdom and called it a land of blessings.
Reaching this point, how strange the calamity becomes! Even if the common people were all to perish, one might still fear that an empty city would remain a foundation for further disaster.
Alas! In the City of Blessings, suffering is most pitiable.
"Sengbingtan" (Lament for the Monastic Soldiers) laments the chaos in Quanzhou during the late Yuan dynasty, when those who consumed meat were so vulgar as to drive monks into military service.
Master Mengguan composed this "Sengbingtan. Today, there are many monks who become soldiers without even being driven; this is the extinction of the Dharma.
Such is their characteristic. Following their dreams and visions, they have acted accordingly;

yet the Awakened King, in establishing the Vinaya, first prohibited killing. Even to merely possess the implements of slaughter was subject to censure. According to ancient tradition, one dares not pluck a blade of living grass;
how much more so for those who follow the military and engage in mass slaughter? Shaking their heads and flailing their arms as they leave the *ārāma*, they constantly think of strife and battle.

Asuras! Your *kāṣāya* robes are cast directly into the flowing eastern waters; you wear armor upon your bodies and shoulder spears upon your shoulders. You are ashamed to speak of dignified deportment and dismiss Aśvajit;
you boast of your own prowess in leaping over tigers and wading through rivers. You possess not a single iota of loyalty or righteousness;

it is only because of delusion and greed that you have raised the trap for disaster. The mountains of knives and trees of swords appear before your eyes; bleached bones lie strewn across the slopes of withered grass. Furthermore—
The three miserable realms inflict agonizing suffering; how shall one pass through a thousand births and a hundred kalpas? Alas! Alas! Why do you not awaken?

To wallow in self-indulgence is like a moth rushing into a lamp’s flame. Rising at dawn, rub your head and reflect within yourself: what can the Buddha of Awakening do for you, though his words are bitter?
Seeing Master Jinghe Return to His Former Retreat:
Lately, Chan practitioners have become as numerous as millet seeds; Everyone they meet is muddled and confused.

They all claim that birth and death do not concern them, Yet they are bound by lotus fibers like calves tethered to their mothers. My Master has realized the Chan of Boshan; For half his life, he has willingly accompanied the white clouds.
Cloud-dwelling: not a single speck is hung upon the human world. Serenely and securely seated within a three-bay cottage, one takes a single staff and enters the deep clouds;
a thousand-fathom cold tree hides in the secluded valley. How can this compare to the defiled Zen of other quarters, which involves bitter racing and pursuit amidst heaps of red dust?
This summer I have returned to Shigushan, where the mountain has admonished me more than twice or thrice. At dawn—
Parting from me to return to his former dwelling, his towering solitary wind is truly beyond the mundane. In this age of the Dharma’s decline, how few are there like you?
You cause those of a thousand years hence to look up in reverence at your fragrant footsteps.
I see off Master Zhuo’an as he returns to the golden corded boundary beneath Mount Huanglong at Shouchang.
Having traveled again to Western India to establish a Brahma-palace, he now preaches the Dharma amidst a single day of blazing flames;
all is swept away, revealing the primordial void. It is no easy matter for you to be entrusted with this task; your iron will supports the heavens once more.
The ancient traces seem as if Nüwa were able to smelt stones; now, indeed, there is the merit of mending the heavens. The stupa of the former master was originally without seams;
it is beneath the shadowless tree that we may meet well. When will you again raise the momentum that soars beyond the clouds?
Standing firm, it shall forever guard the east of Shíxī. You now bid me farewell and depart through the stone gate; your straw sandals shall tread upon the sealed white clouds. My wish is this:
At every step, one must be careful. Skillfully grasp the hoe and revitalize the ancestral wind.
As I escort Upāsaka Benli back to Tanyang, this old monk has reached the age of seventy-five;
though my karma is heavy, I still preside over the drum of Gushan, yet I have not yet attained the peace of a true leader.
I, Qiu, have been prostrated by illness for many years. It is truly difficult for you to come and inquire after my health; like a solitary raft, I have traversed countless green rapids.
Pushing through the clouds, I ascend the path that reaches the heavens, where the frost and snow of the sea and sky are most severe.
To meet you joyfully before this couch and converse face-to-face is as if we were meeting again after lifetimes apart. When I inquire after our old friends, how many remain? How many heroes...

The worthy ones buried it in the earth; forty years have passed since I donned the white robes. My hidden body remains only before Fuxi; all that I studied in my life has been cast into the eastern sea.
With a single *zhilu* staff, I dwell amidst the white clouds. My tongue flaps like wind, like rain from the clouds; the secrets of Gautama are now fully revealed.
How many of the fifteen hundred disciples could hear this? Though my compassionate heart is emptied, in the end there is no remedy.
In days of yore, Zhongni wished to remain silent; only through silent realization can one accord with the original source. Do not say that the drum-sound of Mount Gu has ceased its resonance;
from the beginning, it has been a distinct realm of its own. You are now sixty-four years of age; why would you climb this mountain as a mere casual pastime?
We are both old, like the setting sun; how many times more shall we meet hereafter? This morning, you take your leave of me.
Leaving the Stone Gate, spring birds clamor along the peach and plum paths. I urge you earnestly to remember these parting words:
when traveling to Yan, do not by any means drive your carriage southward. — Composed by Lin Deshan, Military Commissioner.

I recall our meeting long ago on the banks of the Jian River; at first sight, your countenance was like that of a celestial being. With noble spirit, you laid bare your breast to discuss the affairs of state;
how magnificent your resolve, surpassing all other heroes! You were the first to entrust me with the Stone Drums, and we have cemented our friendship among springs and rocks for over twenty springs.
The mountain gate relied upon your weight as if upon a city’s moat; your merit in restoring it is beyond compare. Last year, I urged you...
The final matter: ordinary tea and rice are unfit for presentation. He declared, "I have a path that reaches through the heavens;
how could one of such spirit consent to rank as an ordinary person? Lately, I suddenly heard the news of his passing from his bed; indeed, he has already traveled ahead upon that celestial path.
Standing alone in the empty mountains, I can only look on with regret; I pray that you will not lose your former vow.
Eulogy for Minister Zheng Hanfeng:
I recall in the past, when I went to Jianzhou to offer prayers for the state’s prosperity, it was at Jingci Hermitage that I first met you. From then on, our friendship has lasted nearly a decade;

I have never shied away from the arduous climbs as we traveled between us. Such open-mindedness and profound virtue are not common in this world, and your illustrious reputation and lofty rank—[are truly rare].
Like space, he has true faith in this Way and no longer doubts; his past karmic conditions are focused upon Prajñā.
In days of yore, Yang, Li, Su, and Huang left behind a legacy of the joy of the Dharma. To this day, more than six hundred years have passed, yet only you still possess the spirit of the ancients.
This year’s twelfth month, the weather grows ever colder; snowflakes as large as palms dance across the vast sky. Piercing the clouds—

The ancient tree has suddenly been broken and snapped; both the young and the old lose their composure. Alas! Birth and death are indeed momentous matters, yet even that which is neither born nor dies must be thoroughly investigated.
Casually I have extracted the skeletal bones from the void; clapping my hands, I sing aloud atop the peaks beyond the heavens.
Pentasyllabic Regulated Verse:

Ascending the Shengquan Rock The mountain is high and the world naturally remote; The forest is deep and the scenery uniquely secluded. Hanging vines provide rest for weary birds; Strange rocks splash with cold spring water.
The winding path pierces the clouds as it passes; the empty pavilion awaits the hanging moon. I arrive as the day is already fading, revealing myself before the evening breeze.
[From "Hearing of Border Alarms in the Mountains" (two poems):
War dispatches have arrived year after year; the Heavenly Qiao hordes press upon the Han borders. Bones wither as the mountain grass turns white; blood splashes as the battle clouds turn yellow.
I have not yet seen the heroism of one who offers his silken cord; who will lend him his chopsticks? When shall we see the weapons melted away? This makes me long for the days of Feng Tang.
I hear it said that the Heavenly King is enraged, and a thousand armies march forth from the Han capital. The morning frost sharpens the swords of Chu, while the night rain washes the celestial host.

The brilliance of the borderlands halts the weapons of war; heaven hangs the sun and moon in clarity. The Chanyu’s heart must surely fail him with dread; pointing toward the sun, the smoke of the frontier passes clear.

Dwelling upon Lotus Terrace, the blue lotus blooms in this pure realm. Half a couch is borrowed for our shared lodging. The sound of surging waves is urgent upon the pillow; through the window, the colors of the trees are a blur.
In my leisure moments, I peruse the Buddhist scriptures; upon waking from sleep, I hear the oriole’s song. At evening, I sit by the riverbank; the wind is clear as a tiger crosses the stream.
On a spring day, I go with my disciples to Yunji Mountain.

The solitary pagoda rises high above the clouds; below it lies the Maṇi Palace. The ancient path is thick with long-entrenched moss; the secluded courtyard is so verdant it seems about to envelop one.
Pine branches hang the sea sun; bamboo shadows play in the river breeze. Having drawn water from before the crags, I brew tea to discourse on suffering and emptiness.
To the west of the bridge lies a small garden; half of the garden is a pond. In stillness, I perceive the joy of swimming fish; in leisure, I watch the busy flight of butterflies.

Picking chrysanthemums while wearing the morning dew, planting chrysanthemums to defy the autumn frost—though my cultivation of the garden may be deemed vulgar, within this vulgarity lies enduring flavor.
I visited the stupa of Chan Master Baiyun Yue at the deepest point of Yunshan.
The trees are ancient, vying to pierce the heavens; the stupa is ruined, yet its foundations remain; the stele is fragmentary, still bearing traces of mist.

The transmission of the mind hangs like the bright sun; the preaching of the Dharma invites the chirping cicadas. Do not say that the Master is silent—his thunderous voice shakes the great chiliocosm.
Mountain Dwelling (Four Poems) I alone delight in these lofty, layered peaks; I have chosen my dwelling in the upper reaches. Deep clouds bury the small cottage; dense trees guard the low walls.

The dense cassias are fit for inviting the recluse; the secluded orchids always scent themselves with fragrance. Reflecting back on events from days past, they seem as deep as the madness of one who has lost his head.
With little means for a lifetime’s livelihood, my family is ruined and I accept only poverty. Lodging as a traveler in a half-ruined hut, this seven-foot body is but a bubble upon the flowers.

On the bookshelves, disordered volumes are piled; upon the desk, dust gathers thickly. I lean alone against the cold crags and lie down; like a withered log, I heed not the spring. A valley of white clouds lies deep;
this secluded dwelling satisfies my wild heart. Turning over the sutras, I often let out a solitary啸 (xiào); facing the moon, I delight in long chanting.
I plant bamboo to clear the mossy path; I plant pines to enhance the verdant peaks. Thus I sigh for the worldly traveler—who among them is like the bird returning at dusk?
Having no temperament suited to the vulgar world, with whom could my square peg fit their round hole? My eccentricity only invites others' laughter; my madness brings me shame even in my own eyes.

Frequently gathering medicinal herbs amidst the clouds, Delicately tapping out verses beneath the moon. For now, I learn the tortoise’s way of concealing its six limbs; Facing the breeze, I smile to myself.
A leisurely half-acre by my small pond window has been opened into a tiny square pool: When clouds pass, they briefly cast their shadows here; When the moon arrives, it always sheds its light.
The spring water poured over the flowers borrows their color; the ink washed from the inkstone flows with fragrance. Only the water in the pond remains serene, as if having forgotten itself.
Passing by Baoshan Hermitage, I met a friend and spoke of old times while observing his recent return to his hometown.
We reminisced about our former haunts: we were startled to find a new master within the gate, yet we recognized the aged pines before the steps.
On this ancient path, who asks the way? Among those known to me, you alone have met me here. As we discuss matters of past and present, our laughter breaks open the seal of the white clouds.
Autumn of the Xinwei Year. Staying at Qingxiu Temple, I carve the *Hongshi lu* while my staff hangs in the ancient meditation chamber.
The autumn wind chills the bamboo bed; only the white moon illuminates my heart, and within my curtains there is clear frost.

Longing for the past, I grieve that it cannot be continued; hearing of its transmission, I fear it may not endure long. Yet, with joy I hear that the cassia upon the crag still emits its fragrance in late autumn.
On the eighth day of the sixth month, I visited He-shui-yen (Water-Sound Rock) together with the two masters, Zhiben and Zhidongwei. Following their rhyme, I write:
The sound of the water has long since vanished, yet the empty name of the crag remains. The path is perilous, deceiving one with its steep cliffs; the river seems small, dwarfed by a solitary sail.

Probing the caverns, I know the source is far; rubbing my head against the inscription, I sigh at the moss-encrusted seal. Accompanying friends, we sit upon the flat rock as a subtle resonance issues from the pines and cypresses.
Presented to Master Kōshō upon his restoration of the ancestral pagoda of Zen Master Xuan Sha, following the rhyme of Great Master Ōun:
In life you harbored many far-reaching thoughts; I long remember the ancient Xuan Sha. Time and again you hewed stones from among the clouds; Once more you spread flowers upon the seat.
The terrace is marked by cold leaves falling; the reflection is cast slantwise by the evening sun. One suspects a fisherman has come to revive the old family home.
Inscribed at Xiansha Monastery, entering beneath Lion Peak at dusk: Beyond the forest, the sound of the Buddhist bell resonates; Cool smoke veils the white pagoda; Cold dew chills the green pines.
Old foundations lie hidden in the wild grass; new rafters nestle beside ancient banyan trees. The thunderous sound has now fallen silent; I come in vain to lament the traces of the past.
In response to hearing of the Great Master’s ascent of Mount Dengsheng to sweep his ancestral stupa:
A solitary peak stretches out as he leans on his staff. His vision is so vast it encompasses no other cities. Clouds manifest in a thousand shifting forms; the river flows in but a single pool.
Deep ferns enshroud the darkened pagoda; fine smoke lingers lightly upon the robes. To seek the traces of a former dynasty, I call my servant to clear away the thorns and brambles.
On an autumn day, the Layman Huishan (Huìqiān) came to the mountain seeking a poem.
Standing before Mount Lìzè, he gazed out: how vast and boundless is the sea and sky! Severed mists obscure the distant trees; the autumn waters reflect the pale, slanting sun.

Planting my staff, I listen to the falling spring; leaning against the crag, I catch the fragrance of the cassia. With boundless intent as I gaze from this height, I share a smile beside the white clouds.
In response to Wei Juzhan’s *Visiting Drums Mountain*, I follow his rhyme:
After the rain, the mountain’s appearance is pure; with deepening spring, the verdant hues are fresh. Ascending the peak, the vast ocean seems small; leaning on my staff, I face the towering cliffs.
Observing the transformations, I sigh over past traces; through meditative stillness, I wash away the dust of the world. Do not say this was a mere chance encounter;
the Lotus Society has its prior causes. Inscription for Kaiyuan Temple: The fame of the Buddha-land has been transmitted for long;
the mulberry tree and lotus flower alone enjoy renown. Extraordinary blossoms sprout from the foundations, and auspicious grasses grow covering the courtyard.
The ancient hall stores clouds in its purple depths; the empty altar reflects the sun’s brilliance. I come to inquire of its ancient traces, as golden bells ring out toward the void.

(II) [In this temple there was a divine monk known as the Bare-Shouldered Bhikṣu, a Wayfarer who carried a lamp, and another monk said to be an incarnation of Mañjuśrī who transcribed the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

Once upon a time, this was a land where lotuses grew, where divine monks often took refuge. The Bare-Shouldered One rescued the multitudes drowning; the Lamp-Bearer awakened the world from its delusions.

The corridors stretch long as the sun turns, and the pagoda soars high, level with the clouds. Where are those who once transcribed the treatises? The hall is empty, and the birds cry out of their own accord.

(III) [In this temple is the Amṛta Precept Platform, established by Master Zhaolun. There is a well whose water tastes like nectar, hence its name. Master Jiehuan authored works such as the *Essential Exegesis of the Lotus Sūtra*.

Ancient worthies were able to uphold the Vinaya; how many years have passed since the platform was constructed? Long submerged in the darkness of the mundane world, it is now reopened, its auspicious colors fresh and bright.
Flying flowers constantly enter the hall; a spring flows from the ocean of nectar. How might I obtain a ring and a mirror, so that their radiance may shine upon the great thousandfold world?

(During the Hongwu era, the Emperor commanded Jie’an to come and preside over the monastery. Upon his audience, the Emperor said: "If you simply purify your mind and cleanse yourself, the multitude will naturally submit. Thus, he established the Hall of Purifying the Mind and Cleansing the Self.
Contentedly I dwell by the edge of white clouds; how many times has the spring breeze blown? It is only because I once sowed seeds here that I have returned again.
The stone cauldron emits fresh flames; celestial blossoms dot the ancient moss. I recall from afar the Master’s instructions on purifying oneself;
the Emperor’s words still resound like thunder. Visiting Mida Rock, I passed through Chaoyun Mountain Hermitage. Arriving late at Dadao Rock, I composed this verse:
Ascending a hundred turns by clutching at creepers, A single path hangs suspended above the clouds. Shady ivy grows like stone shoots; A broken cliff hangs with dragon-spring water.
The sounding-stone echoes from the edge of heaven; Flowers fly, scattering before the cave. Coming home at evening to the precious abode, I smile alone amidst the white clouds.

The stone of that southern peak rises high above the southern mountains; In deep spring, its verdant hue is lush. Its cliffs so lofty they seem to mock the sun’s scarcity; Its paths so remote they communicate with the heavens.

The city walls lie within a rain of smoke; towers and pavilions dwell amidst the shadows of trees. Do not say it is as large as a peck-measure; ten thousand *li* enter through the curtains and windows.
Inscribed on a Fragment of Tile at Yan’an (Two Poems): Because its shape resembles a tortoise, it is also called Six-Eyed Cave.
Bees hang from the narrow path; the vast and deep cavern is long and secluded. A fragment of tile holds the golden spire; for a thousand autumns, it has borne the cosmic pattern.
The celestial wind pierces the rocks with a roar; the ocean waves strike the sky as they flow. How can we always come here to grow old together in this single hill?
To escape the summer heat within the city, I have come to roam this minor celestial grotto. The stone pavilion encroaches upon the verdant hues; the pine couch is shielded by misty vapors.
I brew tea to await the new moon; I strike out verses upon the old strings. The novice monk does not understand these matters, yet still asks the old monk about Chan.

Staying at the Fengmu Hall of Layman Xue Jike to seek the excellence of the "Green Stone" (Bisheng), I came to stay in Layman Xue’s room. The path is secluded, piercing through the shadows of pines; the forest is deep, dispersing the fragrance of lychees.

Smoke and clouds shroud the old walls; wind-whipped trees lend a mournful air to the empty hall. Sitting alone at night in the silent, desolate mountains, the sound of the bell emerges from the upper reaches.
Staying Overnight at Longshan Temple:
The hall is so vast that half of it is filled with clouds; the wind arrives from across the sea. The moon divides itself as it rises above the treetops.
Mountain birds warble beyond the groves; the sound of the tide is heard as night falls. Sitting thus, pure and sleepless, I once again burn a small stick of incense.
Visiting the Purple Cloud Chamber, in the style of Mr. He Jing-shan (two poems):
Scratching my head atop the green peaks, I sit in repose amidst the purple clouds. The solitary city by the seashore stretches far away; at the pine gate, the rustic guest is at ease.
Solitary birds cry out in the evening trees; white deer lie resting in the empty mountains. Vast and boundless, the misty waves stretch far away;

from afar, one sees a solitary crane returning. A single glance spans a thousand li; this mountain alone is permitted its supreme dignity. The sea breeze blows through my sleeves; the mountain’s emerald verdure embraces the monk’s gate.
If you wish to learn the dharma of concealing the body, you must first chew on the roots of vegetables. I exhort you, my two or three disciples: do not pursue the proliferation of profit and fame.
Inscribed at the Tranquil Chamber of the Venerable Guzhu:
A single dwelling beyond the dust; Within it lies a realm apart. The shade of locust trees hangs over the secluded path; The color of the grass enters the curtain, fresh and bright.
The chamber is cramped like a peck-measure; the walls are high, barely reaching my shoulders. Though I have lived in poverty for many days, I accept my food and drink according to circumstances.
Composed at Dongyuan while Dwelling in the Garden of the Venerable Miti:
This place is secluded, where the weeds grow even deeper. My roof is broken, relying on the clouds to pass over it; The walls are low, welcoming the moon’s descent.

Gathering vegetables while still dripping with dew, planting trees to provide shelter for birds—do not say that dwelling in this garden is humble; it is here that my long-held aspirations find serene fulfillment.
Returning to Gushan, I send this reply to Fu Youxin of the Palace of Remonstrance, using his original rhyme:
A single staff has lingered here for a long time; now I turn back, flying beside the cranes. The reflection of the autumn river grows ever fainter; the green of the ancient path fades away.
Pengze was still indulging in wine; to whom at Donglin would the robe be entrusted? Entering the gate, they shared a smile—just like wild clouds returning home.
Passing Yan Tan, evening mountains rest upon the setting sun; spring waters ripple with gentle waves. The clouds clear and the river-sky grow tranquil; the cliffs high, the stone walls cold.

I brush aside the thick moss to explore traces of the past; leaning my oar, I inquire about the former rapids. How many heroic guests have there been? Yet none surpass you with a single fishing rod. New Year’s Eve (Four Poems):
Beholding those waters of the Tiáo River, how could they ever be asked about years or seasons? It is only because this floating life is illusory that it cannot share the hardness of the kalpa-stone.
The sound of crackling fire drives away the old year; incense in the burner leaves but lingering smoke. Gazing toward the colors of the eastern sky, the dawn approaches faintly.

In meditative stillness, it is difficult to speak of years; in the affairs of an old man, knowing the right time is what matters. Is this for the sake of ghosts who lack words? It has nothing to do with poems for ancestral sacrifices.
The years and their splendor end with the burning candles; old age advances with the passing watches. Recalling the Elder of Beichan, I touch my heart and sigh in private:
for many years I have lived in self-contentment, yet tonight my heart is struck with alarm. Within the brazier, the red embers are nearly spent; upon the branches, the white frost is about to form.
The springtime light swiftly fades away; noble ambitions are difficult to fulfill from afar. Cease waiting for the dawn at the window of the rooster; I pray we may travel together upon the bird-path.
The longing of the plum blossoms is nearly spent; the eyes of the willows are about to turn green. Firecrackers shatter the cold stillness; pine torches pierce the night’s darkness.
A hundred years are but a long dream of intoxication; how many times can one awaken this night? Yet I cherish the frost-defying cypress trees, standing in dense ranks throughout the courtyard.

Inscribed at Xiangxiang Hermitage: The woods are secluded and the mists are deep; The fragrant elephant lies hidden on the layered peaks. When clouds arrive, the crags turn white; When the wind comes, the bamboos too sing.
Kindling pines to cook the essence of stone, I converse on the Zen mind beneath the moon. From time to time, I hear upon the eastern ridge the rhythmic *ding-ding* of the ancient chisel.

Ascending the jagged peaks of Shiyu Mountain, I tread the narrow path of birds; flying waterfalls drape the fields like robes, while ancient caves hide within dense clouds and deep bamboo thickets accumulate the misty greens.
The host is virtuous and guests arrive in their sandals; the mountain is remote and worldly dust is scarce. Gazing from the small tower at dusk, a crane is returning to the distant heavens.
Staying at Salawu (Two Poems): Deep emerald hues shroud the layered peaks;
Faint mist enshrouds the secluded valley. A white silk banner hangs in the cold sky; Yellow clouds spread everywhere across the earth.
Strange rocks are draped in mossy robes; on empty steps, bamboo rain descends. Gazing longingly amidst the evening light, who is the master of this solitary pagoda stretching into the distance?
To hide one's traces, the mountain should be steep; leaning against the clouds, a few rafters stand. Tattered robes are drenched by the emerald rain; the bamboo hat is satiated by the misty mists.
Mossy moonlight pierces the curtain, cold; pine wind plays with the shadows, leaning. Last night, pure and unable to sleep, I sat alone facing a single hanging lamp.

By Guōděngyán. Composed for the venerable Chōngrú, who selected the site of an ancient sage and rebuilt the palace of a Great Being (Bodhisattva). Mountain mists invade the desk and mats; the Ox and Dipper constellations rest within the curtains and balconies.
The ocean’s cove cradles the solitary moon; the mountain’s end spans a reclining rainbow. Penglai seems not far away, amidst the hazy, drifting white clouds.
Passing by the Mountain Studio of Layman Shao Lianyao on an Autumn Day (Two Poems) The drum-shaped peaks abound in wonders and beauty;
this mound is most pleasing to the heart. River sails occasionally enter the courtyard; stone shoots naturally form a grove.
In the steep gorges, cold jade-like water chimes; in the secluded mountains, evening birds clamor. Far transcending the world of dust, how much more so now that the autumn deepens!

Startled by this strange realm first opened, I, a mountain monk, feel abashed at being the first to travel here. From the roots of clouds, the backs of birds are revealed; from the pine tops, the essence of stone drips.

As leaves fall, the peaks grow ever leaner; With deep mists, the mountain streams turn more secluded. The west wind arrives with a whistling rush, Yet I still rejoice that the evening smoke has withdrawn.
I offer my congratulations on Master Dongbai’s sixtieth birthday;

having ascended to the high age of sixty, his physical seclusion makes his reputation even more manifest. Pine trees lie prostrate like canopies over cold cliffs; Plum blossoms waft their fragrance through the late season.

With a lofty and dignified air, the monk’s appearance is ancient; his exhaling and inhaling stir the winds of virtue as they soar. Wishing to fulfill the aspirations of Jambudvīpa, how could the lengthening of white hair hinder him?

In early summer, bitter rains fall as the solitary yin is about to be exhausted; the mandate of the Red Emperor has just begun to take effect. The clouds remain dense and heavy, and the drenching moisture continues to pour down for a long time.
The cuckoo finds it hard to call as the moon shines; the buehlohn is too lazy to urge the plowing. Embracing my coarse wool, I sit enduring the cold; when shall I see the sun’s bright light?
Sweeping the Patriarch’s Stupa on Qingming Day (two poems):
On this spring day of clear weather, the breeze is truly warm; Fine birds warble amidst the fragrant groves. Pine-clad clouds are dense upon the stupa; Before the steps, the flower-rain falls deep.
A瓣 of incense for the pulse of the former sages; a cup of tea for the hearts of later men. Recalling events of the past, it is as if I hear the sound of the Dharma being preached.
The ancient worthies departed long ago; the stūpa stands alone in its towering majesty. At night, tigers and wolves dwell within; by day, only woodcutters and herdsmen pass by.
The frost is severe and the stone eggs crack; rain-soaked, the mossy garments grow thick. I circle three times in empty desolation—what can be done about this long slumber?

As the autumn deepens with the descent of frost, the cold wind presses on; the grass before the steps is about to wither. The forest is sparse as the wind sweeps away the leaves; the moon sets and the crows cry from the trees.

In the desolate marsh, the cicadas' song is hushed; Upon the cold pond, the wild geese' shadows stand solitary. Though the hard ice has not yet arrived, The frost has already spread across the tall reeds.
*Eulogy on the Fish Drum* (Two Poems) The gates of the Chan school are mostly silent and still;
It is you who lend them a resonant voice. What need is there to gaze upon the abyss with envy? One may instead follow the wood and encounter [the fish].
The insentient responds with skill; unmoving, it is spontaneously pervasive. Why is it able to do so? It is entirely because the belly is empty.
The formation of images is not nurtured by Heaven; timber is selected from the Deng Forest. Scales have not yet been stripped to enter the waters, yet the flowing resonance emerges from the mindless.

Master Quan holds the authority of the monastic community; he can harmonize the sounds of the *brahman* chants. He is truly a companion to the bells and chimes; how could a fisherman ever encroach upon him?

**Autumn Feelings (Four Poems)** The autumn deepens and the air grows increasingly austere; for a wild monk, this is precisely fitting. I do not compose a "Rhapsody on Autumnal Sorrow," but instead chant only the "Poem on Plucking Chrysanthemums."
The golden wind bids farewell to falling leaves; the jade dew moistens the cold branches. There is a natural, detached elegance here that those passing by may yet fail to perceive.

Sitting silently in this desolate glen, the breeze is already pure, yet it becomes even more so. The smoke from the tea blurs the color of the bamboo, while the resonance of the *buddha-śabda* mingles with the chirping of crickets.

Ancient trees and gnarled roots resound with the chirping of cicadas; the empty curtains hang as the moon shines bright. As the night draws to a close, deep reflection arises; a solitary crane calls out from the crest of the ridge.
A cool breeze rises from the horizon’s edge; I lean on my staff toward the western peaks. The river is still at dawn amidst the reeds; the pond is empty as the geese’ shadows lower.
Cold clouds shut in the secluded valley; withered grass covers the path ahead. After one long laugh upon returning home, the color of the silk-like waterfalls is lost amidst the treetops.
Rising from sleep, I stand before the courtyard; I am suddenly transported beyond desolation. The air is pure and the heavens are vast; as the realm extends afar, the traveler’s longing fades away.
The rock-orchids exude their late fragrance; the river maples shed their leaves in intoxication. A white monkey comes seeking fruit, howling at the moon in the dead center of the night.
Walking through the lush forest, Layman Mouqing ascends Drum Mountain in the rhyme of the previous verse:

Throughout the night there are no locks or keys; for five li, one is entirely shrouded in pine shade. The rocks are perilous and the moss remains slippery; though the mountains are empty, the traveler has arrived.
Cranes fly far, soaring beyond the Milky Way; monkeys cry out as they enter the deep forest. The sound of water drinking cannot be sustained; who can transmit this primordial melody?
On the evening of the Mid-Autumn Festival, together with Zheng Hanfeng, Minister of Works, and Lin Deshan, Minister of Agriculture, we walked by moonlight at Shimen and sat in the Shuiyun Pavilion.
The azure sky is as pure as if washed; following my inspiration, I explore the sacred source. Walking by moonlight through the shadows of pines, I follow the cliff to enter the stone gate.
The sound of cicadas comes from distant trees; the light of fishermen’s fires distinguishes the solitary village. Because I sat upon Fengpo Hill, who would have known the autumn dew was so profuse?
As the sun sets, the mountain’s form grows pure; I raise my staff and ascend the steep heights. I linger upon the autumn grass path as a gentle breeze brushes against my face.
Joyfully I follow the drifting clouds away, then return like a wild crane. What business do I have coming and going? My footsteps have worn through the ancient moss.
I dwell upon the heights of the Azure Ridge; my feet are planted atop the Verdant Rock. White clouds touch my robes with cold, while the wind whistles about me.
Distant villages are visible beyond the mountains; the long river flows beneath my feet. Looking closely, I see mountain ants at war; their greed and anger show no sign of ceasing.

Seated amidst the quiet clouds of the tranquil realm, the curtain is rolled back as the moon first brightens. Not yet having realized the intent of Bodhidharma, he sits facing the wall with legs crossed in the double-lotus posture.

His head is shrouded by nothing but a tattered robe; for his mat upon the ground, he uses a round rush mat. Outside the railing, heavenly flowers rain down; does Śāriputra know they exist? Or does he not?
Reclining on the deep mountain, the lotus-hour is long; within this single room, the breeze is serene. My corded seat is but seven feet square; with my arm bent, I sleep amidst the clouds.

I do not reckon at all between existence and non-existence, nor do I discard the distinction between the ordinary and the sage. Do not say there is nothing at all; a solitary clarity hangs like a mirror.
The Extensive Record of Master Yongjue, Volume Twenty-Four;
The Extensive Record of Master Yongjue, Volume Twenty-Five.
Re-edited by the Dharma-heir Disciple Daopai.
A Seven-Character Octave from a Poem:
Gazing at Mount Wuyi from a Boat on the River.

Chiseled from purple jade, it presses against the azure heavens; below, it reflects in the shimmering depths of the green stream. On the moss-covered ruins of the altar, the moon shines cold through the night;

in the ancient pavilion leaning against the clouds, the autumn wind blows chill. The cave has yielded the immortal’s蜕 (shui—molted skin); where is his spirit now? The cliff locks the rainbow bridge; by whom can the path be traversed?
Do not say that the immortal’s boat is safely hidden in the ravine; burdened by the passage of time, one drifts like a tumbleweed.

Ascending Mount Huangyang, several layers of emerald peaks separate one from the dust of the world. In the wild temple, deep mists shroud the pure green moss. When the moon reaches the meditation seat, the monk is in perfect samādhi;

as mist obscures the jeweled trees, the cranes first return. The Ox and Dipper constellations of the Nine Heavens rest within the window, while the ten thousand li of rivers and plains lie in the palm of the hand.
The upper gate is opened; the scenery filling my eyes is still as it was of old. For what reason does Zi Yang not return?
Having received news from home while in the mountains, I send this reply to my friends:
Since our parting at Lengyun Ju, I have heard it said that the scenery is no longer as it was at first. Upon the stream, the rain has added three feet.
The water has washed away the half-tablet of books that fell from the house during the wind; my worn bag is already known to me, so I shall cease my deep attachment to it.
Why labor further with heavy sighs over this broken cauldron? I will not learn like the weary donkey circling the millstone; I shall take the entire great earth as my humble lodging.
In the mountains of Luyang, the snow accumulates at the end of the year. Thus, for the sake of a young monk chanting a verse on Guan Mountain, I compose this:

With his tattered robes mended and resewn, he passes through the depths of the year; How is it that the traveler’s satchel alone leaves Guan Mountain empty? The wind wildly breaks the branches before the window.
Bamboo—its branches weighed down by heavy snow, half the ridge lies broken. The mountain birds must all wait until after spring to arrive. Old acquaintances mostly communicate through dreams.
The earthen stove has not yet reached total stillness; I frequently add firewood, keeping it glowing red throughout the night.
Amidst the mountains, I have received a letter from Magistrate Xiao Jingwei;
our traces, once like floating duckweed scattered upon the waters of Jian, are suddenly reunited through this scroll. My old self of ten years past can no longer be compared to my former state;
yet this stubborn heart of mine remains unrefined. Flowers fill Heyang, where you enjoy such splendor, while I am but a youth with twin buns veiled in green.
Idle and indolent, I know myself to be like a useless, aged piece of wood; I am content to dwell in the empty mountains learning how to plant pines.
In the tenth month of winter in the year of Renxu, I stayed at the Double-Top Peak (Sangjigŭng) in Sabye. Left behind for the Layman Jungyang.
Layered blue cliffs invite the staff-bearer; smoke-wreathed peaks half-revealed compose a poem. Amidst the deep clouds, one may hide a thousand follies;

beneath the dense trees, what prevents borrowing a single branch? I am too lazy to seek the powerful, for my tongue is short; I am content to endure hunger and cold, for I am a fool obsessed with books.
Let people call me a cow or a horse as they please—I laugh until I fall over at the sight of that ancient sage of Vaiśālī.
Ascending North Mountain on an autumn day, the emerald cliffs soar high, where the bird-path hangs suspended. A newly established golden temple presses against the autumn sky;

a thousand peaks, tinted with azure, peer out beyond the curtains, while two rivers carry their boats past my seat. I let forth my long-drawn sighs beneath the bright moon; my walking meditation is mostly conducted amidst the white clouds.
At the edge of the clouds, I dreamt of traversing the traces of the Han and Tang dynasties; the withered grasses and desolate smoke are truly mournful.

From the time of Fuxi until the present, how many springs and autumns have passed through this forest of books? Here on this mound, the cultural treasures and spiritual radiance of antiquity are gathered together; north and south, boats and carriages pass by without ceasing.
Exhausted! Throughout antiquity and today, the mirror of the mind’s eye has been difficult to exhaust. Every stroke carves through the bones of the hero;
every fascicle transmits afar the sorrows of the sages. Only this old monk has not a single word; before even the Yellow Emperor drew his lines, he asked for the source.
Visiting Master Du on Mount Qishan:
He dwells in transcendent seclusion upon the peaks of ten thousand crags. Stone steps pierce the clouds; the bird-path winds its way.

Fragments of jagged rock are revealed halfway to heaven; a few thatched huts hang against the cliffs. To sweep the window, he always relies on the smoke-emitting willows; to wash his bowl, he frequently uses the [flowing] stream.
Hèquán: At twilight, I lean against the railing, pacing back and forth repeatedly. A single long cry of laughter resounds as the moon hangs solitary and full.
At Seven-Stone Mountain in Autumn, facing the Moon, at the request of the Venerable Hónpǔ:

The clouds clear from a thousand crags; autumn is pure and bright. The vast sky is as if washed clean; the solitary moon shines with clarity. All is radiant and serene; for long, the drawn bow has been cast aside.
In the shadows, all is silent; who hears the sound of the pounding silk? I am ashamed of my own negligence and lack of vigor;
I know you possess a spirited and profound heart. Do not trade the moon atop Mount Qishi for your two natural, mother-born eyes.
In the second month of spring in the year Dingmao, while dwelling on Mount He, I was moved by certain reflections and composed this verse:

A green bower has been cleared away to build a hut east of the waters; From the cool air of Pear Peak, fragrance enters the curtains and windows. The tiger, hungry, roars forth from beyond the layered clouds;
The bird, weary, flies back to alight amidst the setting sun. Only in old age do I realize that madness is a disease; Only upon waking do I perceive it to have been a dream.
It is empty. Within the layers of green vines, no one arrives; a single thread of sandalwood incense drifts across the melting stream.

On my fiftieth birthday, half a lifetime’s labors have all been rendered in vain. Suddenly realizing my errors, I grieve for myself in secret. For twenty years, the study window has reflected only emptiness.

Snow. For ten winters, I have ground bricks at the Jiemo Temple; my drowsy words are but leaves used to stop a child’s crying. In propagating and explaining the Buddha’s teachings, I have searched only through long-worn, moth-eaten scrolls.
