To whom can this single piece of secluded heart be entrusted? With head shrouded and tongue rolled back, I pass the remaining years.

Passing West Lake on an autumn day, the level waters shimmer as my small boat glides. A gentle breeze upon the water brushes softly against my face. Sparse bells from the Three Zhuz fall from beyond the clouds;

withered willows line both embankments like reflections in a mirror. On the desolate terrace, the grass grows long, harboring the resentment of the Chancellor; in the ancient temple, the mist deepens, concealing the traces of Wu...
How sorrowful! For a thousand ages, the world drifts on in its endless states; all these things are casually cast aside like a single bubble.

In the first month of autumn in the year Wuchen (1688), I traveled to Xiushui to request the Tripitaka scriptures. On my return, I passed through Qiantang just as the tide of the Yangtze surged violently.
While all the other passenger boats were submerged, my boat alone escaped the peril. Overjoyed, I recorded this.
The ocean clouds gather thickly as wind and waves rage; looking out in alarm at the riverhead, it is truly dismal. In a single moment, the crumbling banks for a thousand *li* are breached;
ten thousand households sink away into several layers of springs. One finds no ground at all to rest in when facing death, yet who would have thought that life remains, with another world ahead?
Surely the dragon spirits protect the precious scriptures; a single sail carries them forth as the rain drifts like mist.
In the first month of autumn, the year Jisi (1629), I returned to Shouchang to sweep the stupa of the Master. Sitting in meditation at night, I was moved by these reflections:
The wind carries the sound of autumn through the evening woods; The incense burner’s embers fade as sorrow deepens. Raindrops fall upon the empty steps, casting shadows on the green lamp;
Clouds rise in the vacant courtyard, darkening the white stupa. I am ashamed to close the iron gate and hide my hundred follies; Yet it is difficult to erase the ink upon the earth to record this.
Lonely Heart: The sacred remains of my former teacher still exist today; amidst white waves surging to the heavens, who would be willing to seek them out?
I visited Master Da Yu at Miaogao Peak;
his former madness has never been cured. For ten years he has wandered aimlessly through the lakes and mountains; on the road back, how could I dare shrink from the heat of the three summer months?
The heat; arriving at the mountain, it was precisely the autumn of a forest. A cool breeze and falling leaves along the east-west paths;
the bright moon and the distant bell echoing through the upper and lower towers. Cherish our old friendship, deep as the sea; lingering and lingering, like drifting white clouds.
I weep for Master Boshan;
his Dharma banner stood tall to the east of the Great River. Alone he grasped the awl to remove the cataracts from the blind masses.

Just as I rejoiced that the Dharma-thunder resounded through the upper realms, I was suddenly startled that the moon of wisdom fell into the front valley. The mist darkens the pond’s edge and the dragon still weeps; the terrace atop the ridge is empty of the phoenix.

I find no place to rest; I feel deep sorrow that the traces of demonic influence still fill the land. Who now beats the war-drum amidst the fray? (Upon the mountain lies the Dragon-Bathing Pool and the Phoenix-Perching Ridge.

Here in the mountains, I sing of my inner resolve as I embrace the withered remains of the scriptures while the years pass by. I eat my fill of wild herbs, accepting whatever karmic conditions arise before me. In vain do I speak of my former studies in "Slaying the Dragon."
Skillful! I am glad you have now studied under Fuhu Chan. You have sheared away the clouds from the pines to release the bright moon; you have drawn forth the rock-essence to pour into the blue sky.
If you should meet someone and ask about the affairs of the mountains, tell them that the dragon-like staff is not yet permitted to be transmitted.
On his birthday, Layman Dayu came to Gushan. We traveled together to Linyuan Cave and composed this verse to offer him our congratulations:
"Upon the sea rise lofty and towering peaks; I rejoice that you have specially followed me with staff and sandals. Who can trace the footsteps of one who has drunk the water?"
An Illusion. In ancient times, the inscriptions were half-concealed by moss. Beyond the heavens, azure shells divide the islands; within our eyes, white waves give rise to dragons and serpents.
With what thing could one possibly offer as a gift for longevity? A thousand-year-old cliff-side pine dripping with sweet dew.
I thank Layman Xu Xingong for visiting me;

he spoke of how there are "phoenix feathers" in Min—your elder and younger brothers who excel in the *fengsao* style. You are accustomed to leaning on your short staff as you wend through the lush green of the pines, reclining amidst the deep clouds to listen to the ocean waves.
You intend to form a literary society to emulate the laughter of Tao Yuanming and Huiyuan, and your chiseling of verse suddenly causes the ghosts and spirits to tremble.
Divine Inscription: Clouds gather and rain disperses; mountain flowers are pure. Upon the towering peaks, the moon is at its highest.
Sitting in meditation at night, I tread upon the Bridge of the Tortoise.
Following the rhyme of Master Dongwei, I step forth with my feet tracing the path of the Golden Turtle. Mountain mists drift down, soaking my tattered robes. Whale-waves surge afar across the river.

The moon; the celestial breeze near the drum-tree stirs the ripples. By the crags, the sound of the jade spring flows with subtle clarity. Beyond the bridge, pines pierce through the rocks as tall as bamboo shoots.
Sitting for so long, I did not notice the lotus-drip hourglass fall. Yet, riding upon this secluded inspiration, I once more take up my brush.
The Dharma Master Nianyi visited me and departed abruptly; I respond with these verses:
With grime on my face and hair in disarray, I dwell beside the rocks. The wind turns the shadow of the pagoda toward the western cave-gate.

From the wall, spring water gushes like falling blossoms in haste; Clouds come from the sea, sweeping low across the earth. Delighting in guests, I part the brambles, forgetting the ruggedness of the path; Following a woodcutter, I ask for directions as I enter.
Zhao Ti. Meeting by chance, we became close friends; parting at midnight, the moon filled the mountain stream.
After the long rains in the mountains have finally cleared, the two Magistrates, Zheng and Ru-jiao, visited me. Using their rhyme, I offer this reply:

This humble monk, a white-haired old man with his head shrouded, sits in silent meditation amidst the sound of rain in the empty mountains. Suddenly, the clouds of the cavern break apart, revealing the morning sky.

The sun rises; forest birds vie with one another in their proud warbling as the morning breeze blows. Choosing a tree, there is no hindrance to the flapping of wings downward. To respond to the opportune moment, one only knows how to raise a single fist.
Together we watch as the candles by the western window are trimmed away; turning our heads, the sun on the eastern peak is red once more.
I went to Saichang to sweep the pagoda. Arriving in Jianzhou, I met Xu Xingong. Responding to his verse:

Our drifting traces have no set purpose, yet we meet by chance; Together we listen to the sound of the waves beneath several pines. Raising my whisk, it is difficult to support the lineage of Xingsheng;

Feeling within my heart, I have often failed the school of Shaocang. The traveler’s journey falls amidst the sorrow of mist and rain; Upon the master’s pagoda, the moss-streaks are as they were in my dream.
Sealed within. On the eve of my departure, I made an appointment for the day of my return: "In early autumn, let us laugh together atop White Cloud Peak.
In the summer of the year Yihai, I returned to Shouchang to sweep the stupa of my late Master.
Having wandered aimlessly and in solitude for many years, I have only upon my return begun to recognize my old fields and gardens. Who shall rely upon as I plow deep and sow shallow?

With little strength, I harvest the full yield, leaving it to external conditions. A single mass of sandalwood clouds joins the shadow of the stupa; several stalks of stone-grown tea are brewed with mountain spring water.
I am ashamed that I, a wandering son, am as poor as washed out; yet to repay my teacher’s kindness, I simply raise my fist.
Dharma Master Maigeng Qiu did not seek out patrons for alms;
he obtained his daily sustenance from beneath the plow. During a year of famine when food was scarce, he made soup of wheat and led the assembly in reclaiming wasteland.
Once the fields were established, the community called him Maigeng Qiu (Wheat Soup Mound). In the summer of the Yihai year, he returned to Shouchang. [He] returned once more.
While wandering through that place, I was moved by a profound sense of melancholy.

"The backbone of Shouchang was as hard as iron; even when opening the fields in the sixth month under a scorching sun, and during years of famine when he could only take wheat to make porridge, he would wield his hoe with an empty belly and refuse to desist.
To this day, the fields are known by the name 'Wheat Porridge Fields,' and the elder residents of the mountains can still [bear witness to it]."
The legend goes: the grain and millet grow tall, gathering like green clouds; all this was formed by the blood my Master shed in sweat.
Returning to the valley, he stayed for a time at Tiantang Monastery.

Moved by emotion, he revisited his native village after many years, thinking idly that the streams and mountains still appear as they were before. His friends and peers showed him sincere compassion for his old age.
The children were struck with wonder and asked about his origins: "Willow tips hang with dew, emerald in the morning; Mulberry shadows sway in the wind, misty at evening.
The light of life is as fleeting as foam—how much longer can it last? Why not study together the Zen of the Patriarchs?"

Returning to the Pond, shown to my nephews: Having left home for ten years, I now return. With white hair and a withered face, how could I dare pity myself? Thus I know that I am no longer as I was of old;
who would say that human affairs remain as they were before? To build a Great Wall out of resentment is still not a wise plan; to leave one’s body behind as a massive boulder—how could this be right?
Attaining steadfastness, worldly affairs are but floating illusions—cease your bitter anxieties. It is well to follow the benevolence and righteousness of former sages.

Dwelling among the green mountains, my hair grows long and loose as I age; planting trees and sowing grain, I learn from the rustic farmer. Poetry flows from my mouth as it comes, mostly composed of my own accord.

Joyful, he shouldered his staff and went out; few people encountered him on the way. Through the window, he stretched forth the moon before White Rock; facing the couch, he gazed upon the peaks over the Blue Sea.
In an instant, white clouds obscured near and far; from the head of the hall, the sound of a single bell was transmitted.
Yang Fu personally visited me on the mountain and presented this gift; I respond in kind using his rhyme.
Treading through the weeds to climb the peak, I alone seek out the wonders. The river breeze, pines, and moon naturally compose a poem. The path at Stone Gate is perilous, thick with creeping vines;
The towering peaks are so high that crows and magpies are scarce. At the pagoda, I recall with deep longing Xingsheng Temple; To brew tea, I need not use Zhaozhou’s staff.
The Mechanism of the State. For a long time we held hands and spoke deeply amidst the clouds; I now recall anew that moment of Vimalakīrti’s profound silence.
Having heard of Great Master Wengu’s Society for Releasing Living Beings, I compose verses in his rhyme to bid farewell (ten stanzas).

Compassionate clouds gather thickly, covering the City of *Zhicheng*; Swimming in rivers and soaring in the void, each finds fulfillment in life. Silently turning the mechanism of slaughter, he upholds the Sage’s Way.
Transforming others, you have extensively nurtured the pulse of benevolence through the sound of the scriptures. Your black cassock has been stained by the heavy mist of the mountain peaks;

your precious staff now rests lightly upon the shadow of cranes. As you prepare to depart, your parting instructions leave no room for other concerns; yet looking back upon these fish and birds, my feelings are redoubled.
A transformative wind blows throughout the city of Puṣpapurī; by the riverbank, grass is planted to encourage the release of living beings.

Just as they encounter the net, their entrails are nearly severed; as the blade and block draw near, they plead in silence. One’s own body is worth more than a thousand pieces of gold, yet the life of another creature is as light as a single grain of dust.
Only our Master’s compassionate vow is most earnest; though separated by distant mountains and passes, he always harbors this deep affection.

With flying staff you came from the south to establish a city of transformation; at Lêng-yen you formed a society to protect all living beings. Within the marketplace, the stench of meat and pungent spices suddenly vanished;
beneath the forest trees, the sound of Buddhist chants was heard from time to time. On the ancient bank, clouds shroud the solitary pagoda in silence; on the cold stream, ripples carry a light sail.
You should know that though the depths of this pool may reach a thousand fathoms, they cannot compare to the compassionate heart of our Master toward all creatures.

Having recently preached the Dharma throughout the city, he sought to realize non-arising by first practicing the release of living beings. Fish freed from their nets leap upon the waves of the former bay;
birds released from their cages warble with cries across the valley stream. Cold moonlight pierces the thatched hut atop the crags; a spring breeze on the river carries the lightness of the oars.
How many creatures, flying or hiding, still enter his dreams? His compassionate heart is vast and profound, far exceeding ordinary sentiments.

Azure waters and vermilion peaks encircle the Forbidden City; The golden temple stands vast and open, protecting the beings of the lower realms. The Zen gates are silently closed, enshrouding the green of the pines;
The precious raft drifts upon the waves, carrying the sound of the Dharma. Fish frolic joyfully among the duckweed as they swallow the moon; Birds fly lightly through the mist above the river.
Yet I still grieve that fishing and hunting can never truly cease; I compose this poem in verse to convey my feelings of parting.
The east wind sweeps across the mountain city; at Qīlǐ Tān, spring waters rise. The pale light of the river trembles with the reflection of the pagoda;
A fine rain of blossoms moistens the sound of the bell. My devotion to the incense and lamps within the monastery grows ever deeper;
In my dreams, whether soaring or hiding, my intent remains unflagging. Neither monk nor layman can detain the departing boat; As I hold this "White Snow" [poem], what shall I do with such feelings?
Whenever I followed my pure companions out of the great city, we formed a society in the desolate wilds to practice the release of living beings.

A solitary pagoda hung its reflection over the cold marsh; at dusk, the bell sent afar the sound of a traveler’s boat. Birds piercing the treetops were accustomed to their pride; scales gathering in the heart of the pool leaped lightly upon the waves.
As the Master’s staff suddenly turned back, my deep affection was boundless; amidst the wind and rain filling the river, I lamented our parting.

The established prefecture is just like the city of Śrāvastī; the Master of Men uses flowing water to sustain the lives of the remaining. It is better to eat fresh food than to have the stench of various raw meats;

do not let the sound of unbearable cries from the slaughterhouse reach our ears. Let them fly as far as they wish amidst the clouds, and let them sport lightly upon the waves at the heart of the river.
As we turn our smoke-wreathed oars back from a thousand li away at the parting of ways, looking back, it is difficult to forget the affection felt for all living beings.
In the past, I once traveled to Jianzhou City to seek the Way; there I heard it said that even birds and fish find joy in life. Beneath the pines, the wind carries the resonance of the monk’s staff;
by the reeds, the clouds conceal the sound of the wooden fish. Yongming’s vows were profound and his compassion ever keen; yet Huanzhu’s dwelling in a hermitage was always treated with lightness.
Since the Dharma-boat first returned to the waters of Zhejiang, I have gazed upon the misty waves until my sight is severed—how can one bear such feelings?

Fish and birds rejoice as they are nurtured within the City of Transformation; relying on the Master’s rain of Dharma, they cross over their remaining lives. Having been ransomed, they are fortunate to escape the suffering of boiling and roasting;

released into freedom, they still hear the sound of liberation. Your precious staff has frequently passed by me, making my sorrow heavy; today we part upon the fragrant boat, my intent is no light matter.
Deep into the night, the moon ripples upon the riverhead, further stirring my compassionate heart to protect all sentient beings.

On the Lantern Festival, I ascend the Zunseng Pavilion; a thousand homes’ lanterns glow amidst the evening clouds. From the sea, the giant tortoise arrives to support the mountain together with us. The world beneath our eyes is ultimately subject to change and illusion;
above the tower, the sun and moon circle again and again. In every place, the music of pipes and strings leaves guests long intoxicated; with every strike of bell and chime, the monks chant.
Solitary and at leisure, it would be well to return home at midnight before the suffering cries begin; do not wait until your hair has turned white.
Reascending the Zunseng Pavilion, I employ the previous rhyme:
this towering pavilion stands amidst purple and azure peaks; returning once more, I long remember the old rivers and mountains. In the past, the Lotus Garden was originally most venerable.

Victory! The precious structure remains, and now I rejoice to have returned. The curtains are rolled back, directly revealing the smallness of the blue sea; the windows are open and vast, facing the eternal leisure of white clouds.
The mansions throughout the city are all like brocade; in the mirror, who can boast that their two temples are not streaked with gray?
Visiting Jiuri Mountain (where there are the Song and Jiang Peaks from the Jin Dynasty, and the stone inkstone used by Qin Xie for annotating scriptures):
Layered ridges and peaks reflect the bright light; after the rain, the spring colors are a deep azure. The ancient trees, though obscured by drifting clouds, still belong to the Jin;

the high peaks reach into the Milky Way and are named after Jiang. I have rubbed several broken steles, yet they remain difficult to read; repeatedly questioning those at the ruined walls, my weariness redoubles.
How tragic! The person who annotated the sutras at this stone inkstone has long since departed, yet the traces of his ink still linger with their fragrance to this day.
Passing through Baqin Temple, I ascend Feilai Ge;

this small pavilion lies to the east of the ancient monastery Feilai. Verdant light is reflected and absorbed within the curtains and windows; beneath the shade of lychee trees, stones gush forth like a thousand fathoms.
Waves. Outside the bridge, the wind blows upon a small floating hut. Clouds emerge from Golden Cock Mountain as they return to Purple Cap Peak; waves part like jade shoots from Yellow Dragon Hill.
The beauty of the ten thousand mountains is as if entirely made of dark ink; north of the river and south of the river, spring is at its peak.

Wandering through Qingyuan Cave, I have transplanted this small Mount Danqiu to the sea. Purple vapors swirl within the ancient, secluded cavern; in several ravines, verdant clouds enshroud strange rocks, while from moss-covered cliffs thousands of feet high, cold streams burst forth.
Having cast away all worldly essence, I beg for the way of the immortals; the sacred traces are difficult to pursue, yet they remain—only...
Enough of this intoxication. At twilight, the wind is mournful and travelers disperse; a single cry of a monkey resounds from atop the emerald cliffs.

To escape the summer heat, I have temporarily borrowed Huang’s mountain cottage to lodge my traveler’s body. The trees are as high as parasols, and the grass is like a lush carpet. Ascending the tower, the path winds as it passes through the precipices.

Stone hearths brew tea as mist curls around dense bamboo; clouds pass the pine gate, their coolness drenching the mats. The moon shifts its reflection from the stupa, its chill gaze piercing the observer.
The heat’s fury has already been swept away by the celestial breeze; alone, I draw in the fresh, invigorating spirit of this pure source.
Wandering among the Five Peaks, in the style of Master Luoyi Feng:
A single robe flows freely as my inspiration alone excels; Piercing the clouds, I choose the finest spots for my wanderings. At the most remote reaches of the Five Peaks, the blue heavens draw near;

On the very edge of the great earth, the vast blue sea floats. A single stone, cold and clear, dispels the heat of the three summer months; A solitary moon, at night, scatters its light across the hundred peaks.
Autumn at the Crags. I recall your steadfast virtue, as lofty as a dipper-star; today we meet here atop the green peaks.
Passing through Anping, I visit the Shifosi Temple;
the ancient temple is desolate, its years long gone. Half of the *Sumeru* throne is encroached upon by moss and lichen; broken steles lie prostrate within the empty pavilion.

Below, a cunning hare dwells long in the shadow of the ruined palace; its auspicious features still remain because it is made of stone. When the steps and foundations crumble, who will spread gold upon them?
Pausing and standing alone amidst the withered mists, I listen with sorrow as cicadas chirp in the evening woods.
Arriving at Gushan, I send this reply to Lü Tiānchí, Minister of Agriculture, using his rhyme:
The waters on the Yangtze above Luoyang are brimming; I have caught the autumn wind to sweep along with my staff. Returning, the mountain peaks are cold with dark dew;
It stirs up light purple clouds beneath my feet. Two periods of blows and shouts emerge from the void; A single assembly of conditions is but a dream.
The interior is complete. How does this compare to Vimalakīrti, who was able to manifest illness? His Dharma discourse amidst the dust remains as clear as ever.

*Eight Poems on Cuiyun Hermitage:* Burying my head and sealing my tongue, I pass the days and nights. In these three thatched rooms, the door is never closed. I plow through the green mountains, dividing the rocks.
The marrow: cutting open the emerald bamboo reveals the cloud-root. At the mouth of Ligu Valley, one watches the returning cranes;
by the edge of the pond, one learns to irrigate the garden with a jar. Last night a tiger passed outside the hermitage; without cause, it trampled the old mossy traces.

In declining years, I am too weary to distinguish between You and Qiu; embracing my simplicity in the empty mountains, every affair is secluded. Beneath the crags, I bask in the sun, deeply loving the light;
before the steps, I weed the grass, knowing the autumn has come. Let the forest flowers fall as they are moved by the wind; it is difficult to make the vegetable leaves follow the flowing stream.
Do not compare this to the ancients whose concealment was not yet thorough—when meeting people, I still speak of the two clay oxen.
Mountains wind and valleys thicken as clouds store deep within; I have built a snail-shell hut beside the emerald peaks. Walking slowly along the stream, I frequently glance at my reflection;

leaning against a pine tree, I gaze alone, glad to unbutton my robe. My traces hidden amidst the dust are as solid as stone; who in this world beyond can discuss friendship with such loyalty that it cleaves gold?
When guests arrive, I speak only of planting bamboo; how many dragon-sprouts do we need to form a grove?
Idle and indolent, I have grown habituated; my laughter is like that of a gourd. To avoid the vulgar, what harm is there in dwelling on high?

Unable to save the world, I have not yet transmitted the *Great Changes*; for leisure, I especially delight in reading the *Li Sao*. The moon peers through the mountain’s gaps, sifting the shadows of the forest;
the wind penetrates the crag’s gate, drumming upon the emerald waves. A single cup of yellow earth is enough to cover the bones; what use is this fleeting life of weary toil?
Deep within the emerald mists, this very place is home. In the stony ravine, the murmuring stream washes away the setting clouds.

Beyond the gate, every mountain is planted with bamboo; before the hermitage, there is not a gap to plant flowers. The iron ox crouches on the ground—no need for the whip; the stone drum hangs in the void—no need to strike it.
For now, learn from the cold cicada and gladly remain shut in; when guests arrive, I shall not serve Zhaozhou’s tea.

Layer upon layer of emerald peaks shield the clamor of the mundane world. When the mossy path reaches its end, one crosses a small bridge. Tending the garden under the stars, he labors with diligent irrigation;
gathering firewood amidst the rain, he ascends the towering heights. White clouds drift away leaving no trace; black cranes return without the need for a call.
He understands that keeping one’s mouth shut brings little praise; like a wild goose on land, he is content to remain far from the crowd.
Awakening from sleep, I scratch my head and find it strangely still; when guests arrive, I brew tea and draw fresh spring water. I take but a few sips of the dew from the golden stem;
facing my companion at the mat, we contemplate only the "Jade Board" Chan. The resonance of the chime follows the clouds through the bamboo path;

the pine wind, chasing the rain, enters the thatched eaves. After a full meal, I rest beneath the west window on a single pillow; in a daze, I am as one with the vast, primordial sky of the age of Xi Huang.
Lazily straddling my yellow ox, I enter the marketplace; in a single valley of white clouds, I bring this final year to a close.
Whenever I ascend the peak, I encounter the mountain lord’s howl; when gathering bracken, I sleep beside the calf. The sound of water in the winding stream intersperses the songs of birds;
the moonlight through the sparse forest tints the wind and mist. Even the mountain flowers know their own seasons; do not seek to explain their flourishing and withering by the treatises of Guiguzi.
Revisiting Yanling Tan (Two Poems) Beneath Mount Fuchun, the waters are like moss;
A single leaf glides lightly, cutting through the waves. The emerald cliffs have not yet melted the snow of last night;
The azure mists still guard the terrace of former times. My feet are light as though they were ten thousand chariots; Heaven reveals its signs, and my will resists the world for a thousand autumns.

With lingering conjecture, I tread upon my sandals and ascend once more to this solitary lodge; my thoughts linger by the river, drifting far away. In this rustic dwelling, years have passed and long green moss has grown.
Having spent five summers here, I return once again. Whenever I encounter the tracks of rabbits across the woodcutter’s path, who can see the one in sheepskin robes hidden at the fishing platform?
My haughty bones refuse to submit to another imperial summons; my solitary figure shall not be permitted to fade into white [old age].
Suspicion and Mistrust. Unable to fully gather up his floating fame, he causes travelers to sigh in regret.
Composed at Wanghui Hermitage (two poems).
Formerly, when the Prince of Jianwen was fleeing in exile, he stayed in this secluded hermitage. His ministers built thatched huts here, hence its name.
A mountain cottage of half a mu is veiled by azure clouds; The winding grass path is covered entirely with falling flowers. Longing for antiquity, I bear to seek the traces of the former Emperor;

Seeking respite from clamor, I lodge temporarily in the home of a former minister. In this small mound, pines and bamboos filter the new moonlight; Ten thousand li of rivers and plains are stitched together with evening glow.
Leaning on my staff before the hermitage, I unroll my aged eyes; From afar I watch the spring geese dotting the level sands.
In the past, someone built a dwelling to borrow the clouds for concealment; they planted only green pines and no flowers.

Fearing that the Master could not yet turn the Sage’s carriage back, they hid their person and temporarily adopted the ways of a mountain hermit. Smoke from cooking rises beneath the forest as cranes return to their roosts;
drawing water at the cliff’s edge, one carries the setting glow of the sunset. Gazing to the limit, how vast is the Lan River! The azure spring colors encircle the bright sands.

Spontaneous Verses Composed at Mount Puming (Two Poems) Treading a thousand mountains with a single short staff, My recent livelihood is now solely that of a farmer. At the edge of the fields, night rain urges on the seedlings;
From the bottom of the ravines, spring thunder rouses the bamboo shoots. Clouded trees obscure the ancient temple; The ponds are vast and tranquil, soaking [the surrounding land].
Cold pines—what has been accomplished by years of blows and shouts? Contentedly lying at the south window, I listen to the distant pounding of grain.

The single lean cane of those days is snapped; Cloud-cloak and rain-hat have transformed me into a farmer. The wind from the heavens lifts the crane in its cage; Clouds at the bottom of the ravine hide the dragon of the sea.
Releasing the calf is most suited to the grass by the stream; Loving the mountains, I have cut away the roof [of my former life].
Tou Song. From afar, I hear the sound of yellow birds answering the evening pounding of grain within the deep mist along the willow banks.
Having returned from Zhejiang to Fujian, I am staying at Baoshan Hermitage. Dharma Master Bai Zhuo has sent me a poem inquiring after my well-being.
In response to your verse, I offer these lines:
In the declining age of the Dharma, learning is shallow and true essence rare. Where can one find a person with a straight hook? My boat, empty, drifted freely as I wandered through Zhejiang;
now that the leaves have fallen, I return to my roots and go back to Min. Do not say that keeping one's mouth shut brings no fame; how could I dare continue to remain like a withered stump?

In the spring of my heart, I suddenly encountered white snow descending from the clouds. Secretly rejoicing that my indolence might find the aid of benevolence, I beheld the bamboo shoots by the river and the misty trees in their deep verdancy.
Shifting my oars into the midstream, I drifted upon the vast and boundless expanse, amidst the sounds of drums and pipes mingled with the chanting of the *buddha-śabda*.

Chant: Amidst the fragrance of flowers, reflections mirror the shimmering waves; golden scales pierce the net as the heavens and sea stretch wide. Jade-feathered wings return to the void as the path through the clouds extends long.
Together we turn the mechanism of cessation to support the flourishing transformation, and further pray for benevolence and longevity for our Sovereign.

Among the various officials who died for their principles in Yanjing, those who perished for the cause are but few; yet one knows that the spirit of righteousness has not entirely vanished. Wielding halberds, they lamented that they could not turn back the sun and sky;

drawing their swords, they truly moved the ghosts and spirits to tears. Their integrity and virtue, as well as their literary talent, cannot be easily surpassed; their loyal and steadfast hearts and livers—
Cheng Lin: To cast away one's life is surely not for the sake of preserving empty fame; yet I could not bear to endure the preservation of this seven-foot body.

The imperial edict bestowing the posthumous titles of Emperor Jianwen and the ranks and honorary names for the various ministers who died in defense of their principles arrived all at once, without cause.
The great vessel has shifted; the profound and silent workings of Heaven are truly difficult to fathom. My solitary self has fled far away, yet my spirit still...

Trembling with fear, ten clans were all executed—a matter universally doubted. In former days, the sovereign’s majesty was indeed too severe; at this time, the minister’s loyalty naturally becomes rare.
That the imperial decree has joyfully reached this desolate grave, it is now the moment for parched bones and sunken souls to release their resentment.
Staying at Shuangji Temple (Two Poems) Last night the western wind pierced the bamboo door;
Red leaves from the treetops flew across the courtyard. This one performance of drama has now just ended;

Of the mountains and rivers of the Hundred Yue, to whom shall they return? I wash my feet beneath the emerald waters of the Shuangji Falls; The firewood of the woodcutter is entangled with the clouds. Five... [fragmentary]

Wearing my patched robes, I am glad that evening finds me free from all affairs. Leaning my back against the pine gate, I face the setting sun; amidst the desolation of a thousand peaks stands this single thatched hut.
For the wild monk, there is a time for both action and withdrawal. Having finished annotating the neglected scriptures, I pass the days; the newly dug taro is better than eating mushrooms.
War has reached this point and can never truly cease; even the most beautiful things are now... (Note: The final line of the source text appears incomplete.)
Suddenly all is lost; yet fortunately, the valley is deep and the clouds grow ever denser. My dwelling is secure, like a tortoise with its six limbs withdrawn within its shell.
On the ninth day, I returned from Shuangji to Baoshan. Along the way, I was moved by these reflections:
Returning now that autumn has deepened, the wild smoke is cool; what strikes my eyes increases the sorrow of Song Yu. After the war, even the chickens and dogs are utterly startled.

Silence. Amidst the rain, it is hard to face the chrysanthemums as the pines and cypresses grow wild. The children cry to their mother for lack of trousers; the young wife seeks her mother-in-law to ask about provisions for the night.
Though the western wind may blow strong enough to knock off one’s hat, how can one bear to carry wine and become drunk on this Double Ninth?
On Hand: Occurrences in the Mountains. Composed in the Rhyme of "Dwelling at Shuangji" (Two Poems).
Deep within the stone gate, thatched huts lie hidden; A desolate chill prevails during this year’s end. It is difficult to lean my staff upon the red dust of the world;

Better to gather numinous fungi from the emerald ravines. Leaves fall repeatedly as I sweep before the steps; Flowers are planted behind the house— (Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-line; the translation reflects the available portion.)
Alternating deficits; such are the changes of the world—who can settle them? I am too weary to consult the milfoil stalks or tortoise shells for omens of fortune or misfortune.

The wind from heaven urges the rain to beat upon my thatched gate. Several times the cold clouds have swept across the earth. On this world, the strife between the "insects" (ants) has not yet ceased;
yet in these mountains, even cranes and monkeys are permitted to return home. It is difficult to seek the four benefits of the *īpū* offering; the thousand needles have already been lost.
Xuan-yi: Every time I wake up, the sound of battle seems ever-present in my ears. I wish to devote my life and soul to the lingering rays of light, continuing my affairs here in the mountains.
Using the previous rhyme: A wild gale blows through the old thatched hut; how can one pass the seasons in such desolation? One need only be satisfied with coarse bran and need ask no more.
Rice; merely picking wild greens while vainly seeking mushrooms. A bamboo staff in the mountains dissolves into the clouds; a mirage-tower upon the sea fades as the sun sets.
One cannot help but sigh for the clever men of old: most who lost their lives were like tortoises bearing the world on their backs.
Ten *li* of pines and clouds meet the thatched gate; when the pines and clouds are all felled, let the cranes fly as they please. The foolish monkey who tries to seize the moon can hardly find rest;
when will the headless madman ever return? All year long I neglect my studies because of many guests;
I sit around the brazier all night for lack of clothing. Who dares compare the world’s profusion and splendor to this? Looking at it, it is but like the glow of the setting forest.
In the fifth month of summer in the year Dinghai, torrential rain poured down like a cascade. The river surged with a great flood, half submerging the city of Zhi;
it was not until the seventh day that the waters began to recede.

I composed this poem to record the calamity: For seven days the deluge raged on, refusing to cease; The vast inundation overflowed the city walls. Fields and dwellings were half swept away by weeds and duckweed.
Depart! The old and the young mostly frolic with fish and turtles; frogs breed within the hearth, making it difficult to kindle the fire. Waves surge at the treetops as boats pass freely;
though this old monk remains outside the torrent, I gaze daily upon the flood and cannot cease my sorrow.

A Reflection on the Double Ninth, Autumn of the Dinghai Year, the Seventh Month. The naval troops arrived at Fuzhou and encamped at Guqi River. Mount Gushan was in close proximity, and the slaughter on the battlefield was witnessed firsthand. By the Double Ninth, the troops had still not been withdrawn; what more can be said of the sublime custom of ascending the heights? Thus, [The original Chinese text continues: 乃作詩曰： 「年年此日登高處，今歲登臨倍黯然。 戰地近山多血刃，軍營隔水少炊煙。 風前落帽悲陶令，月下吹簫憶列仙。 回首故園何處是？天涯流落又經年。」 I then composed a poem, saying: "Year after year, on this day, I ascend the heights; this year’s visit is doubly somber. On the battlegrounds near the mountains, blades are stained with blood;

in the military camps across the water, smoke from cooking is scarce. Before the wind, I lament Tao Ling as his hat fell; under the moon, I recall the Immortals as they blew their pipes. Turning my head, where is my old home? Wandering afar at the ends of the earth, another year has passed."

I compose two regulated verses for him: Tears flow in vain upon Mount Niu; this day, heaven and earth suddenly depart from their constancy. The sounds of drums and horns clamor as clouds darken the sky;
banners and spears unfold while the sun loses its light. Flowers and trees in the rain are faced with sorrow; villages and hamlets after the war are stricken by illness.
Looking back upon the past, though the yellow chrysanthemums and purple *yū* flowers have not yet changed, there are no fine guests at all to inquire after the Double Ninth Festival.
As the season reaches deep autumn, the jade dew is cold; withered lotuses and withered willows are not worth beholding. Warships lie across the rivers, terrifying the turtles and crocodiles;

wild foxes are slaughtered, turning the earth and stones crimson. In the ten thousand villages, the people are despondent and agricultural work has ceased; the thousands of forests are desolate, and ghosts [haunt] them.
I sigh with bitterness. Facing the wind, how can I have any desire to ascend the heights? I grieve alone for the common people, finding it difficult to grant them life.
On this Mid-Autumn Festival, I lie ill;
of the ninety autumns of my life, but half remains. The moonlight scatters its brilliance as I stand alone by the window; the sound of the pestle is mournful and piercing against the Milky Way.
Serene. The shadows of cassia trees interlace as the jade dew thickens. My sickly frame cannot endure the evening breeze; my private longing only delights in bearing the morning warmth.
Let the thousand peaks remain as they are, washed clean as if by rain; I lie alone in an empty room, too weary to step outside.
Self-mockery:

My body, over seventy years old and burdened by chronic illness, is like a single hair trying to pull up a thousand-jin weight. My writings on the Three Schools are but the moon reflected upon ripples;
my propagation at the four monasteries is but dust upon a mirror. By nature lazy, I am content only to remain perpetually simple; my Way is solitary, for it has always been lacking companions.
To be a neighbor—what kind of creature does one become now? How can this compare to studying in seclusion for a lifetime?
Sitting alone, moved by feeling (two poems):

Clouds arrive, sweeping across and half-concealing the pines of the grove. Sitting alone in stillness, I listen to the evening pounding of grain. I lift up my thatched roof, yet it serves as but a mere cover.

The Summit: Spreading the empty net, how many dragons have been caught? In vain one speaks of peaches under the gate, tipsy with wine; one cannot bear to see the grass before the hall completely overgrown.
I always pity these many seekers of profit, who go from village inn to village inn only to inquire after the freshness and richness [of the fish].
In my empty study, leaning on a desk against withered banana leaves, cool smoke from the four walls aids my solitude. I consider my own declining tracks to be like those of deer and wild boars;
how dare I speak of youthful ambitions reaching the clouds and sky? Ancient springs murmur their rhythms over precarious rocks;
leafless trees brush against wild gales. What has been accomplished in these seventy-odd years? I casually cast it all aside, leaving it to the preceding tide.
On this first day of spring, I celebrate the completion of the dwelling of No-Contention;

willow buds open as I face the frosty birds. This newly constructed meditation hall leans against emerald peaks. How often can the traveler’s sandals reach this secluded valley? Tea smoke rises daily from the level forest.
Within these chambers, days and months pass without cold or heat; beyond the gate, let the mountains and rivers be as they are.
Throughout ancient and modern times, he has long bid farewell to the worldly dust and dreams of existence; with head and face covered in ash and soil, he lies deep within the clouds.
On the Yuanxiao Festival in the mountains, the lamps and fires are sparse, yet the moonlight is as bright as day.

For this, I compose a regulated verse: The festive clamor of the lantern festival is but vulgar noise; In these secluded mountain depths, all is naturally still and vast. Though there are no "fire-trees" burning deep within, [the moonlight remains].
In the valley, the moon hangs high through the eternal night; A cold radiance covers the earth like the Snowy Peaks. The dawn light fills the forest as it approaches the Star Bridge;
I sit alone before the courtyard after the third watch. From time to time, I perceive the fragrant breeze drifting several times.
The Licentiate Zou Lianshan visited Gushan Temple and stayed for two nights. He presented me with a poem, to which I respond in kind:

Ascending the mountain, I need not fear the green vines that veil the way; How could my traveling sandals be hindered by the winding stone paths? As I emerge from the valley, the yellow orioles’ song grows ever more melodious.

Exquisite! The red apricot leaning against the clouds still displays its opulence. The meditation cell continues to harbor the dream of the Lacquer Garden; the Buddha-lamp once again blooms as an *utpala* flower.
In the silent, empty courtyard, all is as clear as water; there is no longer the clamor of the green toad under the moon.
The Layman Xie Qiwenzai:
At the ancestral temple in late autumn, a wild gale arose; its momentum was so arrogant it seemed poised to shake Mount Kunlun.

With his hand he supported the crimson sun suspended above the Milky Way, whereupon the wild gale suddenly ceased and all worldly clamor vanished. From this moment on, the waters of the cave grew ever more majestic, surging day and night into the depths.
The ocean tide—be mindful of the power of dredging at this moment; clearly, for a thousand years, its merit has been supreme.
Presented to Zen Master Hunpak on his fiftieth birthday:
for half a lifetime he has personally studied the Dongshan school of Chan. Deep within the Nine Dragons, he sleeps embracing the clouds; in his three-room thatched hut, he relies upon the crags.

Standing, a single-handled golden hoe hangs from his belt, dripping with rain. The hollow fame of a snail’s horn has long since been cast aside; how could he ever be swayed by the meager profits of a fly’s head?
He speaks of worldly cycles only to know the Mandate of Heaven; his integrity remains forever firm as it defies snow and frost.

Seeing off a monk returning north of the river, I rise at dawn and pull on my robes to depart through the stone gate. An autumn wind blows through the village of white clouds. On the chessboard, mountains and rivers shift with every move;

among one's kinsmen in a dream, how many remain? Having sought the Way for four years, I have relied upon the Water-Drawing Master; now, longing for my kin a thousand miles away, I compose this verse.
Summoning the Soul: A Song of Return to My Hometown on West Plain. Withered grass and cold smoke as the day nears dusk.
On the Human Day (Renri), I joined my friends in visiting Linyuan Cave (two poems).
On this auspicious day, the gentle breeze brushes the face softly; Pine-clad clouds veil the small Mount Danqiu. A single thread of jade rainbow still resonates with sound...

Subtle! A thousand fathoms of iron walls, the mist is just now clearing. Drinking water, I personally witness the power of the divine realm; forgetting my way home, worldly sorrows are instantly extinguished.
On the Canglin Pavilion, leaning on my staff and gazing afar, I alone perceive heaven and earth as but a single bubble.
Accompanying friends, we explore the seclusion of the celestial cavern; as the snow clears, the spring light floats everywhere. A thousand layers of emerald ridges stretch like five tigers;
ten thousand acres of vast waves intoxicate the two eyes. Gazing at these poems, I alone rejoice in the verses of Duandaming; lamenting the ancients, I deeply recall the travels of Zizhi.
As the smoke from the tea cauldron fades and the twilight grows dim, a single cry of a monkey echoes from the head of the evening forest.

On the full moon day of the second month of spring, the Minister Tong, along with Mr. Gu Nanjin, Mr. Lin Deshan, and other gentlemen, stayed overnight at the Upper Monastery to sit and gaze upon the moon.
They presented a poem to me, which I now respond to using their rhyme:

Amidst a thousand layers of accumulated green, the monastery is secluded from worldly dust; By chance the Virtuous Star has gathered here, precisely at the vernal equinox. The moonlight from the eastern tower reflects upon the western tower.

The moon rises as clouds above the upper cave connect with those below; when the water-clock strikes its hour, the mountain birds fall silent. Where the sound of the sutras ceases, the Brahma-bell is heard.
These pearls and gems, brilliantly radiant, can never be matched—how could they be the mere trifling artistry of "carving insects"?
On the first day of spring, the Magistrate Xue Yuhai ascended Mount Gu and visited me. I composed this poem to express my gratitude: The gentle breeze begins to stir as the heavens and sea open;
Your literary banner arrives, riding the auspicious fortune of the age. Vernal warmth floats through the willows by the bridge at night;

Auspicious light shines upon the plum blossoms before the cave at dawn. With a staff of bamboo, you have traversed the path that reaches the sky; Pushing aside the weeds, you ascend high to the Embroidered Peak.
Stone Terrace. How can the beacon fires of the southeast be extinguished? I sing aloud as I linger together at the edge of the clouds.
Written on the third day of the first month (four poems).
Eighty-eight years have long since faded away; though my breath is but a lingering gasp, it still persists. How can one endure these shifting forms, like white robes turning to gray dogs?
Love. How could the trifles of a snail’s horn or a fly’s head be worth discussing? Pitying the common world, I cannot forget my far-reaching concerns;
why then reveal these words that spill from the cup when speaking of the heart? So many years have slipped away in vain; sitting here, I watch the river before me rush on day and night.
Seventy-eight years pass in the snap of a finger; how much time remains of this waning life? Cease lamenting over past and present within the dream;

one grows weary of discoursing on the mountains and rivers upon the chessboard. If you do not seek the place of joy found by Confucius and Yan Hui, how can you hope to find ancient words from paper and ink?
On the white clouds and ancient paths, no one arrives; how many heroes and sages have merely rushed outward!
Seventy-eight years spent on worldly affairs; when scrutinized from beginning to end, none can remain. Having read the Confucian classics to exhaustion, they only increased my flowery rhetoric;

having perused the Buddhist scriptures, I lacked essential discourse. Only when my strength was spent did I realize my former errors; with my mind extinguished, I now rejoice in approaching wordlessness.
In this present single breath, a thousand ages are complete—what need is there to speak of peach blossoms chasing the waves?
In the seventy-eighth year, I am already at my end. Reflecting upon my contemporaries, how many can still remain? Carving insects and engraving on mulberry bark are all heterodox pursuits;
whistling at the moon and chanting with the wind are but worldly discourses. Brandishing the fly-whisk, I have cast my hook a thousand feet into the void;

meeting people, it is difficult to find even one word of perfection. Before my gate lies a path as straight as a bowstring; from of old, the weary horse and the noble steed have each galloped their own way.

Providing Congee to Alleviate Hunger (Two Poems) Do not say that once one has donned the black robes, all worldly affairs cease. With destitution filling the eyes, who among us has no sorrow? The fields and gardens lie utterly desolate, yet the mouth still remains;

Wife and children have been scattered, and my own person is filled with grief. In taking this food, I always recall the kindness of the drifting woman; Having abandoned my home, how could I fail to emulate the son of [Zi]?
I have wandered far and long, yet I am ashamed that I have not yet forgotten my emotions. You talkative Fenggan, you urge me to travel everywhere.
Born into this final age of calamity, we endure bitter warfare; bewildered refugees pass by on the roads. With no refuge upon leaving their homes, their spirits are desolate;
they find it hard to tell anyone, their tears falling like rain. A triple-braided bamboo belt remains at their waists, binding them in vain; though many trees are in bloom, there is nothing to eat.
How could it be much? In the past, at the Twin Trees, he wished to refine himself; how could he have known that his aspiration for study would remain unfulfilled?
*The Extensive Record of Master Yongjue*, Volume Twenty-five;
*The Extensive Record of Master Yongjue*, Volume Twenty-six.
Re-edited by the Dharma-heir Daopei:
Poetry, Part Two,
Five-Character Quatrains.

Ascending Mount Xi (Four Poems on the Place Where Master Cai You Shanshan Read His Books) The ancients retired from worldly dust, Building their dwellings beneath Long Rock. Upon the ancient steps, withered weeds remain; The cold crickets chirp night after night.
This cliff is deep and hollow; within it, one may spread a mat and lie down. I took temporary rest there for a while, unaware that the wind and rain had passed.
There, I discovered an ancient, fragmentary stele buried by clouds in a secluded valley. Though I rubbed and polished it two or three times, I was ultimately unable to read it.
I have heard it said that the most excellent place is named the Terrace for Reading the *I Ching*. The path is overgrown and impassable; as evening falls, the wind is mournful.
Evening View from the Pavilion by the Stream (Two Poems):
Clear waters soak the setting sun; a rainbow bridge cuts through the falling clouds. The fisherman goes to buy wine; at the thatched inn, the tavern flag slants.

The river is empty and the clouds cast faint shadows; the banks are distant and the willow mist obscures the view. A traveler in a small boat—where has he come from? He floats upon the moonlight past the western city wall.

Begging for food, he enters the royal city with his almsbowl. How many times does he turn back to look at himself? Upon his return, the rain suddenly falls in torrents; the stream swells so high that he cannot cross it.

Encountering Evening While Traveling on the Road to Linchuan, Thinking of Seeking Lodging: The wind is cold and the sun slants low; Pale mist floats beyond the bamboo. I suspect this must be a rustic dwelling.
Inscribed on the wall of a thatched cottage.
Clouds hide the house before the cliff; buried deep lies one dead man. Reclining forever on the northern window, I am but a commoner of the Ge-tian era.

Sleeping alone beneath the empty pavilion, The empty pavilion holds me as I sleep alone. In the empty window, subtle breezes suffice; A single clear strike of the chime falls Amidst the autumn dew and the bright moon.

Scenic Impressions from the Mountain Study (Two Poems) Having just finished reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, I wave my fly-whisk as I face the slanting rays of the sun. The mountains are still as pine needles fall; the courtyard is empty as swallows return.

With nothing to do, I sit with my chin resting on my hand; clouds of incense cling to my monk’s robe. It is simply because I have long been free of artifice that the wild sparrows settle here with such ease.

On a spring day, I wandered by the southern ravine, casually following the path down the stone cliffs. I sat scattered among the ground where petals fell, greedily listening to the sound of water trickling over the rocks; unaware that the spring rain had arrived.
I entered Donglin.
Walking alone amidst the green clouds, I don my robes and wander at ease. From where has this man of the Way come? He carries a vessel for brewing tea.

*On Feeling Inspired by the South of the City (Two Poems)* Ten li south of the city, there are peach and apricot trees; A commoner owns a few acres of land, Where he has preserved space to plant mulberry and hemp.
Amidst withered grass and desolate smoke, Mound upon mound are many ancient tombs. Beneath a single cup of yellow earth, What difference is there between noble and base?
A Six-Word Quatrain:
Liquezeqi Peak.

The clusters of peaks at the base of the village all bow down; only then does one realize that one’s body has entered the layered heavens. Laughing as I gaze upon the old kingdoms of Min and Yue, their rise and fall are just like the tides of the sea.
The Phoenix Pond—
The sacred realm opens far-reaching toward the celestial horizon. When did the phoenix depart from the empty pond? The green rushes and white birds remain as they were of old;
the yellow tubers have been newly planted at the edge of the clouds. The Cave of the Sacred Spring.

Clouds atop the bridge have just dispersed; the moon over the sea-cave is already full. A white ape passes through the western ravine at night, drinking water at the head of the cliff before settling into a slumber.
Śāri-kūpa (The Śāri Cave).
A narrow path slants toward a distant ridge; from a deep valley, a solitary village suddenly appears. Amidst the clouds, chickens and dogs emerge and vanish;
ancient trees half-conceal the gates of Jingmen.
*Heptasyllabic Quatrain*
General Luo Retires to Live in Seclusion on Mount Dong (Two Poems) From of old, the General has been esteemed for his refined elegance;
Now he returns to hide his traces amidst the white clouds. Having finished reading the *Huangting jing*, he seeks the *zhī* fungi;
As the sun sets and the mountains grow empty, he returns with a solitary roar.
In these mountain groves, I am now delighted to see you; leaning on my staff by the rocks, I attend to my cultivation. To those I meet, I say only that the mulberry and hemp grow tall;
I cannot yet bear to hear of the winds and mists of the north.
Ye Maocai Requests a Title for Two Paintings A few bends of spring stream, wild trees all blurred;
At every sandbar, smoky villages lie hidden. With a single pole, he fishes alone beneath the weeping willows;
A few petals of peach blossom chase the surging waves.
The hibiscus withers as autumn deepens, the river empty; amidst the green cliffs and red crags, the setting sun reflects. Where is the traveler on his small boat upon the river?
He holds his short flute crosswise, playing it against the western wind.
On an autumn night, I long for my friend Weng Zhongshi, the Literatus;
prompted by the moonlight, I have ascended the tower. My reflection is solitary and desolate as I recall our former excursions.
I know not when I shall finish arranging the fragmentary scrolls beneath Du Lin’s study curtains.
I harbor the sincere loyalty of a loyal minister;

before the Hundred-Fathom Tower, the wind and rain are cold. How can Yuanlong find peace while lying high in bed? I am ashamed that, as a man of the mountains and fields, I lack far-reaching foresight;
I leave my seat to the round *kusa* grass and study the wall-contemplation.
The Sutra-Preaching Terrace (all three realms are present at Boshan):

Amidst the towering cliffs half-way to heaven, the stone walls part; The forest light reflects upon the Dharma King’s platform. The sound of the sutras is permitted to be heard only by the solitary peak;
There is no need for celestial flowers to fall and shake the earth.

In the land of the Great Tang, how could there be no Chan within the Chan-cave? Within a single cave amidst the clouds, all is serene and at ease. Sitting and cutting off the myriad peaks, heaven and earth turn dark;
with a single crowing of the cock, the sun hangs solitary once more.
At Lingyuan Bridge, the murmuring waters flow in winding curves like a silver river; a flying rainbow spans across, dipping into the green waves.
To test how deep this Lingyuan spring runs—there, white clouds drift in mystery and azure ivy grows thick.

Miscellaneous Verses from My Hermitage (Six Poems) Looking out in all four directions, a thousand peaks are lost in misty azure; The spring oriole laughs as it sings toward me. Last night a fresh rain fell upon the mountain head;
It has washed the peach blossoms down into the small stream.
Spring rain falls like rich ointment; spring trees grow lush. Smoke and flowers swirl in confusion as one becomes intoxicated by the spring breeze. A cowherd boy happens to come seeking his oxen;
the grass grows long and the clouds are deep, so no trace of him is seen.
At the summit of ten-thousand-fathom peaks, there is but one house; the misty radiance and emerald hues reflect upon the *kāṣāya*. Those on the path below find it difficult to reach;
the rocks are treacherous, the forest deep, and the sun has already slanted.
In the vast expanse of sky, clouds roll away as the moon descends; scattered river stars reflect upon the Jade Stream. In the bamboo groves the breeze is pure and the lotus water-clock flows on;
a solitary crane calls out once, west of the several peaks.
What is this bitter commotion before the mountain? The sound of firecrackers is heard piercingly throughout the night. This idle monk has nothing to do;
he lights his lamp and playfully composes a "Parting from Poverty" essay.
Burning pine and boiling stones by the white clouds; let the spring and autumn pass in secret.
With broken walls and tattered thatch through the old year, when guests arrive, they say it is already the New Year.
The withered plantain stands solitary, its broken leaves turning in the wind; though emaciated, it still retains a countenance that defies the snow. I pity its pure form, for it cannot endure long;
how could I bear to encounter it again at the end of the year?
A Gift to a Monk of Mount Qingliang:
Upon the mountain peaks remain trees of a thousand years; At the bottom of the ravines still lie icicles of a hundred feet. Sitting before these rugged crags, one forgets the summer days;
Deep within the cold clouds dwells a single recluse monk.
Wan Shi paid me a visit and requested my old manuscripts. For him, I composed two quatrains:
Lute and brush cast aside, I have endured separation from my kin; For several years, I have lain across the clouds of the Chu lands. How can a broken drum ever be struck again?
In discussing our friendship, how could I dare speak further of literature?

In this sagely age, I willingly accept being like a scattered piece of wood; in this floating life, I ought only to let things take their course like an empty boat. When I examine myself in secret, I find no place of excellence;
it seems, rather, that you have merely added one more finger (referring to the story of the stubborn stone who, while practicing Chan, failed to realize the truth and had one of his fingers severed).
The reflections of pavilions and terraces on Lake and Mountain Hall fall beyond the empty clarity; the sound of bells and chimes is transmitted amidst the purple and azure peaks.
A courtyard where songs and dances once flourished in broad daylight now hears only the whistling autumn wind through the reeds and rushes.
Seeing Master Bai Zhuo depart for Mount Zhizhe to clear away the heavy clouds and establish his hermitage, I say: May you dwell among pines and stones with your fellow practitioners.
Now that the world’s paths are perilous as wind and waves, let us simply learn from the "Dumb" One by deeply roasting our yellow tubers.

Traveling along the road to Chongfu, the ancient city’s grain fields stretch out in lush rows; turning into the deep forest, the verdant foliage seems to obscure the sky. Supported by my short staff, I cross the wild waters;
half-concealed by pines and clouds lies a small temple.

I stayed overnight in a few-rafters meditation cell at Chongfu Monastery, opening my window to lean against the pines. From the northern ridge, the mountain mists and light rush upon my face. At night, when all is still, a cool breeze comes from beneath the moon;
osmanthus petals are blown down, dotting the gray moss.
Scenic View at Shílín Hermitage:
Beside the Shílín Hermitage, the clouds part to reveal the view. I am told that every green pine was planted by hand. Their lush, verdant growth is now fit for white cranes to nest;
Riding the wind, they fly away and fly back again.

White Cloud Cave towers above the sky, its solitary peaks casting layered shadows; Catching the moon and riding the wind, it conceals its verdant countenance. The great earth, mountains, and rivers are all a mass of falling snow;
I wonder if one has come from Tianmu to visit Gaofeng.
At Mount Damo, the celestial cave opens upon ancient caverns and emerald cliffs; spitting forth the moon and swallowing the clouds, every detail is profound and secluded.
From the stone walls, the flowing nectar glistens as it cascades—why need one sever an arm to seek it in the depths of night?
Upon reaching Damo Cave, I heard the Master’s resonant voice;
the solitary peaks are rugged and towering, resembling those of Shaolin. Within the cave, winding and deep, gathering clouds hang low.
When guests arrive, they face the moon and taste freshly brewed tea, together discussing the mind of the wall-facing years of old.
Master Suxian’s pine-casket stone wall has thorns for its gate; morning and evening, mist and clouds come and go at will.
When the harmonious breath within the cavern has fully permeated, the spring colors will naturally fill the universe.
In Praise of the Ambrosia Pine: A Longevity Poem for My Layman Bai Majestic, it emerges from the edge of the clouds;
its station is lofty. Its gray scales and verdant mane play amidst the wind and waves. Having endured the passage of spring and autumn, it remains as if yesterday.
How many times has it been graced by the falling drizzle of ambrosia?
Inscription on the Stone Boat (Two Poems) Who was it that once steered this stone boat across the sea? Now it stands high upon the white clouds at the edge of the sky.
Because no one came to ask where its shore had reached, It has cast off its moorings and ceased its rowing for years uncounted.

Unmooring the cables and halting the oars, years passed unnoticed. Blown by the wind and scorched by the sun, they were shrouded in evening smoke. Reflecting in stillness, I realize that even hiding in a ravine can never ensure permanence;
to hasten toward the darkness at midnight is truly pitiable.
Crossing the Luoyang Bridge (Two Poems) One need not grieve for crossing the turbulent waves;
who drove the massive boulders to lock the surging flood? The sky and sea stretch vast and empty as the tide rushes on;
the sun sets and the wind rises upon the ancient shore.
Carrying his mendicant’s staff, he crossed the bridge spanning the sea; the portrait of Duannming alone faces the surging tide.
Having finished gazing upon these silver hooks and iron strokes, I look with sorrow toward the ten-thousand-li distance of misty waves.
I have heard that the lay practitioner Huang Kenian’s secondary residence has suffered a fire. I offer these two verses to inquire after him:
For half a lifetime you have cherished this with such intensity; How could it be that tonight it turns to emptiness? One should know that the flames can preach the Dharma;
The white ox is steadily driven, swift as the wind.
Whenever I compose a rhapsody, I delight in ascending the tower. I laugh and roam amidst the rivers and heavens like a tiny bubble. This evening, those known to me do not remain;
a single orb of moon hangs upon the old tower’s crest.
Inscribed at the Study Site of Master Huang Jitao:
The emerald cliffs of Nantai pierce the heavens on high; Upon the terrace, mountain mists reflect his cloth robe. Having finished his reading, he leans against the railing as clouds fill the earth;
Ten thousand li across the sea and sky, they carry away the cold surges.

Living in the Mountains (Five Poems) At the ancient Buddha’s crag, all coming and going have ceased; Only when the moon is bright do I again reach the pine gate. Incense is burned and tea is brewed—there is nothing else to do;
Scratching my head by the clouds, I gaze idly at the crane.
In the south and north of the mountains, smoke from cooking is scarce; behind and before the hermitage, tiger tracks abound. Within lies a recluse who guards his integrity in solitude;
who will come to join him in singing the Song of the Purple Mushrooms?
Carrying my staff across my shoulder, I enter the white clouds; in the deep mountains, silent and still, deer form my herd.
Sitting alone upon the small tower at night, I laugh as I listen to village children reciting the Sanskrit texts.
After the rain, the green mountains seem as if they will drip with emerald; amidst the clouds, the flowing water is as blue as moss.
A guest arrives to inquire after the master of the hermitage, who leans on his staff before the crag, watching the falling plum blossoms.
The reed-fire deeply warms the broken-legged cauldron; with ash on my head and dust on my face, I pass through the final year of the cycle.
By the window, I idly unfold and read the bequeathed sutras, when suddenly I hear a single crow from the golden rooster.
Dwelling in the Crag (Eight Poems) A single rock rests upon the void above; its eight windows are hollow, piercing the celestial light.
Sea clouds, without intent, drift in with the wind, to accompany the mountain monk as he lies upon his stone bed.
Yantou’s pair of cranes fly off against the wind; a solitary sail on the sea comes breaking through the waves. Alone he turns toward his meditation cushion to dwell in profound stillness;
let the heavenly flowers fall as they will upon the gray moss.
In leisure, I lean on my staff atop the emerald peaks; with a single roar amidst the clouds, ten thousand ravines fall silent. The thousand forests are resplendent, as if entirely made of jade;
there is no need to seek the Cinnabar Hill across the sea.
The wind carries the ocean waves to a foreign land; the moon shifts the pine shadows into the mountain hermitage. Having finished my commentary on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, there is nothing more to do;
I simply add another incense stick to the precious burner.
The summer heat is intense and the days are long; across a thousand mu of green clouds, the plowed fields appear like tortoise shells.
Having received a sudden downpour of rain as rich as fat last night, I look with a smile as the banana leaves sprout once more.

Through a small window, one gains a glimpse of the sky within the caverns; borrowing the lingering light of the sun, I read the Buddhist scriptures. The smoke from the tea stove has vanished, yet fragrance fills the room;
when a guest arrives, they tread upon the ancient moss that carpets the ground like coins.
To the south, the perilous blue waves stretch beyond reach; to the north, the miasmic fogs still obscure the void.
As a monk, you should learn from the tortoise to hide its six limbs, so that you may win a pure breeze filling the entire cave (wherein the ancient Chan Master Zangliu once resided).
Suddenly the pines roar like a tidal wave, resounding through ten thousand valleys; thick clouds mingle together, and even by day it is as dark as night.
In a mere moment, after the rain has dispersed and the clouds withdrawn, the distant village on the seashore appears just as before.
Yulin’s Eight Poems:
When did they emerge from the crest of the azure peaks? Vomiting the moon and swallowing the clouds, every matter is profound and secluded.
Having received the Six Secrets of the Spirit Mountain, The world’s fortunes and misfortunes are left to flow eastward (Six-Eyed Cave).
The immortal crane has returned, though years are not counted; it flutters gracefully, forever dwelling amidst the white clouds. Do not say that the city walls remain as they were before;
the vast seas and mulberry fields have undergone many transformations. (Ssanghak Rock)
When the wind comes from between the pines, the night watch is deep; sitting with legs spread wide upon the crag, I unbutton my robe. With a sudden, piercing laugh, the thousand mountains resound;
alone I behold the silver hook hanging in the evening forest (at the Roaring Moon Terrace).
From atop Stone Tower, I long inhale the clouds of the sea and mountains; Reclining alone upon the clouds, I am half-intoxicated. Awakening from sleep, I scratch my head with nothing to do;
Laughing, I gaze at the four walls as they naturally form patterns of cloud-like mist (Zuiyun Lou).
In ancient times, the spring of the Dharma-milk flowed down in twin streams; its waters melted like jade as they poured before the steps.
I have come, and with but a single drop moistening my mouth, the defiled mind is utterly cleansed—no need for further meditation (the Spring of Dharma-milk).

An ancient dragon’s body surges forth from the edge of the rock; majestically soaring amidst the clouds, it seems as if possessed of feeling. Will it not deign to think of how sentient beings are so utterly withered?
May it let fall sweet dew to drench the parched dust (the Tree of Sweet Dew).
I have heard it said that the crest-jewel atop a Wheel-Turning King’s head is difficult even for a victorious general to capture;
yet now, emerging from the peak of a solitary mountain, it dazzles the earth and illuminates the heavens—there is no mirror to reflect it. (The Crest-Jewel Stone)
The golden spire once had its gates made of jade; white clouds eternally guard the locked green mountains. For a thousand autumns, the path of the red dust has been severed;
it does not permit the wandering footsteps of the mundane to come and go at will. (Jade Green Barrier)
Ascending Kai Bao An in the Evening (Two Poems) After several li, a small path winds its way upward; Upon the mountain peak, stone lotuses bloom in full array.
A newly built cottage of half a mu amidst the clouds, Where I sit facing the myriad peaks reflecting the evening glow.
Crows pass over the city walls of a hundred *zhì* at dusk; autumn colors envelop the homes on all four sides.
The monk returns too weary to speak of affairs within the city, yet he envies the leisurely pleasures found among the mountains.
On the Road to Putian (Two Poems) Vast and level fields encircle the city of Putian; The colors of the water and the light of the woods reflect one another in clarity.
Having crossed a small bridge as the mist and rain clear away, I hear the sound of flower-sellers from beyond the groves.

Carrying his mendicant’s staff, the Scholar of Enduring Brilliance returns to his native land; in the desolate ancient road, the slanting sun grows pale. Where have so many worthies and sages departed?
One sees only stately monuments erected by the roadside.
Crossing the Matou River, waves atop Matou River overturn the void; A great vessel crosses athwart, chasing the morning breeze.
Through many perils of ebbing and rising tides, Gushan Mountain still stands amidst the white clouds.
Moved by Feelings at West Lake:
Smoke drifts beyond the willows as the sun reaches its zenith. Sitting here, I watch shrimp and crabs scuttle over the spring reeds.
Before me, all is new song and dance; who will mourn the old capital for the King?
Inscribed on a Painting: Clouds obscure the secluded valley, cold as ice. Ancient trees and frosty crags shelter a monk in tattered robes.
When the woodcutter returns, the sun is already at its zenith; a single cry of laughter rings out from the emerald vines.
Seeing Master [Name] Return to Min:
A single strand of hair bears the weight of a thousand pounds; the momentum is most solitary. The Dharma-gate is desolate; how many are there to support it?
When you return and your old friends inquire after me, Tell them only this: the sky is cold and frost covers my scalp.
Inscribed on Wang Hui’s Hermitage (Two Poems) The spring has come, its profusion staining the green mountains.
Time and again the flowers bloom, reflecting against the bamboo gate. Having dwelt here long, I no longer know my body is a guest;
I smile as I watch the clouds emerge and the clouds return.
Carrying his staff across his shoulder, he enters the verdant mountains; burning incense, he sits in stillness with the pine gate closed.
At times he wanders aimlessly among falling blossoms, then returns from the mountain ahead having gathered bracken.
Arriving at Zhuangping Hermitage, I follow the previous rhyme:
Vast and ethereal, clouds enshroud ten thousand layered peaks; A few thatched huts conceal the wooden gate. The empty forest is silent, flowers fall like rain;
With a single staff, I travel alone amidst the clouds.
Layer upon layer of emerald mist, layer upon layer of mountains. All day long no one comes; the gates remain closed. A vast haze of light smoke obscures the ancient path;
within the shadows of ten thousand pines, a single monk returns.

Autumn Thoughts (Four Poems) Sitting long upon the fishing pier, I cast my straight hook. How many autumns have passed over the misty waters of the blue river? Failing to meet the golden-scaled fish, I withdraw my line;
Yellow leaves fill the ground in the west wind—how much sorrow!
Yellow leaves fill the ground, the autumn wind stirs with sorrow; The wildcat hangs upside down from the treetop. Spreading a net across the heavens—what purpose does it serve?
I deeply regret not having retired early enough in the beginning.
I deeply regret not having retired early at first; mountains of Wu and waters of Yue have left me lingering in vain.
How much better it would be to lie peacefully atop Mount He, with a tattered robe covering my head, growing old in a single hill.

An old man with a tattered robe covering his head dwells in a single hill; a massive cauldron weighing ten thousand *jin* has been cast into the eastern stream. Deep within the green vines, no one can reach;
the empty monastery is silent and profound as the moon fills the tower.
Returning to Min in the Second Month of Autumn, Year Xin Si. Crossing the Xianxia Ridge (Two Poems).
Old and infirm, I return late, crossing the pass. The perilous peaks and long stone steps force me to struggle upward. Upon the pass lies a single slab of mossy stone;
It smiles coldly at the traveler as they pass back and forth so many times.
White clouds and yellow leaves—the autumn of ten thousand mountains. The whistling western wind stirs the traveler’s sorrow. The paths of the world have always been like chasing a deer;
alas, one dies of old age without ever knowing rest.
A late view from the mountain gate:
as the sun sets behind the pine treetops, the celestial cavern grows dark. Moonlight and plum blossoms conceal the temple gates; standing alone upon the stone bridge, cool dew falls.
Fishermen’s lamps flicker on and off, illuminating the riverside village.
Like Layman Li Kefu’s verse:
"On the peak of Qingfeng Mountain, the emerald hues are about to flow; amidst the cries of the partridges, the rain falls like oil.
If a guest should ask for the master of this mountain, he is simply an old bhikṣu, listless and indolent."
Like Layman Li Yuji’s verse:
"On the peak of Qingfeng Mountain, the tree colors are verdant; among lofty pines and ancient cypresses stand young bamboo shoots. Sometimes he ascends straight to the summit of the solitary peak;
with a single roar, the sky is vast and the clouds are far-reaching."
A Gift to General Yuanzuo Pei:
I know you are born of a family of generals; Your soaring spirit and heroic bearing surpass ten thousand men. May you serve the Imperial House with loyal devotion as its very limbs;
With golden halberds and iron steeds, settle the dust of the frontiers.
**Verses on Bao Shan (Four Poems)** The mountain of Bao Shan is deep and the mountain vapors are cool; The autumn wind whistles through the pine-window.
The cicada’s cry reaches the point where there is no sound; A single orb of ice hangs above.
In the deep recesses of Mount Bǎoshàn, guests arrive but rarely. Beyond the forest of *lánggān* bamboo, one gathers fresh *wēi* ferns. At the gate, the small dog does not bark;
it knows that a green monkey is returning with its young.
The deep rains have just cleared atop Mount Bausan; incense burns as I sit alone beneath the rising moon. The empty hall is silent, with no one arriving;
only the drifting fireflies shine brightly in the clear air.
