On the steep, narrow path deep within Mount Bǎoshàn, the lush, shaggy grass reflects the fading glow of the sunset. At the treetops, the cranes rejoice to see those returning;
they need not inquire whether the path through the azure heavens is far.
I stayed overnight at the watchtower above Jianjin City; the sound of the night watches has faded. Frost flies across the water, making my thin robe painfully cold.
I suspect it is the lingering aura of the twin swords from years past, which even now continues to chill the stars of Beidou and Niu.
In the ninth month of autumn, past the full moon, the chrysanthemums have not yet bloomed. I compose two quatrains:
Though the golden wind is cold, the flowers open late; It has missed the occasion for the reclusive man’s wine-soaked gathering. To look closely, they bloom early and wither early as well;
How much better to endure and keep watch over the cold branches.
In the silence between the fences, the evening wind slants; I see alone the Southern Mountain reflecting the setting clouds. I am reminded again of the former Master Tao;
How could his lofty fame have rested merely on gazing at chrysanthemums?
Hearing the Alarm in the Mountains (Two Poems) Winged dispatches race in haste;
the maritime realm is startled. Yet within these mountains, the wooden fish still tolls its sound. As a monk, I know nothing of the affairs of borders;
I simply burn sandalwood, praying for peace.

What need is there to seek the mountains and rivers on the chessboard? This groundless bitter struggle—when will it ever end? The village elder of the eastern hamlet has no one to whom his grief can be told;
his tears have soaked the Yellow Springs, yet they remain unceasing.

Picking Tea (Four Poems) Thunder and rain frequently urge on the spring that fills the clusters. Purple shoots burst forth, laughing at the eastern wind. Before one realizes it, the fingers find them difficult to gather;
once more they enter the misty green of the front slope.

Unfurling banners and spears amidst the cries of the cuckoo; The rain has cleared and the clouds dispersed, leaving the world a vast expanse of azure. They press forward through the steep mountain paths without complaint;
Carrying their baskets back home, they are imbued with the fragrance of heaven.
As spring draws to a close, my mountain dwelling duties are most diligent. Several times I have heard the sound of singing upon the ridges. Climbing high, I pluck leaves that welcome the breeze;
I laugh at myself for having my whole body covered in white clouds.
Stepping out the gate, I gaze afar at layers of azure clouds; Auspicious vapors swirl and gather upon the branches. In twos and threes, we pluck them together;
Singing our way home, we joyfully see the moon rise.
Spring rains fall in drenching torrents, thick with mist; The myriad flowers have washed away their beauty from last night.
So much splendor cannot endure for long— How can it compare to the green pines upon the mountain ridge?
On a spring day, the mist has cleared and the sun first shines beyond the railing. The *xiebao* calls as the flowers bloom, and the *bugu* cries out.
Having passed the mountains ahead to seek bamboo shoots and bracken, I turn my head and see white clouds stretching across the sky.
Inscription on Lion Hermitage (Two Poems) The monastery pole stands tall to the east of Stone Creek; Half-shrouded by pine-clad clouds, the emerald hues are deep.
At midday, having just finished reading the Golden Sutra, A single roar of a lion resounds amidst the white clouds.

The peaks turn back and the terrain stretches far, the scene secluded and profound. Along the winding paths, it is truly fitting for the traveler’s sandals to roam. A single toll from the golden chime signals a monk emerging from meditative concentration;
the smoke from the tea always drifts alongside the white clouds.

A Gift for the Venerable Xian upon His Residence at Wanshou Monastery in Min’an Having traveled southward through countless passes and ferries, you have halted your staff by the shores of the Min Sea. Having finished reading the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, you dwell in the stillness of this Chan monastery;
transcendent beyond the world, you are a person of leisure.
Playfully presented to a woodcutter:
The sound of *ding-ding* as he hews timber mingles with the song of spring birds. At the foot of the Ao-bridge, fallen petals drift lightly.
Casually treading into the mist and clouds, How many times have I seen green monkeys carrying their young along?

On the contrary, the peony urges its own flowering as the spring arrives and a hundred plants vie for beauty. Yet the King of Flowers alone emerges even later; being noble and dignified, he naturally deserves to appear last.
Why must others trouble themselves with poems to urge him forth?

In return, I offer this peony, intoxicated and satiated by the spring breeze, its national beauty perfected. Its delicate form naturally provokes the passions of the mundane; in a mere moment it withers and falls—where will it go?
I recall how former sages praised it with singular refinement.

The World’s Hardships (Six Poems) The world’s hardships are as bitter as they are now, with no cure in sight. Besieged by war for ten months, there is still no end in view. As people scramble for their livelihoods, they become emaciated corpses in the ditches.
Even the Thousand Buddhas would shed tears upon hearing this.

In the midst of the battlefield of blades and arrows, the blood of war remains fresh; how much more so now that a single *dou* of rice costs a thousand coins? A leaking cup cannot fill the cauldron of the world’s end;
how many of the hundred million common people can hope for safety?
Whenever I see the noble, I sigh that gold and jade are not worth a single spoonful of rice that can cure hunger. That wife and children scatter is but a trivial matter;
I fear even my solitary self may not be sustained.
Ruined walls and broken tiles mark the desolate village; of ten hearths, nine no longer hold rising smoke. Grass grows waist-high, obscuring the traveler’s path;
in the mournful wind and rain, my soul is darkened with sorrow.

Banners and flags fill both banks, shrouding the river’s edge; roads are cut off, the people flee, and it is hard to find food to beg. Since ancient times, these mountains and rivers have endured a hundred battles;
the clouds and rainbows of hope are severed—how often can peace be found?

Enduring hunger and cold as they pass the final watches of the night; day and night, one hears only the sound of drums and horns. Corpses lie scattered across the four fields—whom can they find to bury them?
Blown by the wind and scorched by the sun, their grievances remain unappeased.
Composed by Huai Xu for Xī Yú Guǎngwén (Two Poems) For several years we shared the study of the classics and histories;

Since our parting at Miaofeng, I have been separated from my peers. When shall we again trim the candles by the western window, To spend the entire night together discussing the subtleties of the texts?
Gazing from atop the Water-Drawing Rock, the mountain before my eyes is the official residence of an old friend.
It is only because the sash of our distance has long separated us that the vast misty waves have cut off all coming and going.
Presented to the Venerable Benji:

Entering the empty mountains alone, ten thousand cares turn to ash. Why would you begrudge the water-jar and hand-towel their approach to the dust? How many times have floating clouds been seen passing through the forest?
Now they follow the western wind back into the cave.
A Gift to the Venerable Kuicun:

On the northern ridge, the azure hues are thick beside the clouds; Within the stillness of the pine-window and bamboo desk, He burns incense and sits in silence, contemplating only his breath, Leaving the mountain flowers to be white or red as they may.
Presented to the Senior Monk Zhong:
At the summit of Ten-Thousand-Fathom Peak, there is but one house. Layer upon layer of verdant hues reflect upon his *kāṣāya*. Having finished reading the golden sutras, he has no further concerns;
he draws water himself to brew the Guyu tea.

Seeing Off Huang Zhi, Third Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, on His Northern Journey to Retrieve the Tripitaka (Two Poems) His banners and pennants flutter as he journeys north; The western wind blows across the marshes of white artemisia.
Having discovered the Great Treasure of Gautama, He has thoroughly gathered the vast ocean of the Dharma.
The *Garuḍa*’s bequeathed words, transmitted upon palm leaves, have spread effortlessly among humans and devas. Only those with great strength can bear this burden;
now that the gate of ambrosia has opened, it shall drench the great trichiliocosm.
Sent to the Two Chan Practitioners, Taxdan and Jinghui, on their Request for the Tripitaka (Two Poems) On an autumn day, riding the wind, I depart from Shimen.
White clouds drift and vanish over the riverside village. Having traversed every pass and ferry, the distance was not at all great;
My staff bears the entirety of the words of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Fluttering and flying, yellow leaves fill the mountains in autumn. With golden staff piercing the clouds, you travel beyond the ridges.
Having obtained the priceless treasure from the Dragon Palace, Auspicious light already shines upon the peak of Gushan.
For the Layman Li Wusheng: An Inscription on a Painting of Mount Emei Ten thousand layers of steep crags suddenly open;
The Great Being Samantabhadra emits light and arrives. Within Lingyuan Cave, deep realization dawns;
It is as if attending the Dharma-preaching Terrace amidst the mountains.
Reading Zhou Luoyuan’s Account of the Auspicious Lotus (Two Poems) The teachings of righteous upbringing have been imparted for many years;
His integrity and prudence in office are shared by all in the world. Auspicious signs emerge before his courtyard, bringing double smiles to the elders;
One should know that his son has once again drawn near to the Heaven of Yao.
The ways of the world have long been fraught with adversity; it causes heroes’ sleeves to be ever drenched in tears.
Where the white tuft of light shines through the void, the auspicious petals of the spiritual branch reveal a steadfast heart.
The setting sun casts its light across the horizontal stone cliffs by the ancient shore; the mountain’s radiance reflects in the water as a sky within the waves.
A monk returns late, leaning on his staff, smiling as he points toward the lingering sunset mingled with the evening mist.

Fishing by night on the Jin River, the moon reflects upon the cold waters in a single hue of autumn. A small boat drifts past the White Reed Isle. Having not yet caught the silken-scaled fish, the wind and smoke grow chill;
yet how could I dare cease my thousand-fathom line?

The spring colors of Jianxi are locked before the mountain, where emerald mists swirl; Clustered mountain flowers display patterns as fresh as brocade. The yellow oriole has finished chanting the gāthā of Huating;
It brings laughter to the fisherman, who remains fast asleep in his intoxication.
The Extensive Record of Master Yongjue, Volume Twenty-Six;
The Extensive Record of Master Yongjue, Volume Twenty-Seven.
Re-edited by the Dharma-heir Disciple Daopai.
The Preface to the *Dongshan Guchè*, Volume One, states: "The Way has neither past nor present, yet that which possesses past and present is the transformation of the world.
The Way leaves no tracks, yet that which possesses tracks is the safeguarding of the world. The Way of Shaolin was transmitted through six generations until it reached Caoxi. Caoxi...

This was the gateway [to the Dharma]. Those who succeeded to the Dharma were numerous, yet Qingyuan Xingsi was called "one who obtained the marrow. Later, after five transmissions, it reached Dongshan Liangjie.
At that time, the capacities of practitioners were gradually declining and their studies increasingly diverged from the fundamental principle.

The masters of the Dharma grew concerned and thus established the essential tenets and instituted regulations, so that those of high capacity would not be stalled in the realm beyond kalpas, and those of lesser capacity would not fall into the constraints of the present moment. They [sought to] prune away...
It cuts through the dense forest of various views and severs ten thousand strands of speculative fabrication.

Its mastery as a forge and its skill in refining are beyond compare. Yet, its method is so refined that those with talent cannot display their talent, and those with wisdom cannot exercise their wisdom.
Even the slightest trace of coarse ambition or the turbidity of emotional consciousness finds no place within it.
Furthermore, while other schools focus solely on the ground of view—whether singular or layered—our school discusses both the ground and its meritorious accomplishments.

Thus, only when one is recognized as having attained realization according to the standards of other schools do we permit them to enter our gate. Since the time of Xinfeng, those who have transmitted this Way have been as rare as stars at dawn.
Among those who study it, few do not grow weary of its difficulty and instead gravitate toward what is easy. This single thread of the lineage is now as if severed.

Furthermore, it is not surprising that this is so. During the era of the victorious dynasty (the Yuan), those who presided over the Dharma often bypassed subtle realization while discussing the fundamental tenets (*zongzhi*).
It was like someone wishing to travel to Yan who merely calculates the daily distance, yet whose feet have never actually crossed the threshold;

Yanjing remains a vast ten thousand *li* away. This continued until the Hongzhi period of our Ming dynasty, when there appeared the *Sunggu Zhu* (Commentaries on Ancient Cases) by four masters. In the Jia... [text continues].

Within the "Jingzhong" [Record], there are works such as the *Caodong Zongzhi Yuyue* (The Residue of the Caodong School’s Tenets) and the *Shaolin Biji* (Notes on Shaolin), all of which are erroneous and delusive, causing confusion among later students.
It is like pointing to the narrow, winding paths of sheep-guts, secluded valleys, and desolate trails, and claiming they are the main thoroughfares to Yan;
is this not lamentable? This old monk was born in the final age of the Dharma, yet fortunately he caught a glimpse of light through a narrow opening and beheld these [errors].
He wrote the *Bimowang* (Errors and Absurdities) and the *Pomie Zhengfa* (Destroying and Annihilating the True Dharma), totaling two fascicles.

He completely excised heterodox teachings and selected only the ancient precedents of the virtuous masters, compiling them into a book. Occasional insights and critical examinations were added; thus, he disregarded even the peril of his own destruction.
I have directly offended against taboos and prohibitions. Alas! How could I have helped it? This old monk’s twilight years are spent, and moreover, the demon of illness daily encroaches upon me;
my breath is faint and I stand on the very brink of death. Yet, despite my failing strength, I have exerted myself to compose this work.

Is it because I still cling to the notions of self and other in the midst of emptiness, or compete over right and wrong in this world? Rather, it is simply that I cannot bear to see this Way remain long obscured and shrouded in darkness.
Through the long night, I have sought to cause all under heaven to look up together toward the morning sun of Fusang; this is the day of great abundance and prosperity.

Whether they understand me or condemn me, let it be this book alone. Written on the full moon of the second month in the Jia-shen year of the Chongzhen era, by the Elder Yongjue Yuanxian at the Shengjian Hall on Mount Gu.
This commentary on the *Cantong qi* is the source of the Dong lineage. During the Song dynasty, there was a commentary by the Great Master Fayan which was universally revered;
however, it has now been lost and can no longer be consulted. Therefore, without measuring my own abilities, I have ventured to imitate its style.
"The mind of the Great Sage of the land of Chu (India) was secretly transmitted from east to west. Though human faculties may be sharp or dull, the Way has no Southern or Northern patriarchs.
First, he brings forth the word "mind" to establish the fundamental principle. How can the mind be transmitted? It is simply the mind-sealing the mind.

It does not fall within the realm of verbal explanation; therefore, it is called the "Secret Transmission. Although the Southern and Northern Schools are distinguished as Sudden and Gradual, this is precisely because the capacities of people's faculties differ.
For those of sharp faculties, the Sudden Dharma is taught; for those of dull faculties, the Gradual Dharma is taught.
While the expedient means differ, the Way itself is without distinction; in sum, it is simply to accord with this wondrous mind.

The spiritual source is bright and pure; its branches and tributaries flow on in obscurity. To cling to phenomena is fundamentally delusion; to accord with principle is likewise not awakening. The "spiritual source" is the mind.
Originally it does not fall within the realm of names and words, yet through clarity, its brightness and purity are perceived. The "branches and tributaries" are phenomena.
Originally they possess no substantial reality, yet through obscurity, their flowing and pouring forth are perceived. These flowing branches and tributaries are what is called—
"Attendant, to mistake the delusory for the real is certainly confusion. That the source of spirit is bright and pure is called 'conforming to principle.

But if there is a principle to which one conforms, how can that be true awakening? These words clarify that both light and darkness, as well as the manifestation and concealment of clarity, are all delusory;
students must not rely upon them to delude themselves."

In every gate, all objects are either interpenetrating or non-interpenetrating. When they interpenetrate, they mutually enter one another; otherwise, they abide according to their respective positions.

"Gates" refers to the faculties (*indriya*); "objects" refers to the sensory fields (*viṣaya*). Regarding these faculties and objects, there are two meanings: interpenetration and non-interpenetration.
What is called "interpenetration" means that the various faculties and objects mutually enter into one another, like the jewels in Indra’s net. Non-interpenetration means...

This means that the sense faculties and their objects each abide in their own respective positions, never becoming intermingled. Although they mutually penetrate one another, they in fact each abide in their own positions;
although they each abide in their own positions, they in fact mutually penetrate one another. This is not an object within the domain of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Form originally possesses distinct substantial characteristics; sound fundamentally differs as pleasure or pain. Darkness accords with words of superior and middling quality; clarity and turbidity correspond to phrases.
The natures of the four great elements return to themselves, like a child finding its mother.
This clarifies that while the various phenomena of form and sound are vividly distinct when illuminated, they cannot be distinguished as superior or inferior in darkness;

yet when illuminated, the clear and the turbid are clearly differentiated. All of these are stuck in the traces and are unable to return to the fundamental nature. If one were to return to the nature...
How could there be anything to be said regarding light and darkness? It is just as when a child finds its mother;
they naturally and wondrously accord, such that both "knowing" and "not knowing" are insufficient to be spoken of.
Fire is hot, wind is mobile; water is moist, earth is solid. The eye perceives form, the ear perceives sound; the nose perceives fragrance, the tongue perceives saltiness and acidity.

Yet for each and every phenomenon, they are distributed according to their roots and branches; from beginning to end, one must return to the fundamental source. Whether noble or base, one employs the appropriate terminology.
Although all phenomena (*dharmas*) differ, they are collectively rooted in the mind. The mind is the source; all phenomena are its branches. Yet, there must be a fundamental principle (*zong*).
This principle is the secret essence of all Buddhas and the profound intent of the successive patriarchs. If one does not penetrate this principle, then both source and branches are false;
if one can penetrate this principle, then both source and branches are true. Once this principle is attained, one emerges from it accordingly.
A single word, a single command—there is nothing that is not the true seal of Vairocana. Who could fail to follow and employ it?
When there is light within, do not encounter it with darkness; when there is light within darkness, do not perceive it with light.
Light and darkness are each mutually opposed, like the steps of walking back and forth.
This [passage] further refutes the claim that light and darkness are not real. At the very moment of light, darkness is already present within it;
it is simply that the characteristic of that darkness cannot be encountered. At the very moment of darkness, light is already present within it; it is simply that the characteristic of that light...
It cannot be perceived. What is the meaning of this? It is established through the mutual dependence of light and darkness.
It is just as when a person walks: the preceding step receives its name because of the succeeding step. If there were no succeeding step, how could the preceding step be named?

Furthermore, the succeeding step receives its name because of the preceding step. If there were no preceding step, how could the succeeding step be named? The principle of light and darkness is likewise so.

It is thus. For the most part, brightness is established in dependence upon darkness; therefore, it is said that there is darkness within brightness. Darkness is established in dependence upon brightness;

therefore, it is said that there is brightness within darkness. That arising and ceasing manifest alternately is not the ultimate reality. If this were the wondrous light that is primordially present, [it would not be so].
Being utterly devoid of duality, how could there be any talk of arising and ceasing? Delusion does not exist, and awakening is likewise not established;
this is the true illumination of the wondrous nature.
All phenomena possess their own efficacy; one should speak of their function and their locus.
Previously, it was stated from the perspective of the mind that light and darkness are not real; here, it is stated from the perspective of the object that all phenomena are not real.
Those in the world who cling to phenomena as being real do so because each possesses its own efficacy. If, indeed, they were [inherently existent]...

If there were merit, one should speak of how its application benefits things. Now, observing the extent of its application, we see that it is entirely dependent upon external conditions before it can be accomplished.
Without external conditions, it cannot reach or benefit things; thus, we know that it has no merit in itself from the very beginning.
Since it possesses no merit in itself, it is nothing more than something empty and illusory.

The facts exist as a box and its lid meeting; the principle should be like the point of an arrow meeting its target. When receiving words, one must understand the source; do not establish your own rules and regulations.
If you grasp at mind and objects as real, then both fact and principle are violated. If you realize that mind and objects are illusory, then both fact and principle are wondrous. Facts exist;
there is no need to discard them, for they naturally accord with principle without deviation. Principle is transcendent.
When words are brought forth for practical application, they naturally meet like the points of two arrows, never missing their mark.
This is due to nothing other than being able to grasp the essential principle (*zong*). Therefore, when receiving and employing words, one must necessarily grasp the essence.
If one deviates from the fundamental principle and establishes one's own arbitrary rules, then one’s actions and understanding will be erroneous; such a person is either a fool or a madman.

When you encounter it with your eyes, you do not realize the Way; when you set foot upon it, how can you know the road? Advancing forward is neither near nor far, yet delusion keeps one separated by mountains and rivers.
I respectfully address those who investigate the profound mystery: do not let your time be spent in vain.
This is a summary, intended to exhort one to diligently seek the convergence with the Way. The Great Way is right before one’s eyes; it is present in everything one encounters.
If one does not grasp at phenomena or cling to the Dharma, then one cannot achieve this convergence. Thus, it is like a blind person walking: they have no means of advancing forward.
How could it be that the road itself has distance? It is simply that if one is not deluded, then as one walks, one knows the way; there is no distance.
If one does not reach this point, one will remain lost; then mountains and rivers will stand forever firm, and even a distance of a few inches will be impassable.
How can those who study the profound mysteries fail to strive diligently to realize the Way? If you unite with the Way, your time may perhaps not be spent in vain;

otherwise, it will be nothing more than a hollow life and a futile death. In the past, Fayan commented on this, saying: "Stop! Stop! Your kindness is too great to be repaid. How profound his meaning was!
The *Baojing Sanmei Zhu* (Commentary on the Jewel Mirror Samādhi) is a single work that was secretly transmitted by Dongshan to Caoshan within his quarters.
Dongshan said, "I received the direct seal of the Jewel Mirror Samādhi from my late teacher Yunyan"; thus, one knows it was not composed by Dongshan himself.
This was composed by Yunyan; some even claim it was transmitted by Yaoshan, though this cannot be verified today.
The various masters of the Dongxia (Linji) school feared that if this text were to circulate widely, it would instead bring disgrace upon the Great Dharma.

Therefore, they secretly bestowed it within their chambers to establish the fundamental tenets and prevent its leakage. In the Song dynasty, Zhu Shiying obtained it from an old monk, who then entrusted it to Jue.
Fan’s commentary proceeds by way of practice; however, Juefan did not penetrate this school and was further characterized by a disposition toward negligence.
Consequently, his judgments are half-right and half-wrong, leading later students into confusion and error. Having no other choice, I have therefore composed a separate commentary.
Such a Dharma has been secretly transmitted by the Buddhas and Patriarchs; now that you have received it, you should protect it well. That principle is not otherwise is called "such" (ru);
that phenomena do not fail to accord with it is called "is" (shi). As for "transmission," it is transmitted in this manner;
as for "receiving," it is received in this manner; as for "protecting," it is protected in this manner. Should there be even the slightest deviation from this, [it is no longer so].
It is not merely a matter of common grasses. A silver bowl filled with snow; the bright moon hidden by a heron—these are alike yet not the same; they are confused, yet their places can be known.
Such a Dharma is fundamentally neither orthodox nor biased; yet if one forcibly names it, it may be called both orthodox and biased. This...
The principle of the correct and the biased is fundamentally neither divisible nor unified. Yet, if one speaks forcefully, it can be said to be both divisible and unified.
The ancient sages, having no other choice, employed the metaphors of "silver bowls filled with snow" and "the bright moon hidden by a heron.

These analogies are not identical; however, when mixed together, their respective locations become known. This is precisely the interpretation of the meaning of the first two lines. If a student, regarding this point, can—
Do not be obstructed by words and phrases; if you divine and clarify them, then the teachings of Dongshan will leave nothing behind.
The meaning does not reside in the words; when the opportune moment arises, the response follows.
Although the meaning is not confined to words, one may still employ words to respond to the occasion in order to convey that meaning.
Movement creates habitual patterns; deviation results in fixation.
That which is not at ease within the ordinary is called movement. When there is movement, the mind inclines toward a particular direction, thereby forming a habitual pattern;
this is not the state of transcendence and non-abiding. That which does not accord with principle is called deviation. Deviation causes one to lose the light that is inherently present.
One immediately falls into the realm of the mundane. To look back and dwell upon it with thought is merely the livelihood of ghosts.
Neither turning away from nor touching it, it is like a great mass of fire.
Prajñā is like a great mass of fire: if you touch it, you are burned; if you turn away, it is not fire. It simply seizes you by both ends.
Do not cling. Thus, one avoids the mutual conditioning of suffering and pleasure, or light and darkness.
To merely manifest patterns and colors is to belong to defilement.
Baizhang said: "From the beginning, it has never been any thing at all. Do not seek to know it or understand it; do not say 'it is' or 'it is not.'"
It merely cuts off the phrases of both extremes; it cuts off the phrases of existence and non-existence, and the phrase of neither non-existence nor existence.
It is not deficient, nor is it complete. It is neither holy nor ordinary, neither bright nor dark.
It is not possessing knowledge, nor is it lacking knowledge. It is neither bound nor liberated. It is none of these names and designations; this is called the Buddha.
This is defilement; this is what is called the "Dharma. This is defilement.
At midnight it is perfectly bright, yet at dawn it does not manifest.
To call it "perfect" implies the partial, so it cannot be said to be perfect. To call it "partial" implies the perfect, so it cannot... [be said to be partial].
This refers to partiality. Because one does not wish to transgress the Middle Way, it is clarified in this manner. The pivot of the Dongshan school values indirectness and mutual interpenetration;
its source truly originates from this.
He acts as a model for all beings to pull them out from all sufferings. Although this is not conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is not a state of silence. Guishan said:
"In the ground of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), there is fundamentally not a single dharma; therefore, one does not delight in grasping or attachment.
When acting as a model for beings, one employs what is necessary at that moment. Yet, at other times, not even a speck of dust shall bind one's thoughts. This is *nirvāṇa*."
The Sūtra says: "That which can be spoken of is called conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma). Yaoshan, however, replied:
"First of all, one must not cut off speech. When he utters a word, it is to manifest that which is beyond words."
It is like standing before a precious mirror, where form and reflection behold one another. You are not that; that is precisely you.

For one who perceives the Way, it is like a person standing before a mirror and illuminating themselves: form and reflection face each other, unimpeded by names and words, silent yet radiantly manifest.
If you were to consider [the reflection] merely as "you," then "you" would exist apart from "that," and thus "you" would not be "that. Thus it is said.
"It is not you. If one further takes 'it' (the river) to be the river, then the river would be entirely devoid of being a river, yet the river is precisely you.
To speak of 'it' is also incorrect. As soon as one enters the realm of names and words, it becomes defiled; how could this possibly be in accord with the intent of this Way?"
It is like an infant of the world, complete with the five characteristics: neither going nor coming, neither arising nor abiding;
it is *baba* and *hehe*, possessing both phrases and non-phrases, yet ultimately unable to grasp any object, for its speech is not yet correct.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "What is called 'infant-like conduct'? Good son, being unable to arise, abide, go, come, or speak—this is called infant-like conduct.
The Tathāgata is also like this. 'Unable to arise' means that the Tathāgata never gives rise to the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
'Unable to abide' means that the Tathāgata does not cling to any phenomena. 'Unable to come'..."
As for "the Tathāgata’s bodily actions are without movement": it means that the Tathāgata has already attained Great Parinirvāṇa.
As for "he cannot speak": it means that although the Tathāgata expounds all dharmas for the sake of sentient beings, in reality, there is nothing spoken.
In the sutras, the conduct of an infant is cited as an analogy for the conduct of the Tathāgata; here, it is cited to illustrate that within the Dharma there are five stages.
The hexagrams of the *Zhongli* (Hexagram 30) involve the interplay of the biased and the correct; when these are layered into three and their transformations exhausted, they form the five.
"Alternation between the biased and the correct" refers to the transformation of yin and yang. "Layering them to form three" means layering these transformations until the third line is reached.
"The transformations complete to form five" means that when the aforementioned three lines undergo transformation, they form the hexagram *Ji-ji* (Water and Fire in Completion).
The hexagram image is "centered within the biased. When the three lower lines change, it becomes the hexagram *Wei Ji* (Fire over Water).
The hexagram image is "biased within the centered. When the interlocking trigrams formed by the middle lines—lines three, four, and five—change, it becomes *Yi* (Wind over Thunder).

The hexagram image is "reaching the center from both sides. When lines two, three, and four change, it becomes *Sun* (Mountain over Lake). The hexagram image is "arriving at the center from both sides."
In the two hexagrams Ji (Fire) and Wei (Water), fire is paired with the biased and water with the orthodox; their meaning is thus evident.

The two hexagrams Sun (Diminution) and Yi (Increase) both arise from the *hu* (interchange) lines, which signifies the principle of inclusion. Wind and thunder both move, symbolizing the manifestation of inclusion in its function (*yòng*).
Mountain and marsh both are still, symbolizing the return of inclusion to its substance (*tǐ*). The hexagram Li originally derives its image from the central line.
The hexagram Li represents the departure from the mind’s images. The mind dwells within the body, yet it emerges from the center;
its image is black inside and white outside, which is precisely the image of Li. The five positions correspond to the five trigrams;

not only do their meanings all accord, but even the names of the hexagrams Unfinished (Wei Ji) and Finished (Ji Ji) are directly opposed to one another, as are the names of Diminution (Sun) and Increase (Yi). Viewed in this light, [the correspondence is clear].
It can be seen that the establishment of the five ranks was created by Heaven and ordained by Earth; it is not the slightest bit a human contrivance.
That "reaching the ultimate within the central" (jiānzhōng zhì) was changed to "reaching the ultimate within the partial" (piānzhōng zhì) only serves to further reveal its error.
It is like the taste of the *kakkō* (Chinese yam) and like a vajra.
The *kakkō* possesses five flavors; this serves as an analogy for how a single dharma fully encompasses the five positions.
A vajra is broad at both ends and narrow in the middle; likewise, in this dharma, there is "the partial within the central" and "the central within the partial."
The two positions are at the front: "Simultaneously in the Middle" and "Simultaneously Arriving in the Middle. The two positions are at the rear.
Only "Coming from the Center of the Middle" occupies the central position. Because the two ends are broad while the middle is narrow, its symbol is the vajra.
The "wondrous embrace" within the center; striking and singing raised together. Penetrating the source and penetrating the path; carrying the source and carrying the way.
Within the position of correctness, there is originally not a single thing, yet it truly wondrously embraces all phenomena.
Therefore, one must raise both the correct and the biased; one must not fall into partiality or barrenness. To "penetrate the source" is to be in dark resonance with the samādhi of self-enjoyment.

The primary aim is to be without obstruction. "The common path" refers to the samādhi of the other-enjoyment body, wherein guest and host communicate through sound and message, and the life-force of the lineage remains unbroken.
"Carrying along" means to skillfully embrace and penetrate the fundamental source. "Traversing the path" means to skillfully embrace and traverse the common way.
"To be startled is auspicious; one must not offend or oppose [it].
The line for the first nine of the Li hexagram says: 'Treading upon something, one is startled; if one respects it, there will be ultimate good fortune.

This is used here to speak of the central position, which is a place of honor and nobility. One should be startled and respectful toward it; one must not violate or provoke it. Dongshan’s verse also [states this].
It is said: "If one can refrain from touching upon the taboos of the present age, this surpasses the 'tongue-cutting' talent of former dynasties.
It is natural and wondrous, belonging neither to delusion nor enlightenment; through the conditions of time and season, it is serenely manifest."
The Way is fundamentally natural; it does not belong to delusion or enlightenment. Delusion and enlightenment are matters of the person.
However, when the proper time arrives, it transcends all verbal expression and becomes vividly manifest.
Subtly it enters the Avīci hell; vastly it transcends all spatial dimensions. A deviation of even a hair’s breadth would fail to accord with the musical scales.
This Way is manifest: when speaking of its subtlety, it enters the Avīci hell; when speaking of its vastness, it transcends all spatial dimensions.
This may be called the ultimate in thoroughness. Although the Way is thus all-pervasive, those who seek to realize it must value the acquisition of its method.
If one acquires the method, one will naturally merge in profound harmony with it; if one loses the method, [the Way remains distant].
Thus, the more one seeks, the further one strays. It is just as with those who compose music:

if there is a discrepancy of even a hair’s breadth within a single inch, the sounds of all twelve pitch-pipes will fail to harmonize. This speaks to later students, who ought to examine the ancient tracks with meticulous care.
Yet it must not be treated with negligence.
Now there are sudden and gradual [teachings], established based on conditions. Once the fundamental tenets are distinguished, they serve as the standard and rule.
They are inherently natural and wondrous; all things are thus. It is only because the capacities of sentient beings differ that the "sudden" teaching is formed.
Gradually, the divisions of the fundamental tenets (zong) and the ultimate goals (qu) emerged, such that their standards became distinct.
When the tenet is fully realized and the goal reaches its ultimate limit, it flows as true permanence.

Even when the tenet and goal are wondrously perfected, they still constitute a "barrier of principle" (lizhang), obstructing correct knowledge and vision; therefore, it is called the "flow of true permanence. (From the *Xuanshi*)
The Master said: "You all must believe that there is a portion of true, eternal flow which extends through antiquity and continues unto the present;
there has never been anything that is not this, nor anything that is not non-this. This single phrase constitutes the Dharma of equality. Why is this?

Because words are pursued by words and principles are dispelled by principles; it is through the ordinary nature and characteristics that the Dharma is preached to deliver sentient beings. Yet even so..."
They understand what precedes but not what follows; they have never produced a phrase that transcends the ordinary. They die within the words themselves.
Outwardly tranquil, yet inwardly wavering—like striking a foal or subduing a rat.
Those whose so-called "true permanence" is merely a continuous flow appear tranquil on the outside, but inside they are truly restless, like a tethered foal that never forgets to gallop.
The prostrate rat represents the thieving mind.

The former sages took pity on it and established the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā) for the sake of the Dharma. In accordance with its delusions, they treated black as white; once these inverted perceptions were extinguished, [the truth was revealed].
To resolve with sincere conviction—this very resolution is itself the mysterious path of the golden lock. Thus, there is the account of observing the tree for ten kalpas.
To accord with the ancient tracks, please look to the ancients: when the Buddha-way was about to be perfected, he observed the tree for ten kalpas.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas, yet the dharmas of all Buddhas did not manifest before him.
Only after ten kalpas had passed did the dharmas of all Buddhas finally manifest. Caoshan said: "Because he had not yet forgotten the great fruit.
I [Yuanwu] say that the ten kalpas symbolize the completion of the ten stages; that ten kalpas have passed symbolizes not being obstructed by the completion of the ten stages.
It is like the "defect of the tiger" and the "white hoof of the horse.
Regarding the tiger: one name for it is *Li-er*. When a tiger eats livestock, it does not reach their ears; yet whenever it eats a person's ear, that ear is invariably left with a single defect.
This is used as an analogy for the principle of not daring to violate a taboo name. As for the "white hoof": it refers to a white mark on the hind left leg of a horse.
This is form. This uses an analogy to avoid the completion of the ten [categories].
Because there is that which is inferior, such as a jeweled stand or a precious carriage; because there is that which is startlingly extraordinary, such as a dark-skinned slave or a white ox.
Ordinary sentiment and the vision of the sages constitute the mysterious path of the golden chain; therefore, the former sages refined them with the Dharma.
When Hou Yi, through his skill and strength, shot an arrow that hit a target a hundred paces away, the arrowheads met point-to-point—what role did skill and strength play therein?

To shoot at a distance of a hundred paces is a matter of strength. To hit the mark at a hundred paces is a matter of skill. But when the arrowheads meet face-to-face, it is beyond the reach of either skill or strength.
The wooden man sings; the stone woman dances. This is beyond the reach of emotional consciousness; how could it admit of thought or deliberation?
This precisely clarifies that the wondrous function of true suchness is not within the scope of intellectual power; it is like the meeting of the tips of two arrows.
A minister serves his sovereign; a son obeys his father. To be disobedient is not filial; to fail to serve is not to provide support.
This clarifies that the partial should assist the whole, just as a minister serves a ruler and a son serves a father.

Thus, Dongshan further established the five ranks of "Establishing Merit," and Shishuang further established the five ranks of "The Prince's Son"; both were intended to minutely clarify the meaning of service and obedience.
Moving in concealment and acting in secrecy, appearing as if foolish or dull-witted, yet able to maintain continuity—this is called the "Lord of Lords.
These four lines clarify the matter of the sovereign-father; his station is the pinnacle of honor and nobility, and fundamentally no active function can be perceived.
Yet, in reality, it is the pivot of all transformations. Thus it is said that its activity is latent and its function subtle.

Although its illuminating essence is uniquely suspended, it is in fact devoid of the discrimination of cognition and perception. Therefore it is said: "As if ignorant, as if dull-witted. Furthermore, this essence is eternally such of itself;
it continues without interruption, possessing no distinction between movement and stillness, nor any difference between manifestation and concealment. Thus...

This is called the "Lord among Lords. If there were distinctions between movement and stillness, or differences between manifestation and concealment, it would be a "Lord among Guests," not a "Lord among Lords."

In the preface to the Five Ranks of Dongshan by Master Danxia Zhen, it is said: "When black and white have not yet been distinguished, it is difficult to speak of 'this' and 'that. After the differentiation of dark and light, one establishes 'self' and 'other.
Thus, one borrows black to represent the provisional and the correct, and relies on white to indicate the partial. The correct does not sit in the correct; at midnight..."

Vast clarity. When partiality does not sit upon partiality, when dawn breaks amidst the gloom, the whole body is function. When the flowers bloom on the withered tree, total function is the essence; the fragrant clusters do not flaunt their beauty.
When destruction and preservation are held together, the profound mystery is exhausted. The jade phoenix and golden crane cannot be further distinguished.
Therefore, beyond the limit of Vipaśyin, do not speak of "how. To accommodate the present age, it is established according to human capacity.
I briefly set forth my humble views to indicate the general direction, hoping that those of like mind will not merely clap their hands in derision.
Before the signs of black and white had appeared, the primordial chaos was already divided; from this it evolved into three, and through transformation, the five elements were fully formed.
The General Diagram of the Five Stages:
The Single Aperture Facing Upward; Black and White Interchange; Like the Taste of the *kṛtavedhana* Herb; Like a Vajra.
Explanation of the Diagram of the Five Stages.
The first supreme characteristic represents the state prior to the emergence of black and white; it is what is called the matter of the upward-pointing vehicle of the lineage (*zongcheng*).

Students should first awaken to this. If one has not awakened to this yet speaks of principle and phenomena, or distinguishes essence and function, how does this differ from those who study and lecture according to the teachings?
The next characteristic represents the period after black and white have already been distinguished; it is what is called the "center."
There is partiality; within partiality there is correctness. The principle of the mutual interpenetration of the partial and the correct is fully revealed herein.
The single empty circle remaining in the center represents the matter of the upward direction; it is likewise now hidden between the black and white.
Furthermore, if this principle of the mutual interpenetration of the partial and the correct is expanded, it forms five positions—that is, one becomes five, and the five together become one.
How could this be a matter of artificial arrangement? That which has much black and little white is called "the partial within the correct" (*zhèngzhōngpiān*).

Because this position contains the partial within the correct, there is much black and little white. That which has much white and little black is called "the correct within the partial" (*piānzhōngzhèng*).

Because this position contains the correct within the partial, there is much white and little black. That which is black in the center and white on the outside is called "coming from the correct" (*zhèngzhōnglái*). This is because...
The former two positions create the most supreme and noble station; yet, not remaining in that nobility, they turn directly toward the partial.
Thus, while the direct does not abide in the direct, the partial emerges from the direct, and the partial does not fall into the partial. Therefore, black is within while white is without.
That which is entirely white constitutes the "Ultimate within the Comprehensive. This occurs after the "Coming from the Center of the Direct," wherein the wondrous seal faces the wind, even as it...

Heng Wujì was one who illuminated both principle and phenomena simultaneously and employed both light and darkness together. Because his entire being was function, his manifestation was entirely white.
That which is entirely black represents "arriving within the integration" (*jiānzhōngdào*); therein, the wondrous function is exhausted and effort forgotten, blending seamlessly without trace.

Principle and phenomenon are both dissolved, and neither right nor wrong is established. Because his entire function is substance, his manifestation— [Note: The source text appears to be incomplete at this point.]
It is entirely black. The first two positions are mutually exclusive and do not encompass one another; the latter two positions are mutually inclusive and do encompass one another.
Only the single position of "Coming from the Center" has no counterpart; it skillfully embraces the four surrounding positions, just as [the center] stands among the five directions.
The "trust" among the Five Constants and the "earth" among the Five Elements both have no counterpart. With two positions before and two behind, there is only one position in the middle;
thus, it is broad at both ends and narrow in the center, which is why it is symbolized by the *vajra*. As soon as one position is distinguished, all five positions are manifest.
It is like worldly objects: as soon as one speaks of "front," there is immediately a "back. Once front and back exist, left and right necessarily follow.
The "right" and the "middle" constitute one stage, which together comprise five stages; thus, they are likened to the taste of *tiktaka* (bitter) grass.
Popular traditions regarding diagrams of these five stages are spurious, false, and uncanonical; therefore, I have now specifically established this diagram to inform future students.

Furthermore, I have observed that some attempt to correlate the five stages of meritorious achievement, the five stages of a prince, and the five stages of ruler and minister with these five [stages] respectively.
As for "position," it cannot be followed. For both "merit" (*gongxun*) and "prince" (*wangzi*) are matters pertaining to partial positions.

Furthermore, merit is a vertical discourse on the depth of one's cultivation, whereas a prince refers to the internal and external lineages within the central division; thus, there is a difference between them.

The five ranks of ruler and subject consist of two distinct positions for ruler and subject; this is the method for receiving others, and it is derived from within the single rank of "Arriving at the Center" (jiānzhōng zhì).

Jiyin changed "Arriving at the Center" to "Arriving at the Partial" (piānzhōng zhì) in order to pair it with "Coming from the Center" (zhèngzhōng lái), which is a great error for later students. Now...

To establish this, the "Coming from the Center" (Zhèngzhōnglái) occupies a single position; it is the pivot of the four positions. Those who enter via the two preceding positions do so through this, and those who emerge via the two succeeding positions do so from this.
It is precisely like the position of supreme honor, which must not have a counterpart. This is the first reason why it cannot be paired with another.

Furthermore, if one were to pair "Arriving from the Partiality within the Center" (Piānzhōngzhì) with "Coming from the Center," there would be two positions in the middle, which is not the Golden Mean.
The image of the vajra: it cannot be followed; this is the second [point]. Furthermore, "arriving from the side" is the image of being entirely white.
"Coming from the center" is the image of being black within and white without. These do not correspond at all; it cannot be followed; this is the third [point].
Moreover, "reaching through the integration" is the image of being entirely black, which directly corresponds to the image of "arriving from the side," which is entirely white. How could...?
This may be called "arriving within the simultaneous" (*jiānzhōngdào*). It stands alone at the end, without a counterpart. That it cannot be followed is the fourth [point].
Jiyin says: "The various masters and great monks of antiquity all employed 'arriving within the simultaneous,' yet none understood its meaning.
Therefore, I shall now set it forth here."
Dongshan’s Five Ranks Verse:
Commentary on "The Centered Amid the Deviant. Before the moon shines bright at the third watch of the night, Do not blame us for meeting yet not recognizing one another;
Hidden within, we still harbor the resentments of days past.
"Centered in the midst of the partial. This is established based on the initial moment of awakening to this principle. The principle is "centered," while the awakening is "partial.

The third watch of the night—dark and without light—symbolizes the principle. Yet, because the moonlight becomes manifest before its brightness, it is at the very moment the darkness is revealed that brightness exists within it;
likewise, the principle must necessarily be manifested through awakening. At the moment the principle is manifested, brightness already exists within it.
To "awaken" implies there is a principle (li) that can be seen; thus, the traces of awakening have not been eliminated.
Since even this principle is not yet the ultimate reality, though they may meet face-to-face, they do not recognize one another, and the resentment of former days cannot yet be avoided.

It is incorrect for masters of this stage to explain this as "function arising from within the essence," for according to Dongshan’s intent, this is already partiality within the absolute center (zheng). It is not [the ultimate].
This refers to the partial arising from within the correct. This can be discerned by examining the two verses of Chang and Dong.

"The correct arising from within the partial": An old woman at dawn encounters an ancient mirror; clearly facing it, there is nothing else that is real. Do not further lose your head by still recognizing its reflection.

"Deviation within correctness" (*piān zhōng zhèng*) is established in reference to the period of diligent practice following the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*). "Diligence" (*gōngxūn*) represents deviation;

the principle one upholds represents correctness. "The old woman who has lost her way at dawn" symbolizes deviation within correctness; "the ancient mirror that is no longer bright" symbolizes correctness within deviation.
This stage, through the power of reverently upholding [the principle], results in a vision even more intimate than before, yet it is still not yet possible to personally manifest it.
This principle means that what is recognized exists only within the realm of reflected images; hence it is said, "mistaking one's head for its reflection.

It is incorrect for masters of this stage to frequently provide an interpretation that shifts toward the essence (*tǐ*). According to Dongshan’s intent, the correct is already present within the partial;
it is not a matter of returning to the correct after having been in the partial.

"Coming from the very center: there is no path within it, for dust stands in the way. If one can simply avoid touching upon the taboos of the present age, this surpasses even the talent of those who had their tongues cut off in a former dynasty.
This "coming from the very center" constitutes one rank; it is precisely the attainment of the Dharmakāya and is also the Right Position (*samyak-sthāna*). The first half [of this verse] is...
"Transforming merit to reach the station" refers to the latter half [of the verse]. "Transforming the station to accord with merit" refers to the middle [section], which is the station of nobility.
"Non-existence" (wu zhong) is the true station (*zhengwei*). "The existence of a path" refers to partiality.

"Separated from dust and grime" means that because one has internally transformed the body and has not yet entered the secular world, one is separated from dust and grime. There are those who interpret this as "transcending dust and grime," but that is incorrect. Why? Because...
The meaning of the character "emergence" (chu) is that one emerges only after having entered the mundane world. This position of honor and dignity must not be violated;
to violate it is to fall under defilement. One must skillfully employ mutual interplay (*huìhù*). When one can so interplay, one strikes and reveals from the side:
there is speech within silence, and silence within speech. Therefore, this surpasses the talent of mere verbal disputation. This is recorded according to the fundamental tenets of the Caodong school.
It is said that during the Sui dynasty there was a debater named Li Zhizhang. Whenever he engaged in debate, everyone else would be left speechless;
thus, people called him "the talent who cuts off tongues. Regarding this position, later generations who composed eulogies mostly used the phrase "shrouded in fur and wearing horns."

Statements such as "entering the marketplace with hands hanging down" are all incorrect. Only Caoshan’s verse—“Without leaving the Tuṣita realm, the black bird walks upon the snow”—profoundly captures the essential meaning of the Dongshan school.
Later, there was an ancient worthy who divided this single stage into the "small five ranks," which is the most precise and subtle interpretation.
Tiantong Jue’s “four turns of the spiritual mechanism” is likewise a clear elucidation of this.
This is something students must know.
Reaching the pinnacle within the midst of both [sides], two blades clash—there is no need to avoid them. A master hand is like a lotus in the fire;
it possesses, quite naturally, a will that soars toward the heavens.

Simultaneously reaching the center: when the positions of function and status are manifested in unison, the primary [the absolute] having arrived, the secondary [the relative] must necessarily accompany it.
At the moment of encounter between masters, light and darkness intersect, and yielding and seizing are employed interchangeably, without involving even a hair’s breadth of deliberation or conjecture.
Naturally, one will not suffer injury to the blade or wound the hand; like a lotus flower within fire, one ultimately remains unharmed.
This is the samādhi of "other-enjoyment," which is precisely the penetration of the Dharmakāya and constitutes great capacity and great function.
Dongshan’s departure from the three leaks and Linji’s possession of the three mysteries and essentials are both nothing other than this.

Reaching within the simultaneous: not falling into existence or non-existence, who would dare to harmonize with it? Everyone desires to escape the common flow, yet when brought to the final reckoning, one returns to sit amidst the charcoal.

Reaching within the simultaneous: established at the moment when both function and status are concealed. As for "reaching within the simultaneous" mentioned previously, although the biased and the correct arrive together, [they are here transcended].
There still remains the trace of partiality and correctness; here, however, no trace is to be seen. Therefore it is said: "It does not fall into existence or non-existence.
This is indeed the ultimate attainment of the Way and the exhaustion of the present moment. Returning to the source and merging with the root, it is therefore said:
"When brought to its final conclusion, one returns to sit within the charcoal. This is like the meaning of the Buddha’s teaching on ultimate *nirvāṇa*: it is the *samādhi* of self-enjoyment. Since...
Having attained this samādhi, although its great functions arise in profusion, they do not, in total, transcend this. Dongshan, at the time of his death, said:
"My idle name has already faded away; this precisely clarifies the essential meaning. Jiufeng Qian said: "Though there may be arts for concealing one's form amidst the dust,"
"How can this compare to entering the Imperial Capital with one's whole body? Yunmen said: "Even if you manage to penetrate through the Dharma-body, it still cannot be let pass.
If one examines it closely, what kind of 'fragrance' (or trace) is there? This too is a sickness; the meaning lies right here."
According to the *Zhengfayan zang* (Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma), it records a single verse by Mahamati explaining the five stages (*wuwei*). This must absolutely not be trusted.

For instance, in the line "The third watch, the moon bright before nightfall," he explains that this is speaking of black while pointing toward white; by transposing the word "black" (*hei*), he avoids violating taboos.

In the line "An old woman who has lost her way encounters an ancient mirror," he explains that this is speaking of white while pointing toward black; by transposing [the terms], [he avoids the taboo].
"White characters do not violate taboos. This is truly as he said. In his response to "The Partial within the Central," the Great Deceased Elder replied:
"A lacquer-black old woman wears a white sash. Furthermore, in his response to "The Central within the Partial," he said: "An old man with white hair wears a black robe."
Hongzhi Jue’s verse on "Correctness within Partiality" says: "The woman’s hair is white, hanging down like silk. He further answers:
"An old woman with white hair is ashamed to look in the mirror. Zide Hui says: "White clouds shroud the mountain peak;
its towering majesty is never revealed. Can these all be faulted for violating taboos? Moreover, the function of the Dongshan school values indirectness and circumlocution precisely in this manner.
Furthermore, how does one transcend birth and death? Those who study this school must examine this carefully:
"The Five Ranks of Fenyang: A General Verse.
One must thoroughly know the essentials of seeking within these five ranks; the moment there is the slightest movement, one is at odds [with the truth]. Who can pass the diamond through the casket?"
In its application, there is only the foremost faculty of Nātha: a single glance can cause the three realms to fall silent; shaking his bell, he causes the nine heavens to return to their place.
In the midst of the correct, the subtle and the grasping interpenetrate and revolve; should one hesitate to deliberate, the sharp edge of the blade loses its majesty.

Cimingyuan’s General Verses on the Five Ranks: Returning from the Partial to the Correct is profoundly mysterious; From the Correct departing and the Partial arriving, principle and phenomena are complete. One must know that the Correct Position is beyond words and speech;

Its subtle signs are faintly perceived through conditions. When both arrive, the coming and going give rise to wondrous function; Once one has reached this state of "both," why would one pursue anything further?
Regarding the power of words to explain: how could their appearance and disappearance encompass the entire world? Vast and without reliance, the Bird Path is profound and mysterious.
Touzi’s Verse on Blue (with Preface):
Now, when the long sky is of one color, how can stars and moon be distinguished? When the great earth is without partiality, withering and flourishing naturally differ. Therefore—

In the Dharma there is no separate dharma; how could delusion and awakening ever reach it? The mind is not of itself the mind; it is only through the provisional use of words and symbols that it is proclaimed.
These words are both partial and complete, direct and ultimate, inclusive and harmonious. As for this Dharma, it does not fall into the extremes of right and wrong.
How could this concern the myriad phenomena? Once the profound intent has merged with the moon in the water, the source of the school blends its tributaries in the Golden River;
it does not fall into empty stasis, but returns to the path through the subtle wonder.
The Centered Deviation: The stars and river-crossing moon turn across the sky before dawn; colored vapors mingle at night while heaven is not yet bright.
Faintly manifest, they are perfectly complete within the darkness.
The Deviation within the Center: The half-moon shines at night, its reflection in the water bringing shame; amidst the hazy mist, how can one distinguish? All is blended, indistinguishable.
The mirror of the Qin dynasty has fallen;

it comes from the very center. A golden rooster sits upon a phoenix terrace amidst the flames. The profound path leans against the heavens, leading out onto the main thoroughfare; traversing the clouds on the bird-track, one emerges from the dust and toil.
Simultaneous Arrival: A blade of snow encasing the body, there is no avoiding it. A natural warrior, neither side is harmed;
in secret, he fully provides for all contingencies.
Simultaneous Reaching: One who knows how to run does not touch the Way. This common act of grasping is different from what you possess; it does not fall into being or non-being.
Not square, yet this is the wondrous.
Master Hongzhi’s Verse (of the five verses following those of the two houses, Dongshan and Caoshan, these five are considered the most supreme):
The Center Amidst Deviation: The clear blue sky, the stars and river coldly soak the heavens. At midnight, the Wood Child knocks at the moon-gate; In the darkness, he is startled.
A jade figure lies asleep, leaning toward the center.
Sea clouds rest upon the summit of the immortal’s head; a woman’s hair, white and hanging like silk, feels shame before the cold reflection in the Qin Terrace.

Coming from the very center: on a moonlit night, the great whale sheds its shell and opens it wide. Its vast back brushes the heavens as it spreads its cloud-like wings; soaring along the path of birds, it is difficult for any category to encompass.

Reaching through the "concurrent" [state]: facing one another, there is no need for mutual avoidance or concealment. The transformation of wind and movement is the profound meaning of the unblemished intent; within the light, there is...
The paths are naturally different;

arriving within the "Simultaneous Middle. The handle of the Dipper hangs slantwise as the sky is not yet dawn; the crane’s dream has just awakened, the dew-drenched leaves are cold. From its old nest it flies forth;
the cloud-pine lies prostrate.

Spontaneously Attained Radiance praises the "Middle Deviating from the Partial": When primordial chaos first divided, before the midnight hour, The wooden man turned over, startled by the breaking of his dream;
Snow and reeds fill the eyes, and sleep can no longer be found.

Entering from the side into the center: The precious moon is full and round, the golden hall is cold and still. Facing the light, one does not fall into darkness; withdrawing the body, the shadow turns at the peak of the western mountains. Coming from the very center:
The Emperor’s mandate is distributed to the sides, revealing the talent for transformation. As the bright sun first rises, the lands of the sands are tranquil. Spiritually resonant, it has never...
Without a speck of dust.
Reaching the ultimate within the integration. One plays forever on the great road of Chang’an. Everywhere there is no self; emptiness merges with emptiness.
Every dharma returns to the same source; water sees water.
Simultaneously reaching the center. The Master says: "At the place where the heavy judgment is passed, the home mountain is fine. He smashes the bright moon pearl of the black dragon;
Kunlun enters the sea without a trace.
—Verse by Xian of Gushan.
The partial within the absolute: A black-lacquered Kunlun man sleeps in the void. Though he has not yet attained intimate realization, the images before his eyes are nonetheless vividly clear.
The absolute within the partial: The general holds the seal of no-words; with iron horses and golden spears, his labors are diligent and ceaseless. He has not yet found rest.
At such a time, it is difficult to have self-confidence.

It comes from the very center: at midnight, plum blossoms vie with the snow to bloom. A gust of fragrant wind wafts out from the valley; only then does one know that they shall not be permitted to remain buried deep in the snow.
Simultaneously Reaching the Center: A blue serpent emerges from its case, beyond the reach of deliberation. The reversal of yin and yang—how constant can such affairs be?

Do not say that meeting is merely a matter of personal spirit. Simultaneously Arriving at the Center: Affairs and principles are entirely dissolved; there is nothing to be said. This is not merely standing alone on a cold cliff in emptiness; fundamentally, there is no change.
Yi Xian’s name was Sǎo.

Regarding Cao Shan’s “Verses on the Five Phases” (the versions of these verses found in the *Wudeng Huiyuan* are all erroneously arranged; here they are corrected according to the *Zongmen Xuanjian Tu*):

“Though one in white robes may receive the rank of a high minister, this matter is not considered extraordinary. As for those whose families have held office for generations, do not speak of their falling into ruin.”

At that time, this is precisely "the partial within the central" (zhèng zhōng piān). The initial awakening to this principle is likened to a commoner in white robes being appointed as a high minister;

yet in reality, one is originally noble and dignified, having merely been temporarily submerged in obscurity. Thus, there is the metaphor of those with generations of official lineage who, for a brief moment, fall into a state of ruin.
On the day he first descended into the royal palace, how could the jade hare have been able to leave? Having not yet received the mandate of non-action, why are humans and devas so slow?
This refers to "attaining correctness within partiality. His descent into the royal palace is a metaphor for first awakening to this principle; it must necessarily rely upon effort.

Merit is preserved through such guarantees; thus, the jade hare is used as a metaphor for meritorious achievement. Since one cannot yet be entirely without merit, one remains lingering within the realms of humans and devas;
hence it is said: "How very slow are humans and devas!"

At the hour of Zi (midnight), one should abide in the Correct Position (*zhengwei*). Clarity resides precisely in the relationship between ruler and subject; not yet having left the realm of Tuṣita, the black hen walks upon the snow.
This is precisely "coming from the midst" (*zhengzhonglai*). Since the hour of Zi corresponds to midnight, it is used as a metaphor for the Correct Position. Clarity resides precisely therein.

"Ruler and Subject" refers to clarifying this correct position (*zhengwei*). It is like a ruler looking upon his subjects: one must not sit [with them] as if they were equals, for their dignity is supreme.
It is also like a subject serving his ruler: one must neither turn one's back on him nor violate him.

"Not yet leaving the Tuṣita realm" is a metaphor for being currently turning about within the correct position, having not yet entered the mundane world. "Black chicken" is a metaphor for the Correct; "snow" is a metaphor for the Deviant. "Black" refers to the Correct.
A rooster walks upon snow: this is the image of turning from the correct toward the biased.
Within the flames, cold ice forms; willow flowers fly in the ninth month. The mud ox bellows upon the water’s surface; the wooden horse chases the wind and neighs.

This refers to the simultaneous arrival within both the partial and the absolute. "Flame" represents the partial; "cold ice" represents the absolute. This is the absolute contained within the partial.
"Willow blossoms" represent the partial; "the ninth month" represents the absolute. This is the partial contained within the absolute. "Mud ox" and "wooden horse" both represent the absolute;
"roaring on the water's surface" and "neighing after the wind" both represent the partial. This is the simultaneous arrival of principle and phenomenon, where the partial and the absolute intersect.
Three. It is that which cannot be grasped through thought or deliberation.

● The principle and phenomena are stored in total浑然 (unity); their initial signs are ultimately difficult to clarify. Even King Bhīṣmagarjitasvaranāda was not yet enlightened; how could Maitreya be so alert?
This is precisely "reaching within the simultaneous" (jiānzhōngdào), the ultimate limit of cultivating the Way. Here, both principle and phenomena are utterly extinguished;
it is not only that the ordinary eye cannot perceive it, but even all Buddhas of the past and future cannot perceive it.
This is because one has returned to the cavern of primordial chaos, which by its very nature cannot be made manifest.
Regarding the essential meaning of the Five Ranks, one should take the verses of Dongshan and Caoshan as one’s guide;
therefore, I have now annotated them in detail. As for later authors, many have lost the intent of their predecessors.
As for the verses of the two masters Dayang Xuan and Fushan Yuan, they are all spurious compositions that entirely deviate from the ancestral meaning; I have now deleted them.
Regarding the fifth position, the response to the question asked by a monk: "What is 'the partial within the central'?
Fenyang Shao replied: "Once the jade hare has illuminated the end of the first watch, the golden rooster must crow before the fifth watch."
Hongzhi Jue said: "After the clouds have dispersed across the vast sky, the moon shines brightly in the empty hall. Zide Hui said:
"Last night at the third watch, the stars filled the heavens. Dasiweng said: "A lacquer-black old woman wrapped in white silk."
Gushan Xian said: "A lamp burns at night at the bottom of a thousand-fathom well.
He was asked: "What is 'correctness within partiality'?
Puxian Xiu said: "Light smoke veils the bright moon; thin mist locks the cold cliff. Hongzhi Jue said: [as follows].
The white-haired old woman is ashamed to look in the mirror. Dasi Weng said: "The white-headed old man wears a black robe.
Zide Hui said: "White clouds shroud the mountain peak; it never reveals its towering majesty. Gushan Xian said: [as above].
The General held the Seal Without Characters.
He asked, "What is it that comes from the very center?
Fenyang Shao replied, "Lotus blossoms bloom one after another upon dry land. The monk asked, "What is it like after they have bloomed? Fenyang said:
Golden stamens and silver filaments receive the jade dew. The eminent monk does not sit upon the phoenix terrace.

Puxian Xiu said: "The pine withers, yet how could it ever grow old? The flower blooms, yet its sprouts have never emerged. Hongzhi Jue said: "With frosty brows and snow-white hair, he emerges from amidst the flames;
majestic and imposing, he never falls into the present moment. Daowu Zhen said: "The heavens and earth are pure and bright."
Thundering Earth and Trigram: Zide Huigu said, "Do not say that the whale and the kun lack wings; today they have personally come by way of the birds' path.
Gushan Xian said, "With the talisman suspended behind the elbow, he emerges from the forbidden city."
Question: What is "reaching within the inclusive"? Puxian Xiu said:
"The sound of the monkey’s cry cannot be distinguished; the call of the crane is difficult to clarify. Hongzhi Jue said: [The same].
When the great function manifests, no rules or regulations remain. Dasi Weng said: "The blade of snow covers the body, yet one does not wound oneself.
Zide Huiyun said: "There should be no tracks; in its application, there is no trace. Gushan Xian said:
"A precious sword brandished in the void—no one asks who it is."
Question: What is "reaching within the simultaneous"?
Puxian Xiu said: "Clearing the path beyond the clouds; shedding oneself before the moonlight. Hongzhi Jue said: [as above].
At night, the ranks are already formed outside the bright curtain; atop the Hall of the Empty King, no one understands the sound.
Daishi Weng said: "Kunlun walks through the night. Zide Hui said: "The stone man’s robe is torn;
there is no one on earth to sew it. Gushan Xian said: "In the night, ink dyes the black gauze cap."
A monk asked Dōngshān about the five ranks and their meritorious functions:
"What is 'facing'? The Master said, "When eating a meal, what do you do? He further said, "If you have gained strength, you must forget your fullness;
if you cease taking grain, you will no longer hunger."
"Directing toward" means to move toward. However, one must first know that it exists; if one does not first know that it exists, toward what would one direct oneself?
The answer, "What is it like when eating a meal? means that amidst the activity and stillness of daily life, it must not be forgotten for even a moment.
"To gain strength by forgetting satiety; to cease taking grain and yet not be hungry" means that if one is single-minded in directing oneself [toward this], then [one will not be hungry].
He reckons leisure by his hunger and satiety.
The verse says: The Wise Lord has always followed the way of Emperor Yao; he governs the people with propriety, bending his dragon-waist. Sometimes he passes through the midst of a bustling market;
wherever he goes, civilization flourishes as we celebrate the Sage Dynasty.

Question: "What is 'offering'? The Master said: "When you have your back turned, what then? He further said: "One knows only the nobility of the crimson and purple robes, but fails to honor the person of original nature."

"To serve" (*bōng*) means as in "to serve" (*chéng-bōng*). It refers to serving after having first turned toward [the object], just as when a person serves a superior, they must first offer reverence before they can serve.
If one turns away, one cannot serve. To say "turning away" means being greedily attached to external objects.
This is to turn one's back on one’s fundamental duty. Knowing only the nobility of purple and crimson robes, one betrays the person of original nature.
This refers to greedily engaging with external sensory objects.
The verse says: Washed clean and heavily adorned, for whom? Amidst the cries of the cuckoo, it urges people to return home. The hundred flowers have all fallen away.
Crying without end, he cries even deeper into the midst of the chaotic peaks.
A question was asked: "What is 'merit'? The Master said, "When you set down the hoe. "How about then? [The Master] said again, "Cast off your hands and sit upright;
idly amidst the deep white clouds."
Holding the hoe is "turning toward" [the Way]; putting down the hoe is "not turning toward.
