Because of the merit of the former turning toward, one suddenly forgets it upon reaching this state; hence it is said, "Put down the hoe.

"Casting off [all concerns] and sitting upright, idly deep within the white clouds" refers to entering the True Position (*bhūtatathatā*). That it is still called "merit" is precisely what is meant by "joy like a spring bubbling forth."
This refers to establishing the merit of the Middle Way; it pertains to the merit within the Middle.
The verse says: A withered tree blooms with a spring beyond the kalpas; Riding backward upon a jade elephant, one pursues the qilin.
Now, high-secluded beyond a thousand peaks, The moon is bright and the wind is clear—a most auspicious day.
Question: What is "shared merit"? The Master said: "One cannot grasp at form. He added: "White powder is difficult to settle on the road;
one does not dwell long in Chang'an."
Regarding "shared function" (*gònggōng*): all dharmas arise together; hence it is called "shared. Dongshan said:

"Not obtaining form" refers to the preceding stage, wherein there is but a single color and all dharmas are concealed. In the present stage, this single color is exhausted and all dharmas manifest together.
"A single color cannot be obtained again; it is difficult for traces to settle upon plain powder.
As for "not dwelling long in Chang'an," this also refers to the aforementioned "single color," meaning that one cannot dwell there for long.

The verse says: Sentient beings and all Buddhas do not encroach upon one another; the mountains are naturally high and the waters are naturally deep. Amidst ten thousand distinctions and a thousand differences, the fundamental reality is clear:
where the partridge cries, the hundred flowers are fresh.

Question: "What is 'Gong-gong' (the function of function)? The Master said: "Not shared. He further said: "In the state of total integration where there is nothing to avoid, what more could one seek beyond this?
As for "Gong-gong," this function is even deeper than the former; therefore, it is named "Gong-gong. Dongshan said: "'Not shared' means—"
Previously there was the shared; now it is the unshared. It is not that the Dharma alone cannot be attained; neither can non-Dharma be attained.
It is a state of total integration where there is no place for concealment. Beyond this, what more could one seek?

This means that principle and phenomena are integrated, entirely without any trace of hiding; this is the ultimate pinnacle of realizing the Way. What further could there be to seek? Yet, it is still called by a name.
As for "merit" (*gong*): if one views it in relation to matters directed upward [toward the ultimate], it is likewise something achieved through human effort;

thus, it is also merit. The verse says: "As soon as its horns begin to grow, it is already unfit; To set the mind on seeking a Buddha is truly shameful. Vast and remote, the empty kalpa has no one who knows it;
Who would consent to travel south to consult the fifty-three [patriarchs]?"
Yongjia’s Eulogy:
Meeting everywhere yet not recognizing; sometimes not recognizing yet meeting. Master Xiang has no eyes yet sees as if he did;
Master Kuang can hear so well he is just like one who is deaf. (Xiang)
Gold needles stitch the mandarin ducks closely; brocade seams layer upon layer with long jade threads. Hung in the spring garden, no one recognizes it;
it draws the bees and butterflies over, making them busily flit about. (Offered).
Master Yan lived in a humble lane, unable to bear his sorrows; all day long he appeared as if ignorant, finding joy in his freedom.
To say that "sitting and forgetting" (zuowang) was beneficial was merely a pretext; it brought a measure of grief upon Confucius himself.
The Daoist of Huainan wears true crimson; do not say that when emotions are forgotten, form is empty.
When the rite at the Jade Altar concludes and the handle of the Dipper shifts, he chants a single verse of *Buxu* facing the spring breeze (Gonggong).
When Emperor Gao of Han first rose in the region of Pei and Feng, his imperial enterprise was secured by a three-foot long-sword;
yet it took the time for Shusun Tong to establish the rites and music—truly, he would not have shared a single meal with you (Gong).
Dongshan spoke of the "Three Kinds of Leakage" to Caoshan, saying:
"In the age of the Dharma’s decline, many people possess only dry wisdom. If one wishes to discern the true from the false, there are three kinds of leakage;
you must truly possess the eye [of insight]."
First: Leakage through Views. When the faculty does not leave its station, one falls into a sea of poison.
Ming’an said: "This means that when views stagnate within the known, if one does not shift one's station, one remains fixed upon a single form."
Second, the leakage of emotional states. One becomes stagnant in terms of preference and aversion, and one's perspective becomes biased and withered.

Ming'an said: "This means that the state of emotion is not perfect; one stagnates in grasping and rejecting, becoming biased and withered from beginning to end. One's discerning awareness is incomplete;
this is the flowing of the waves of consciousness, a matter of the near and far shores along the way. One must simply, in every phrase, remain free from the two extremes."

Not being obstructed by the circumstances of the situation. Three: Leakage of Speech. To exhaustively investigate the subtle while losing the fundamental source; for the capacity [of the student] to be obscured regarding the beginning and end; turbid wisdom flows on and turns. Ming’an said:

“To exhaustively investigate the subtle while losing the fundamental source” means to be obstructed within the pathways of speech, whereby the phrases lose the fundamental source of the doctrine; the capacity is obscured regarding the beginning and end.
"Beginning" refers to when the listener's faculties are obscured and the essential principle within the discourse is not fully realized.
Within every phrase, there must be "speech where there is no speech" and "no-speech where there is speech"; only then does one attain the subtle sound that is secretly perfect.
Letang Zhao’s Verses (These three verses were inverted in the old edition; they have now been corrected).
The wooden man lightly opens his mouth atop the ridge; The stone woman secretly nods her head by the stream.
How laughable that Li Bai of old, Spent the night once more aboard a fishing boat.
The world’s most exquisite and secluded mountain streams— Who can hold my hand and roam them together? Turning my head, I suddenly hear the cry of the cuckoo;
Laughing, I point to the white clouds and say: "Go home and rest. (Sentiment)
In years past, I was once a seeker of the profound mystery; I knocked everywhere at the pivot of the arcane to exhaust its vital veins. When the night was deep, ink stained my black robe;
when I spoke it to others, their mouths were too narrow. (Verse)
Regarding Dongshan’s “Guest and Host” phrases:
When the Master visited Longshan, he asked, "What is the guest within the host? Longshan replied, "Green mountains shroud white clouds.
He asked, "What is the host within the host? Longshan replied, "Never leaving the door for years. He asked, "How far apart are guest and host? Longshan...
[The Master] said: "Waves upon the waters of the Long River. He asked: "When host and guest meet, what words are exchanged?
Shanshan said: "A clear breeze brushes the white moon. The Master then bowed twice.
The Master asked a monk, "Who is your true master? The monk replied, "The one currently responding to you.
The Master said, "Alas! Alas! People of this age are all like this; they take that which follows behind the donkey or the horse to be themselves.
This is a sign that the Buddha-dharma is sinking. They have not yet clarified the 'master within the guest,' let alone the 'master within the master.'"
A monk asked, "What is the master among masters? The Master said, "You, Reverend, should say it yourself. The monk said, "What I can say is only the master among guests.
(Yunju spoke on his behalf: "What I can say is not the master among guests. [The monk asked again: "What is the master among masters?
The Master said, "I am not unwilling to tell you, but for it to be continuous is also very difficult."
A monk asked, "Regarding the meaning of 'universal virtue' (guǎngdé): what is the guest within the guest? The Master said, "The profligate has no home or means;
drifting and homeless, he does not even know it himself. The monk asked, "What is the host within the guest? The Master said, "A pearl curtain hanging at a thatched door.
The monk asked, "What is the guest within the host? The Master said, "A grass mat spread in the imperial palace. The monk asked, "What is the host within the host? The Master said:
Although the Crown Prince is the legitimate heir, he does not behold the sacred countenance of Yao.
Regarding the four "hosts" (zhǔ) and "guests" (bīn): the "host" refers to the correct, the essence, and the principle; the "guest" refers to the partial, the function, and the phenomenon.

That which is the fundamental substance of principle and does not involve function is called the "Host of Hosts. It is metaphorically like an emperor dwelling in deep seclusion within the Nine [Palaces].
That which is internal is the "Self" (zhòng). That which issues forth from the substance to manifest its function is called the "Guest within the Host" (zhǔ zhōng bīn);

it is like a minister who has received an order and gone out. That which is the substance within the function is called the "Host within the Guest" (bīn zhōng zhǔ); it is like the Son of Heaven in a bustling marketplace.
When the function and the substance are at odds and there is as yet no host, it is called the "Guest within the Guest" (bīn zhōng bīn); it is like one outside the civilized realm.
These people are guests without a host. These four types of guest and host differ from those of Linji; let students examine this carefully.
Furthermore, there is a book recording the words of Ming’an that attempts to correlate the four guest-host relationships with the four kinds of "selective testing" (lìjiǎn);
this is an egregious error, for it is a spurious compilation.
Tiantong Jue’s Verse:
The affairs of my life have knotted my brow; A face covered in dust, hair already autumn-tinted. In truth, when setting out, one has no skillful means;
Alas, today’s road is poor and filled with sorrow. (Guest within Guest)

By day one should engage in commerce to profit ten thousand pieces of gold; at dawn, one asks for news of one’s family on the ancient road. Having clearly received the report that one’s honored parents are well, what can be done?
It is difficult to rely upon a heart of joy and fear. (The Host within the Guest.)
The horns blow atop the imperial pavilion as the six thoroughfares brighten; the General of the Golden Horse emerges from the forbidden city. His authority beyond the borders is truly well-founded;
without harming social customs, there is spontaneous peace and prosperity. (Host within, guest without)

The Immovable Golden Wheel possesses all myriad virtues; the moss has grown thick upon the imperial abode, and the ranks have not yet been arranged. The tabooed name stands at the head, forbidden throughout the realm;
who would dare to approach it even slightly, offending the Sacred Countenance (the Lord of Lords)?

The Verses on the Essential Principles and the Verses on the Double Locks of the Golden Needle state: The Golden Needle and Double Locks are complete; They encompass the hidden path and include all. The Precious Seal is wondrous as it faces the wind;
Layer upon layer, the brocade seams unfold.

The "Golden Needle" phrase refers to the simultaneous employment of the biased and the orthodox, such that one does not fall into either extreme, yet it is also not a matter of clinging to the Middle Way.
The "Tucked-in Path" phrase refers to the path that responds to capacities; the orthodox must necessarily embrace the biased, and the biased must necessarily embrace the orthodox.

Although one of these may be hidden and not manifest, in reality, neither the biased nor the orthodox fails to be fully encompassed. The "Treasure Seal" phrase refers to the orthodox within the midst.
The seal of "Excellently Clutching" corresponds to the responsive resonance of sentient beings' capacities.
As for the "repeated layers of brocade seams," it means that due to the responsive resonance of sentient beings' capacities, the fivefold dharma-gates manifest in successive layers.
The Verse on the Mysterious Path of the Golden Lock says: Where light and dark intermingle, effort becomes as difficult as turning back;
When strength is exhausted and one forgets how to advance or retreat, The golden lock’s net is spread all around.
Brightness symbolizes great function; darkness symbolizes the true position (*bhūmi*). When first applying effort, one borrows function to advance toward the position;
this is "darkness within brightness. Next, one borrows the position to clarify the function; this is "brightness within darkness.

When function and position are both fully manifest, it is still valued that function and position revolve together. If one’s strength is exhausted and cannot effect this revolution, then one remains stuck in the traces of phenomena and principle.
It has not yet been digested; the sentiments of the holy and the ordinary have not been exhausted. This is called the "Mysterious Path of the Golden Lock.

Not falling into the categories of ordinary or holy, the verse says: When both phenomena and principle are not involved, The returning illumination cuts off all subtlety. Turning one's back on the wind, there is neither skill nor clumsiness;
Like a flash of lightning or a spark, it is difficult to pursue.

The preceding two verses clarify the mutual functioning of the correct and the biased; this verse clarifies the simultaneous dissolution of both the correct and the biased, which is the return to the fundamental source of the Way.
When one turns the light back to illuminate this realm, not only are there no visible forms or traces, but even the subtle and minute is utterly transcended.
Yet it cannot be seen. Regarding the absence of skill or clumsiness when facing the wind: when there is an interaction with the mechanism, then skill and clumsiness take form.
In a place where this interaction with the mechanism does not reach, how could there be skill or clumsiness? "Skill and clumsiness" refers here to the sage and the ordinary person.
Regarding "the lightning fire that is difficult to pursue": because it has form, it can be pursued; because it is formless, it cannot be pursued.
This is a metaphor for the fact that wisdom cannot reach it. This is precisely "reaching the ultimate within the simultaneous."
Shishuang’s Five Ranks: "The Prince is Born, the Prince is Born" refers to the initial nurturing.
From the very beginning, one knows that there is; thus, one is able to enter immediately into the single color, without borrowing anything at all.
The "Merit" (Gongxun) is like the eldest legitimate son of a king who receives the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) immediately upon birth.

This differs from Dongshan’s "the biased within the central" (*zhengzhongpian*). "The biased within the central" merely refers to the initial realization that [Buddha-nature] exists; it is not yet the sudden entry into the single color (*yise*).
Entering the single color is the matter of "coming from the central" (*zhengzhonglai*).

The noble scion of nature is fundamentally not a product of effort; his virtue harmonizes with heaven and earth, and his nurtured influence is magnificent. From beginning to end throughout this single period, there is no admixture of other strains;

though divided into six palaces and six residences, they do not belong to different lineages. Above and below, they are harmonious and concordant; yin and yang flow in accord. Sharing the same vital breath, their branches are linked, and their capacities and measures are identical.
If you wish to recognize the father of the Prince at his birth, it is like a crane soaring through the clouds and mists, emerging from its silver cage.
The first phrase states that he is noble by nature, without depending on meritorious achievement. "Virtue accords with Heaven and Earth" means his virtue is identical to that of his parents.
"The power of his upbringing is exalted" means the force of his birth and rearing is exceedingly magnificent; he is originally of royal lineage.
The initial and final phrases state that he is not mixed with the achievements of external succession. The phrase regarding the division of the palace refers to the six... [text ends].
Although the functions of the faculties differ, they do not deviate from the fundamental principle. The first line, "harmonizing with the father," speaks of its accord with the father.
The line on "sharing the same vital breath" speaks of the six consciousnesses being like brothers who share the same capacity and all accord with the father.

The final two lines clarify that the prince’s father is the silver cage; this metaphor for "one color" signifies transcending that single color, whereupon one first perceives true nobility. This serves as a metaphor.
Regarding his status as a father:
"born in the morning" means that he was born in the outer court; he occupies the rank of a minister and was not born within the palace precincts. This son—
Being unable to know existence, one merely halts at the merit of external succession; thus, one cannot transform that merit into the station of the king.
This is precisely what is called the "royal lineage" or the "prince," which the Nine Peaks [Master] refers to as the "external succession of the royal clan.

This differs from Dongshan’s "correctness within partiality," which is internal succession but has not yet attained the station. This is because "correctness within partiality" is internal succession while still remaining unestablished in the position.
This man is one who has inherited the legacy from without yet does not occupy a formal position;

in his arduous studies and sincere character, none in the world can rival him. Having emerged into the world, he excels in all affairs beyond his peers. When his five-character verse is complete, it is like the snow of three winters;

when his brush falls, even a hair’s breadth becomes clouds across the four seas. Through the accumulated merit of ten thousand scrolls, he brings glory to the sagely age, and with a single mind of loyalty and filial piety, he assists the state.
"An enlightened ruler: salt and plum are not obtained through innate knowledge. Why labor over the golden scroll to manifest supreme merit?
The first line speaks of the diligence with which he applied his efforts. The second line states that because of this diligent effort, every undertaking upon its inception transcends the ordinary;
this is the manifestation of his achievement. These two lines of the poem precisely illustrate this transcendence.
Regarding the affairs of governance: the two lines concerning "accumulating merit through ten thousand scrolls" serve as a metaphor for borrowing external achievements to assist one's sovereign.

"Salt and vinegar" (the seasoning of salt and the sourness of vinegar) precisely metaphorize the duties of a minister. This indicates that it is not innate knowledge; rather, it speaks of reaching such a state through study.

The final line serves as a metaphor for how, although great merit may be manifest—like one’s name being inscribed upon the golden list—it ultimately remains within the domain of a subject’s office and does not ascend to the rank of a king.
What need is there for such labor?
As for the "last-born, last-born," this refers to those who achieve perfection only after a long period of diligent effort. This child has distantly transcended all such things.
Devoting oneself solely to internal succession, one attains entry into "one color. Compared to this, birth has both sudden and gradual aspects;
yet, as for the destination reached, they are one and the same. This is also different from "coming from the very center.
This refers to one who enters the correct position only after long application of effort, whereas "coming from the very center" refers to one who enters the correct position and then turns the body.

Long dwelling in mountain caves, he applied himself with diligent effort; upon a grass mat and a wooden door, he maintained his solitary resolve. For ten years, he surrendered his mind to what he saw and heard;

throughout winter and summer, his single body possessed not even a piece of silk for clothing. With a serene and composed smile, he harbored thoughts for three autumns; through pure austerity, he attained a lofty reputation, a plan of the highest sages.
His studies perfected, he achieved the highest honors to fulfill his ultimate ambition; yet recently, the ministers and officials have not held the path of power.
The first two lines mean: not coveting the distinction between crimson and purple (the noble and the lowly), but focusing solely on the person who is one's original nature.
The line "ten years" means that one does not place weight on what is seen or heard. The line "one body" means that one does not cling to worldly conditions.

The two lines beginning with "clear and concentrated" mean that one delights the spirit in the realm of purity, emptiness, tranquility, and detachment; these all express the intent of internal succession. The two lines beginning with "vocation accomplished" express the internal...
When his merit was accomplished, he ascended to his position through the transformation of kalpas; he did not establish himself in the rank of a minister.

As for those who are "transformed by birth," it means they are collateral branches of the Emperor’s transformation, being the sons who have shifted their positions to achieve merit. The ancients called them—
The talent of the General Who Goes on Missions is that of Dongshan; he is one who reaches the center through the intermediate.

Branching out from the imperial mandate to uphold the Dharma, his administrative prestige is spread across ten thousand li of mountains and rivers. The crimson reflection of the sun’s orb gathers beneath the realm;

the green oil-silk banner is cooled by the wind during the heat of summer. How could the distinctions of high and low ever neglect the service of honor and humility? His five-garment robe brings relief to distant lands.
"Recently attained knowledge. Holding the seal of wondrous mastery, he uses smoke to block stillness; facing the sun, how could he be willing to reveal even a trace of his subtle mechanism?
The first phrase: occupying the position to manifest merit, carrying out the imperial transformation. The "ten-thousand-li" phrase:
the diamond sword, brandished horizontally across the world. The "red shadow" phrase: wisdom-illumination is impartial, shattering all deep obscurity. The "azure oil" phrase.
The workings of the divine are unfathomable; it purifies all afflictions and torments. "Azure Oil" is the name of a ceremonial banner.

During the Han dynasty, the Prefect erected an azure-oil banner at his gate to signify the majesty of the orthodox transformation. The two lines concerning "high and low" collectively describe the vast and far-reaching operation of divine transformation.
High and low alike receive [this teaching]; far and near all know it. "The Five Pants": when Han Lian Shudu was serving as Governor, the people sang a song:

"Lian Shudu, why did you come so late? Formerly there were no travel permits; now there are five pairs of pants for each. "Su-t'u" (Soothing the Roads) refers to soothing the people who were suffering like charcoal in fire.
"The Sentence of the Wondrous Seal" means that if one alone maintains the Mind-Seal, the ten directions are cut off at once. Heaven... [text ends].

This refers to the "Tàipíng" (Great Peace) watchtowers. Regarding "smoke barriers": smoke mounds were established at the foot of the barriers; when bandits approached, they would raise a signal fire to transmit the report.
Hence, they are called "smoke barriers. The final phrase states that although its wondrous function is manifest in action, its mechanism is so secret that it cannot be fathomed.
Regarding "born within, born within": this refers to one who has long resided within the inner palace. This is the ultimate state of perfection.
Being of no different body from the Father means that principle and wisdom are of one suchness; it signifies a profound union without division. Yet, it is still said that there is a Father.
In this regard, the son still guards the precious treasure, while the father has no house to sit in and no lineage to be established.

Furthermore, the father is entirely devoted to non-action (*wuwei*), so profound that he cannot be fathomed. Within this state, one who hangs up the tattered robe and responds to the call to act on behalf of the father is also a son;
this is precisely the same as Dongshan’s "Arriving Amidst the Synthesis" (*jiānzhōngdào*).
How can the profound secrecy of the nine-layered palace be proclaimed? The hanging of tattered rags has long served as a manifest and wondrous transmission.

Solely serving the One Person is the honor of Heaven and Earth; all other paths follow their own allotted authority. When the purple silk curtains close, ruler and subject are separated; when the yellow gate’s drapes hang down, the prohibitions are complete.
Because you, officials and subordinates of the various regions, harbor lingering attachments, I have thus used "yellow leaves" as money to stop children's crying.
The first phrase states that he is of one essence with the Father, silent and without speech. The second phrase states that at times he emerges again to manifest his wondrousness.
The "Reverently Serves" phrase states that true wisdom realizes the principle.

The "From Another" phrase states that while the six sense organs each perform their respective functions, the sovereign source remains unmoving. The two phrases concerning the purple silk state that since he is of one essence with the Father...
When the essence is unified, the ministers and officials are set apart, for its essence is fundamentally non-action (*wuwei*).

The two phrases "for you" and so forth mean that although it is indeed non-action, there are times when it responds to the capacities of sentient beings and teaches the Dharma through skillful means; this is expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).
The eulogy for the noble scion’s birth:
the wheel-tracks of his destiny fill the void. With tinkling jade pendants, he dwells in the Eastern Palace; when the moon hall shines forth, he attends to his sovereign and father.
He directly knocks upon the steps of Yao, yet borrows this merit from his birth.

His learning in the Odes and Documents and his virtuous conduct were complete; he presented his strategy at the Golden Gate and entered the ranks of the Purple Microcosm. Yet like a guest star, he could not remain apart from his reed-clothed fishing;
how could he have failed to attend morning and evening at the Sacred Countenance? (Born at Court)
Poverty has reached its ultimate clarity and emptiness today; I rejoice that all is still and void, without a single thing.
I wish at once to ascend as a nine-tufted phoenix, dwelling alone upon a moonlit nest amidst the misty clouds and trees. (End) — Composed by Mosheng.

The Emperor commanded that it be brought down from the Nine Heavens; within and without the Forbidden City, its transformation was proclaimed far and wide. Upon his return journey, he again held the wondrous golden seal;
of the true mandate, not a single character has been transmitted (through birth).
A great man, soaring like a phoenix and galloping like a dragon, is naturally noble and distinguished from the six palaces. Moss seals the ancient halls where no one enters;
how could ordinary folk ever recognize him in their haste? (Born within).
The Prince answered the monk’s question.
When asked by Shishuang, "What is the Prince at Birth? he said: "A noble lineage of extraordinary seed; born of Heaven, his station is most supreme.
When asked, "What is the Prince Born at Court? he said: "In white robes, he serves as the highest counselor; he points directly to the inner palace."
[In the] Middle [Section]. Question: What is the "Prince Born at the End"? Answer: Following the path, one only then realizes his nobility; advancing gradually, he does not know his own majesty.
Question: What is the "Prince of Transformational Birth"? Answer: His sovereign authority is beyond compare; his divine function has no equal. Question.
"What is the Prince Born Within? He replied: "In the layered curtains, victory and defeat cease; upon the golden hall, one lies in the pure breeze.
Regarding the essential instructions on Cao Shan’s Five Ranks of Sovereign and Subject, Cao Shan said:
"The Correct Position is the realm of emptiness; fundamentally there is no thing. The Partial Position is the realm of form; there are the myriad phenomena."
"Form. "The center within the partial" refers to turning one's back on principle to follow phenomena. "The partial within the center" refers to relinquishing phenomena to enter principle.
"The simultaneous inclusion" refers to responding to all conditions in profound stillness, without falling into any state of existence; it is neither defiled nor pure, neither central nor partial.

Therefore, it is called the Great Way of Empty Space, the True Teaching of Non-attachment. The former masters of antiquity have maintained that this single stage is the most profound and the most wondrous; one must truly realize this.

Examine and discern this in detail: the ruler represents the position of correctness, while the minister represents the position of partiality. When the minister faces the ruler, it is "partiality within correctness";
when the ruler looks upon the minister, it is "correctness within partiality. When the way of ruler and minister is harmonized, it is the time of "comprehensive integration.

A monk stepped forward and asked, "What is the Ruler? He replied, "Sublime Virtue honors the universe; lofty brilliance illuminates the great void. The monk asked, "What is the Minister? He replied, "Spiritual..."
The pivot expands the holy Way; true wisdom benefits all living beings. What is "the subject facing the sovereign"? It is said: "Not falling into any of the various realms of existence.
What is "the sovereign looking upon the subject"? It is said: "Though the wondrous countenance does not move, its light illuminates all without partiality.
What is "the way of sovereign and subject in harmony"? It is said: "Blending seamlessly without interior or exterior, harmoniously fused above and below."

"Even," he said, "those who speak in terms of ruler and minister, or partiality and correctness, do so because they do not wish to offend the central [principle]. Thus, when a minister refers to his ruler, he does not dare to name him directly;
this is correct. This is the essential method of our school. He then composed a verse, saying: "A student must first recognize their own school."

Do not conflate the true limit with insentient emptiness; the wondrously luminous essence fully knows how to avoid injury and offense. Its power lies in encountering conditions without depending on the "middle.
When speaking, ensure that even fire cannot burn it; its hidden practice must accord with the ancients. To have affairs while lacking a body transcends all divergent paths;
to lack both affairs and body falls back into the cycle of beginning and end.
The Great Sun’s Mysterious Eulogy:
Without establishing merit or achievement, he sits upon the hall of the ancestral temple. How could the ministers dare hope for his pure radiance?
Deep and profound is the palace of the inner court, most majestic and solemn; it is silent and empty, yet the night is not yet ended (O Sovereign).

With the Classics as warp and the Military Arts as woof, he settled the Middle Kingdom; establishing every stage of advancement, he served the state. His meritorious achievements having reached their zenith, he was granted the nine emoluments;
yet his divine spirit remains but slightly separated from yours, O Minister.
Though his rank was as honored as the "Nine-Five," he never dwelt therein; he always shared the same path with his ministers. He did not conceal his later offices, and the world was well-governed;
thus he spared the barbarians from looking toward him for salvation (as the ruler regards his subjects).

In every thought and every moment, they offer loyalty, not daring to deceive; head bowed and heart humble, these sons of true men pay their respects. Behold the long road to Chang’an for a thousand li:
those with jade-bridled steeds all hasten toward the palace gates to return to their sovereign. (The subject bows toward his ruler.)
Minister and Sovereign forget each other as the ancient halls grow cold; The ten-thousand-year-old locust trees are shrouded in vast snow. A thousand gates remain closed, silent as still water;
Only the weeping willows dance in the emerald mist. (The Way of Ruler and Minister is in perfect harmony.)
There is no middle path leading to Chang’an; who would dare to grasp the numinous branch beyond the kalpas?
Moss grows upon the precious palace—the honored and the weighty—while at the third watch, the red sun is shrouded in vast darkness. (Total)
Caoshan’s Four Prohibitions:
Do not travel the path of the mind.
Wherever the mind finds delight, it is a state of partiality and obscuration; even if it be most profound and subtle, it must not be pursued.
One must have a mind that is nowhere to be found; only then is this the conduct of a patch-robed monk.

To be "unattached to the original garment"—that is, having recognized the *dharmakāya*—yet not forgetting the attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) such that one's own views still persist, is to fall into [delusion].
Regarding the section on the Dharma-body: one must overturn the habitual mold before the wondrous function can be fully manifested.
Why need it be "just so"? The Way has no fixed direction; to conceptualize it is to lose it. To say "it is just so" is already not "just so. Therefore, it cannot be [grasped].
Draft: One must strictly avoid [fixating on] the time before birth.
The Way penetrates past and present; how could it be restricted to the time before birth? If you merely recognize that single segment prior to the birth of your parents...
To take the realm of emptiness and stillness as one's own self—do you not see what Tong’an Cha said? "The distant void of kalpas cannot contain it.
Those who hold such a view fall into the stream of those who lapse into emptiness and stray outside [the Way]; therefore, one must strictly avoid this.

Regarding "The Three Falls" of Caoshan, Caoshan said: "Ordinary sentiment and the vision of sainthood constitute the mysterious path of the golden lock; one must necessarily employ indirectness and mutual interrelation.
Now, one who takes the food of right livelihood must possess three kinds of 'falls': first, wearing fur and bearing horns; second, not severing sound and form; third..."
[The Master] would not accept food. Choubunna asked, "What kind of fallacy is it to have fur and horns? The Master said, "It is the fallacy of being of that class.
He asked, "What kind of fallacy is it to not cut off sound and form? The Master said, "It is the fallacy of following along.

He asked, "What kind of fallacy is it to not accept food? The Master said, "It is the fallacy of nobility. He then said, "To eat is simply one's own fundamental matter; it is to know that there is [this]."

One does not grasp at them; therefore, it is called "the fall of the noble. If one clings to the initial mind, perceiving the existence of a self and the stages of sainthood, it is called "the fall of the similar.

If, at the initial moment of knowing one's own affairs, one casts aside form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and phenomena upon turning the light back within, and attains tranquility, this constitutes achievement.
However, if one subsequently fails to remain unattached to the six sense objects and so forth, one will gradually become obscured.
If you let it take its own course, it will become an obstruction. This is why the six heretical teachers were your teachers;

where those teachers fell, you too would have fallen—only then could you have taken this food. "Food" here refers to the sustenance of right livelihood. It also concerns the gates of the six sense organs: seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
It simply means not being defiled by them, which they mistakenly regard as falling. Furthermore, it is not the same as heading toward [the same destination].

The preceding was already equalized; even the fundamental matter itself is not grasped, so how much less so other matters? Whenever the Master speaks of "falling," he means that things cannot be mixed and their categories cannot be made uniform.
Whenever he speaks of a "beginner," he means that those who have attained awakening are the same as those who have not yet awakened.

Regarding "right livelihood as food": within the teachings, there are four types of livelihood—wrong livelihood, right livelihood, *ūrdhvamukha* (upward-facing) livelihood, *adhomukha* (downward-facing) livelihood, *tiryagmukha* (horizontal-facing) livelihood, and *vidig-mukha* (intermediate-facing) livelihood. These are what they are.

As for "right livelihood as food," it refers solely to sustaining oneself through the pure practice of begging for alms. Now, when Caoshan establishes "right livelihood as food," his intention is as follows:
To accept all dharmas is called wrong livelihood; to accept none at all is right livelihood. Regarding the "three falls":
although a great practitioner of the Way fundamentally has no place of abiding, they may temporarily find a point of reliance, remaining sovereign wherever they are.

It is like a wild goose passing through the vast sky; its shadow sinks into the cold water—how could there be any obstruction? Therefore, this word "falling" (duo) is used figuratively; it is not its literal meaning.
In the *Wudeng Huiyuan*, following the section on "Falling from the Noble and Precious," there is another passage beginning with "Furthermore, there was one who said, 'The eater...
The text and meaning of this are erroneous, and I have long harbored doubts about it. Upon seeing that later masters generally state—
The term "falling" (*duò*) appears in the character "master" (*shī*). One can only then know that these are the words of later commentators. I shall not discuss them exhaustively here;
let me cite one or two instances to verify this. For example, it says: "Because one knows the fundamental matter exists yet does not grasp it, it is called 'falling into the noble'.
Here, the character "falling" is used in a metaphorical sense. Furthermore, the subsequent text states: "One clings to the initial knowledge that [it] exists..."

To claim that "oneself" and the "sages" constitute the "falling into categories" (lei-duo) is already a mistake; to further treat this as a "falling into reality" (shi-duo) is an even greater error. Furthermore, Cao Shan said:
"Having fur and wearing horns is 'falling into categories'; this is acting within the heterodox classes, which is a path for those at later stages."
Now it is said: "The initial mind knows that there is a self, as well as the state of sainthood. How could this be Cao Shan’s intention?

Furthermore, this passage is also included in the *Sengbao zhuan*, though it has been extensively revised and altered. Of the fourteen phrases, their meaning remains distorted; for instance, the first phrase is changed to:
"Mysteriously harmonizing with the initial mind, one knows that there is [a self]. This kind of fallacy—how could the initial...?
The mind knows that they exist, yet this is not the meaning of "shaggy-haired and horned" (referring to animals).

Furthermore, in the *Zhizhengzhuan*, it is stated that the names of the three types of "falling" (san-duo) all originate from the sacred scriptures; however, the term "falling into categories" (lei-duo) was changed to "falling into never severing sounds and colors" (bu-duan-sheng-se-duo).
This has caused great error among later students. I shall now correct this here as well.
Ming’an once explained these three "falling into" (san-duo) as follows: "These three phrases must clarify the turning of the station before they can be understood.
'Becoming a water buffalo' is the falling into a category. The Master said: 'This is the speech of a śramaṇa’s transformation of his body; it is a matter within the realm of different categories.

If one does not understand this meaning, there will be an obstruction. It simply requires that one’s single thought be free of self-interest; then, one immediately possesses the means to emerge from the body."
1. The Path. 2. Not accepting food is the "Fall from Nobility. The Master said: "You must first realize the state beyond before you can practice within this state.
If you do not leave this position empty, you will remain seated in nobility. 3. Not severing sound and form is the "Conformist Fall."
The Master said: "Because they do not understand sound and form, they fall into them at every turn. One must find a way to emerge from within sound and form.
What is the single phrase beyond sound and form? He then said: "Sound is not sound by itself; form is not form by itself."
Therefore it is said: "It is not cut off. "Pointing at the palm"—at which palm does one point?
According to Caoshan, one must possess the three kinds of falling away (*di*). Only by being free from even a single thought of self-interest can one fall away into the category [of the ordinary].
Only by not clinging to what is noble can one fall away into nobility. Only by penetrating through sound and form can one...
"Being able to follow along with falling" is merely the name for "falling," established as a provisional designation. Now, Dayang asserts that these three types must clarify the turning of positions;
there is actually something to fall into, and therefore it is necessary to turn. This greatly diverges from the intent of Caoshan.
However, upon examining the *Ming'an bie lu* (Separate Record of Ming’an), I find that it contains the "Five Ranks Verses" and the commentary on Dongshan’s "Five Ranks Verses.
Furthermore, it correlates the four guest-host relationships with the four "selections" (*liao jian*) and includes the theory of these three "falls" (*tui*).

These various points are erroneous and contradictory; I suspect they were fabricated by impostors after Dayang had passed away and there was no one left to inherit his Dharma, who then falsely claimed his name.
He did so, yet Juéfàn failed to notice this and consequently included it within his *Sengbao zhuan* (Biographies of the Jewel of the Sangha), thereby misleading later students.
Let those who examine this matter investigate it in detail.
— Bai Zhang’s Verse by Duan.
I put on a tattered robe with split lapels and cast off my mother-born trousers. I walk with confidence into the wild weeds, forgetting the road to Chang’an.
I sing of the moonlit nights at the Qin towers and am intoxicated by the spring breeze at the Wei palace gates. After the ruin of my home and nation, news from my hometown has been lost.

(Suì). Sitting alone on the peak of a solitary mountain, wheels and hooves have ceased their coming and going. How pitiable are these two feet; they have never once trod upon the human world. (Zūnɡuì)
Clouds do not cling to the green mountains; a mirror does not enclose beauty or ugliness. Failing to pass through the Ghost Gate Barrier, one falls into a habitual trap at every turn.
(Total) Furthermore, there is a verse:
Clad in fur and wearing horns, he moves freely among his kind;
his head and horns mingle with the mud and dust, clearly manifesting this very body. By the green willows and fragrant grasses on the bank, where is there that does not honor him?
Seeing forms and hearing sounds, one is at ease wherever one is:
the monkey cries out under the frosty night moon; the flowers laugh amidst the spring of Qinyuan. Amidst the vast expanse of red dust, every single thing is an old friend.
His ritual standing transcends all officials;
noble and sovereign, his painted hall has no locks or keys. Who would dare to cross its threshold? Do not wonder at the absence of guests; from time immemorial, he has never seen another person.
General Verse:
Last night I stayed in a desolate village; this morning I roam the Imperial Garden. Originally there is no fixed position; where can one seek its traces?
—Tongan’s Examination of the Ten Mysterious Discourses.

The *Ten Mysterious Discourses* (*Shixuantan*) extensively propagates the principle of the "wondrous embrace within the correct center. The first five verses demonstrate the essential points of the great purport;
the final five verses are intended to lead one toward actual practice.
Regarding the Heart-Seal, I ask you: what is the appearance of the Heart-Seal? Who dares to bestow and transmit it? Through kalpas it remains serene, never changing its color;
to call it the "Heart-Seal" is already a hollow word. You must know that it is inherently the nature of numinous emptiness; it is likened to the fire in a red furnace.
Li Lian: Do not say that a mindless state is itself the Way; even a mindless state still stands at one more barrier.

The meaning of the Patriarchs, the meaning of the Patriarchs, is like space, yet it is not empty. How could the mysterious pivot fall into the realm of existence or non-existence? Even the Three Sages have not yet clarified this.

The Essential Meaning: How could the Ten Sages reach this school? A golden fish that has passed through the net still lingers in the water; a stone horse returning from its path emerges from the silken cage.
I earnestly declare the meaning of the Westward Transmission: do not ask about the West or the East.

The profound mechanism is so remote that even the void kalpa cannot contain it; how could it be bound and detained by the mechanisms of mundane dust? The wondrous essence is fundamentally without location;
throughout the entire body, what further traces could there be? A single phrase, spirit-like, transcends all phenomena; it stands far beyond the Three Vehicles.
A provisional cultivation: casting off the hand beyond that realm, one stands outside the thousand sages; returning the journey, one is fit to be a bull in the fire.
The turbid is turbid by itself, and the clear is clear by itself. Bodhi and afflictions are equal as empty space. Who says there is no one for the Bian jade?
Jian: "In my Way, the dragon pearl shines wherever it goes; when the myriad dharmas are extinguished, the whole body is revealed. Where the Three Vehicles are divided, names are falsely established.
A man of true stature possesses a will that soars to the heavens; do not walk where the Tathāgata has walked."

The Buddha sequentially expounded the golden words of the Three Vehicles; these were likewise proclaimed by the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time. At first, when he spoke of emptiness and existence, all people clung to them as real;

later, when he negated both emptiness and existence, the multitude took them as their object of reliance. The medical treatises and their meanings filled the treasuries of the Dragon Palace; at the final discourse beneath the Śāla trees, he exhausted the ultimate principles.
Not yet profound. Within the realm of true purity, it takes but a single thought; yet on Jambudvīpa, eight thousand years have already passed.
Do not seek the King of Emptiness halfway home; you must take up your staff and return to your original hometown. When clouds and waters part, do not [despair].

Abiding in the depths of the Snowy Mountains, I have not forgotten you. Reflecting on the day I departed, your countenance was like jade; sighing over the time of your arrival, your hair is like hoarfrost.
Casting off my hands, I reached home, yet no one recognized me; I have nothing left to play with in the honored hall.

To break through and return to one’s hometown—to revert to the root and source—is already a deviation. Originally there is no abiding place, which is not called a "home. The path of the ten-thousand-year pine is buried deep in snow;
a range of peaks is further shrouded by clouds. When host and guest are in harmony, it is all mere delusion; when lord and subject are united, it is precisely [the state of reality].
Possessed by an evil spirit. How should one sing the melodies of the local tunes upon returning to one's hometown? "The withered tree blossoms before the Hall of the Bright Moon.
Turning the position, even within the City of Nirvana there is still peril. Meeting on a crossroads, there is no fixed time [for parting]. Temporarily hanging up the soiled robe, it is said to be...
The Buddha has returned his precious regalia; who else could it be? A wooden man puts on boots at midnight; a stone woman returns home wearing a cap at dawn.
The moon in the empty sky over the ten-thousand-year-old azure pool—only after repeated scooping and searching will you finally know it.
Turning the mechanism of the mind, they don the fur and horns and enter the dark abyss; the *utpala* flower blooms amidst the flames. Amidst the sea of afflictions, they act as rain and dew;
upon the mountain of ignorance, they become clouds and thunder. They blow out the fires of the boiling cauldrons and the glowing coals; at the sword-trees and knife-mountains, they simply shout.
The messenger is crushed; the golden lock at the mysterious pass cannot detain him. Wandering among the heterodox classes, he revolves in saṃsāra.
Before the state of correctness (also called "after the single color"), there are many divergent paths before the withered tree at the cliffside.
When practitioners reach this point, they all falter and waste their efforts. The egret standing in the snow is not the same [as the snow].
Form: the bright moon and reeds amidst the flowers are not like others. When there is total clarity, there is nothing to clarify; even where the profound is most profound, it must be rebuked.
With earnest diligence, I sing this song of the midst of the profound: can one grasp the light of the toad in the void?
Daiyō’s Three Phrases.

One day Daiyō addressed the assembly, saying: "All you practitioners of Zen, you must clarify the phrase of ordinary non-arising, the phrase of wondrous profundity and lack of partiality, and the phrase of essential clarity and inexhaustibility. The first phrase opens a single path; the second phrase has neither guest nor host."
The three phrases are interconnected: the first phrase expresses the lion’s growl; the second phrase expresses the lion’s leap; the third phrase expresses the lion’s crouch.
Question: What is the phrase of ordinary non-arising? Answer: White clouds cover the green mountains;
the peaks of the green mountains are not revealed. Question: What is the phrase of wondrous mystery and impartiality? Answer: A jewel... [text ends]
In the palace, there is no one who does not stand in attendance. By not planting the *wutong* tree, one avoids the arrival of the phoenix.
Question: What is the phrase of infinite clarity of essence? Answer: When the finger points to space, heaven and earth turn; on the path of return, the stone horse emerges from the gauze cage.
Question: What is the lion’s roar? Answer: It has no intention of looking back; how could it deign to fall into the ordinary? Question: What is...?
The Lion’s Backward Leap: It is said that every movement and return is entirely returned to the Father; though manifold activities and great functions arise, their essence remains undiminished.
Question: What is the lion crouching on the ground? Answer: Utterly transcending the mechanism of coming and going, it has remained unchanged through all time.
Jue of Langya, while responding to a monk’s request for instruction, said: "I, this mountain monk, also have three phrases to answer Dayang.
The monk asked: "What is the phrase of ordinary non-arising? He replied: "Before words, there is no definitive meaning; beneath the phrase, all seeking ceases. The monk asked:
"What is the phrase of wondrous mystery and impartiality? He replied: "The golden phoenix does not perch on a shadowless tree; the jade hare..."
"How have they ever descended from the azure heavens? He asked: "What is the phrase of the body’s inexhaustible clarity? He replied: "In the three months of winter, withered trees flourish;
in the nine months of summer, snowflakes fly."
The phrase "ordinarily non-arising" refers to the initial realization of existence. The phrase "the wondrous mystery is without partiality" refers to entering the noble station.
The phrase "the essence is luminous and inexhaustible" refers to the subsequent stage of transforming one's position into merit. [This is from] the *Xuánjiàn*.
Furthermore, there are diagrams of three phrases that are entirely devoid of meaning; they were merely fabricated by later generations.
The "three kinds of lions" represent advancing one step further within each of the aforementioned three phrases; they are the shifting positions within those three phrases.
The teaching style of Master Fuyong Kai is a wondrous song that is not confined to a thousand tongues;

it is discoursed upon in every land, within every atom, and in every place. Without even the need to snap one's fingers, Sudhana has attained realization. Even Śāriputra understands how to fully assimilate this.
Breath ceases; before the Flower-Rain Rock, birds do not carry it away (Furong Kai).
Suchness is tranquil and still, as if without sentiment; this single phrase has been fundamentally perfected from the start.
The broad and long tongue functions without interruption; Xuefeng met him at Wangzhou Pavilion (Zide Hui).

The ancient Buddhas stand majestic, their bodies vast and long; Interlacing light and jeweled nets manifest throughout the dust motes of the lands. One knows they do not require the tongue born of a mother;
The rock-olibanum and courtyard flowers skillfully proclaim them. (The Ancient Sage)
A dead snake leaps startled from the grass, scorched by the sun and blown by the wind as it lies buried therein. Its poisonous breath still strikes out erratically;
in the darkness, its dead mouth suddenly opens, yet Chang’an remains as ever, with no one coming. (Furong Kai)
The golden whip points afar as the Jade Hall grows cold; it startles the General to emerge from the pass by night. With his three-foot Mohe sword, he clears the four seas;
with one sweep of his banner, he eradicates all folly and stubbornness. (Zidehui)
A dead snake beaten to death reveals its frost-white fangs; an unfathomable basket filled with stench beyond measure. Since it is well-summoned, it must be well-dispatched;
otherwise, its poisonous breath will strike down the entire family (as the Ancient Worthies said).
Chanting over a Needle and a Withered Bone:
To find life within death is truly extraordinary; its secret application possesses a further depth. At midnight, a skull chants a single song;
though a fiery flame erupts from an icy river, it is yet cool and refreshing. (Furong Kai)
The palace leaks deep as the night grows dark; lamps wane and fires die out, leaving no one to understand. The wooden man turns his station as the jade cords of heaven dawn;
the stone woman awakens from her dream, frost filling her breast (Self-Attained Radiance).

His merit equals that of the divine; how profound is his intent! How could he allow those with incurable ailments to sink into oblivion? The true secret instructions were not transmitted from father to son;
yet he could resolve the needle in a withered bone so that it sang like a dragon (the Ancient Sage).

The dance of the iron saw performs upon three stages without missing a note of the *gong* or *shang* scales. Who can join in for a single performance? What could Boya have done about it? This melody has long been known as "The Everlasting" (by Fuyong Kai).
An iron ox without horns lies on the hillside; when whipped, it flies—do you see it? Riding across the bustling market, no one recognizes him;
lifting his head, the hawk soars to Silla. (Zide Hui)
The Gandharva King’s drum resounds like thunder; the music offered at Vulture Peak never ceases.
The ocean waves surge and Mount Sumeru quakes—what prevents the iron saw from dancing upon the three terraces? (An ancient worthy).
There is no interval between past and present. (This title is not found among the recorded sayings of other masters; it appears only in that of Fuyong.
The One Dharma is fundamentally non-existent, and the ten thousand dharmas are empty. Within this, how could there be any realization of perfect penetration?
I thought the news from Shaolin had been cut off, but the peach blossoms still smile at the spring breeze.
The ancient masters established five minor stages;
as soon as great function is activated, one borrows these stages for birth, and the burden is suddenly forgotten.
Upon first arriving at the single color, one attains the noble portion of the lineage; therefore, it is called "Birth" (Tan).
When a prince is born, it is only when his singular color fades that he is called noble;
when his singular color fades, he attains the very position of nobility. Yet, as long as he merely maintains that nobility, he remains but a child.
Regarding the matter of the grandson’s side: thus did the ancient masters say, "One must know that those of noble status do not abide in their noble positions;
they shift their feet in secret, like a crane emerging from its silver cage."
This is not maintaining one's noble status. It is precisely at the moment of transitioning positions that Tong An said, "Even within the city of Nirvana there is still danger;
therefore, one must transition."

Returning the mechanism to enter the secular world, the moon spreads across the golden ground—this is precisely the matter of extending the hand to receive others. Tong’an Cha said: "Clad in fur and wearing horns, he enters the monastery."
"The *utpala* flower blooms within the fire"—this is it.
Tiantong Jue’s four turns of the spiritual mechanism have not yet turned the spiritual mechanism; he has completely forgotten the burden he carries.
This is the correct turning of the great function until one reaches the single color; it is simply sitting within that single color. As the saying goes:
"The crane in its moon-nest dreams for a thousand years"—this is the function of being deluded by the single color within a snow-covered house.
Although the mechanism has turned its pivot, the seal has not yet formed its pattern.

Once the single color has vanished, it is like the turning of a mechanism’s pivot; yet because one still clings to nobility, the functional application of the mechanism has not yet been fully revealed.
The spiritual mechanism operates in secret; the seal has already formed its text.
Turning within the position, one proceeds from the orthodox to the deviant; the patterns and colors are fully manifest, such that application is without deficiency.
The Precious Seal is suspended in the void, utterly transcending all literary expression and color.
This is the state where the entire body leaves no shadow and its application leaves no trace; it is beyond the reach of thought or deliberation.
Regarding "One Color" in the *Tiantong Jue San*:

"One Color" refers to the initial establishment of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), which occurs when one turns back from effort to abide in the position [of realization], thereby realizing a state of singular, pure vacuity.
This section is divided into three parts. "One Color of Great Effort" refers to that which still retains the traces of effort, as it is achieved through the power of cultivation.

"The single color of the true position" refers to the emptiness and stillness of the realm of principle. "The single color of the present time" refers to the purity and brightness of the realm of phenomena.
*Verse on the Single Color of Great Accomplishment:*
The white ox leaves no trace sought amidst the snow; when effort is exhausted, the body is transcendent and vasty harmonious.
Moonlight on the reeds and flowers, though the sky is not yet dawn—the numinous sprout moves spontaneously, shearing through the spring breeze.
In the verse on the single color of the true position:
"In the shadowless forest, birds do not perch; in the empty steps, they cry out densely toward the edges. How could the fragrant grasses on the cold crags ever turn green?
Sitting upright and majestic, one loses the way and becomes lost."

At this moment, within the single color of the skull-verse, let consciousness be exhausted; do not make too many distinctions. As soon as the dog’s mouth opens, two or three fall out. One must urgently realize it within the light of daily life:
the green mountains are simply amidst the white clouds.
Tiantong Jue’s “Four Borrowings”:
Borrowing Function to Clarify Status.
The wind has ceased at the surface of the water; the night is not yet over. Heaven and water are empty and azure, sharing the autumnal light. The moon-boat does not infringe upon east or west.
The bank. One must trust that the boatman’s intent is skillful. Borrowing a position to clarify merit, the six gates are empty;
the path is open and not lost. Within the shadow of the great sun, one does not rely on the immediate trigger. Transversely and vertically, the wondrous is displayed without partiality.
Transformation. Just as one travels by the path of birds to return, one does not rely on anything (this refers to both the stages of attainment and the ultimate state).

Having fully experienced the bitter and the sweet at the tip of every blade of grass, the nose is free from the tethering rope and attains leisurely ease. Not knowing that there is "going," one achieves true knowing.
There is. Only now do I truly believe Nanquan called it "the ox.
Completely transcending all dependence (speaking from the standpoint of simultaneous attainment), the frost is heavy, the wind is severe, and the scene is desolate.
The jade pass and golden lock—my hands are too weary to strike them. Through the long night, the cold pines remain without a single false note.
The reed flute: the old crane shifts its perch to the empty moon-nest;
naturally attaining radiance, it transforms through five stages as the green serpent roars within its case.
The precious sword lies askew as the sky has not yet dawned; its cleansing of demons and Buddhas strikes one with chilling cold. From within the scabbard, a faint radiance emerges;
disciples in patched robes should simply regard it with the correct eye.
The golden needle departs and returns;
the Great Way of pure emptiness is the road to Chang’an. In its coming and going, how could there ever be any interval? It departs in darkness and arrives in light, yet its edge remains unexposed.
From the very beginning, it has never fallen into the extremes of center or periphery.
The Qin palace makes one’s gallbladder shiver with cold;
the mountain hermitage is silent and still as ice. Wondrously attaining the hidden tally, he is efficacious everywhere. Turning over, there is no dependence as merit takes its place;
looking back, he has lost the city of King Chu.
At noon, the silver candle of heaven shines;
at noon, the jade wheel of the sky is solitary and bright. A single point of radiance divides the Mirror Lake. Strolling idly, I come once more to wander through the illusory sea;
throughout the ten directions and all dust-mote worlds is the Great Vairocana.
The white-browed tiger hides deep within the crags;

the white-browed one is hidden deep, shrouded in mist and smoke. Coming from amidst the strange, he naturally startles the herd. The grass is so deep that he goes straight down, leaving no trace to find him.
A light touch, and disaster reaches the door.

The ancient tracks of the caves and the subtle words of the former masters—the functional application of the teachers—originally have no fixed rules. Yet, why did the ancients necessarily establish their fundamental principles? Precisely...
It is like a pearl rolling upon a tray; though it may twist, turn, and slide in every direction beyond comparison, it can never leave the tray.
Now, from Youshan downward, all those who have clarified the fundamental principles of the school have been recorded here to serve as a model for future students.
Chan Master Yaoshan Weiyan was asked by a monk, "What should I do when I intend to return to my hometown?
The Master said, "Your parents' entire bodies are covered in festering sores as they lie amidst a thicket of thorns; where would you go upon returning?
The monk said, "If that is the case, then I shall not return. The Master said, "You must return. If you do return, I will give you a prescription for ceasing the intake of grain."
The Master said, “I request you to do so. The Master continued, “When ascending the hall for the two periods of formal teaching, you must not chew even a single grain of rice.

[The Master] asked Yunyan, “What are you doing? Yunyan replied, “Carrying manure. The Master said, “And who is that? [Yunyan] said, “He is here. The Master said, “For whose sake are you coming and going?
[Yunyan] said, “To carry his belongings for him. The Master said, “Why not have them walk side by side? [Yunyan] said, “Do not slander him, Master. The Master [laughed].
[The Master] said, "It is not appropriate to speak in such a manner. [Zun] asked, "How then should one speak? The Master said, "Have you ever carried it?
When Zun Puna was bathing the Buddha, the Master said, "This one you are bathing from—can you also bathe that one? Zun said, "..."
"Bring that one here. The Master then ceased speaking.
Among the assembly, this was called "a statement of simultaneous inclusion.
Governor Li Ao asked, "What are precept, concentration, and wisdom? The Master replied, "In my humble abode, there are no such things as 'other households' (extraneous matters)."

[The Governor] was equipped [with robes]. Unable to fathom the profound purport, the Master said: "If you, Prefectural Governor, wish to take full responsibility for this matter, you must stand atop the highest mountain peak and walk upon the deepest ocean floor.
If you cannot relinquish the things of the inner chambers, it will immediately become a leakage."
Chan Master Zongzhi of Daowu Mountain left Yaoshan and went to see Nanquan. Nanquan asked, "What is your name, *dàolǐ*?
The Master replied, "Zongzhi. Nanquan said, "How do you establish the 'principle' (*zōng*) where wisdom does not reach? The Master said, "One must strictly avoid speaking of it."
Jianquan said, "It was certainly spoken to the point; immediately, his head and horns have grown.

Three days later, while the Master and Yunyan were mending clothes on the rear rack, Jianquan saw them and asked, "Dharma-teacher Zhi, the other day you said that where wisdom does not reach, one must strictly avoid speaking to the point."
"As soon as one speaks of the Way, horns grow on one's head. How should one go about practicing? The Master then withdrew his body and entered the Sangha hall;
Nanquan returned to the Abbot’s quarters. The Master came back again to hold the needle. Yanguan said, "Disciple, why did you not respond to the Master just now?
The Master said, "You are remarkably sharp-witted. Yanguan did not realize this, so he instead asked Nanquan, "Just now, regarding 'The Head of Wisdom'—"
Touzi said, "He was truly no match for the Master. Quan said, "He was indeed acting among those of a different species.
Touzi composed a verse: Beneath the adamantine limit lies an ancient skull; For many years it has been trodden by people until blood splatters the void.
Let you freely scoop up the bright moon; How could the cold pines ever abandon their shroud of white clouds?
Danxia’s verse says: Hungry, he eats tender grass as he departs for the distant mountains; Thirsty, he drinks clear spring water as he returns by the winding ravine.
Roaming freely upon the empty ground of the kalpa before time began, At twilight, what need is there for the call of the cowherd’s song?
Yan asked, "What is 'walking among those of different species'? Quan replied, "Have you not heard it said:
'Where wisdom does not reach, one must strictly avoid speaking; if one speaks, horns will grow. One must simply walk among those of different species. Yan still did not understand.
The Master realized that Yan’s karmic conditions did not lie there, so they returned together to Yaoshan. Yaoshan asked, "Why have you returned so quickly? Yan replied:
"Simply because our karmic conditions did not coincide," said Shanshan. Yunyan asked, "What are those conditions? Yunyan recounted the previous conversation.
Shanshan asked, "How do you understand this? Yunyan had no reply, whereupon Shanshan laughed heartily. Yunyan then asked, "What is it like to walk among those of different species?"
Mount said, "I am weary today; wait for another time to come. Yan said, "I have returned specifically for this matter.
Mount said, "Go on then. Yan then departed. As the Master stood outside the abbot’s quarters, hearing that Yan had not attained realization, he unconsciously bit his finger until it bled.
The Master then came down and asked Yan, "Brother, when you went to question the Abbot, what was the reason?"
"What is the condition? Yan asked. "The Master will not speak to me," [the monk] replied. The Master then bowed his head.
I observe that the two elders, Yaoshan and Nanquan, were like water merging with water; how could there be any difference between their two houses?
Any difference arises from later generations. Any difference arises from later generations, and thus my Way has declined.
Guishan asked the Master, "Where have you come from? The Master said, "I have come to visit the sick. Guishan said, "How many people are sick?
The Master said, "There are those who are sick and those who are not sick. Guishan said, "Is the one who is not sick perhaps the Venerable Zhi?
The Master said, "Whether sick or not sick, it has nothing to do with him. Speak quickly! Speak quickly! Guishan said, "Even if you could speak it..."

Transcending entirely the era before the Awesome Sound (Vaiśvānara), he strides alone through the void of kalpas; this is the perfection of stillness. Heaven covers and earth supports;
this is the movement of transformation: the crow flies and the hare runs.
