The Preface to the *Yuyan* states: The void world is a single dream-scene; the Three Vehicles and Four Teachings are the dream-dharma;
all Buddhas and sentient beings are dream-people within this dream. Dream-people, occupying the dream-scene and receiving the dream-dharma, how can they ever be secure?
Is this not being "dreamless" within a dream? Thus, there are those who speak within a dream while claiming they are not dreaming; these are precisely those in a great dream.
There are those who, within a dream, recognize it as a dream; and those who, within a dream, seek to emerge from it. All of them remain within the realm of dreaming.
Only when one suddenly shatters the dream and emerges is there no longer any distinction between the dream-field, the dream-phenomena, and that which is within the dream.
All people have utterly perished; only this primordial luminosity remains, perfectly illuminating and sovereign.
Originally, it has never been dreaming, nor has it ever been waking. *Tsk!* This too is but a dream-talk. Alas, the mountain hermit-monk remains unawakened from his great dream;

his wild mind has not yet ceased, and thus he utters these delirious words, chatter incessantly. To an onlooker, they seem to form a coherent sequence, so I have recorded them for private preservation.
These are handed down as traditional practices; they are all matters of dreams. A guest asked, "Who is it that does not dream? He replied, "This foolish fellow is dreaming even during the day.
At this time, in the ninth month of the autumn of the *Chongzhen* *Renshen* year, I inscribed this at the Hermitage of Heshan:

"The Way is profound and subtle (*xuánmiào*), yet the profound and subtle are not the Way. If there were a 'profound and subtle' to be spoken of, then even that profound and subtle would be a dharma."
It is a dharma-dust. The Way is fundamentally ordinary, yet the ordinary is not the Way. If there were an "ordinary" state to be settled upon, then that ordinariness would also be a dharma-dust.
The Way is fundamentally mindless, yet being mindless is not the Way. If there were a "mindlessness" to be realized, then that mindlessness would also be a dharma-dust.
The Way is fundamentally spontaneous, yet spontaneity is not the Way. If there were a "spontaneity" to be...
If there is a school (zong), then nature is likewise a mental object (dharmāyatana).

For where there is that which can be explained, that which can be settled, that which can be realized, and that which can be taken as a school, then speech and thought have not ceased and subject and object are not forgotten; how could this be anything other than delusion? Therefore, the wise do not give rise to various views.
In the mundane world, it is held that the sense organs are inherently organs and the objects are inherently objects, arising only through their mutual encounter to give rise to function.
Our Buddha, however, teaches that fundamentally there are no organs; rather, the organs arise because of objects. Fundamentally there are no objects; rather, objects manifest because of the organs.
Just as when separated from the two objects of light and darkness, where else could seeing exist? When separated from the single object of movement and stillness, where else could hearing exist?
Thus, these faculties must manifest in dependence upon their respective objects. Furthermore, when a wooden man sees flowers and birds, where else could there be form?
When a wooden horse hears drums and flutes, where else could there be sound? Thus, these objects must [depend upon the faculties].
The faculties (*indriya*) are likewise manifest and luminous. Since objects (*viṣaya*) depend upon the faculties, the objects have no substantial reality.

Since the faculties depend upon the objects, the faculties also have no substantial reality. Faculties and objects intersect in emptiness; there are merely false causes and conditions, and it is only through delusion that various functions arise.

Those who are deluded do not realize this and cling to the faculties and objects as being substantially existent; this constitutes attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*). They cling to the faculties as "self" and cling to the objects as...
This is what is called human attachment. From the arising of these two attachments, beauty and ugliness are produced; from the production of beauty and ugliness, views and thoughts arise;
from the arising of views and thoughts, the paths of karma are established; and once the paths of karma are established, retribution becomes manifest.

When the wise person thoroughly realizes that the faculties and their objects are fundamentally empty, they no longer calculate "self" and "other. When self and other are not calculated, beauty and ugliness do not arise. When beauty and ugliness do not arise...

Then views and afflictions (dṛṣṭi-kleśa) subside; when views and afflictions subside, the constant light (nitya-prabhā) spontaneously becomes perfect. When the constant light spontaneously becomes perfect, the ears can see and the eyes can hear;
there is no faculty among the six sense organs that cannot function interchangeably. To speak in the ultimate sense, this extends to every faculty and every object of the senses.

All things pervade the Dharma-realm; how, then, could there be any obstruction? Viewed from this perspective, these very sense organs and their objects constitute bondage when one is deluded, and liberation when one is awakened.
As a sutra says: "The sense organs and their objects share the same source; bondage and liberation are non-dual. It further states:
"To establish knowledge within seeing and knowing is the root of ignorance; to have no seeing within seeing and knowing—this is nirvana. Although the Buddha-dharma...
These points are fully exhausted by these few words.
The two meanings of existence and non-existence in Buddhism are diametrically opposed to those of the mundane world; therefore, there are few in the mundane world who believe in them.

That which the Buddha calls "existence" must persist through successive kalpas without ever being diminished in the slightest—this is what he calls existence. That which the Buddha calls "non-existence"...
If something does not abide moment by moment and cannot persist eternally, it is called "non-existent.
Therefore, that which the Buddha possesses is what none in the world can lack; that which the Buddha lacks is what none in the world can possess. This is the ultimate, true Dharma.
That which has substance and a name is called "existence"; that which lacks substance and a name is called "non-existence. These are the conventional notions of existence and non-existence.
This existence arises from non-existence and must inevitably return to non-existence; thus, although it exists in the present, it does not abide for even a single moment.
One thereby knows that to speak of "existence" is an illusion. This non-existence can be realized through existence, and it may also manifest instantaneously.

When things transform within existence, although they do not exist in the present, they do not remain still for even a single moment. Thus, one knows that to say "they are non-existent" is a delusion.
Some claim that this existence is inherently existent and this non-existence is also inherently existent, thereby establishing the thesis that "all is existent.

Others claim that this non-existence is inherently non-existent and this existence is also non-existent, thereby establishing the thesis that "all is non-existent. Still others claim that to take existence as one's thesis is to fall into the trap of existence, and to take non-existence...

Those [who hold such views] fall into non-existence. For this reason, they establish both [existence and non-existence] as their thesis, or they establish neither [existence nor non-existence] as their thesis;
or again, in contrast to these four views, they establish that which is not the four views as their thesis. When subdivided in detail, there are ninety-six types in total.
All these are the teachings of external paths. Their error lies in attempting to perceive the Way through views; yet they do not realize that the Way cannot be perceived by means of views.
Only by awakening to and entering into the single mind do all views vanish. When all views vanish, the eternal light becomes spontaneously perfect.
Although one may say that existence exists, or that non-existence exists, or that both existence and non-existence exist, or that neither existence nor non-existence exists—
this is because one who truly knows existence finds every word returning to the root; all such speech accords with the True Dharma, and is surely beyond the capacity of worldly people to fathom.
Everyone knows that Śākyamuni is a sage who has transcended the world, yet they do not know him as a sage who has truly entered the world;

for one cannot transcend the world without first entering it. Everyone knows that Confucius is a sage who has entered the world, yet they do not know him as a sage who has truly transcended the world;
for one cannot enter the world without first transcending it.
The study of the Buddha’s teaching requires nothing more than recognizing that all phenomena (*dharmas*) lack intrinsic nature.

Once one recognizes that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, then the body, the mind, the physical world, and even the boundless void will all vanish away; there remains only the single mind, its perfect luminosity revealed alone.
Without seeking Buddhahood, one has already become a Buddha; without delivering sentient beings, they have already been delivered. If one does not know that all phenomena...
If there is no inherent nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), then one falsely gives rise to attachment, engenders delusion, and creates karma; how could this ever come to an end? Question:
Mencius said that human nature differs from the nature of dogs and sheep. Does it follow, then, that there are two types of nature? Answer: Nature is not dual. Question:
If so, do other beings obtain only a partial portion of it, while humans obtain it in its entirety? Answer: Nature has no partiality.
"It is complete. [The interlocutor] asked: "If that is so, then are humans and things the same? He replied: "In their unchanging essence, there is nothing that is not the same;
in their functioning according to conditions, there is nothing that is not different. This is what the Sūtra means when it says: "The Dharma-body flows through the five paths of rebirth."
Question: Mencius spoke of the inherent goodness of human nature (*xing shan*). Many practitioners of Chan Buddhism have criticized this view;

only Master Donglin Zong upheld it, asserting that this primordial goodness does not stand in opposition to evil. Is this correct? Answer: The essence of nature (*xingtǐ*) is quiescent extinction and transcends all names and words.
All such specific designations deviate from its original nature. It is not only that Mencius was inappropriate to praise it as "good";
even Yao and Shun called it "the Mean," the *Great Learning* called it "clarity," and the *Doctrine of the Mean* called it "sincerity.

Extending further, the Buddhas call it "True Suchness" and "Perfect Enlightenment"—how could these be used to speak of "nature"? As for the expedient means of instruction, [they employ various names].
Thus, it does not abandon the power of linguistic expression. Because it is not partial, it is called "the Mean" (zhong).

Because it is not obscured, it is called "clarity" (ming). Because it is not false, it is called "sincerity" (cheng). Because it is neither false nor subject to change, it is called "True Suchness" (zhenru).

Because it encompasses all virtues and illuminates the masses of darkness, it is called "Perfect Enlightenment" (yuanjue). Furthermore, because it is inherently free from evil, it is called "good" (shan). It is also...
What is so wrong with this? Furthermore, that which is called "good" is precisely what is called "the Mean" and "clarity-and-sincerity," and it is these that constitute goodness.
However, if one understands that goodness is a skillful and expedient application, then Mencius is indeed a follower of Zhongni (Confucius).
But if one clings to goodness as an ultimate, real doctrine, then Mencius would likewise belong to the school of Gaozi.
Question: Laozi takes emptiness and non-being (*śūnyatā*) as his fundamental principle, yet the Buddhists criticize him, calling him a non-causal heretic.
However, I have heard the Buddhist teachings which state: "From the root of non-abiding, all dharmas are established," and "The essence of empty space is the source of sentient beings.
How does this differ from Laozi? Answer: Laozi’s adherence to emptiness and non-being is [a form of] insentient...

It is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). The Śākya [Buddha] spoke of the essence of empty space, asserting that among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṭa-dharma*), there is none that does not originate in ignorance (*avidyā*).
Yet this ignorance has no substantial nature (*svabhāva*) and nothing upon which it can dwell or cling.

Because it lacks a substantial nature and has nothing to dwell upon, it is able to manifest all phenomena in accordance with conditions (*pratyaya*), establishing them in full vigor. Therefore, it is said: "From..."
"The root of non-abiding establishes all dharmas. It is further said: "The foundation of empty space is the source of sentient beings.
How could this not be the meaning of Laozi’s "emptiness" and "spontaneity"?
Question: The study of philology and glosses is something that cannot be discarded in the world; why then do you, Master, strenuously condemn it?
Answer: How could philology itself be condemned? What is condemned is falling into mere glosses while failing to understand the actual meaning.
If one knows the actual meaning, then philology becomes miraculous and profound; if one does not know the actual meaning, then even the most ingenious [explanations] are of no avail.
To engage in forced interpretation and to exhaust one’s ingenuity in speculative conjecture are both the habitual tendencies of those who wear the scholar’s cap (the Confucian literati).
How can they be worthy of serious discourse? The Confucians maintain that the nature of humans and things is fundamentally bestowed by Heaven (*tian*).

Many Buddhists disparage this view, yet they fail to realize that what the Confucians call "Heaven" does not refer to the actual celestial realm. Rather, it refers to the state prior to the involvement of deluded consciousness; thus, they designate it as "Heaven. As for humans...
When there is that which cannot be acted upon, one says it is "Heaven. When there is a point where deliberation and planning fall short, one says it is "Heaven.
Thus, the *Wenshi jing* says: "That which cannot be contrived, cannot be brought about, cannot be fathomed, and cannot be divided—forcing a name upon it, we call it 'Heaven.'"
It is called "destiny" (ming). Mengzi also said: "That which acts without being acted upon is Heaven; that which arrives without being brought about is destiny.
This is an excellent discourse on the mandate of Heaven. If this explanation is indeed correct, then the Confucianists derive the nature of man from Heaven.
It is not different from the Buddha; it merely draws forth [the truth] without yet concluding it, remaining hidden and unrevealed as a provisional teaching of skillful means.

As the Book of Documents says: "The Great Sovereign God bestowed the innate goodness upon the people below. And as the Classic of Poetry says: "Heaven produced the multitudes of the people; they have their things and their norms.
This refers precisely to the time before deluded consciousness has intervened, the day when human artifice had no part in it, and before one could engage in conceptual deliberation.

This refers to the state of "attaining. Furthermore, such expressions as others' claims of "reaching Heaven and knowing fate," or "attaining the will and mind of Heaven," all do not go beyond this meaning.
Later Confucianists, failing to comprehend its essential intent, instead asserted that there is a presiding agent within the dark and obscure realm.
That which is considered the pivot and nexus of the two vital energies (*qi*) and the five elements (*wuxing*) is called "Heavenly Mandate" (*tianming*).

All persons and things receive this to form their physical structures and establish their natures. Now, the pivot and nexus of the two energies and five elements is in fact none other than the wondrous mind of our own selves;
hence it is said that "the three realms are nothing but mind. To now discard the mind and claim that there exists some other sovereign ruler within the obscure and indistinct is untenable.
Within this [framework], there is a cause external to the mind. My Buddha has categorized such a view as that of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), because its cause exists outside of the single mind.
Furthermore, it is said that in the heavens it is called "fate" (*ming*); it is unified and not yet differentiated. In humans it is called "nature" (*xing*); it is differentiated and not unified.
Thus, nature is held to possess differentiation and unification. When the vital energy (*qi*) gathers, it gives rise to life, and at that point its nature begins...
There is [the case where] the vital breath disperses and one dies; its nature (xing) is then extinguished. Thus, it would follow that nature possesses arising and ceasing.
Since there is division and combination, and arising and ceasing, one cannot speak of these as "nature," much less call them "Heavenly Mandate" (tianming) or "the Way" (dao).
This is certainly not the fundamental intent of the Confucian tradition.
Zhouzi said: "From the Poleless (Wuji) comes the Great Ultimate (Taiji). The Great Ultimate moves and generates Yang; it rests and generates Yin.

These few sentences are the source of Song dynasty Confucian Neo-Confucianism. Yet, those who are confused about them are by no means few. Why is this? It is because of the doctrine of the Great Ultimate.
When Laozi and Zhuangzi refer to the primordial state of the One Qi (One Breath), it can be described in terms of movement and stillness.

However, when the Song Confucians directly identify the substance of the Dao as the Great Ultimate (Taiji), it is simply a single, undifferentiated principle; how could there be movement or stillness therein? Someone asked:
"If the Great Ultimate has neither movement nor stillness, does it not give rise to the Two Polarities? I replied: "That which is neither moving nor still is the substance of the Great Ultimate."
That there is movement and stillness is the function of the Great Ultimate (*taiji*). Function issues forth based upon the substance; it is provisionally named "arising.

Yet the substance transcends function and is, in reality, itself without arising. When function is subsumed back into the substance, arising is immediately non-arising. When the entire substance gives rise to function, there is non-arising yet arising.
The reason for this is that the transformations of yin and yang and all things are like shadows—neither existent nor non-existent, yet not non-existent.

Therefore, the process of creation and transformation does not obstruct the occurrence of arising and ceasing; yet because [the ultimate] is not a substantial entity, the true substance is ultimately and eternally without arising.

Furthermore, as for the creative transformations of yin and yang and their relationship to the true substance: they are neither one nor two. Because they are not one, the Great Ultimate (Tàijí) transcends the Two Polarities (Lǎngyí);
because they are not two, the Two Polarities are entirely identical to the Great Ultimate.
Someone asked: "In the *Commentary on the Diagram of the Supreme Ultimate* (*Taiji tu zhu*), it says: 'The Supreme Ultimate is the wondrousness of the primordial state;

movement and stillness are the mechanisms upon which it rides. It further says: 'The Supreme Ultimate has no movement or stillness, yet it is that which moves and rests. If one explains it in this way, would there not seem to be no error? I replied:
"If he takes the Supreme Ultimate to be the 'rider' (*neng cheng*) and movement and stillness to be the 'vehicle' (*suo cheng*), then movement and stillness would reside within the Supreme Ultimate."
Beyond the Ultimate (Taiji), one cannot say that the Ultimate moves or that the Ultimate is still.

Furthermore, if it were said that the Ultimate sometimes rides upon the mechanism of stillness and sometimes rides upon the mechanism of movement, then the Ultimate would be a thing possessing dimensions and subject to coming and going.

How could it not be erroneous? Furthermore, regarding his claim that the Great Ultimate (Taiji) is devoid of motion and stillness, while there is something else that moves and rests—the Great Ultimate—does he mean that outside of the Great Ultimate there is a separate "Qi" (Vital Energy) which causes the Great Ultimate to move and rest?
Or does he mean that there is no such separate Qi, and the Great Ultimate itself moves and rests? If he claims there is a separate Qi, then this Qi would not be produced from the Great Ultimate.
If one were to say that there is no single qi apart from these, then that which moves would move what, and that which stills would still what?
Someone might say: "This refers to the yin and yang produced subsequently. I reply:

If this were so, it would mean that within the Great Ultimate (Tàijí) there suddenly arises a mechanism capable of movement, whereby it moves and becomes yang; and suddenly arises a mechanism capable of stillness, whereby it stills.
And thus the aggregates (skandhas) are formed. Does not the Great Ultimate (Tài jí) also possess movement and stillness?

Now, as for the Great Ultimate, it is the single principle in its entirety, without any trace or sign, and devoid of names or characteristics. If within this there were suddenly to arise the mechanism of movement and stillness, [it would no longer be the Great Ultimate].
If there were signs and omens that could be discerned, or names and forms that could be pointed out, how could it be called the Great Ultimate (Tài jí)?
Question: The Song Confucians say that the Great Ultimate is divided into Yin and Yang. Is this correct? Answer: Yin and Yang are differentiated within the Great Ultimate;
it is not that the Great Ultimate itself is divided into Yin and Yang. Generally speaking, whatever can be divided must possess form and substance, yet the Great Ultimate...
The Supreme Ultimate (Taiji) is utterly formless and substanceless. Generally speaking, whatever can be divided must necessarily undergo change; yet the Supreme Ultimate is without change.
Whatever can be divided must necessarily possess partiality or completeness; yet the Supreme Ultimate is without partiality or completeness.

To claim that the Supreme Ultimate is divided into Yin and Yang—is this not erroneous? Formerly, those of the school of Laozi and Zhuangzi designated the beginning of the single vital breath (yiqi) as...
Because it is the Great Ultimate (*tài jí*), there is the doctrine of its division into Yin and Yang.
Now, if Confucian scholars directly designate the Great Ultimate as the substance of the Way (*dào-tǐ*), they ought not to merely adopt this doctrine without investigating it. Someone asks:

"If the Great Ultimate cannot be divided, do all things still possess the Great Ultimate? He replies: "They do. [The questioner] asks: "Since the whole cannot be divided, how is it that each individual thing..."
He replied: "This is precisely that which cannot be understood through discursive thought or conceptual discrimination.

If one were now to proceed with such discrimination, the substance of the Great Ultimate (*tài jí*) is such that, when speaking of its greatness, it encompasses the vast void; when speaking of its smallness, it is fully present within a single speck of dust.

Although it is fully present within a single speck of dust, it simultaneously encompasses the vast void; although it encompasses the vast void, it is simultaneously fully present within a single speck of dust."
If it can encompass the great void yet cannot fully contain a single speck of dust, it is limited by the large.
If it can fully contain a single speck of dust yet cannot encompass the great void, it is limited by the small. How could the Great Ultimate (Tàijí) possess the dimensions of large or small?
Therefore, the universal whole is one Great Ultimate, which is precisely each individual thing possessing its own Great Ultimate.
The Supreme Ultimate (Taiji). Each possesses its own Supreme Ultimate, which is identical to the universal Supreme Ultimate as a whole.
If the individual Supreme Ultimates are derived from the universal one, then those that possess them individually cannot be complete.
Since the universal Supreme Ultimate has been divided into individual instances, the universal one itself has already lost its completeness. Can it still be called the "Supreme Ultimate"?
It is appropriate for those who study the Way to forget their emotions and realize it through silent verification.

Someone asked: "The *I Ching* states that 'the refined essence forms things' and 'the wandering soul constitutes transformation. Does this explain the meaning of saṃsāra? He replied: "One should not rely on this as proof.
Saṃsāra clarifies the three periods of time, whereas Confucianists clarify only the present. Saṃsāra clarifies the six realms of existence."

The Confucianists clarify only the Way of Humanity (ren-tao). Therefore, the Confucianists do not speak of saṃsāra. A comprehensive examination of the Five Classics and the various Masters reveals that none contain such a teaching. Only the single phrase in the *I Ching*, "the wandering soul undergoes transformation," seems similar; however, since there is no other evidence to corroborate it, one cannot force an interpretation upon it. Moreover, the subsequent line states: "Therefore, by knowing the nature and circumstances of ghosts and spirits, one will not [be deluded]. Thus, it does not refer to rebirth. Furthermore, the *Analects* records that when Yan Hui asked about death, Confucius replied: "As for life, we know its origin; as for death, we know its destination. This indicates that he did not speak of rebirth. Moreover, the *Mencius* says: "Those who know the Way of Heaven do not speak of the Way of Man; those who know the Way of Man do not speak of the Way of Heaven. This shows that the two ways are distinct and do not intermingle. Furthermore, the *Zhou Li* states: "The Grand Historiographer is responsible for the sacrifices to the ancestors. This implies that the spirits of the dead remain within their ancestral temples and do not wander through the six realms. Even if one were to grant that there is rebirth, the Confucian Way does not require one to seek it. For the sages established the rites and music solely to regulate human conduct and transform customs; they did not establish them to enable people to escape suffering or attain bliss. Therefore, the Confucian Way is sufficient for governing the world and regulating the people; it does not concern itself with the affairs of the afterlife. As for the Buddhist Way, it is intended for those who have exhausted the worldly path and seek transcendence. It is like a ferryman who provides a boat for those crossing a river. If one has already reached the other shore, what further use is there for the boat? Thus, the two teachings serve different purposes and do not conflict. To claim otherwise is merely to confuse the masses and lead them astray. This is why the Confucianists do not speak of rebirth. It is only because the Buddha’s Way is profound and subtle, and his teachings are vast and far-reaching, that he spoke of rebirth to save sentient beings. If one understands this, one will not harbor doubts. If one does not understand this, one will surely fall into error. Therefore, I have explained this at length to resolve your confusion. I hope you will reflect upon it carefully. Do not let your mind be disturbed. If you can set aside these doubts, you will find peace of mind. If you cannot, you will only increase your distress. You must choose between these two paths and settle your mind accordingly. Do not allow yourself to be swayed by external influences. This is my earnest exhortation to you. It is said that when a person dies, they simply become a ghost. Since the circumstances of a person becoming a ghost after death can be known, how could those who claim that existence is utterly annihilated after death possibly represent the intention of the Sage?

Question: When the Confucians state that after death there is total annihilation, is there any evidence for this? Answer: There is no such evidence. What the Confucians discuss is based on the Six Classics, the foundational texts.
These Classics merely state that when a person dies they become a ghost (*gui*), and furthermore, they all maintain the doctrine of [spirits] abiding in Heaven.

Thus, there are regulations for ancestral temples and canons for the *Chunqiu* (Spring and Autumn Annals). Although it is said that one serves the deceased as if they were alive, this is precisely how the benevolent person fulfills the requirements of filial piety.
The nature of the human spirit cannot yet be hastily declared to have vanished into unconsciousness and returned to total dissolution.
As for what the *Zuozhuan* records—such as spirits transforming into foxes or becoming malevolent ghosts after death—these are particularly manifest examples.

It was only from the Han dynasty onwards that the theory of annihilation after death first emerged; this contravenes the Classics and opposes the sages, being merely the indulgence of one's own arbitrary speculations.

Yet the world at large fails to examine this; they all contend to cite it as authoritative evidence. Thus, they are bound by what they have been accustomed to since childhood and are unable to liberate themselves from it. How tragic!
Someone may say: "The mechanism of creation is one of ceaseless production; it does not need to rely on qi that has already been exhausted to produce qi that is currently unfolding.
Therefore, the doctrine of rebirth seems untenable. I reply: That which is ceaselessly productive in the process of creation is *qi*.
How could it rely on qi that has already been exhausted to produce qi that is currently unfolding? As for this mind—

This spirit is not merely qi. Although it receives qi and assumes form such that it appears to undergo birth and destruction, its wondrous essence is eternally firm and remains unchanged throughout kalpas.
It is therefore able to preside over and direct the processes of creation and transformation, and is thus called the most spiritual and most wondrous of all things.

If one were to claim that death is eternal extinction, then one would be identical to grass and trees; how could it be said that the spiritual intelligence of the human mind perishes along with grass and trees?
Indeed, the human body is a microcosm of heaven and earth. While heaven and earth undergo formation and decay, the sovereign master of heaven and earth never perishes.
Therefore, after decay they are formed again; likewise, while the human body has birth and death, [the spirit does not].
As the sovereign of the human person, it has never ceased to exist; therefore, one dies and is born again.
This principle is as clear as day, yet many people do not believe it. It is truly lamentable that they equate this superior body of heaven and earth with the ignorant grasses and trees below.
Someone asked: "The *Zhongyong* speaks of the state where joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure have not yet been manifested, calling it 'Centrality' (*zhong*).

Is this not close to our Buddhist teaching of 'the non-arising of a single thought'? I replied: "No. 'The non-arising of a single thought' means that while this mind is active, it is constantly quiescent;
while quiescent, it is constantly active. It simply means remaining constantly detached from all objects within one's own thoughts, such that thoughts do not arise because of external objects."
It is so. There is no distinction between the unarisen and the already-arisen, nor is there a division between what constitutes the nature (*xing*) and what constitutes the emotions (*qing*).

Someone asked: "Can the Five Constant Virtues (*wuchang*) be spoken of as the nature? He replied: "When one points to the function by means of the substance, or returns to the substance by way of the function, one may speak of the Five Constant Virtues as the nature;
yet, in reality, the nature is not the Five Constant Virtues. For the nature is a single,浑然 (holistic) unity, fundamentally without [differentiation]."

Regarding names and forms: from the single principle following conditions, there arise the names of the "five constants. It is like gold following conditions to become a bowl, a ring, a hairpin, or an armlet.
Therefore, when speaking of function in terms of essence, one says that within the gold are fully present the bowl, the ring, the hairpin, and the armlet.

Or, when returning to the essence by way of function, one says that the bowl, the ring, the hairpin, and the armlet are all simply gold. If one points directly to the fundamental nature of the gold...
As for substance, how could it be merely defined as ingots, rings, hairpins, or bracelets? The Song Confucians did not comprehend this principle;
they took the Five Constants to be the nature (*xing*), asserting that within nature there exists the differentiation of these five. Thus they said:

"Within the complete body of the Confucian, there are many principles, each with its own distinction and its own right and wrong. That which is bestowed by Heaven and inherent in humanity (*zhòngzhōng bǐngyí*) is without exception...
Each possesses this principle. To explain it is merely to point to a single, undifferentiated whole—a thing without distinction, without right or wrong.
Now, to speak of "many principles" existing within the total body [of reality] is nothing other than names and marks (*nāma-rūpa*). One must realize that principle has no name;
therefore, it can serve as the progenitor of all names. Principle has no mark; therefore, it can serve as the source of all marks. If there were...
Those who fall into names and signs all take this principle and apply it according to conditions; they establish names based on phenomena and manifest their signs.
How could one possibly deliberate upon the true essence that is fundamentally quiescent?

That true essence which is fundamentally quiescent cannot be expressed by words and cannot be cognized by consciousness; if even "one" cannot be apprehended, how much less can it be divided into five?

Indeed, the nature still prefers strong designations; how much more so when it is designated as benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom? Therefore, to speak of the nature in terms of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom is an error.

Someone asked: "If nature cannot be designated by benevolence, righteousness, propriety, or wisdom, then 'neither good nor evil' is the essence of nature, while 'possessing both good and evil' is its function.
Since both good and evil equally emerge from nature, why must the gentleman abandon evil and follow good?
I replied: "Although nature itself is neither good nor evil, that which accords with nature will necessarily be good, whereas that which opposes it..."
Human nature is inherently good. The manifestation of evil arises from attachment to the self and attachment to phenomena. The ultimate state of goodness returns to non-thought and non-action.
Non-thought and non-action are the way that accords with nature; attachment to the self and attachment to phenomena are obstacles that oppose nature.
Therefore, the gentleman must abandon attachments in order to attain the Way. Someone may say: "Nature is not found apart from the Five Constant Virtues."

If one remains fixed in samādhi, one will be vast and indeterminate. How, then, can one respond to stimuli with precise appropriateness? It is said: Responding to phenomena has its principle; it does not depart from the single mind.
The mind is empty yet spiritual; the mind is still yet wondrous. When objects arrive, the response occurs, shining forth clearly in every instance.
This is like a mirror that is empty and formless, yet all forms manifest their reflections within it; or like a scale that is empty and contains no object, yet all things are thereby weighed.
This is to ensure its levelness. If a mirror or a scale were not empty [of their own nature], how could they adapt to objects and respond with precision?
Someone asked about the doctrine of "investigating things" (*gewu*). I replied: Among various scholars, some gloss *ge* as "rectifying," meaning to rectify the movement of one's intention.
Now, if the numinous mind is still obstructed, deluded thoughts will arise crosswise; if one forcibly attempts to rectify them, one cannot succeed in rectifying them.
Some explain "ge" (to rectify) as the "obstruction" found in the term "hange" (resistance/obstruction), and explain "wu" (objects) as "object-desires.

They claim that if one rectifies away the obstructions of object-desire, then the original luminosity will manifest of itself. Now, when right view has not yet opened, principle and desire are often conflated;
if one mistakes desire for principle, how can it be removed? Some explain "ge" as the "obstruction" in "hange," and explain "wu" [as object-desire].
Regarding "for the sake of all external objects": this means that by completely severing ties with external objects, the mind will not be obstructed.

Now, principle and phenomena are non-dual, and the internal and external are without interval. To now insist on removing objects in order to clarify principle is like trying to find water by beating away the waves.
This is merely a one-sided and biased view. Only Hui-ān’s interpretation of it as "exhaustively reaching the principle of things" comes close to the mark.

However, what he calls "principle" (lǐ) refers specifically to the normative standard of how things ought to be; what he calls "exhausting principle" (qióng lǐ) refers specifically to following after objects to exhaust their respective standards of what they ought to be.
Thus, this "principle" is something that falls within the reach of names and words, and within the scope of thought and deliberation.

Wherever one goes, the views of difference and distinction only increase further; the path to returning to the source is not reached. One seeks that sudden, expansive illumination—can it truly be achieved?
I, a fool, say that one who investigates things (*ge wu*) must exhaust their true substance and penetrate directly to the fundamental root.

This is what the *I Ching* calls "refining the meaning until one enters the divine" (*jing yi ru shen*). When one refines the meaning to the point of entering the divine, one does not fall into the narrow paths of conceptual meaning, but attains awakening.
Furthermore, form is forgotten as it transforms into nature; vital energy (qi) transforms into the Way (Dao); and things transform into the mind.
The spiritual light shines forth alone, utterly transcending the sense organs and their objects. There is nothing vast that it does not illuminate, and nothing subtle that it does not penetrate.

That the Way of exhaustive inquiry is necessarily thus—when compared to those petty attempts at conjecture within the realm of external forms and traces—is it any more than the difference between a torch and the sun and moon?
Reaching the state where there is neither one nor many, the myriad responses are inexhaustible; because true emptiness is not empty, the myriad transformations encounter no obstruction.
This is why the Great Foundation is established and the Way of Attainment is practiced. The Song Confucians did not comprehend this principle, and thus they said:
"The Buddhists claim that all principles are empty, whereas we Confucians claim that all principles are real. Principle is a reality, yet they have rendered it empty."

This is why the fundamental basis is not established. When they claim that "all principles are equally real," they are referring to the normative rules (*dangran zhi ze*) inherent in things and affairs.
These normative rules have names by which they can be recognized and forms by which they can be pointed out; therefore, they say they are all real.
Yet they do not realize that principle resides within oneself and not in objects, and that principle resides in the mind and not in affairs. If [principle were merely] in things and affairs...
Thus, these are but shadows of this subtle and wondrous response to principle, receiving their names based on material things.
They undergo sudden change and transition, possessing no substantial reality whatsoever. Therefore, what others call "substantial," I call "empty. It is like water:
whether it takes a square shape, a round shape, a curved shape, or a straight shape, it does not fail to differ according to the vessel that contains it.
As for the nature of water, it is simply moisture; it possesses no such qualities as squareness, roundness, curvature, or straightness.
Therefore, squareness, roundness, curvature, and straightness are empty, while the nature of moisture is real.

Now, to insist that all principles are real is to insist that squareness, roundness, curvature, and straightness are real—is this not erroneous? Furthermore, take the moon as an analogy: sometimes it is in the river, and sometimes...
Whether in the Yangtze, the Huai, or the Han, there is nowhere that does not have a round moon; yet the actual substance of the moon resides in the heavens.
Therefore, that which is in the heavens is real, while that which appears in the Yangtze, the Huai, and the Han is empty.
To now insist that all phenomena are real is to grasp at the moons in the Yangtze, the Huai, and the Han as being real. Is this not a grave error?
The Song Confucians, because they clung to this principle as being substantial, pursued objects to exhaustively investigate them.
With their discriminating and deluded minds, they attempted to gauge illusory phenomena that are like shadows and echoes, claiming that objects could be mastered and knowledge could be attained.

They did not realize, however, that the transformations of things and events are as swift as a flash of lightning, and that the complexities of phenomena are as vast and chaotic as dust motes in the sand; thus, they were unable to penetrate their fundamental source.

Yet, how can one who busily pursues external objects hope to achieve complete illumination? Furthermore, there is the mind that discriminates, which is called the attachment to the person (*pudgala-grāha*);
there is the principle that is discriminated, which is called the attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*). When these two attachments coexist, all manner of faults arise.
Though one may strive to do good, one’s departure from the Way becomes ever more remote. Alas! The Song Confucians lost the root while seeking the branches, mistaking the branches for the root.
Fundamentally, such is their perversion; how can it be said that the Great Root (Dàběn) is thereby established?

Worldly scholars claim that the Supreme Ultimate (Tàijí) possesses motion and stillness; this implies they regard the Supreme Ultimate as something subject to arising. They claim that the Five Constant Virtues constitute human nature;

this implies they regard nature as possessing phenomenal characteristics. Once one is confined to the realm of existence, there arise the distinctions of self and other, beauty and ugliness, and [good and evil].
Affection and aversion involve acceptance and rejection; thus one discriminates and cultivates them in order to return to the good. Yet these are all phenomena subject to arising and ceasing.
Therefore, although it is said that there is no thought, in reality there is thought; although it is said that there is no action, in reality there is action.
Its application can only serve Heaven and govern people; it cannot yet transcend humanity to enter into Heaven.

Laozi and Zhuangzi revered the non-existence (*wu*) of antiquity; this was because they had not yet transcended non-existence. They loathed the existence (*you*) of the present; this was because they had not yet transcended existence.
Their vision being thus confined to existence and non-existence, they conceived the thought of abandoning the existence of the present to return to the non-existence of antiquity.

Consequently, they caused the limbs to wither away, rejected the clarity of the intellect, severed sage-like wisdom, and discarded benevolence and righteousness, practicing the arts of the primordial chaos (*hundun*). All of these were merely [the products of] life.
This is the cessation of phenomena. Therefore, although it is called "no-thought," it is not truly no-thought; although it is called "non-action," it is not truly non-action.
Its function can only allow one to leave the human realm and enter the celestial realm, but it cannot yet allow one to leave the celestial realm and enter the state of the Sage.
Some say: "The learning of Master Zhuang does not fall into nihilism. His words state: 'There is that which has being; there is that which has non-being;
there is that which has never yet begun to have non-being; and there is that which has never yet begun to have that which has never yet begun to have non-being.'"
Since it is said, "There has never even been that which has never begun with non-existence," one thus transcends both existence and non-existence; what else could this be but the true nature?
[The opponent] says: "No. Zhuangzi was unable to detach from the views of existence and non-existence; therefore, he exhausted existence in order to enter non-existence."
Exhausting "non-being" (wu), one enters "the non-being of non-being" (wuwu). Exhausting "the non-being of non-being," one enters "the non-being of the non-being of non-being" (wuwuwu).

Although one can thus penetrate deeply into the layered mysteries (chongxuan), in sum, this involves abandoning being and grasping at non-being; taking the ultimate limit of recognizing non-being as the pinnacle, one ultimately cannot transcend non-being. Therefore, it is said:
"That from which things have never begun to exist—this is the ultimate, the exhaustive, that to which nothing more can be added. This is not [the case].

To be confined by non-existence—how can that be? Furthermore, if one discusses the nature [of things] and insists on seeking it prior to form and prior to qi, one will inevitably miss it after form and after qi has manifested;
this is to mistakenly identify the state of desolation as the nature. How could this not be being confined by non-existence?
Someone says: "Zhuangzi did not take desolation to be the nature. He pushed his analysis to its ultimate limit...
That which precedes the non-existence of all things is the very moment when the substance of nature (*xingti*) first manifests, by virtue of being prior to the non-existence of things.

It is said that for one who awakens to nature, objects are themselves nature; how could this hinder seeing it after the existence of things? Although there are things, they have never begun to exist as such.

For one who is deluded regarding nature, nature itself becomes an object; how then can they exhaustively reach back to the point prior to the non-existence of things? Although there is no thing, it is...

It is likewise a phenomenon. To use a mirror as an analogy: the substance of the mirror is not the reflection; yet the substance of the reflection is precisely the mirror. The wise person recognizes the mirror through the reflection;
once the mirror is recognized, they no longer concern themselves with whether the reflection exists or not. The deluded person clings to the reflection as being the mirror.
Upon hearing that the reflection is not the mirror, they then cling to the absence of the reflection as being the mirror. Or, upon hearing that there is no...
The shadow is not the mirror either; yet one further clings to that which is before the shadow as being the mirror.
If this were the way to obtain the mirror, the teachings of Zhuangzi would for the most part be similar to this. Therefore it is said: "They are merely confined by non-existence."

Someone said: "Zhuangzi did not take 'silence and stillness' (jimo) as the nature [of things]. The reason he necessarily traces back to the point before anything had begun to exist is to exhaustively discover the source from which all transformations arise;
this is precisely what is called 'nature. One says that the root-source of the myriad transformations does not transcend the single mind.
Therefore it is said: 'The three realms are mind-only; the myriad dharmas are consciousness-only. Now, let us seek this."
Before the time when things had not yet begun to exist, the further one seeks, the further away one becomes. This "time before things began to exist" refers to the end of a preceding kalpa;
it is the kalpa of emptiness (*śūnyakalpa*). Although this realm is utterly devoid of form or appearance, a single qi (*qì*) is turbid and swirling, operating silently and without ceasing.
From the minute to the manifest, it produces the earth and produces the heavens. Laozi and Zhuangzi refer to this very realm of emptiness by the name...

They call it "emptiness and non-being" (*śūnyatā*) and also name it the "Ultimate Limitless" (*ananta*). This very same *qi* (vital energy) is named the "Great Ultimate" (*taiji*) and is also called the "Great One" (*taiyi*).
They claim that heaven and earth arise from this single *qi*, and that this single *qi* arises from the realm of emptiness.
Consequently, they cling to this emptiness as the source of all transformations and the true nature of ultimate reality. Yet they do not realize that this—
Space comes into being through the preceding kalpa of destruction; this is "arising. Once heaven and earth have been produced, space is consequently lost;
this is "ceasing. To have arising and ceasing is merely a single illusory and false phenomenon—how could it be the root source of the myriad transformations?
Furthermore, this single qi does not arise from space; rather, it has been produced life after life since beginningless kalpas.

It does not cease; it is that which exhausts neither in closing nor opening. If a student can, through this, penetrate the source of perpetual generation, then the myriad phenomena of the three realms are truly nothing other than themselves.
Thus, past and present can be understood as a single thread, and existence and non-existence can be seen as non-dual.
Now, when Zhuangzi claims that qi is born from emptiness, he misses the mark by a great distance. Therefore, it is said: "To identify with the silence and stillness..."
This is the nature of things.
A Song dynasty Confucianist said: "The entire *Gengsangzi* consists of Chan; while other chapters also contain Chan-like expressions, it is only this chapter that contains them from beginning to end.
Alas, this is what the Song Confucianist calls Chan! How could he have understood Chan? Indeed.

The school of Master Zhuang claims to have exhausted the profound and reached the ultimate subtlety; yet, when its essential aim is examined, it does not go beyond finding peace in emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and spontaneity (*svabhāva*), regarding this as the ultimate limit.
Now, the Way (*dharma*) transcends existence and non-existence and is free from the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*);
therefore, that which speaks of emptiness is not the Way itself, but rather its sphere. He wishes to practice emptiness to accord with the Way, yet emptiness...
This has become a mere conventional trap. The Dao has no self-originated nature; how then could there be such a thing as "so-being" (ran)?
It is so-being only by following conditions, yet it is not self-originated. Thus, that which is called "spontaneity" (ziran) is not the Dao itself, but rather its mechanism.
Those who wish to practice spontaneity to harmonize with the Dao find that spontaneity instead becomes a fetter. This is why Zhuangzi regarded it as a heterodox learning.
If one studies according to our Śākya school, it is not so; one does not grasp with a mind that exists, nor does one unite with a mind that is non-existent.
The essential point lies solely in the perfect realization of the one mind. Once this one mind is realized, the sovereign mastery resides prior to the workings of the spirit;
there is no need to speak of "following its natural course. Its operation transcends the realm of existence and non-existence; there is no need to speak of "returning to the void."
There is no such thing. The acute ear hears everything, yet this is not a case of having extra ears; the clear eye illuminates everything, yet this is not a case of having extra eyes;
the wise mind knows everything, yet this is not a case of being wounded by artificial excavation; the sage is all-pervasive, yet this is not a case of being excessively preoccupied with the arts.
How could one remain so narrow-mindedly confined to dull silence, concluding one's life solely upon these [limited faculties]?
The Song Confucianists say that Buddhists use Laozi and Zhuangzi to embellish their teachings; this is the delusion of the Song Confucianists.
Those [thinkers] such as Laozi and Zhuangzi take what precedes the Great Ultimate (Tài jí) to be non-being and what follows the Great Ultimate to be being.

By taking non-being as right and being as wrong, their views on being and non-being have not yet been eliminated, and their sentiments of right and wrong have not yet been extinguished. This itself constitutes [the error].
It is the root of saṃsāra and the basis of falsehood; how much more so when one feels joy or aversion toward it, or grasps at it or rejects it!

Though you claim to roam in the void and merge with the vast emptiness, taking this to be the ultimate realization of the Way, you have instead fallen into the prison of nihilism and are bound by the tether of spontaneity (*ziran*).

Consequently, you produce conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), and as a result, you invite outflows (*āsrava*). To use such a state to compare with dhyāna is no different from the Lord of the River [who was humbled by the Ocean King].
How vast is the ocean! As for the Song dynasty Confucian scholars who claim that Buddhists used Laozi and Zhuangzi to embellish their teachings—how dare they so slander the Buddha?
Furthermore, the various sutras spoken by the Buddha all predate Laozi and Zhuangzi; how could it be that the Buddha first took them to embellish his own doctrine?
Since the Han dynasty, the various sutras have arrived in succession; though the phrasing was produced through translation, the meaning was in fact [already present].
Regarding the emergence from the Sanskrit: could it be that the translator himself took passages from Laozi and Zhuangzi to embellish the text?

Within the Translation Institute, all the eminent scholars gathered together—there were those who provided oral translations, those who performed the pen-recording, and those who verified the meaning.

How could it have been permitted for a single individual to privately take from Laozi and Zhuangzi to embellish the work? Once a Sanskrit manuscript was obtained, it might be translated several times; there may be omissions by a predecessor, which a successor [corrects].
One may rely upon the Sanskrit original to examine it in detail. When a later master has access to the Sanskrit original, he can correct the errors of his predecessors.

How could one possibly allow oneself to arbitrarily adopt the writings of Laozi and Zhuangzi at that time to embellish the text? However, when translating from Sanskrit into Chinese, one must necessarily employ the syntactic structures of this local dialect.
Since the books of Laozi and Zhuangzi are the preeminent works for discussing the Way in this land, many of their expressions were adopted; and yet—
The meanings are vastly different; one must not fail to examine this. For instance, when Laozi and Zhuangzi speak of "non-action" (*wuwei*), our Buddha also speaks of "non-action.
When Laozi and Zhuangzi speak of "no-self," our Buddha also speaks of "no-self. When Laozi and Zhuangzi speak of "the Way and its Virtue" (*daode*), our Buddha also speaks of "the Way and its Virtue.
How could these possibly be compared and treated as identical?

Formerly, Huizi composed the "Discourse on Pointing to Objects" (*Zhìwù lùn*), employing forceful sophistry to unify all things. Zhuangzi criticized this and thus composed the "Discourse on Equalizing Things" (*Qíwù lùn*).
Its essential aim was to set aside the self and accord with things; then, while things remain inherently disparate, the self remains naturally equanimous.
This is Zhuangzi’s discourse on approaching the Dao. Yet, it is a pity that he was unable to fully exhaust its meaning. Now, the non-uniformity of things is a delusive form;
the perception of the non-uniformity of things is a delusive emotion. If one uses principle to break through emotion, there will be no perception of non-uniformity;
if one uses nature to subsume form, there will be no form of non-uniformity. It is like a potter taking clay to make [vessels].
There are various vessels; when the deluded grasp at the forms of these vessels, the myriad appearances then diverge.

When the wise realize the substance of the vessel, they see that in reality there is but the single earth. Now, you merely wish to abandon yourself, yet the nature of your own self has not been shattered;
you merely wish to rely on external objects, yet the forms of those objects have not been rendered void. How can this be considered a definitive discourse?
Zhuangzi was at peace with time and lived in accordance with the natural order; he viewed life and death as a single path.
He was able to equate life and death, yet he had not yet forgotten them. If one has not yet forgotten life and death, how could one possibly be without life and death? His words say:

"As for parents toward their children, wherever they may go—east, west, south, or north—the children must simply follow their commands. As for yin and yang toward humans, they are no less than parents. Regarding that—
"He was close to death, yet I did not listen to him; I was indeed obstinate. What crime was there on his part?
He knew that it could not be averted and accepted it. Could he have truly forgotten life and death? My approach through the study of liberation is otherwise: the One Reality is eternally quiescent;
though there is birth, there is no birth. The wondrous essence is ever-present; though there is death, there is no death. Birth is but an illusion."
Birth is, in truth, non-birth; death is likewise illusory death, for death is non-death. Being thus, one may simply say that there is neither birth nor death.
How could it be merely a matter of man’s inability to overcome Heaven, and then resigning oneself to it?

Question: The sutra states that the realm of sentient beings arises from ignorance (*avidyā*). If ignorance has not yet arisen, then all is a single, undifferentiated reality; would there then be no realms of sentient beings? Answer:

The sutra speaks in terms of principle (*li*) to investigate their ultimate origin. It means that the two types of retribution—the primary (the physical body) and the secondary (the environment)—exist by virtue of karma.
Karma exists by virtue of ignorance, and ignorance exists by depending upon True Suchness (*tathatā*). However, [ignorance] is... [unreal].
This clarifies that there is truly no time when [delusion] first arose. As the Sūtra says: "The source of delusion is beginningless. Question:

If delusion is indeed beginningless, does it mean that delusion has existed from the very beginning? Answer: Both truth and delusion are equally beginningless; yet, while the essence of truth is unchanging, the essence of delusion is entirely empty.
Therefore, it is said: "From the beginning, there is no delusion. Furthermore, since delusion exists in dependence upon truth, one cannot say that truth itself is delusion.

It exists in dependence upon delusion, like a wick and its light. Although there is no sequence of before and after, the light necessarily exists in dependence upon the wick. Therefore it is said: "Originally there is no delusion.
Question: True Suchness is one alone; why is it divided into all sentient beings? Answer: There are those who have divisions and those who have not; [the former] is limited.
That which pertains to form is transcended by True Suchness (*tathatā*). That which possesses both unity and multiplicity is confined within the realm of numerical categories;
True Suchness transcends such numerical categories. How could there be a time when True Suchness is the unified whole, and another time when it is the individual parts?
Indeed, that which each sentient being individually possesses is precisely the possession of the entire body of this Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). The Dharma...
Regarding the totality of the *dhātu*: it refers to the entirety of what each sentient being possesses. From the perspective of its unchanging essence (*tattva*), there has never been any difference;
from the perspective of its functioning in accordance with conditions (*pratyaya*), there has never been any sameness.

Essence does not depart from function—thus they are the same yet different; function does not depart from essence—thus they are different yet the same. Since beginningless time, this has been so by nature.
It is so. Yet, if one seeks how these could be distinguished, can they truly be so obtained?
Konggonglong composed the *Shangzhi bian* (Compilation on Uprightness), in which he claimed that the learning of the Song Confucians all derived from Buddhism.

Now that the books of those various Confucians are fully extant, can it truly be found within Buddhism? If one were to say that what the various Confucians attained was precisely [that of] Buddhism...
As for the Way of this Master (Zhu Xi), he not only lacked knowledge of Confucianism, but was likewise ignorant of Buddhism.
Regarding the single diagram of the Great Ultimate (*Taiji*), he claimed it was obtained from the Buddhists. Now, the Great Ultimate Diagram is originally a core tenet of Confucianism;
that the Buddhists possessed it and transmitted it to Luoxi (Zhou Dunyi) means that Luoxi simply recovered his own family heirloom. How could this be considered theft?

"You say that I have stolen the learning of our Śākya [Buddha]. For instance, when Master I-ch'uan saw a monk leave the hall, he sighed and said, 'The rites and music of the Three Dynasties are all contained herein.
This was simply I-ch'uan seeing his own rites and music through the sight of a monk; how could it be considered stealing the learning of our Śākya?
As for the statements in your own writings, where you occasionally employ the scriptures of the Inner Canon (Buddhism), it merely appears as if you have derived them from the Śākya tradition."
One must recognize that while the phrasing may be identical, the underlying principles are in fact vastly different.

If you insist that Confucianism originated from Buddhism because Buddhist scriptures employ many Confucian terms, then one might as well claim that Buddhism originated from Confucianism. This is especially true when it comes to your forceful denunciation of Master Lu Jiuyuan (Hui-ang).
There is no factual basis for this; it is nothing more than a private conjecture of his intentions and a biased pointing out of his flaws.
The language is inflammatory and false, not a dispassionate assessment. From this, one can discern the cultivation of Konggu.
When Buddhists discuss *xing* (nature), they most often describe it in terms of cognition and awareness (*zhijue*).

However, what is called cognition and awareness is that wherein the numinous light shines forth alone, utterly transcending the sense organs and their objects; it is a cognition and awareness that is independent of conditions.

When Yangming propounded his doctrine of "innate knowledge" (*lingzhi*), he held that knowledge arises in dependence upon objects and perishes when the objects vanish. How could this be the light of the true nature? When Cheng and Zhu discussed *xing*, they directly [took it as]...
To speak in terms of principle: cognition is the mind; the principle inherent within the mind is its nature (*xing*);
when this is manifested through the four beginnings, it is emotion (*qing*). Yangming’s "innate knowledge" (*lingzhi*) is precisely this emotion.

If one wishes to observe it deeply, then in the interval between when this emotion is about to move and before it has moved, there is a state that is luminous and unclouded, neither good nor evil—this is the rectified mind. How could it be anything else?
Is this the principle of nature? Generally speaking, the learning of Yangming took Confucianism as its foundation and augmented it with Chan Buddhism;
thus, its profundity, subtlety, and ingenuity were so startling that they shocked the common world. Yet, people remained unaware that they were merely sitting within a state of "luminous clarity.
This luminous clarity is precisely the "grit" already sifted out by Hui-an (Zhang Zai), and it is what the Buddhists deeply condemn.
It is the very root of birth and death. To then use it to look down upon the present and the past, boasting that one has attained something unique—is this not an error?
The two elders Longxi and Jinxi lectured on the learning of Yangming and frequently employed Chan terminology; they did not, however, possess any genuine realization of it.
"Chan. This is using Confucianism to explain Chan. When one uses Confucianism to explain Chan, how could Chan not be Confucian?

Nevertheless, it is not surprising that this is merely the discourse of another school. But as for Zhuowu, he claimed that the learning of these two elders (Confucius and Mencius) can correspond to the purport of the "Separate Transmission.
He further asserted that no monk should lack this book at his bedside. How is this any different from calling a bell a jar?
Alas! In the past, people borrowed Chan terminology to augment Daoist learning; today, people conversely borrow Confucian terminology to represent the primary vehicle of our school.
The Great Way remains obscure, and the blind lead the blind in mutual delusion. I know not when this darkness will break into dawn.
The words of the Chan school (Zongmen) are like pearls on a tray: they roll, turn, slant, and intersect; they are ever-shifting and cannot be grasped.

How could they ever tolerate commentary? Lately, I have observed that several great masters frequently use the school to comment upon the teachings (Jiao), or use the teachings to comment upon the school.

Thus, the Heart-Seal of the Patriarchs has been cast aside in the wilderness. Someone may ask: "The school is the Buddha’s mind, while the teachings are the Buddha’s words. For what reason [do you disparage them]?"

He granted that they could be mutually understood, saying: "The principle of the school (zong) and the teaching (jiao) is one; how could they not be mutually understood? To clarify the school while turning one's back on the teaching is identical to the speech of demons.
To expound the teaching while remaining deluded about the school results merely in frivolous discourse. The essential point lies in awakening to the underlying meaning upon hearing the words;

one must by all means avoid stagnating in the language and giving rise to emotional attachments. It is not only the language of the school-gate that cannot be pointed out or annotated; even interpreting the meaning based on the sutras is called being an enemy of the Buddha."
The Buddha’s words are subtle, profound, vast, and great; they cannot be fathomed or fully comprehended.

Even if the sages of this world were to share the seat and expound upon them, each person would differ, and it would be difficult for even one person to grasp the Buddha’s secret intent. Although they do not grasp the Buddha’s secret intent, they nevertheless all...
One does not contradict the Buddha; therefore, those who comment on the sutras may each present their own perspective to mutually illuminate one another.

The essential point is simply that the fundamental principles are not lost and that one does not contradict the Buddha. Why must it be that what was done in the past is wrong and what is done now is right?
"What others deem wrong, I take to be right. The great masters who propagated the scriptures during the Tang and Song dynasties composed commentaries on various sutras;

although it cannot be said for certain whether those that have been transmitted to the present day accord with the Buddha’s intent, an examination of their essential principles reveals they all do not contradict the Buddha. For beginners, these works serve as steps and ladders. Furthermore—
What is so wrong with that? It simply requires one to delve deeply into the divine principles; it depends entirely upon the person themselves.

Prior to the Jiajing and Longqing eras of our dynasty, those who studied the Classics were for the most part bound by ancient commentaries, not daring to look beyond them. They were like those born blind leaning on a staff, unable to take even a single step without it;
their pedantry was hardly worth observing. During the Wanli era, Xuelang arose and shook things up, completely setting aside all [the old constraints].
This commentary alone elaborates upon the scriptural text, providing a singular pleasure for those who lecture.

Nevertheless, there are those of frivolous and arrogant disposition who, wishing to imitate it, recklessly indulge their own arbitrary opinions and hastily carve it into woodblocks. The harm of such acts—contravening the scriptures and betraying the sages—is far more than mere vulgarity.

The Mind-Seal of Shaoshi—how could it ever fall into the realm of literary ornamentation? The ancients merely employed words as a means of guidance; they first allowed them to hang upon the lips and mouths.

Yet these were all浑朴 (hún pǔ, simple and unadorned) and 簡直 (jiǎn zhí, straightforward and direct), intended to point directly at the mark for others. It was not for the purpose of boasting of understanding or displaying cleverness, nor was it merely for external embellishment and aesthetic appeal.

In later generations, this was by no means the case; they carved out ornate characters and chiseled refined phrases, clustering flowers and gathering brocade, exhausting their ingenuity in contrivance and manipulation.
Each vies for novelty; how could this be anything other than the intent of lewd artifice? It violates the original character of the patch-robed monk.
Thus, the principle is obscured by the words, and the Way is lost through speech. How difficult it is, then, to trigger the spark of spiritual awakening beneath even a single word or half a phrase!
A certain scholar said to the Master, "When the moon shines upon the paper window, I hurriedly took up my rush mat to face it;
it was quite another realm. The Master asked, "Before the moon had risen upon the window, where was that realm? The scholar said, "It was non-existent.

The Master asked, "After the moon has set behind the window, where is that realm again? The scholar likewise said, "Non-existent. The Master said, "If it is non-existent before and after, where is it in the middle?"

"How could there be anything in between? It is just like when the moon is directly above the window; if one does not give rise to thoughts of grasping at its appearance, where would the objective realm be?
The Master said, "In that case, you do not see the moon or the window; how then can you know that there is an objective realm?

[The student] said, "I know that this objective realm certainly does not exist on the side of the person, because if there is no moon and no window, then there is no objective realm. [The Master] said, "Nor does it certainly exist elsewhere..."

By the moonlit window: because there is no person, there is no objective realm (*viṣaya*). Since both the moonlit window and the person are each non-existent, how could they possibly exist when combined?
Thus, this objective realm is exactly like the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit;
it arises as a false appearance solely due to the discrimination of deluded thoughts. It is not only this; the body, mind, world, and all things of prosperity [are likewise so].
Honor and disgrace, profit and loss, life and death, calamity and fortune—none are otherwise than this.

If you can discern and penetrate these through and through, then both mind and objects will vanish, and the original radiance will be perfectly complete. Within the state of no-objects, there is the true realm; fundamentally, there is neither coming nor going.

It is neither manifest nor obscure; the Buddhas have realized it and provisionally designated it as "Nirvana. How could the fleeting moments of a single kṣaṇa ever hope to approximate even a fraction of its reality?
Question: "In practicing Chan, one must give rise to the 'doubt-mind' (*yiqing*). When the doubt-mind does not arise, what should be done? Answer:
"This is a common malady among students of recent times. The reason the doubt-mind does not arise is simply that the sense of urgency regarding birth and death (*shengsi*) is not keen enough.
If one were truly like someone living in a dilapidated house where a fire suddenly breaks out, with only a single door and no other way out—how could one not [give rise to it]?"
One must race forward with urgency to emerge from it. Thus, if one presses with one part, there will be doubt in one part; if one presses with ten parts, there will be doubt in ten parts.
There has never been a case where one presses and yet does not doubt, nor has there ever been a case where one doubts and yet does not awaken.

However, the arising of this state of doubt originates from a heart of intense inquiry; it is not something that can be contrived through deliberation or forced to arise. It is, for example, like a parent...
Upon hearing the news of a funeral by sudden accident, I looked up to heaven and wailed once; my heart was nearly broken.

How, then, could one employ deliberation and fabrication to force such a response? If there were even the slightest intention to force it, the sentiment of grief would instead become thin and insipid.
The late Master Shouchang once said: "When I first began, I had no understanding of Zen practice at all.
One day, while reading the *Transmission of the Lamp*, before I had even finished the volume, a sudden sense of doubt and distress arose within me.
I forgot both sleep and food for eight months until, all of a sudden, I shattered the lacquer bucket. Today, each of you is deliberating: how to apply effort, how to exert yourself?"
Advance! Though you may deliberate with the utmost precision, you do not know how many layers of obstacles you have already added.
The three characters for "practicing the work" (gongfu) are already spoken out of necessity; they are already a concealment of the true person.
How much more so today’s incessant exhortations? Today, my fellow practitioners are not those who do not recognize the practice of the work.

Now, the true illness lies in explaining too elaborately and recognizing [the student's state] too early. To meet [the student] with preconceived intentions, or to anticipate and avoid [certain responses] based on prior thoughts—both are manifestations of the "thieving mind.

In antiquity, those who served as teachers merely found it difficult to apply their tongs and hammers skillfully and to exert pressure through rigorous interrogation, so that those who aspired to the Way would do so without conscious deliberation or intellectual artifice, yet their inner feelings were spontaneously stirred and their spirit naturally roused.
Bravely pressing forward, one possesses a sense of being unable to stop even if one wished to; thus, suddenly striking upon it, the great matter is completed.
Therefore, I have often said that the single thought of practicing Zen is like General Li’s arrow:
with spirit leaping forth, it shoots through stone and sinks its feathers, yet one does not know how it comes to reach this point. If there were even the slightest deliberation—
The mind cannot enter. Those who practice Chan today are all like those who aim and shoot at a stone;
failing to penetrate it, they blame their lack of precision in their aim. Are they not profoundly deluded?
Question: "A single thought tied to the slightest hair leads to the karmic causes for the three miserable realms; a fleeting emotion arises and one is shackled for ten thousand kalpas.
If, right now, you are being instructed to contemplate the *huatou* (critical phrase), this is precisely a 'tied thought' and precisely the arising of emotion.

How can one avoid these karmic causes and shackles? Answer: "The slightest trace of emotional perception cannot avoid saṃsāra. Right now, while the *huatou* still remains, there is the doubt-mind (*yiqing*)."
This has not yet been explained. Who allows that one can escape birth and death? It is simply this focused mindfulness and this state of doubt;
these are worldly dharmas borrowed as causes for transcendence, what the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* calls "using illusion to cultivate illusion.

When you reach the point where the path of the mind is cut off, vast and transparent with nothing to rely upon, then both person and phenomena vanish together, and both mind and objects are discarded. Is there still anything left?
Can one attain it through focused mindfulness? Can one attain it through the state of doubt? Can one be bound by karmic causes?
This focused mindfulness is the gateway to non-mindfulness; this state of doubt is the method for forgetting emotions.

It is the Great Path by which sentient beings escape the mundane and enter the sacred, and the subtle skillful means by which all the Sages gather, transform, and deliver living beings. Such is the teaching of all the Buddhas.

Who is there who does not experience this? Why then do you alone harbor doubts regarding it? The monk said, "The *Perfect Enlightenment Sūtra* states: 'To know illusion is to be free from it; no expedient means are required.
To be free from illusion is awakening itself; there is no gradual progression. How could there ever have been such a thing as 'fixing the mind'?

[The Master] said, "The crux of this sūtra lies in the single character 'know' (*zhī*). When one truly knows it, there are indeed no expedient means—this is precisely what is meant by 'the path of the mind is cut off.'"
The locus is vast and penetrating, without dependence. Yet, how many people throughout past and present have truly known it upon being pointed out?
Since you have not yet been able to know it immediately, surely there must be expedient means prior to such knowledge. The sutras contain explicit clarifications; why not go and examine them?
