Question: Baizhang taught people only to let go completely, which is like the sun rising when the clouds part; is this not direct?
As for later generations being taught to contemplate the "head-word" (huatou) and searching for it by every possible means—is this not an excessive amount of business? Answer:

If one were truly able to hear such a teaching and immediately let go of everything with one’s whole being, it would indeed be a matter of simplifying affairs. However, as for me teaching you now to let go—do you still...?
Can you let go? Even if you can let go, you are still sitting within this "letting go.
Even if this "letting go" itself can be let go of, you still harbor a conceptual understanding of that letting go. Even if you do not form such a conceptual understanding...
This state of not forming intellectual understanding yet being unable to let go is, in short, like a monkey climbing a tree: it abandons one branch only to grasp another.
For this reason, the masters of former generations specifically employed extraordinary skillful means (*upāya*) to advance them; these skillful means are numerous.
It is not limited to a single path. For the most part, it is because one cannot see through or pass beyond a single word or half-phrase;

thus, one searches with a hundred stratagems and presses forward with a thousand maneuvers. As the state of doubt becomes increasingly bitter and the self-exhortation more urgent, one suddenly breaks through.
When there is nowhere to which one can point as an object of comparison, then birth-and-death and nirvana are but a dream from yesterday;

enlightenment and afflictions are both merely flowers in the sky. What, then, remains that cannot be let go? Thus, for people today, contemplating the "head-word" (huatou) is simply a skillful means for letting go.
Question: Baizhang only said that once one has penetrated beyond the three phrases, that is where the student lets go of body and life.

Yet later generations established so many formal gateways and produced so many strange and eccentric doctrines; this is all because their understanding of the mind was not yet severed, hence such things occurred.
Answer: Lately, in the region of Chu, there have been many who advocate this view precisely because they themselves lack any genuine realization.

One merely takes such texts as the *Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch*, the *Extensive Record of Baizhang*, and the *Essentials of Huangbo’s Mind*, and attempts to grasp their meaning through intellectual understanding alone.
Consequently, one conceives within the mind an image of a state of empty stillness, calling it "the atmosphere before joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure have been aroused.
Yet, regarding the pivotal mechanism of the Patriarchs' teaching, there is no way to break through it; thus, one slanders the various masters. Above...

The informal sermons in the hall, the picking up and commenting on verses, and the answering of questions—all these arise because the mind of conceptual understanding has not yet been severed; thus, such matters exist.
Little do they realize that for one who has directly penetrated through the three phrases, the mind of conceptual understanding is already severed.

A thousand mechanisms are suddenly unleashed, naturally allowing for seven maneuvers and eight traversals, turning heaven and earth upside down. Without a drop of water, waves and billows are stirred; without a single thread, the net of heaven is spread.
This ground is for the treading of dragons and elephants; it is not something a donkey can endure.

When practitioners of the Way reach the point where their diligent effort presses them to the brink of awakening yet they have not yet awakened, and their conceptual understanding has not yet ceased, clever insights often arise abruptly.
This is called the realm of intellectual cleverness, and it is also called the army of demons beneath the tree. Thus...
One must cut them off and extinguish them completely; only then will there be a path for progress, and the Great Matter may be expected.

If you can skillfully see that all is extinguished, then before your parents were even born, you will stare wide-eyed with the True Eye open. To realize this is not impossible; yet, if you look toward the matter beneath the patched robe, it remains as it was.
It remains as if separated by a river. You must undergo a thorough refinement under the bitter hammer and tongs;
only then will you penetrate the profound barrier above and master the myriad gateways of differentiation, whereby the Great Matter is completed.

The single word "awakening" (wu) derives its name from the existence of delusion. People today have completely misunderstood this word; they assume that awakening occurs only when one can understand some principle, and thus they claim it is "awakening.

They do not realize that if there is a principle to be understood, then the one who understands that principle is called false consciousness (*vikalpa-vijñāna*), and the principle that is understood is called a false object (*vikalpa-viṣaya*). How could this be anything other than delusion? There is goodness...

When knowledge perceives things in this way, it immediately claims that their fundamental nature is empty and quiescent, asserting that there are no manifold principles and that only when all things are utterly extinguished does one reach the true radiance of the original ground.
Yet they do not realize that the very presence of "emptiness and quiescence" means it is no longer truly empty and quiescent.
This knowing of emptiness and quiescence is called deluded consciousness; the existence of emptiness and quiescence is called a deluded object. It is not through delusion...
"What is it? [The Master asked. "There was a lay devotee who urged you to build a vihāra," [the disciple replied. The Master said, "I eat one *sheng* of food a day and sleep on seven feet at night;

what is the use of overexerting myself for the offerings of the faithful? The devotee said, "To establish a monastery is the legacy of former Buddhas; it is to welcome those with the potential for awakening."
The Bodhisattva’s compassion and vows—why must one strive for such lofty heights as to confine oneself to the narrow scope of self-benefit? It is said:
"Only when the Way is full and virtue is established can one truly extend a helping hand. For one as dull-witted as I to be in haste to receive others is merely to bring disgrace upon myself."
Moreover, what is currently lacking in the world is not monasteries. [Rather, it is that they] act as decoys for fame and snares for profit;
they nourish the greed of later students and level the teachings of former masters—nothing is more extreme than this.

The reason I hasten away and do not dare to look back even once is not because I am violating the regulations of the Buddhas of the past or abolishing the rules of Baizhang; it is simply because I wish to remain uninvolved.
To assimilate [to others] means to lose oneself for the sake of becoming another. I would rather avoid others to preserve myself. It is not that preserving oneself is considered virtuous;

however, while preserving oneself may still allow one to serve as a human being, losing oneself inevitably leads to skillfully deceiving the multitude. This is to give rein to one's evil and recklessly employ it.
Yet they take much. I would rather take little and use frugally. It is not that I consider frugal use to be a mark of worthiness;
however, frugal use can still nourish integrity, whereas reckless expenditure inevitably leads to conflict with the multitude and fosters greed.
A scholar cited ancient precedents to judge the present and pass judgment on the character of individuals. The Master said: "The merits and faults of individuals are not easily discerned;
they cannot be measured by the standards of old cases. For instance, deposing a ruler or executing a ruler was unheard of in antiquity; it began only with Tang and Wu.

If one were to judge by citing ancient precedents, then Tang and Wu would have to be considered disloyal subjects. Regarding the matter of going back and forth five times [to seek counsel], this too was unprecedented in antiquity.
It exists. Its existence began with Yi Yin. If one were to judge by citing antiquity, then Yi Yin would be deemed disloyal.

Thus we know that there are matters universally approved throughout the ages that must necessarily be rejected today, and likewise matters universally condemned throughout the ages that must necessarily be accepted today.
This applies not only to the distinction between ancient and modern; it holds even for the Spring and Autumn period.

Second, regarding Confucius: the era of his birth was the same, and the circumstances of his life were likewise the same; yet, as for when to serve or retire, and whether to remain long or hasten away, there must necessarily have been differences.
Although there were differences, how could one judge right and wrong between them? Generally speaking, those who have realized the Way possess an unfathomable interplay of illumination and function;

whether moving vertically or horizontally, in accordance with or contrary to the flow, nothing fails to accord with the standard. You alone were able to grasp his mind, and thus you may [be considered his equal].
In discussing the scholars of the world, the Buddhist doctrine of "mind-only" differs from the principle of the "One Thread" (yīguàn) taught by Confucius.

The intent of the One Thread lies in breaking through the tendency to scrutinize phenomena individually; thus he said, "My Way is unified and runs through all things. This, however, was a provisional expression. If one investigates deeply...
If so, what is this "one"? And what is it that this "one" penetrates? When the whole mind creates phenomena, the whole phenomenon is the mind.
It is like a statue cast from gold; the statue is not outside the gold. It is like a reflection appearing in a mirror; the reflection exists within the mirror.
This is precisely the meaning of "Mind-Only."
Confucius said, "When it is grasped, it remains; when it is abandoned, it perishes. Its coming and going have no fixed time, and its direction is unknown.
This was precisely spoken with reference to the deluded mind. Commentators say: "How could the mind actually have coming and going? It is merely spoken of in terms of being grasped or abandoned."
Since it can both be grasped and relinquished, how could it not be illusory? Question:

Many who have attained prior awakening have said that the three teachings share one principle; is this so? Answer: Since the teachings are divided into three, those who forcibly claim they are the same are deluded.
Since the principle is in fact only one, those who forcibly claim they are different are confused. Therefore, let us speak from the perspective of their differences.
Thus, it is not only that the three teachings differ; even within the single teaching of Buddhism, the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna differ.
Even within the same Mahāyāna, the provisional and the ultimate differ. For since the capacities of sentient beings are myriad and diverse, the teachings are not of a single form.
If one speaks from the perspective of their commonality, then it is not only that the three teachings are one, but even all Māras, non-Buddhists, and ordinary beings [share this].

Livelihoods and other such activities all accord with the True Dharma; for there are no teachings outside of principle, and thus teachings must ultimately return to principle. This is similar to the Confucian teachings here:

these beings within this realm have physical forms that arise and spirits that develop, yet they daily incline toward desire. If one does not restrain them through regulation, how can they be brought to a halt?
Therefore, the Sage, in accordance with the circumstances of the time and observing human nature, expounded benevolence and righteousness for their sake and established [these principles].
The administrative framework is transformed through ritual and music and bound by penal law so that disorder does not arise.
Even if the Buddha were to reside in the land of Zhendan (China) and preach sutras on worldly laws, would he not surpass the Duke of Zhou and Confucius?

However, since sentient beings are already constrained by the Confucian classics and cling to names and appearances, the realm of names and appearances instead becomes a place of shackles and fetters. How could this be...?

This was indeed the intention of the Confucian sages. From this arose Laozi and Zhuangzi, who expounded the Way of non-being (*śūnyatā*) and spontaneity (*svabhāva*), enabling those who heard them to attain a state of leisure, vastness, and transcendence, so as not to be burdened by external things; they served as a skillful means for entering the Way.
As for what our Buddha taught, however, it is the actual Dharma that transcends both humanity and heaven, the reality that exhausts all principles and fulfills human nature.

This is learning. What the Master [Confucius] once said—"I wish to remain without words"—and what the descendant of Du [Zengzi] referred to as "hearing that which lies beyond the written word," how could they possibly differ from this?
Thus we know that while the principle is one, the teachings cannot help but be differentiated;

yet though the teachings are differentiated, the principle has never been anything other than one. Those who cling to difference or cling to sameness are all engaged in frivolous discourse (*prapañca*).
Nowadays, when people see the Buddhas, they immediately conceive thoughts of them as extraordinary and marvelous; yet regarding themselves, they conceive thoughts of being inferior and lowly.
They do not know that the Buddhas are merely ordinary people living their natural lot, and that ordinary people are merely Buddhas who have failed to live up to their own nature.
They cast aside the precious treasure within their own reach, while willingly accepting hardships beyond their station. How lamentable!
Question: When Dharma certified Shen Guang, he was merely verifying the essence of the mind of non-thought.
Why do later generations further say that "non-mind still leaves one separated by a single barrier"? Answer: It is because his vision had not yet reached complete penetration;
he remained stuck within the conceptual trap of non-mind. Once a trap is formed, it is no longer true non-mind. Therefore, one must once again exert oneself with intense alertness and brilliance.
To overturn it with a single kick—whether one is with mind or without mind—both constitute slander. Shen Guang performed three prostrations and stood in his place;
he realized this very point.
Someone asked: "Many masters have extensively explained that sudden enlightenment must rely upon gradual cultivation.

Yet Zhongfeng alone did not permit the doctrine of gradual cultivation, stating that as long as habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) have not been eliminated, it is simply because the awakened mind has not yet become perfect;

one must strive to seek thorough penetration. Between these two views, I do not know which is correct. I replied: "Once the awakened mind is perfected, the life-root (*mūla*) is suddenly severed. Although habitual tendencies may still exist..."
The karmic breath has not yet been eliminated; one need only attain right view so that it is not obscured, and habitual tendencies will naturally and gradually subside.
There is no need for any separate practice. It is like a woodcutter who, having severed the root of a tree, finds that although the branches and leaves remain, they wither and fall away in no time.

There is no necessity for a separate method to cause them to fall. If the realization of the mind is not yet perfected, then the life-root has not been severed, and habitual tendencies will continue to run rampant.

Birth. Since suppressing and treating [the afflictions] proved ineffective, it was necessary to strive for thorough awakening. Furthermore, examining the intent of Zhongfeng, it is not that he entirely disallowed gradual cultivation;
rather, it was because at that time, as soon as a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) had just gained an initial entry point, they would claim to have attained thorough realization.
When their habitual tendencies (vāsanā) were subsequently not eliminated, they instead blamed it on the fact that their gradual cultivation had not yet reached its goal. Thus, Zhongfeng...
This is merely a statement made out of narrow-mindedness.

Deng Huoqu of Xishu compiled the *Nanxun Lu* (Record of Southern Inquiry), wherein he pointed to the state where the spiritual mechanism has not yet been activated and termed it "non-arising" (*anutpāda*).
This is simply his own personal and biased interpretation; it is not the orthodox teaching of our Buddha. When our Buddha spoke of "non-arising," it was because ordinary people...

Now, when one observes within the Dharma-realm that there is a blazing proliferation of birth, it is because the impulse of birth gives rise to delusion, leading to the creation of karma and the summoning of retribution;
thus, saṃsāra continues without ceasing, with no time of escape in sight. Therefore, our Buddha taught the Dharma of non-arising to shatter this [delusion].

He declared that all phenomena do not arise from themselves, do not arise from another, do not arise from both, and do not arise without cause. Since they do not arise through any of these four ways, then...
In reality, there is no arising. To speak of "arising" is merely because the eyes contain a cataract, leading one to falsely perceive flowers in the sky.

If one takes the state where the stimulus is still and has not yet been triggered as "non-arising," then one must necessarily take the state where the stimulus moves and has already been triggered as "arising.
If that which is moving and already triggered is taken as "arising," then non-arising would ultimately result in arising; how could this be considered true non-arising?
Once, a friend rose at dawn and asked Huoqu, "When one has just awakened from sleep and there is no time of discursive thought, what is that?
Huo said, "This is precisely the state before one's parents were born; it cannot be described. The Sixth Patriarch said: "Do not think of good..."
"Do not think of evil. Which one is the original face of Elder Ming? This refers precisely to this.

I, the fool, say that if upon waking from sleep there is no thought, or if one falls into a state of non-discrimination (*avyākṛta*), then this is the totality of ignorance (*avidyā*). Can this be pointed out as the "original face"?
Furthermore, within the teachings there are five states of mindlessness, all of which lack both wholesome and unwholesome thoughts; can these be pointed out [as the original face]?
Is this not the original face? As for the Sixth Patriarch’s instruction to Master Shiming, its purport is quite distinct.
When Shiming requested the Dharma, it was certainly not a state of non-recording (amūrchita). When Shiming turned his light back upon himself, it was likewise not a state of non-recording.
Since it was neither of these, it transcends the two thoughts of good and evil; what else could it be but the original face?
Huo Qu said: "When one is fast asleep and not dreaming, that is precisely the realm where there is neither good nor evil.
The Chan school calls this the 'Great Ocean of Quiescent Extinction. Students study for nothing other than this; Buddhas realize nothing other than this.
I say that when one is fast asleep and without dreams, one must recognize the true master’s place of descent. Once the true master’s place of descent is recognized, then—"
Whether asleep or awake, whether dreaming or not dreaming, it is all the Great Ocean of Quiescent Extinction (*mahā-śānti-nirvāṇa-samudra*).
When the pillow falls from the high peak, one realizes this. Now, it is directly pointed out that being fast asleep without dreaming is called the Great Ocean of Quiescent Extinction.
Thus, one would mistakenly identify the deluded state of ignorance as the true nature; how could this not be an error?
When masters meet, their dynamic function transcends all bounds; whether they praise or revile, they do not fall into conventional patterns.
If one attempts to fathom this with ordinary conceptual consciousness, one will be far, far removed from it. Long ago, there was a laywoman who supported a monk residing in a hermitage. Once...
She sent a young woman to offer alms. One day, she had the woman hold the monk firmly and asked him, "At this very moment, what is it like?
The monk said, "A withered tree leans against a cold cliff; for three winters there is no warmth. When the woman returned, she reported this to the old woman (the nun).
The old woman said, "In three years, I have only managed to support one worldly monk. She then ordered the hermitage to be burned down and drove him out. That monk ultimately departed.
Their actions were beyond words. These two men were utterly inverted in their ways. The laywoman (po) possessed the capacity to reach the heavens;
the monk (seng) possessed the stratagem to enter the earth. The laywoman had the hand of one who chases elephants; the monk had the scheme of one who traps tigers. Thus, a former master remarked:
"Casually sitting and cutting off the surging tide of heaven, in the end his body has not a single drop of water. This may truly be called penetrating.
This has penetrated to the very depths of my entrails. Having been startled by the monk’s assessment of my worldly sentiments, I went to that monk to seek out my faults;
because he told me that I must simply eliminate deluded thoughts, I was rebuked and sent away. Did you truly see this monk in a dream?
Question: Some masters say that those who practice Chan must first study the teachings to understand their general meaning before they can apply themselves to the work;

otherwise, they fear falling into heterodoxy. Other masters say that one need not study the teachings when practicing Chan, for such study may increase intellectual pathways and obstruct the gate of self-awakening.
Between these two views, it is unknown which is correct. Answer: In some cases it is appropriate to study the teachings, while in others it is not.
Regarding the teachings: this depends on the differences in the capacities of individuals; one cannot insist upon a single approach for all.

For those of brilliant intelligence, why would they need to study the teachings before they can engage in Chan meditation? As for those of duller faculties, they may find it difficult even to comprehend the teachings, let alone practice Chan.

Furthermore, there are those with heavy karmic obstructions who must first rely on the power of the teachings to cultivate themselves and eliminate their coarse attachments. If [the obstructions are...]
For those of lesser capacity, it is sufficient to enter directly with a single blade; why must one deliberate over every preceding and succeeding step, thereby creating obstacles for oneself?
However, if one truly falls into heterodoxy or stagnates halfway through the practice of Chan meditation, it is essential to receive the guidance of a master;
this is not something that those who merely study the scriptures can save themselves from.
Question: A master said, "In practicing Chan, one must investigate the 'meaningless phrase' (wuyi ju). One must not investigate the 'meaningful phrase' (youyi ju).
Those who enter through the meaningful phrase mostly fall halfway; only those who enter through the meaningless phrase can reach their destination. Is this so?
He said: "In Chan practice, it matters not whether there is a 'meaningful phrase' (*yìjù*) or a 'meaningless phrase. What is valued is that you do not fall into a trap upon the path of meaning.
For instance, when the numinous light shines forth alone, completely detached from the sense organs and their objects—this was Baizhang’s ‘meaningful phrase.
Can you recognize this solitary shining? The very moment you wish to recognize it, you have already fallen into the realm of the sense organs and their objects. As it is said:
"Radiant light, quiescent and illuminating, pervades as many grains of sand as there are in the Ganges. These are the meaningful words of Zhang Zhuo.

Can you recognize that which pervades the sands of the Ganges? The moment you seek to recognize it, you are already obscured by clouds. For the most part, this was the case prior to the Sixth Patriarch.
Most [teachings] prior to the Sixth Patriarch consisted of sentences with explicit meaning; those after the Sixth Patriarch mostly consist of sentences without explicit meaning.

The skillful means differ, but in reality there is no superiority or inferiority. Students who investigate this must seek its true essence deeply. If one seeks its true essence deeply, it matters not whether the sentences have meaning or not;
ultimately, one cannot fathom them through intellectual calculation. When one cannot fathom them through calculation, doubt naturally arises.
Once the spirit of inquiry has arisen, dullness and distraction will naturally vanish. Once dullness and distraction have vanished, the sense faculties and their objects will naturally fall away.

Once the sense faculties and their objects have fallen away, the numinous light will naturally manifest. Once the numinous light has manifested, one turns back to look at both meaningful and meaningless phrases.

All are like the sky-like heavens or tattered rags. If one does not seek their true meaning deeply, but merely attempts to grasp them through the literal words, then even those "meaningless" phrases—such as "three pounds of hemp," "a dried piece of dung," and so forth—would all possess a transmissible meaning.

This is precisely what is found in the current commentaries on the *Gusō* (Verses on Ancient Cases) by the four schools and in various texts such as the *Shaolin Biyao* (Secret Essentials of Shaolin). How could such works ever penetrate the pivotal mechanism of the Ultimate?
Ah! Question:
The teachings regarding the Pure Land have been analyzed in detail by various masters. Yet, as for the claim that Chan meditation is inferior to the Pure Land, this doubt remains unresolved.
Answer: This lies with the master who advocates for the Pure Land; therefore, he employs exaltation and praise to encourage others to take refuge in it.
This is merely a matter of reciting the Buddha’s name. If one discusses it from the perspective of ultimate truth, there is certainly no distinction of superiority or inferiority between them.

In Zen, the essential point is to awaken to one’s own mind; in the practice of nianfo (reciting the Buddha’s name), the essential point is likewise to awaken to one’s own mind. Although the entryways differ, the destination reached is the same.

However, those who reach the destination through Zen may lack the karmic affinity for the Pure Land, which constitutes a slight difference. Nevertheless, once the light of the mind is manifested, one has already interfused with the vital energy of all Buddhas.

[The Master] replied: "Why must it be the Pure Land? Whether in the heavens or among humans, one may entrust oneself wherever one pleases; having severed all longing and aversion, why not [choose] the Pure Land?
Moreover, if you wish to draw near to and make offerings to the various Buddhas, this too depends on nothing more than a single turn of thought.
Why should the Pure Land be difficult? Someone said: "If both paths lead to the same destination, they are indeed no different. However, as for the practice of Chan meditation..."

As for those who have attained awakening, they cease their lingering in the realms of humans and devas. For those who have not yet awakened but practice the recitation of the Buddha's name, rebirth [in the Pure Land] is still possible.

Judging by this comparison, it seems that the practice of Chan meditation does not equal the practice of reciting the Buddha’s name. It is said: "Those who attain rebirth without having attained awakening must certainly recite the Buddha’s name with the utmost sincerity."

If those who practice Chan meditation are likewise as sincere and earnest as they, then even if they remain temporarily stalled within the realms of humans and devas, their awakening will not be far off.
When they emerge once more, their roots of wisdom will suddenly blossom, and they will transcend to realize Bodhi beyond measure.

As for those who recite the Buddha's name but have not yet attained awakening, although they may achieve rebirth in the Pure Land, they will ultimately fall into the womb-prisons of the City of Doubt; there they must wait until their emotional consciousnesses are completely refined away.
Only then can one first behold the Buddha. How could this not surpass those who practice Chan?

Generally speaking, while the two gates of Chan and Pure Land differ in how they respond to individual capacities, their efficacy is no different. For those suited to the Pure Land, the Pure Land path excels Chan;
for those suited to Chan, the practice of Chan excels the Pure Land. To do otherwise is not merely to fall short—it will certainly result in failure. This is what students must understand.
One should carefully discern this.
Question: Regarding Yongming’s “Fourfold Selection,” it states that while Pure Land may be practiced without Chan, Chan cannot be without Pure Land.
This seems to suggest that Chan practice is inferior to Pure Land. Answer: Yongming’s Fourfold Selection is likewise a form of rhetorical emphasis and praise.

This is merely an exhortation to return to the practice of *nien-fo*. To speak of it in truth: for those who possess meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) yet whose habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) remain heavy, there may indeed be the peril of "shadowy realms" (*antarābhava*).
However, their merit lies in daily practice; they should constantly apply mindfulness so that the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*) do not grow dim.

This is not a matter of relying solely on the Pure Land. If one recites the Buddha’s name and succeeds in beholding Amitābha, one will truly have no cause for concern regarding the attainment of enlightenment.

Yet, before one has seen [the Pure Land], how could there not be the perilous realm of the *gandharva* (intermediate state) to be feared? For as long as right vision (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*) has not opened, the realm of the *gandharva* will not be shattered;
and as long as the realm of the *gandharva* is not shattered, karmic obstructions (*karmāvaraṇa*) will be difficult to escape.

Even though Amitābha’s compassionate vow embraces all, what can it do for one who is blind and cannot see the sun? Therefore, those who attain birth [in the Pure Land] without having realized this are but one or two out of a hundred.

Question: Is it permissible to practice Chan meditation while concurrently cultivating the Pure Land? Answer: The merit of Chan meditation lies solely in the value of unifying the mind on a single path.

If the mind is divided between two ends, there will be no accomplishment whatsoever. For instance, if a Chan practitioner harbors even a single thought of waiting for enlightenment, it becomes a great obstacle;

if they harbor a single thought of fearing they will not attain enlightenment, it becomes a great obstacle; if they harbor a single thought of desiring immediate enlightenment, it likewise becomes a great obstacle.
The mind itself is a great obstacle; how much more so are the various pleasant matters of longing for and admiring the Pure Land?

How much more so are the anxieties over not attaining enlightenment and thus failing to be born in the Pure Land, or over failing to be born there after one has already attained enlightenment? All such concerns belong to the "thieving mind" (*tōshin*); you should swiftly and utterly eradicate them.

However, apart from formal inquiry (*shōsan*), you may engage in all other practices—such as prostrating to the Buddha and reciting his name—as they arise, allowing them to proceed spontaneously and concurrently with your practice.
It is not abandoned; it is like the ordinary acts of dressing and eating. Thus, the Pure Land is both not practiced as a separate endeavor and yet is practiced simultaneously.

Once the Great Matter has been realized, if one’s aspiration is to personally behold the various Buddhas or to guide sentient beings, there is no reason why one cannot vow to be reborn there; for this is birth within non-birth.
Although all phenomena (*dharmas*) are numerous, they are ultimately exhausted by their state of dependence. Whatever is dependent is known to be illusory. For example, space is not empty of itself;
it is empty in dependence upon form. Form is not form of itself; it is form in dependence upon space. If form exists in dependence upon space, is that form truly form?
If space exists in dependence upon form, is that space truly space? By reasoning from this, one knows that whether regarding the present or the past, or the great...
Whether small, whether beautiful or ugly, whether true or false—none are otherwise. All lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Furthermore, they are all established only by depending upon a single moment of thought. If a single moment of thought does not arise, then all phenomena have nothing upon which to depend;

if they have nothing upon which to depend, then each individual phenomenon likewise has nothing upon which to depend. If each has nothing upon which to depend, then although all phenomena may appear to be arrayed in dense profusion...

All things are manifestations of light that is entirely without dependence; this is the seal of the true reality (*dharmatā*). Therefore it is said: "When one person attains Buddhahood, even walls, fences, tiles, and rubble all attain Buddhahood."

All phenomena ultimately depend upon conditions; thus, one certainly knows them to be illusory. If one’s innate capacity is profound, by virtue of that dependence on conditions, one immediately realizes there is no self.
Just as the self is originally without a self, yet depends on others to have a self; so too, others are originally without a self, yet depend on the self to exist as others.

Furthermore, just as one substance is non-self and depends on two to become one, and two substances are non-self and depend on one to become two, it is because they are non-self that they possess dependence;
and because they possess dependence, their non-selfhood becomes even more evident.
Applying this reasoning, whether it be body or mind, person or object, or even the encompassing of heaven and earth and the vast expanse of empty space—all are [non-self].

This is the pervasive light of the single non-self (*anātman*). Once everything is unified within this single non-self, the self need not be expanded to accommodate things, for there is nothing that is not the self;
and things need not be gathered to be assimilated into the self, for there is nothing that is not the self.
To understand this clearly is called the study of the sages (*ārya-śikṣā*); to be ignorant of it is called being a heterodox path (*tīrthika*); and to realize it is called [enlightenment].

The Sage. One who loses this is called an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). Although the teachings established by the Sages of the Three Teachings differ, that which they necessarily share is this absence of self (*anātman*).
Confucius realized this; therefore, he spoke of "cutting off the four" (*jue si*). To cut off the four is to be without self.
After Confucius, only the Yan clan was able to overcome the self (*ke ji*); overcoming the self is what comes closest [to this realization]. Thus it is said: "There is..."
Whether [the other] be real or false, whether one be offended or not, he does not take it to heart. But when it comes to Mencius, he takes "the Self" as his master.

By taking "the Self" as his master, the very bloodline of "no-self" (wu-wo) is severed. Although he speaks of the nature of the Way being good and extols benevolence (ren) and righteousness (yi), how can he truly be considered a follower of Confucius?
For although benevolence and righteousness are indeed good, they all achieve their virtue through "no-self. If he were to allow "the Self" to exist...
I must necessarily force things to conform to me; when things possess me, I must necessarily lose myself to conform to them.

Thus, what is called benevolence and righteousness is either artificial or partial. Even if one claims it is neither artificial nor partial, if it is achieved through forced effort and external compliance, the heart will not find peace therein;
can this truly be called being capable of benevolence and righteousness? The Confucian scholars of the world do not realize that both the self and things...
There is no self, yet they grasp at it as real, holding fast to it so that it cannot be broken; thus they say, "I study Confucius! I study Confucius!"—this is increasingly perverse. Question:

Regarding the various schools' theories on human nature (*xing*), how should one reach a balanced synthesis? Answer: Xun Qing spoke of nature as evil (*xìng è*); Yang Xiong spoke of it as both good and evil.

Confusion. Han Yu asserted that human nature consists of three grades; the Song Confucians criticized him, claiming it was because he discussed nature in terms of *qi* (material force) and *zhi* (disposition).
Only Mencius spoke of the goodness of nature; Donglin [Zhang Ji] maintained that this refers to the inherently good, which does not stand in opposition to evil.
Zhu Hui-an also said, "These words are indeed correct. Consequently, for five hundred years, Confucian scholars have taken them as their standard, none daring to deviate from them;

only those who study the teachings of Śākyamuni occasionally find them unsatisfactory. I shall not now use Buddhist doctrine to critique Confucianism, but shall instead critique it using Confucian terminology itself.
For instance, when Mencius argued for the goodness of human nature, he used the analogy of water: [water flows downward].

To use the necessity of water’s downward flow as an analogy for the necessity of human nature’s goodness implies that what is called "goodness" is not an inherent goodness, but rather a goodness that stands in opposition to evil.
Once it is opposed to evil, how does this differ from the arguments of Xunzi, Yangzi, and others?
In short, the four masters' discussions on human nature all refer only to its manifestations. To use water as an analogy: goodness is water flowing downward;
evil is water flowing upward; and the mixture of good and evil is water flowing both ways. These constitute the three grades.

Thus, although it moves between the upper and lower, it is neither exclusively above nor below. Since its application has four distinct modes, the discourse concerning it likewise possesses four distinct modes.
If one can recognize the essence of water, then it is neither separate from these four modes nor identical to them;

thus, the various arguments regarding these four modes will collapse of their own accord without needing to be attacked. Someone may say: "The Śākya [Buddha] said that one follows conditions (*pratyaya*)."
"Transformation" refers to "nature" (*xing*). This is a designation that unifies both essence and function. To speak of "non-transformation" expresses the virtue of the nature's essence;
it does not directly point to the essence itself. For example, a *maṇi* jewel possesses the nature of being non-transformative while following conditions;

how could one point to this "following conditions while non-transformative" as the very substance of the jewel? Some may say: "In the past, Heze elucidated the essence of nature by taking 'cognition' (*zhi*) as..."

Regarding the school: Guifeng (Huihong) claimed that he alone had attained the essence of the pearl. Is this true or not? I say: to discuss nature by means of cognition is like discussing a pearl by means of its radiance;

this too expresses the virtue of the pearl’s essence. Moreover, since the essence possesses both the virtues of quiescence and illumination, to speak solely of its illumination when referring to cognition fails to fully express its virtues.
One must provide an explanation for this, saying: "Cognition that is empty and quiescent" is what constitutes completeness.
Someone said: The Great Master Fu composed a verse: "Empty-handed, he grasps a hoe; walking, he rides a water buffalo.
A person passes over the bridge; the bridge flows, but the water does not flow. The Venerable Dushun composed a verse: "The ox of Huai Prefecture eats the grain;
the horse of Yi Prefecture has a bloated belly. The world seeks a physician; he applies moxibustion to the left shoulder of a pig. These two Great Masters... from... [text continues].

"Is it possible for the substance of the finger to be fully revealed by not recognizing it? He replied, "The two Great Beings (Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra) exhausted their efforts to proclaim it, yet they did so only by striking from the side;
in the end, it was not the direct pointing. Someone asked, "What kind of eyes do you possess? All the sages and worthies of the Three Teachings have scrutinized this very point."
"I request that you, Master, point it out directly. [Dongshan] said, "This essence is not something that even Yuanxian alone could point out;
even Śākyamuni was only able to remain silent in Mahādeva’s room, and even Vimalakīrti was only able to keep his mouth shut in Vaiśālī."
Indeed, there are no words that can be spoken and no principles that can be set forth.

Therefore, although all the Buddhas and Patriarchs have exhausted their tongues through indirect hints and circuitous manifestations, they have never, in reality, moved even a single hair’s breadth within the fundamental substance.

When a single thought does not arise, the entire body is profoundly still and nothing is lost. When a single thought briefly arises, one is separated by ten thousand miles and it is difficult to find.
When a single thought does not arise, the positions of the four sages have no place to stand. When a single thought briefly arises...
Then the shadows of the six realms of ordinary beings cannot be escaped. When not a single thought arises, the self is vast and empty space is small;
when a single thought momentarily arises, the self is small and even a mote of dust is large. When not a single thought arises, the sense faculties and their objects pervade the entire Dharma-realm;
when a single thought momentarily arises, the sense faculties and their objects are each confined to their own respective positions. When not a single thought arises...

Then the ears and eyes function interchangeably, and the physical body (*āśraya*) and its environment (*niśraya*) merge. When a single thought momentarily arises, the ears and eyes assume their separate offices, and the physical body and its environment are forever divided.
When not a single thought arises, numerical categories cannot constrain one, and retributive results cannot reach one.

When a single thought momentarily arises, fortune and misfortune become distinct realms, and suffering and joy diverge onto different paths. When not a single thought arises, one moves with speed without haste and acts without exertion.
When a single thought momentarily arises, one moves with haste yet fails to reach the goal; one acts but does not arrive.

When not a single thought arises, one is reverent without moving and trustworthy without speaking. When a single thought momentarily arises, one moves without reverence and speaks without trustworthiness.
When not a single thought arises, both emptiness and form vanish together; seeing is transformed into the nature. When a single thought briefly arises, emptiness and form stand in opposition;
the nature is transformed into seeing. When not a single thought arises, the world can be moved and empty space can be extinguished.
When a single thought briefly arises, even a mote of dust becomes an obstruction, and a single film creates a barrier. This single thought is precisely birth and death.

It is the very root and core [of enlightenment], and also the broad highway to nirvana. If a person can forge their state of having thoughts into a state of no-thought, what further task remains for them to achieve Buddhahood?

The Preface to the *Xu yiyán* states: Formerly, while I resided at Mount He, I encountered various scholars who posed questions and engaged in debate. Consequently, I synthesized the teachings of Confucianism and Buddhism and composed the *Yiyán*.
It has been twenty years since it was carved into printing blocks and circulated. Recently, having returned from Zhejiang to Fujian, I once again reside at Mount Gu. With my own eyes...
Bound by the transformations of the world, he at times uttered what he felt compelled to say, thereby composing the *Xu yuyan* (Continued Words from a Dream).
Now, as for the worthy, they are originally followers of the "Black Robes" (the monastic order); their proper course is to remain hidden in deep mountains, content to be like the silent cicada.

Why, then, do they clamor toward others like Mencius’s fondness for debate or Jia Yi’s bitter lamentations? Is it because the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of many lifetimes have not yet been suddenly subdued? Or is it also...
Is there anyone who, driven by necessity, utters but a single cry? This book now stands complete; every fragment is the product of painstaking effort.
I leave it solely to the lofty discernment of the Great Ones. Written on the Buddha’s Birthday in the summer of the Renchen year at Seongjeondang Hall.

Those who are arrogant and conceited generally do so because their attachment to the self (*ātman-grāha*) is deep; thus they give rise to this affliction recklessly, which constitutes a grave obstacle to the Great Way. Today’s scholars exclusively esteem this habit, calling it "stiffness" or "aloofness. Yet, when they encounter even a slight matter of profit or loss, they become as supple as a twisted wire, completely lacking self-mastery. This is what Confucius meant by: [The passage continues with the quote: "When he is in a position of authority, he is firm and upright; when he is not in a position of authority, he is gentle and compliant. This describes the true gentleman. Those who are arrogant and conceited are the exact opposite of this. They are like a great tree that has grown tall for a thousand years, yet its roots are shallow; at the first gust of wind, it topples over. How can one call such a person a man of integrity? It is said: "If you wish to know the person, observe them in times of adversity. This is precisely why the ancients valued the practice of "refining oneself through hardship" (*nan-jing*). Only by enduring the trials of poverty and distress can one truly test whether one's resolve is firm or fragile. If one cannot maintain one's integrity when facing minor difficulties, how could one possibly achieve anything in the face of great calamity? Therefore, the sages taught us to cultivate ourselves through adversity. If one does not undergo this refinement, one will surely fall into the trap of arrogance and conceit. One must constantly examine oneself to ensure that one does not harbor such faults. If one harbors such faults, one will inevitably become a vessel for ruin. Thus, the Buddha taught: "One who is arrogant and conceited will never attain liberation. This is a warning against the dangers of pride. One must always remain humble and cautious. If one is not humble and cautious, one will surely invite disaster. Therefore, the sages taught us to cultivate humility. If one cultivates humility, one will naturally avoid arrogance and conceit. This is the way to enter the path of the sages. If one wishes to enter the path of the sages, one must first eliminate arrogance and conceit. If one eliminates arrogance and conceit, one will naturally attain liberation. Therefore, the Buddha taught: "Only by abandoning arrogance and conceit can one attain liberation. This is the ultimate teaching of the Buddhas and patriarchs. One must study this deeply and apply it to one's own life. Do not let it become a mere empty word.
