One must not fail to heed it. If one fails to heed it, one will surely suffer great regret. Therefore, I exhort all of you to take this to heart and diligently practice it. Do not let it be in vain. If you practice it diligently, you will surely attain the Way. This is my earnest exhortation to you all. May you all take it to heart and put it into practice. Do not let it be in vain. If you put it into practice, you will surely attain the Way. This is the ultimate teaching of the Buddhas and patriarchs. One must study this deeply and apply it to one's own life. Do not let it become a mere empty word. If you practice it sincerely, you will surely attain great benefit. This is the essential point of the Buddhas' and patriarchs' teachings. One must not fail to heed it. If one fails to heed it, one will surely suffer great regret. Therefore, I exhort all of you to take this to heart and diligently practice it. Do not
To be stern in appearance but weak within is the mark of a petty person who acts like a thief or a housebreaker. They do not realize that the ancients were not like this at all.
In the past, Master Yuanlü (Dongshan Liangjie) said to Chan Master Yan (Wuzu Fayan): "If you simply attain wondrous awakening, your mind will naturally become tranquil and your breath harmonious;

your countenance will be respectful and your demeanor dignified. Wuzu Fayan replied: "Be long-suffering in embracing the vast and indifferent; be generous in concealing faults; be humble in making friends; and be diligent..."
Jizhong. A letter from Dahuì, the Chief Seat of the Precepts, repeatedly and earnestly exhorted [the recipients] to practice humility, modesty, and yielding.
Since you all are called Chan monks, you look down upon the common world; how can you not contemplate emulating the ancients?
The dignified deportment of Chan monks is not a matter of external formalities; rather, it is for the purpose of internally examining the mind by first binding the body externally.
There has never been one whose body was lax and dissolute who could nevertheless achieve mental stillness and unity.

Therefore, the Buddha established rules for bhikṣus requiring that their deportment be strictly solemn. Baizhang’s ritual laws are observed by all schools. When Master Yichuan of the Song dynasty saw a monk...
He emerged from the hall and sighed, saying, "The ritual and music of the Three Dynasties are all contained herein. Judging by this, what must the majestic deportment of those days have been like?

Today there are certain reckless people who indulge their passions and run wild, tearing asunder the rites and laws, yet they mock those who observe the rules of decorum as being narrow-minded and pedantic.
What kind of heart is this? In the past, Da-jue Lian was dignified and solemn in both motion and stillness."

Upon meeting Tongne once, Huanglong Nan immediately expected him to be a man of great capacity. In his daily conduct, Nan was measured in his movements and sat with his robes adjusted and his back straight.
Were these two elders men of narrow-mindedness? One can thus know that those who are frivolous and restless certainly lack great capacity;
though they may achieve initial awakening, they will ultimately fall short of perfect virtue. I only wish that students would not settle for themselves as men of small capacity.
There are certain practitioners of dhyāna who claim that while their speech precedes the soaring dragon, their conduct lags behind the limping turtle;
yet they say, "In our school, we value only the realization of the ground (jian-di), not the practice of conduct.

They do not realize that under Qingyuan, what is called "merit" (gong-xun) is like a minister serving his sovereign or a son serving his father—how could one dare to be in opposition? Under Nanyue, what is called "tending the ox" (mu-niu) is because one has attained...

If even one who already possesses an ox still requires a skilled herder, how much more so for one who has not yet obtained an ox? Furthermore, beneath the patched robe (*kāṣāya*), good is not permitted to be worn;
how much less can evil be indulged? Even the Buddhas and Patriarchs could not do it; how could one pursue power and profit with partiality?
This is a petty person devoid of all restraint, who uses the words of the Sages to gloss over their own faults—one who enters hell as swiftly as a shot arrow. There is [a saying]:...
Those of resolute character should reflect deeply upon themselves:
the public cases of the ancients all flow forth from within the inconceivable; as soon as one engages in discursive thought, one is separated by a thousand mountains.

People nowadays generally rely on intellectual speculation and conceptualization. They study with teachers and friends using texts such as the *Shaolin Notebooks* and the various commentaries and verses on ancient cases (*gū*) by the four solitary masters;
yet every word and phrase therein is nothing but the spittle of delusion. To be confused by them is to block the gate of awakening forever.
Furthermore, to compose verses or "picks" (critical comments) is like painting a latrine with vermilion and cinnabar—it only increases its stench.
Listen! Those who today truly aspire to participate in Chan meditation must decisively sever these kinds of evil cognitions and habitual tendencies.

They must single-mindedly drill and investigate the seamlessness where there are no cracks, with a sense of indignation as if encountering a mortal enemy—one must surely destroy this before eating breakfast.
If one can apply the mind in this way, the treasure-store is near; you will certainly not be deceived.
The practice of the staff and the shout exists in all five schools, yet it flourishes most prominently in the traditions of Deshan and Linji.
This is like a crossbow capable of launching a thousand-jin bolt; how could it ever be discharged recklessly?

Alas, ignorant people have grown accustomed to this as a mere custom, much like commoners who rashly brandish weapons—such acts lead either to rebellion or madness. Therefore, Xinghua warned them, saying: "I have heard that in the front corridor..."
"Ye-he! [The Master] shouts. Then, from behind the screen, he shouts again. "Do not blindly shout or recklessly shout, everyone!
Even if you could shout so that Xinghua were cast into the void and fell down with not a breath of life remaining, and waited for me to recover and rise up, I would still say to you:
'Not yet. Why? Because I have never yet scattered real pearls within a purple silk curtain."
"You are with me; why do you shout so recklessly and confusedly? Later, the elder Yuanwu did not employ staff or shouts throughout his life;
was he not a master of the Linji lineage? When his son, Dahui, resided at Mount Jing, he imposed fines in money and meals upon those who uttered shouts.
This was because he deeply understood the abuses of the practice; thus, he sternly punished and vigorously sought to rectify them.
Regarding the distinctions between the various lineages, there are five schools to which they adhere; yet in reality, they are all one and the same Way.
Therefore, one who truly knows Linji will certainly not disparage Caodong, and one who truly knows Caodong will certainly not disparage Linji.

For example, although Fenyang Shanzhao was skilled in the Three Mysteries (Sanxuan), he nonetheless sent Langye Huijue away [to study elsewhere]. Fushan Fayuan studied the principles of the Dongshan school under Dayang Jingxuan, and Yun... [text ends]

Although Shoumen inherited the transmission from Xuefeng, he subsequently traveled to study under various masters of the Dongxia (Cao-Dong) lineage, such as Caoshan, Shushan, Qianfeng, and Jiufeng, with whom he shared karmic encounters.
This shows that the Great Way is impartial and that the Dharma knows no favoritism.

It is only those of later generations who recklessly give rise to notions of self and other, carving up the void of reality. Those who succeed Linji slander Cao-Dong, while those who succeed Cao-Dong [slander Linji].
To slander Linji and destroy the Dharma-gate is to lose one’s own life of wisdom; is this not deeply lamentable?
Now I pray that all people will broaden their perspective beyond the external and embody an illumination free from partiality, so that this Way may flourish.

The mind-teachings of the Confucian school have rarely found a successor since the time of Mencius. Among the various scholars of the Han dynasty, most took the interpretation of texts as their primary occupation;
only Dong Zhongshu came close to this tradition. The "Three Memorials on Heaven and Man" submitted by Master Dong were all pure, correct, and without flaw.
His response to the question regarding those who surpassed the "three men of benevolence" was particularly refined and essential. — Cheng [Yi-cheng] (or Cheng Hao)
It is indeed true that both Yi-chuan (Cheng Yi) and Zhu Kaoting (Zhu Xi) all extolled him as surpassing all other disciples.
However, regarding his study of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*, he insisted on seeking out the specific events that provoked the recorded portents and omens;
thus, he was pedantic and far-fetched, a scholar whose views were muddled by the *chan* and *wei* traditions of divination. How, then, can he be considered a pure Confucian?
Yang Xiong’s profound contemplation and refined, elegant diction were rarely encountered in his time.

He composed the *Fayan* (Discourse on the Law) to emulate the *Lunyu* (Analects) and the *Taixuan* (Great Mystery) to emulate the *Yi* (Book of Changes). He lived with such confidence that he considered himself a sage or worthy;
had he not been born during the era of Wang Mang, or had he died before Wang Mang usurped the throne, he would surely have been the preeminent Confucian scholar of his generation.
Since he first lost his integrity by serving Wang Mang, how could he have guaranteed that his obscurity would remain pure? With both his person and his reputation ruined, the world laughed at him.
Such is the difficulty of defining a person's character.
The talent and wisdom of Kongming truly combined the three great heroes of the House of Han into one person, yet his loyalty surpassed theirs.
At the conclusion of his "Memorial on Sending the Army," he wrote: "I shall bend my body and exhaust my strength, dying only when my task is done.
This is how I repay the grace of the late Emperor and fulfill my duty of loyalty to Your Majesty. As for success or failure, advantage or disadvantage—"
It was not within my humble intelligence to foresee these few words; yet this sincere heart and loyal spirit shine forth through all time.
Among the Three Heroes, they were not only unwilling to do so, but indeed incapable of speaking such things. Therefore, I say that their loyalty and integrity surpassed those of the others.
From the Wei and Jin dynasties down to the Tang, Confucian learning was sparse; only Wang Tong may be said to have resembled it.
His *Zhongshuo* contains insights and arguments that are largely pure and refined, far surpassing what Han Yu could achieve.
However, as for the factual details within it, they mostly resemble the *Lunyu*, leading one to suspect they were composed through embellishment. As for the Five Classics he authored:
This is merely a triviality, like the joke of dust on the rice and paint on the soup. Was Confucius truly such a person? How extreme is the obscuration caused by the love of fame!
When Ou-yang Hsiu wrote the *History of the Five Dynasties*, he claimed that there were no outstanding figures during those five dynasties.

I say it was not that there were no figures, but rather that they were constrained by their times. Take Zhou Shizong alone: had he appeared during the flourishing eras of the Han or Tang dynasties, could you gentlemen have [even] known him?
As for those who withdrew to dwell among the mountains and forests, such as the various sages of the Five Houses, their brilliance illuminated both past and present;
few in later generations have been able to equal them. Therefore, I say: it is not that there were no outstanding individuals, but rather that they were constrained by their times.
Han Yu possessed a spirit that was exceedingly bold and unrestrained; he constantly compared himself to Mencius, wishing to practice his Way through diligent effort.

Yet, he was impatient in seeking advancement, submitting three memorials to the Chancellor without ever hearing of the principle of not appearing before feudal lords. This remained so until his later years.
Having been employed at court, he has not produced a single constructive proposal; instead, he spends his days occupied solely with poetry and wine. How does this differ from the common vulgar?
Can this be called "exerting oneself to practice the Way"?
After Mencius, Tu (Han Yu) uniquely selected Xun Qing and Yang Xiong, stating that while Xun and Yang were "substantially correct with minor flaws," Mencius was "perfectly correct.
In my humble view, the writings of the Master Xun contain much that is artificial and eccentric.
For instance, Zisi and Mencius elucidated the Way of the former sages and refuted heterodox doctrines to rectify the human mind; this established the foundation for the world.
This is a matter of the greatest gravity. Yet they say that those who bring disorder to the world are Zisi and Mencius—is this not strange?
If Mencius maintains that human nature is good and always cites Yao and Shun as his authority, he provides a target for all generations to pursue.
They, however, claim that nature is evil—that the nature of Jie and Zhou is what is natural, while Yao and Shun were merely hypocrites—is this not strange? As for Yangzi—
Although he was not as eccentric as Xunzi, who held that human nature is a mixture of good and evil, he nevertheless identified habitual conditioning with innate nature;
this already deviates from the intent of Mencius. Furthermore, he served as a high official under Wang Mang, failing his moral duty.

In the final chapter of his *Fayan*, he lavishly praised Wang Mang’s merits, claiming they were comparable to those of the Duke of Zhou and the Duke of Shao. He even composed the "Jiqin Meixin" (Praising Qin and Glorifying the New) to eulogize Wang Mang.
Since their fundamental principles are already deficient, what can be said of their learning?
These two individuals viewed the Way of Mencius as being as far apart as the wind and cattle or horses that do not meet;
how could they be described as "mostly correct with minor flaws" and placed in the dust-trail following Mencius? How egregious was the error of Han Yu!

In my examination of Liu Zhitou, I find that when he finally passed away in Liuzhou, he was only forty-seven years old. Thus, at the time he served as one of the "Eight Simas," his age was very young.
Had he been able to fulfill his ambitions with ease and not suffered such frustration, I do not know what his condition would have been later on.
It was precisely because he underwent this period of exile and demotion that he was able to settle into solitude and devote himself wholeheartedly to learning.
Therefore, as for his literary style, it was only after he arrived in Liuzhou that he began to achieve its ultimate refinement. Having resided in Liuzhou for a long time, the common people loved him;

upon his death, they continued to offer him blood sacrifices in that region. Could one achieve such a thing without being virtuous? Zhu Xi said, "Zi Hou actually gained the power [of his literary genius] from Liuzhou," which is indeed correct.
Sickness can kill a person, yet it can also benefit them. Take the Tang dynasty’s Bai Juyi (Le-tian) as an example; he was one who received benefit from illness.
Bai Juyi was most renowned for his refined elegance and sensuous charm, yet in his later years, having fallen ill, he was able to restrain himself and turn toward simplicity and substance.

He daily cultivated the practices of the Western Paradise to bring his life to its end. This may be called "losing at the eastern corner, but recovering at the mulberry trees"—a case of gaining in the latter part of life what was lost in the former.
If Dongpo’s errors in his later years were as grave as those, he would fall far short of even Bai Juyi.
Dongpo prided himself on Chan, and others likewise attributed him to Chan;
yet though he had moments of realization, he died under the seal of Donglin and failed to achieve thorough penetration, remaining instead trapped within the realm of cleverness. How so?
He was able to contend with the cycle of birth and death; yet in his later years, he took a liking to the arts of longevity.
On the day of the winter solstice, he closed his gates to cultivate his vital breath (*qi*). Ultimately, he fell ill because of this and passed away. Is Chan like this?
Is Chan like this?

Zhu Huiweng said: "When Buddhism first arrived, they merely discussed causes and karma in a humble manner; later followers magnified these teachings until they reached the height of mystery and subtlety.
I say that when Kāśyapa Mātanga first came to this land, the work he translated was the *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections*.
This sūtra originally belonged to the Hīnayāna, and its principles were naturally shallow and mundane. Nevertheless, its shallowness was certainly no inferior to...

Regarding Confucianism, even those aspects that are somewhat profound are beyond the capacity of the Confucians to understand. Zhu [Xi] claims they merely discuss causes and karma in a petty, mundane manner;
how groundless such a statement is!
Among the various scholars of the Yuan dynasty, those recommended for inclusion in the ancestral temple sacrifices were Xu Heng and Wu Cheng.

Yet, regarding the conduct of these two gentlemen during their periods of official service and retirement, they failed to grasp the great principles of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*. How difficult it would have been for them to claim a place within the gate of Confucius!
Liu Yin, Jin Lixiang, and Xu Qian all lived in seclusion and declined office, teaching disciples and composing works; the scholarship of these men followed the lineage of the aforementioned masters.
Kaotang was the preeminent among the Confucian scholars of the Yuan dynasty; yet, when it came to promotion for inclusion in the temple sacrifices (*congsi*), he was not accorded such status.

This was because his name and rank had not yet become widely renowned. During my time as a layman, I delighted in the study of learning but was negligent in the pursuits of the civil service examinations.
A friend once teased me, saying: "My elder brother delights in the study of learning, yet you must wear that silk cap [of office]; if you do not wear it..."

"To wear a gauze cap indicates that one's learning is not profound. Although these were merely words spoken in jest at the time, they nonetheless strike the core of the defects prevalent in secular society.
Therefore, I have recorded them here together.
Yangshan asked a monk, “Where are you from? The monk replied, “I am from Youzhou. Yangshan said, “Do you still think of that place? The monk said, “I constantly think of it.
Yangshan said, “That which is capable of thinking is the mind; that which is thought of is the object.

In that place there are towers and pavilions, groves and gardens, and crowds of people and horses. When you reflect upon that which is thinking, do you find that it contains all those various things? The monk said, “Yes.”
"Such-and-such a person has come here," [the monk] said, but he did not see anyone at all. Yangshan said, "The fact that you still have a mind to 'see' is precisely the stage of faith;
it is not yet the stage of a realized person. I, Yongyue, consider that Yangshan’s such instruction was not merely administering medicine for this particular monk.
It is because everyone who does not truly perceive the Way falls into this very trap. This is because both seeing existence and seeing non-existence are both pitting the mind against [reality].

Regarding the objective realm (*viṣaya*): it is like looking at a mountain from across a river. It may be called the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*), but it cannot be called the stage of the person (*pudgala-bhūmi*).
This is because the stage of the person requires the forgetting of subject and object; the mind does not see the mind, just as a mirror does not illuminate itself.
Qixian Bian once traveled through Jiuyang carrying a single staff and wearing a pair of sandals. When the Elder Hunrong of Donglin saw him, he rebuked him, saying, "A master is a model for others.

To behave in such a manner—how can you not be self-deprecating? Your reception of guests is extremely neglectful. Bian laughed and said, "In human life, one finds joy in the fulfillment of one's own aspirations. What fault is there in mine? He then took up his brush and wrote a verse:

The staff is my companion; My feet follow the path. The mountain peaks are my home; The clouds are my clothing. The world is vast and boundless; Who can measure it? If you wish to know the Way, Look at this very moment.
And so he departed. The verse says: Do not say that Xiqian is destitute; though his body is poor, his Way is not. His straw sandals are as fierce as tigers; his staff is as lively as a dragon.
When thirsty, he drinks from the Caoxi stream; when hungry, he swallows the thorny chestnuts. The men with copper heads and iron brows all dwell within my mountains.
I, the fool, say that a single staff and a pair of sandals are the true vocation of a patch-robed monk; this is precisely what may be called the standard for later students.
To claim that the Master’s ritual was lax and fragmented is surely erroneous. When Master Bian took up his brush to write a verse, every word was full of self-aggrandizement;
this is entirely the habit of pride. The waters of Caoxi should not be like this.
Hong Juefan’s calligraphy comprises six types. The Elder Daguan greatly delighted in them and carved them for circulation. What I myself delight in is merely his "literary Chan" (wenzizi chan).
This elder’s calligraphy is truly that of a master, rare among monks. As for his understanding of the Buddha-dharma, however, the pure and the flawed are mixed together.
It is not my view that worldly people, out of their love for his calligraphy, should accord equal weight to his Buddhist realization as well.
I dare not say for certain.
At that time, Juefan’s reputation was already widely established; he would arbitrarily disparage and rebuke those from all quarters, and most of them were intimidated by him.

Only Lingyuan deeply knew that he had not yet attained awakening. He once wrote a letter of admonition to him, saying: "I have heard that while you were in the South, you were constantly investigating..."
To provide a special commentary on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* is not what this unworthy person hoped for. For the study of mere words cannot penetrate the source of a person's own nature;
it merely serves as an obstacle for later students to the wisdom-eye of the former Buddhas. The ailment lies in relying on others to form one's interpretations.

If one blocks oneself at the gate of self-awakening and relies on words and speech, one may surpass those of shallow learning; yet if one expands the divine mechanism of the mind, it will ultimately be difficult to reach the ultimate wondrous realization.
Consequently, there are many discrepancies between practice and understanding, and in daily life and perception, obscurity and confusion increase even further. I am well-acquainted with Fa-jian;
his wisdom and insight are sharp and keen enough to reflect upon this. If he continues to diminish and further diminish [his attachments], when we meet again in the future, he will certainly...
There is indeed another wondrous point. This letter of Lingyuan serves as a potent medicine for Juefan;
yet, since his chronic ailment has not been cured, what can truly be done?
Dahui said: "A thousand doubts and ten thousand doubts are but a single doubt. Once this one doubt is shattered, there are none among the thousand and ten thousand that are not resolved.

Some may not yet believe this. I, the fool, say that although a thousand doubts and ten thousand doubts differ from one another, they all ultimately consist of calculations based upon illusory reflections.
If one personally perceives the reality, then these illusory reflections will completely vanish. Since the illusory reflections have [vanished]...
It is extinguished. What further doubt remains that has not been shattered?

It is commonly said that the Buddhas are devoid of mental deliberation and have transcended intellectual understanding; yet, to possess even a single instance of mental deliberation or intellectual understanding is what defines a sentient being.
The fool thinks that while sentient beings possess mental deliberation, the Buddhas also possess mental deliberation—only that the Buddhas' mental deliberation...

It arises from non-selfishness. Yet the emotional thoughts of sentient beings are obscured by selfishness. Sentient beings possess cognition and understanding, and the Buddhas likewise possess cognition and understanding;

however, the cognition and understanding of the Buddhas are subtle because they are perpetually awakened, whereas the cognition and understanding of sentient beings are stagnant because they are unawakened.
Among the "Verses on Ancient Cases" (Sònggǔ) transmitted by the four masters of our tradition, Xuedou should be considered the foremost; Tiantong comes next.
Xuedou is like one who enters directly with a single blade, striking down the leader of the enemy at once. Tiantong, however, must array a great formation, which involves considerable effort.
This is because Tiantong’s learning was so extensive and his diction invariably elegant; yet, he was hindered by these very qualities, and thus often could not express himself freely.
Indeed, after Touzi and Furong, those who were able to revitalize the school of Dongshan were Tiandong Jue and Zhenxie Le.

The insights of these two masters were intimate and direct, and both possessed lofty conduct and great virtue, such that they could truly not bring shame upon their predecessors. However, as for their teachings...
Regarding the Dharma, there are indeed differences. Tiantong followed the ancient tracks, never straying by even an inch or a foot from the established order;

yet, in terms of manifesting extraordinary and divine transformations, his strengths were not yet apparent. Zhenxie’s language was transcendent and elegant, his intent free and unrestrained, and his expositions were illuminating and penetrating.
It does not require the expenditure of effort. Although one is not confined by the Dharma, one truly does not turn away from it.
The language of Linji is straightforward and direct; the language of Caodong is circuitous and winding—this is the general outline.

However, among the great masters, there are also those who do not conform entirely to this pattern. For instance, Fengxue said: "The fishing boat carries [the fish] to the banks of the Xiao and Xiang rivers; the breath is choked."
In his moments of boredom, he asks the white gulls; again he says: "The wooden cock crows at midnight; the straw dog barks at dawn.
These are all closely akin to the Cao-Dong (Caodong) school. When the Boatman struck Jianshan twice, Yaoshan would simply say, "Look at the arrow!
These are all closely akin to the Linji school. This is what Dahui meant by Chan encompassing all styles; it cannot be confined to a single path.
Ciming visited Shending and presented only the phrase, "I have attained but this: 'The house has fallen over. Shending sighed and said, "Fenyang now has such a son.
He then vigorously recommended him. From this, Ciming’s reputation spread far and wide. As for his sharpness of wit (*jīfēng*), it was truly extraordinary.
Jungjie remarked, "Ciming was certainly a master of the Way. However, he fostered a trend of frivolity among later students, the evils of which are beyond description.
When Shending offended his juniors, Ciming did not become angry but instead recommended him with great vigor. How could Shending have been easily surpassed?
Thus we know that while Ciming was like a swift hawk or a sharp falcon, Shending was like the vastness of heaven and the depth of earth."
When Baiyun Yuan initially resided at Chengtian Monastery in Jiujiang, Yantong Ne yielded the position of Abbot of Yantong to him and retired to the West Hall himself.
After some time, a group of petty individuals began to incite discord between them. Unable to endure it, Ne complained to visitors;
consequently, the petty individuals claimed that Ne could not bear the solitude and suggested he intended to return to the abbacy of Yantong. Thereupon, Yuan took his leave and departed.
To remove him was indeed correct. However, as for his words upon retiring from the monastery and ascending the hall, they seem to place the blame on [his own] lack of eloquence;
this is merely because he was obscured by petty people and failed to examine himself.
Wang Shanti had long served Da Mingbao as his attendant. One day, Shanti packed his bedding and departed. The assembly was suspicious and asked, "Where has Attendant Shanti gone?
Bao replied, "He came from all quarters; he goes to all quarters. Why ask him? They further asked, "How was his study of the Way?
Bao said, "If I say he has it, I would be stifling his potential. If I say he does not have it, I would diminish him."
Because of his majestic aura, the assembly only then realized that he had been secretly entrusting his teachings while his physical body was away.
He subsequently withdrew once more into the deep seclusion of Mount Wang in Taiyuan for over ten years, where he first established a Chan monastery and opened the hall to expound the Dharma.

Whether master or disciple, their profound concealment and meticulous secrecy were such that they may both serve as a model for future generations. Observing the affairs of recent times, however, one sees that they are as vastly different as heaven and earth.
How tragic! After Master Shouchang had attained the essential meaning [of the Dharma], he remained hidden on Mount E for nearly thirty years before finally emerging to reside at Baofeng Monastery.
There, he personally tilled the soil and fields, refusing to engage in any form of solicitation. On the day he moved to Shouchang, there was a Minister Zhang in the village who built a hall for him.
The record of the circumstances: My late Master accepted it with a smile, yet ultimately did not reveal the identity of the patron. Ten years later, a great monastery was magnificently restored;
wealth and silk arrived of their own accord without being sought. Alas! My late Master has passed away; his solitary style and stern integrity remain.
Who is there capable of succeeding him?
Our former master wore coarse clothing and ate plain food; he personally held the plow and the hoe until the age of seventy, never ceasing for even a moment.

During a time of great famine, he ground wheat into a porridge and led the community to open up fields. Those fields are still called the "Wheat Porridge Mound" (*mài-gēng qiū*) today. It is said that [he cultivated] a hundred...
Since the time of Master Zhang, there has been but one such person. Now we of our generation do not tread upon the grass before us nor grasp the grass across us;

we sit at ease and enjoy ourselves. Whenever I reflect on this, I feel as though I have no place to hide my body—how much less dare I indulge in heedlessness and fall into the agony of the hundred punishments within the Iron Ring Mountains?
One day my late teacher said to me, "Mazu and Baizhang taught people to 'tame the ox. This matter is not at all easy.
Since the roots and stem have been established for so long, they cannot be severed abruptly; how could one act with such recklessness?
When I was on Mount Emei, I thought to myself that nothing in the world could move my mind. Later, while at Shouchang, because of construction work, I had to purchase [materials]."
The wood was finished and the contract fulfilled. He agreed with the man that he would come to collect the payment. When the appointed time arrived, however, he had nothing with which to respond.
While he was in a state of extreme distress, he suddenly saw several sedan chairs arrive outside his gate. Upon seeing them, he obtained more than one hundred pieces of gold.
The old monk could not help but show joy upon his face, whereupon he said to himself in self-reproach: "For thirty years I have practiced the Way, yet I have been turned around by this thing."
Go. By this, you may know with certainty that [the truth] is entirely as it is. When the ancients constantly called out "The Host," they were not deceiving me.

The doctrine of cause, effect, and retribution is not something proclaimed by the Buddhists alone; the sages of this land, such as those of the *Great Changes* (*Da Yi*) and the *Great Plan* (*Hong Fan*), have also explained it in detail.
However, where there are instances of retribution that do not seem to correspond exactly, one should simply set them aside and return to the principle.
To attribute destiny to Heaven—is Heaven indeed partial? Is destiny truly something that can be attained by mere chance?
This is likely because one has not yet understood the causality of the three periods of existence.
There is a discourse in the world which claims that every sip of drink and every morsel of food is predetermined by fate and cannot be avoided through human effort.
If this were so, then those who do good would be destined to do good, and those who do evil would be destined to do evil;

the sages and worthies would have no merit in their teaching and transforming, and the common people would have no means of pursuing what is right or avoiding what is wrong. Consequently, the petty man would remain at ease.
In times of indulgence, even the noble person becomes negligent in their cultivation; how could one possibly enumerate the resulting harms?
Now, among the calamities and blessings of the world, none are greater than birth and death. Furthermore, there are those who die when it is not their destined time to die;

the Buddha calls these "untimely deaths" (*akālamṛtyu*), of which there are nine types. Therefore, within the Bodhisattva precepts, there is the rule against traveling while disregarding dangers, for fear that one might encounter such peril.
And yet, one may die an untimely death. Mencius also said, "The man of wisdom who knows his destiny does not stand beneath a collapsing wall.
He further stated, "Those who die in shackles and fetters do not meet their true destiny. Inferring from this, can one entirely resign oneself to fate?
Generally speaking, the workings of heavenly mandate and human effort are in fact intertwined; therefore, the gentleman must cultivate himself to await what comes.
The members of the Sangha entrust their traces to the mundane world while dwelling their bodies beyond the realm of material things. They should still sever ties with all worldly dust and turbidity;
how much more so should they not covet official rank or emolument? Even literary affairs are not to be engaged in, let alone military matters.
It was during the Yuan dynasty that Liu Bingzhong first initiated this prohibition, which Yao Guangxiao subsequently followed. This was a greedy and deluded error.
Their fame and achievements have destroyed the great transformation of compassion; they are sinners against the Buddha-dharma for ten thousand generations. Someone might say:
"Regarding the Bodhisattva precepts, there are times when killing is permitted as an opening [of the path]. These two masters were surely men of great expedient power (*mahā-upāya*);
they cannot be constrained by the laws applicable to ordinary *bhikṣus*. I replied: "As for what is called 'killing being permitted as an opening at certain times'..."
This is the duty of a lay bodhisattva. Just as one protects a lord or a father, or wards off bandits and thieves, once one has personally undertaken such a responsibility, how could one not kill?
Moreover, if by killing one person one can save hundreds or thousands of others, then it is permissible to kill.
If by killing one person one can accomplish hundreds or thousands of good deeds, then it is permissible to kill. Now, these two individuals have already taken the precepts of the Śākya.
Your son is not like those who remain at home. Furthermore, what he has done destroys the fundamental principles of social order and spreads calamity across the four seas.
What benefit could there be in calling this "great authority"? He is not merely a sinner against the Buddha-dharma;
he is also a sinner against the teachings of the secular world.
Prior to the Tang dynasty, monks who had audiences with the sovereign did not address him as "minister" (*chen*); it was only during the Tang that they began to do so.

Nevertheless, masters such as Huisi and Hongshou, when receiving offerings within the palace, were all treated with the etiquette due to a teacher. When these masters addressed the Son of Heaven, they called him "donor" (*dānapati*);

when referring to themselves, they called themselves "the poor practitioner" (*pindao*). By the Song dynasty, this practice had completely disappeared; yet, there still remained instances of being granted a seat upon ascending the hall or entering the palace.
Regarding matters such as ascending the throne [to preach], these too have disappeared in recent times. Monks who were permitted to have an audience with the Son of Heaven were extremely rare;
there were only a few during the Hongwu era. Even then, they were limited to composing verses in response to imperial compositions or being dispatched on missions to foreign lands.
Furthermore, there are those who forcibly compel others to maintain their hair and appoint them as officials;
there are those who compose poetry using a single unconventional character and are subsequently executed. Where, then, lies the propriety of treating monks?

It is because the virtue of the Sangha has declined successively through the ages that the rites of treating monks have likewise descended generation after generation; this is an inevitability of the current trend. From this point forward—
It has gone on; it has progressed further and further downward. The Dharma-gate is being extinguished; its destruction may be expected at any moment. How can one bear such grief!

The three schools of Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya originally share a single source; that later generations divided them into three was simply because their intellectual capacity could not encompass all of them.
It is with these that the Dharma-gate of Śākyamuni is established, like the three legs of a tripod—none may be lacking. They must be united.
If they are integrated, both are perfected; if they are separated, both are impaired.

Alas for later students who, driven by the passions of self-attachment, give rise to views of arising and ceasing, and thus mutually revile one another—just like brothers slaying each other—claiming, "I alone can glorify my ancestors' lineage. Are they not truly foolish?
Among the three schools, nothing is more difficult than Chan; the Teaching (Dharma) is next, and the Vinaya is next after that.

This is because Chan transcends emotion and leaves behind views; its wondrous realization lies beyond words and letters. It cannot be grasped through conjecture as the Teaching can, nor mastered through study and recitation;
therefore, it alone is difficult. As for the Vinaya, its ritual matters and appearances are superficial and accessible, and all have...

The Vinaya-dharmas are such that anyone possessing even a modicum of wisdom can learn them; they do not possess the profound subtlety and perfect elegance of the doctrinal teachings (śāstra), which no one but those of great intelligence can fathom.

Yet, for several hundred years, while the lineages of Chan and the doctrinal teachings have maintained a slender thread of continuity, why is it that the study of the Vinaya has become so rare as to be virtually silent?
This is likely because those of brilliant intellect and eloquence have mostly [neglected] the Vinaya...
People treat this study as shallow and trivial, neglecting it; they feel no sense of shame in confining themselves to such a limited scope.

Furthermore, according to human nature, people prefer ease and dread restraint, and thus they are unwilling to settle their minds upon this discipline. Therefore, the Vinaya studies are the most accessible.
Yet this has become the most difficult task of all. How tragic!

Regarding the study of the Vinaya, since the time of Lingzhi Zhaoyi, few have been seen who truly embody it. As for those in later generations who merely claim the title of "Vinaya Master," they are even fewer still.
If one does not even recognize the names, how much less can one understand their meaning? If the meaning itself is not grasped, how much less can one personally practice it?
As for the two ordination platforms at Tanzhe and Zhaokeng, their degeneration and abuses are such that they are difficult to speak of;

if Your Majesty’s clear decree does not prohibit them, who knows what state affairs will become in the future? Toward the end of the Wanli era, various regions were permitted to administer the precepts themselves.
This perfectly accords with the Buddha’s intention; yet, it is exceedingly coarse and superficial. Alas! One who wishes to revive the fallen Vinaya school today must surely be a person of rebirth;
otherwise, it cannot be done. How tragic!
The *Shao-lin Xuān-jì* says: "In later times, those who understand the Way will be many, but those who practice the Way will be few;

those who explain principle will be many, but those who realize principle will be few. I say that if one understands the Way but is unable to practice it, then that understanding is not true understanding.
It is like a person sitting peacefully in a single room, poring over maps, and saying, "The whole world is already within my eyes. Its [meaning] is...
In truth, he has never moved even a single step. If one explains a principle but fails to reach its core, that explanation is likewise not a true explanation.
It is like a person skilled at painting dragons; though every stroke and detail is masterful, when a real dragon actually appears, they are struck with terror and unable to discern it.
As for the events of today, there is something even more extraordinary: having seen the map of Min and Yue, and...
Zhidi said: "The destiny of the world rests upon this. Yet you merely study the painting of horses and claim, 'I am able to know dragons.
Is this not something even the prophetic records of Shaolin could not have anticipated? Will the anxiety for the Dharma not grow all the deeper?"
The single work titled *Rendiantiyanmu* was compiled during the Chunxi era of the Song dynasty; it already contained errors and corruptions.
By recent times, as further materials were added, its scope expanded, yet the errors and corruptions became even more numerous.

This is likely because individuals such as "the crane in the floodwaters" have fabricated content under false names, or perhaps because those with knowledge of the teachings were not proficient in this school and forced interpretations upon it. How could their misguiding of later students be considered anything but profound?

Alas! Generally speaking, a Zen practitioner must first possess the correct Dharma-eye; as for the various pedagogical devices employed in the lineage, these are truly matters of secondary importance.
Today, those with the ambition to study Zen often prioritize this book above all else, like someone who, lacking eyes themselves, wishes to borrow another’s as their own.
They will inevitably be obscured by it, and there are those who spend their entire lives without realizing their error.

In propagating the Dharma during the final age, demonic activities will inevitably be many. Those who greedily pursue advancement will surely incur disgrace; those who exceed the bounds of moderation will surely invite calamity.
To know this is the foremost strategy for subduing the armies of Māra. As was the case during the Wanli era with Daguan and Hanshan.
These two elders were both renowned throughout their time; yet because they did not grasp this meaning, they ultimately met with disaster.

How can it be said that these were "calamities of the unprovoked" (*awāṅ zhī zāi*) and thus entirely attributed to fate? Only the Elder of Yunqi was cautious, discreet, frugal, and parsimonious, never acting with even a single step of negligence.
Thus, although he enjoyed great fame, he began well and ended well, remaining entirely free from demonic hindrances. He was truly [a model] for the Dharma-ending age.
These are excellent precedents.
Banners and flags obscuring the sky, corpses covering the ground—these are my sorrows, not my anxieties.
White blades encircling one’s person, with no sustenance of porridge or rice to follow—this is my destitution, not my anxiety. What I truly fear is the Māra.
A ghost has entered the room; calamity arises from within the inner chambers. Regarding future events, there is something most unspeakable that is already at hand.

Long ago, Māra made a vow before the Buddha, saying: "I can do nothing with you now; I shall wait for the age of the Dharma's decay (mofa), enter your gates, wear your robes, eat your food, and call myself your disciple, thereby destroying your Dharma. The Buddha said: "As for your destruction, let it destroy itself; my Dharma..."
It is indestructible; yet today, there are no signs of its own destruction that do not manifest.
Though it is said that the Dharma cannot be destroyed, the gateway of the Dharma has been breached and the ritual of transformation has ceased. Even a Buddha—what could he possibly do about this?
This realm is called Sahā (The Enduring). There is certainly no place here of peace and ease.

As soon as one steps before others, various circumstances—whether differing or identical, favorable or adverse—are presented in a chaotic array. This is unavoidable even for a Buddha who appears in the world, let alone others.

The essential point lies in gathering everything back into the emptiness of the fundamental limit of equality. Thus, what are called difference and sameness, or favorability and adversity, are none other than grounds for refining the mind.
At the time of refining one's practice, these possess profound benefit throughout daily life; this is not something that worldly people can understand.
If one merely follows one's own emotions and pursuits, generating delusions within oneself, then not only will external conditions be unable to [harm], [but internal stability will likewise be lost].
All is at peace; even for oneself, there is no place to set foot.
This is the method of the ancients for responding to the world: they must maintain it with stillness, await its unfolding with patience, and act according to their own capacity.
If my strength were always sufficient, I would neither be distressed nor exhausted, and my undertakings would surely succeed.
However, if one is fond of grandiosity and great achievements, and is in haste to act, then one’s strength will be small while the burden is heavy; it is rare that such a person does not fall.

One will inevitably have to seek extensively and toil bitterly to meet these demands. Once one has reached the point of seeking extensively and toiling bitterly, what leisure will there be to attend to anything else? It is inevitable.

They dispatch and employ people in such chaotic confusion that they no longer distinguish between cause and effect. They entangle themselves in petty dependencies until their integrity and sense of shame are utterly lost.

Let alone the fact that they fail to obtain what they seek; even if they do obtain it through their seeking, they cannot bear the thickness of their own faces. How could this be the way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs?
When people are young, having not yet experienced many lifetimes, their resolve is keen and their strength is robust; thus, many strive with indignation toward the upward path.
However, as the years pass and worldly thoughts deepen, their initial aspirations gradually decline. Subsequently, being turned by external conditions, many lose what they have maintained.
There was once a monk who left the white robe for the saffron in his early years and devoted himself to inquiry and investigation.
He transcended the mundane world and did not associate with the common folk. Dwelling in the mountains in solitude for over twenty years, many praised him.

Yet, in his later years, upon unexpectedly gaining a few worldly men who took refuge in him, he suddenly desired to enter the world of public ministry; he thus built temples, established a monastic community, opened the hall, and transmitted the Dharma.
He performed all these things with forced effort, only to end up losing both his reputation and his life, becoming a laughingstock for the whole world. [Poem]
It is said: "There is nothing that does not have a beginning, yet few are able to reach the end. How can one not be cautious?

After the Buddha entered *parinirvāṇa*, the True Dharma (*saddharma*) and the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpakadharma*) each lasted for one thousand years, and the Final Dharma (*antarmārga*) lasted for ten thousand years;

this merely states the general outline. If one were to discuss it in detail, there is a period of the Final Dharma even within the True Dharma, and there is also a period of the True Dharma within the Final Dharma.
The True Dharma depends entirely upon the person who receives it. Mencius said, "As for those who are heroic and eminent men, they will flourish even in the absence of King Wen.
This shows that those of superior faculties and sharp wisdom are certainly not restricted by the three periods [of the Dharma's decline].
Furthermore, since the Buddha-dharma is at all times perfect, luminous, transcendent, and absolute, how could it ever undergo waxing or waning? A person of resolve ought to...
Take the highest as your standard; do not allow yourself to fall into the base and low, and you will be fortunate.
To kill people for food—I have heard of this in North China, but it was unheard of in South China. Now it has already been seen in Min.
To exchange one's own child for food—I have heard of this in ancient sayings, but I have never heard of a mother eating her own child. Now that too...
This has been witnessed in Min. Alas! Among all forms of love, none surpasses that between father and son;
yet a mother’s love for her child is even greater than a father’s—even among tigers and wolves this is so. Yet by our own day, humans have come to fall short of even tigers and wolves.
Is this not indeed a great transformation since the dawn of antiquity?
The saying goes: "Of all that humans love, nothing is more cherished than life; of all that they loathe, nothing is more detested than death.

Yet, observing from the present day, we know that the love for fame and profit is even weightier than the concerns of life and death. If there is an opportunity to seize, not even nine oxen can pull one back;
even life and death would not be spared a second thought. Since the upheaval of the Jiashen year, whenever I have encountered those who know me...

Friends, you must certainly exhort one another to restrain the body and mind to survive this calamitous era; do not allow yourselves to be moved recklessly by the winds of circumstance, thereby inviting disaster upon yourselves.
In the end, not a single person believed [this warning], and many suffered the ruin of their families and the loss of their lives beyond all hope of rescue.
Those who managed to escape by luck were few indeed. Such is the power with which fame and profit entangle human beings.
I am now seventy-one years of age; I have long observed the ways of the world. That which has never occurred since antiquity has now come to pass.

That which I did not believe throughout my life, I now believe. I know deeply that the three poisons of greed, hatred, and delusion are boundless in their transformations and boundless in their calamities.
Even when they result in corpses strewn for ten thousand *li* and blood flowing until it forms rivers, the mind—
It has not yet ceased. Its beginning was merely a single moment’s lapse of thought. Should we not reflect upon this and guard against the subtle while blocking the gradual?
Should we not sternly punish ourselves and strive to turn back from it? Otherwise, if a flickering flame is not extinguished, it will eventually consume the plains and wilds;
if a tiny stream is not dammed, it will ultimately transform the mulberry fields. Even if one wishes to save oneself then, it would be like biting one's own navel—too late to be of avail.

The three karmas of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct are the very root of saṃsāra. If these karmas are not severed, then even if one possesses meditative concentration and wisdom, they will collectively result only in becoming a māra or a non-Buddhist.
Some frequently claim that the nature of karma is fundamentally empty; what then is there to sever and what to continue?

They fail to realize that while the nature of karma is indeed fundamentally empty, sentient beings grasp at it as real, thereby giving rise to karma and inviting its fruits. How can one say [it is empty] in such a case?
Emptiness. Formerly, during the Liang dynasty, there was a Dharma Master named Yunguang who was skilled at lecturing on the sutras and treatises but did not observe the precepts.
Master Zhi rebuked him, to which he replied: "I do not fast, yet I am fasting; I eat, yet it is not eating. Later, as a karmic retribution, he became an ox.
He was yoked to a cart in the mud and, despite his strength, could not move forward. The lashes and whips grew increasingly severe. As Master Zhi passed by, he saw him and called out, "Yunguang! Ox!"
He raised his head. Master Zhigong said, "Why do you not say today, 'I pull without pulling'? The ox shed tears and departed with a mournful cry.
Observing this, one sees that empty-headedness and wild interpretations can do nothing to oppose saṃsāra; though one wishes to deceive others, it only results in deceiving oneself. How lamentable!

Many Chan practitioners of recent times boast grandly without shame and fail to observe the *vinaya*. They constantly claim to abide in a state of expansive liberation and disregard the maintenance of reputation and integrity.

They always rely on the rhetoric of "perfect interfusion" (*yuanrong*) as an excuse; yet when they suddenly pursue power and profit, they are like hungry ghosts scrambling for spit, and when they contend over self and others, they are like vicious dogs guarding their homes. What, then, can be said of their so-called "perfect interfusion" and "expansive liberation"?
The single school of Dharma transcends emotion and leaves behind views; thus it is called "a separate transmission outside the teachings.

It cannot be deliberated upon through mouth or ear, nor can it be approximated by means of words and phrases. Therefore, the admonitions of former masters, who earnestly and repeatedly exhorted us toward true investigation, were not spoken in vain.
Lately, however, Zen practitioners have come to regard the words of these predecessors as incorrect, devoting themselves instead solely to the collective study of *songgu* (verses on ancient cases).

Regarding the study of *ji* (critical pivot) and *feng* (verbal wit): if one spends days studying until they have mastered the texts somewhat and their speech becomes somewhat slick, the master hands them a whisk (*buzi*).
Thus, masters and disciples deceive one another; where, then, is the true intent of Bodhidharma? Not only this:
I have seen those to whom the whisk was entrusted who died in a state of madness, those who abandoned the Way to return to secular life, and those...

Those who啸聚山林 (gather in the mountains and forests) and take plundering as their business, as well as others who are licentious, treacherous, and evil, and are held in contempt by the secular world—such people exist everywhere.
It is surely these types who will extinguish the lineage of the Tathāgata. Alas, how perilous!
Chan Master Boshan Lai said to me, Ji Sheng: "In the affairs of the Zen school, what is valued is the accord between heart and marrow, not the succession of formal lineages.
If one truly finds such a person, then whether it is through direct perception or hearsay, the priority and the sequence will be of one accord."
It is a severance, yet not a severance. If one does not encounter the right person, it is like adding water to milk, which dilutes its flavor;

or as the characters for "crow" (*wū*) and "three" (*sān*) can be mistaken for "horse" (*mǎ*). In such cases, does what remains truly remain? Therefore, my view is that it is better not to find the right person than to transmit the teaching to an unsuitable vessel.

If the right person is not found, although the lineage may be severed, the truth of the Way remains intact and does no harm to the Great Dharma. However, if it is transmitted to an unsuitable vessel, although the lineage may persist...
Yet those who propagate falsehoods instead undermine their own ancestral school. A person of wisdom ought to know how to exercise discernment.

According to my humble assessment, Bozan’s words such as these may be called truly dedicated to the Great Dharma. Although his successors are now few, the world still looks up to him as one would to a qilin or a phoenix;
when compared to those of recent times who recklessly transmit the lineage to unworthy persons, Bozan’s legacy is seen to have brought honor rather than disgrace to his ancestral school.
Furthermore, how could the difference between these two be anything less than that between heaven and earth?

There was a man surnamed Zhang among a gathering of scholar-officials enjoying a banquet who said: "Lately, monastics have been fabricating strange wonders, opening halls to preach the Dharma at every turn, and using their flattery to incite the common people.
I wish to compose with each of you gentlemen a 'Treatise on the Refutation of Chan' to extinguish this practice."
A man surnamed Chen said, "If you wish to abolish it, I beg to hear your reasoning. Zhang replied, "To have no father and no ruler is to be a pest to the state and a harm to the people;
these four crimes—how could he possibly escape them? Chen said, "It would be acceptable if you had some other lofty insight."

"If these four offenses are truly irremediable, and if China is now submerged and its people are suffering in the mire of calamity—if those who are said to be 'without father and without ruler,' who corrupt the state and harm the people, are all practitioners of Confucianism themselves, what does this have to do with the monks?
At this, Zhang was left speechless. A guest came forward from among the assembly and reported these words to me. I said: "The Chan of today is indeed..."
It may indeed be refuted. It is a pity that this gentleman did not grasp its true meaning.

I myself actually intended to compose a "Refutation of Chan," but fearing I might incur the wrath of others, I did not dare to do so. Alas! Is it Chan? Is it Confucianism? Where shall I turn for refuge?
One night, Wang, a commander of a thousand households at Quan, dreamed that someone told him: "I am Zhang Jie. I have now been reborn as a deer.
Unluckily, I was captured by a man who used me as a gift to curry favor with high officials. I am now being sent to the nun who is the younger sister of Marquis Hou."
"May you rescue and deliver me; do not kill me. The King woke slightly, reflected on this, but did not recognize Zhang Ji as anyone in particular.

Shortly thereafter, he fell back asleep and again dreamed that Ji entreated him with extreme sorrow. The King’s mind was moved by this; he rose early and informed his younger sister, a nun. The nun said, "I know of him.
She then related her brother's words to the official (the Duke) and begged for his life. The official would not grant it.
In the end, he killed him. Alas! Did Master Zhang come to such a pass? At that time, the Master prided himself on his talent and learning;
though he associated with Han Yu, he refused to take him as his teacher. Why, then, has he now fallen like a deer into a trap?
To seek to escape being killed while in the form of a deer is likewise impossible; why is this so?
It is because one is dragged by the karma of killing and flows into the ranks of other species to repay past debts, for which there is no skillful means to avoid.
I do not know when Master Zhang’s suffering will end. How tragic!
A Brief Record of the Conduct and Deeds of the Great Monk Master Yongjue Xian of Yongquan Chan Temple on Baiyun Peak at Gushan in Fuzhou.
The Master’s name was Yuanyuan;
his courtesy name was Yongjue. He was a native of Jianyang and the fourteenth-generation descendant of the great Song dynasty Confucian scholar, Mr. Cai of the Western Hills.

He was the great-grandson of [his grandfather]. His father was Yuntin and his mother was Lady Zhang; his birth mother was Lady Fan. He was born on the nineteenth day of the seventh month in the Wanyili戊寅 year.
The Master’s original name was Maode and his style name was Anxiu. He was a renowned local student (*zhusheng*) who took a deep interest in the learning of Zhou, Cheng, Zhang, and Zhu.
At the age of twenty-five, while reading in a mountain temple, he heard someone reciting a verse from the *Lotus Sūtra* that began: "I and you..."
At that time, he manifested a body of pure radiance. Suddenly filled with joy, he remarked, "Beyond Confucius and Mencius, there is yet this one great matter.
He then visited Zhao Yuzhai of the same district and received the *Śūraṅgama*, *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and *Awakening of Faith* (Yuanjue) sutras.

The following year, he encountered Master Wuming Shouchang, who was expounding the Dharma at Dongyan. The Master went to pay his respects and engaged him in a series of rigorous inquiries. Shouchang said:

This matter cannot be resolved through intellectual understanding; it requires diligent investigation to achieve resonance with it. Consequently, he was urged to contemplate the "dry dung shovel. After a long time, he made no progress.
One day, while hosting a monk for a night-long sitting, he brought up the story of Nanquan’s beheading of the cat.

At that moment, he attained realization and composed a verse: "The two halls were in a chaotic clamor, utterly groundless; When the precious sword was swung, all courage turned cold. Fortunately, there was Zhaozhou arriving late..."
The Governor’s Old Man stood alone atop the crown of Vairocana. He presented this to Shouchang, who said: "A student of the Way must by no means take a single phrase or a single scene as a standard.
Even if one passes directly through a hundred layers and a thousand folds with hands extended, one must still encounter the person.
As it is said: 'Though the body may already be upon the blue clouds, one still further enters the multitude of treasuries.'"
This is the eye of one who studies the Way. A verse of distinction says: "The skillful means of the Great Square House—encountering an object, it cuts it in two with a single stroke.
Zhaozhou saved this cat, yet he could not avoid being thoroughly deceived once more. If one were a spirit possessing a path, one would ultimately demand his life in exchange.
Upon reading this verse, the Master gained even greater clarity. When his two parents passed away in succession, the Master was forty years old; he then finally tore [his monastic robes].
A young man in his blue scholar’s robe who had been abandoned by his wife went to Shouchang to shave his head and receive the name Anjin (Anjin).

Whenever the Master requested instruction, Chang would simply say, "I am not as good as you. One day, encountering Chang returning from plowing, the Master went up to him and asked, "What is the pure, radiant body?
Chang stood up straight. The Master said, "Is it only this, or is there something else? Chang then walked away.
The Master suddenly attained a state of vast clarity, as if casting off a heavy burden. He followed [Chang] into the abbot’s quarters;

as he was about to prostrate and explain what he had realized, Chang struck him three times with his staff and said, "Henceforth, you must not be careless. He then presented this verse: "Each time one penetrates through, it becomes deeper;
From of old, Buddhas and Patriarchs have not permitted others [to know]. Even if one were to leap onto the back of the Golden-Haired One, I would still have them receive a blow from my staff."

He turned himself around. The Master did not even utter a word before withdrawing. Yet he still harbored doubt, wondering: "Why must one further turn oneself around beneath the staff? The following year, in the Wuwu year, Shouchang passed away. When Master Bowshan Wuyi came to attend the funeral, the Master went with him to Mount Bo. Mount Bo asked, "Have you yet paid your respects before the portrait of the late Master? The Master replied, "I have. Mount Bo said, "Then why did you not prostrate yourself? The Master said, "I was afraid that if I prostrated myself, I would lose my life. Mount Bo said, "If you had lost your life, you would have gained it. The Master said, "I am already dead. Mount Bo said, "How can you say you are dead when you are still here? The Master said, "I am dead, yet I am not dead. Mount Bo said, "What do you mean by 'dead'? The Master said, "It means that I have no more life. Mount Bo said, "What do you mean by 'not dead'? The Master said, "It means that I have no more death. Mount Bo said, "What do you mean by 'dead yet not dead'? The Master said, "It means that I have neither life nor death. Mount Bo said, "What do you mean by 'neither life nor death'? The Master said, "It means that I have neither life nor death, and yet there is neither life nor death. Mount Bo said, "What do you mean by 'neither life nor death, and yet there is neither life nor death'? The Master said, "It means that I have neither life nor death, and yet there is neither life nor death; I have neither life nor death, and yet there is neither life nor death. Mount Bo said, "This is truly the turning over of oneself beneath the staff. The Master said, "It is not so. Mount Bo said, "How can you say it is not so? The Master said, "It is not so, and yet it is so. Mount Bo said, "How can you say it is so? The Master said, "It is so, and yet it is not so. Mount Bo said, "How can you say it is not so? The Master said, "It is not so, and yet it is not not-so. Mount Bo said, "How can you say it is not not-so? The Master said, "It is not not-so, and yet it is not not-not-so. Mount Bo said, "How can you say it is not not-not-so? The Master said, "It is not not-not-so, and yet it is not not-not-not-so. Mount Bo said, "How can you say it is not not-not-not-so? The Master said, "It is not not-not-not-so, and yet it is not not-not-not-not-so. Mount Bo said, "How can you say it is not not-not-not-not-so? The Master said, "It is not not-not-not-not-so, and yet it is not not-not-not-not-not-so. Mount Bo said, "How can you say it is not not-not-not-not-not-so?
