When it was finished, Mount [Shan] asked, "Did you still see the Master? The Master said, "I saw him. Mount asked, "What is that which you saw?
The Master said, "It is the same as what the Master saw back in his own day. Mount said, "I grant you one point for now. Not long after, he received full ordination (*upasampadā*).
When his biological mother fell gravely ill, he returned home to visit her. After she passed away, he went again to Boshan to receive the Bodhisattva precepts.
He resided at Incense Burner Peak (Xianglu Feng), where he and Mount Shanshi frequently discussed profound mysteries. The Master never shied away from taking the lead when it was his turn to speak;
Mount Shanshi sighed and said, "This man has always been self-assured throughout his life. In the future, no one in the world will be able to withstand him.

After three years had passed, he returned to Min Province and stayed at Double-Top Peak (Shuangji Feng) in Sha County. The following year, he went back to Jianyang to bury his parents. While crossing the Sword River (Jianjin) by boat, he encountered the following:
He heard a fellow monk chanting the sutras, saying: "At one time, they coughed simultaneously and snapped their fingers together;

these two sounds reached everywhere throughout the worlds of the Buddhas of the ten directions. At this, Master Kuò attained great enlightenment and thoroughly realized the point of Shouchang’s teaching.

He then composed a verse, which says: "The golden rooster pecks through the azure lapis lazuli; Ten thousand ceasings and a thousand restings are known only to oneself. Lying peacefully upon a fragment..."
The sky was bright and clear; on the mountains ahead, the rain had ceased and only cuckoos sang. It was the ninth month of autumn in the year of Guihai;
the Master was forty-six years of age. He resided at the Jinxian Hermitage in Oning for three years, reading the Tripitaka, before moving to Heshan in Jian’an.
The following year, in Jieli, he requested that the Tripitaka be returned and composed the *Hongshi Lu* (Record of the Propagation of Śākyamuni) for Jianzhou.

Previously, while the Master was residing at Boshan, Wuyi Heshang had once entrusted him with the task of establishing the various Buddhist centers in Jianzhou. The Master replied, "My great matter is not yet concluded;
I have no leisure to attend to this. When the Master went into seclusion at Heshan, Wuyi returned from Shigou and passed through Jianzhou on his way back. The Master...
Wu was different from [his experience at] Guangxiao Temple. Upon seeing him for the first time, Wu recognized him and said, "This must be the monk from Jianzhou.
The Master smiled but did not answer. Wu then asked, "Have you swept the pagoda at Shouchang yet? The Master replied, "I have not neglected the sweeping;
it is simply that I do not allow others to know of it. Wu said, "In that case, you must be sweeping it in secret. The Master said, "Monk..."
He asked again, "How so? Zhenyi replied, "Sweeping is not neglected; it is simply that nothing has been moved. The Master said, "In that case, you, Master, seem as though you have never swept at all.
They laughed and parted. When this book was completed, Zhenyi wrote the preface and circulated it.

Furthermore, he sought to harmonize Confucianism and Buddhism, composing the *Yiyanyan* (Words from a Dream). In the year Xinwei, he went to Jianyang to edit the posthumous works of Cai Yong and other Confucian scholars.
On the *renshen* day, I visited Master Wengu at Baoshan Hermitage. Upon our first meeting, we found ourselves in perfect accord, though I lamented that our encounter had come so late.
It happened that Cao Anzu, Military Commissioner of Yixing, requested the Master to compose eulogies for the portraits of the various patriarchs;

consequently, he commissioned the Master to take up his brush. The Master completed over a hundred eulogies, which left the Master so profoundly amazed that he remarked, "I shall not enter the monastic order."
The Duke was about to depart this world and concealed his intentions from all people. He immediately conferred the Great Precepts upon the Master.

The following year, when my late father went to the imperial court, I accompanied him on the official journey (*jìxié*). Passing through Fén and Cháng, I visited the Great Master Wén, where I first beheld the Master’s model of the Way.
Subsequently, together with Cáo Yànzé, the Minister of Rites, and various faithful adherents, we invited him to preside over Gǔshān. In the year Jiǎxū, he entered the monastery.

He was requested to open the hall for formal sermons, but he did not grant permission; instead, he only preached the precepts for the fourfold assembly. To those who requested the Dharma, he merely instructed them using the etiquette of an abbot.
That autumn, he constructed the Hall of Heavenly Kings (Tianwang Dian) as well as the two pavilions for the bell and drum. In the year Yihai, he went to Shaoshang to sweep the pagoda;
on his way back, he passed through Jianzhou and, for the sake of Jingci Monastery, composed the *Jingci Yaoyu* (Essential Words of Jingci). That winter, Zhang Ershui visited him.
Minister Guo Lütiánchí, admiring the Master’s spiritual transformation, led the assembly in inviting him to enter Kaiyuan Temple in Quanzhou.
Knowing that the karmic conditions were now ripe, the Master finally opened the hall to begin the formal retreat; the fourfold assembly gathered like clouds.

From within his robe, he specially offered the fragrant incense for the Elder Wuming. The following year, Minister Cóng Yúnyún, then serving as a provincial governor in Southern Quanzhou, visited him.
The Master built a hall for him at Kaiyuan Temple. Because the meaning of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* was profound and abstruse, he requested the Master to compose a commentary on it.

In the autumn, he returned to Gushan Mountain and constructed a Tripitaka Hall to the east of the Dharma Hall. In the year Dingchou, he received the news of the Great Master’s passing and personally went to Zhenji Temple to pay his respects.
The various masters of Western Zhejiang, in accordance with the Master’s final instructions, jointly requested him to serve as the abbot.

They carved the Master’s parting words, enshrined his remains in a stupa, and composed an inscription for it. In the year Wuyin (1638), following the request of the Imperial Censor Yugou Cao Gong, they again compiled the *Biographies of the Images of the Patriarchs*.
In the year Gengchen (1640), he established Cuīyún Ān at Xīshè in Yúháng. In the year Xinsi (1641), he moved to Wǔ.

He went to Puming Temple in the prefecture, and in autumn returned to Min to reside at Baoshan. The following year, he traveled to Kaiyuan Temple in Quanzhou for the commencement of the retreat (jie-zhi) and compiled the *Kaiyuan Zhi*.
He subsequently returned to Gushan, where he renovated the main halls, the mountain gate, and all the various monastic quarters one after another until they were newly restored and fully adorned.
Furthermore, he erected the stupas for the two masters Focen and Han’an Sheng on Mount Xianglu.

He returned home and further constructed a stupa to enshrine the robes and bowl of Master Boshan, inscribing a commemorative stele for them. In the year Guiwei, he accepted an invitation from Xingfu Temple in Jianzhou;

upon the conclusion of his term there, he went to Baoshan to construct a stupa for śarīra relics. In the winter, he returned to Gushan and carved the *Chan-yu nei-wai ji* (Collected Works on Chan Leisure, Inner and Outer).
In the year Yiyou (1645), he composed the *Brief Commentary on the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and compiled the *Gushan Gazetteer*.
In the year Bingxu (1646), Zheng Ruirui, the Minister of Works, along with various scholar-officials, again invited him to Jingtian Monastery in Jianzhou to offer prayers for the state;

following this, he moved to Baoshan to administer the precepts and composed the *Summary of the Meaning of the Four-Part Vinaya Precept Text*, which served as a starting point for the study of Vinaya. In the year Dinghai (1647), he returned to Gushan and composed...

He traced the ancient tracks of the Tōng (Dong) lineage and continued the *Yìyán* (Sleeping Words). In the year Jǐchǒu (1639), he composed the *Bǔdēnglù* (Supplement to the Lamp Record) to fill the omissions in the *Wǔdēnghuìyuán* (Five Lamps Meeting the Source).
In the year Gēngyīn (1650), he collected over a thousand unclaimed remains and buried them. In the year Xīnmǎo (1651), he produced the *Jìdēnglù* (Continuation of the Lamp Record).
Previously, those who recorded and transmitted the lamp of the Chan school had ceased with the Song dynasty; from the end of the Song until the Ming, for over four hundred years, there was [a gap].
The tradition of the lamp had been passed down, yet no one had yet practiced it. The Master searched widely and gathered extensively until, at this point, he produced a completed work.

In the summer of the Renchen year, he carved the *Wanlu* (Evening Record). In the autumn, he constructed a memorial pagoda for his parents at the eastern corner of the Śarīra Cave, and further repaired the tombs of the two Chan masters Shantang and Huaitang.
He dispatched a disciple to retrieve the Great Tripitaka from Jinling. In the Jiawu year, he authored the *Xinjing Zhizhang* (Pointing to the Palm of the Heart Sutra).
He collected more than two thousand eight hundred remains. In the spring of the year Yiwu, Fucheng and Changle in Xinghua suffered a military upheaval;
starving men and women flowed into the southern suburbs of Huicheng, their piteous state such that people could not bear to look upon them.

The Master then gathered the assembly and dispatched his disciples to establish soup kitchens for relief. He provided coffins for those who had died and buried them, totaling over two thousand people. By the time he reached...
He ceased [teaching] after fifty days. On the day of Dingyou, the Master was eighty years old.

On the first day of the Yuanxuan festival, he took up his robe and whisk and entrusted them to his senior disciple, Master Weilinpai, immediately appointing him to lead the assembly and share the teaching seat; the assembly was greatly delighted and submissive.
On the nineteenth day of the seventh month in autumn, coinciding with the Master’s birthday, those from all quarters gathered to request that he open the Dharma. Since the year of Xinmao...

He was forbidden from ascending the hall; though he pleaded with all his might, it was not permitted. Upon reaching this point, he joyfully ascended the seat. However, he frequently expressed his intention to pass away.
On the first day of the ninth month, he indeed manifested illness. He did not eat for over twenty days, yet his daily activities remained as usual.
Thereupon, he spoke a verse, saying: "The old man’s nature has been too biased since birth; I refused to follow the stream into the worldly marketplace. This stubborn nature remains to this day..."
"Still not transformed, I shall use my stubborn and haughty bones to rescue Confucianism and Chan. In Confucianism, the true pursuit of fame and achievement has already perished;

in Chan, the reverence for intellectual skill makes perfect conduct difficult to maintain. Now that I am on the verge of death, what further use is there? I shall simply offer this thought as a repayment to the dragons and devas.

He said, "Monks, all matters of both the mundane and the supramundane are fully contained within this verse. Do not neglect it! Thereupon, he closed his eyes and passed away in the auspicious posture.
He lay down. When he had entered samādhi for several days, the Head Seat asked him: "How shall the final phrase be entrusted? The Master took up his brush and wrote:
"The final phrase is personally entrusted; within and without the three realms, there is no place to be sought.
Three days later, at midnight, he said to the Head Seat, "I am not ill," and ordered his attendant to help him sit up. Once seated, he cast off his body.

He passed away at the hour of the rat on the seventh day of the tenth month. Three days later, the coffin was finally closed; his countenance remained as if alive, causing the assembly to all marvel at this wonder.
The Master’s demeanor was lofty and extraordinary, and he possessed the physical marks of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa*). Throughout his life, he presided over four monasteries.

Wherever he went, he dwelt deeply within his private chamber, remaining serene and free from worldly concerns, appearing as if he were not occupied with affairs; yet donors vied with one another to offer their support, and all matters of business were successfully managed.
He raised [the topic]: "Scholars from the four quarters come without being refused and depart without being detained;

beneath his seat there are always many eminent monks, all of whom he exhorts toward true inquiry and actual realization, while strictly warning them against the poisonous mixture of intellectual understanding.

When he ascends the hall to preach the Dharma, his eloquence and discernment are纵横 (zōnghéng—unrestrained and pervasive), like clouds spreading across a vast sky. When he takes up the brush and pen, pearls and gems roll forth; even a single phrase or a solitary character is without exception [profound]."

Exquisite and absolute. Regarding the fundamental principles of the Caodong school, those who from of old had been corrupted by turbid wisdom and delusion were all rectified by means of the mind-seal (xinyin), returning them once more to the ancient path.
Throughout his life, he was cautious and reverent toward the Great Dharma; for nearly thirty years since opening the hall, he never lightly granted instruction to students.
It was only at the age of eighty that he finally selected Master Pei alone to receive it. All quarters of the monastic community marveled at his strictness. Furthermore—

His character was as steadfast as a mountain, and his conduct as pure as ice and frost. To protect the Way and save the world, he would not have been deterred even if a blade of white steel were held before him.
Alas! How could the Master have been an ordinary man? The world calls him an ancient Buddha returned to this age;

that his merit and wisdom are perfectly luminous and that his compassion and insight are fully endowed is truly no exaggeration. Furthermore, wherever he went, he manifested extraordinary traces. In the *ding* year of the Heavenly Stem cycle...
In the year Mǎo, he resided at Heshan in Jian’an. One day, while walking outside the mountain gate, a tiger suddenly rushed toward him.
The attendant fell to the ground in alarm, but the Master pointed his staff at it; the tiger turned around, roared, and departed. In the year Jiǎxū, the Master took up residence at Gushan.
On the eleventh day of the fourth month, sweet dew descended upon the pine trees at the mountain gate. The Master composed a verse, saying: "A holy omen should descend upon the Great Capital;
How could this remote mountain alone be moistened? At dawn, leaning on my staff outside the triple gates, I smile as I watch jade beads cluster upon the pines.
On the nineteenth day of the ninth month of that same year, sweet dew descended once more. The Master again composed a verse, beginning with: "Jade..."

The mist drifts and falls once more; throughout the grove, flowers and trees are all in full bloom. Be careful not to say it is as sweet as honey, for fear it might entice wandering travelers into the Stone Gate.
When the Master was traveling to Wénlíng, Mr. Lǚ led the monks of Kāiyuán Temple to meet him at Luóyáng Bridge.
At that time, the tide had already receded, but upon the Master’s arrival, the tide surged back again. The assembly...
Everyone was struck with astonishment. A monk asked, "The timing of the tides has never failed for a thousand years;
why have they arrived again today? The Master said, "Ask the Lord of the Tides. The monk said, "Is it not because of you, the Master? The Master said, "Do not defile me, monk!
In Quanzhou there is a deity called Lord Wu (Wu Zhenren), who was the disciple of Xu Jingyang of the Jin dynasty, namely Wu Meng.
This deity is a native of Nanan. Many people in Quanzhou offer sacrifices to him. In the fourth month of the Bingzi year, the Master was preaching the precepts at Kaiyuan Temple.
One day prior, the deity appeared in a dream to the ritual master (zhù) and said, "Prepare one thousand coins for me; I wish to go to Kaiyuan to receive the precepts.
The following day, the deity arrived at the temple riding in a palanquin. He used the pole of the palanquin to write upon the ground, requesting a dharma-name and five [other items].
The Master gave him the name Daozheng and conferred upon him the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts before departing. Shen was skilled at treating illnesses, so many people went to invite him;
however, since receiving the precepts, he no longer accepted such invitations. Whenever anyone entered his temple to offer sacrifices, he would never use pungent foods or wine.
In the spring of the Renwu year, the Master returned to Ch’uan. The True Man (Chen-jen) came once more and requested the Bodhisattva precepts.

A local deity from a neighboring village named Chang Hsiang-kung also came together with him to seek the precepts; the Master conferred upon him the Dharma name Tao-ch’eng, and both received the Bodhisattva precepts.
Furthermore, the mother of the Yu family of An-p’ing, whose name was Tao-chiao, received the five precepts from the Master. One night she fell ill and passed away. The official of the underworld...
Question: "What meritorious deeds did you perform in your previous life? Qiao replied, "I once went to Kaiyuan Temple and received the five precepts from Master Yong.
The official said, "Since your observance of the five precepts was not greatly violated, you shall be reborn in a good realm.
You should go to Master Yong's place for me and request a verse. Qiao then revived; he sent his son to request the verse, and the Master gave him this verse: "Clearly there is one..."

"The path to the West lies solely within a single thought-moment of the person. When one sees through the body and mind as being like horse-horns, the sword-trees and knife-mountains are instantly empty.
Having uttered this verse, Qiao closed his eyes and passed away. In the year Wuyin, the Master was at Zhenji Monastery in Hangzhou.
At that time, there was a scholar from Guian named Mao Weiqi, who had never been a follower of Buddhism. One night he dreamed that a messenger of the underworld came to summon him.
Weiqi rose up and pleaded bitterly not to go. The messenger said, "I will go for a moment; can you be diverted? After about ten days had passed—
The ghost messenger returned and said, "This matter cannot be altered; however, I shall grant you seven days of respite. It would be well for you to gather your things.
The next day, Weiqi went directly to Zhenji to seek salvation from the Master. The Master said, "How can I save you? But can you subsist on vegetarian food? He replied, "I can.
"Can you resolve to attain the Unsurpassed Mind and receive the Bodhisattva precepts? He replied, "I can."
He then conferred the precepts upon him and he returned home. For one month, nothing untoward occurred. However, his parents again pressured him with wine and meat.
One day, having become heavily intoxicated, he was seized by a spirit and brought before the underworld authorities.

The official rebuked him, saying, "Because you were able to resolve your mind and receive the precepts from Master Yong, I did not take you [to hell]. Why have you now brought this downfall upon yourself? Wei Qi pleaded, saying, "I..."
"I do not dare break the precepts. My mother had only me as her child; fearing that my body would become weak from a vegetarian diet, she forced me to eat meat.
Hereafter, I swear never to commit this offense again. The underworld authorities granted his request, whereupon he awoke and recorded these events for posterity.
In the summer of the *Xinsi* year, the Master was at Puming Temple in Jinhua. At that time, there was a great famine, and many of the residents were without food. Lanxi—

There was a man surnamed Zhao whose family was poor and who made his living by burning limestone. He would sell a kiln’s worth of lime and use half of the proceeds to provide offerings for a vegetarian feast.
The Master marveled at how difficult this was for him to do. Later, in the autumn, he fell ill with malaria. One day he died; from noon until the hour of the Dog (7–9 p.m.), he returned to life.

He said of himself: "When I first departed, everything was vast and indistinct, and I did not know where I was going. Later, after traversing several layers of high mountains, I suddenly encountered Master Yongjue.
He asked me, 'Why have you come here? I replied, 'I do not know. He asked, 'Do you wish to return? I replied,"
He was in great haste to return, but did not know the way. The Master said, "Just follow me. After traveling several *li*, the Master pointed and said, "This is Jinhua Prefecture.
After another several *li*, he pointed again and said, "This is Lanxi County.
After yet another several *li*, he pointed once more and said, "This is your home," pushing him with his hand. He then woke up. At the time, people spread the story far and wide. The Master said:
"How could I possibly enter the underworld to save people? It was entirely due to his single thought of wholesome roots that this phenomenon appeared.

In the summer of the Guiwei year, while the Master resided at Baoshan on Jianjin, a great drought occurred; for three months there was no rain, the vegetation was as if scorched by fire, and the hearts of the people were filled with dread.
The local officials visited every spirit shrine in turn, but none responded. The Commissioner of Military Affairs, Lord Sun, dispatched a messenger...
A military officer went to Baoshan and requested the Master to offer prayers on his behalf. The Master ascended the hall and said: "O worthy ones, from where does the wind come?

From where does the rain arise? When the Thunder King flies forth from the head of the black clouds, if one asks where he ultimately dwells—when the Dragon King Sāgara sends down rain, he need only stir a single thought, and the rain will pervade the entire Sahā world. Son.
Look closely: it does not depart from this very place. What kind of place is this? Do you know? [The Master] raises his staff and says:
"The old monk’s staff has transformed into a dragon, spitting mist and raising clouds that obscure the heavens and hide the sun.
It pours down a great torrent, pervading the entire Jambudvīpa. The assembly, tell me: by what power of grace is this received? [He] plants the staff firmly in the ground.

As he set down his staff and descended from his seat, rain immediately poured down like an overturned basin, filling the valley to a depth of three feet; that year’s harvest was exceptionally bountiful.

In the year Dinghai, bandits plundered Gushan. As they carried the Master on a sedan chair halfway up the ridge, the bearers suddenly stumbled and fell. Consequently, they escorted the Master back to the mountain.
His boat was moored in the river, and its mast was struck by lightning; the pirates were terrified and did not dare to attack again.
A Buddhist monk from Kapilavastu came to present the Master with a wooden bowl, which he used regularly during his two daily meals.

In the first month of spring in the year of Gui-si, a fire broke out at the pavilion beside the abbot’s quarters; only this wooden bowl remained undamaged. The following day, it was recovered from the ashes.
Regarding various supernatural occurrences, the Master declined them all and would not take credit for them, admonishing that they not be passed on.
Those who followed him numbered over three hundred, while those who sought the Way and received the precepts were no fewer than tens of thousands.
The total number of those who attained ordination was several thousand; he conferred the precepts upon six disciples: Cunsimong, Seogyo, Ugong, Jangam, Jin-gong, and Mokwi.

The *Jingxinming* (Inscription on the Mind of Vigilance), the *Gongzong shengshan gong suoshuo fayu lu* (Recorded Sayings of the Venerable Master Gongzong Shengshan), and his various other writings comprise over eighty volumes in total.
On the twenty-first day of the first month of the Wuxu year, his entire body was enshrined at the Shou-ta Pagoda in his native Xiyu.
Among those who served as attendants to the Master, none had been under his tutelage for as long as I. I am thus thoroughly familiar with the Master’s life.

Furthermore, at the earnest request of Master Pài, I have carefully recorded these accounts to transmit them. Every word is based on actual fact; I dare not add any embellishments or paint upon the void.
My sole purpose is to reveal the Master’s true conduct and manifest it for ten thousand generations. Thus it is said.
Composed respectfully by Lin Zhifan, a recipient of the jinshi degree, Grand Officer of the Second Class (Fengzheng Dagu),
Langzhong of the Kaogong Qinglis司 (Bureau of Examination) in the Ministry of Personnel, formerly Yuanwailang of the same ministry’s Wensuan Qinglis司 (Bureau of Selection),
Censor of the Zhejiang Dao, and Disciple of the Bodhisattva Precepts.
According to the biography of Master Yongjue of Gushan, the Master entered the Buddhist path from Confucianism. He once said: "Śākyamuni is a sage who enters the world;
Confucius is a sage who transcends the world. Indeed, one cannot enter the world without first transcending it. Thus, after attaining the Way, he spoke of governing the world.
The Dharma has the power to rescue the defects of both Confucianism and Chan. Through direct investigation and genuine realization, it is vast and all-encompassing.

A master such as he was truly a singular figure among the enlightened ones of the past three hundred years. In the year Wuxu, the year following the master’s passing into stillness, I privately reflected that I had no means to pay my respects in person.

Having followed the Chief Seat Lin throughout my life, I have acquired a very detailed understanding of the master’s life from beginning to end. Thus, I have carefully prepared this plain record for him.
This preface is offered merely to convey my inexhaustible thoughts. The Master’s name was Yuánxián (元賢), his courtesy name Yǒngjué (永覺). He was a native of Jiānyáng, surnamed Cài.
He was the fourteenth-generation descendant of the Song dynasty scholar Xīshān Xiānshēng (Xīshān Xiānshēng). His father was Yúntín, his mother Zhāng, and his birth mother Fàn.

He was born on the nineteenth day of the seventh month in the Wànlì year of the Earth-Tiger cycle (1618). The Master’s original name was Mào dé (懋德) and his courtesy name was Ànxīū (闇修). He was a renowned figure of the county...

All you students: I have been fond of the teachings of Zhou, Cheng, Zhang, and Zhu since my youth. At the age of twenty-five in the year of Renyin, while reading in a mountain temple, I heard someone reciting a verse from the *Lotus Sūtra*:
"At that time, I appeared for him in a body of pure radiance. Immediately, I realized that beyond the teachings of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius, there was this other great matter.
In the year of Gui-mao, the Venerable Wuming of Shouchang opened the Dharma at Dongyan; I went there to him.
He went to visit him. After several rounds of questioning and cross-examination, Chang said, "This matter cannot be resolved through intellectual understanding;

one must exert oneself in practice to achieve realization. He then urged him to contemplate the "dry dung pellet. One day, upon hearing a monk cite the story of Nanquan’s killing of the cat, he attained awakening.
He then composed a verse and presented it to Chang. Chang said, "A student of the Way must by no means grasp the truth through a single phrase or a single scene."
"Thus, even if there were a hundred circuits and a thousand layers, he would pass straight through with his hand hanging down, yet he would still encounter people. This is what is meant by:

'Though one's body is already atop the azure clouds, one still further enters the storehouse of the multitude. This is the eye of one who studies the Way. The Master responded, "Yes, yes," and respectfully accepted the instruction.
When his two parents had passed away in succession, in the year Ding-si, the Master was forty years old.

He finally tore his scholar’s robes, abandoned his wife and children, and went to Shouchang to shave his head, where he received the name Anjin (Anjin). Whenever the Master requested instruction, Chang simply said, "I am not as good as you."
One day, Chang returned from plowing. The Master went out to meet him and asked, "What is the pure, radiant body?
Chang stood up straight. The Master said, "Is that all? Is there something else? Chang then walked away. At that moment, the Master suddenly attained great clarity, as if casting off a heavy burden.
He followed Chang into the abbot’s quarters, intending to communicate what he had realized. Chang turned the handle of his hoe upside down and struck him three times with force, saying, "Speak!"
He was not to be dismissed so lightly. The Master then spoke a verse: "Each time one penetrates through, it grows deeper; From of old, Buddhas and Patriarchs have never permitted it to others.
Even if you were to mount the back of the Golden-Haired Lion, They would still force you to turn yourself around beneath the staff. The Master’s whole body broke into a sweat;
he did not even manage to utter a word before withdrawing. Yet he remained in doubt, wondering: "For what reason must one still turn oneself around beneath the staff?"
In the ninth month of autumn, Huaixiang entered the abbot’s quarters to request a record of his life and deeds. Chang composed about six hundred words by hand and bestowed them upon him.

On the eighteenth day of the twelfth month, Chang manifested slight illness. At the stroke of New Year’s Eve, he personally instructed his attendant to hang the signboard for the formal lecture hall (shàngtáng).
The Master knelt and said, "The Abbot is unwell; we do not dare trouble him with matters of daily life. Chang replied, "That which has a beginning must have an end—do you understand this?
It is because he personally received my final entrustment. On the seventeenth day of the first month of the following year, the Wumu (57th) year, Chang wrote a verse and passed away while seated.
The Master wept bitterly for him and specially composed the *Xingye* (Account of Conduct) and the *Heilin* (Heling Monastery) [biographies].
He recorded this in his collection. As for Chang’s life and career, the Master alone possessed this knowledge. At that time, Boshan arrived to attend to his father’s funeral;

when he returned, the Master went with him to receive the full precepts (*upasampadā*). They remained together for three years, frequently discussing the profound mysteries of the Dharma, during which time creative insights spontaneously emerged.
Boshan sighed and said, "This man has always been self-assured; in the future, people throughout the world will not [be able to surpass him]."

"What can be done about him? he said. In the year of Wuchen (1082), he returned to Min and resided at Shuangji Peak in Sha County. In the year of Guihai (1083), he returned to Jianyang to bury his parents.
As his boat passed the Jian River ferry, he heard fellow monks chanting the *Lotus Sūtra*, saying: "At one time, they all coughed and snapped their fingers together;
these two sounds reached throughout the worlds of the Buddhas in the ten directions. At this, the Master attained great enlightenment.
He then clearly perceived the point of Shouchang’s application and composed a verse, saying: "The golden rooster pecks through the azure lapis lazuli;
Ten thousand cessations and a thousand restings are known only to oneself. Reclining peacefully on a single sail under a clear sky, On the mountain ahead, the rain-birds no longer cry.
At that time, the Master was forty-six years old. He subsequently hung up his staff at the Jinxian Hermitage in Ouning to read the Tripitaka. In the Ding year...
In the second year of the Mǎo year, he moved to Heshan in Jian’an. One day, while walking outside the mountain gate, a tiger suddenly appeared.
The attendant fell to the ground in alarm. The Master pointed at it with his staff; the tiger turned around, roared, and departed.

In the spring of the Wùchén year, Boshan returned from Shigǔ to Jianzhou and met him at Guǎngxiào Temple. Boshan asked, "Have you swept the pagoda of Shòuchāng yet? The Master replied: [text fragment].
The Master said, "Sweeping is not neglected; it is simply that you do not permit others to know of it. Yunmen said, "In that case, you have been sweeping in secret.
The Master said, "I am just like this. But what about you, Reverend? Yunmen said, "Sweeping is not neglected; it is simply that I have never moved a muscle.
The Master said, "Then you, Reverend, seem as though you have not swept at all. He then laughed and departed. (Guiyou year)
I heard that the Great Master had met with Bao-shan like water and milk merging; it was as if they were bound by a karmic affinity from a former life.

At that time, Cao Anzu, the Military Commissioner, requested that he compose eulogies for the portraits of the various patriarchs. Consequently, the Master was commissioned to take up his brush and composed over a hundred eulogies.
The Great Master was startled and said, "I shall not enter Jian. You intend to deceive all the people of the world! He then conferred the Great Precepts upon the Master.
In the year Jiashu, Cao the Court Grandee, Lin the Military Commissioner of Yanze, Deshan, and various lay devotees invited him to preside over Gushan.

Although they requested that he open the hall for formal preaching, he did not consent; instead, he only preached the precepts for the fourfold assembly. To those who requested the Dharma, he served as the abbot of the hermitage.
The Master merely showed this to the assembly. On the eleventh day of the fourth month, sweet dew descended upon the pines of the mountain gate.
The Master composed a verse, saying: "A sacred omen should descend upon the great capital; How could this remote mountain alone receive its moistening?

At dawn, leaning on my staff outside the triple gates, I laugh as I behold the jade beads clustering at the pine tips. On the nineteenth day of the ninth month, it fell again. He composed another verse, beginning: "Jade dew..."

A fresh flurry of blossoms once more; throughout the groves, flowers and trees are all in full bloom. Be careful not to say they are as sweet as honey, for fear of drawing in travelers to the Stone Gate.

In the following year, the year of Yihai (1075), Zhang the State Councilor, Ershui, and Lü the Court Gentleman invited him to Quanzhou Kaiyuan Temple to inaugurate the Dharma. Upon his initial arrival at Luoyang Bridge, the tide had already receded. At that time—
The waters surged and overflowed once more, leaving everyone astonished. A monk asked, "The timing of the tides has never failed for a thousand years;
why have they returned today? The Master said, "Ask the tide-god. The monk said, "Is it not because of you, the Master? The Master said, "Do not defile me, old monk.
Knowing that the karmic conditions were now ripe, he finally opened the hall; the incense in his breast—
I have specifically brought this forth for the sake of the old man Wuming. He once said: "Chan is fundamentally Shouchang; Precepts are fundamentally Zhenji. One must not misrepresent them.
During the Upoṣadha ceremony in the fourth month, a Real Man (Zhuren) named Wu arrived at the temple in a palanquin.
He sought a Dharma name and received the five precepts before departing. At that time, a monk asked: "For thirty years at Dongshan, the local deity has been searching..."
[The Master] said, "I do not cling. The Abbot asked, "For what reason did you bestow the precepts upon the Immortal of Wu? The Master replied, "To rescue those drowning, one must go to the water;

to chant to the moon, one must ascend the peak. In the autumn, he returned to Gushan. In the year Dingchou, hearing the news of the Great Master’s passing, the Master personally went to Zhenji to pay his respects.
The various masters of Western Zhejiang, following the dying instructions of the Great Master, jointly requested him to succeed to the seat; thus, his reputation for the Way spread widely.

At that time, Mao Weiqi, a student from Gui’an, dreamed that a messenger of the underworld came to seize him. He went to Zhenji Temple to seek refuge with the Master, who conferred the Bodhisattva precepts upon him before he departed;
consequently, no harm befell him. Later, when Mao violated the precepts, the ghost came again to seize him and reprimanded him for his transgressions.
Because of the sin of his broken precepts, Mao bitterly lamented and repented his transgressions; only then was he released and allowed to return. Mao himself recorded these events for posterity.
In the year Gengchen, he established Cuīyún Ān (Cuiyun Hermitage) at Xīsā in Yúháng. In the year Xīnsì, he moved to Pǔmíng Sī in Wùzhōu.
During a great famine, many residents were deprived of food. A man named Zhào from Lánxī was poor and made his living by processing lime. Suddenly—

A patron donated capital to establish a *zhāi* (vegetarian feast) for universal illumination. The Master praised this for a long time. One day, he died of malaria from the fifth watch until the eleventh.

In the underworld, he encountered the Master who guided him back; he revived at that moment. People of the time spread the account widely. The Master said, "How could I have entered the underworld to save people?
This occurred entirely because of his own single thought of wholesome roots, which manifested this event. In winter, he returned to Min and opened the precept platform for ordination.

The treasure of his sword was excellent. At that time, more than a thousand people received the precepts. In the *Renwu* year, he went to Kaibian Monastery in Quanzhou for the commencement of the retreat (*zhì*).

There, the local deity Zhang Fu and Wu the Real Man took refuge in the Triple Gem and requested the precepts. In winter, he returned to Gushan. Disciples gathered like clouds, and all necessary conditions converged.
He renovated the Great Hall, the mountain gate, and all the various monastic quarters one after another, restoring them to their former glory until they were fully adorned.
He was the preeminent leader among the monastic forests of the Eight Mins. Because he had previously received the full precepts from Boshan, they shared the bond of teacher and disciple;

thus, a stupa was erected to enshrine his robes and bowl, for which a commemorative inscription was composed. In the year Guiwei, he accepted an invitation to Xingfu Temple in Jianzhou. Upon arriving at Baoshan, he constructed a stupa for śarīra relics.
During a severe drought, Sun Bingxian dispatched an official to Baoshan to request prayers. The Master ascended the hall to preach, and immediately after concluding his discourse—

There was a timely rain, pouring down like water from a basin until the ground was three feet deep; that year’s harvest was abundant. Later, returning to Gushan during the Dinghai and Wuzi years, the provincial capital was in great turmoil.
When bandits were about to plunder Gushan, they carried the Master away in a sedan chair, but midway up the ridge, the vehicle suddenly shook and overturned.
They then escorted the Master back to the mountain. Bandit ships were moored in the river, but their masts were struck by thunderbolts, so they did not dare to attack again.
In the year Gengyin, various Chan masters of the Wu and Zhejiang regions vied with one another in their polemical claims, even resorting to legal petitions.

He sent a letter to the Master [Zhaozhou], who smiled but gave no reply. In the winter, he constructed a funerary pagoda on the western fields of the temple and composed an account of his own life’s conduct.
And he inscribed this upon it, saying: "Whose skull is this that has erected this stūpa? It is the son of Shouchang and the master of the Stone Drum.

He was oblivious to worldly sentiments, being of a single, coarse nature. His aspirations were great and his words were grand; his eyes looked upon the Buddhas and Patriarchs with utter disdain. He occupied the seat of Xingsheng."
Rebuking the present and reviling the past, he employed spirits and drove the winds to rebuild this edifice. Now, casting aside his skin-sack, he is interred in a desolate grove.
Do not say he has no mouth; his voice is like a tiger’s roar. Whether he be alive or dead, please unravel these words. This is proclaimed to all who come.
"Who shall succeed to my martial legacy? Reading this even to this day, its vital energy remains chillingly present, causing one to straighten one's robes in reverence.
In the spring of the Guisi year, the border pavilion of the Abbot’s quarters caught fire. Among the ashes was found a single water bowl;

it had been presented to the Master by a monk from Kapilavastu, whom he had met previously, and which the Master used regularly during his two daily meals. To this day, it remained completely undamaged. The following day, it was recovered from the midst of the charred ruins.
In the spring of the Year of Yiwei, Fucheng and Changle in Xinghua suffered military upheavals. Starving people flowed into the provincial capital in all manner of wretched conditions.
The Master then gathered his assembly and dispatched his disciples to establish soup kitchens for relief; he provided coffins and buried those who had died, totaling more than two thousand people.
In the Year of Dingyou, when the Master was eighty years old, the assembly was deeply concerned for him, as they felt no successor to the Dharma had yet been found.
On the first day of the first month of the year, he suddenly struck the bell to assemble the community. Holding up his robe and whisk, he entrusted them to Vinaya Master Weilnpei, saying in verse:
"Once I passed over the Shauchang Bridge; How could I follow worldly custom to sprout branches in vain?

If one single hair is to preserve the lineage of a thousand sages, How many people can truly understand this mind? In my declining years, now eighty years old, The Great Matter is finally settled here."
Entrusted to Yi. Regarding the matter of salt and sauce for thirty years, there is an ancient saying: "One does not deceive others.

Only by wielding the helm with a thousand-jin strength against a headwind can one firmly establish the foundation of peace and stability. He immediately ordered Yi to preside over the assembly and share his seat, and upon hearing his formal discourse, [the Master] was deeply impressed.
The assembly was all delighted and submissive; there was not one who did not congratulate another, considering that the tradition of the Upper Cavern (Dongshang) now had a reliable leader.
On the nineteenth day of the seventh month of autumn, coinciding with the Master’s birthday, people gathered from all quarters like clouds to request him to open the Dharma for them.

Since the year of Xinmao, the Master had strictly prohibited ascending the hall, and though they pleaded with him earnestly, he would not grant permission. Upon reaching this occasion, he joyfully ascended the seat. There followed a succession of congratulations and condolences.
The disciples said, "Those who understand know that the Master has already departed from this world. On the first day of the ninth month, he indeed manifested a slight illness.
He did not eat for more than twenty days, yet his daily activities remained as usual. He then spoke a verse to the assembly, saying: "Since birth, this old man’s nature has been too biased."
I refused to follow the stream into the worldly marketplace; my stubborn nature remains unrefined to this day. I have merely used my haughty bones to rescue both Confucianism and Chan.

In Confucianism, the pursuit of fame and achievement has truly been lost; in Chan, lofty wit and eloquence make right conduct difficult to perfect. Now that I am on the verge of death, what further use is there?
I shall simply offer this thought as a repayment to the dragons and devas. He said, "The Elder's affairs, both mundane and supramundane, are all contained within this verse."
"Do not neglect this," he said, and then closed his eyes and lay down in the *śrīvatsa* posture.
When he had entered samādhi, the Head Seat asked, "How shall you deliver the final phrase? The Master took up a brush and wrote: "The final phrase is personally delivered;
it is to be found nowhere within or without the three realms. Three days later, at midnight, he said to the Head Seat, "I am not ill."
He had his attendant help him rise; once he was seated, he surveyed the great assembly with his eyes for a long while before passing away.

This was actually at the hour of the rat on the seventh day of the tenth month. Three days later, the shrine was finally closed; his countenance remained as if alive, and the multitude all marveled at this wonder.

The Master presided over four monasteries in succession; wherever he went, he lived in deep seclusion within his private quarters. Though he did not engage in worldly affairs, donors vied with one another to offer their support. One hundred...
He attended to all duties with diligence. Scholars from the four quarters came to him without being rejected and departed without being detained;

those under his guidance were always many eminent monks, all of whom he exhorted toward genuine inquiry and authentic realization, while strictly warning them against the poisonous admixture of intellectual understanding.

Throughout his life, every word and deed was as decisive as driving a nail through iron, without the slightest trace of artifice or embellishment. Regarding the fundamental principles of the Caodong school, which had been muddled by the turbid intellects of former ages, [he restored them].
Kai used the mind as the seal. He returned once more to the ancient tracks; for thirty years he presided over the hall, never lightly granting permission to students.

It was only at the very end that he selected Master Pei alone to receive the transmission. The Master himself described his life: "I entered the world [of teaching] most belatedly and responded to the needs of the age most clumsily.
Furthermore, I did not strive to gather many disciples or create a bustling, noisy gate. This was because I had certain realizations. Such was the Master throughout his life.
His recorded sermons and various writings comprise twenty works totaling over eighty fascicles, which have circulated widely throughout the world.
Those who rely on him at the mountain monastery number approximately three hundred, while those who seek his guidance and receive the precepts exceed tens of thousands.

He attained the degree [of ordination] together with several others. He entrusted six disciples with the precepts. While he was alive, he contemplated the purity of Xueqiao and the discernment of Feizhao;
he never deviated from the truth, and his "Inscription on the Mind" served as a warning and a model for the holy goodness of the school.

On the twenty-first day of the first month of the Wuxu year, he enshrined his entire body in the Shouta Pagoda at Benshan. This was in accordance with his final instructions. Daojing had been a disciple since childhood. Tai was a teacher who resided [there].

When he was at Mount He, he was immediately able to pay his respects. In the seventh month of the Dinghai year, when the Master was seventy years old, [the author] accompanied his late father to Baoshan to offer him a long-life celebration;
he wept and rejoiced wildly, congratulating himself on having attained what he had never experienced before. In the Xinjia and Dinghai years, he entered Gushan three times.
Twenty days before the Master’s nirvana, he finally succeeded in receiving the Master’s personal instructions in person; his only regret was that his... (roots/knowledge remained incomplete).

Though my faculties are dull and I stand at the gateway of the Master’s school as if gazing upon the heavens, the Master has constantly nourished me with the milk of the Dharma and drawn me forth through manifold means, refusing to cast me out from his door.
Therefore, disregarding my own meager ignorance, I venture to record in truth what I have attained.

This is manifested for the sake of the future, comparable to the birds singing in spring and the insects chirping in autumn; it is to propagate the Dharma-transformation throughout the Great Creation. Thus it is said.
The disciple Daojing of Jian’an and Pan Jin-tai respectfully record this with a hundred prostrations.
